14504-experiments-and-considerations-tou:
Robert Boyle, fellow of the Royal Society, published this treatise on colours in London in 1664, as the beginning of an experimental history of the subject. Boyle wrote first for a friend, then let the essays reach print.

He reports trials with glass, powders, microscopes, and dyed stuffs, asking why a body looks white, red, or blue. A clear glass ground to powder turns white, he notes, because its many small surfaces scatter light. The book helped found experimental chemistry, and its careful method still reads as modern science in seventeenth-century dress.
18068-five-years-in-new-zealand-1859-to-:
Robert B. Booth wrote Five Years in New Zealand, 1859 to 1864, printed in London in 1912 by J. G. Hammond. Booth, a civil engineer, tells how he came to emigrate, and what five years on sheep runs taught him.

Chapters run from a voyage with rats, a white squall, a shark, and burial of twins, to Port Lyttelton, Christchurch, and a cadet's life on a sheep run. Scab, shepherd work, and wild sows fill the later pages. Booth writes with a pioneer's plain vigor. It is a lively settler memoir, and a fine window on early Canterbury life.
18453-the-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-1:
The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy, issued this volume for January to June 1864, published in New York by John F. Trow. The volume index lists tales, essays, and reports on American finances, army organization, and the national academy, alongside poems and aphorisms.

This number belongs to the Civil War years, when the magazine weighed literature steadily against the nation's crisis. Its pages mix fiction, finance, and military writing, giving a broad view of how Northern readers in 1864 thought about war, money, and art in the same monthly journal.
18820-the-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-4:
This April 1864 issue of the Continental Monthly, a magazine of literature and national policy, opens with a long essay on Sir Charles Lyell and the antiquity of man. Its writer recalls Thomas Chalmers, who sixty years earlier startled Scottish orthodoxy by saying "the writings of Moses do not fix the age of the globe."

Geology, the essay argues, has since pushed the earth's origin back to a vast, undated antiquity, and the age of man may follow the same path. The piece weighs how sacred writings might adjust to new findings, as they already had on the earth's age. As a whole, the issue shows an American magazine of 1864 joining science, scripture, and public questions in one monthly conversation.
2128-narratives-of-new-netherland-1609-1:
J. Franklin Jameson edits firsthand narratives of New Netherland, from Henry Hudson's voyage of 1609 to the Dutch colony's end in 1664. Van Meteren on Hudson, a letter of Isaack de Rasieres, and Megapolensis on the Mohawks lead the set. Jameson edited the series for the American Historical Association, setting a scholarly standard.

Father Isaac Jogues adds a Jesuit view, and the documents together give the Dutch years in America in the writers' own words. The collection remains a key source for early New York, New Jersey, and the Hudson Valley. Hudson's voyage of 1609 opened the Hudson River to Dutch trade and settlement.
3161-narratives-of-new-netherland-1609-1:
J F Jameson edited this collection of Dutch colonial accounts for the years 1609 to 1664. The narratives cover the founding and growth of New Netherland, from Henry Hudson's voyage to the English seizure of the colony. Traders, settlers, soldiers, and officials speak in their own words, or in close translations of them.

Read together, the pieces show a colony built on trade rather than on farming towns alone. Beaver, ships, and land deals matter as much as forts and churches. The volume serves students of early America well: it puts firsthand voices beside one another, so the Dutch years on the Hudson can be heard before the English story takes over.
32247-the-battle-of-allatoona-october-5t:
William Ludlow's paper on the Battle of Allatoona, October 5, 1864, was read before the Michigan Commandery of the Military Order of the Loyal Legion at Detroit on April 2, 1891. It was printed there by Winn and Hammond. Ludlow, major in the Corps of Engineers and brevet lieutenant-colonel in the United States Army, issued it as War Paper Number Seventeen.

Ludlow finds it strange that so brilliant an exploit should lack an adequate historian. All who mention the action agree in calling it one of the most brilliant of a war thickset with deeds of gallantry. He compares the war's gallantry to blossoms thick on a rose bush. The contest was famous. The issue was glorious. The day was still vivid in survivors' minds, so material for a satisfactory narrative could not be lacking. Readers get a veteran's Civil War battle paper, part history and part tribute.
33436-the-irish-ecclesiastical-record-vo:
The Irish Ecclesiastical Record, volume one, December 1864, is a Catholic journal of theology, history, and church life in Ireland. Its first volume gathers articles, notes, and reviews for clergy and educated readers, with careful editing of punctuation and printer errors. The journal's Latin and Irish terms are transcribed with care, including lenition marks and crosses.

The volume suits readers of Irish church history, offering a window on Catholic thought in the 1860s. Its tone is scholarly and devout, aimed at priests and scholars. For researchers, it is a valuable source on the Irish church at a time of change, from seminaries to parishes, in the years after the Famine.
4146-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-26-jan:
January 1663 to 1664 opens, like the full year, after midnight, Pepys going to bed between four and five with his mind in good temper. Sleeping till eight, he wakes to callers, among them a bearer of the best New Year's gift he ever had: a bill of exchange from Mr. Deering.

The two-month volume follows that bright start through office, Change, and family talk. Pepys's satisfaction runs through the entries, tempered by work and weather. Readers who want the year's opening in short form will find this volume a brisk, cheerful slice of 1664.
4147-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-27-mar:
March 1663 to 1664 opens with office business, then at the Change after noon, where Pepys meets his uncle Wight. Wight tells how Mr. Maes was nearly trapped the day before but was forced to run for it, a scrap of city danger in a business day.

Pepys goes home to dinner with Creed and Mr. Hunt, closing a day of trade talk and family news. The volume carries the diary into its fifth year with the same brisk mix of work, kin, and gossip. Readers will enjoy Pepys's London as a place where a near trap and a good dinner share one afternoon.
4148-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-28-apr:
April 1664 sends Pepys to his office till noon, then to the Change, where merchants gather with complaints to present to Parliament's committee against the Dutch. Home to dinner, then by coach, Pepys carries the city's commercial anger with him.

The volume moves toward war, as trade complaints turn into policy and policy into fleets. Pepys sits between merchants and ministers, recording both sides. Readers get the spring when London's counting houses began to beat the drum for war. Merchants, ministers, and clerks all crowd these spring pages. Pepys stands in the middle, notebook open.
4149-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-29-jun:
June 1664 opens late, after accounts kept Pepys up past midnight. Rising, he finds Mr. Hollyard waiting with unwelcome news: despite past assurance that the stone could not return, the doctor now fears it has come again.

Health, money, and office work tangle through these summer entries, as Pepys counts his gains and guards his body. The volume shows the diary's private side, where a medical worry matters as much as a Navy order. Readers get Pepys the patient, frank about pain and fear in a summer of reckoning. His accounts, kept late into the night, show a man measuring health against wealth.
4150-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-30-aug:
August 1664 finds Pepys's mind very light from last night's accounts, and up with Minnes, Batten, and Pen to St. James's. Each man has prepared his part that very morning, for fear the others should consider it or dispute it beforehand.

The volume shows the Navy Board at its most political, with officers guarding their papers like cards. Pepys's light mind comes from money in order, a base for confidence. Readers who like office intrigue will enjoy this late summer of accounts and alliances. Prepared papers and guarded talk rule the board room here.
4151-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-31-oct:
October 1664 finds Pepys busy at the office forenoon and afternoon, and pleased to be so. That pleasure breaks when Mrs. Lane, now Martin, comes like a foolish woman to the Horseshoe nearby and sends a sealed note asking him to speak with her.

Pepys records the interruption with annoyance and care, guarding his time and his name at once. The volume mixes steady office work with the social traps of a rising man. Readers see how even a sealed note could threaten a reputation in Restoration London. The sealed note lingers in his mind long after the office day ends.
4152-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-32-dec:
December 1664 sends Pepys betimes to Whitehall for a Committee of Tangier, then straight home to business at his office till noon. Dinner done, he sits all afternoon, then works at his office again till past one in the morning, home to supper and bed.

The volume closes the year in a rush of committees and accounts, with Pepys working past midnight as a matter of course. Tangier, trade, and war preparation fill the winter days. Readers see the diary's work ethic at full stretch, in a December of long hours.
4808-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
This eighth volume of The Rise of the Dutch Republic, dated 1855, covers 1563 to 1564. Chapter four opens with a joint letter to Philip from Orange, Egmont, and Horn, followed by Egmont's quarrel with Aerschot and with Aremberg. Philip's answer to the three nobles, with instructions to the Duchess, follows, and Egmont declines the king's invitation to visit Spain.

A second letter from the three seigniors, a mission by Armenteros, and a letter from Alva lead to Granvelle's secret letters to Philip. The cardinal's insinuations and instructions fill much of the chapter. His complaints about Berghen and Montigny's lukewarmness in the inquisition's cause join anecdotes to their discredit, privately chronicled by Granvelle. The supposed necessity for the king's presence, correspondence of Lazarus Schwendi, an approaching crisis, and Granvelle's anxiety to retire carry the volume on. Readers get Motley's account of conspiracy and intrigue.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: John Tyler, William and Mary graduate and violin player, fills this fourth volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Born in Virginia in 1790, Tyler studied law and entered the legislature in 1811. The volume prints his messages and papers as president after Harrison's death. Richardson's series preserves Tyler's official record. The volume adds a full record of a short and troubled presidency.
a-family-man-in-three-acts-pg4764:
John Galsworthy's A Family Man, a play in three acts, studies a provincial tyrant at home. John Builder, of the firm of Builder & Builder, rules the Midlands town of Breconridge. His study, where nothing is ever studied, opens the action after breakfast. His wife Julia, daughters Athene and Maud, and brother Ralph complete the family.

Builder's creed is respectability enforced by will. A young person in blue, a poacher's figure, and a flying man named Guy Herringhame disturb his order. The mayor's study hosts the second day's reckoning. Galsworthy lets the family man's certainties destroy what they claim to protect. The play belongs to his fifth series of plays, printed with full stage directions. Its comedy is cold: a good citizen discovers that owning everyone is not the same as loving anyone.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume thirteen of Robert Kerr's voyages describes the island of Otaheite in detail. Its sections treat the produce and inhabitants, their dress, houses, food, domestic life, and amusements. Manufactures, boats, navigation, and the division of time follow. Kerr's volume preserves a full eighteenth century picture of Tahitian life. The full account gives a vivid view of island life long ago.
an-amiable-charlatan-pg9664: Edward Phillips Oppenheim writes An Amiable Charlatan, a tale of a charming rogue whose schemes entangle him with wealth, love, and danger. With illustrations by Will Grefé, the novel moves at Oppenheim's smooth, popular pace through society and crime. The amiable villain at its heart made it a favourite of its time.
arxiv-2412-00864:
Kyriakos Flouris, Anna Volokitin, Gustav Bredell, and Ender Konukoglu encode data by flowing it downhill into a compact code, skipping the encoder network, in work from 2024. Autoencoders squeeze data through a learned encoder, but that learned squeeze can be sloppy. In the physical sciences, sloppy codes cost real accuracy.

Their method keeps only a decoder and pushes each data point along a gradient flow into the code space, as a differential equation demands. Training uses an adjoint trick that avoids pricey integrals at small cost in accuracy. A second-order flow, echoing a fast descent method, speeds convergence. Stiff cases get an adaptive solver. Data-thrifty tests favor the approach.
arxiv-2412-01064:
Taekyung Ki, Dongchan Min, and Gyeongsu Chae present FLOAT, a system that animates portraits from speech, in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Diffusion-based portrait animation produces strong results, but its iterative sampling makes videos temporally inconsistent and slow to generate. FLOAT instead builds on flow matching, a generative approach that samples more directly. It also works in a learned orthogonal motion latent space rather than a pixel latent space, which supports efficient generation and editing of consistent motion.

A transformer-based vector field predictor, conditioned frame by frame, drives the motion synthesis. The method additionally supports speech-driven emotion enhancement, folding expressive motion into the performance naturally. Extensive experiments showed FLOAT beating state-of-the-art audio-driven talking portrait methods on visual quality, motion fidelity, and efficiency. The work targets applications from virtual presenters to film dubbing, where a still portrait must speak convincingly.
arxiv-2412-05264: The XENON Collaboration reports results on the neutron veto of the XENONnT experiment, run with demineralized water. XENONnT is a dark matter search. Its neutron veto is the system around it that tags neutrons. That keeps their signals from being taken for dark matter hits. The 2024 paper, by the large global team, shows how the veto worked in this setup. Veto work sets how well the search can reject background in its hunt for rare events.
arxiv-2412-05964:
Şevval Çakıcı and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on the state of sentiment analysis for Turkish, the task of judging whether a text sounds positive or negative. Turkish data sets are scarce, so the same few get reused across studies with wildly varied results. The team reviewed a decade of work to bring order.

They gathered thirty-one studies and twenty-three data sets, then sorted them with a shared taxonomy. Leading sentiment tools were run across the data sets to see how scores move. Tool performance hinged heavily on the kind of text, from tweets to product reviews. The map should help Turkish language researchers pick data and tools with eyes open.
arxiv-2412-06464:
Songlin Yang, Jan Kautz, and Ali Hatamizadeh merge two memory tricks to make sequence models both forget fast and edit precisely, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Linear transformers promise cheaper long-context modeling than standard attention, but they lag on retrieval and long documents.

Two recent mechanisms attack different halves of the problem. Gating lets the model erase memory quickly when content turns stale. The delta rule makes surgical updates to what is stored. The authors observe the two are complementary, so they fuse them into a gated delta rule. A parallel training algorithm makes the fused rule fast on modern hardware. The resulting architecture, Gated DeltaNet, beats Mamba2 and DeltaNet across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, and long-context benchmarks. Hybrid versions that mix in ordinary attention layers push performance further.
arxiv-2412-07264:
Salvatore Calcagno and a large team present QuantFormer in a 2024 arXiv paper. Forecasting brain activity could power predictive models of brain dynamics and real-time interventions. Neural signals are sparse in space and time, which makes them hard for standard transformers to predict.

QuantFormer reframes forecasting as classification. It quantizes the neural signal on the fly, so the model picks among signal levels rather than regressing raw values. The data come from two-photon calcium imaging in the mouse visual cortex. This design suits the sparse, tangled structure of neural activity. The authors aim for sharper forecasts of future activity in brain circuits.
arxiv-2412-07864:
Subhroneel Chakrabarti and Renann Lipinski Jusinskas published this theoretical physics paper in 2024. It examines a family of theories defined directly by their equations of motion rather than by a Lagrangian, the usual starting point of field theory. Such third-way theories raise a basic worry: does scattering in them respect unitarity, the rule that probabilities must add up correctly? The authors test this using a method that builds scattering amplitudes piece by piece.

They find that unitarity fails already at the simplest, tree level. They then identify a unique change to the equations of motion that restores it. The price is that a Lagrangian comes back, and it turns out to be a higher-dimensional version of the known Freedman-Townsend model. Currents and a higher-rank symmetry in the original theories are shown to descend from that parent model.
arxiv-2412-09464:
Akbar Davlataliev and co-authors study how waves fade near a regular black hole of the Simpson-Visser type when a magnetic field is present. They track a charged, massive scalar field disturbed near the hole and compute its ringing tones, known as quasinormal modes. The question is how long these tones can ring before they die away into late-time tails.

The team found that both the magnetic field and the mass of the field slow the fading sharply. The tones may ring for very long times, close to resonances that barely decay at all. In the time picture, the ringing passes into slow, wavy tails that differ from the smooth tails seen without a magnetic field. For waves with angular structure, the tail's envelope itself oscillates and resists a simple formula. The work links field strength and mass to the lifetime of black hole vibrations.
arxiv-2412-09964:
Ontivero-Ortega and four co-authors split feature weight into solo and group parts in this twenty twenty-four paper. Feature weight scores help explain why a model makes its calls, but a feature may matter only when paired with others. The team builds on a known score that drops one feature at a time and checks the error change.

Inside, their method hunts for the feature group that makes the score as large as it can get. It also hunts for the group that makes the score as small as it can get. That split shows which partners add shared weight and which add fresh, joint weight. The team shows the method on test data that sorts two types of tiny particles apart.
arxiv-2412-10064:
Makbule Gulcin Ozsoy, Leila Messallem, Jon Besga, and Gianandrea Minneci build Text2Cypher, a tool that turns plain questions into graph database queries, in a paper from 2024. Knowledge graphs store facts as nodes and links, and the Cypher language reads them. Writing Cypher takes training that most users lack. Their tool aims to open graph data to non-experts.

Large language models can draft Cypher, but they often miss fine points. Fine-tuning on good examples works better, yet public training sets were scarce. The team merged and cleaned several sets into more than forty-four thousand examples. Models tuned on that pool gained a lot on match scores over plain models. The work shows data quality drives this task. It also gives the field a shared base for later gains.
arxiv-2412-10764: Aschenbrenner, van den Dries, and van der Hoeven settle in twenty twenty-four a conjecture from nineteen eighty-one about Hardy fields, which order fast-growing functions. They study when a field can be closed under solving differential equations without leaving the analytic world. Using their earlier work on such equations, they prove that the common core of all largest analytic Hardy fields matches that of all largest Hardy fields. They also widen a key proof step and give a warning example marking where it stops working.
arxiv-2412-10864:
Zeno Capatti and Mao Zeng published this physics paper in 2024. It connects two ways of computing how black holes and other heavy bodies deflect each other, a calculation needed to predict gravitational waves from merging pairs. One route starts from particle scattering amplitudes; the other follows the bodies' worldlines directly.

Working in a standard amplitude framework, the authors show the divergences plaguing the classical limit cancel cleanly, term by term, beyond the first loop order. The trick is rewriting propagators in a worldline-like form before combining them. The cleaned-up result matches the worldline formalism exactly in their examples, proving the two routes equivalent. Causality emerges on its own instead of being imposed. They demonstrate the method on impulse calculations in electrodynamics and a scalar model at two loops, plus families of harder diagrams.
arxiv-2412-12864:
Yoontae Hwang and Yongjae Lee build GFTab, a way to learn from mixed tables of data when few rows are labeled. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Tables join smooth numeric fields with class fields, and their shape is hard for many tools to read. GFTab has three new parts. It mars each kind of field in a way that fits its type. It weighs how near two rows are by a flow measure on a curved space. And it uses tree-based codes to draw facts from the labeled rows. The team built a test set of twenty-one tables from varied fields. GFTab beat known tools on many of them, most of all when labels were scarce.
arxiv-2412-13264:
Mengyuan Xiao and co-authors announce a monster spiral galaxy seen when the universe was under a billion years old, in this 2024 paper. Found in a Webb telescope survey, the galaxy sits at redshift about 5.2 and sports a classic bulge, a wide flat disk, and grand spiral arms spanning nineteen kiloparsecs. They name it Zhúlóng, the Torch Dragon. Its star mass rivals the Milky Way's.

The core is red and quiet, packed dense with old stars, while the outskirts still form stars, a sign of inside-out growth. Its total star birth rate is modest for its size, far below dusty peers of the era. The team says such maturity this early strains formation models. Zhúlóng caps how fast galaxies can assemble structure.
arxiv-2412-14164:
Shengbang Tong and co-authors show that a language model taught to understand images can also learn to create them, in a 2024 paper. Their method, Visual-Predictive Instruction Tuning, trains the model to predict both word tokens and picture tokens from mixed sequences of images and text, all framed as instructions. The model they trained this way is called MetaMorph.

Two findings stand out. First, the power to generate images seems to grow out of better understanding, and it can be unlocked with surprisingly little generation training data. Second, understanding and generation feed each other, but understanding data does more for both. MetaMorph matched strong rivals at answering questions about images and at making them. When generating, it could lean on the world knowledge and reasoning from its language training, dodging failure modes that trip up other image makers.
arxiv-2412-14464:
Tung Do and co-authors present a method that builds 3D scenes from one or a few photos and renders new views of them. Their 2024 paper faces an ill-posed problem: hidden surfaces cannot be recovered from a single image by geometry alone. Their design splits the job between reconstruction and imagination.

A first model lifts the input images into a coarse volume, then a finer three-plane representation. A diffusion model then fills in plausible detail for regions the cameras never saw. The two steps repeat in rounds, each pass refining the scene and its renderings. Tests on car scenes, real-world captures, and a large object data set beat prior methods on quality while keeping views consistent with each other. Better view synthesis serves product previews, games, and robot training.
arxiv-2412-15664:
Xiaohan Zhang and five co-authors present SCENIC, a model that generates human motion shaped by both the 3D scene and a text instruction. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Animating people who move naturally through cluttered places is hard. Older models assume flat ground or ignore the meaning of the requested action.

SCENIC reasons about the scene at two levels. A goal-centered frame handles the broad navigation target. A body-centered distance field captures the ground and obstacles up close. Text alignment at each frame lets styles blend smoothly mid-motion. The model can spin out motions of any length that fit the terrain. Tests show plausible moves like stepping over obstacles or climbing stairs in character. The work serves games, film previsualization, and robot training worlds.
arxiv-2412-16064:
Humza Ikram, Rumaisa Habib, Muaz Ali, and Zartash Afzal Uzmi present a design to shield anonymous web services on the Tor network, in two thousand twenty-four. Hidden services are often attacked by methods that reveal their address and location. Their design adds a volunteer host, called a vault, between the service and its visitors.

The vault runs the service's web content inside a trusted hardware enclave and serves as the contact point. The real provider then needs far less uptime, which shrinks the chance of being traced. The setup also protects the content while it is hosted elsewhere. Tests showed only a small slowdown for visitors, a few percent at most.
arxiv-2412-16564:
Thomas Henzinger, Fabian Kresse, Kaushik Mallik, Emily Yu, and Djordje Zikelic study how to warn of risk in systems we cannot see inside. Their twenty twenty-four paper deals with black-box systems, where we can only watch the state at set times. The goal is to guess future states and flag harm before it comes.

Their method mixes a classic math tool for curves with a way to find rates of change from past data. They also prove a bound on how far the guess can stray, if the system is smooth. Tests on hard cases show the method is light to run and more exact than past tools of this kind.
arxiv-2412-17064:
Debashis Panda and six colleagues wrote a 2024 study of waves on a fluid surface. When a fluid layer is shaken up and down, the surface forms standing waves called Faraday waves. These waves arrange themselves in patterns such as squares and six-sided shapes.

The team studied what happens when the surface also holds a soap-like film. Such films create stresses, named Marangoni stresses, that pull on the surface. As these stresses grow stronger, the shaking needed to start waves grows too. The patterns also change, moving from squares to uneven squares and then to wavy stripes. The work helps explain how thin films shape surface patterns.
arxiv-2412-17264:
Chengran Yang, Hong Jin Kang, Jieke Shi, and David Lo present ACECode, a training framework for code-generating language models, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. These models often write code that works but runs slowly. Slow code wastes energy and hurts software in resource-limited settings.

Earlier fixes traded correctness for speed or needed ready-made test environments. ACECode instead uses reinforcement learning to pursue both goals together. An actor model generates code samples. A reward signal comes from actually executing that code, with no predefined test cases required. The signal scores efficiency and correctness jointly. Fine-tuning against it teaches the model to produce fast code that still passes.
arxiv-2412-17664:
Bradji and Benkhedir use computer modeling to study a single layer of the material MoSe2, pure and with added arsenic, in a 2024 study. They test three changed forms: a missing molybdenum atom, an arsenic atom in its place, and an arsenic atom tucked into a gap in the sheet.

The team finds the swapped-in arsenic form is the most stable, while the tucked-in form is less so. Each change opens new energy levels inside the material's band gap, and the gap itself grows wider. Two forms behave like p-type material and one like n-type material. The authors suggest the swapped form could suit uses in cleaning chemistry with light, or in solar cells.
arxiv-2412-19164:
Devibala Esakkimuthu and Basherrudin Mahmud Ahmed show how to get the best light squeezing from a conditional measurement setup with plain optics and photon counting. Squeezing cuts noise in one trait of light below the plain limit, and such setups breed non classic light states. Their work came out in twenty twenty-four.

The setup feeds a coherent state and a number state into a beam splitter, then counts photons. By writing the output as shifted finite level systems, the team can compute the max squeezing the setup can give. Fixing the count at one photon and tuning the beam split and input strength reaches that max, at least for low number inputs. Flawed sources and weak detectors are also weighed.
arxiv-2412-19364:
Elisa Postinghel and Artie Prendergast-Smith wrote a 2024 mathematics paper on shapes built from pairs of projective spaces. They introduce bilinear secant varieties, a paired-space version of a classic geometry tool. Secant varieties join points on a shape to fill new spaces.

These new objects sit at the heart of the authors' main study: blowups of the product space at a set of general points. A blowup replaces each point with a small space that records approach paths. The authors compute the key cones that describe curves and surfaces on the blowup. They also show the blowup is log Fano in the cases they cover. Such cones guide the broader study of shape changes.
arxiv-2412-20164:
Andrzej Bedychaj, Jacek Tabor, and Marek Śmieja present StyleAutoEncoder in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Modern image generators can make fine pictures and edit traits like age or smile. But training them from scratch costs a great deal of computing power. The authors offer a light add-on module instead. It plugs into a ready-trained generator and lets users steer image traits.

They tested the module with StyleGAN, a leading generator. In their trials, the add-on matched top methods that rely on invertible flows. It did so at much lower training cost. That makes trait editing open to teams with modest hardware. The paper should interest image researchers who want strong editing tools without huge budgets for computing.
arxiv-2501-03464:
Shubhr Singh, Emmanouil Benetos, Huy Phan, and Dan Stowell introduced LHGNN in twenty twenty-five, a graph-based model for classifying and tagging audio. Transformer models lead audio tasks but focus on pairwise links, missing the higher-order patterns that define distinct sounds. LHGNN builds a graph over audio features that joins local neighborhood detail with cluster-level structure from fuzzy grouping.

On three public audio data sets, LHGNN beat transformer-based rivals across the board while using far fewer parameters. Its edge was clearest when no ImageNet pre-training was available, a common bind in audio work. The results suggest graph models that respect both fine and coarse structure offer an efficient path for sound understanding, without leaning on huge pre-trained backbones.
arxiv-2501-03964:
Bingran Wang and four co-authors study how random wind gusts affect the wing of an electric aircraft design called Lift-Plus-Cruise. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Gusts and flight conditions are never exact, so the team asks how much that doubt changes the wing's response.

The authors couple an air flow solver with a shell model of the wing structure. They then compare five ways of measuring risk, among them Monte Carlo sampling and polynomial chaos. Each method estimates tip movement and strain energy. Results show wide spread in the outputs even when inputs vary only a little. Which method works best depends on which risk measure a reader cares about.
arxiv-2501-06164:
Satchel Grant introduces, in a 2025 paper, a method for judging whether two neural systems do a task in the same way, by swapping activity between them. Simple similarity scores can miss how a system truly uses its inner signals. Grant's method moves activity both ways and reads the change in behavior as the similarity measure.

The method can mimic a known stitching trick when wanted, or focus tightly on shared causal facts. It also cuts the cost of comparing many models, since the needed matrices grow in a straight line. Case studies show number coding can differ by task inside like models, and that fine-tuning can misalign a model's inner steps. A bonus loss term helps when one system cannot be probed.
arxiv-2501-06964:
Ma and co-authors test whether language models can stand in for patients when judging discharge summaries. Models are adept at role play when given a concrete profile. That skill could replace costly user studies in some checks. The team focused on summaries handed to patients leaving intensive care. They asked whether models can judge how clear those summaries are. Simulated replies were compared with real human replies.

Diverse backgrounds were assigned to the simulated patients. The team checked whether the fake replies stayed consistent and matched real patterns. Clear discharge text matters for safety after hospital stays. If models mirror patients well, hospitals could pre-test wording cheaply. The study weighs that promise with care.
arxiv-2501-08264:
Inácio Rabelo presents a 2025 mathematics paper on the Lipschitz geometry of a family of singularities. Singularities are points where a shape stops being smooth. The Pham-Brieskorn family is a classic test bed, built from power-like equations, and the mixed version allows complex variables and their conjugates together.

Rabelo finds conditions under which two such singularities count as the same under topology and under the stricter bi-Lipschitz lens, which also controls stretching. As a payoff, he builds endless families that are topologically identical yet distinct in the stricter sense. For surfaces in two variables, he separates inner, outer, and ambient versions of the question. One invariant of the outer shape turns out to be fixed by the exponents alone.
arxiv-2501-08964:
After two black holes merge, the newborn hole rings like a bell, and its tones carry its fingerprint. Ariadna Ribes Metidieri, Béatrice Bonga, and Badri Krishnan ask whether the radiation falling into the hole rings with the same tones. Simulations had hinted yes; this paper explains why.

The authors set up the problem with data placed on the horizon and on a surface that catches outgoing waves. Splitting the signal into modes, they show the infalling and outgoing tones are tightly linked. They give formulas that connect the wave measure at the horizon to the one far away. The result turns the horizon into a readable mirror of the ringdown. Future gravitational wave observations could use that link to test the nature of the remnant.
arxiv-2501-10064:
Keita Miwa and four co-authors introduced One-D-Piece in twenty twenty-five, an image tokenizer whose length adapts to the image. Tokenizers turn pictures into discrete codes for generative models, but fixed-length codes waste tokens on simple images. Their one-dimensional tokenizer instead supports variable-length, quality-controllable compression.

A simple trick, Tail Token Drop, trains the tokenizer to pack the most critical information at the head of the sequence, so cutting the tail degrades quality gracefully. On reconstruction metrics it delivered better perceptual quality than JPEG, WebP, and other variable-rate methods at smaller sizes. Downstream tests — classification, detection, segmentation, depth estimation — confirmed versatility. The authors validate the trick with detailed analysis of how tokens organize themselves.
arxiv-2501-10264:
Preston Smith and five co-authors test an economic model of university supercomputing in a 2025 paper. Research computing is costly to buy and run, yet it helps win grants, draw faculty, and train students. University leaders need a way to judge what a given investment returns and to plan capacity.

The authors apply the production function model, borrowed from economics, to top-tier research universities. The model, built in earlier work on fewer schools, held up across the wider set: investment in machines and staff showed positive returns in research output. The exact balance between inputs and outputs varied by school, for reasons the authors trace to local factors. They also show how to run the model backward for planning.
arxiv-2501-11464:
Silvano Rosenau and co-authors present a 2025 paper on splitting ocean flow into slow and fast parts. Ocean currents mix a slow, balanced drift with fast waves riding on it. Separating them is essential for studying how waves are born from currents. Simple splits by size or speed are too crude. Optimal balance and normal mode methods handle nonlinear effects but worked only in idealized setups. Real coastlines, depth changes, and varying Coriolis force broke them.

The authors modify optimal balance with a time-averaging step that projects onto the slow part. The trick removes the need for the idealized assumptions. Ocean modelers get a decomposition that survives realistic geography. Spontaneous wave emission is a small energy leak with big climate model consequences. Cleaner splits sharpen estimates of that leak in real ocean simulations.
arxiv-2501-11864:
Venkata Duvvuru and three co-authors present a testing framework for small drones in a 2025 paper. Small uncrewed aircraft must be checked in simulation across weather, terrain, and mission types before they fly. Today that work is mostly manual: people invent scenarios, set up simulators, plan missions, and sift results by hand.

Their framework, AutoSimTest, hands those steps to a team of large language model agents. The agents create scenarios, prepare the test setup, generate missions, and offer an interactive way to explore results. The design adapts to different drone uses and simulators. The team tested it on two widely used flight controllers, PX4 and ArduPilot, in simulation.
arxiv-2501-13364:
Jianglin Qiao and co-authors model task allocation in two sided markets in this 2025 paper. In older models, companies set prices first and customers respond. New markets like crowdsourcing do not fit that pattern, because customer needs are diverse and personal. The authors flip the order and let customers lead.

Customers start tasks, and companies then shape their offers to meet them. The paper proves that stable outcomes exist for both sides under stated conditions. A test case uses satellite constellation services, where customers buy satellite tasks. Customer payments fell by 23 percent in the test. Company revenue rose sharply at the same time. The model aims at lower cost and better market performance.
arxiv-2501-13464:
Osama Saleem and four co-authors build a neural receiver for vehicle-to-network links in future 6G systems, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The receiver replaces the hand-built chain at a base station with one learned model. It takes the raw frequency-domain signal and outputs the decoder-ready likelihood values, handling channel estimation and equalization inside.

The team trained variants with different sizes and kept the best for wider use. The receiver was then fed many kinds of traffic, images, video, position data, lidar clouds, and radar returns, to test its range. In simulation it beat leading receiver designs, holding its edge at low signal strength where links usually fail. The authors frame it as a step toward learned radio infrastructure.
arxiv-2501-14864:
Thong Nguyen and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on dark matter that loves leptons, the light particles like electrons. The Sun can trap such dark matter when it bumps into free electrons. Trapped dark matter may then clash and vanish in pairs, which sends out neutrinos. A huge tank in Japan, Super-Kamiokande, can catch those neutrinos.

Ten years of data from the tank show no such excess. That null sets tight caps on how hard dark matter can hit electrons. For light dark matter, the caps beat ground based hunts by more than ten fold. The caps reach down to very faint cross sections.
arxiv-2501-14964:
Kartik Sharma and colleagues let each node in a graph choose its own network depth in a 2025 paper. Graph neural networks classify nodes by pooling information from neighbors, layer by layer. One fixed depth for every node is standard, yet some nodes need only close neighbors while others depend on wider context, and over-smoothing hurts the first group.

Their MetSelect algorithm builds a prototype for each class within each layer's representation, then classifies a node at the layer where it sits closest to a prototype, scaled by that layer's spread. Across ten datasets and three network types, accuracy rose significantly in plug-and-play fashion. Variable depth also let networks grow deeper and resist poisoning attacks better.
arxiv-2501-15464:
Anoushkrit Goel and six co-authors present TractoGPT, a GPT based design that segments white matter bundles in the brain. Such maps serve brain link studies, surgery plans, and nerve disease work. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Segmentation is hard because streamlines look alike, people vary, and the two brain halves mirror each other. The model trains apart on streamline, cluster, and fusion forms of the data. It runs fully on its own, keeps bundle shape data, and carries across data sets. Tests on two sets beat top rivals on overlap and overreach scores, the authors report, with cross set checks to prove it travels.
arxiv-2501-15664:
Sophie Middleton outlines a proposed muon facility at Fermilab in a 2025 paper. Muons, heavy cousins of electrons, can betray new physics by changing flavor, an act standard theory nearly forbids. Three current experiments hunt that change in different channels, each set to sharpen past limits greatly this decade.

The proposed facility would gather the hunt in one ring-based site with far greater reach. If today's experiments spot a signal, the new site could measure its character and identify the physics behind it. Design work is young, and Middleton surveys the early research and the design's ties to a possible muon collider. The paper is a roadmap for keeping the United States in the flavor hunt.
arxiv-2501-15864:
Sanjeev Nahulanthran, Leimin Tian, Dana Kulic, and Mor Vered explain a face-reading model's decisions in terms of the facial muscle movements that expression science already uses. Systems that recognize facial expressions are headed for emotion-aware agents, but users must understand and rightly trust them. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team built explanations from facial action units, the coded twitches of brow, cheek, and lip, delivered as text, as pictures, or as both. A user study compared their approach against leading general-purpose explanation tools, measuring how well people understood the model and whether their trust was well placed.

Explanations in text alone and text plus pictures improved user understanding over the rivals. Every form of the action-unit explanation improved appropriate trust, meaning users relied on the model when it deserved it. The paper argues domain-native explanations beat generic heat maps for face technology.
arxiv-2501-16964:
Bilot and three co-authors built a network attack detector that learns from almost no labeled attacks in twenty twenty-five. Graph neural networks model network traffic as a graph and detect attacks well, but labeled examples are scarce in practice. Unsupervised methods flag anomalies yet confuse them with true attacks.

Their system, FEAE, trains with self-supervised learning plus few-shot learning. A hybrid objective mixes contrastive and reconstruction signals, teaching the network normal traffic structure without labels. Then a handful of labeled attack events, drawn as edges in the graph, teach it to separate real attacks from odd but harmless traffic. On two standard datasets it matched supervised and unsupervised rivals. Just one example per attack type brought substantial gains, and on one dataset it beat some fully supervised systems.
arxiv-2501-17364:
Sekar Nugraheni and Paolo Giordano opened a series of papers in 2025 by defining broadened holomorphic functions, holomorphic functions that can contain objects like the Dirac delta. Classic complex analysis forbids this: distributional answers of the Cauchy-Riemann equations are holomorphic, and the identity theorem bans delta-like spikes. The escape route is a non-Archimedean extension of the complex numbers, a number ring where infinitesimals and endless amounts exist again.

Inside that setting the authors prove the theory still works. Cauchy-Riemann equations, and the theorems of Goursat, Looman-Menchoff, and Montel, all extend; broadened differentiability forces smoothness; compactly supported spreads embed; and the class closes under composition and other nonlinear operations. The program is positioned against the older Colombeau theory, whose holomorphic version it aims to boost, with a proof including the Cauchy integral among its later goals.
arxiv-2501-17464:
Abel Azze, Guglielmo D'Amico, Bernardo D'Auria, and Salvatore Vergine modeled a wind farm battery in twenty twenty-five. Wind farms face fines when their power output rises or falls too fast, a rule called a ramp-rate limit. A battery can store or release power to smooth those swings, but poor control still draws penalties.

Their model treats the battery as switching between charging, draining, and idle states, with the switch pattern drawn as a semi-Markov process. Within each stage, the stored energy follows a bent random path known as a Brownian bridge. The team tested the model on ten years of real wind power data. Simulated fines matched the real ones, which supports using the model to price the cost of breaking the ramp rule.
arxiv-2501-18164:
Kanata Oowada and Hideaki Iiduka analyze optimization on manifolds in twenty twenty-five. Riemannian stochastic gradient descent trains models whose parameters live on curved spaces. Batch size is a key knob in that training. The authors study what happens when the batch grows over time instead of staying fixed.

Theory shows an increasing batch converges faster than a constant one. The gain holds for constant learning rates and for decaying ones, including cosine and polynomial schedules. The error term that lingers with constant batches vanishes in the increasing case. Tests on principal component analysis and low-rank matrix completion confirm the theory. Increasing batches also cut the total oracle cost. Readers get a simple schedule change with proven speed benefits.
arxiv-2501-19264:
Orion Weller and nine co-authors introduce a test set from 2025 for search systems that follow written instructions. Most search tests use short queries in English only. Their new set uses longer task notes in Russian, Chinese, and Persian, drawn from a news search task, with small changes made to the notes on purpose.

The team checks if search models notice those small changes and adjust their results. Models trained with English instructions did well when queries crossed languages. They did worse when both query and task were in the same non-English language. The authors say more training data in those languages is needed.  The full test set is shared so other teams can score their own search models the same way.
arxiv-2502-00264:
Binchi Zhang, Zaiyi Zheng, Zhengzhang Chen, and Jundong Li find a new symmetry in transformer networks and use it to merge models, in a 2025 paper. Neural networks can be reshaped without changing what they compute. For plain networks, swapping rows in set patterns gives the same model. Transformers resist that trick because their swaps are discrete and limited.

The authors show transformer attention weights can instead be rotated, a smooth and wider reshaping. Rotation grows the set of equal models far beyond swaps. On that fact they build a matching method with a proven best answer for aligning two models before merging. Across language and vision tests, rotation-based matching improved merged models a lot. The work opens parameter symmetry as a tool for model fusion.
arxiv-2502-01164:
Sirui Lin and co-authors tighten causal bounds by weaving background variables into an optimal transport method, in this 2025 paper. When a study cannot pin a treatment effect to one number, it reports a range instead. Those ranges can be too wide to guide decisions. Adding covariates can narrow them, but the math becomes a conditional transport problem, which is harder than the standard kind.

Their fix is a tight relaxation that turns the conditional problem back into standard transport, with a penalty term. Any penalty value gives narrower ranges than ignoring covariates, and huge penalties recover the exact answer. They build an estimator on common transport software and rate its convergence. Simulations show it beats existing methods in practice.
arxiv-2502-01364:
Abhinav Pratap reads Meursault as a data point in two thousand twenty five. Camus's Stranger lives detached from feeling and social sense. Datafication turns human lives into metrics with ease today. Pratap asks what algorithms make of such a literary figure.

Emotion detection, sentiment analysis, and entity tools scan the novel. BERT, VADER, and spaCy quantify Meursault's acts and moods. The tools misread alienation and moral ambiguity throughout the text. Those failures expose limits of algorithmic takes on human life. The study argues for humanistic values inside modern AI design.
arxiv-2502-01464:
Masahito Hayashi, Yu-Ao Chen, Chenghong Zhu, and Xin Wang present, in twenty twenty-five, a method to predict symmetries of quantum dynamics with the fewest possible samples. Symmetries include invariance under time reversal or the identity. Spotting them matters for quantum technology. Their framework blends group representation theory, the math of symmetry, with subgroup hypothesis testing. They derive an exact formula for the best failure rate in detecting a symmetry. That formula gives a working meaning to a quantum entropy measure.

They prove that running tests in parallel does as well as adaptive or exotic control schemes. For key cases they give explicit sample counts. Identity testing needs fewer samples than symmetry testing, by the stated scaling laws.
arxiv-2502-01564:
Xinyue Chen and co-authors present a system from two thousand twenty-five that maps meeting talk into diagrams in real time. Video meetings show speech as a straight transcript, but ideas in a meeting branch and reconnect. Their tool, called MeetMap, uses large language models to build a visual map of the dialogue as it happens.

The team explored two versions with unlike levels of AI help. In one, the AI drafts summary nodes and people draw the links. In the other, the AI draws the map and people edit it. Ten pairs of users tried both versions against a standard baseline. Users preferred the mapping tool, liked the low effort of the AI-drawn version, and valued the hands-on sense-making of the other.
arxiv-2502-01864:
Zhiyang He, Vinod Vaikuntanathan, Adam Wills, and Rachel Yun Zhang construct quantum error-correcting codes with unusually flexible operations in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Good codes should correct errors well and support transversal gates, operations applied qubit-by-qubit that resist spreading faults. Earlier work mostly forced such gates to act on all logical qubits at once. This work targets addressable gates, applied to chosen logical qubits only.

The headline construction is an explicit qubit code with a special addressing property. Any triple of logical qubits, in one block or spread across up to three blocks, can receive a logical CCZ gate. That gate is implemented by a depth-one circuit of physical CCZ gates. The code's parameters are asymptotically good up to polylogarithmic factors, and the idea generalizes to wider controlled-phase gates. A broader framework, addressable orthogonality, extends classic triorthogonality theory to systematic code design.
arxiv-2502-02164:
Mark van den Bosch and two co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on waves that travel through a noisy medium. The waves solve reaction and diffusion sums on a tube shaped domain. Noise nudges the wave as it goes. The team asks how the noise shifts the wave's speed and shape, in a strict math sense.

They use a freezing trick that pins the wave in place while the noise is read. Small noise expansions then split the shift into clean terms. That gives a firm sense for the speed shift due to noise. Its size can be found to any order in the noise strength, as long as the wave is smooth enough. The work aids models where waves move through random settings.
arxiv-2502-03364:
Tom Hoddes, Alex Bijamov, Saket Joshi, Daniel Roggen, Ali Etemad, Robert Harle, and David Racz establish scaling laws for wearable activity recognition, in a 2025 paper. Scaling laws link model size and data volume to performance. They are well known in language and vision. This field, reading human activity from body sensors, lacked them. The team ran an exhaustive grid search. Both pretraining data amount and model size were varied.

Pretraining loss followed a power law in data and size. Adding more users beat adding more data per user. Data diversity, they conclude, drives gains. That finding contrasts with some earlier reports. The laws carried over to real tasks. Three benchmark datasets covered postures, walking styles, and daily activities. The authors suggest some past studies used undersized models. Revisiting them with proper capacity may change conclusions. The laws give builders a principled way to size models and datasets.
arxiv-2502-04264:
Jyothilakshmi and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on how neutron stars ring when disturbed, and what the ringing reveals about exotic matter inside them. At crushing densities, neutrons may give way to heavier cousins like hyperons and delta baryons, softening or stiffening the star. The team built equations of state for both mixes from a tuned particle model.

They computed each star's structure, its fundamental vibration frequencies, and how tides deform it. The delta mix proved stiffer than the hyperon one. The two agreed at low masses but diverged sharply for heavy stars, in step with sound speed differences. The predicted masses, sizes, and frequencies fit current pulsar and gravitational wave observations, giving future detectors a sharper test.
arxiv-2502-04864:
Aditya Kapoor and co-authors present a method from two thousand twenty-five for sharing credit fairly among cooperating AI agents. When a team earns one joint reward, each agent's true share is hidden. Splitting the reward well speeds learning, but any split must keep the team's best strategy unchanged, or learning aims at the wrong target.

Their method learns raw contribution scores with a neural network, then applies a fixed normalization step that forces the shares to sum to the team reward. They prove this is a valid form of reward shaping, which protects the optimal policy no matter how rough the learned scores are. On hard game benchmarks, the method learned faster and scored higher than strong rivals.
arxiv-2502-05064: Berlai presents a math paper from twenty twenty-five on a new family of sofic one-relator groups. Sofic groups form a broad class studied for their approximation traits. One-relator groups are defined by a single relation among generators. The new family is infinite in size. Its members are neither residually solvable nor residually finite. The proof takes a route apart from earlier Magnus-style decompositions.
arxiv-2502-06764:
Kiwhan Song and co-authors present a video diffusion architecture that uses past frames as history in this 2025 paper. Guidance methods improve how well generated video follows its conditions. Video models, though, must handle a varying number of past frames. Fixed size designs cannot do that well, and simple dropout guidance performs poorly.

Their model, called DFoT, trains with a goal that supports flexible history length. On top of it they build History Guidance, a family of steering methods. Even the simplest form raised video quality and time consistency. A stronger form improved motion and held together on very long videos. It also handled history unlike anything seen in training.
arxiv-2502-07464:
Arthur Alexandre, Thomas Guérin, and David Dean derive how dissolved material spreads in channels with strongly wavy walls, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The spreading, called Taylor dispersion, mixes the effects of flow and molecular diffusion, and it governs transport through porous media like rock and filters.

The channels they study repeat periodically but are far from straight. In the limit of a short channel period, they obtain exact formulas, to next-to-leading order, for the long-time diffusion constant and the drift along the channel. Those formulas let them recast the wavy channel as a straight one with extra surface effects. The surface absorbs and releases material, the flow slips there by an effective amount, and surface diffusion takes a universal value. Numerical checks confirm the formulas. The result gives a practical way to upscale transport in tortuous pores.
arxiv-2502-07864:
Fanxu Meng and five co-authors present TransMLA, a frame that turns models built with one attention style into another called multi-head latent attention. The target style is used by DeepSeek and unlocks its speed tools. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The shift squeezes the stored key and value cache by a vast share. On a known seven billion weight model, that gave a more than ten fold speed up at long text lengths while output stayed sound. Only a modest pool of training text was needed to bring scores back to par across test sets. The authors pitch the frame as a hands on path for moving older models to the new style.
arxiv-2502-07964:
Anthony Blaom and Samuel Okon introduce software for comparing math models of tumor growth, including a new kind that learns its equations from data. Classic models describe growth with fixed formulas, and a forecast is only possible after fitting the formula to a patient past measurements. Their tool, described in twenty twenty-five, automates fitting for a battery of models side by side. They apply it to a human data set covering lung and bladder cancer lesions under two treatments, rechecking earlier claims about which model works best.

On cases with at least a handful of size measurements, one classic model, the general Bertalanffy model, performed best on average, and earlier reported gaps were tested for statistical strength. The authors add a caveat: when many measurements are available, richer models that can capture rebound and relapse may be the wiser choice despite their complexity.
arxiv-2502-09264:
Sellier-Prono and three co-authors chart how clusters of oscillators fall into step when their natural frequencies vary across space. Think of rhythms in living tissue, where each region prefers its own tempo. The team studies a classic model with a steady frequency slope.

With steep slopes and strong coupling, the system rests quietly. As conditions shift, plateaus of locked rhythm grow, split by defects where the wave dies out. The team traces those defects to a nonlinear reshaping of how activity spreads. They also work out how the number and size of defects scale with the settings. Two end states appear, smooth plateaus or a fully locked pattern.
arxiv-2502-11264:
Caleb Maresca wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It asks how the mere hope of transformative AI could move money behavior today, well before such AI exists.

In the model, when AI arrives it shifts labor pay from workers to those who own the systems, and each household's share tracks its wealth at that date. Households thus race to pile up wealth now. With forecasts of AI timing fed in, even mild set-ups push short-term interest rates far above their no-race level. Rates part from capital rents, since wealth buys a strategic edge, not just yield. The tale warns central banks to watch beliefs, not just tech.
arxiv-2502-11764:
Zi-Yang Huang and Jia-Hui Huang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It computes the ringing tones, called quasinormal modes, of a massive scalar field around five-dimensional Myers-Perry black holes that spin on two axes.

Since the wave equation splits into radial and angular parts, the team solves each part by numeric means, using both a continued fraction method and a matrix method. All modes found decay, as their imaginary parts are negative. The authors track how spin rates, field mass, and the wave's angular counts shift the tones. For heavy fields, long-lived modes appear. The results also show the expected symmetries of the mode set.
arxiv-2502-12364:
Gregg and co-authors, listed by initials in the record, build a way in 2025 to compute the gamma-ray spectra from positron annihilation in molecules. A positron is the antimatter twin of the electron. When one meets an electron inside a molecule, both vanish and gamma rays fly out, and the spread of their energies carries clues about where the meeting happened.

The team derived a workable formula using smooth math functions for the electron and positron states, and coded it into a public program. They show how the pairing between the two particles reshapes the spectra. For two test molecules, the share from each electron orbit depended on symmetry, not just on energy.
arxiv-2502-12464:
Seanie Lee and co-authors present SafeRoute, a way to run safety checks on user prompts at lower cost, in a research paper from 2025. Large language models need guard models that catch harmful prompts before the main model answers. Big guard models work well but cost a lot to run, while small ones miss hard cases.

SafeRoute adds a small router that sorts each prompt as easy or hard. Easy prompts go to the small guard model, and only hard ones go to the big model. The team notes that most prompts are easy, so the big model is needed for just a small share. Tests on several benchmark sets showed a better balance of cost and safety than rival methods.
arxiv-2502-16264:
Henrik Garde, Markus Hirvensalo, and Nuutti Hyvönen prove steady recovery for a classic inverse problem, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The Calderón problem asks whether boundary voltage data can reveal how well a body's interior conducts. Past work gave only weak guarantees for broad material classes, and strong ones only for narrow classes. The authors study the unit ball in any number of dimensions.

They give a plain proof that strong, Lipschitz-type stability holds for many broad material classes. The key is expanding the material in basis functions whose weights fall fast enough near the boundary. They build such bases in general dimension from Zernike functions, known from optics. The result marks a step change in what can be promised for this old problem.
arxiv-2502-16364:
Peter Forsyth and Yuying Li weighed how to state risk when a retiree spends down a pension pot. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with defined contribution plans. Such plans have spread as the old promise based plans fade. The spend down phase needs a plan for draws over time. Cast as a control task, it needs a clear prize and a clear risk.

The prize is plain: total draws over the retired span. Risk, to most, is to run dry. The team tests three left tail risk forms, from mean shortfall to the chance of shortfall. They show that, on set terms, the best controls for prize and risk lines share a form. Readers who plan pensions get a firm way to weigh dry risk.
arxiv-2502-16464:
Josh Green and Jingbo Wang encode data into quantum states in twenty twenty-five. Loading a general state vector into qubits normally takes exponentially many gates. That cost blocks many quantum machine learning ideas at the door. Matrix product states offer a compressed representation that can dodge the worst of it.

The authors show such states can represent useful functions compactly. Low-degree piecewise polynomials are prepared with shallow circuits at very high accuracy. They extend the method to approximate encoding of pixel values. A medical chest image of substantial size was prepared on fourteen qubits. Its fidelity exceeded ninety-nine percent in a circuit of modest depth. Readers get a practical loading route for structured data onto quantum hardware.
arxiv-2502-17064:
Kevin Smith wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. Its text studies an Lp analogue of Bohr's abscissae of summability for Dirichlet series. The frame is the Phragmén-Lindelöf theorem in strips.

For functions that grow at most like a polynomial in a strip, an order function tracks that growth. The paper ties shape traits of the abscissae to shape traits of the order function. When the order function obeys a Selberg-class type law, the tie is the same as the Lindelöf hypothesis, save for one case. In that case the order function turns out smooth, with fast decay near one. The work is pure analytic number theory.
arxiv-2502-17264:
Konstantina Bairaktari and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on prediction sets that keep their accuracy promise not just on average, but for overlapping groups of people at once. Conformal prediction builds sets that contain the true answer at a set rate. That rate can quietly fail for subgroups, which is unfair in high-stakes uses.

Older methods guard disjoint groups only, like tiles in a grid. Their framework, named for the painter Kandinsky, allows groups that overlap and even partial membership, defined over both traits and labels. The algorithm folds older methods in as special cases and hits the best possible worst-case coverage bound. Tests on real data show it runs in practice.
arxiv-2502-17364:
Yorùbá is a tonal language spoken by millions, yet language technology barely serves it. Toheeb Jimoh, Tabea De Wille, and Nikola Nikolov review a decade of research, from 2014 to 2024. Their systematic search gathered 105 studies. The pattern is scarcity: few annotated corpora and few pretrained models. Tone marks and rich word forms add technical difficulty. Code-switching and fading digital use of the language add social difficulty.

Rule-based methods feature often, a sign of data poverty. Still, shared datasets and multilingual models are growing. The authors map the resources that exist and the gaps that matter most. Their aim is to steer new work where it counts.
arxiv-2502-18064:
Wang and Zhao built a neural network system in twenty twenty-five that upgrades cheap accelerometer signals. Accelerometers measure motion in phones, cars, and wearables. Low-cost versions are small and easy to mass-produce but suffer noise and a narrow measurement range.

Their system, HEROS-GAN, learns to rewrite a cheap sensor's output so it resembles a costly sensor's. Paired cheap and costly recordings rarely exist, so a method based on optimal transport theory supervises learning from unpaired data. A second addition feeds tuned energy into the generator so it can exceed the cheap sensor's range and capture fine detail. The team also released a dataset of tens of thousands of paired-style samples, the first of its kind. Tests doubled the range and cut noise a hundredfold, they report.
arxiv-2502-18364:
Yifan Pu and co-authors present ART, a transformer for generating multi-layer transparent images, in a research paper from 2025. Layered images let users isolate and edit parts of a picture, which single flat images cannot do. Past systems used semantic layouts that fix what each region must show, which limits freedom.

ART uses an anonymous region layout instead. The model itself decides which visual tokens match which text tokens from a global prompt. A layer-wise crop keeps only the tokens of each region, cutting attention cost sharply. The method runs more than twelve times faster than full attention. It can build images with more than fifty distinct layers.
arxiv-2502-19364:
Ali Ismail-Fawaz's thesis applies deep learning across the main tasks of time series analysis, with human motion as the flagship use. Sequences measured evenly over time appear in medicine, energy, and telecommunications; the thesis covers classifying them, clustering them, making stand-ins for them, and predicting outcomes from them. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the contributions include classification boosted by feature engineering, early foundation-model work for series, a compact architecture that still reaches top performance. Self-supervised methods for when labeled data are scarce.

For motion, the work distinguishes normal from abnormal movement in skeleton recordings for action recognition and rehabilitation, and makes synthetic motion useful to film and games. A shape-based tool creates extra training samples for regression when data are thin, such as forecasting patient recovery. The thesis closes by criticizing shaky evaluation habits and proposing a standardized, robust structure.
arxiv-2502-20664:
Kenneth Hinkle and co-authors measure, in twenty twenty-five, the star pair behind T Coronae Borealis, a nova that flares about every eighty years. The pair holds a red giant star and a white dwarf, the dense core of a dead star. A fresh flare was expected in twenty twenty-five. The team took spectra of the giant from twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four. Light patterns in spectra reveal how fast the star moves toward or away from us.

They combined new and old speed data to refine the orbit. It is near circular, with a period of about two hundred twenty-eight days. At the known distance, the white dwarf is heavy for its type. The giant is lighter. The paper weighs paths to refine these values.
arxiv-2502-20764:
Junpeng Wang, Chin-Chia Michael Yeh, Uday Singh Saini, and Mahashweta Das build a viewing tool, in a 2025 preprint, for a new kind of vision model. The models, based on the Mamba design, scan an image as a sequence of patches. Trainable weights let the scan mimic attention, picking which patches matter. How patches influence each other across the flat sequence is hard to see. The scan order itself bends that influence. Without a window into it, users cannot tell what the model has learned.

Their visual analytics tool shows attention across patches block by block. Users can watch the pattern shift as data flows deeper into the model. The team used it to compare ways of ordering patches into a line. Different orders produced clearly different attention maps. The authors offer the tool as a step toward models whose inner focus can be inspected, not just scored.
arxiv-2502-20964:
Zhengxuan Zhang, Yin Wu, Yuyu Luo, and Nan Tang upgrade the memory that image-question systems consult. Big multimodal models answer questions about pictures well, until the question needs niche or fresh facts. Bolting on a knowledge base helps, but older setups translate the image into words first and lose visual detail in the process.

Their answer is to organize knowledge into fine-grained units that keep text scraps and entity images together in one structured bundle. A framework called KU-RAG then retrieves those units for the model and runs a correction chain that double-checks the facts before answering. Across four benchmarks the approach beat existing knowledge-based systems by about three points on average and up to eleven at best. The authors argue that how knowledge is structured matters as much as how it is fetched.
arxiv-2502-21164:
Christian Komusiewicz, Diptapriyo Majumdar, and Frank Sommer shrink the long-path enumeration problem with polynomial-size kernels that preserve listing speed. Their paper from twenty twenty-five asks for every path on exactly k vertices in a graph, a classic enumeration task. Kernelization pre-chews the instance into a smaller equivalent core. The catch for enumeration is delay: solutions must keep flowing at polynomial pace.

Three structural parameters each admit such kernels: vertex cover number, dissociation number, and distance to clique. Each parameter measures how far the graph sits from a tame class. Small parameters, small kernels, fast listing. The work extends a young theory of enumeration kernelization, refined only a few years ago, into concrete path problems.
arxiv-2503-00464:
David Snee and four co-authors test a quiet weak point in language research: the wordlists used to trace language history. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with multilingual wordlists, where one concept is translated into many tongues. Family trees of languages are built from such lists, so their quality sets the quality of the trees.

The team paired ten lists built on their own and compared the translations concept by concept, across nine language families. On average, only about eighty-three percent of pairs gave the same word form. When the sound transcription had to match too, the share fell to about twenty-three percent. They urge care in judging tree studies built on such data.
arxiv-2503-00864: Thomas Foertsch, Alexander Lytchak, and Elefterios Soultanis prove a clean split for spaces defined only by the gaps between their points. Their short paper is from two thousand twenty-five, in pure math. They show that each full such space breaks, in just one way, into a product of two parts. One part is a Hilbert space, which may be flat or have a finite count of dims. The other part is a space that does not split off straight lines at all.
arxiv-2503-02364:
Andrei Marin and Adrian Stefan Carstea wrote a math paper in 2025 on a wave equation. The equation mixes smooth change with steps on a grid. The authors blend two tests for well-behaved equations: one about smooth solutions, one about how spikes shrink and vanish.

From the step test, they find a surprising spread of helper functions. Only one of them fits the classic two-line form used to solve such equations. The rest give forms with more lines, yet all link to the main one by fixed relations. They also study two changed versions of the equation. There, repeating patterns show up next to the shrinking spike patterns. The paper ends with full step versions and a fast way to work out a growth score.
arxiv-2503-02864:
Markus Lohrey and Andreas Rosowski study how hard it is to find a permutation with a given cycle shape inside a group. Their 2025 paper starts from a known hard problem in computing. A permutation group is a set of rearrangements closed under combining and undoing moves.

The pair show sharp splits by how the group is given. For a group made from a single generator, the search can be done with very little memory. For a group made from two generators, where the moves commute, the problem stays as hard as the general case. The same hardness holds for asking whether such a group holds a move that fixes no element. The results map the edge between easy and hard cases in group algorithms.
arxiv-2503-03064:
Victor Wang, Michael Zhang, and Eunsol Choi improve machine judges by using their full score spread in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Language models often grade text in place of humans. Most setups take just the judge's top pick under greedy decoding.

The judge in fact holds a spread of scores over options. Averaging that spread beat taking the top pick in every test style: single, paired, and ranked grading. Methods that add risk caution often did better still. Chain-of-thought prompting shrank the spread and often hurt scores. The authors urge using the spread rather than the text alone.
arxiv-2503-05264:
Mark Russinovich and Ahmed Salem present a 2025 paper on a simple way to break the safety rules of AI chat systems. Most known jailbreaks need heavy prompt crafting or costly search. Their attack instead edits the chat history itself.

The method plants a fake past exchange in which the model seems to have agreed to the harmful request already. Faced with that false context, many models comply as if staying in character. The team tested the attack on a wide range of open and commercial models. It slipped past top tier safety setups in many cases, they report, and they propose fixes.
arxiv-2503-05864:
Yuxuan Zhang and Maissam Barkeshli present a 2025 physics paper that joins two ways of gauging charge drift in Chern insulators. Such materials hold an inborn sideways drift, a polarization, despite loose edges and spread-out electron waves. One school reads the drift from body-wide clues: trapped charges at defects, edge charge piles, and momentum. That read hinges on where the cell's origin is set.

The other school reads it from a wave phase, hinged on a chosen point in momentum space. The authors show the two reads agree when origin and point are matched as a pair. A long split between bulk and wave views closes. Polarization in these odd materials is now one number, not two.
arxiv-2503-07864: Ilijas Farah gives a clear new write up of an older proof, in work from twenty twenty-five. The proof comes from two thousand one. It asks when a function truly depends on just one input. The functions live on a cube built from many binary choices. A function may seem to use many inputs. Yet in effect it may rest on only one. Farah states a test for that trait. The test is both needed and enough in the local case. He adds limit results too.
arxiv-2503-07964:
Tadaki and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on warm gas swirling near a supermassive black hole seen as it was thirteen billion years ago. Quasars shine so brightly that their X-rays should heat nearby gas to hundreds of degrees. Sharp telescope views of one distant quasar caught the glow of dust and of carbon monoxide in very high energy states.

The signals come from a compact disk hugging the black hole. The balance between the two carbon monoxide lines matches models where X-ray heating dominates and the gas column is extremely dense. The team argues such high-state lines are a promising way to find dust-buried quasars in the early universe.
arxiv-2503-08964:
Rongxia Tang, Henry Liu, Yueping Shi, and Chenming Wang introduce list versions of rainbow connection numbers in a twenty twenty-five mathematics paper. In a rainbow path, every edge carries a different colour. Classic measures count the fewest colours that link every pair of vertices by such a path.
