The list versions let each edge choose from its own allowed colour list.

Results give the new numbers for several specific graphs. The authors also sort out which pairs of values can occur together. One pair links the ordinary and strong list measures. Another links the strong measure with its list form. The paper closes by asking whether the ordinary and list numbers always match.
arxiv-2503-10064:
Alok Nath Singh, Bibek Bhandari, Rafael Sánchez, and Andrew Jordan published this quantum physics paper in 2025. It poses a foundational question: can a particle be caught in a virtual state, a classically forbidden place it should pass through without truly occupying? Their test bed is a chain of three quantum dots, tiny electron traps. The middle dot is set at an energy electrons avoid, so tunneling from one end to the other is normally described as virtual.

The team studied what happens when the middle dot is watched continuously, under two styles of measurement. Individual electron paths differed wildly between the styles. On average, though, watching raised the chance of finding the electron in the middle dot. Weak watching partly localizes the particle there, while strong watching forces a sharp yes-or-no outcome. The authors say the paradox dissolves: observation itself reshapes the tunneling.
arxiv-2503-10864:
Marziyeh Karmand and four co-authors studied electron waves in twenty twenty-five crossing a junction where a Dirac cone tilts by different amounts along its length. In such materials, electrons act like massless relativistic particles, and a position-dependent tilt warps their world into an emergent curved spacetime. The team solved the resulting Dirac equation numerically after a change of spinor that stands the cone upright locally.

As waves cross the tilt texture, key quantities oscillate, with wavelengths shrinking where tilt is strong — a pattern echoing gravitational redshift. They derived formulas for the local wave number that explain the pattern and matched them with simulations. Wider tilt bumps damp the oscillation size but add peaks. Smooth tilt profiles also transmit electrons remarkably well, suggesting devices that engineer redshift on a chip.
arxiv-2503-10964:
Watanabe and Zheng revisit core claims about a classic tool for steering systems in twenty twenty-five. The tool, called the linear quadratic regulator, picks the best control for a system with smooth costs. It looks simple, but the math of tuning it by trial has subtle traps. The pair ask when the tuning task acts like a much nicer, curved task.

They use equation based tools and a new lifting method to sharpen past results. Under standard checks, the tuning task shows strong pairing between its two forms. Under a bit stronger checks, the slope of the task points firmly toward the best answer. Their broader test for when that holds is a main new result.
arxiv-2503-11064:
Ziqi Wang and five co-authors improve contactless breathing monitors in twenty twenty-five. Breathing waveforms carry more than rate: they can reveal irregularities for diagnosis and guide rehabilitation. Ultra-wideband radar can capture them without touching the patient. Prior work chased rate estimates and treated waveforms as a by-product.

That neglect let waveform deformation and inversion slip through. Their system, MobiVital, targets waveform quality directly. A self-supervised autoregressive model extracts the breathing signal. A biology-informed alignment step then corrects its shape. Readers get radar monitoring judged by the waveform doctors would actually read, not just a beats-per-minute number. The work aims at signals fit for clinical pattern reading.
arxiv-2503-11364:
Bacteria spreading through soils or body ducts switch between swimming freely and skimming along walls, and the gap between surfaces shapes how far they get. Renaud Baillou and co-authors track a model flagellated bacterium in three dimensions between two plates in this 2025 study, varying the gap height.

They measure for the first time how spread speed and time spent in the open versus at walls depend on the gap. A detailed random-motion model that includes the cell's inner chemical memory matches every measurement without tuning. A simpler memory-free version then yields a clean formula for spread, giving a general frame for how microbes navigate tight spaces.
arxiv-2503-11464:
Aryan Eftekhari, Michel Juillard, Normann Rion, and Simon Scheidegger extend, in a 2025 preprint, the Dynare economics platform to solve big nonlinear models globally. Dynare is the workhorse for dynamic economic modeling, but its standard methods are local approximations. They wobble when models grow many dimensions and strong nonlinearities. The authors bolt on two tools. Adaptive sparse grids place points where the action is, taming the growth of points with dimension. A hierarchical expansion writes policy rules as sums of low-dimensional pieces.

Benchmarks use an international business cycle model solved by time iteration. Both tools beat the dimensionality curse in their tests. Models with at least one hundred dimensions solved accurately on ordinary hardware in modest time. The authors present the upgrade as a bridge: Dynare users gain global methods without leaving their platform. Machine learning solvers could plug into the same frame later.
arxiv-2503-11564:
Yang Wang, Alexander Craddock, and four peers link a phone-band photon with a quantum store that works at room heat. The work came out in 2025. Such links are a key step toward quantum relay posts. Those posts are what a long-range quantum net will need.

Range is the foe in this work. Photons get lost in glass fiber as they fly. The no-clone rule bars a plain boost of their signal. The team used plain rubidium kits to make the photon and to store its mate. The photon sits at 1324 nm, in the phone band that set fiber bears well. The shared link hit a truth score past 90 percent. The team also made linked pairs at rates up to 1200 per second. That rate came at a truth score of 80 percent. A room-heat build like this could make relay gear much less hard to place.
arxiv-2503-12164:
Yacob Alemiye Mamo, Leonid Berdinkov, and Elena Pastukhova wrote this astronomy paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on pulsing stars called Type II Cepheids. These old, low-mass stars swell and shrink in steady cycles, and slow shifts in the cycle length can reveal how the star is evolving.

The team tracked thirteen short-period stars using records that span about a century. Their timing charts curve in a smooth arc, the mark of a steady rise or fall in the cycle length. Seven of the stars are speeding up their pulses, and seven in the wider known class were newly counted here as slowing down. A standard test confirmed the shifts are real, not noise. The pattern matches new theory on how these stars live out their later stages. The work grows the sample that theory must explain.
arxiv-2503-12464:
Alessio Xompero and Andrea Cavallaro show that judging image privacy needs far less machinery than assumed. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Whether a photo is private is a subjective call. Graph networks paired with convolutional ones have led the field. Those models carry millions of parameters and many parts. End-to-end training can hide which part does the work.

Their simpler route pairs transfer learning with one convolutional network. Scene types link images to privacy judgments. Only hundreds of parameters are tuned, not millions. Performance matches the graph-based methods. High-dimensional features per visual entity prove needless. The graph part itself adds almost nothing. Privacy prediction gets a leaner, clearer baseline.
arxiv-2503-13064:
Suryadevara designs HERMES in twenty twenty-five, a memory system for an open chip design used in machine learning. Learning models need data fed fast, and slow memory can starve them. HERMES tunes the layers of memory in RISC-V chips for image, sequence, and attention models. It adds smart pre loading, caches that know tensor shapes, and mixed memory types.

A shared top level cache links to a special learning accelerator chip. The team tested the design in two standard simulators under typical learning loads. The report lays out the main design choices and the hard parts that remain. It aims at memory that stays fast as models and chips scale up.
arxiv-2503-14164:
Hiroki Takahasi studies rare fluctuations among the repeating patterns of a symbol system called the Dyck shift. The system models balanced strings, like correctly nested brackets. Its periodic points are the patterns that repeat forever. Large deviation theory prices how unlikely atypical repeating patterns are.

Takahasi proves a level-two large deviation principle for these points. The rate function is built from the entropies of the system's invariant measures. Unlike the well-mixed Markov case, this rate function is not convex. At level one it splits into a sum of two convex continuous pieces. Thermodynamic tools then show the level-one rates are smooth in some key cases. One displayed example bends without convexity and kinks inside its domain. The work extends rare-event theory to a system with memory and constraints.
arxiv-2503-15464:
Alexander Held and a large team of co-authors report the 200 Gbps Challenge, a stress test of the analysis facilities built for the High-Luminosity LHC. Their paper from twenty twenty-five describes the IRIS-HEP institute's Grand Challenge format: staged exercises of rising scale to prove readiness. This round aimed to sustain two hundred gigabits per second into live analysis pipelines. Software, data services, and facilities teams joined, inside and outside the institute.

Around two hundred terabytes flowed through test pipelines in CMS and ATLAS formats. The target rate held across pipelines, and event-hungry ones processed tens of millions of events per second. Lessons for working at this scale feed the next exercise, planned at double size. The baseline for HL-LHC analysis now exists.
arxiv-2503-15564:
Tung Sum Thomas Kwok, Chi-Hua Wang, and Guang Cheng published this data study in 2025. Making fake but realistic tables is useful for sharing knowledge without exposing real records. A recent framework, GReaT, feeds whole table rows to a language model as text. That avoids splitting numbers from categories, but two problems remain. Rows carry little plain meaning, so the model cannot use its background knowledge well. Linked multi-table data also resists the approach.

Their upgrade, GReaTER, attacks both problems. A semantic enhancement step maps table entries into richer descriptions the model can reason about. A cross-table method then links related tables so they can be generated in a coordinated way. Tests showed the new system outperforming the original framework. The authors present it as a better route to synthetic data that mixes numbers, categories, and text across several tables at once.
arxiv-2503-15964:
Daria Schumm, Katharina Müller, and Burkhard Stiller wrote a 2025 survey of decentralized identity, where a person holds their own credentials and presents them as they choose. Such systems have grown fast in recent years, with a flood of standards, designs, and products. Earlier reviews of the field lean on academic work and skip the grey literature and the real deployments.

This team read both, and surveyed company and government efforts to map where the systems stand in real life. Their emphasis falls not on the technology but on the obstacles in its path to wide use. Those obstacles include the old central hubs that hold data now, laws, and plain habits. The survey finds that the value of self-held credentials is clear. The drag lies in the shift away from hub-held systems, and the authors name why that shift stalls.
arxiv-2503-16164:
Kříž and Vonásek sped up optimal robot path planning in twenty twenty-five. The standard algorithm, RRT star, grows a random tree through configuration space and slowly refines the path toward optimal. Its weakness is slow convergence; sampling the whole space wastes effort on regions that cannot improve the current route.

Only samples inside the so-called omniscient set can possibly help. The authors approximate that set in two ways: with several small ellipsoids fitted along sections of the current best path, and with a convex hull built from the current solution. Both samplers keep the guarantee of eventual optimality and work in any dimension. Experiments in three- and six-dimensional spaces showed superior performance over existing approaches in multiple scenarios, reaching good paths faster.
arxiv-2503-17064:
Leiming Chen, Patrick Jentsch, Chiu Fan Lee, Ananyo Maitra, Sriram Ramaswamy, and John Toner wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It takes a fresh look at the fluid-like theory of flocks, groups that move as one, as in birds or active matter.

The authors split flocks into two kinds: ones where birth and death keep the density steady, and ones where the head count is fixed. For the first kind they derive two exact scaling laws that link the three exponents of long-range behavior, and argue such flocks can hold true long-range order in two dimensions. For the second kind, extra terms block any exact law. They conclude that past claims of exact exponents for both kinds were wrong.
arxiv-2503-18364:
Chenxi Xie and four colleagues introduce MaSS13K, a dataset for high-resolution semantic segmentation, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Semantic segmentation labels every pixel in an image by category. Existing datasets often have low resolution and coarse masks with poor boundaries.

MaSS13K contains 13,348 real-world images, all at 4K resolution. Its masks cover seven categories, including human, vegetation, ground, sky, water, and building. The masks are far more detailed than those in earlier datasets. The team also presents MaSSFormer, a model built for this resolution. A final learning scheme mixes the labeled categories with pseudo labels for new classes. That lets the model transfer its accuracy to fresh object types.
arxiv-2503-18664:
Vito Crismale, Manuel Friedrich, and Joscha Seutter present a 2025 mathematics paper on computing how cracks grow slowly in a brittle sheet. Their method uses a mesh of triangles that is itself part of the unknown: the mesh adapts at each step to follow the crack. Both the mesh size and the time step shrink together in the analysis.

They prove the approximations settle into a true crack path for the classic Griffith model of brittle fracture with even surface energy. The limit path obeys three rules: cracks never heal, the state is stable at each time, and energy balances. The work also gives a fresh proof of an earlier static result.
arxiv-2503-19164:
A fibered version of the Burnside ring splits into indecomposable pieces, and a 2025 arXiv paper by Benjamín García and Alberto Raggi-Cárdenas describes each piece from the ring's standard basis. The fibered ring tracks group actions together with extra data attached to each orbit.

For each factor the authors give a second description, as the solvable component of the matching ring for a Weyl group. The two views together pin the structure down. The paper is brief and technical, aimed at algebraists who work with Burnside rings and their variants.
arxiv-2503-19664:
Timofey Kozhukhov, Benjamin Loewe, Kristian Thijssen, and Tyler Shendruk find that swirling defects can kick tiny beads into faster wandering. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Colloids in nematic fluids carry defects of their own. Active nematics spawn extra defects that move on their own. The mix creates a turbulent, topological soup. Mesoscale simulations track how beads move inside it.

At low activity, traveling defects shove the beads' own defects around. Rearrangements speed up, and bead diffusion rises. At high activity, interactions turn uniform and directionless. Bead motion decorrelates and diffusion falls again. The non-monotonic curve is the paper's striking result. Active matter gains a knob for tuning transport.
arxiv-2503-20264:
Yunrui Zhang, Gustavo Batista, and Salil S. Kanhere question a basic belief about sorting time series data. Their two thousand twenty-five paper tests the UCR archive, the standard benchmark for this task. The field assumes that the order of values over time is what sets time series apart. The authors scramble that order and watch what happens to accuracy.

For a large share of the datasets, scrambling changed almost nothing. Many sets are tabular in nature, or rest on tabular traits, not on timing. That flaw can make timing-focused methods look better or worse than they are. The team builds UCR Augmented, a fresh benchmark that rewards true use of time order. Tests across seven families of classifiers showed clear gaps on it.
arxiv-2503-20864:
Camila de Sá-Freitas, Dimitri Gadotti, Francesca Fragkoudi, and a wider team wrote this astronomy paper, published in 2025. It dates, for the first time, the stellar bars at the hearts of nearby galaxies, reading their ages from the young nuclear discs the bars themselves built.

Bars drive a galaxy's slow internal evolution once its disc settles. The method uses spectrograph data from the MUSE instrument to separate the star-formation history of each nuclear disc from the older background. Since bars and nuclear discs grow up together, the disc's birthday dates the bar. Twenty galaxies, mostly from the TIMER survey, yielded bar birthdays from one to thirteen billion years ago. Disc settling, it turns out, is both an ancient and an ongoing process. The implied bar fraction across cosmic time matches counts of distant galaxies surprisingly well.
arxiv-2503-21864:
Jay Desai and Diptimoy Ghosh pushed positivity bounds for photon and gluon theories to one loop. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with bounds that tie a low energy theory to any sane high energy whole. At tree level such bounds are stock. At one loop the photon case stays finite and clean in the forward limit, but old tries hit a snag: the arc term hung on a fake low scale.

A close read of the high side of the spread link kills that hang. The bound comes out safe and flow fixed. The gluon case, with worse flaws, still yields a sound bound. Readers in field theory get loop grade fences for light and strong force toys.
arxiv-2503-21964:
Yanting Yang and Xiaoxiao Li present NeuroLIP, a 2025 method that aligns brain imaging data with text descriptions of a person. The imaging data come from functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, connectivity. The text can hold a disease label or demographic facts such as age and sex. Joining the two could sharpen what scans reveal about brain conditions, but older methods hide how the link is made and can bake in bias.

NeuroLIP links brain regions to disease-related words in the text, using token-conditioned attention. Its attention maps can be read and checked against known brain patterns. A special loss term pushes attention on disease words away from attention on sensitive traits, cutting false links between them. A negative gradient technique weakens the pull of those traits still further. On two shared datasets, it scored best on fairness while holding top marks on standard scores.
arxiv-2503-22364:
Lukas Eriksson and a large team find cryoEM structures of proteins after soft landing in two thousand twenty-five. A protein's gas phase shape underlies native mass spectrometry reads. How folds react to drying was never seen at fine scale. Their method lands proteins gently from an ion beam, then images them cold.

Four soluble complexes gave near atomic structures by that route. Main and side structure held up well after the landing. Change tracked how exposed each residue was to solvent. Inner residues stayed sharp while outer zones rearranged. The tool links mass selection to near atomic views at last.
arxiv-2504-01864:
Xiang-Dong Li and Enrui Zhang prove entropy laws for heat flow on rough spaces with bounded curve. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. The spaces, called RCD, blend length and mass in a way that mimics smooth curved worlds. Entropy tracks how a spread of heat evens out.

They give the W-entropy form and show it falls in a steady way, with a hard case that pins its least shape. The Shannon entropy power bends in a set curve sense on such spaces. From that flow a sharp isoperimetric-style bound and a log-Sobolev bound of Stam type, with a stiff case for the last on full spaces.
arxiv-2504-02364:
Kulkarni and Ghiasvand build a test suite for stream tools on big compute rigs in this twenty twenty-five paper. Stream tools sort live data as it flows, but their growth caps on big rigs were not well gauged. Past test suites were built for desk rigs and cloud packs, not for such hubs.

Inside, the suite is built in parts that swap in and out with ease. It runs on the queue frames that big hubs use and takes three known stream tools. Hub tests show flow rates far past those of past test suites. Full knobs, auto run care, and free code set the suite apart, the team says. It aims to be the yard stick for stream work on big rigs.
arxiv-2504-02464:
Ruixiao Zhang and co-authors rethink 3D object detection for self-driving sensors in a 2025 paper. Lidar sees only the near side of an object, so detectors that aim at the object's center lose accuracy when moved to new settings. Judging whole boxes also leans on size quirks of one data set. The authors argue the near surface matters most, since avoiding a crash depends on it.

They propose two new scores that grade how well a model finds the surface closest to the sensor. They also add a training head that steers models toward those surfaces. Their detector, CornerPoint3D, instead predicts the nearest corner of each object. In cross-setting tests it beat the standard center-based detector on both new and old scores.
arxiv-2504-02864:
Peter Adelson and Julian Nyarko release a giant public set of business contracts in a 2025 paper. The set holds over a million contracts that public companies filed with the United States securities regulator between 2000 and 2023. Each contract is sorted by agreement type and linked to the parties who signed it. Machine learning tools, including a tuned language model, did the sorting and linking.

The records also carry filing form, file format, and whether a contract amends an older one. The authors chart how contract length, wording, and complexity drifted across two decades. Job and securities deals dominate the filings. An open trove this size lets scholars study how real deals are written, not just how books say they should be.
arxiv-2504-03864: Pavel Turek, writing alone in 2025, studies the Mullineux map, a rule that links certain symmetry modules and entries of key tables in algebra. He asks what the map does to partitions whose rim hooks meet a size condition tied to two whole numbers. A new tool, called a runner matrix, is built for each such partition. Turek shows the matrices for a partition and its image agree. That match pins down the image in full, and a new abacus method drives the proof.
arxiv-2504-04764:
Shyam Sundhar and co-authors build a model to spot leaf diseases in a 2025 paper. Early, cheap detection of crop disease protects yields and food supply. Their model treats each leaf photo as a graph: the image is split into small like-colored patches, and the patches form nodes joined by edges.

Two graph methods work together in the hybrid. One weighs which neighbors matter most, and the other pools traits across the patch network. Extra edges and tuned starting weights make the model tougher and more general. On apple and potato leaves, scores for precision and recall sat near zero point nine eight. Sugarcane proved harder, with scores near zero point eight eight. The authors offer the tool as support for greener farming and less crop loss.
arxiv-2504-04864:
Christina Sauer and colleagues look at how statisticians build simulation studies on real data with no self-deception. Simulation studies are a must to test statistical methods. The common parametric kind draws data from a fitted model. Critics call it unrealistic. To base the data-making process on real data is the standard fix. But how its parts are drawn from data varies a lot and is poorly grasped.

Teams also tend to reuse a small set of real data sets. Their grounds for picking them are unclear. The paper reviews how each part of a parametric data-making process can be drawn from real data. It also treats how data set choice can be made in a set way. Two cases show the build: one on ordinal outcomes in randomized trials, and one on gene expression work.
arxiv-2504-06264:
Jisang Han and nine co-authors present D2USt3R, a method for reconstructing three-dimensional scenes that contain moving objects, in a two thousand twenty-five computer vision paper. Earlier pointmap regression methods such as DUSt3R work elegantly on static scenes but break under motion.

Motion disrupts alignment based only on camera poses. D2USt3R instead regresses static-dynamic aligned pointmaps that capture both the still background and moving geometry together. By treating space and time jointly, the pointmaps encode dense three-dimensional correspondence across frames. Extensive experiments on datasets with complex motion show consistently better reconstruction than prior approaches, which should help downstream tasks that need reliable dynamic geometry.
arxiv-2504-06364:
Xiuyuan Cheng, Zheng Dong, and Yao Xie reviewed deep learning for events scattered across space and time in a 2025 article. Spatio-temporal point processes model happenings like crimes, earthquakes, infections, and social posts, where each event raises or lowers the odds of the next nearby. Classical models assume fixed parametric kernels for that influence, which struggle with heterogeneous, nonstationary reality. Neural versions either learn the intensity function directly or learn flexible influence kernels from data.

The review centers on the deep influence kernel approach, which keeps an interpretable kernel inside the model while gaining neural expressiveness. Basis decompositions, graph networks for structured spaces, likelihood-based and likelihood-free estimation, and scaling to large datasets are all covered, along with open theoretical questions. The field guide serves researchers choosing machinery for event data.
arxiv-2504-07264:
Aleksandr Cariow wrote a solo paper in two thousand twenty-five on faster ways to run a core signal-processing transform. The Fourier transform turns a signal into its mix of frequencies, and fast versions of it are standard tools. Almost all of them treat each complex number as a single unit.

In some setups it pays to keep the real and imaginary parts apart, for example when later steps handle them in separate channels. Cariow proposes a fast algorithm built exactly for that split form. He lays out the method as a chain of matrix and vector steps, so the order of operations is clear and formal for builders.
arxiv-2504-07464:
Li Li and a large team charge a superconducting quantum battery in two thousand twenty five. Quantum batteries store energy in tiny quantum devices. Fast, stable charging must respect quantum speed limits. Their platform is a capacitively shunted flux qubit.

Counterdiabatic pulses in a Raman passage scheme drive the charging. Two norm constraints bound the driving strength in the tests. One run reaches the quantum speed limit itself. A new parameter S unifies speed and stability scoring. It tracks ergotropy stability where power and efficiency metrics fall short. The platform suits three level quantum batteries well.
arxiv-2504-08264:
Justin Feng, Amirmohammad Haddad, and Nader Sehatbakhsh survey device fingerprinting under modern machine learning attack, in a paper from 2025. Fingerprinting identifies internet-of-things devices by their physical or behavioral quirks, to authenticate them and spot eavesdroppers. Generative models now let attackers mimic those quirks, so old defenses need a fresh audit.

The authors propose a simple generic model of fingerprinting and sort existing methods for authentication and eavesdropping detection under it. They map shared trends between the two tasks and catalog current threats. Future directions aim at schemes that stay sound when attackers wield strong learning tools.
arxiv-2504-08864:
Kacha Dzhaparidze wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025, reproducing a chapter of a forthcoming book. It develops series expansions for random processes whose increments are stationary, processes whose step sizes behave the same whenever they are taken.

Such expansions write a wiggly random path as a sum of fixed wave-like pieces with random weights, the Karhunen-Loève pattern. The author uses a theory of Hilbert spaces built from entire functions to revisit old results and add new ones. Fresh decompositions of the Karhunen-Loève type are a highlight. The chapter also covers processes associated with the stationary-increment family. The paper serves specialists who model noise, signals, and other random motion, offering a unified view of how these processes can be broken into orthogonal parts.
arxiv-2504-08964:
Qisai Liu and co-authors published a 2025 paper on a sequence model that reads data in both directions at once. Forecasting tasks, from weather to energy demand, need models that spot patterns across time and across several data streams. Transformers do this well but slow down steeply as sequences lengthen. Classic recurrent models scale gently but usually read only forward.

Their model, BLUR, runs two linear recurrent units, one forward and one backward. Together they capture what came before and what comes after each point, while keeping the gentle scaling of recurrent designs. The system is built for fusing multiple sources at the sequence level, not just stacking their outputs. The authors present it as an efficiency play: bidirectional awareness without the transformer's quadratic cost. For long records, like sensor streams, that trade could matter more than raw size.
arxiv-2504-10464:
Teixeira and co-authors ask whether a basic rule linking two cosmic distances might be broken, in this 2025 paper. The rule ties how big an object looks to how bright it looks, through the universe's expansion. Breaking it could explain the clash over the expansion rate, called the Hubble tension.

The team tested five forms of rule-breaking against new survey data, supernova records, and early-universe clues. Two simple forms eased the tension. One shifted supernova calibration, while the other bent the rule at low distances and paired with steady dark energy. Evidence slightly favored the second, which motivates hunting for a physical cause.
arxiv-2504-11464:
Li Lu, Lingyu Guo, and Victor Guo sharpen bounds on a kind of weighted sum used in the study of special primes, in a paper from 2025. The primes in question are the whole parts of powers of whole numbers. Such primes, named for Piatetski and Shapiro, follow a sparse pattern. Sums of this kind are the main tool for proving where they fall.

Their new bound comes from a fresh attack on one part of the sum. With it, the range of a key condition from Balog and Friedlander grows wider. That wider range improves a known result on writing numbers as sums of three such primes. The methods also bear on how these primes spread across arithmetic patterns. They even touch primes shared by several beat-like sequences at once. The paper is a step in a long analytic program.
arxiv-2504-14064:
Leo Boisvert, Mihir Bansal, Chandra Kiran Reddy Evuru, and a multi-institution team present DoomArena in this two thousand twenty-five paper. DoomArena is a framework for testing AI agents against evolving security threats. It plugs into existing agent environments such as BrowserGym for web agents and a tau-bench setup for tool-calling agents. Threat models are configurable: users specify which components can be attacked and what the attacker targets.

The framework separates attack development from environment details, so one attack can run across many settings. Tests on leading web and tool-calling agents produced surprises. No agent dominated across all threat models, combined attacks often reinforced each other, and guardrail-model defenses failed where stronger model-based defenses held up better. The authors use these results to probe trade-offs between vulnerability and task performance.
arxiv-2504-14164:
Kisung You, Dennis Shung, and Mauro Giuffrè build a transport-style distance for bell-shaped spread laws on a sphere, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such laws model arrow-like data, yet fair ways to compare two of them were scarce. Hard normalizing math blocked older routes.

The new distance splits into two plain parts: the angle between centers, and a spread gap term. A bell-curve shortcut in the tight-spread case yields a closed form. Tests on fake data and real text and image codes show clean sorting. A mixture shrink method built on it keeps model shape while cutting bulk. Readers get a yardstick that respects the sphere.
arxiv-2504-14664:
Jixiang Sun and colleagues attacked a stubborn weakness of AI image deblurring in 2025: it fails on photos unlike its training data. Deep networks restore sharp images impressively on familiar datasets, then falter elsewhere, because they lean on dataset-specific patterns. The authors argue the missing ingredient is the blur kernel itself, the mathematical fingerprint of the blur, which does not depend on image content. Traditional algorithms already exploit kernels in the frequency domain.

Their design adds a Frequency Integration Module that fuses kernel information into a frequency-based transformer network for deblurring. Working in the frequency domain mirrors classical deconvolution while keeping deep learning's power. Experiments test whether this hybrid generalizes better to out-of-domain photographs. The broader lesson appeals beyond deblurring: when a classical prior is truly content-independent, building it into the network can free the model from dataset habits.
arxiv-2504-15564:
Musfiqur Rahman, SayedHassan Khatoonabadi, and Emad Shihab present a large set of real Python classes for language model research. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Past class-level sets were made by hand or were too small for the needs of new training and tests.

Their set, OpenClassGen, holds classes drawn from close to three thousand open-source projects. Each class comes with its frame of names and notes, plus a set of code measures on size and links. The team tests three large models on a small run-ready slice. The models write code close in sense to the true code, but much of it fails when run. The set can serve training, search-based help, and study of failure modes.
arxiv-2504-16064:
Theodoros Kouzelis and co-authors present a way to train image generators that also learn what their pictures mean, in a 2025 paper. Standard latent diffusion models make fine images but learn little about the content of a scene. The team ties generation to feature learning by having one model produce both the image code and a set of meaning features at once.

The features come from a strong self-taught vision encoder, and the model learns to denoise the image code and the features side by side. The change needs only small edits to a standard transformer design. As a bonus, the learned features can steer generation at run time, a trick the authors call representation guidance. In both prompted and unprompted tests, images came out better and training converged faster than with plain diffusion.
arxiv-2504-16264:
Francisco Valentini, Diego Kozlowski, and Vincent Larivière built a search data set across languages for scholarship in a 2025 paper. Researchers miss key work printed in other languages, and academic search across languages needs test data to improve. CLIRudit pairs English keywords written by authors themselves with non-English abstracts from a Canadian platform. It starts with French targets, in a recipe other repositories can copy.

Benchmarks of sparse and dense first-stage retrievers, with and without machine translation, hold surprises. Dense embeddings without any converting nearly matched translated systems, translating documents beat translating queries. Classic sparse retrieval with document translation stayed competitive while running cheaper. The data set, a first for English-French academic search, is put out for reuse.
arxiv-2504-16564:
Zhongtao Wang and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on labeling each pixel in satellite images by land type. Crisp edges and even traits in each class are both a must. Standard layered models blur edges and mix class traits. Their network, SAIP-Net, works in the wave band domain to sharpen both.

The net filters wave bands in a way that adapts to the image. It also widens the span each part of the net can see. Those two moves curb clashes in class traits and firm up edge lines. Tests show clear gains over the best known methods. The authors say wave aware design is a sound path for remote sensing labels.
arxiv-2504-17564:
Jean-Paul Allouche, Manon Stipulanti, and Jia-Yan Yao study a simple number map and its wide echoes, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The map doubles a number and wraps it around an odd limit. It shuffles positions, and a known equality counts the cycles of that shuffle in two ways.

The authors first prove that equality directly. To do so they widen the map, multiplying by any whole number instead of just two, and count its cycles too. The second half of the paper tours the map's surprise appearances. It turns up in word patterns, number theory, error-correcting codes, and even in card shuffling, juggling, bell ringing, poetry, and music.
arxiv-2504-18164:
Anna Jarosz-Kozyro and Jerzy Baranowski review data-driven ways to model wear and decay across fields in two thousand twenty-five. Slow decline limits the life of materials, machines, and bodies alike. Though the settings differ, the math used to track decline has much in common.

The review sorts methods from plain regression and cluster tools to Bayesian models, hidden state models, and deep learning. Tables lay out where each method has been used in medicine, power systems, and materials work, and what each revealed. The authors group the methods by how they infer, forecast, and learn. The survey is meant to let one field borrow tools proven in another.
arxiv-2504-19264:
Angel Mary John and two co-authors compare how world regions write rules for artificial intelligence in a twenty twenty-five paper. They look at the United States, Europe, China, and Singapore, grouped by IEEE regions. The focus is on how each place treats human rights in its rules.

Europe, they find, has strict rules that guard the rights of each person. The United States leans toward free rein for new ideas, with looser rules. China stresses state control and social order, while Singapore uses advice and self-rule by firms. The authors call for more talks across borders so rights stay safe as the tech grows.
arxiv-2504-21664:
Stephen McKean, Giosuè Muratore, and Wern Juin Gabriel Ong wrote a math paper in 2025 about lines that touch a hypersurface very closely at a single point. For such highly tangent lines they study the local type. A piece of information that feeds into a count valued in quadratic forms and tied to an Euler number that depends on a chosen orientation.

The authors give two shape-based readings of that local type. One uses the Wronski map, and the other uses the basic forms of the hypersurface itself. The two views connect an algebra-based counting problem with the surface's own geometry.
arxiv-2505-00664: Álvaro Otero Sánchez presents a key exchange protocol in twenty twenty-five. Two parties must agree on a secret key over a public channel. His protocol rests on circulant matrices acting on matrices over a congruence-simple semiring. That algebraic setting replaces the number theory behind classic protocols. He describes how to compute matrices with the properties the protocol needs. He also analyzes the computational cost of running it. Its security against known attacks is examined as well.
arxiv-2505-01064:
Telling apart near-identical categories, like bird species, is hard for image models. The task normally needs big labeled datasets from experts. Hari Chandana Kuchibhotla and co-authors remove the label list entirely. In their vocabulary-free setting, a model must name fine-grained classes it was never given. Big multimodal models can do this, but querying them per image is slow and costly. Their method, NeaR, uses such a model to label a small unlabeled set once. A CLIP model is then fine-tuned on those noisy labels.

The approach is built to absorb noise and open-ended answers. It sets a new benchmark for efficient fine-grained recognition without a vocabulary.
arxiv-2505-01664:
Yi-Ming Zhai, Chuan-Xian Ren, and Hong Yan tackle image classification when the target set covers only some of the source classes, in a paper from 2025. A learner trained on labeled source images must adapt to unlabeled target images. Extra source classes can poison the match if they are not held back.

Their method first estimates how much each class matters in the target. It then rebuilds a weighted source set for fair class-by-class matching. A soft-masked cost table steers the transport toward same-class pairs. A dual form of the transport problem keeps the math fast, solved by gradient steps. A neural network stands in for the transport potential.
arxiv-2505-02364:
Weihua Yang and Yicong Zhou merge in 2025 two kinds of camera images into one clearer picture. Visible-light images hold color and detail but fail in darkness or fog. Infrared images reveal warm targets in those conditions but lack texture. Fusion aims to keep the best of both.

Their method works in quaternion math, a number system that keeps color structure intact instead of splitting channels. One part pulls heat targets and fine texture out of poor-quality inputs. Another sharpens detail while balancing brightness. A statistical fusion step then blends the pieces. Across many test sets the fused images beat leading methods, especially in low-visibility scenes.
arxiv-2505-03064:
Daniel Revier and Jeffrey Lipton print foams whose tangled fibers are placed by design, not by chance. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Tangled networks appear in nature and in engineering, but programming them in patterns has been hard.

Their method joins a printing style that lays down coiling threads with a design algorithm. By changing print height and speed, they set how dense the coils are in each spot. The algorithm places dense and sparse zones to hit target traits. The result is one-piece foams with tunable stiffness and sideways stretch. One foam even couples sideways pull with shear in a strong, unusual way. Tests and simulations agree that the patterned foams beat uniform ones.
arxiv-2505-04164:
Ariful Hoque and co-authors survey outflows from forming massive stars using a new tracer molecule, in this 2025 paper. Young stars shoot out gas jets as they feed, and those outflows stir the parent cloud. Slow outflow gas mixes with cloud gas and is hard to isolate. The team used the molecule HC3N in 146 massive star-forming regions from the ALMA-ATOMS survey.

They found forty-four two-sided outflows and one explosive case. Host clumps sat at varied growth stages, so the tracer works across the whole formation span. The molecule proved slightly better than the standard tracer at catching slow gas, and it also caught fast narrow jets. Outflow mass, push, and energy scaled moderately with clump mass and brightness. The authors offer HC3N as a partner tracer for outflow studies.
arxiv-2505-04264:
Lebo Molefe, Tomas Fullana, François Gallaire, and John Kolinski show that a water drop can bounce for minutes on a shaking solid plate, in a 2025 paper. Drops on a vibrating liquid bath famously bounce forever on a film of air, mimicking quantum behavior. On a rigid solid, drops usually wet the surface in under a second. The team vibrated an atomically smooth mica plate and stretched the hovering time to several minutes, orders of magnitude longer.

The drop's squashing rhythm decides its fate: one mode gives high leaps, another locks the drop into a bound state riding above a thin air film. A spring model that includes the drop's deformation predicts the paths. A solid-based bouncer frees the effect from bath dynamics and opens controlled study of drop motion.
arxiv-2505-04364:
Kai Ruan, Mowen Huang, Ji-Rong Wen, and Hao Sun published this paper in 2025. It benchmarks whether language models can act as a swarm: many simple agents coordinating with only local views and local chatter, like ants or birds. Existing tests rarely impose such strict limits.

Their benchmark, SwarmBench, sets five classic group tasks on a grid: pursuit, synchronization, foraging, flocking, and transport. Each agent sees only a small window around itself and talks only to neighbors. Leading models, tested without training, showed flickers of coordination but broke down on long-range planning and on adapting strategy when conditions shifted. Results varied widely by task. The authors release the toolkit openly, with environments, prompts, and scoring scripts. They argue swarm-style tests expose weaknesses that single-agent benchmarks hide, and that future decentralized systems will need exactly these skills.
arxiv-2505-05064:
Xinyang Lu and a team of co-authors present WaterDrum in two thousand twenty-five. WaterDrum grades how well a language model has unlearned data. Utility based grades can fail when kept and dropped data read alike. Retraining from scratch to check is often out of reach as well.

Their metric is data centric and rests on robust text watermarking. Marks in the data reveal if its sway truly left the model. New benchmark sets vary how alike the kept and dropped parts are. That lets unlearning methods face a strict, fair test. Code and data sets are shared in public.
arxiv-2505-05464:
Chen and seven co-authors fuse two models to pour thought skill into a sight-tongue model in this twenty twenty-five paper. Sight models see well, while tongue models think well, and the join is still dim. Fuse-by-weights is their bridge, with no fresh drill rounds at all.

Inside, fused models gain thought skill from the tongue side in test after test. The team then maps where sight and thought live in the stack of layers. Sight skill sits most in the first layers of the stack in their maps. Thought skill sits most in the mid-to-late layers of the stack. Past the fuse, all layers pitch in on thought, while sight spread stays put.
arxiv-2505-05564:
Nicolas Esser studies a new way for primordial black holes to pair up with stars and merge, in a physics paper from 2025. These black holes, born in the early universe, may sit inside small halos of dark matter. A star passing through such a halo loses energy to friction against the dark matter.

If the loss is large enough, the star is captured into a binary with the black hole. Friction keeps draining energy, so the pair should merge quickly. The author estimates the merger rate and checks two signals. The channel could explain a small number of fast-fading X-ray binaries seen in our galaxy. It also predicts a modest gravitational wave rate, with odd mass ratios. Most mergers would occur in small galaxies.
arxiv-2505-06864:
Shunyao Wang, Ming Cheng, and Christina Dan Wang feed financial news into an asset pricing model in a 2025 paper. Pricing models usually ignore text. Their system, NewsNet-SDF, embeds about 2.5 million news articles with a multilingual language model, pairs them with market and firm data across 10,000 securities, and fuses everything through adversarial training.

On US stocks from 1980 to 2022, the model reached a Sharpe ratio of 2.80. It beat the classic CAPM benchmark by 471 percent and cut pricing errors by 74 percent against the Fama-French five-factor model. Tests that removed parts of the system showed news text contributed more than macroeconomic features. The authors present text as a first-class input to pricing.
arxiv-2505-07564:
Louis Gallard and Riccardo Hertel introduce a finite-element method to measure the Hopf index of magnetic textures, in this 2025 paper. Hopfions are knotted swirls of magnetization in three-dimensional materials. Counting their knot number in complex shapes is hard, and errors creep in when the texture varies sharply. The authors base their method on a classic field formula that keeps results gauge-safe, even in ring-shaped samples.

A variance-based fix cuts errors in rough textures, and the index settles fast as the mesh refines. Tests on a known analytic Hopfion confirm the accuracy. A simulation then watches a Hopfion break into a simpler toron under a field, marked by a sudden index jump. The tool lets researchers quantify knotted magnetism in realistic device shapes.
arxiv-2505-08264:
Ahmed Abouelazm and four co-authors teach self-driving agents with lessons that grow harder on their own. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Reinforcement learning agents are often trained on a fixed set of road scenes. They then fail when real roads differ. Randomizing scenes helps, but wild variety makes training slow and patchy. Hand-built lesson plans add expert bias and do not scale.

Their framework adds a teacher that builds and mutates driving scenarios. Difficulty adapts to the agent's current skill. Easy cases come first, and harder ones follow as competence grows. The process needs no human-designed curriculum. Training becomes both sturdier and faster in their tests. The work targets driving policies that hold up outside the simulator.
arxiv-2505-10164:
Ikhsanov, Piotrovich, and Beskrovnaya work out how magnetized wind feeds neutron stars in bright binary systems in a 2025 paper. In high-mass X-ray binaries, a neutron star pulls gas from a giant companion's wind. The gas carries its own magnetic field, and that changes everything about how it lands. The authors lay out when each landing style occurs.

Three regimes compete: a near-spherical rain, a standard Keplerian disk, and a magnetically arrested disk, where piled-up field chokes the flow. In the arrested case, the star's resting spin period depends not only on the orbit but on the wind's speed, heat, and magnetization. Assuming the best-studied pulsars sit at that resting spin, they back out the wind traits each system must have. The scenario ties a star's clock to its partner's breath.
arxiv-2505-11364:
Pierre Marchand and five co-authors release a software environment for modeling newborn stars, in a 2025 paper. Interpreting telescope views of protostars needs chemistry and fake observations, and both need the physical scene: densities, temperatures, and flows. Building that scene from scratch is a barrier for many teams.

Their code assembles the whole setting, star, envelope, disk, and outflow, from analytic formulas. It hands the scene to public tools for chemistry, light transport, and synthetic telescope images. Dust grain sizes are handled consistently so the light calculations stay honest. An example maps five molecules in a young system and fakes the matching telescope view. The package aims to make full modeling a routine step, not a specialist's project.
arxiv-2505-11464:
Bao Bach, Filip Maciejewski, and Ilya Safro scale a quantum optimization algorithm to large binary problems by working through a multilevel hierarchy. QAOA is promising for combinatorial optimization, but today's hardware is small and noisy. Their solver shrinks the problem, solves the coarse version, and carries the solution back up.

The key move is parameter transfer: settings tuned at the coarsest level seed the finer levels, because their relaxation-based coarsening preserves the structure QAOA needs. Genetic algorithms reinforce the sampling at the shallowest circuit depth. Quantum relax-and-round rounds out the pipeline. The authors present the hybrid as a practical route to high-quality, low-depth solutions on near-term devices.
arxiv-2505-12864:
Yu Fan and co-authors published this paper in 2025. It introduces LEXam, a benchmark that tests language models on real law school exams. Long legal reasoning, where an answer must spot issues, recall rules, and apply them step by step, remains a weak spot for these models.

The set holds 7,537 questions from 340 exams across 116 courses, in English and German. It mixes open written problems with multiple choice items. For the open problems, marking guides spell out the reasoning path a good answer should take. Current models handled choice questions far better than the open ones, which demand structured multi-step work. The authors grade model reasoning with a panel of judge models, checked against human experts, and the grades lined up well. They offer the setup as a scalable way to score legal reasoning.
arxiv-2505-12964:
Shanshan Liu and co-authors present a 2025 framework that finds biomedical concepts in text, even when the text never names them. Concept spotting feeds knowledge maps and ontology upkeep. Old tools hunt for exact mentions, so hidden concepts slip past. Their frame, MA-COIR, recasts the task: each concept owns a semantic index, and the tool assigns indexes to text, much like a search engine.

A mid-size pretrained model, fine-tuned on small data, does the core work, which keeps costs low for domain teams. Model-made queries and fake data shore up thin fields. Tests on three sets show the frame catches both stated and implied concepts. It needs no mention-level labels at run time. Ontology teams gain a lighter path to full concept maps.
arxiv-2505-13064:
Yannik Wotte, Arne Sachtler, Alin Albu-Schäffer, and co-authors study families of natural oscillations in mechanical systems in this 2025 paper. Machines from pendulums to robot arms have internal rhythms that cost little energy to sustain. Controllers would like to ride those rhythms, but the rhythms shift with the system's settings.

The families in question gather periodic swings that pass near a resting state. Using the time symmetry of energy-keeping systems, the authors show that mild conditions force every swing in the family to run between two points of zero speed. They prove the family grows from a single one-dimensional curve of those rest points. When the machine also has a mirror symmetry, all swings pass through one shared posture, which suits control well. Tests on a double pendulum and a five-link pendulum matched the theory. The results could guide energy-saving motion in robots.
arxiv-2505-13164:
Iris Kaplan and Or Ordentlich give high rate quantized matrix multiplication with small lookup tables in two thousand twenty-five. Nested lattice codes quantize each column of the matrices at hand. Dequantized matrices are then multiplied in the standard way. Lookup tables speed the inner products in that scheme.

Past tables blew up in size past low rates, capping their use. Their layered frame splits each vector across many layers. Table size then rests on rate per layer, not full rate. Bounds show the loss against standard quantizers stays small. Numeric tests call that loss negligible in practice.
arxiv-2505-13564:
Aymeric Capitaine and colleagues take decision-focused learning online, where the world will not sit still. That paradigm trains predictors to minimize the cost of the decisions they feed, not mere prediction error. Prior work assumed one fixed batch of data and a frozen objective. Real settings stream data while objectives and distributions drift.

Two obstacles block the online version: decision losses have useless gradients, and the problems are non-convex. The team smooths the objective to restore gradients. Perturbations plus a near-optimal oracle tame the non-convexity. Two algorithms emerge, with the first static and dynamic regret bounds for this problem. A knapsack experiment shows both beating standard benchmarks. The guarantees matter for logistics and pricing systems that learn while operating. Prediction, in this view, is only as good as the decisions it survives.
arxiv-2505-15064:
Sho Sonoda, Yuka Hashimoto, Isao Ishikawa, and Masahiro Ikeda present a 2025 theory study of when deeper neural networks learn better than shallow ones. Their model treats each hidden layer as a map on a state space and stacks up to k of them before an output layer. Depth is compared fairly: deep and shallow nets share the same layer building blocks. The key cost of depth, they show, is the size of the set of all stacked maps, measured by metric entropy.

Under smooth layers, that cost grows at most polynomially with depth. Under shrinking or special layers, it stays flat or grows only like a logarithm. Balanced against fitting error, the theory yields a best depth that grows with sample size. Worked cases include deep ReLU networks and chain-of-thought computation. Every claim was machine-checked in the Lean proof system.
arxiv-2505-15564:
Hossein Hassani, Soodeh Nikan, and Abdallah Shami build TinyDrive, a light sight-language model for driving scenes. It answers asks on views from many sides at once. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such models are heavy, which bars them from cars with scant compute. TinyDrive has two core parts. A sight encoder reads views at many scales, by a scale mark and cross-scale gates. A two-level pick then routes work. At the token level, just the most telling tokens are worked. At the chain level, chains are scored by loss, doubt, and spread, and the best are kept. The aim is keen answers at a cost a car can bear.
arxiv-2505-16264:
Sebastian Janampa and Marios Pattichis present a faster method for finding lines in images in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Line detection is a basic step used by many higher image tasks. Newer transformer models are more accurate than older ones, but they run slowly and need large pre-training sets.

Their method, called LINEA, uses a new attention step shaped for lines, so no large pre-training is needed. Tests show it runs much faster than earlier transformer methods. It also beat prior models on a test set drawn from a different source than the training data. The authors aim to bring accurate line detection to video and other jobs that need low delay.
arxiv-2505-17164:
Thiago Bergamaschi gives a teaching-first walk through the black hole information problem for readers who know relativity and basic quantum theory. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The puzzle asks whether information that falls into a black hole is lost for good as the hole slowly evaporates. It has fueled decades of debate in physics.

Bergamaschi lays out the core ideas in a pedagogical order, building each step on plain terms. His stance is firm: there is no true paradox of information loss. He argues that fixes which bend well-tested theories at random scales clash with themselves. The paper suits students meeting the topic for the first time. It offers a clear map of the concepts before readers dive into the research fray. Teachers may also use it as a lecture base.
arxiv-2505-17264:
Giuseppe De Giacomo and co-authors show, in twenty twenty-five, how to solve Markov decision processes whose goals are stated in two new temporal logics. Temporal logics specify what should happen over time. The logics, LTLf+ and PPLTL+, match the expressive power of classic LTL on infinite traces. Yet they allow efficient automata-based methods, the trick that made finite-trace versions scale. Markov decision processes add probabilities: actions have uncertain outcomes. Their tailored technique exploits that structure.

The approach is simpler than its counterparts in reactive synthesis and planning, they argue. It tolerates a controlled form of nondeterminism in the automata, one that is good for probabilistic systems. Compositionality, solving pieces and combining them, makes the method implementation-friendly and suited to symbolic code.
arxiv-2505-18264:
Boiza and co-authors test an alternative theory of gravity against two stubborn mismatches in cosmology, in this 2025 paper. Measurements of the universe's expansion rate and of matter clumping disagree with the standard model. The rival framework, called f(Q) gravity, reshapes gravity's rules at large scales.

The team fit three versions of the theory to supernova data, cosmic clocks, gamma-ray bursts, and early-universe distance clues. Most versions raised the expansion rate, easing one mismatch. One version also weakened effective gravity in a way that suits the clumping data. Mixed signals between data sets kept the standard model ahead overall, but the authors urge more work.
arxiv-2505-19964:
Eric Zhao, Jessica Dai, and Pranjal Awasthi study a limit on learning from human preferences in a 2025 study. Preference data give rankings between outputs rather than scores, and they are easy to collect at scale. Teams hope such rankings can train models for tasks like research help or trip planning, where success is qualitative.

The authors show a basic obstacle, even with perfect, endless, noise-free rankings. Ordinal feedback alone can block a learner from reaching even near-optimal outcomes. They formalize that impossibility result, which warns against treating preference training as a full substitute for richer outcome measures. The claimed limit is a theoretical one, proved under stated ideal conditions.
arxiv-2505-20064:
Matteo Scandi and Álvaro Alhambra study how open quantum systems settle to thermal balance in a 2025 arXiv paper. They start from a microscopic picture of weak contact between a system and its bath. From that base, they derive a master equation without a common simplifying shortcut.

The equation obeys a general form of detailed balance, called KMS, which forces exact convergence to the correct thermal state. Their dynamics match the true evolution with error growing at most linearly in time, a sharp gain on past bounds. The equation can be simulated well on a quantum computer. It also reduces to the classic Davies dynamics in a stated limit.
arxiv-2505-20164:
Dairu Liu and six co-authors teach multimodal models to think with visual sketches instead of long verbal chains, in a 2025 paper. The head of the text titles the approach Thinking with Visual Abstract. Images carry rich detail but also clutter that drags reasoning down. People facing a complex scene compress it into a simple abstract first. The authors prompt the model with such a visual abstract rather than with wordy step-by-step thoughts or tool calls.

Stripping redundancy concentrates the model's perception on the essential elements and structure. The approach is compared against chain-of-thought and tool-using methods that add complexity. If a glance-sized summary beats a paragraph of reasoning, multimodal systems could get faster and more accurate at once.
arxiv-2505-20464:
Samuel Rhys Cox, Rune Møberg Jacobsen, and Niels van Berkel test whether a chatbot should act like an old friend or a stranger in a 2025 study. People pour feelings into chatbots, but does the bot's claimed memory change what they share? One version presented itself as a companion that remembers past talks; the other as a fresh stranger each time. Participants chatted across two days, once about feelings and once about facts, in counterbalanced order.

When feelings came first, the stranger bot made people more comfortable disclosing. When facts came first, the familiar bot was enjoyed more. Order flipped the winner, a warning that disclosure design has no one-size answer. Interviews added the reasons behind the numbers.
arxiv-2505-22864:
Weitzel and a large team described the National Research Platform in twenty twenty-five. The platform is a shared computing system for science, built on Kubernetes, a tool that runs software across many machines. It spans over seventy-five locations in the United States and abroad, run by many tenants at once.

Sites contribute anything from single nodes to large clusters of graphics and central processors. Users can work through friendly interfaces such as JupyterHub or control resources directly at a low level. The paper covers daily operations, including threat detection built into the system, wide monitoring, and detailed accounting of use. The authors present the platform as a scalable answer to rising demand for shared research computing.
arxiv-2505-23164:
Jonathan Husson, Guido Mazzuca, and Alessandra Occelli present a 2025 paper on a random process built from plane partitions, three-dimensional stacks of cubes. Their Muttalib-Borodin ensemble weights each stack by its volume. The team studies the stacks' typical shape when they grow very large, in both discrete and continuous versions. A key feature is a hard cap on how dense the particles can pack.

They prove a large deviation principle that prices rare shapes, then solve for the limit shape exactly in all parameter ranges. The solution passes through a phase transition, which they track in both mild and extreme regimes. They also give the curve that separates frozen from fluid regions of the shape. The edge behavior departs from classic random matrix patterns. The work is a first for this kind of constrained analysis.
arxiv-2505-23864:
Wei Zhuo, Zhaohuan Zhan, and Han Yu personalize federated learning for graph data in a 2025 paper. Each client in their setting holds a different piece of one big graph, such as a social or citation network, and the pieces differ in character. Sharing raw data or node embeddings is off the table.

Their method, FedAux, gives each client a learnable projection vector that squeezes node embeddings into a ranked one-dimensional signature. The server compares signatures to judge which clients resemble each other, then mixes their models in proportion. Each client ends with a personal model that still borrows strength from similar peers. Tests on graph benchmarks beat the baselines on both accuracy and personal fit, with theory supplied for convergence.
arxiv-2505-24264:
Xin Quan, Marco Valentino, Louise Dennis, and André Freitas present a 2025 method for checking machine-written logic with a theorem prover. Language tasks ask whether a claim follows from a set of facts, and good answers show their steps. Provers can certify steps, but only in formal code. Turning prose into code can drop meaning or break form. The team attack both faults: guard the meaning in the turn, auto-fix form slips, and let the code steer the model's proof drafts.

Prover feedback then feeds repair rounds. On three data sets, gains over the best past system ran large on both the turn step and the polish step. Faithful steps matter when AI explains itself in court or clinic. This loop keeps the story and the proof in step.
arxiv-2505-24564:
Yu-Cheng Chang and co-authors build a tiny heat sensor from graphene that can spot single microwave photons, in work from twenty twenty-five. Such sensors, called bolometers, matter for reading out quantum processors. The team grows the graphene on silicon carbide to get a strong heat response.

By keeping charge low and even, they reach a state where heat leaks away very slowly. That makes the sensor react more to faint signals. The devices work at very low heat and reach a noise level the authors call state of the art. They can also be made at scale. The results point to low disturbance detectors for next stage quantum machines.
arxiv-2506-00164:
Agustín Roca and six co-authors monitor endangered deer with drones and deep learning in two thousand twenty-five. Hand counts of rare deer cost time and trained labor. High resolution aerial images plus vision models can take that load. Two projects in Buenos Aires province anchor the study.

One tracks marsh deer in the Paraná Delta wetlands. The other tracks Pampas deer in a national park. A YOLO based detector trains on drone images from both sites. Marsh deer were spotted with high accuracy in tests. Pampas deer results are early, with clear limits noted.
arxiv-2506-00464:
Donghao Qu and five co-authors design and test a digital receiver for a new radio telescope array. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, describes the unit's build. It takes eight analog inputs and samples them at very high speed and depth. On-board chips split the signal into channels in real time.

Field tests pointed the system at the Sun, a satellite beacon, and a supernova remnant. The team studied the fringe patterns that prove the array works as one. Signal delays were fixed two ways, by math and by a fitted curve. Both agreed to under a billionth of a second. The unit suits planned telescopes, one of them in Brazil.
arxiv-2506-00964:
Dren Fazlija, Arkadij Orlov, and Sandipan Sikdar build the first benchmark for sensitivity awareness in language models in a 2025 paper. Companies increasingly let models answer questions over internal documents. A model that ignores access rights can leak secrets to staff who should never see them. Simple filters by clearance level, though, can hurt both usefulness and privacy.

Their concept, sensitivity awareness, asks the model itself to respect access rules while it talks. Their test environment, styled as a fictional firm named in the title, Access Denied Inc, throws both forbidden and legitimate requests at models. Results varied widely across models: some leaked, some refused too much. The benchmark gives builders a shared yardstick for a skill that corporate deployment cannot skip.
arxiv-2506-01564:
Angarita and seven co-authors present a 2025 astronomy survey of starlight polarization in the Milky Way's spiral arms. Starlight becomes polarized when it passes through elongated dust grains lined up by magnetic fields. By pairing polarization readings with star distances, astronomers can map the galaxy's magnetic field layer by layer. The team used visible and near-infrared data from three regions along the galactic plane.

Both data types pointed the same way, with visible light showing two to three times stronger polarization. Two analysis methods separated the signal into nearby, middle, and distant dust clouds. These matched known structures in the local bubble wall and two spiral arms. In two regions, the field's direction changed clearly along the line of sight. The results refine maps of the galaxy's magnetism in the arms.
arxiv-2506-01764:
Guan-Hao Feng, Jun Quan, and Yusheng Hou ask, in a 2025 paper, what symmetry alone can say about how a new nickel-based superconductor pairs its electrons. The material conducts without resistance at strikingly high temperature under pressure. Grown as a thin film, it still superconducts at normal pressure, but at only about half that temperature. The gap between the two forms begs an explanation.

The authors build a symmetry-based method that combines crystal structure, the measured transition temperature, and density-based calculations. Both forms, they find, share the same pairing symmetry and a two-gap structure. What differs is which electron orbitals do the pairing: between layers in the pressed bulk, within layers in the film. A shift in hopping strengths between the layers drives that switch, and with it the temperature drop. The method, they note, should transfer to other odd superconductors.
arxiv-2506-02864:
Changyi Xiao, Mengdi Zhang, and Yixin Cao improve a training method used to teach language models to reason, in a 2025 paper. Recent models gain reasoning skill from rewards that are simply right or wrong. The training methods behind them scale rewards in fixed ways, or not at all, which can make learning unstable as the model changes. The authors propose scaling rewards with a beta distribution whose shape updates during training.

Their method, BNPO, keeps the reward scale matched to the model's current behavior. Steadier scaling should give cleaner learning signals and smoother training. The paper compares BNPO with the group-based method used by recent reasoning models. Better training stability matters because these long training runs are costly to restart when they go wrong.
arxiv-2506-03064:
Balázs Németh and Ronojoy Adhikari show, in a 2025 physics paper, that a classical charged particle that moves on its own can respond to a magnet in a way long thought impossible. A classic theorem says charged systems at restful balance cannot be magnetized. Active matter breaks that balance by burning energy to move.

The authors study one such particle held on the surface of a sphere. They track its random paths in simulations and compare them with exact math at low and high heat. Both agree that the system gains a real magnetization and leans with the field, not against it. The result hints at ways to steer and harvest work from charged active matter.
arxiv-2506-04564:
Huaying Wei and Michel Zinsmeister study two ways of measuring rough functions on a curve, in this 2025 paper. One space is defined through harmonic extensions inside and outside a Jordan curve, weighted by distance to the boundary. The other sums squared differences between points on the curve itself. On a circle both match the classic fractional Sobolev space.

On a general curve the two can part ways. For the borderline exponent, equality needs the chord-arc property; for other exponents that condition stops being decisive. The authors prove equality does hold for Lipschitz curves. They then turn to the Plemelj-Calderón problem, linking the Cauchy integral to these spaces. The work sorts out when interior and boundary views of smoothness agree.
arxiv-2506-05664:
Chao Zhang and three co-authors allocate bits wisely when shrinking language models in a 2025 paper. Quantization stores model weights in fewer bits to save memory and compute. Most schemes hand every weight the same bit count or follow rough rules, ignoring that weights differ in sensitivity.

A curvature-based proxy measures how much each layer suffers from rounding noise. Under stated assumptions, each layer's loss becomes an explicit formula in its bit count. That turns bit allocation into a convex problem with a tidy closed-form answer. The optimal answer equalizes loss in a pattern the authors exploit. Their algorithm slots into standard quantization pipelines with little friction. Tests show a strong balance between accuracy kept and complexity added.
arxiv-2506-07164:
Qiong Chang and co-authors published a 2025 paper on speeding up a vision step used by robots that map their surroundings. Such systems, called visual SLAM, pick out feature points in camera images to track motion and build a map. A popular method spends about half its time on one step: finding corners with their orientations. On small mobile hardware, that cost breaks real-time work.

The authors attack the two slowest parts of that step. For finding candidate points, they encode the test in binary form so weak points are rejected fast. For scoring corners, they split the math into separable passes and use special low-level instructions of the graphics chip. Tests ran on a Jetson TX2, an embedded board. The result was an average speedup of more than seven times over the OpenCV library.
arxiv-2506-08364:
Jash Parekh, Pengcheng Jiang, and Jiawei Han present a 2025 paper on retrieval-augmented generation. Language models answer better when given retrieved proof. Standard pipelines hand the model loose text chunks. Multi-hop questions then fail, since facts scatter across documents. Their framework, called SARG in the head, builds explicit reasoning structures from the retrieved text. The catalog title names a related graph framing; the head governs the system described.

Three stages run after retrieval. Relation triples are pulled from documents with few-shot prompts. Those triples form a structure the model can reason over directly. Answers can then trace a visible path across sources. Search teams get a post-retrieval layer that fits existing stacks. Explicit structure also aids audit: a wrong answer can be traced to a wrong triple. That traceability is a step past black-box context stuffing.
arxiv-2506-08564:
Törö, Suni, and Šimko present a study from twenty twenty-five on what speech models reveal about language kinship. Languages relate through family lines, word stock, and contact between neighbors. The team take speech vectors from a model trained to name languages by ear. They study recordings of one hundred six world languages. They group the vectors and compare their gaps with family, word, and map distances. The speech gaps match the classic measures closely.

The match holds for both world-scale and local patterns. Charts of the links prove tricky, since language change is fluid. The authors discuss data size and space shape as method concerns. They see speech vectors as a scalable tool for language studies. Future work targets rare languages and social variation.
arxiv-2506-08764:
Benjamin Dadoun and four co-authors prove stability results for deep neural networks in a 2025 paper. As networks grow deeper, gradients can explode or vanish during training. That failure ties to how the network's input-output Jacobian behaves across layers.

Earlier work found safe starting settings only for plain fully connected nets with independent random weights. Real networks break both limits through pruning and through training itself. The new theorem covers sparse weights and weakly linked randomness as well. It leans on fresh advances in random matrix theory. The guarantees give modern initialization schemes a firmer base. Designers of pruned or structured networks gain theory that matches their practice more closely.
arxiv-2506-08864:
Maria Vittoria Chiaruttini, Lukas Pin, and Sofía Villar design a trial method that steers patients by safety, not cure speed. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, tackles non-inferiority cancer trials. In such trials a new drug need only match the standard, while being gentler counts as a win. Efficacy data like survival arrive too slowly to guide assignments.

Their SAFER design watches early side-effect data instead. Assignment shares shift toward the arm looking safer so far. The split also weighs how safety and efficacy relate in each case. A simulation modeled on a real phase three cancer trial tests the design. The authors show it balances proof power with patient protection.
arxiv-2506-09564:
Quentin Griette and Franco Herrera prove the existence of slow wave-like solutions in a population equation, in a mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five. The equation, a form of the Gurtin-MacCamy model, tracks how a population feeds back on itself over time. Without the symmetry that older methods rely on, standard tools for pinning down such waves fail.

The pair build a special set of starting conditions whose solutions must keep the slow oscillating character. They then link that set to a convex set in another space, giving it the fixed-point property needed to prove a repeating solution exists. In a limiting case the wave matches a known discrete equation's solution. Computer plots round out the argument.
arxiv-2506-10164:
