The team also releases AraLongBench, a large Arabic benchmark spanning single documents to collections of hundreds of pages. Their evolving pipeline beat static alternatives and strengthened leading Arabic vision-language models on long-context comprehension. A separate automated workflow gathers the long documents themselves.
arxiv-2509-02964:
Victor Solomon and 3 co-authors introduced a 2025 image model called EdgeAttNet for outlining solar filaments. Filaments are dark, thread-like clouds of cool gas held above the Sun's surface. Their handedness, called chirality, helps predict how solar eruptions will behave once they leave the Sun.

Older models often miss the thin barbs that branch off a filament's spine. EdgeAttNet builds a learnable edge map straight from each image and feeds it into the attention step, where the model decides which areas to compare. That structural hint sharpened boundaries and barb detection in tests. The model beat several U-Net based rivals on a filament dataset while using fewer adjustable parts. It also ran fast enough for practical use.
arxiv-2509-03464:
Kenzie Fontenot and two co-authors wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on Cops and Robbers, a pursuit game played on a graph. Earlier work mostly covered finite boards and counted how many cops guarantee a win. Their board is the endless integer lattice, which stretches without bound in every direction.

Because that lattice would need infinitely many cops under the old measure, the authors study cop density instead. Density asks how thinly cops can be spread while still forcing capture. Their coordinate matching strategy, which pairs cop positions across directions, yields winning layouts with density zero. A full classification follows, giving exact conditions on cop placements across coordinate directions that decide whether the robber is caught. Future variants are also sketched.
arxiv-2509-03564:
A systematic error affecting LiteBIRD, a planned satellite mission to measure polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, occupies a 2025 research paper by S. Stellati and twelve co-authors. That faint early-universe light carries signals of primordial gravitational waves. LiteBIRD rotates half-wave plates to modulate the polarisation it records.

The team studies a small, fixed tilt between a reflective plate's rotation axis and its optical axis, which acts like a wedge. Simulations insert that tilt into time-ordered data and rebuild sky maps and power spectra. The tilt creates pointing errors locked to the plate's rotation and adds spurious B-mode patterns, which mostly mimic gravitational lensing effects rather than primordial signals. More detectors dilute the contamination. From the error implied for the tensor-to-scalar ratio, they set an upper limit on the allowed wedge angle.
arxiv-2509-03764:
Han Wang and four co-authors' 2025 research paper focuses on using fine-tuned large language models to judge search relevance at Pinterest. Relevance evaluation checks whether results truly match a user's query and intent. Human annotation is the traditional route, but it is expensive and slow, limiting how much of a web-scale search system can be tested.

Their system automates relevance labels for online experiments with models tuned specifically for the task. Alignment between machine judgments and human annotations is validated rigorously before the labels are trusted. With cheap, fast labels, the team can expand the query set, design sampling more cleverly, and assess more kinds of search experience. Relevance metrics become higher quality as a result. The smallest change an online experiment can reliably detect also shrinks significantly, so weaker real effects stop slipping past measurement.
arxiv-2509-03964:
In a 2025 research paper, Philippe Bergault and three co-authors focus on inferring yield curves for cryptocurrencies, markets with almost no bonds. A yield curve shows interest rates across maturities for one currency. Ordinary currencies get theirs from deep bond markets, which set rates at many maturities directly.

Cryptocurrency markets, as of early 2025, have almost no fixed-rate lending and essentially no bonds, so no curve can be read off directly. The authors show how mathematical tools can construct one anyway. Their source is the highly developed market for cryptocurrency derivatives, contracts whose prices embed expectations about future rates. Extracting a full curve from those prices gives crypto markets a basic instrument they lacked. With a curve in hand, stochastic interest rate models can be calibrated for digital currencies, and standard pricing machinery becomes available to a bondless market.
arxiv-2509-04064:
Pedro Carvalho and three co-authors built a working analog version of a brain-inspired computing model for a 2025 research paper. The model, called HORN, uses networks of oscillators, parts that cycle rhythmically, instead of standard digital neurons. Such oscillating networks promise speed and low energy use. The team first trained a four-node version on a computer for a handwriting task using the MNIST data set, which holds images of digits.

Circuit behavior matched the computer model in most tests. One readout layer copied from the digital version agreed poorly, because analog parts lack digital precision. Retraining a simple readout on the circuit's own signals restored accuracy, proving the hardware kept the needed information.
arxiv-2509-04164:
Arjun R and one co-author, A V Anil Kumar, introduce a new magnetic model with clashing influences in a 2025 physics paper. Their system extends the classic Ising model, a grid of tiny magnets that flip up or down. Two kinds of sites push each other in a one-way fashion, called nonreciprocal coupling, while a random field adds disorder that spreads unevenly. Theory tools and computer simulations with Glauber dynamics, a standard flipping rule, map the behavior.

Under weak disorder, orderly group oscillations begin smoothly. Stronger fields switch the onset to an abrupt jump with hysteresis, meaning the path back differs. The boundary between those regimes is a special tricritical point. At high field strength, droplets trigger a phase cycling through eight states.
arxiv-2509-04364:
Emanuela De Negri and four co-authors prove a partial reverse of a known result about a singularity-control technique in a 2025 mathematics paper. Frobenius splitting works in characteristic p algebra, where arithmetic wraps around a prime, and it tames bad geometric points called singularities. Knutson earlier showed such splittings survive a breakdown process called geometric vertex decomposition under certain types. The present paper asks the reverse question: when can a splitting be lifted back?

When a splitting compatibly handles both halves of the breakdown, called the link and the deletion, lifting succeeds under one extra condition on its form. An example proves that extra condition cannot be dropped. The argument leans on liaison theory, which links geometric objects together. Double determinantal varieties are also shown to be Frobenius split.
arxiv-2509-04464:
Yang Nan and three co-authors show that a language model's several answers can reveal why it is unsure in a 2025 research paper. Models sometimes produce unreliable output, and knowing the amount of uncertainty is less useful than knowing its source. When uncertain, a model's multiple sampled responses disagree in telling patterns. An auxiliary model reads those patterns and guesses the cause: a vague question, missing knowledge, or both.

For knowledge gaps, the helper also names exactly which facts or concepts are missing. Tests on three benchmarks, AmbigQA, OpenBookQA, and MMLU-Pro, confirmed the diagnosis works across distinct uncertainty sources. Targeted human fixes could then address the real problem instead of treating all doubt alike.
arxiv-2509-04564:
Mark Eberlein and one co-author, Ravit Helled, show that heat flow assumptions can shift the predicted sizes of Neptune-like planets in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Modelers usually treat these planets as layered and fully churning, but formation suggests smeared composition gradients instead. Stagnant layers then carry heat by radiation, electrons, and vibrations, each with its own conductivity. The team simulated planets of several masses, starting energy budgets, and two starting composition profiles.

The assumed conductivity significantly changed how planets cooled and contracted. The commonly used value proved inappropriate for this planet class. Inferred radii swung by about twenty percent with conductivity, and by a quarter with starting heat uncertainty. Those swings dwarf observational errors, so better laboratory conductivity data are badly needed.
arxiv-2509-04664:
Why do language models sometimes state falsehoods with confidence instead of admitting doubt? Adam Tauman Kalai, lead author with three co-authors, argue in a 2025 paper that training and grading reward guessing. Hallucinations, in their account, begin as ordinary errors in binary classification, sorting statements into true and false.

When a model cannot tell a false claim from a fact, statistical pressure produces confident errors. The authors say most benchmarks keep the problem alive because guessing raises test scores. Their proposed fix is social and technical: change how existing dominant benchmarks score uncertain answers.
arxiv-2509-04764:
Corruption can spread through groups, not just pairs of people. Elisa Bretón-Fuertes, lead author with six co-authors, extend a social contagion model to group interactions in a 2025 paper. Their higher-order version of an honesty, corruption, and ostracism model lets influence travel through group structures of any size.

Analytical and numerical results show abrupt, explosive transitions between fully honest and fully corrupt states. A bistable phase separates the two regimes. That abrupt behaviour disappears when only pairwise interactions remain. The authors also connect their model to broader social contagion dynamics, arguing group structure can destabilise honest norms.
arxiv-2509-05064:
Graph Nim turns a small graph into a two-player contest over edge weights. Sayar Karmakar, lead author with three co-authors, analyse that game on all graphs with exactly four edges in a 2025 combinatorics paper. On each turn, a player picks a vertex and reduces the weights of its edges, removing a positive total amount.

The player who makes the last move wins, so each starting weight pattern is either winning or losing for the first player. The authors characterise those patterns almost completely across the four-edge graphs. One graph resists full characterisation, and for it they provide substantial partial results.
arxiv-2509-05264:
Magic, the quantum resource that lets devices go beyond easy simulation, gets a measure for mixed matter in a 2025 paper by Matthieu Sarkis and two co-authors. No resource theory existed for systems that combine bosons, particles like photons, with fermions, particles like electrons.

Using a phase-space method from Cahill and Glauber that handles grass-like algebra, the authors define hybrid magic from the size of a combined Wigner function, a map of the quantum state. They test it on a polaron, where electrons couple to lattice vibrations, and on a fermion version of the Jaynes-Cummings model. At gate level they also derive an exact formula for one key operation.
arxiv-2509-05664:
Tail chances for a finance-tested law get new asymptotic formulas from Nico M. Temme in a solo 2025 paper in analysis. The normal inverse Gaussian law, a flexible law used for skewed heavy-tailed data, has a cumulative function with no simple closed form.

Using a recently derived integral written with elementary functions, Temme derives fresh expansions for that function. Such expansions give good estimates where direct work is hard, mostly far in the tails. One form runs through the normal Gaussian law, or the error function paired with it. The results extend the toolkit for working with this law in chance and finance.
arxiv-2509-05964:
A single strontium ion keeps time with record precision in a 2025 report led by T. Lindvall with six co-authors. Optical clocks tick by counting light oscillations. This one's systematic uncertainty sits below one part in a quintillion's neighborhood. Tiny radio-frequency losses, careful blackbody temperature evaluation, and a fresh polarizability measurement enable that precision. The paper lays out the full uncertainty budget.

Two absolute frequency checks anchor the clock: one against a remote cesium fountain over twelve days, and one against International Atomic Time across ten months of high uptime. The second gives, to the authors' knowledge, the most accurate optical frequency measurement yet reported. Both values agree with other recent work and suggest the current recommended value for this frequency sits slightly too high.
arxiv-2509-06164:
Political bias in language models is measured against real parliamentary votes in a 2025 paper by Jinrui Yang and two co-authors. Their benchmark, EuroParlVote, links European Parliament debate speeches to roll-call outcomes and adds each member's gender, age, country, and political group. Models are then tested on guessing a speaker's gender and predicting their vote.

Consistent skews appear. Models often misclassify women members as male and simulate votes for women speakers less accurately. Politically, they favor centrist groups and underperform on both far-left and far-right speakers. Proprietary models such as GPT-4o beat open-weight rivals on robustness and fairness. The dataset, code, and demo are released to support accountability research in political language technology.
arxiv-2509-06264:
Private deep learning usually buys privacy with one noise knob, and Qin Yang and eight co-authors widen that control in a 2025 paper. Standard private training perturbs gradients with Gaussian noise set by a single scale, tying privacy loss and accuracy loss together. Their framework, PLRV-O, searches a broad family of noise distributions whose privacy loss can be characterized tightly yet tuned more independently.

The noise adapts to model size, training length, sampling, and clipping, in training and fine-tuning alike. Under strict privacy budgets, gains are large: a fine-tuned vision transformer on CIFAR-10 and a large language model on SST-2 both far exceed their Gaussian-noise counterparts at the same budget. The authors frame privacy loss itself as the object to optimize.
arxiv-2509-06364:
A comb made of light can sweep every vortex out of an ultracold gas, show Shrohan Mohapatra and four co-authors in a 2025 paper. Vortices, tiny whirlpools in a Bose-Einstein condensate, are useful but often unwanted leftovers. The technique applies a one-dimensional optical lattice to the condensate and then removes it, taking the vortices with it.

Simulations reveal a second removal route in the narrow channels the lattice carves. When a channel is about as wide as a vortex core, the core's density dip separates from its phase swirl and the vortex dissolves. Scanning lattice strength and spacing finds an optimal parameter set that clears all vortices efficiently. The authors add the method to the experimental toolkit for condensate control.
arxiv-2509-06764:
The rational Chow ring of a space parametrizing bundles over genus-two curves is computed by Shubham Saha in a solo 2025 algebraic geometry paper. The space is the universal moduli space of semistable rank-two bundles over smooth curves of genus two. Chow rings encode how algebraic cycles intersect, and rational coefficients simplify the accounting.

Saha determines the ring completely and shows it is generated by certain tautological classes, standard classes built from the universal bundle itself. Along the way he computes Chow rings of universal Jacobians over genus-two curves with marked Weierstrass points, and of the universal pointed Jacobian. Those intermediate rings are of independent interest in the study of curve moduli. The results also give alternate computations matching earlier work on the genus-two case, a useful consistency check in a subject where calculations are long and error-prone.
arxiv-2509-07064:
Bartolomeo Trefoloni and 20 co-authors present observations of a distant quasar in a 2025 paper from the GA-NIFS program. The James Webb Space Telescope opened a new observational window on the primordial universe. Their target is the quasar ULAS J1342+0928 at a redshift corresponding to the early universe, observed with integral field spectroscopy that records a spectrum at every point in an image.

Low-resolution data reveal ionized oxygen emission on scales of about seven kiloparsecs, well above the typical galaxy size at that redshift, likely associated with a past outflow event. High-resolution observations show a more energetic ionized outflow on nuclear scales. The total ionized mass outflow rate is estimated within a broad range, with significant spread mostly due to lack of tight constraints on electron density. The data give a complete description from ultraviolet to optical bands.
arxiv-2509-07264:
Zhiyuan She and 3 co-authors offer a unified way in 2025 to build small stand-in models for large Hamiltonian systems. Hamiltonian systems conserve energy and include many molecular and mechanical setups. A reduced model tracks only a few key variables, but the discarded ones leave a memory effect, where past states keep shaping the future in ways that depend on the current state.

A consensus-based sampling scheme gathers the data needed to learn both the free energy landscape and the memory behavior at once. Auxiliary variables, extra learned quantities that stand in for memory, turn the reduced system into an extended Markovian one, where the future depends only on the present extended state. Trials on a small molecule, alanine dipeptide, show the model captures jumps between its stable shapes. Getting memory right matters whenever a big system is replaced by a cheap surrogate.
arxiv-2509-07364:
Ytterbium atoms are workhorses in cold-atom experiments and in optical lattice clocks, among the most precise timekeepers known. Kanta Asakawa and 4 co-authors report a simple protection trick in a 2025 research paper. Over long runs, ytterbium sticks to the windows of vacuum chambers. That coating slowly clouds the glass and cuts the light getting through.

The authors show that a surface coating of tetracontane, a waxy paraffin compound, effectively suppresses the sticking. Their short report gives experimenters a cheap way to keep chamber windows clear for longer. That matters for clocks and quantum experiments that must run for months without being opened for cleaning.
arxiv-2509-07564:
Raúl Alonso and 2 co-authors compare two Euler systems in number theory in a 2025 paper. An Euler system is a family of algebraic objects with tight compatibility rules, used to bound arithmetic quantities such as class groups. One system here comes from diagonal cycles tied to the convolution of two modular forms, in the anticyclotomic setting; the other is the cyclotomic Beilinson-Flach system.

The comparison extends landmark work linking Heegner points to the Beilinson-Kato system. The proof leans on a close study of p-adic L-functions and Perrin-Riou maps, and on how diagonal cycles degenerate along Hida families to an irregular Eisenstein series in weight one. Arithmetic applications are derived from the bridge between the two systems. Such bridges let results proved for one family of objects transfer to another, widening the reach of Euler system methods.
arxiv-2509-07664:
The DUNE Collaboration studies in 2025 whether a movable near detector can deliver nearly mono-energetic neutrino beam measurements. Neutrino-nucleus cross sections are critical for oscillation studies. Current measurements average over broad neutrino energy fluxes, though. That makes them hard to interpret, and it exposes gaps in interaction models. DUNE, the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, needs better data to reach its physics goals.

The DUNE-PRISM concept moves the near detector across off-axis positions. Each position samples a different energy spectrum. Combining those views builds narrow virtual fluxes, under 100 MeV wide. Cross sections can then be extracted at set energies, as functions of the outgoing lepton's motion. A dedicated simulation tests the idea. It uses realistic event counts and flux systematics, with an almost-perfect detector assumed. The study shows the approach is feasible. Cleaner cross sections would anchor the models that oscillation analyses depend on.
arxiv-2509-07864:
Tiancheng Yang and 5 co-authors trace why multimodal language models sometimes describe things that are not in an image, in a 2025 paper on model reliability. Such models answer questions about pictures and write captions, but they can hallucinate details that conflict with what is shown. Weak attention to the image is one suspected cause.

Earlier fixes adjusted attention evenly across the whole network, which hides where errors begin. The authors introduce two diagnostics: one flags layers whose image attention looks abnormal, and one scores individual attention heads inside those layers. Targeting the exact faulty spots should let engineers correct hallucinations more precisely, instead of shifting the whole system and hoping the problem moves with it.
arxiv-2509-08064:
Anna Hallin and 3 co-authors hunt stellar streams in Gaia data with an anomaly detector borrowed from particle physics, in a 2025 astronomy paper. Stellar streams are ribbons of stars torn from small galaxies and clusters, tracing the Milky Way's gravity and history. Their search framework, Via Machinae 3.0, is newly optimised for the task.

The detector, CATHODE, is model-agnostic: it learns what ordinary sky looks like and flags what stands out, without a stream template. The combined method rediscovers known streams and confirms many candidates found earlier with a related technique, while turning up further candidates. Borrowing tools across fields pays off here, because rare, faint structures hide in any huge dataset the same way.
arxiv-2509-08164:
Daniel Arean and 2 co-authors put disorder on a black hole and watch what survives as it cools, in a 2025 physics paper. Their black branes live in anti-de Sitter space. That makes them mirror images of strongly linked matter with flaws, through the holographic link. The chemical drive on the horizon varies from place to place, and the geometry bends in response.

At warm levels the horizon is lumpy. Yet its averages match the clean, known shapes. Cooling splits the cases. In three dimensions the lumps fade away. Disorder stops mattering at the lowest energies. In four dimensions the lumps persist. The split hints at how real dirty materials, like strange metals, may act at low heat, a regime labs find hard to probe.
arxiv-2509-08364:
The system that translates website names into addresses can authenticate itself, until one broken link voids the whole chain. Aduma Rishith and 3 co-authors address those breaks, called islands of security, in a 2025 research paper. DNSSEC protects name lookups with a chain of trust down the server hierarchy. Where a level lacks proper signatures, domains can authenticate on their own but not across levels.

Earlier fixes relied on a central authority keeping a bulletin board, which demands trust and infrastructure. The authors propose a decentralized alternative using TLS and IP-based certificates. Their method authenticates between hierarchy levels directly, without uniform DNSSEC deployment everywhere. It also reduces dependence on registrars to maintain signature records. The result aims at stronger internet naming security that real operators can actually deploy in stages.
arxiv-2509-08564:
Bouazza Kacimi and 2 co-authors study two kinds of maps between curved spaces in a 2025 paper. A smooth map between Riemannian manifolds, spaces with a distance rule, has a tension field that measures how far it is from being harmonic. That field can itself be viewed as a map.

One class requires the tension field to be a harmonic map, called HM-tensional. The other requires it to be a harmonic section, called HS-tensional. The target bundle uses the Sasaki metric, a natural distance rule on tangent vectors. The paper examines basic properties of both classes. Such maps extend classic harmonic map theory in differential geometry.
arxiv-2509-08664:
Pablo A. Cano and 2 co-authors compute quasinormal modes of fast spinning black holes in higher-curvature gravity in a 2025 paper. Quasinormal modes are the fading tones a black hole rings with after a disturbance. This is the first such work for arbitrary rotation in this theory.

A master equation governs large momentum gravitational waves, solved with WKB methods. Corrections to Kerr frequencies grow much larger near extreme spin, especially for modes near a critical boundary. A geometric optics study links special graviton orbits to mode frequencies. The link between orbit instability and frequency changes from the usual rule in this theory.
arxiv-2509-08964:
F. A. Martynenko and 2 co-authors study production of heavy tetraquarks in rare Higgs boson decays in a 2025 paper. A tetraquark is a particle made of four quarks; here all four are charm type. The relativistic quark model frames the calculation.

Several decay mechanisms are considered, involving quark-gluon, Z boson, and loop processes. Relativistic amplitudes are built for each channel. Decay widths are calculated with corrections for the relative motion of quarks and antiquarks. The work is theoretical particle physics. It estimates how often a Higgs decay could create a fully charmed tetraquark, a rare process that experiments could in principle search for.
arxiv-2509-09464:
P.-J. Stas and 15 co-authors demonstrate entanglement-assisted interferometry over a quantum network in a 2025 experiment. Dim light spread across distant telescope stations is hard to measure sharply. Shared entanglement between remote quantum memories can raise sensitivity, and their work puts that idea into practice with silicon-vacancy centres held in diamond nano-cavities.

The team combined event-ready remote entanglement, erasure of which-path information, and non-destructive heralding of incoming photons. With those pieces they measured a phase difference for weak light arriving at two separate stations. The link between stations ran through fibre up to a kilometre and a half. Success points toward a new family of quantum-enhanced imaging tools.
arxiv-2509-09764:
Emiliano Merlin and 20 co-authors hunt systematically for galaxies that quit forming stars early in cosmic history in a 2025 survey paper. Using deep James Webb imaging across six fields and a uniform catalogue, they seek massive quiet systems beyond redshift three. Careful colour fitting under three possible life histories, plus checks against spectra and simulated catalogues, guards the list against impostors.

They gather 633 candidates and mark 291 as gold grade by a reliability score weighing quiet against star-forming explanations. Heavy systems mostly stopped at least 150 million years before being seen. Lighter ones had usually quit only recently, a split the authors read as downsizing caught in the act, with small galaxies shutting down fast and late.
arxiv-2509-10064:
Erik Bertram and 4 co-authors lay out a working routine in 2025 for turning customer survey answers into actual software changes inside a large company. Feedback piles up in every big software firm, yet the hard part is rarely collecting it: drawing the right conclusion and feeding it into development is where value leaks away. Their end-to-end account covers choosing metrics, gathering responses from end users, and testing them with inferential statistics.

Transparency comes next, through a prototype experience dashboard that shows stakeholders the findings in a form they can act on. The authors close the loop by describing how results were pushed into decisions that changed the product. For product teams drowning in survey exports, the paper offers a tested plumbing diagram rather than another plea to listen.
arxiv-2509-10264:
Inside a T-shaped mixer, two liquid streams collide head-on. They must blend as they travel down one channel. Huixin Li and five co-authors study the turbulent version of that flow in this 2025 fluids paper. Their new setup has a channel four centimeters wide. It allows optical measurements at small scales.

The team uses particle image velocimetry and laser-induced fluorescence. First, they copy flow patterns known from tiny mixers at gentle speeds. Then they turn to turbulence. They measure the flow's kinetic energy and how fast it dissipates. They also track the spread of the mixed substance and its spectrum. The spectrum shows early signs of Batchelor scaling. Last, they tie the velocity and concentration fields together. They check all of it against standard models and their own simulations.
arxiv-2509-10364:
Christopher Beem and Niklas Garner study a special class of vertex algebras in this 2025 paper. Their tool is the relative semi-infinite cohomology of those algebras. Vertex algebras encode the algebra of quantum fields. A loosened form of unitarity, graded unitarity, gives many of them a Hilbert space structure. Without it, they would lack one. The loosened notion comes from supersymmetric field theories.

The authors focus on algebras with a chiral quantum moment map. The map targets a current algebra of affine type, taken at double the critical level. For these algebras, the chain complex behaves like a familiar object. It mirrors the differential forms on a compact Kähler manifold. That echoes classic work by Banks, Peskin, and Frenkel, Garland, and Zuckerman. Consequences follow. The cohomology is itself graded-unitary. An extra symmetry action appears. And the complex matches its own cohomology, like a famous formality theorem.
arxiv-2509-10764:
Siqi Zhang and eight co-authors turn earbuds into heart monitors in this 2025 ubiquitous computing paper. The subtle vibrations of heart valves opening and closing, captured in seismocardiography and gyrocardiography, carry fine timing information, but normally require chest-mounted sensors. Their system, LubDubDecoder, uses the one component every hearable has: its speaker, repurposed as an acoustic sensor.

The speaker picks up the coarse lub-dub of heart sounds, and the system reconstructs the subtle vibration waveforms from their shared timing and spectral structure, extracting the moments of key cardiac events. In an approved study with twenty-five users, reconstructed signals correlated strongly with chest references, between roughly 0.88 and 0.95, held up across users and across remounting, and even generalized to earbuds the system had never seen, with music playing.
arxiv-2509-11064:
Jin Woo Jang and Chanwoo Kim prove a long-time stability result for plasma physics. This 2025 mathematics paper treats the Vlasov-Maxwell equations in three dimensions. The system couples a particle density to electric and magnetic fields. A half-space setting models the solar wind at a boundary.

The authors first build steady solutions of the boundary-value problem. They then prove those states are stable. Small disturbances decay at a sharp rate over time. The particle density and both fields decay together. One wave part decays too slowly to sum directly. A new device turns that part's spatial focus into time decay along light cones. The result is billed as the first of its kind for the full nonlinear system.
arxiv-2509-11164:
Diego Eustachio Farchione, Ramzi Idoughi, and Peter Wonka wrote this 2025 computer vision paper on measuring coral. Reef monitoring needs accurate estimates of coral volume and surface area, but coral shapes are so tangled that building a full three-dimensional mesh is slow and fragile.

Their method skips the mesh entirely. A pre-trained vision module turns a handful of ordinary color photos into dense point maps, which are merged into one point cloud carrying confidence scores. Two network heads then read the cloud and report volume and surface area, each with its own confidence estimate. The system stayed accurate on coral shapes it had never seen, offering a light, scalable way to track reef growth from sparse photos.
arxiv-2509-11664:
Aimeric Malter and Artan Sheshmani build exotic resolutions for a class of singular spaces. This 2025 algebraic geometry paper treats non-commutative crepant resolutions. Such a resolution swaps a singular variety for a well-behaved algebra. The algebra plays the role of a smooth space. The targets are affine toric Gorenstein varieties.

The authors prove a shared generalization of two past results. One is by Špenko and Van den Bergh. The other is by Iyama and Wemyss. The proof extends work of Novaković to cones over polytopes that hold interior points. A special case takes reflexive polytopes with few vertices. There, results of Borisov and Hua supply the resolutions.
arxiv-2509-11864:
Lichao Wu and five co-authors attack the safety training of large language models at the neuron level. This 2025 AI security paper treats alignment. Alignment teaches models to refuse harmful requests. It leans on a sparse set of specialized safety neurons. That concentration is itself a vulnerability.

Their framework is NeuroStrike. With white-box access, it finds safety neurons by feedforward activation analysis. It prunes them at inference time. Removing well under one percent of neurons in targeted layers let plain harmful prompts succeed often. More than twenty open models were tested. In the black-box setting, a profiling attack trains prompt generators on open surrogate models. The generators transfer to proprietary targets. Success came in a majority of attempts. Safety neurons transferred across fine-tuned and distilled relatives too.
arxiv-2509-12264:
Black holes dressed in extra ingredients bend the paths of nearby particles in new ways. Faizuddin Ahmed and two co-authors study such an object in 2025. It is a charged anti-de Sitter black hole. It uses nonlinear electrodynamics. A cloud of strings wraps it. A halo of perfect fluid dark matter surrounds it.

The team derives the effective potentials for light. They do the same for massive neutral particles. Then they track three features as each ingredient varies. The photon sphere shifts. The shadow size shifts. The innermost stable orbit shifts too. Wave perturbations and thermodynamics follow. Heat capacity shows dividing points between stable and unstable regimes. The free energy profile stretches into new parameter territory.
arxiv-2509-12464:
Reasoning models write long chains of thought, which makes them expensive, and pruning them the usual way backfires: the shrunken model thinks longer and worse. Ryan Lucas and five co-authors diagnose that failure in 2025 and offer a drop-in repair called Reasoning-Aware Compression.

Standard pruning rebuilds only the input-side activations, but reasoning is dominated by decoding, the model's own generated text. Their fix also rebuilds activations from the model's own chain-of-thought traces during pruning. Plugged into an existing pruning workflow, the change restores much of the lost performance on reasoning tasks without extra machinery.
arxiv-2509-12864:
Jorge Acuna Flores, Giuseppe De Nittis and Javier Lorca Espiro lift Kitaev double models to shapes of any size in 2025. The models are lattice toys for phases that guard quantum data. A strict algebra frame was missing past flat cases.

Ground states with no strain are classed via a logic algebra. Its state space matches the strain-free ground set. Swap rules of a broad type hold. When hole counts are finite, the algebra splits into a classic part and a full matrix part. Vanishing holes mark exactly when a core pair forms. That pair may help class heat states next.
arxiv-2509-13064:
Irina Serban, Dimitra Dritsa and six co-authors ask in 2025 how bowel cancer patients feel about remote watch during pre-surgery fitness work. Fitness plans before surgery cut post-surgery harm. Remote watch aids clinical choice, but patient views in this phase were thin.

Five patients who did four weeks of fitness with constant watch were asked in depth. Willingness was shaped by drives, felt gains, and worries. Themes point to design rules for patient-first systems. The small set gives a base for larger studies. It lifts patient voice in a field led by clinical metrics.
arxiv-2509-13564:
Arman Pourghorban and Dipankar Maity analyze a pursuit game in a 2025 paper on target defense. One defender guards a target inside a cone-shaped region while attackers arrive one at a time, each racing straight for the target at top speed. An attacker that slips past scores a breach; one that is caught ends its run, and the next attacker appears.

Where each chase ends sets the defender's starting point for the next, so attackers plan with future rounds in mind, using limited-range sensors to spot the defender. The authors derive equilibrium strategies for both sides built around a capture distribution, a way of scoring the defender's long-run success rate. Monte Carlo trials with random scenarios confirm the theory.
arxiv-2509-13864:
Jovana Videnovic, Matej Kristan, and Alan Lukezic make video object tracking distractor-aware in a 2025 computer vision paper. Memory-based segmentation models such as SAM2 track a target through a video. They remember earlier frames as they go. Look-alike objects, called distractors, pull the tracker off course. Occlusions can lose the target entirely.

Their add-on for SAM2 is named DAM4SAM. It combines a distractor-aware memory module with introspection-based memory management. Drift toward look-alikes drops, and re-detection after occlusion improves. To study the problem, they also built DiDi, a distractor-distilled test dataset. The system beat SAM2.1 on thirteen benchmarks. It set new best results on ten. The same memory also lifted two real-time and edge trackers.
arxiv-2509-14164:
Javad Zakeri, Armando Perez-Leija, and Andrea Blanco-Redondo generate high-dimensional topological entanglement with light in a 2025 quantum photonics paper. Scaling quantum states to many entangled modes is central to quantum computation. Topology offers protection: information encoded in such features resists local damage. A practical route to many entangled topological photonic modes had been missing.

Their platform is a silicon photonic chip patterned into carefully designed topological superlattices of waveguides. Inside it, a nonlinear process creates energy-time entangled photon pairs. The pairs spread as one blended state across several modes at once. Measurements and theory together show the effect spanning up to five topological modes. It holds up despite the small flaws that real chip-making always leaves. That is a step toward scalable, robust quantum light.
arxiv-2509-14264:
Gautam Kishore Shahi and Tim A. Majchrzak survey research on toxic content online in 2025, a problem that spikes during crises, elections and unrest. Their review pulls together a large body of work on finding hate speech, offensive language and other harmful posts with machine learning.

Working from a synthesis of many prior studies, the authors compare how toxicity is defined, where data sets come from, and which learning methods get used. The data they cover span dozens of languages and topics from elections to sudden events. Gaps remain around clear definitions, fair data and methods that transfer across platforms. The survey gives new researchers a map of what has been tried and where detection still fails in practice.
arxiv-2509-14364:
Guillermo Gallego, writing alone in 2025, identifies dual pairs of multiplicative Hitchin fibrations, a construction in algebraic geometry with roots in gauge theory. A fibration organises a space into fibres over a base. Duality here pairs systems from Langlands dual groups.

Three pairings are matched. An untwisted system for a group pairs with one for its dual group. A twisted system for a simply connected group pairs with an untwisted system for a dual invariant group. Two twisted systems also pair in a third case. In each pairing the bases coincide and generic fibres are dual objects called Beilinson motives. Such matches are concrete instances of Langlands duality, a vast expected mirror between geometries for dual groups.
arxiv-2509-14764:
Yuanyuan Yao and three co-authors address initialisation bias in 2025 in unsupervised auditory attention decoding, which infers from brain signals which speaker a listener attends to. Label free decoding removes calibration sessions for hearing devices, a major usability win. Its self adaptive training, though, starts biased.

The bias comes from the initial model used to bootstrap stimulus reconstruction without ground truth labels. An unbiased variant exists but leaves efficiency or accuracy concerns. The authors develop efficient solutions that mitigate the bias while keeping the unsupervised advantage. Neuro steered hearing aids depend on such decoding: a device that follows the wrong voice in a crowd fails its core promise, however elegant its signal processing.
arxiv-2509-15164:
Daniele Tancini, Riccardo Rastelli, and Francesco Bartolucci fit hidden Markov models that shift over space and time in a 2025 paper. Such models hide a state process behind the data. Here the hidden states spread across sites with an autologistic form. Their joint odds are known only in trivial cases, so most users swap in pseudo-odds and accept skewed fits.

The team runs Bayesian inference with an exchange method that steps around the model's intractable constants. The sampler aims at the true posterior, not a stand-in. A fresh start-up step for the method also cuts run time. Skipping pseudo-odds matters most where hidden links are strong, which is just where these models earn their keep.
arxiv-2509-15464:
Junhong Lin leads a team that helps language models reason over facts that change over time. Facts can be stored in a knowledge graph, a web of linked items. Most tools treat that web as fixed, yet real facts shift and clash. The team build a system that both reasons over time and keeps the web fresh.

Their reasoner grounds items in both broad and local views, splits a query into routes, and scores answers by time. A second part updates the graph from raw text, settles clashes by trust scores, and tracks trends. Tests on time based question sets show the system beats plain prompts and older graph tools. It also narrows the gap between small and large models.
arxiv-2509-15964:
Tianyu Li, Yan Xin, and Jianzhong Zhang sharpen channel estimation for wireless links with a team of expert networks. Knowing the channel, how a signal warps on its path, is basic to robust communication. Deep learning methods often fail to travel across noise levels, block counts, and channel types. Their frame, MoE-CE, attacks that travel problem directly.

Several expert subnetworks each specialize in a kind of channel. A learned router picks the right experts for each input. Capacity and adaptability rise without a matching rise in cost. The frame fits any backbone model and training rule. On fake data across many settings, including unseen ones, it beats standard deep methods in a steady way.
arxiv-2509-16064:
Animators often sketch a scene with a few rough poses, then spend hours adding natural detail and timing. Purvi Goel and three co-authors use diffusion models to turn those sparse blocking poses into full, lifelike motion. Their trick blends the model's free output with the fixed poses at set steps, with a slack weight for each pose.

The blended result then feeds a prior model that fixes timing. Tests show this works far better than adding detail by blending outputs or by soft guidance alone. The result is presented as the first diffusion method that robustly lifts rough poses into plausible finished animation.
arxiv-2509-16264:
Can language models predict how European lawmakers will vote, and do their errors fall unevenly across groups? Wenjie Lin and seven co-authors build ParlAI Vote, a web platform that links parliament debates, speeches, and roll-call votes with data on gender, age, country, and party group. Users can browse debates and compare real outcomes with model forecasts, broken down by group.

The platform shows where leading models show steady bias in both vote forecasts and gender tasks. It also displays model reasoning, so users can see what cues drive errors. By joining data, models, and visuals in one place, it eases audits and teaching.
arxiv-2509-16564:
Jun Rong Brian Chong, Yixuan Tang, and Anthony K. H. Tung study how false claims change as they spread, in a 2025 paper. A claim can shift its wording, framing, and moral tone for new readers. Most detectors, though, treat false claims as fixed. The team build a tool that mimics this drift across rounds.

Their system uses set personas to rewrite claims step by step. It then tests common detectors on the changed claims. Detector scores fell sharply, in one case by close to half. That drop shows how brittle fixed detectors can be. The work gives researchers a way to stress-test tools before real campaigns hit them.
arxiv-2509-16664:
Simone Ricci and co-authors keep old and new image models in sync in a 2025 paper. Search systems turn images into lists of numbers for matching. When a model is retrained, its lists often clash with lists from the older model. Retraining everything is costly. The team add a training rule that keeps the lists compatible.

Their rule pushes certain directions in the lists toward right angles. Tests span many model types and datasets. The rule kept zero-shot skill intact, with no prior examples needed. It also let old and new lists work together after updates. Code is shared in public. Compatible lists could save firms from costly full rebuilds.
arxiv-2509-16764:
Eleonore Faber surveys number patterns called friezes in a 2025 solo math paper. A frieze is an endless array where each diamond of four numbers obeys one rule. Coxeter introduced them in the late 1960s, and work with Conway followed. The topic then slept for over thirty years.

Faber reviews striking links that woke the field up. Friezes tie to polygon splits, to cluster algebras, and to categories built from them. The focus then shifts to recent results in those categories. A simple counting rule thus opens into deep modern algebra. The survey gives newcomers a guided entry to a revived field.
arxiv-2509-16964:
C. Daoutis, A. Zezas, and M. L. N. Ashby use mid-infrared light to spot typical star-forming galaxies in a 2025 astronomy paper. A galaxy's mid-infrared spectrum carries clues about its radiation, star birth, and dust. The team test which spectral traits mark galaxies on the main sequence, the common path of steady star formation.

Dust features called PAHs track star formation and radiation hardness well. Alone, though, they cannot pick out main-sequence galaxies reliably. The team also built a physical spectral library spanning ultraviolet to far-infrared light. That library gives modelers a reference set for nearby galaxies. Better markers help surveys sort millions of galaxies by type.
arxiv-2509-17864:
Shi Chen and 4 co-authors rebuild moving 3D scenes from a single camera video, live as it plays. Their 2025 method, ProDyG, uses Gaussian splatting, a way to paint a scene from soft 3D blobs. Past live tools tend to drop moving parts or need a depth camera.

Their system splits the scene into still and moving parts. A mask keeps pose tracking steady, while a motion graph guides how the moving parts are rebuilt bit by bit. New views from the rebuild rival off-line tools in tests. Tracking also matched top dynamic tools, and both colour and depth inputs work.
arxiv-2509-18564:
Particle accelerators rely on superconducting cavities whose surfaces must waste as little energy as possible. Hannah Hu, Young-Kee Kim, and Daniel Bafia compare two ways to treat niobium cavities in this 2025 paper. Adding nitrogen into the metal is known to cut surface resistance sharply. Oxygen treatment has lately emerged as a rival with similar gains.

The team measured cavities treated with varied nitrogen and oxygen recipes. They also studied cut-out samples treated the same way, to size each element's share of the gain. Nitrogen proved ten times more effective than oxygen at cutting resistance at the tested field strength. The two impurities' effects also added together when both were present. The authors discuss the results through ideas about gap enhancement and hydrogen trapping. The findings guide recipes for higher-quality accelerator cavities.
arxiv-2509-18664:
Textbooks are static, but AI can turn a chapter into a mix of visuals, audio, and quizzes. Courtney Heldreth and nine co-authors test whether that mix actually helps students learn. Their 2025 paper evaluates Learn Your Way, a platform that rebuilds textbook chapters into varied, interactive forms. The open question is whether such tools beat a plain digital textbook.

The team ran a mixed-methods experiment with sixty students in the United States. One group learned through the platform; the other used a digital textbook with the same content. The platform group reported a better learning experience. They also scored better on learning outcomes. Choice among several forms of the same content seems to be part of the gain. The authors present AI-driven choice as a promising route for course design. They frame the result as early but positive evidence.
arxiv-2509-18764:
Earthquakes, floods, and blackouts often arrive in bunches rather than evenly spread. Sarvesh K. Upadhyay, Vimal Kishore, Sanjay Kumar, and R. E. Amritkar study that bunching on networks in this 2025 paper. Their model sends a random walk across a complex network as a stand-in for transport. Extreme events are the walk's rare, largest excursions.

In a modular network, one small cluster hangs by sparse links to the rest. That cluster shows bunching and correlations among its extreme events. The bunching emerges on its own from the structure, with no added mechanism. The team quantifies it with several tools, from recurrence times to burstiness measures. Their message is that network shape alone can drive event bunching. That insight matters for risk planning on grids and other networked systems. Structure, not just load, sets the rhythm of extremes.
arxiv-2509-18864:
Apps want a profile of each user, but labels for training are scarce and user data is messy. Yingxin Li and 10 co-authors present Conf-Profile, a label-free profiling framework, in this 2025 paper. They also built ProfileBench, a benchmark from a real video platform. It pairs varied user data with a structured trait taxonomy.

Conf-Profile works in two stages. Strong models first draft labels, guided by their own confidence hints. Confidence-weighted voting cleans those labels, and calibration balances them. The drafts, reasons, and scores are then distilled into a small model. A second training phase uses confidence to filter hard cases and weight rewards. On a standard base model, the full pipeline lifted the F1 score by about fourteen points. The authors pitch confidence as the steering signal that replaces missing labels.
arxiv-2509-18964:
Xingtu Liu, writing alone, proves limit theorems for a workhorse method of reinforcement learning called Q-learning. In Q-learning an agent learns the value of each action in each state from rewards it collects. The version studied here updates entries at uneven times, as data arrives, and then averages the results over time, a scheme tied to the names Polyak and Ruppert.

Liu proves a central limit theorem for the averaged values, the kind of result that says errors settle into a bell-shaped distribution. The proof gives an explicit rate that depends on the number of steps, the size of the state-action space, the discount factor, and how well the agent explores. A second result shows the running sums of the process behave like Brownian motion, the standard model of a random walk.
arxiv-2509-19164:
What if dark matter and dark energy trade momentum as the universe expands? G. N. Candlish and Y. Jaffé simulate that exotic idea, in which dark energy takes the form of a quintessence field coupled to dark matter by momentum exchange. Using a modified version of the RAMSES simulation code, they grow cosmic structure and compare dark matter halos with the standard model. Both signs of the coupling are tested.

The sign matters a lot. A negative coupling boosts substructure inside halos, while a positive one suppresses it. Host halos also end up in odd dynamical states: under-virialised for negative coupling and over-virialised for positive, compared with the reference run. Positive coupling makes halos less concentrated and less sharply peaked at the center. Negative coupling does the reverse. The study gives observers concrete fingerprints to look for if such a coupling exists.
arxiv-2509-19264:
Noam Soker, writing alone, argues that jets which jitter around while exploding a massive star also help the star's remains form dust. He examines dust shapes in several supernova remnants and finds jet-like forms among them. In Cassiopeia A and the Crab Nebula, some dust-rich structures sit in point-symmetric patterns, mirror images across the center. In supernova 1987A, the dust follows the two-lobed shape of the inner ejecta.

Earlier studies had credited those shapes to jets within the jittering jets explosion mechanism, where jets from the newborn neutron star, changing direction, unbind the star. Soker proposes the jets' properties and their clash with the core and envelope also set how much dust forms and where it lands. The study adds dust to the list of remnant features the jittering jets picture claims to explain.
arxiv-2509-19364:
Angelina Wang and two co-authors argue that the standard way of grading language models, offline and one question at a time, does not match how the models behave in real use. In practice, the same model answers differently inside one person's chat session than in another's, because personalization and conversation state shape its behavior. A stateless benchmark run erases exactly those forces. The authors gather field evidence with 800 real users of ChatGPT and Gemini.

Those users posed benchmark and other supplied questions through their own chat interfaces. Comparing the field answers with offline scores shows systematic gaps the authors document. The same question to the same model can earn markedly different responses across sessions. They conclude that evaluations must account for personalization to say anything trustworthy about deployed behavior. The paper is a call to redesign model evaluation around real usage.
arxiv-2509-19464:
Before a learned control policy is used in the real world, someone must check how well it will do. Shripad Vilasrao Deshmukh, Will Schwarzer, and Scott Niekum argue that the check itself should shape training. Their method, EvA-RL, trains policies that are both strong and easy to judge with low error. Standard methods train first and leave the check for later, where it can be noisy or skewed.

The team gives the method a form that can be built and tested. Theory and trials show a trade between top performance and ease of judging. That trade can be softened when the policy and the judging tool are learned together. The work treats trustworthy checks as a core goal of learning, not an afterthought. It speaks to safe use of learned systems in risky settings.
arxiv-2509-19564:
A weak heart pump in children born with heart defects is dangerous and easy to miss early. Yuting Yang and five co-authors improve an AI tool that reads standard heart tracings to flag that weakness. Such tools usually need huge labeled data sets, which children's hospitals rarely have. The team adds synthetic noise that mimics real-world signal flaws, made by nudging tracings along their natural shape.

Training then mixes that noise with an uncertainty-aware method that works across model designs. On real pediatric data, the tool detected the weakness reliably despite the small data set. The cost stays low, since a tracing is cheap and painless to record. The authors aim at clinics with few resources. Wider use could catch failing hearts sooner, when treatment helps most.
arxiv-2509-19864:
Solar active regions store twisted magnetic energy, and flares release it in bursts. K. Moraitis and J. K. Thalmann ask how much of that twist sits near the polarity inversion line, the seam where the field flips sign. They study about forty active regions that produced over two hundred strong flares. Three-dimensional field reconstructions feed a line-based helicity measure.

During the strongest eruptive flares, the seam's relative helicity fell by more than a tenth on average. Weaker or confined flares showed smaller drops. The current-carrying part of the helicity fell harder still. Such drops mark energy leaving the seam region at eruption. A measurable pre-flare signature would aid space weather forecasts. The study quantifies one candidate signature across a large sample.
arxiv-2509-20464:
Rings and gaps in young planetary discs are usually modeled on a flat two-dimensional grid. Alexandros Ziampras and three co-authors ask whether that shortcut is safe in a 2025 arXiv paper, the second in a series. Real discs cool by radiation and stir vertically, effects a thin model can miss. The team ran gap-opening planet simulations in both two and three dimensions.

They compared four heat treatments, from simple isothermal assumptions to full radiative transfer with diffusion. Simple cooling recipes tracked the fully radiative results well, slightly overstating gap opening near the planet. Two-dimensional models captured the essential gap physics with remarkable accuracy. Vertical flows, which only the three-dimensional runs can show, explained the remaining differences without changing the verdict. The authors encourage modelers to include radiative effects, even in simplified form.
arxiv-2509-20664:
Drug discovery needs molecular properties predicted before costly synthesis. Peng Zhou and six co-authors fuse language model knowledge with graph learning in a 2025 arXiv paper. Graph neural networks learn from molecular structure directly, reducing hand-crafted features. Yet human prior knowledge still adds value that structure alone misses. Their framework extracts that knowledge from large language models.

The models are prompted to produce domain knowledge and executable code that turns molecules into knowledge-based features. Those features are then fused with structural representations from pretrained molecular models. Three leading language models supplied the knowledge in the experiments. The combined method beat existing approaches across their tests. The authors are candid that language models hallucinate and have gaps on obscure properties. Their fusion design is meant to gain the knowledge while the structural channel keeps predictions grounded.
arxiv-2509-20864:
Eye scans reveal retinal disease, but hand-labeling every layer and lesion is slow. Botond Fazekas and five co-authors present SD-RetinaNet in a 2025 paper on optical coherence tomography segmentation. The model targets age-related macular degeneration and similar conditions.

The system learns in a semi-supervised way, using some unlabeled scans alongside labeled ones. Its key part is a differentiable topology engine for biomarkers. The engine forces segmentations to stay anatomically plausible, respecting how layers and lesions fit together. Earlier methods often produced impossible layouts and weak layer-lesion modeling. Joint learning of layers and lesions under topological rules aims at outputs doctors can trust for diagnosis and for tracking patients over time.
arxiv-2509-21064:
Many practical choices are yes-or-no, yet the resulting binary optimization problems are hard to solve at scale. Wenbo Liu and five co-authors attack them from a primal-dual angle in a 2025 paper. Their framework recasts an unconstrained binary problem as a continuous minimax problem.

The reformulation has a strong max-min property, meaning the two sides of the game meet cleanly. Smoothing the discrete problem this way lets gradient methods take over. The authors design a simultaneous gradient descent-ascent algorithm that parallelizes well on GPUs. They prove it reaches a near-optimal solution in linear time. Experiments on large instances back the claims, offering an alternative to heuristic solvers with weak guarantees.
arxiv-2509-21164:
Different open language models specialize in mathematics, code, or general reasoning, and combining them usually means picking just one per query. Jacob Fein-Ashley and three co-authors introduce Mixture of Thoughts in a 2025 paper. The method lets expert models collaborate inside their hidden states, not just trade finished text.

For each query, a lightweight router picks the top experts and names one as primary. Interaction layers, placed at uniform depths, project hidden states into a shared space so experts can exchange partial thinking. Earlier approaches routed queries, ran costly multi-turn exchanges, or merged weights, which demands identical architectures. Mixture of Thoughts works across heterogeneous models. The authors argue aggregation should capture what experts think, not only what they say.
arxiv-2509-21264:
Drone paths must respect rotation as well as position when space is cluttered. Its authors are Babak Salamat and 5 co-authors. A drone must plan a path that respects how it moves and turns. Past planners worked only in flat position space. The authors plan in SE(3), a space that joins position and rotation. That allows joint learning of travel and turning dynamics.

Their framework, GMP cubed, plans in phases and uses a Bellman guided update rule. Bellman rules estimate the value of future steps. Agents each refine one segment of the path and share updates with neighbours. A consensus scheme lets local updates shape a global path. The paper also adds DroneManager, a modular ground control tool for running the system.
arxiv-2509-21864:
Janis Keuper and Margret Keuper argue that the hunt for fake images rests on a shaky idea: a clear notion of a real image. Their 2025 position paper notes that image generators are now cheap and easy to use, which raises real fears of misuse. In response, researchers have built many detectors that sort images into real and fake. The authors say the real side of that split has been neglected.

Almost all detectors, they point out, are trained and tested against a few old, low-resolution collections of real photos. Meanwhile, photography itself has changed. Most photos now come from smartphones that build one image from several sensors and several moments, using neural networks much like the generators that make fakes. The authors call for a clear technical definition of a real image and for fresh benchmark data, and they ask whether fake detection is even a sound goal.
arxiv-2509-22264:
Michael Ridley and Eliahu Cohen review two rival ways of treating time in quantum mechanics. Most quantum theory gives time a special role: it is a background parameter, not a quantity the theory measures. One family of approaches, called timeless, removes the background clock and recovers time from correlations inside the system, in the style of Page and Wootters. Their 2025 paper weighs that family against a less studied alternative due to Bauer.

Bauer's two-time approach enlarges the state space with an extra degree of freedom, pictured as a pseudospin, which effectively adds a backward-running time direction. That addition allows a genuine time operator to be defined. It also links up with other time-symmetric formulations of quantum mechanics. They close by sketching a framework in which the timeless philosophy and two-time mechanics can be combined.
arxiv-2509-22364:
Nicola Fabiano, writing alone, proves three no-go theorems about fuzzy metric spaces and quantum state geometry. Fuzzy metrics grade distances rather than fixing them, and they have been proposed as a language for uncertainty. Quantum states, by contrast, live in a geometry shaped by phase. His 2025 paper argues the two are structurally incompatible: the fuzzy framework cannot capture features that are essential to how quantum states behave.

The first theorem shows fuzzy metrics cannot model destructive interference between concepts, because they are blind to phase. The second proves no embedding of quantum state space into any fuzzy metric space can preserve distances. The third shows fuzzy logic cannot distinguish symmetric from antisymmetric combinations of concepts, a basic structural distinction. Taken together, the theorems claim that fuzzy frameworks cannot represent intrinsic uncertainty of the quantum kind. The author presents quantum mechanics as the geometrically coherent alternative for that job.
arxiv-2509-22564:
Kevin Brune, Tobias Huber, and Lars-Thorben Moos finish a missing piece of a rare B-meson decay rate. The decay of an anti-B meson into a strange hadron plus a photon is a sensitive probe of new physics. Most parts of its rate are known to second order in the strong coupling, but multi-parton final states at first order were missing. The team computed the four-body decays with an extra quark pair and photon.

Five-body radiation with an added gluon completes the set. Modern integral reduction and analytic phase-space integration did the heavy lifting. Results come out in exact analytic form with multiple polylogarithms. The net effect on the decay rate is small, thanks to a partial cancellation between orders.
arxiv-2509-22864:
Yixuan Hu and 4 co-authors synthesize training data for event cameras from image diffusion models. Event cameras report pixel changes with fine timing and wide dynamic range, but labeled event data is scarce and costly. Their model, ControlEvents, generates event streams guided by text labels, two-dimensional skeletons, or three-dimensional body poses. The key move is to borrow the prior of a foundation image model, Stable Diffusion, so little fine-tuning and labeled data are needed.

Synthetic labeled events improved models on recognition, skeleton estimation, and pose estimation alike. The generator could also produce events for text labels never seen in training. That ability flows from the foundation model's text grounding, inherited through the diffusion prior.
arxiv-2509-22964:
Actor-critic methods learn well off-policy, but the policy under review keeps shifting. Qinxun Bai and 3 co-authors argue that functional critics are a must, not a luxury. A functional critic takes a code for the policy as input, not just states and actions. Past tries with such critics lagged behind standard methods. The team find two reasons they matter.

First, functional critics calm the clash known as the deadly triad plus moving target. The team give an algorithm that provably settles, with fewer harsh assumptions than before. Second, such critics capture policy-linked uncertainty that exploration tools miss. A small neural version matched top methods on control tests.
arxiv-2509-23064:
Weak solutions of parabolic equations can in principle blow up, so bounds matter. Thuyen Dang and Duong Minh Duc prove global boundedness for a hard class of such equations. Their operator may have unbounded coefficients. It need not be strictly or uniformly elliptic either. It also need not be of Muckenhoupt type, a common weight condition.

Even so, the solution stays bounded on the whole space-time domain. The result covers solutions that vanish on part of the boundary and initial set. Elsewhere on the boundary, the solution is left free. The proof widens the safe ground for degenerate, non-uniform parabolic problems.
arxiv-2509-23364:
Text-to-music tools promise fast creation, but how they change real producer workflows is little studied. Francesca Ronchini and 3 co-authors ran a user study on that question. Producers made tracks with a custom tool that joins text-to-music and source separation models. Semi-structured interviews followed the sessions. Thematic analysis sorted what producers said into patterns.

Challenges, opportunities, and ethical concerns all surfaced. The findings show where these models help and where they grate in practice. Integration into daily workflows lags the raw capability. The study is a case study, with a small producer pool. It offers grounded insight for tool builders and musicians.
arxiv-2509-23564:
Human ratings that teach language models carry noise, and dirty preference data can warp the result. Samuel Yeh and Sharon Li ask whether cleaning that data first makes alignment more reliable. They built PrefCleanBench, the first broad benchmark for preference data cleaning in this setting. It compares thirteen cleaning methods under one protocol.

The tests vary data sets, model designs, and optimization methods to check both alignment gains and how well each cleaner generalizes. The authors pinpoint factors that decide whether cleaning helps or hurts. They release modular code for all methods, arguing that data preparation is a crucial, understudied lever for responsible model alignment.
arxiv-2509-23964:
One wrong label can teach a network the wrong lesson, and big data sets hide many wrong labels. Dang Huu-Tien and 2 co-authors detect and fix them using only a trained model's penultimate features. Their observation: a mislabeled point's features sit closer to its true class than to other classes, so the label pattern inside a tight cluster betrays errors. The methods are post-hoc and model-agnostic.

Theory and experiments show strong detection across varied, realistic noise patterns. The approach can also relabel errors automatically, lifting data set quality. The authors release an implementation for public use.
arxiv-2509-24064:
Ting-Wei Chao and 3 co-authors pose a new question about how often a small graph can sit inside a larger one. Edge inducibility refines two classic topics at once: the Kruskal-Katona theorem and the inducibility question of Pippenger and Golumbic. The twist is to count edges, not just points, in the copies that appear.

First comes a hardness result: for any graph, a related graph can be built whose edge count settles the point count of the first. The team then settles every graph with at most four points and makes headway on two larger cases. A wider hardness result uses graphs with a special matching, set out through locally directed graphs.
arxiv-2509-24164:
Large language models learn tasks from examples in the prompt, but where inside the model does that learning live? Haolin Yang and 2 co-authors split in-context learning into two jobs: recognizing the task and learning the task. They built a method that scores each attention head for its role in each job.

The heads they found for each job worked well alone and together. Steering tests show recognition heads pull hidden states toward the task's region, while learning heads rotate states within that region toward the right label. Old findings on induction heads and task vectors fit the same picture. One frame thus ties together results that had seemed separate.
arxiv-2509-24464:
Xueyuan Yan develops a numerical method for first-principles electronic structure in one-dimensional systems, based on a sinc basis set. Sinc functions are known for high accuracy and a nonlocal character, meaning each one reaches across the system rather than sitting at one point. That reach suits long-range couplings, which local bases handle poorly.

As a proof of principle, Yan studies a molecule inside an optical cavity. The code computes the spectrum direct and shows the emergence of energy level splitting, the signature of the molecule coupling to the cavity light. The study offers the sinc basis as a clean tool for cavity problems in one dimension.
arxiv-2509-24564:
Particle detectors for space experiments need silicon ladders aligned to microns over lengths of a meter. Feng Wang and Xuhao Yuan present a high-precision assembly method built on a gantry system. The approach was used for mass production of all flight-model modules for the L0 tracking detector in the AMS experiment upgrade.

Alignment along the strip direction reached a few microns of precision over the full maximum length. The workflow is fully automated and uses machine vision to hold accuracy through production. The authors offer it as a viable route for future large-area, high-precision detector manufacturing, where hand assembly cannot scale.
arxiv-2509-25564:
Faizan Farooq Khan and eight colleagues wrote a 2025 paper testing whether multimodal large language models, AI systems that read images and text, can do marine biology. Identifying fish species accurately is critical for monitoring marine ecosystems under human pressure. Yet specialized scientific skill is exactly where general-purpose AI may be weakest.

The team systematically evaluated state-of-the-art models on fine-grained fish species recognition. The results were sobering: the best open-source models achieved less than ten percent accuracy. The paper, called FishNet++, analyzes these capabilities and limitations in depth. It also investigates whether targeted approaches can close the gap. Honest benchmarks like this steer the field toward tools that conservation scientists can actually trust.
arxiv-2509-25864:
Matteo Leonard, Dilip Maity, Nicolas Vandewalle, and Tadd Truscott showed in twenty twenty-five that two simple grooves can hold a wide, steady film of water on a vertical plate. Thin water films are prized for cooling, water harvesting, and self-cleaning surfaces because they cover area and drain well. Pure water's high surface tension usually breaks films apart, and past fixes relied on costly coatings or fine patterns.

A pair of laser-engraved grooves anchors the film sideways, with no other treatment. The film stretched over thirty centimeters, more than one hundred capillary lengths, and its thickness could be tuned by flow rate and groove shape. At the grooves' ends, the film cycles through rupture, retraction, and droplet release. Models predict the film's traits well. The method is cheap and scalable.
arxiv-2509-26164:
Zschocke wrote a solo study in twenty twenty-five on how light bends as it passes near a body in space. Work that tracks stars now needs facts at a very fine scale. At that scale, the shape and mass of a body change the path of its light.

He works out the key steps that give the path of the light at the point where it is seen. The steps let users find the bend from a round body and from a body that is not quite round. He gives size values for rays that graze the giant planets. The steps could feed a future space task that maps stars.
arxiv-2509-26364:
Kirill Tamogashev and a co-author solve a sampling problem that arises when no samples exist, in a 2025 paper. The Schrödinger bridge problem asks for the most likely random path between two distributions. It connects to diffusion models and flow matching, tools behind much modern generative AI. All known methods need actual samples from both end distributions. Sometimes only the formulas for those distributions are available, with no data behind them.

The authors give the first general method for that data-free case. It extends a classic fitting procedure, borrowing ideas from recent work on training diffusion samplers without direct feedback. Tests show the method recovers the bridge dynamics well. The advance widens where generative modeling can be used, including physics problems stated only as energy formulas.
arxiv-2510-00064:
Hollis Williams and Holger Hofmann wrote this 2025 theory paper on a basic puzzle in quantum physics. Measuring a quantum system always disturbs it, so gaining facts always costs some change. The authors study that trade-off with mathematics, focusing on the operators that describe a measurement. Their aim is a cleaner way to state how much disturbance each outcome must cause.

The authors show that the gentlest measurement operators split into a set of unitary steps. Each step stands for a pattern of disturbance that an experiment could tell apart. The observed pattern then sets a tight upper bound on the information a measurement can gain. That bound could help check quantum cryptography tools, where leaked information is the central risk. The work gives physicists a sharper language for a trade-off built into every quantum measurement.
arxiv-2510-00364:
Tara Kemp and James Lefevre wrote this 2025 mathematics paper settling a conjecture about Latin squares. A Latin square is a grid where each symbol appears once in every row and column. Inside a big square, smaller subsquares can sit disjointly, sharing no rows, columns, or symbols. A partition of the size lists the subsquare orders one hopes to realize.

Little was known when a partition mixes three or more distinct subsquare sizes freely. The standing conjecture covered partitions whose three largest parts are equal. Kemp and Lefevre prove that conjecture in full. Their proof shows a realization always exists under the stated ordering conditions. The result unlocks existence guarantees for many general partitions at once. Such constructions feed design theory, where Latin squares model balanced experiments and error-correcting schemes. The paper closes a case that earlier partial restrictions had left open.
arxiv-2510-00964:
Gautam, Shrestha, Harrison, and Tatar report an ethnographic study of sex-trafficking survivors in Nepal, published in the journal PACMHCI. Photo-elicitation is a research method where participants discuss photographs to surface feelings and values. Asking traumatized survivors to speak alone can silence them, so the authors reshaped the method into a communal activity inside an NGO's protected living home.

Working together around shared images let the women speak through the group rather than as exposed individuals. The study describes their complex path through rehabilitation toward a hoped-for new normal after rescue. It also shows the survivors hold limited but real social capital, such as craft skills and mutual support, which reintegration programmes could build on. The authors reflect carefully on when technology design can ethically intervene in such a setting at all.
arxiv-2510-01364:
Gornet and Mo import control theory into bandit exploration, for problems where rewards emerge from a hidden dynamical system. A learner must probe for information while harvesting reward, and here the payoff is a noisy system's output. Two algorithms structure that trade-off around the Kalman filter's own uncertainty.

One adds an optimism bonus scaled by prediction error. The other, IDEA, rewards actions that shrink the filter's state uncertainty, exploiting the system's observability. Hyperparameter tuning is the motivating application, where each probe is an experiment. Treating estimation error as a compass gives exploration a principled direction. Linear Gaussian dynamics keep the filter's mathematics exact and tractable. Observability, a classic control property, becomes an exploration resource. Washington University and Tsinghua host the two authors. Optimism and information gain are the two compasses compared. Exploration earns a control-theoretic foundation at last.
arxiv-2510-01464:
