Their classifier works with language-grounded parts. A diagnostic model trained on X-ray reports supplies the inner features. A bank of sparse decoders then breaks those features into single-meaning visual patterns.

Training one hundred decoders on a large hospital X-ray collection yields about five thousand patterns. The patterns cover heart, lung, membrane, structure, device, and artifact themes. Each prediction decomposes into twenty to fifty patterns. Every pattern comes with a gallery of images that trigger it. A clinician can verify the evidence by eye. Accuracy on five key findings stays competitive with opaque models. The team also plans natural language labels for the patterns.
arxiv-2510-22064:
Eduardo B. Molinero leads a nine-author team writing equations for how crystals respond to ultrafast light. The standard Bloch equations work in reciprocal space. In that view, gauge choices that should not matter keep muddying strong-field work. High-harmonic generation is one case that suffers.

Their Wannier equations move the description into real space and real time. They track the electron density matrix in a basis of localized states. Electron interactions enter at a screened-exchange level. Three damping channels cover dephasing and relaxation. One channel depends on distance in real space. The authors argue the result keeps semiclassical intuition. It also stays clean of gauge artifacts. The platform targets nonlinear optics and attosecond spectroscopy in solids.
arxiv-2510-22464:
Anik Burman and two co-authors address spatial confounding, where an unmeasured factor that varies across space can distort the estimated effect of an exposure. Standard methods assume the exposure changes at finer scales than the confounder, an assumption that may fail. Their framework relaxes that demand and instead needs only a few basis shapes tied to the exposure but not the confounder.

Their estimator, basis voting, builds many candidate estimates, each from one basis shape, and takes the most common answer. They also supply a sharper candidate estimate than the usual projection based one. Simulations and theory support the approach for spatial health and policy studies.
arxiv-2510-22564:
Finding ore bodies underground can use both gravity and magnetic measurements, which should point to related structures. Yanfei Wang, with five co-authors, examines in 2025 how to optimize a neural network they built earlier for jointly inverting those two fields in three dimensions.

Two lower networks separately recover gravity and magnetic sources from surface readings. An upper level compares the two source shapes and trains toward making them geometrically close. The paper tests choices in datasets, training, and loss functions for this hard, unstable inverse problem. Trial calculations on synthetic and field data check whether the tuned elements improve the recovered sources.
arxiv-2510-22664:
A random process forced to end at a fixed point may secretly follow a straightest possible path in information space. Tomoi Koide and Armin van de Venn report that result in 2025, studying a Brownian bridge, which is random motion tied down at both ends in time.

When the bridge must satisfy a canonical condition, its evolution matches a special geodesic curve on the space of Gaussian distributions. Random processes therefore travel along informationally straight lines, much like objects follow geodesics in general relativity. The authors argue the asymmetry of informational distance has real physical meaning, offering a step toward an equivalence principle for information.
arxiv-2510-22764:
Noisy past and future data can help fill a gap in a sequence. Maksym Luz and Mykhailo Moklyachuk study that interpolation task in 2025. Their sequence has stationary increments. That means step changes have stable stats over time. A linear functional sums unknown middle values with weights.

Observations come from before the gap in clean form. After the gap, noise corrupts the sequence. The team derives the best linear estimate. They also give its mean square error. When spectra are known, the formulas are exact. When spectra are only known within a set, they use minimax rules. Those rules guard against the least favorable spectra.
arxiv-2510-22864:
Time series experiments switch treatments back and forth over time. Zhexiao Lin and Peng Ding unify two inference views in 2025. One view is regression based. The other is design based, using only design randomness. Switchback trials and N-of-1 trials are examples.

They study design based traits of regression methods. Treatment effects can be estimated by ordinary least squares. That needs a suitable working model and transformed regressors. Many effects can be estimated at once. Even a diverging number is allowed. Estimators stay consistent and asymptotically normal. Variance estimators stay conservative under their results. Model misspecification does not break the design based logic.
arxiv-2510-23064:
Wenwen Li leads a team of eight researchers with LightPFP, a method to reach quantum-level accuracy in atom simulations at far lower cost. Machine-learned potentials can mimic quantum results, but task-specific ones need costly quantum data for each new material. Universal ones are flexible yet heavy to run at scale.

LightPFP uses knowledge distillation to train light models from a teacher, cutting the quantum data needed. The resulting potentials aim for ab initio accuracy with the speed large simulations demand. Modelers could study bigger systems for longer times, from batteries to catalysts, without giving up trustworthy forces.
arxiv-2510-23264:
Xinhai Wang and six co-authors present PAHQ, a method to speed up automated circuit discovery in language models. Circuit discovery finds the sparse subnetworks responsible for a task, a cornerstone of mechanistic interpretability. The standard ACDC method is too slow and memory-hungry for large models, and faster versions rely on linear shortcuts that hurt faithfulness.

PAHQ instead optimizes mixed-precision inference to cut cost while keeping the analysis faithful. The authors aim for circuit maps of large models that researchers can actually compute. Trustworthy circuits help explain how models produce their answers internally.
arxiv-2510-23364:
Hyeongkyun Kim and Orestis Oikonomou introduce ZeroFlood, a framework that maps flood hazard from radar satellite images alone. Flood maps guide disaster prevention, but data-scarce regions lack the geophysical inputs that traditional hydrodynamic models demand. Geo-foundation models, pretrained on Earth observation data, offer a shortcut.

The authors built a data set pairing observation data with simulated flood hazard maps across Europe. They evaluate several recent geo-foundation models on the segmentation task. Strong results would let emergency planners sketch hazard maps in regions where ground surveys and river data are missing.
arxiv-2510-23664:
Eranga Bandara and fourteen co-authors propose Agentsway, a software development methodology built for teams where AI agents do much of the work. Classic methods like Agile, Kanban, and ShapeUp assume human teams, and they strain when autonomous agents plan, code, test, and learn on their own. The authors argue the gap is methodological: agent teams need their own lifecycle and rules.

Agentsway centers on human orchestration, with specialized agents for planning, prompting, coding, testing, and fine-tuning, collaborating under privacy-preserving rules. Outputs and feedback from each agent feed fine-tuned models in a retrospective learning loop, sharpening domain reasoning over time. Responsible AI principles are woven through, using several models and reasoners to keep decisions balanced and explainable. The framework also defines metrics for productivity and trust, and the authors present it as the first methodology designed expressly for agent-based engineering teams.
arxiv-2510-23764:
Abigail Loe and two co-authors build a statistical framework for alternating recurrent events, where people cycle between two states over time. Examples abound: cancer patients swing between clotting emergencies and recovery, people with alcohol use disorder between addiction and sobriety, caregivers between depression and recovery. The analysis is tangled by censoring and by gaps where a person who just had the main event is not yet at risk for another.

Their method pairs random forests with inverse probability weighting and pseudo-observations. The weighting corrects bias from the informative missing stretches spent in the secondary state, and the model estimates the restricted mean time until the primary event. Simulations show sound performance whether the two event types are independent or correlated. The team applies the framework to a mobile health study, measuring how self-care push notifications affect the mental state of caregivers of traumatic brain injury patients.
arxiv-2510-24264:
V. M. Gordeeva and six co-authors predict ultrastrong coupling between magnons and photons in a layered structure at terahertz frequencies. The stack places an antiferromagnet between two superconductors. Magnons are waves of magnetic order, and their mixing with light forms hybrid magnon polariton states whose character depends on the applied magnetic field.

At zero field, only the lower frequency antiferromagnetic mode couples to the photon, while a field switches on coupling for both modes. The coupling strength, near one hundred gigahertz, exceeds ten percent of the resonance frequency, placing it in the ultrastrong regime. The superconductors also modulate the spin of the resulting hybrid states.
arxiv-2510-24364:
Louis Jourdan and Patrick Cassam-Chenaï show that a classic split formula for matrix exponentials turns simple under one mild rule. The Zassenhaus formula expands the exponential of a sum of two non commuting operators into an endless product. That product is hard to use in most cases. When the two operators meet what the authors call the no mixed adjoint rule, the expansion collapses to a short, closed form.

The chief use is a unitary coupled cluster method for electron systems with strong links between electrons. The method runs on a quantum computer. It needs no Trotter step, a common source of error. It is exact with a fixed count of Givens gates, equal to the count of free constants. The formulas also show why and when tuning after a Trotter step can give exact results in split forms of the method.
arxiv-2510-24664:
Parker Riley, Daniel Deutsch, Mara Finkelstein, Colten DiIanni, Juraj Juraska, and Markus Freitag test a two step way to grade machine made translations. In the known MQM scheme, raters mark each error span by type and weight. Their twist adds a second pass where a rater edits marks that are already there.

The first marks may come from the same rater, a new rater, or a machine rater. In trials, the second pass found errors missed the first time, and rater acts lined up with the goals of the scheme. The gain is a grade set with less noise as translation tools get strong.
arxiv-2510-24764:
Manuel Zechmann and Helmut Hlavacs built two real time world makers for fake planets in a game engine, then matched them head to head. One maker stacks a known rough noise in layers. The other copies a layered noise style known from a block game, with its own twists.

Both makers share a tree based detail scheme that adds mesh detail near the viewer. A small user study had fifteen players roam worlds from both makers plus two past world tools. The work lays out how each maker is built, mesh snags they hit, and what users made of each world. It is a hands on guide for small teams.
arxiv-2510-25164:
Yogesh Thakku Suresh, Vishwajeet Shivaji Hogale, Luca-Alexandru Zamfira, and Anandavardhana Hegde write captions for MRI scans with a transformer stack built for the clinic. Their stack joins a small vision transformer that reads the scan, a health text model that codes the words, and a custom loop decoder that writes the line.

Loss mixes a like score with a squared score to pull sight and word codes in line. At test time, a contrast step picks the line whose code sits most close to the scan. On a known care set, brain lone scans beat mixed scans on right and sense match. Past top tools serve as the gauge.
arxiv-2510-25364:
Luca Capone, Alessandro Bondielli, and Alessandro Lenci study small language models. Their 2025 paper asks if instruction tuning helps them. Instruction tuning trains models to follow user directions. They test conversational and question-answering data sets. Models had about one hundred million parameters. Training used merged or sequential curricula as options.

Evaluation covered fine-tuning and zero-shot settings both. SuperGLUE measured fine-tuning performance gains in tests. Other sets tested grammar, world knowledge, and tracking. Psycholinguistic correlation with human data was also checked. Instruction tuning gave small but consistent gains. Sequential curricula beat merged data for fine-tuning. Gains did not always transfer to zero-shot tasks. That suggests a trade-off in adaptation focus. Interaction-focused training may hurt broad linguistic generalization. Hybrid curriculum approaches may help future low-resource models.
arxiv-2510-25464:
Amirhossein Azarbahram and Onel L. A. López wrote a 2025 paper on tracking moving objects with radio signals. Their system uses reflected signals, called echoes, to follow several targets at once over time. The work sits within radio frequency sensing, where wireless waves help locate objects in space.

The authors build a method around a conditional denoising diffusion model, which learns by removing noise step by step. A second part, a variational autoencoder, squeezes each echo into a short code. That code then guides the model to predict where each target will be next. Those predictions help choose the best beam direction for the next signal. In computer tests, the method made smaller errors in angle and distance than older approaches. The results suggest learning tools could support future systems that sense and communicate together.
arxiv-2510-25664:
Kristof Berczi, Karthekeyan Chandrasekaran, Tamas Kiraly, and Daniel P Szabo build a new chain of splits for submodular maps. Their 2025 paper in pure math grows on work by Narayanan. Such chains of splits help with fast methods and with grouping tasks. Their chain is made to keep two named points, s and t, on split sides.

They define the chain, prove it is there, and give a fast way to build it. The build runs in time that grows in a tame, polynomial way. Two uses show why the chain counts. First, it gives good near-best splits for a class of split tasks. Those tasks cover maps that rise in one way, and maps with a like sign rule. Second, it gives a fast way to aim the edges of a hypergraph. The aim task asks for strong links all round, and strong s-to-t links at once.
arxiv-2510-25864:
Daniel Shaffer and Alex Levchenko review theories of the superconducting diode effect, where a superconductor carries current more easily in one direction than the other. A superconductor conducts with no resistance below a cold threshold. A diode like effect in such a material could serve computing, quantum devices, and sensitive detectors.

Shaffer and Levchenko first trace the history and the basic Ginzburg Landau picture, a simple theory of superconductors. They stress that both time reversal and mirror symmetry must break at once for the effect to appear. They then survey microscopic proposals, with focus on Rashba Zeeman materials that lack a center of symmetry, plus ideas based on magnets, valleys, topology, and driven systems.
arxiv-2510-25964:
Ritesh Kanchi, Miya Natsuhara, and Matt X. Wang share an experience report on scaling accessibility work in very large computing courses. Their introductory programming sequence serves over three thousand five hundred students a year with about one hundred teaching assistants. At that scale, course files, slides, and tools can easily shut out disabled students if access is treated as an afterthought.

Kanchi and the team first describe auditing and fixing existing materials, then argue that fixing after the fact is reactive and scales poorly. They built technical systems for web first, accessible by default content, alternate views, and automated checks. They also built human systems that train staff and students in good practice, so new content starts accessible.
arxiv-2510-26064:
David Otte, Jorg K. H. Franke, Arber Zela, Fabio Ferreira, and Frank Hutter run the first systematic study of scaling laws for symbolic regression. Symbolic regression searches for a short math formula that explains data, which can yield insight and models that people can read. Deep learning versions now rival genetic programming methods, but how performance grows with scale was largely unknown.

Otte and the team train a transformer pipeline at five model sizes across three orders of magnitude of compute, on carefully generated data. Both validation loss and the share of problems solved follow clear power law trends with compute. They also map how best batch size and learning rate grow with model size, giving guidance for training larger systems.
arxiv-2510-26364:
Daewoong Cheong, with Gennian Ge, Doowon Koh, Thang Pham, Dung The Tran, and Tao Zhang, studies how many different distances a set of points must contain. Their setting is a finite field version of space, where points sit on a grid with wrap-around arithmetic. The question grows out of the Erdős-Falconer distance problem, a known hard problem in this area.

Cheong and his five co-authors look at a flexible class of sets called Salem sets, which spread their points in a fairly even way. They link a key measure of the set to its additive energy, a count of repeated sums. Gains in that energy force many distances to appear, and their size bounds beat older ones in some ranges. Uses include sharper bounds for sets on curves and surfaces.
arxiv-2510-26564:
Sejal Babel and Martha Łącka work in ergodic theory, the study of systems that evolve over time and the measures that describe their long-run behaviour. They place a special metric, a way of measuring distance, on the set of invariant measures of a dynamical system. That metric gives a stronger topology than the usual weak-star one, meaning it sees finer differences.

Babel and Łącka ask whether ergodic measures inside a fixed characteristic class form a closed set under this metric. They show that if generic points tied to such measures converge in the Besicovitch pseudometric, the limit point is generic for an ergodic measure in the same class. Combined with a result from earlier work with other authors, that proves the set is closed. The result sharpens how the space of measures is understood in this setting.
arxiv-2510-27164:
Hankyeol Lee leads five co-authors in a pipeline that writes richer, more accurate captions for high-resolution photos. Vision-language models train on small images, so shrinking a large photo for them loses fine detail and drops objects. The pipeline instead starts with a draft caption, then asks a language model which objects are present and which related objects likely appear too.

Object detectors verify those guesses on the real image. Newly confirmed objects missing from the draft get focused, region-specific captioning, while mentions of undetected objects are removed to cut hallucination. Judging uses pairwise comparison, quantitative scoring by large multimodal models, and a hallucination benchmark. On a curated high-resolution set the pipeline yields more detailed and reliable captions than single-model baselines.
arxiv-2510-27464:
Aslan Ahadi, Elham Sarvari, and four other co-authors map how a shape-shifting alloy behaves in tubes, in a 2025 study. The alloy is NiTi, a nickel-titanium mix that snaps between two crystal states under stress. Such superelastic tubes serve in medical and engineering parts. Cameras tracked the tube surface in three dimensions during pulls and bends.

Stereo image matching, pairing photos to read surface strain, synced with force records. Under tension, thick-walled tubes formed few fat, diffuse bands, while thin tubes formed sharp slim ones. The boundary between states went from finely fingered to coarsely fingered, then to a smooth front in the thickest tubes. Size alone could flip the pattern: a small thin tube showed diffuse fingers too. Bending patterns shifted with size as well.
arxiv-2510-27664:
Niloy Saha, Noura Limam, Yang Xiao, and Raouf Boutaba present Kestrel in 2025, a lean telemetry system for 5G user planes. Telemetry means the live gauges a network keeps on its own traffic. Coarse counts are cheap but hide brief, per-flow faults. Full per-packet notes catch all faults, yet their cost grows with line speed and soon swamps the system.

Kestrel packs per-packet gauges into compact sketches, which are small summaries that keep key patterns. Buckets gain small charts and are split by queue to guard tail delays and gap times. Math bounds that count sketch clashes guide size and bin choices. The design aims for fine views of faults at a small share of full cost.
arxiv-2511-00064:
Randolph Wiredu-Aidoo presents SPORE, a clustering method built on skeleton propagation over recalibrating expansions, aimed at data that is not linearly separable. Centroid methods like k-means fail on such data, while density methods struggle when local densities vary widely and give unclear boundaries. A single density threshold cannot capture clusters at several density scales at once.

The proposed propagation and recalibration design targets heterogeneous densities and clearer boundary delineation. Machine learning readers get a new density-style option for awkwardly shaped clusters. Real datasets, from biology to geography, routinely mix dense and sparse clusters, which is the gap addressed.
arxiv-2511-00164:
Theophile Jegou du Laz, Michael Coughlin, Peter Bachant, and colleagues introduce BOOM, a real-time optical alert broker for the flood of transient alerts from wide-field surveys. Current facilities already produce up to a million alerts a night, and the Rubin Observatory will produce far more, alongside multi-messenger instruments. Building on the system that ran in production for the Zwicky Transient Facility's first seven years, BOOM processes those streams at scale.

Alert brokers filter, classify, and route events so telescopes can follow up the interesting ones before they fade. Astronomy readers get production software for time-domain science. Broker quality decides which cosmic explosions get observed in their first hours.
arxiv-2511-00964:
Hai Hoang Thanh and colleagues ask a practical question: can synthetic data stand in for a large labeled test set when judging a trained model's true error? Labels are costly, so often only a few are available, yet deploying a model on a bad error estimate is risky.

They develop new generalization bounds that include synthetic data, showing how much the quality of the generator matters. Guided by the bounds, they propose a method that optimizes the synthetic samples used for evaluation. On simulated and tabular data, their estimates of test error proved more accurate and more reliable than existing baselines. The work gives a principled footing to a practice many teams already use informally.
arxiv-2511-01164:
Emanuele Contini and colleagues model the stellar halos of bright central galaxies, the diffuse starlight surrounding the dominant galaxy in a cluster, across cosmic time. They use a semi-analytic galaxy formation model on merger trees from high resolution dark matter simulations, with updated treatment of intracluster light.

Halo mass tracks both the central galaxy's mass and the intracluster light mass, the latter more tightly. The transition radius between galaxy and halo stays near thirty to forty kiloparsecs at most epochs but can grow far larger in the most massive halos. Halos and intracluster light share colors and redden toward today, and both start far more metal poor than the central galaxy, with the gap shrinking by the present. Comparisons with deep imaging surveys mostly agree, though observed metallicities run lower than predicted.
arxiv-2511-01364:
Pavan Kumar Perepu searches for mathematical expressions by meaning rather than by text. Formulas have two dimensional structure, with symbols nested at any depth in superscripts and subscripts. String matching retrieval methods see only the syntax. They miss expressions that say the same thing in different notation.

His approach extracts semantic features with a deep recurrent neural network. The network is trained to classify each expression's complexity, quantified by its nesting depth into simple, medium, and complex classes. Features are taken from the layer just before the final classifier and stored in a database. A query expression is passed through the same network, and its features are matched against the database to retrieve semantically close expressions.
arxiv-2511-01564:
Sai Shruthi Srinivasan and Siva Nadarajah write on a flaw of high-order flow codes. Near a shock wave, sharp methods such as discontinuous Galerkin sprout wiggles that are not real. Entropy-stable flux reconstruction schemes curb the wiggles and keep provable entropy promises. But they pay for this with lost accuracy and small time steps.

Their fix is a lifting operator that adapts. The operator is the part of the scheme that punishes jumps at cell faces. Switching it as the flow demands keeps the scheme's provable traits, restores accuracy, and allows larger time steps. With a limiter that keeps values positive, the scheme gives sound results through shocks in hyperbolic conservation laws.
arxiv-2511-01664:
Duaa Abdullah and Jasem Hamoud examine how Western Orientalist scholars have judged the scientific legacy of the Arab and Islamic world, with astronomy as the central case. The study traces how Arab scholars' work reached Europe and asks what stance European historians took toward it.

Particular weight falls on the zij, the astronomical tables compiled by Arab astronomers, and on their influence on Western astronomy through translations of Arabic books. The authors also consider the view of David King, a leading historian of Islamic astronomy. They credit Orientalist scholarship itself with analyzing Arab scientific output. They also trace its effects on the West. The method is historical retrieval, working from previously documented contributions and records of transmission.
arxiv-2511-02264:
Nicholas Kocurek and Chinmay Nirkhe work on certifying the lowest possible energy of a quantum system, a central problem in many-body physics. Their Hamiltonians are random: sums of signed local Pauli operators acting on many qubits. The authors build a spectral technique that produces an efficiently computable certificate, guaranteed to sit below the true ground energy, and usually close to it when the system has enough terms.

The method extends classical tools for refuting constraint problems, using a quantum version of the Kikuchi matrix. The second half of the work maps the technique's limits: on worst-case Hamiltonians it can fail, and the authors prove matching lower bounds for the non-commutative sum-of-squares method. They also construct a family of Hamiltonians, built from quantum codes, whose low-energy states provably require deep circuits, sharpening complexity guarantees for such systems.
arxiv-2511-02564:
Md Rashidunnabi, Kailash Hambarde, Vasco Lopes, Joao Neves, and Hugo Proença tackle one of surveillance vision's hardest matching problems. The task is recognising the same person across cameras that see from wildly distinct angles, such as a drone above and a camera at street level. Viewpoint shifts, scale differences between altitudes, and changes over time conspire against video re-identification. Their framework bolts seven modules onto a vision transformer backbone, each aimed at one failure mode.

The modules normalise features across cameras, harmonise them across resolutions, remember identity traits, model motion, align features between views. They also learn temporal patterns at several scales, and enforce identity consistency across views through contrastive learning. The additions cost only about two million parameters, and the system runs in real time. It set state-of-the-art results on an aerial-ground benchmark at every altitude and generalised well to two datasets.
arxiv-2511-02864:
Bogdan Georgiev, Javier Gomez-Serrano, Terence Tao, and Adam Zsolt Wagner report on AlphaEvolve, an AI system that hunts for new mathematical constructions. The system pairs a language model with automated evaluation in an evolutionary loop: it proposes code, tests it, and refines the survivors. Their 2025 paper tries the tool on sixty-seven open problems across analysis, combinatorics, geometry, and number theory.

In most cases the system matched the best known solutions. In several it improved on them. Sometimes it generalized a pattern found for a few inputs into a formula valid for all inputs. The team also combined the search with Deep Think and AlphaProof, which add proof generation and deeper reasoning. The work presents machine-guided search as a partner to human intuition in math.
arxiv-2511-02964:
F. Gentile, E. Daddi, and the Euclid Collaboration use the telescope's first release to ask how galaxies stop forming stars and change shape. Nearly one million galaxies, complete above a set mass, were split by star formation and by form, then mapped against mass and local crowding. The 2025 study covers a wide span of cosmic time when the universe was younger.

Two orders of events emerged. In crowded regions, galaxies stopped forming stars while still disc-shaped, and only later grew bulges. In open field regions, the bulge usually came first, with star formation still running, driven by slow internal processes. Quiet discs were common among light galaxies in dense areas, while star-forming bulge systems favored the field at high mass. The split paints environment as the switch.
arxiv-2511-03064:
L. Bazzanini, G. Angora, and the Euclid Collaboration train a neural network to find giant glowing arcs in Euclid images of galaxy clusters. Those arcs are distant galaxies stretched by strong gravitational lensing, and they probe cluster mass and cosmology. Wide surveys produce far too many images for human scanning, so detection must be automated. Their 2025 framework uses mask region-based convolutional networks to find and outline the arcs.

Training used over 4,500 simulated images, built by injecting fake lensed sources into Hubble pictures of ten well-mapped clusters. On a held-out test set the network reached 76 percent precision and 58 percent recall, scanning small fields in a fraction of a second. On real Euclid lenses it recovered two thirds of confirmed arcs above its size threshold. False alarms and faint arcs remain weak spots.
arxiv-2511-03264:
Manuel Ratz, Alessandro Parente, and Miguel Alfonso Mendez free two classic data-splitting tools from the need for neat grids. Methods that pull out main patterns from flow data usually assume samples sit evenly in space and time. Particle simulations and particle tracking in labs break that rule, scattering points unevenly as they move.

Their fix fits the scattered data with smooth radial basis shapes, then uses those smooth forms to do the math the pattern tools require. Holding the basis fixed in time cuts cost sharply. Tests show the mesh-free route can recover the leading patterns where sample counting fails. The approach opens pattern study to a wide class of particle-based data that grids cannot serve.
arxiv-2511-03464:
Mihriban Kocak Balik, Pekka Marttinen, and Negar Safinianaini introduce POEMS, a model that merges several molecular data layers while staying readable. Deep generative models often trade clarity for accuracy, or gain clarity by flattening their math and losing power. POEMS avoids that bargain by keeping the network nonlinear yet decoding through sparse links.

Sparse links tie each hidden factor to few measured features, so factors read as candidate biomarkers. Layers share one hidden space, which lets cross-layer links surface as well. A product-of-experts design fuses the layers under one probabilistic roof. The authors aim at disease studies where a model must both predict well and tell biologists which molecules drive its call.
arxiv-2511-03564:
G P A Nobre and a large collaboration announce ENDF/B-VIII.1, the newest recommended library of evaluated nuclear reaction data. Such libraries feed reactor design, shielding, medicine, and basic science with agreed cross sections for neutrons hitting hundreds of materials. Six years of advances since the prior release are folded in.

A flagship plutonium file was reevaluated by a joint international effort, and updated files for oxygen, uranium, iron, and many other key elements come from a coordinated international collaboration. Dosimetry cross sections join from a specialist library, and thermal scattering and other data see broad refreshes. Every simulation that leans on the library inherits its accuracy, so a careful community release of this scale quietly upgrades nuclear work worldwide.
arxiv-2511-03664:
Elsa Jochl and colleagues tune ultrastrong coupling between a single terahertz resonator and a sheet of electrons with an electric gate. The resonator is a circuit-style split ring at terahertz frequencies, and the electron gas sits in a strong magnetic field for spectroscopy. Gating squeezes the electrons into a patch far smaller than the wavelength.

That squeeze lets standing plasma waves appear even at zero field and changes how many electrons join the coupling. Coupling strength can be dialed down across a wide range in place, without swapping hardware. In-situ tuning matters for terahertz devices that must adapt, from sensors to quantum optics test beds. A single meta-atom with a knob offers a compact lab for light-matter extremes.
arxiv-2511-03864:
Noga Alon, Martin Milanic, and Pawel Rzazewski revisit two graph parameters built from tree decompositions: tree-independence number and induced matching treewidth. Each replaces ordinary bag size with a different measure, one using independent sets and the other using induced matchings touching a bag.

Induced matching treewidth never exceeds tree-independence number, yet complete bipartite graphs show the reverse gap can be huge. Earlier work bounded one by a function of the other when a fixed biclique is excluded, but the bound was exponential. Using the Kovari-Sos-Turan theorem, the authors improve that dependence for biclique-free graph classes. The note sharpens how closely the two parameters can be tied together.
arxiv-2511-03964:
Yinrui Liu, Laura Munteanu, and Stephen Dolan warn that how final-state interactions are modelled can distort how neutrino energy is rebuilt as much as the swing effects experiments hope to measure. The next round of long-baseline experiments aims for very precise oscillation parameters, so a hidden modelling confusion matters.

Using the DUNE flux and baseline as a case study, realistic changes in final-state interaction modelling shifted reconstructed energy spectra by amounts comparable to or larger than shifts from oscillation parameter changes. Those distortions can mimic changes in key parameters. Better study of the effect, theory-driven uncertainty models, and dedicated new measurements are urged so near detectors can deliver robust constraints.
arxiv-2511-04064:
Zhengran Zeng, Yixin Li, Rui Xie, Wei Ye, and Shikun Zhang benchmark language-model agent systems that claim to develop software end to end. Simple benchmarks and tangled implementation differences have made fair comparison hard, so the team build a demanding, dynamically curated benchmark that mimics realistic development work.

Evaluation mixes test-case functional checks with fine-grained, model-based verification of requirements. Three agent architectures were rebuilt on one shared foundation so workflow design alone explains differences. Leading agents met about half the requirements, with success hinging on task decomposition and collaboration strategy. Missed requirements and weak self-verification emerged as the main bottlenecks, more than raw coding ability.
arxiv-2511-04164:
Zoltan M Balogh, Karoly J Boroczky, and Agnes Mester prove quantitative stability results for distortion minimization in quasiconformal mapping theory. Catalog evidence attached a funding note to the title and named a spiral-stretch focus; the arXiv record gives the extremal mappings title used here, and that record governs.

For the mean distortion functional, sharp stability estimates cover the linear stretch and spiral stretch maps, which are extremals under suitable boundary conditions. If a mapping's mean distortion sits close to the minimum in its class, then the mapping itself must lie close to the extremal in stated Lebesgue norms. Near-optimal energy therefore forces near-optimal shape, with an explicit rate.
arxiv-2511-04264:
Qing-Cang Shui is the lead author among ten authors analysing a quasi-periodic oscillation in the active galaxy 1ES 1927+654, home to a supermassive black hole. X-ray flickering near black holes can map accretion geometry, but its physical origin is often unresolved, so a phase-resolved study of this signal is valuable.

A U-shaped lag-energy spectrum appears for the first time in a supermassive system, alongside coronal spectral changes across the oscillation phase. Plasma resonant oscillations inside the corona explain the signal adequately. Modelling and reverberation mapping place a contracting corona within a few gravitational radii of the hole, matching predictions for the shrinking, roughly ten-minute oscillation period reported.
arxiv-2511-04364:
Daniel Brosch and three colleagues extend Ramsey numbers to ordered and canonical settings. Classic Ramsey theory asks how large a graph must be before a set pattern must appear. Here the vertices sit in a fixed order, and copies must respect that order.

The team studies ordered Ramsey numbers for edge-colored complete graphs. They also treat canonical colorings, where the copy must be one color, rainbow, or ordered by its first or second vertex. New lower and upper bounds are proved for small cases of both types. Such bounds test how far known proof methods reach in one of combinatorics' oldest problem areas.
arxiv-2511-04664:
Phat Nguyen leads seven authors with SAFe-Copilot, a shared autonomy framework for driving. Self-driving systems still fail in rare and ambiguous scenes where humans cope well. Most shared control schemes only arbitrate low-level paths, which lose the driver's intent.

Their framework blends human input with planners at the level of strategy instead. A vision-language model reads driver actions and scene context to infer intent. It then synthesizes coherent plans that mediate between person and machine. Keeping intent in the loop aims to make handovers smoother and safer in the odd cases that break automation.
arxiv-2511-04764:
Madhurjya Changmai and two colleagues simulate small-scale dynamics inside a solar prominence. Prominences are dense, cool structures hanging in the hot corona. Their density contrast makes them prone to Rayleigh-Taylor instability, forming bubbles and rising plumes.

High-resolution magnetohydrodynamic runs use the open MPI-AMRVAC code on a thirty megameter square. Grid cells reach about twelve kilometers, and the run covers ten minutes of solar time. Secondary Kelvin-Helmholtz roll-ups appear along plume edges in the flow. Signs of magnetic reconnection inside the turbulence match recent observations, tying simulation to the limb views telescopes record.
arxiv-2511-04864:
Kyle Fogarty leads five authors rebuilding surfaces from point clouds with a self-learned attention prior. Recovering a clean surface from scattered points needs strong shape assumptions. Their method distills a prior from the input cloud itself, with no outside training data.

A small dictionary of learnable embeddings trains jointly with an implicit distance field. At each query point, the field attends across the dictionary by cross-attention. Repeating structures and long-range links inside the shape get captured and reused. Only self-supervised reconstruction losses drive the training. Shapes with repeated motifs, from chairs to ornaments, stand to benefit most.
arxiv-2511-04964:
Lingyu Zhang, Mitchell Wang, and Boyuan Chen show that expert judgment of science ideas shifts over time. Most AI idea tools treat human ratings as a fixed gold standard, as if a rater would score the same idea the same way twice.

In a two-wave study, 63 active scholars gave 7,938 ratings, with one fixed control idea mixed in each time. Scores for that same idea moved a fair amount, though the weight placed on traits like novelty and clarity stayed steady. A model tuned to first-wave ratings then picked ideas that fit the drifted second-wave taste less well.
arxiv-2511-05064:
Jinglin Liang and co-authors ask whether language models share hidden patterns in how they gather context. Past work looked at single models or single attention heads, so cross-model traits stayed out of view.

The team defines order-level attention, built by splitting a known attention rollout method by order. They find that this measure lines up across models at the same order, a shared trait they call a latent commonality. That shared pattern could deepen grasp of how models work and may help move knowledge from one model to another in time.
arxiv-2511-05664:
Seo Hyun Kim and co-authors speed up masked diffusion models, which write text by filling blanks over many rounds. The slow, fixed pace of that process is their main drawback. The team's sampler, KLASS, watches how much each token's prediction shifts between rounds.

Tokens whose predictions have settled are treated as stable and safe. KLASS then unmasks many such tokens in one step, with no extra training. On reasoning benchmarks it ran up to nearly three times faster than before while also beating standard greedy decoding. The authors checked the sampler on text, image, and molecular tasks, and present it as a broadly usable tool for diffusion models of many kinds.
arxiv-2511-05764:
Samvrit Srinath and co-authors address a skill new programmers need more than ever: breaking a big problem into small, well-defined parts. That skill, problem decomposition, is often missing from first computer science courses. With generative AI writing large amounts of code for students, the need to plan structure first has grown urgent.

The team built questions to test decomposition and describe how students received them. Long question contexts are a known hurdle, so they use question suites: staged question sets that build understanding before the hard part. They also had students draw decomposition diagrams by hand. The paper shares its materials and design lessons for teachers who want to assess this skill in beginners.
arxiv-2511-06164:
Constantinos Daskalakis, Vardis Kandiros, and Rui Yao study how many samples it takes to learn the wiring of a Gaussian directed graph model. Under an equal-variance assumption, earlier methods already used few samples. Their hidden cost was dependence on the covariance matrix's condition number, a measure that can grow large and ruin the sample counts.

The authors give an algorithm whose sample needs do not depend on that condition number at all. Matching lower bounds show their count is nearly the true cost of the problem. With one extra bounded-variance assumption, they also obtain a polynomial-time version, and simulations on synthetic data confirm the predicted behavior.
arxiv-2511-06364:
Yash Palan compares two workhorse methods for finding ground states of quantum systems: imaginary-time evolution and gradient descent. Both are usually run inside a chosen family of trial wavefunctions, here Gaussian states. The two methods are widely assumed to be fully equivalent ways of sliding toward the lowest energy.

Palan shows the equivalence holds formally for fermionic systems, where the particles obey Pauli exclusion. For bosonic systems, though, gradient descent consistently converges faster in the tests reported. That gap challenges the standard assumption and matters for practical simulations of bosonic many-body systems, where ground state searches consume large amounts of computing time.
arxiv-2511-06464:
Daniel Jaud and Lei Zhao study Kepler billiards, where a particle moves under gravity-like attraction and bounces off a conic wall. The playing field is part of a conic section with the Kepler center at a focus, and the dynamics turn out to be integrable, meaning hidden conserved quantities tame the motion. Attention centers on what the trajectory's second foci trace out.

For nonzero-energy orbits, the lines joining consecutive second orbital foci all touch one fixed circle. Building on that fact, the authors analyze motion inside and outside an elliptic wall in detail. They identify the elliptic curve where the dynamics straightens into a shift, and spell out exact conditions for orbits that repeat after a set number of bounces.
arxiv-2511-06564:
Michał Szyfelbein studies how to hunt for a hidden vertex in a graph when each query costs money and vertices carry different weights. Asking about a vertex either finds the target or reveals which connected piece remains after removing it. The goal is the strategy that minimizes the weighted average cost of the search.

Even with uniform weights and costs, the problem is NP-hard. Borrowing momentum from progress on the edge-query variant, Szyfelbein ties searching to vertex separation. That link yields an approximation algorithm for general graphs whose factor grows like the square root of the logarithm of the graph size, and a tighter factor, just above four, for trees.
arxiv-2511-06764:
Pu Wang and co-authors remove purple flare, the hazy violet fringe that blooms around bright spots in photographs. Classic fixes rely on rigid hand-crafted rules, and deep learning starves for paired training examples of this artifact. Their network instead corrects color through look-up tables in hue, saturation, and value space, adjusting each component on its own.

A chroma-aware tokenizer first reads the image and encodes the flare's status as semantic tokens from the hue and value channels. Those tokens drive a module that generates separate correction curves for all three channels. The team also built the first large-scale purple flare dataset with fresh metrics and a tailored loss, and their model led on every quantitative measure.
arxiv-2511-06864:
Pallav Jain, Yuvraj Agrawal, Ashutosh Nigam, and Pushpak Patil describe MetricSynth, a system that gathers engineering metrics from many tools into one place. Large software organizations keep their data siloed across platforms, so leaders lack a single view of team performance and system health. MetricSynth computes DORA and other key performance indicators across productivity, quality, and operational efficiency.

Scheduled ingestion jobs feed a dual-schema store, a processing engine pre-computes the metrics, and alerts flag problems proactively. Dashboards run on the open-source Metabase tool, guarded by role-based access control. The authors report the system cut manual reporting by an estimated twenty person-hours per week and sped up bottleneck detection, and they discuss how it scales.
arxiv-2511-07364:
Vaibhav Mavi, Shubh Jaroria, and Weiqi Sun teach language models to grade their own multi-step work so failures get caught early. Confidence estimation for self-evaluating models is well studied for single answers, but multi-step reasoning can go wrong midway, and a single end-of-task score may miss where. The authors extend self-evaluation to multi-step tasks and compare two natural designs: holistic scoring of the whole solution and step-by-step scoring of each intermediate step.

On two multi-step benchmark data sets, stepwise evaluation generally outperformed holistic scoring at detecting potential errors, improving the AUC-ROC by up to fifteen percent relative. The finding is useful guidance for deploying language models in high-stakes settings: ask the model to check each step. Its confidence becomes a meaningful failure alarm rather than a vague overall feeling.
arxiv-2511-07564:
Trishit Mondal, Ricardo Vinuesa, and Ameya Jagtap teach an algorithm to calm shocks on a wing. At transonic speeds, shock waves batter the boundary layer over an RAE2822 airfoil, causing oscillation and drag. Synthetic jets that puff and suck air can tame those unsteady flows.

Deep reinforcement learning steers the jets inside a high-fidelity flow solver with sharp spectral methods and adaptive meshing. The learner faces shock motion and trailing-edge waves at moderate Reynolds number. Successful control would cut buffet and improve efficiency for fast aircraft. The study tests whether learned policies can handle one of aerodynamics most stubborn unsteady problems.
arxiv-2511-07764:
Terry-Ann Suer, Edgar Steenstra, and Simone Marchi reconstruct the iron-rich baby planets whose cores survive as metal asteroids and iron meteorites. Such bodies formed where oxygen was scarce in the early inner Solar System. Differentiation models test how their interiors split into core and mantle.

Bodies about two hundred kilometers wide are modeled across oxygen levels and starting compositions drawn from known meteorite classes. Under oxygen-poor conditions, core fractions stay fairly consistent despite composition changes. Knowing how iron planetesimals formed clarifies the first steps of planet building and why some asteroids today are almost pure metal.
arxiv-2511-07964:
Clarissa Astuto checks time stepping methods for the Poisson Nernst Planck system, which models two ion species diffusing jointly. An electric potential couples the ion flows, and a small Debye length makes the system nearly neutral. That quasi-neutral limit reduces the model to one diffusion equation with an working factor.

Standard methods face strict balance limits and trouble with starting settings at small Debye lengths. Implicit explicit schemes, by contrast, stay asymptotically stable for all Debye lengths and need no special starting assumptions. Astuto validates a recently proposed asymptotic preserving scheme and checks how varied discretizations behave as neutrality approaches.
arxiv-2511-09164:
Jamil Khalouf-Rivera, Miguel Carvajal, and Francisco Pérez-Bernal ask how quantum systems can show paired energy levels without the usual parity symmetry. Many one-dimensional systems split into a symmetric phase and a doubly degenerate broken-symmetry phase. The authors show an antiunitary symmetry can protect the same pattern through momentum or coordinate instead.

Their example is a Kerr parametric oscillator with one- and two-photon drives, which keeps doubly degenerate levels despite broken parity. Such oscillators matter because squeezed versions serve as effective models for driven superconducting circuits. Degenerate levels there could help build protected qubits in setups that break parity. The observed spectral features also hint at further hidden symmetries in the system.
arxiv-2511-09264:
Zhihang Chen and Junwu Tu extend a theorem of Keller about cyclic homology to schemes over a general base ring. Keller showed that the cyclic homology of a scheme over a field equals that of its category of perfect complexes. The result highlights the categorical nature of cyclic homology.

In this note, the base field is replaced by an arbitrary commutative ring, a substantially wider setting. The same canonical isomorphism between the scheme's cyclic homology and its perfect-complex category survives. That generalization matters because many schemes in arithmetic geometry live over rings such as the integers, not fields. The note keeps Keller's conclusion intact while widening where it applies.
arxiv-2511-09564:
Yuxin Gou, Aming Wu, Richang Hong, and Meng Wang use the Mamba architecture to predict ground-state molecular shapes. A molecule's preferred 3D shape underlies its properties, so predicting it matters for chemistry and drug design. Mamba, a state space model built for long sequences, had barely been tried on molecules.

Their approach reads a molecule through three perspectives: atom types, atom positions, and the connections between atoms. Three dedicated scanning strategies build a full view of each perspective, and a bright-channel mechanism highlights the atoms most relevant to shape. On the QM9 and Molecule3D data sets the method clearly beats existing approaches, the authors report. It stays superior even with few training examples.
arxiv-2511-09664:
Quentin Marsal, Hui Liu, Emil J. Bergholtz, and Annica M. Black-Schaffer sharpen the tools used to diagnose topological phases in materials without tidy crystal order. Local quantum geometric markers can locate topological behavior in disordered or glassy systems. This paper studies what the markers' nonlocal structure reveals.

The markers behave like correlation functions for any material structure, the authors show. They vary sharply near topological transitions and paint a distinct real-space pattern for each transition. Even inside one symmetry class, varied transitions produce qualitatively distinct signatures, allowing finer discrimination. Nonlocal geometric indicators, the authors argue, offer a quicker, more versatile way to predict how stable topological phases are.
arxiv-2511-10164:
Periklis Mantenoglou, Luigi Bonassi, Enrico Scala, and Pedro Zuidberg Dos Martires speed up automated planning for problems carrying trajectory constraints, such as safety rules, ordering conditions, and intermediate goals. A standard trick compiles the constraints away so ordinary planners can run, but existing compilers ground the problem first. Grounding explodes on problems with many objects and complex actions, which is exactly where planning matters.

The authors propose two compilation methods that skip grounding entirely, working at the lifted level. They prove both compilers correct and analyze their worst-case running time. On domains from the latest International Planning Competition, the methods produced planning specifications orders of magnitude smaller than grounded compilers, while staying competitive in actual planning with a state-of-the-art planner.
arxiv-2511-10264:
Gal Hadar, Forest Agostinelli, and Shahaf S. Shperberg improve how reinforcement learning trains heuristic functions for shortest-path search problems. A heuristic estimates the remaining cost to a goal, and recent methods learn it with deep approximate value iteration. Those methods update each state from its single best neighbor, a one-step view that can learn slowly and noisily.

Their generalization runs limited-horizon searches during learning. Each state's heuristic is updated from the true shortest path to the search frontier, combining the edge costs along that path with the frontier states' current heuristic values. Better state sampling accompanies the richer updates. The paper positions limited-horizon search as a principled upgrade over single-step Bellman updates for learning search guidance.
arxiv-2511-10464:
Tao Jing and Cheng Li compare cold gas emission with mid-infrared light in 19 nearby star-forming galaxies from the PHANGS survey. Their maps combine ALMA observations of carbon monoxide with JWST images tracing dust and large carbon molecules called PAHs, reaching scales below 100 parsecs.

Using a new regression method designed to handle uncertainties and outliers, they find that the gas and infrared emissions follow log-log linear relations for most regions. The relations shift with local ionization conditions and vary from galaxy to galaxy, mainly through an intercept that shows a clear two-group pattern tied to star formation activity. The coupling also changes with measurement scale, and the brightest regions flatten away from the main relation.
arxiv-2511-10864:
Jose Vasquez and Xuping Zhang present WetExplorer, a self-driving tracked robot that takes over the laborious work of measuring greenhouse gases in wetlands. Counting those emissions matters for climate modeling and restoration, but manual chamber sampling across saturated terrain is slow and exhausting.

The robot combines low-ground-pressure locomotion, a centimeter-accurate sampling lift, dual real-time-kinematic sensor fusion, obstacle-avoiding planning, and deep-learning perception, all packaged in a containerized ROS2 software stack. In outdoor trials its localization error averaged under two centimeters, and its vision system estimated object poses within millimeters. Indoor trials showed the full planning pipeline placing the sampling chamber within a global tolerance of seventy millimeters, avoiding obstacles with no human help. The authors say this enables dense, long-running emission datasets.
arxiv-2511-10964:
Andrea Maurino asks how flaws in training data change the trust we can place in machine learning scores for loan risk. Banks use such scores to judge who may not repay, but real files often have gaps, noise, stray extremes, and wrong labels. Each flaw can hurt a model in a different way.

Maurino breaks a clean open data set on purpose with a software tool and tests ten common models, from forests of decision trees to logistic fits. The models differed a lot in how well they stood up to each flaw. The method and tools give banks and scholars a hands-on way to test data pipelines.
arxiv-2511-11064:
Sujoy Majumder, Nabadwip Sarkar, and Molla Basir Ahamed study the Bohr phenomenon for stable harmonic maps built with several Schwarz functions. The Bohr question asks how large a disk can be while a function's early terms still control its total size. Stable harmonic maps are smooth maps that keep a steady form under small shifts, and Schwarz functions are the bounded building blocks used here.

By mixing several Schwarz functions in careful ways, the authors prove sharp Bohr-type bounds and find the exact radii for some classes. They also derive Bohr-Rogosinski bounds, which skip early terms. Each radius is shown to be best possible, so the results close those cases.
arxiv-2511-11264:
Tobias Kappé, Alexandra Silva, and Jana Wagemaker wrote this booklet as an introduction to Kleene algebra, a set of laws for proving that two programs behave the same. Programs are modeled with regular expressions, the pattern language familiar from text search, and those expressions are tied to automata, the simple machines that run them. That tie is the engine behind the theory's central result.

The central result says an equality between regular expressions holds exactly when it can be proved from the Kleene laws alone. Each chapter closes with exercises to build intuition. An optional final chapter develops automata theory through coalgebra, a lens on systems defined by how they act.
arxiv-2511-11564:
Albert Tan, Mohsen Bayati, James Nordlund, and Roman Istomin study randomized experiments where treatment spills over between connected units and only some units may receive it. Think of a marketplace trial where treated sellers affect untreated ones, so the effect of full rollout is not what a simple comparison shows.

Two target quantities are defined: the total effect on eligible units and the total effect on ineligible ones. Estimators combine exposure mappings, generalized propensity scores, and flexible machine learning, with a projection linking treatment-level and outcome-level effects. Simulations and theory show when full-deployment effects can be recovered honestly despite interference.
arxiv-2511-11764:
Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar and three co-authors describe redesigning an introductory computer science survey course so students learn to use large language models with judgment. The course, taken after the first programming class, now weaves AI tools through its tour of computing subfields under a demystify, use, reflect structure.

Students are taught how the models work, shown live demonstrations with verification of outputs, and guided to use the tools inside a larger problem-solving loop. Disclosure of AI assistance is required, and reflection assignments ask students to examine their own habits and the shifting landscape of programming. The goal is graduates who are informed users, not dependent ones.
arxiv-2511-11964:
A. Rothstein and four co-authors parallelize two real-time physics codes that steer plasma experiments on the DIII-D tokamak, so control decisions can use heavier physics without missing their deadlines. TORBEAM traces electron cyclotron waves used for heating, and STRIDE evaluates ideal plasma stability limits, both central to future fusion plant operation.

A safe multi-threading library built for the plasma control system runs real-time TORBEAM consistently under twenty milliseconds and STRIDE in about one hundred. The library itself is reusable for other real-time codes. Fusion control is a race between physics and the control clock, and this work buys the physics more time.
arxiv-2511-12064:
Hiroshi Hirai works on optimization over curved spaces known as Hadamard manifolds, where the aim is to make a measure based on a function's gradient as small as possible. Earlier work studied the special case of minimizing the gradient norm itself. Hirai broadens that problem by allowing a wider class of measures on the space of differentials.

For a natural class defined by convexity and by invariance under parallel transport, he defines a generalized gradient flow meant to drive the measure down. For basic spaces, including products of positive definite matrix spaces, the flow reaches the lowest possible value in the limit. The result is then applied to tensor problems linked to entanglement polytopes.
arxiv-2511-12264:
Anna V. Kononova and sixteen co-authors argue that benchmarking in evolutionary computation needs a rethink if it is to serve real practice. Popular synthetic test suites isolate clean effects, but they poorly match the structure, limits and missing information of real optimization problems. That gap leads to misuse in contests, algorithm choice and industry decisions.

The authors list gaps in current suites and tools, from few real-world-inspired problems to weak support for noisy and multi-objective cases. Their vision centers on curated benchmarks drawn from real problems, feature spaces that practitioners can use, and shared performance databases kept by the community. They call for a living system that grows with real insight.
arxiv-2511-12364:
Matteo Battisti describes the X-ray and gamma-ray detector planned for a NASA balloon mission that will study ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and very-high-energy neutrinos from high altitude. The balloon will fly at about thirty-three kilometres, where nearly horizontal air showers develop slowly through thin air. Those early shower stages are poorly understood.

At those stages, fast electrons and positrons in the shower can emit X-rays and gamma rays by synchrotron radiation. The detector is built to catch that emission in place, during the flight from New Zealand planned for spring 2027. Its readings should help reveal how horizontal showers begin and grow, ahead of a planned satellite mission.
arxiv-2511-12764:
Hao Wei, Aleksandra Franz, Bjoern List, and Nils Thuerey fix an error problem in hybrid solvers for partial differential equations. Hybrid solvers pair a coarse numerical solver with a learned corrector to simulate physics faster. The usual design applies the corrector's fix directly to the solver's state at each step. The authors show why that fails: small perturbations get amplified as the simulation rolls forward, and errors snowball, especially in chaotic systems over long runs.

Their Indirect Neural Corrector instead weaves the learned correction into the governing equations, so the solver itself produces the corrected state. Theory shows this cuts the error amplification sharply, and the design accepts any neural network and solver pairing. Across benchmarks from a one-dimensional chaotic system to three-dimensional turbulence, the method greatly improved long-term accuracy, stopped blowups under aggressive coarsening, and delivered large speedups. It offers stability without giving up learned speed.
arxiv-2511-12964:
Mehrab Mustafy Rahman and three co-authors fix a quiet flaw in semi-supervised image classifiers: they are confidently wrong. Semi-supervised learning trains on few labeled and many unlabeled images, but its predictions claim more certainty than they earn. Mixup, blending pairs of training images, improves calibration in supervised settings, yet random mixup fails here because the pseudo-labels assigned to unlabeled images are overconfident and unreliable.

CalibrateMix instead reads the training pattern to sort samples into easy-to-learn and hard-to-learn, then mixes easy with hard examples. Across several benchmark image datasets, the targeted mixup lowered expected calibration error while matching or improving scores against rival methods. Honest confidence matters wherever a model's stated confidence drives a decision. Steering mixup by difficulty, rather than chance, gives semi-supervised models a more honest sense of what they know.
arxiv-2511-13264:
Keshav Gupta and 5 co-authors propose SymGS, a compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. Splatting renders new views fast and with sharp detail, but scene files can grow to several gigabytes. Most current tools shrink files by finding similar parts and quantizing them, which leaves a clear limit.

SymGS adds learnable mirrors to a scene so repeated parts made by reflection can be stored once. It plugs into strong existing methods such as HAC and improves them further. Across benchmark scenes it reached about one hundred eight times compression on average while keeping image quality, with larger gains on big scenes.
arxiv-2511-13364:
Hangxu Liu, Yifei Zhu, and Zhenggang Lan automate the hunt for the motions that steer excited molecules toward different decay paths. In non-adiabatic dynamics, experts once picked reaction coordinates by hand and by intuition, a slow bottleneck for photochemistry. Their framework learns those coordinates straight from surface-hopping trajectory data.

An autoencoder compresses the motion, while clustering and information entropy sort trajectories into channels and name the structural moves that govern each one. Applied to keto isocytosine and the methaniminium cation, the method found the channels and active coordinates quickly and accurately. The work turns raw simulation output into clear reaction stories.
arxiv-2511-13564:
Péter L. Erdős and 3 co-authors show that degree sequence regions where every sequence is graphic can be sampled rapidly. A degree sequence lists the connection counts of a graph's vertices, and a region fixes length, total sum, and upper and lower bounds. Sampling such regions quickly matters for testing network models against random graphs.

They prove every fully graphic region of this kind meets a strong stability condition with an explicit polynomial bound. That stability implies the switch Markov chain, which swaps edges at random, mixes rapidly on all such sequences. They also prove a converse direction: strong stability across a region forces the vast majority of its sequences to be graphic.
arxiv-2511-14164:
Yibo Meng, Rong Fu, Lyumanshan Ye, and four co-authors ask what smart screens can do for people who are dying alone. Tech work on death tends to deal with plain tasks, such as who keeps a person's files. It often misses the deep lone-ness of the last stage of life. The team held long talks with fourteen people who were both lone and near death.

From those talks they built a map of needs of mind, body, social life, and spirit. They also set out a design frame of three pillars and twelve rules for screens that act as kind companions. One clear rule stood out: aim to go past what people can give, not to fake it. Fake warmth can deepen the lone feeling.
arxiv-2511-14564:
Ali Eidi and Richard Dwight study spread in averaged turbulence runs coupled to a pressure fluctuation model. Exact fluctuation forecasts matter for flow induced vibration and fatigue. The authors combine global sensitivity analysis, surrogate modeling, and Bayesian inference. Two test cases are used: turbulent channel flow and turbulent annular flow.

In channel flow, calibrated setting distributions improve agreement with source data. In annular flow, settings are harder to identify from data, yet predictions still follow high fidelity trends. The results show both promise and limits of calibration for wall bounded turbulence. The work helps engineers judge when tuned models can be trusted for fluctuation loads.
arxiv-2511-14764:
Mariya Hendriksen, Svitlana Vakulenko, and three co-authors study when an online shopping assistant should suggest moving to a screen. People now shop across voice assistants and displays, and a photo can help a lot for some products. A switch prompt that fires too often, though, just annoys the user.

The team defines a new task: predicting from a spoken query whether the shopper truly wants to see images. They train and test the idea on large-scale production data with hundreds of thousands of voice queries and linked product records. Getting this call right would let assistants offer a device switch only when it clearly improves product discovery.
arxiv-2511-15464:
Dabin Jeong, Amirhossein Vahidi, and twelve co-authors present SIGMMA, a method that learns from two views of the same tissue at once. One view is a stained tissue image, the standard microscope slide used in pathology. The other is a spatial gene map that shows which genes are active at each spot. Earlier methods matched the two views at only one scale.

SIGMMA aligns the views at several scales and models cells as a graph, so links between nearby cells shape what is learned. That design captures fine cell detail and broad tissue layout together. Across data sets it improved gene activity prediction and matching between the two views by clear margins over prior methods.
arxiv-2511-15864:
David O. H. Cutler, Jonas Karlsson, and Neil J. A. Sloane extend a playful classic problem about cutting a pancake into the most pieces. A well-known textbook chapter counted pieces from cuts made by a straight blade, a V-shaped blade, and a Z-shaped blade. The new work asks what happens with far more exotic cookie-cutter shapes, including many-armed stars, chains of segments, and long-legged letter shapes.

Other shapes include a convex polygon, a circle, figure forms, star polygons, and a lollipop shape. Constrained versions of several letters, where cuts must obey extra rules, are also treated. In most cases the authors determine the exact maximum number of pieces, while for the constrained letter A and the lollipop they give bounds.
arxiv-2511-16464:
Koki Otaki, Yudai Kazuno, and Masao Mori estimate how often dark matter subhaloes inside a Milky Way-like galaxy crash into each other. In the standard cold dark matter picture, small structures build galaxies by colliding and merging, so the collision rate shapes how subhaloes evolve and how dwarf galaxies interact.

The authors first build an analytic model for the distribution of subhalo pairs in relative distance and velocity, based on the host halo's phase-space distribution. They then track subhalo orbits in cosmological simulations of Milky Way-like hosts. Violent encounters, closer than the sum of the scale radii, happen about two hundred times per billion years. Their time scale is far shorter than the host's dynamical time, so collisions are a frequent part of subhalo life.
arxiv-2511-16664:
Ali Taghibakhshi and fifteen co-authors present Nemotron Elastic, a framework for training one reasoning language model that contains several smaller models inside it. Training a separate model for every deployment size is prohibitively expensive, and standard pruning or distillation still burns hundreds of billions of tokens per compressed model.

Nested submodels share the parent's weights and can be extracted at deployment with no extra training, selected by an end-to-end trained router and a two-stage curriculum built for reasoning models. Applied to a twelve-billion-parameter parent, the method produced nine- and six-billion-parameter models using only about 110 billion training tokens. That is a cost cut of more than three hundredfold versus training a family from scratch. Each nested model matched or beat the state of the art at its size.
arxiv-2511-16864:
Leighton Barnes and Alex Dytso study when the optimal estimator of a signal in Gaussian noise is nearly linear, and what that forces the signal's distribution to be. Under squared error, a linear conditional mean occurs exactly when the prior is Gaussian; under absolute error the optimal rule is the conditional median, where orthogonality tools fail.

Recent work showed Gaussianity is also the unique prior giving an exactly linear conditional median. This paper builds the stability theory: approximate linearity quantitatively forces closeness to a Gaussian prior. For the mean, explicit rates are given in the Lévy metric. For the median, the authors develop a Hermite expansion and adjoint operator framework to prove the same moral, that near-linear optimal estimation is a fingerprint of near-Gaussian data.
arxiv-2511-17064:
František Bartoš, Suzanne Hoogeveen, Alexandra Sarafoglou, and Samuel Pawel tackle a synthesis problem created by many-analysts and multiverse studies. In those studies, many teams analyze the same dataset in different reasonable ways, and results scatter. Averaging them with standard meta-analysis would double-count the single dataset and produce overconfident conclusions.

Their fix, single-dataset meta-analysis, uses a weighted likelihood that counts the dataset's information at most once. It still yields an average effect across analytic choices, plus a measure of how much analysts disagree, and it works with common software after small input changes. They test it on studies of racial bias in soccer refereeing, marital status and heart disease, and technology use and well-being. The method gives these robustness studies the careful summary statistics they lacked.
arxiv-2511-17464:
Tanzim Hossain Romel and four co-authors design a patient-centric system for sharing electronic health records, built on a blockchain but keeping the records themselves off it. Encrypted health resources in the standard FHIR format sit in ordinary storage, while the public blockchain records only cryptographic commitments and patient-signed, time-bounded permissions. Keys reach authorized parties by public-key wrapping, so storage providers can be curious without being able to read anything.

The authors formalize the security goals, confidentiality, integrity, attributable authorization, and auditable permission history, and provide a working contract implementation organized per patient. Permission grants cost modest transaction fees on the main chain and far less on layer-two networks, and retrieving a megabyte record took about a second. They discuss metadata privacy and health privacy regulations, arguing the design returns real control to patients.
arxiv-2511-17764:
Patryk Michalski, Arturo Konderak, Wojciech Bruzda, and Remigiusz Augusiak build new Bell inequalities, tests that separate quantum links between particles from any classic local story. For most such tests the best possible quantum score is hard to find exactly, which limits their use.

Their construction gives that bound exactly and generalizes two classic inequalities. Under stated conditions the tests can certify Majorana fermions in a device independent way, meaning the claim rests on observed data alone. They also identify a new equivalence that must be part of self testing, the standard for certifying a quantum setup.
arxiv-2511-17864:
Adrian Goldwaser, Michael Munn, Javier Gonzalvo, and Benoit Dherin show that the effect of a prompt's context on a modern transformer can be rewritten as a small change to its weights. Earlier work proved this for a basic transformer, using a rank one patch that depends on the input tokens.

For a Gemma style block they give an exact solution, patching both the main weight matrices and a normalization scale. A general framework then covers many layer types, including gated and mixture of experts blocks, under two controllability conditions. The result gives a simpler lens on how prompts reshape a model from inside.
arxiv-2511-18064:
Szilard Revesz and Imre Ruzsa develop a theory of means and densities on groups, in a paper titled Densitometria, its first part treating discrete groups. An upper mean is a kind of average for bounded functions that ignores local behavior, formalized by a restricted additivity rule for shifted copies of a function.

They ask when a functional defined on part of the domain is a mean. They also ask how to recover the upper mean behind it, whether it is unique, and what values an upper mean can take on a given function. They find the extreme means and propose clearer names for them, with partial answers for the parallel questions about densities.
arxiv-2511-18464:
Jiayi Guo and Zijun Gao pick the best method to estimate how a treatment's effect varies across people. The true effect per person can never be seen, so a direct score for each candidate method is out of reach. A wrong pick can mislead care or policy choices built on the estimate.

They recast the pick as a multiple testing task. A cross fitted score, weighted by a decaying factor, ranks candidates with no ground truth. A two way split keeps the nuisance fits apart from the weight learning, which steadies the test. A stability based limit theorem gives control of the family error rate. On three health test sets the method cuts false picks sharply next to common tools.
arxiv-2511-18964:
Antonia Wüst and five co-authors turn visual concepts into small programs that a vision language model helps write. Such models ace broad multimodal tasks yet fail at systematic visual reasoning, with outputs that clash or break logic. Neuro-symbolic tools promise order, but their perception parts tend to be rigid and domain bound.

Their Vision-Language Programs keep the model's flexible perception and move reasoning out. The model drafts structured visual descriptions, which compile into programs that run on the image itself. Programs stay consistent with task rules and yield human readable explanations, which ease shortcut fixes. Tests on synthetic and real sets beat direct model calls. Interpretable steps are the gain.
arxiv-2511-19264:
Amirtha Varshini A S, Duminda S. Ranasinghe, and Hok Hei Tam test what probing tools can truly show about GFlowNets, models that build molecules step by step. Chemists hesitate to use such models because their choices are hard to read. The study examines SynFlowNet, a synthesis-aware version trained toward drug-like molecules.

Probes, saliency maps, and sparse autoencoders are checked against strict controls, including shuffled labels and an untrained twin network. Chemical traits decode easily from the trained model, but the untrained one does almost as well. That result means the signal comes mostly from graph structure, not learned policy.
