Their plan breaks the jump into steps led by sense. Each step narrows the kind of thing the user may want next. By the last step the code is picked with the full chain in view. A chain of steps could give picks that fit taste with more care. It could also let staff see why a pick was made, step by step.
arxiv-2601-18764:
Sahil Satapathy, Projjwal Kanjilal, and A. Bhattacharyay give a plain way to chart the phases of a trapped cloud of cold atoms with three spin states. Such a cloud sits in a trap that holds it in a near line. Its atoms can pair their spins to pull close or push off, and that choice sets the phase of the whole cloud. To chart the phases by the full rules is slow and dear.

Their way takes a smart guess at the cloud's form and tunes the guess to the least force. From that tuned guess they read the form of the cloud in each spin state. The full phase chart drops out at low cost. A cheap chart helps labs pick trap sets that land on the phase they want. It also gives a first map for more strict work to check.
arxiv-2601-18964:
Karen Meagher and Hermie Monterde study quantum walks that refuse to leave home. In a quantum walk, a particle spreads across a graph's nodes by quantum rules. A node is called sedentary if a walk that starts there tends to stay put, which is odd for such a spread prone process.

The pair prove that almost all planar graphs and almost all trees have at least two such stay at home nodes. The result holds for any choice of edge weights. Sedentariness, it seems, is not a quirk but a common trait of these graph families, a fact that may shape quantum search design.
arxiv-2601-19064:
David Bryant, Celine Scornavacca, and David L. Swofford present a new way to score an evolutionary tree. Few tools in the field are used more than Felsenstein's pruning method, which computes how likely a tree is given DNA data. Their method, LvD, rests on a different split of the tree's structure.

LvD works for all standard models of how DNA letters change over time. A rival route to the same score gives software writers a check on old code and, in some cases, a faster path. Tree scores sit under nearly all modern work on how species relate, so even small gains spread wide.
arxiv-2601-19764:
Guram Donadze, Manuel Ladra, and Pilar Páez-Guillán revisit a classic theorem in group theory. Schur's theorem links a group to its Schur multiplier, an object that measures how the group can be extended. A natural hope is that the multiplier of a Noetherian group is always finitely generated. The authors show this hope is false.

They give cases where the multiplier of such a group is not finitely generated. They also study the non-abelian tensor product of groups, a construction with wide algebraic use. They prove it preserves the polycyclic property, even when one factor is only Noetherian. New versions of Schur's theorem round out the paper. The results correct assumptions that specialists may have taken for granted.
arxiv-2601-19864:
Thomas Bieske and Frederic Bowen study a kind of solution to partial differential equations in an unusual geometry. Martinet spaces lack the algebraic group law of Carnot groups. They also lack the triangular vector fields of Grushin-type spaces. That makes standard methods hard to apply.

The authors establish the basic properties of viscosity solutions in these spaces. Viscosity solutions are a weak notion designed for equations with no smooth solutions. They then prove uniqueness for strictly monotone elliptic equations and for the infinite Laplace equation. Uniqueness matters because a model with several right answers predicts nothing. The work extends a workhorse theory to a setting that had resisted it. The proofs are strict and step by step. Each claim rests on the last.
arxiv-2601-20164:
Jim Maar, Denis Paperno, Callum McDougall, and Neel Nanda ask whether language models plan ahead while they write. A model picks one word at a time, yet it may pick a word now to set up a word it expects later. A prior study of rhyming verse suggested this kind of implicit planning in one model.

The authors build metrics to measure such planning and apply them to rhyme generation and question answering. Clear measures would help researchers test when a model is truly planning and when it is only reacting. That question bears on how much trust to place in model outputs on longer tasks.
arxiv-2601-20464:
Alejandro Benito-Santos and five colleagues survey how research where visualization meets the humanities is evaluated. The field, called VIS*H, is marked by a tension between chasing analytical insight and interpretive meaning. Standard evaluation frameworks judge tools by analytical utility and communicative power.

That yardstick can mismatch the interpretive aims of humanities scholarship, which does not always seek a single right reading. The authors survey evaluation practices across this borderland. Their map can help both sides judge work by goals the work actually has, rather than by imported standards. The field is young, and its rules are still being set by the work now in print.
arxiv-2601-20664:
Dimitrios Karapiperis and three colleagues present ALER, an active learning system for entity resolution. Entity resolution links records that refer to the same real thing across datasets. Supervised deep models do it well but need massive labeled datasets that are expensive to build, which blocks many real uses.

Active learning cuts the labeling need by asking humans about the most informative pairs. Existing approaches, though, hit scalability bottlenecks. ALER is a hybrid design aimed at efficient resolution. Cheaper record linkage would help hospitals, governments, and firms merge messy data with confidence.
arxiv-2601-20764:
Saeed Akbar, Muhammad Waqas, and Rahmat Ullah design control software for fog computing. Their 2026 paper presents Agentic Fog, a policy-driven framework. Fog computing places small servers near users, between devices and the cloud. These systems face strict latency limits and workloads that change by the minute. They also see only part of the picture at any time.

Recent agentic AI tools lean on large language models to reason. The authors argue such tools fit infrastructure poorly. They cost too much compute, act at random, and resist formal analysis. Their framework instead drives agents with explicit policies. The paper aims at distributed intelligence that stays fast, cheap, and open to checking. It speaks to builders of edge systems that cannot wait on the cloud.
arxiv-2601-20864:
Chloe Cheng and a large team of co-authors argue that early galaxies hide more mass than they seem to. Their 2026 paper concerns the initial mass function, the mix of star masses a galaxy is born with. JWST has shown that massive galaxies formed far faster than models predicted. Many had built a large mass in stars about twelve billion years ago. That speed strains the standard picture of galaxy growth.

The authors point to a bottom-heavy mass function as the key. Bottom-heavy means far more small, dim stars than usual. Such stars add mass while adding little light. A galaxy can then be heavier than its glow suggests. This hidden mass could ease the clash with models. The paper reframes how astronomers read the light of the first galaxies.
arxiv-2601-21564:
Antonio Almudévar and Alfonso Ortega remove the trace of chosen training data by compressing a model's inner representations. Unlearning is needed for privacy law and for fixing models trained on bad data. Most methods tweak the model's weights, which can be unstable and costly.

Their framework works in representation space instead of weight space. Compression squeezes out the information tied to the data to be forgotten. Working one level up may give cleaner removal with less damage to other skills. The approach offers a fresh route for honoring deletion requests in trained models.
arxiv-2601-21864:
Jinhao Pan and co-authors study how large language models pick up social bias. Models can repeat harmful stereotypes, which limits their safe use. Most attempts to debias them work by suppression: changing parameters, prompts, or the neurons tied to biased behavior.

The authors argue that suppression is brittle, generalizes weakly, wastes data, and can damage general ability. Their 2026 preprint, called KnowBias, takes the opposite road and enhances neurons tied to knowledge about bias itself. Strengthening a model's own grasp of stereotypes, rather than muting parts of it, could offer a steadier fix. The debate matters because these models now answer questions for millions of people every day.
arxiv-2601-22164:
Christos Tsourveloudis tests whether detectors that find anything in ordinary photos can cope with the view from above. Open-vocabulary detection uses vision-language models to recognize new categories from text alone, with no retraining, and it performs strongly on natural images. Aerial imagery is a different world of tiny objects and odd angles.

Tsourveloudis presents the first systematic benchmark of this transfer. Five state-of-the-art open-vocabulary models are evaluated on an aerial dataset of several thousand images across eighty categories. His 2026 preprint maps which models survive the move to drones and satellite views. That map matters for search and rescue, farming, and disaster mapping, where new object types appear without warning.
arxiv-2601-22364:
Eghbal Hosseini and four co-authors show that the shape of a text can bend how a model lays out its inner states. Past work found that models straighten these paths in deep layers, which may aid next-word calls. Their 2026 preprint asks how the build of the context itself reshapes that layout.

They track how the inner paths curve or align as the input form changes. The work links surface form to deep structure inside the model. That link can help explain why some prompts work and others fail. It also guides safer, clearer prompt design.
arxiv-2601-22564:
Takashi Shimada and Kunihiko Kaneko show that microbes feeding on each other's leaks can coexist in wild, chaotic swarms. Species trade chemicals: each leaks metabolites that others take up. Their 2026 preprint studies a simple model of that cross-feeding web.

In the model, many species persist past what the exclusion rule would allow. The system can even fall into high-dimensional chaos, with counts swinging in complex ways. The result helps explain the rich mix seen in real microbial worlds. It ties food-web shape to diversity itself. The model is simple, which makes the result striking.
arxiv-2601-22664:
Zixuan Huang and a team align reward models with human taste in real time, past mere word sense. RLHF trains models from human likes, yet the policy can overfit the reward model and game its quirks. Their 2026 preprint targets that reward overoptimization, where scores rise while true quality stalls.

Their reward model updates as it is used, staying in step with the policy it grades. A live, aligned grader should cut gaming and drift. The work matters for every lab that trains by feedback. It treats alignment as a moving target. That honesty is the point.
arxiv-2601-22764:
Deepak Kumar, Emmanouil Karystinaios, Gerhard Widmer, and Markus Schedl test how far pre-trained language models go on symbolic music. Music and language share deep parallels, which invites the swap. Their 2026 preprint runs controlled comparisons of supervised tuning against preference-based tuning for music tasks.

The checks cover both grasp of music and generation of it. Knowing which tuning wins, and by how much, guides music AI design. It also shows where language skill fails to transfer. The work is a careful bake-off, not a hype claim. Its value is the clean comparison.
arxiv-2601-22964:
Yufei He and a large team present EvoClinician, a medical AI that learns as it works through a case. Most medical AI judges a complete patient file in one shot. Real diagnosis is a chain of questions and tests, chosen step by step while watching cost and time.

Their agent evolves at test time, improving its approach across many turns with one patient. Stepwise inquiry matches how good clinicians actually narrow down a disease. An agent that asks better questions could cut needless tests and reach answers sooner. Test-time evolution lets the agent adapt within a single case, rather than waiting for a future round of retraining.
arxiv-2601-23064:
Hari Krishna Gadi and six co-authors locate photos by learning geography's natural hierarchy. Visual geolocation predicts where an image was taken, a hard task at global scale. Older methods need huge image stores, ignore how places nest inside each other, or blur fine detail.

Their HierLoc embeds entities in hyperbolic space, a geometry that fits tree-like structure well. Continent, country, and city levels can then guide the search together. Better geolocation helps organize photo archives and verify where images were really shot. Hyperbolic embeddings fit geography's nesting naturally, since space in that geometry grows like a tree of regions.
arxiv-2601-23164:
Daniel Ezer, Alon Peled-Cohen, and Yishay Mansour study bandit learning where the reward rule itself is noisy. In their stochastic linear bandit model, each action's reward depends on a parameter vector. That vector is resampled independently, adding parameter noise on top of ordinary randomness.

Bandit algorithms must learn well despite never seeing a stable target. The model fits settings like ads or dosing, where each user's response rule differs. Theory for noisy parameters helps set realistic expectations for adaptive systems. Independent resampling of the parameter vector each round defines the noise model whose regret behavior the study analyzes.
arxiv-2602-00164: Khairul Alam and coauthors study why fix related pull requests from AI coding agents stay unmerged. Such agents, including Codex, Devin, and Copilot, now draft many fixes in real repositories, but value depends on maintainer acceptance. The team analyzes 8106 fix related pull requests from five agents in the AIDEV POP data set, tracking merged, closed unmerged, and still open outcomes. They then read 326 closed unmerged cases in depth, over about 100 person hours. Their catalog lists 12 failure reasons, led by test failures and prior fixes by other pull requests.
arxiv-2602-00364: Jiate Li and team propose query agnostic black box attacks on LLM based retrieval, titled Someone Hid It. Existing attack studies mostly presume a known query and rely on victim model parameters or interactions, which are rarely accessible in practice. The new method generates transferable injection tokens from zero shot surrogate language models without victim queries or victim model knowledge, exposing practical security risks.
arxiv-2602-00564: Xiang Zheng and colleagues build ReasoningMath-Plus, a benchmark of 150 curated problems testing structural reasoning, not final answers alone. Existing sets lean on template computation and shallow arithmetic, missing coordination, synthesis, and spatial inference skills. Each problem stresses interacting constraints, constructive solutions, or insight, with a skeleton for process scoring. They also introduce HCRS, a deterministic step-level score, and a reward model trained on traces. Leading models reach up to 5.8/10 on answers yet score lower under HCRS, showing answer-only metrics overstate robustness.
arxiv-2602-01364: Lile Wang and co-authors simulate ultra-hot Jupiter WASP-121b from surface to escaping winds, joining fluid flow, non-equilibrium chemistry, and ray-traced light. The base run shows day-night churn low down and near-sonic winds high up, bent into two spiral arms by star pull. Iron traces spin-ruled inner layers, sodium marks thick spiral arms where recombination offsets photoionization, and hydrogen and helium trace wider gas. Spiral speeds near 40 km/s match fast sodium and hydrogen absorption without strong super-rotation jets.
arxiv-2602-01664: Mingda Zhang and colleagues propose FlowSteer, where an agent designs the workflow an executor runs, replacing human dependent construction. Existing construction lacks graph feedback and cannot repair errors in loop. FlowSteer adds a Workflow Canvas, a graph state environment returning checked feedback for every atomic edit. On it, an agent issues one edit per turn from live canvas feedback, trained by reinforcement learning, under the name Reinforced Progressive Canvas Editing. It plugs into operator libraries and backends, and tests on twelve data sets show it beating baselines across tasks.
arxiv-2602-02164: Pengfei He and others propose Co-RedTeam, a multi-agent method mirroring professional red-teaming for auto vulnerability finding and exploitation. Earlier methods falter through weak contact, poor grounding in execution, and no reuse of experience. The team splits analysis into coordinated finding and exploitation stages fed by security knowledge, code-aware thought, and long-term memory. Agents plan, run, validate, and refine actions from real execution feedback. Across demanding benchmarks, the system beats strong rivals on several backbones with high exploitation success and a clear finding gain.
arxiv-2602-02464:
Or Shafran and 5 co-authors argue that concepts inside a language model live in regions, not single directions, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Interpretability methods usually hunt for one global direction per concept, assuming concepts separate cleanly along a line. That misses concepts with curved or multi-dimensional structure.

Their tool, a mixture of factor analyzers, models activation space as a collection of Gaussian regions, each with its own center and local pattern of variation. Trained at large scale on Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B, the model captured complex nonlinear structures. On localization and steering benchmarks it beat unsupervised baselines, rivaled supervised methods, and often steered behavior more strongly than sparse autoencoders. The authors propose local geometry as the right unit for discovering and controlling concepts at scale.
arxiv-2602-02564:
Subhodeep Ghosh and 4 co-authors coordinate teams of AI agents to produce trustworthy labels without any ground truth, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Labeling is essential for supervised learning, yet human workflows are costly, slow, and uneven as data sets grow in size and kind. Their system, AURA, targets reliability-aware machine annotation at scale.

Multiple agents make and check labels together. At the core sits a classical probabilistic model that jointly infers the hidden true labels and each annotator's reliability through confusion matrices. Expectation-maximization settles conflicting annotations and merges noisy predictions into final labels. Across four benchmark data sets, accuracy improved by up to about six percent over rivals. With poor-quality annotators, gains reached fifty percent. AURA also scores annotator reliability, so label quality can be audited without pre-validation.
arxiv-2602-02764:
Jared T. White settles a question in Banach algebra theory by exhibiting one algebra whose bidual behaves differently under its two natural products, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Every Banach algebra's bidual carries two Arens products, two competing ways to extend multiplication. Whether the Jacobson radical, a measure of an algebra's degenerate part, can differ between those products was asked by Dales and Lau.

White's answer is yes. The example is a Beurling algebra, a weighted convolution algebra, built on the free group with three generators. For that algebra, the radical computed with the first Arens product does not equal the radical computed with the second. The construction is concrete. It closes a named open question and warns that bidual arguments must track which product is in force, since even basic invariants can split.
arxiv-2602-02864:
Self-driving cars think too slowly when they reason step by step, and Yi Gu and 10 co-authors tackle that delay in 2026. Vision-language-action models use chain-of-thought reasoning, written steps before acting. Writing each step in order creates latency that real-time driving cannot afford.

Their method, FastDriveCoT, maps the reasoning steps into a dependency graph. Steps that do not depend on each other, like spotting key objects and summarizing traffic rules, run in parallel. Other steps still follow in order. Experiments across several model designs follow. Reasoning ran three to four times faster, and total delay fell sharply. The driving benefits of the reasoning itself were preserved.
arxiv-2602-02964:
Migrating Python test suites between frameworks with language models is tested by Altino Alves and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Many projects want to move from unittest to Pytest for simpler assertions and reusable fixtures. Doing that migration by hand is slow, so automation could modernize suites faster.

The authors built a dataset of real migrations from the top hundred Python open-source projects. They evaluated two leading models under three prompting strategies and two temperature settings. Generated migrations were actually run in their test suites. Slightly under half passed, so models can accelerate migration but with caveats. One model migrated conservatively, keeping class-based tests. The other transformed more aggressively toward function-based tests.
arxiv-2602-03064:
Crowded real-world scenes of people are captured for robot perception by Sandika Biswas and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Most three-dimensional human pose datasets show one person or a laboratory setting. Robots, though, must estimate poses, track movement, and understand activity in busy indoor and outdoor spaces from their own moving viewpoint among many nearby people.

Their dataset, JRDB-Pose3D, was recorded from a mobile robotic platform. It provides three-dimensional pose annotations with consistent body-shape parameters and track identities over time. Frames average five to ten people, with up to thirty-five at once. Frequent occlusions and truncated bodies reflect real conditions. The dataset inherits two-dimensional pose, social grouping, activity, and semantic annotations from its parent dataset, supporting many downstream tasks.
arxiv-2602-03164:
Forecasting that remembers its own past is proposed by Xiaoyu Tao, leading 6 other authors, in a system called MemCast. Time series forecasting supports decisions in many fields. Language-model forecasters perform well but rarely build up experience explicitly or keep evolving after deployment. So hard-won lessons from earlier predictions are lost instead of guiding the next forecast for a similar pattern.

MemCast organizes learned experience into a layered memory. Historical patterns summarize past predictions, reasoning wisdom distills inference paths, and general laws capture time patterns. At inference, patterns guide reasoning and wisdom selects better paths, while laws drive second looks. A confidence adaptation strategy updates entries without leaking test information. Tests across datasets beat previous methods throughout.
arxiv-2602-03264:
Hyperbolic geometry, where space curves away ever faster, helps medical image models generalize in research by Francesco Di Salvo with 3 co-authors. Clinical data has layered form that flat Euclidean geometry captures poorly. Shifts from other scanners, plans, and patient populations further hinder reliable results and slow clinical adoption of deep networks trained at one site and deployed at another hospital or device.

Their method adds an unsupervised consistency constraint between branches in hyperbolic space, promoting domain-invariant traits. It is presented as the first comprehensive review of hyperbolic representation learning for medical image analysis. Gains were clear across many standard datasets and three vision transformer models. On domain generalization benchmarks spanning skin, histopathology, and retinal imaging, the method beat Euclidean methods on average.
arxiv-2602-03564:
Forecasting a time series means understanding its context and modeling its noisy wiggle at the same time. Mingyue Cheng and 4 co-authors build CoGenCast in a 2026 paper. The framework couples a pretrained language model with flow matching, a generative technique for continuous dynamics. Neither ingredient alone covers both sides of the problem.

The team reshapes a decoder-only language model into a forecasting encoder-decoder by changing only its attention pattern. That backbone produces a representation capturing the context, and the flow mechanism then generates the series' random evolution on top of it. The design also supports multimodal inputs and unified training across domains. On several benchmarks CoGenCast performs well against earlier forecasting baselines.
arxiv-2602-03664:
Yang Wan and 6 co-authors name a failure mode of chatty agents: conversational inertia. Their 2026 paper shows that in multi-turn settings, language models copy their own earlier replies as if those were demonstrations to imitate. Attention analysis reveals a strong diagonal pattern toward previous responses, tied to an imitation bias that strangles exploration.

The key observation is that identical states answered with longer context show stronger inertia than with shorter context. That gap builds preference pairs without any environment reward. Context Preference Learning then trains the model to favor low-inertia responses. Inference-time context management adds a second lever. Across eight agent environments and a deep research scenario, the framework reduces inertia and improves performance.
arxiv-2602-04064:
Citizens asking government questions need answers that are right, not just fluent. Neil Majithia and 7 co-authors built CitizenQuery-UK, a benchmark of twenty-two thousand question-answer pairs drawn from official UK government information. Their 2026 paper covers benefits, taxes, immigration, employment, and health topics.

Pairs were synthetically generated from gov.uk content, with a documented curation method. An evaluation pipeline adapts FActScore to grade factuality across eleven language models. Wrong answers here can quietly cost someone benefits or legal standing, so invisible errors matter more than obvious ones. The benchmark gives developers and agencies a shared yardstick before deployment.
arxiv-2602-04364:
Safety guarantees should hold at whatever moment you check them, not only at a preset sample size. Bror Hultberg and 2 co-authors extend conformal risk control to be anytime-valid in a 2026 paper. Conformal methods build prediction sets with controlled error from calibration data, but standard versions control error only on average over fixed-size calibration sets.

Their guarantees hold with high probability over a calibration set that grows cumulatively, at any time point. Quantile-based arguments deliver the bounds, and a matching lower bound shows they are asymptotically tight. Demonstrations include settings with distribution shift, where yesterday's calibration grows stale, exactly where anytime validity pays.
arxiv-2602-04564:
Turbulent flow in a channel drags against its walls, and that friction is called wall shear stress. Le Yin, Yongyun Hwang, and John Christos Vassilicos derive exact equations for it in a 2026 paper driven by the Navier-Stokes equations, which govern fluid motion.

Using direct numerical simulation data at high Reynolds numbers, the authors relate average and fluctuating stress to integrals through the near-wall buffer layer. The average is approximated well by shear combined with acceleration, plus a shrinking pressure correction. Fluctuations need a pressure term that grows instead. Splitting acceleration into parts reveals a peak tied to turbulence production, especially events known as sweeps.
arxiv-2602-04764:
Luis Frentzen Salim and 4 co-authors test how far example-based learning scales for low-resource translation in a 2026 paper. Languages such as Javanese and Sundanese lack the large parallel datasets that translation systems usually need.

Instead of training, the method conditions a long-context language model on demonstrations at inference time. The team scaled the context budget up to a million tokens and compared three supervision sources. Monolingual data, instruction-style data, and parallel sentence pairs were each tried. Gains from extra context saturated quickly and could degrade near the maximum window. Corpus type strongly shaped the scaling behavior. Some monolingual supervision rivaled parallel data despite offering less direct guidance. Bigger context windows did not guarantee proportional quality gains.
arxiv-2602-04864:
Soumya Jahagirdar and 3 co-authors shrink the visual token load of vision-language models in a 2026 work called Mask-LLaVA. Autoregressive models usually represent images with many tokens, which costs computing power, especially when generating answers.

Their framework combines three levels of visual features: mask-based object representations, global tokens, and local patch tokens. All tokens are used in training. At test time, however, the model can flexibly drop many of the object tokens without retraining and without a significant performance loss. On standard benchmarks, results rivaled current token-efficient methods and approached the original LLaVA baseline while using only a fraction of the visual tokens. The design adapts its cost to the task at inference time.
arxiv-2602-05064:
Live music is spontaneous, social, and hard to pin down, which makes it a rich testbed for creative AI. Yewon Kim and 9 co-authors map the field of live music agents in this 2026 human-computer interaction paper, accepted at CHI 2026. These are intelligent systems that perform or interact in real time alongside human musicians.

Drawing on perspectives from HCI, AI, and computer music, the team analyzed 184 systems from papers and videos. From that census they built a design space covering usage contexts, interactions, technologies, and ecosystems. The map exposes trends and gaps left by fragmented work across communities that rarely talk to each other. The authors release their annotated collection as a living online artifact, hoping the shared lens helps researchers, designers, and musicians build the next generation of co-creative performance systems.
arxiv-2602-05264:
Compressible magnetohydrodynamics describes electrically conducting fluids, from liquid metals to stellar plasma, and its equations are notoriously hard near vacuum. Jiaxu Li and 2 co-authors prove a local existence and uniqueness result in this 2026 analysis paper. Their domain is the exterior of a body in three dimensions, with slip conditions for the velocity and perfect-conductor conditions for the magnetic field at the boundary.

The difficulties stack up: the density starts out nearing vacuum far away, and the viscosities are powers of the density, so they fade exactly where the fluid thins out. For regular, even large, initial data, strong solutions exist and are unique for a short time. A contrast with the matching Navier-Stokes theory carries the paper's point: the magnetic field keeps its faster decay rate throughout the evolution. That persistence is what tames the singularities the density-dependent viscosity creates.
arxiv-2602-05564:
JUNO, a reactor neutrino experiment now running in China, has one main goal: finding whether the middle neutrino mass state is heavier or lighter than the others. Sandhya Choubey and Andreas Lund warn that this measurement could fail if neutrinos also feel a new kind of interaction. The risk comes from non-standard interactions mediated by a scalar particle beyond the standard model.

For plausible values of the new coupling, the authors find that JUNO's sensitivity to the mass ordering can drop sharply, and past a threshold it vanishes altogether. The cause is a previously unnoticed resonant boost to a mixing angle, which makes the two orderings look alike in the data. The analysis fixes the ordering and lightest mass at stated values to map the danger zone. The short paper cautions the JUNO program: a headline measurement may hinge on physics the experiment was not designed to see.
arxiv-2602-06064:
Scheduling interlocking jobs on shared renewable resources is a daily problem for cloud platforms. Yi-Xiang Hu and 5 co-authors present iScheduler, a system that learns to build such schedules step by step. Exact solvers find great answers on small cases but slow down badly as jobs grow into the thousands.

The team frames scheduling as a game-like process over smaller subproblems, picking one process at a time. When a plan changes, only the affected parts get rescheduled. They also released a large test set drawn from real cloud work, with thousands of tasks per case. Their system reached workable plans far faster than solver-based rivals.
arxiv-2602-06164:
People differ in whether they turn their heads or just move their eyes to look around, and Jinghui Hu and 3 co-authors map that difference in virtual reality. They call the range the eye-head mover spectrum. Data came from viewers watching all-around video freely.

A simple hinged curve model captured how much of each gaze shift the head supplied, for dozens of viewers. A second study paired video watching with a target-finding task. Values shifted between tasks, yet people partly kept their rank in the group, so the tendency is real but shaped by setting. The authors point to uses in adaptive rendering and shared virtual spaces.
arxiv-2602-06664:
Dominic Hirschbuehl reports precise measurements of top quark pair production from the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. The data come from proton collisions at high energy and cover a large recorded sample. The analysis selects events that produced an electron and a muon of opposite charge together with jets tagged as coming from bottom quarks.

Beyond the total production rate, the paper measures how the rate is spread across lepton properties, giving a detailed profile for testing theory. The total rate is also used in reverse: because predictions depend on the top quark's mass, the measurement pins down that mass in its pole definition. A companion measurement treats top pairs and single-top-plus-W production together as one combined signal.
arxiv-2602-06864:
Zhuocheng Zhang and four co-authors plan robot paths where the exact moment of contact is unknown. A robot arm or cart that hits a wall or catches an egg cannot count on a fixed hit time, and most planners just assume one. Their method, SURE, plans a tree of paths that split from each possible pre-hit state and later merge back into one shared path.

That split-and-merge plan buys safety without paying for a whole set of separate plans. In a cart-pole test with a wall in an unsure spot, letting the controller switch branches lifted success by about 22 percent. In an egg-catching test with a robot arm, success rose by 40 percent over the plain method. The same one-plan setup thus covers both jobs.
arxiv-2602-07164:
Language models shift personas with context, but do they need outside help to do it?  Ruimeng Ye and six co-authors argue the personas are already inside the model, as specialized subnetworks in its settings, and they set out to find them.

Using small calibration data sets, they identify distinct activation signatures for other personas and build a masking method that isolates lightweight persona subnetworks.  The work suggests that steering action may not always require prompting tricks or retraining.  It also raises a sharper question for interpretability research: how much of a model's apparent flexibility is structure already present, waiting to be switched on?
arxiv-2602-07764:
Agents that must balance competing goals, such as speed against safety, often collapse onto a narrow set of behaviors. Tanmay Ambadkar and four co-authors diagnose two causes: early merging of objectives cancels useful learning signals, and policies lose diversity across different preferences.

Their framework, D3PO, keeps each objective's signal separate until after trust-region stabilization, then weights preferences late, while a diversity term pushes behaviors apart in proportion to preference distance. The result recovers fuller Pareto fronts, the set of trade-offs where no goal improves without harming another. Multi-objective reinforcement learning researchers get both a diagnosis of a common failure and a fix that stays within efficient standard practice.
arxiv-2602-08264:
Quantum groups at generic readings behave in new ways from those at roots of unity, and the Gaiotto class sits at that edge. Aleksandr Popkovich asks whether a known match, guessed by Gaiotto and proved by Travkin and Yang for generic q, survives when q is a root of unity. It links twisted D-modules on the affine Grassmannian to codes of a quantum super-group.

As a first step, he weighs basic objects, showing a natural pairing between basics in the Gaiotto class and those in codes of the super-group GL(M|N) in positive characteristic. The proof adapts Serganova's algorithm as formulated by Brundan and Kujawa. Representation theorists gain evidence that the match may extend, plus a concrete pairing to build on.
arxiv-2602-08564:
Merging trained models by averaging their weights is cheap, but it can blend in features that do not generalize, especially when weights differ sharply. Tiantong Wang and four co-authors introduce M-Loss, a metric that judges whether merging is compatible with ensembling, using only a little unlabeled data. Their arXiv paper fills a gap between experimental hints and theory.

M-Loss measures the gap between weight averaging and output averaging at layer and node levels. It serves both as a feasibility criterion for merging and as a guide for which parameters matter when pruning. Theory and experiments show that folding M-Loss into merging aligns merged models far better with ensembles. Readers get a scalable check before merging models blindly.
arxiv-2602-08664:
This branch of algebra replaces ordinary arithmetic with max-plus operations, and these lecture notes introduce the subject from the ground up. Jeffrey Giansiracusa and three co-authors expand a 2025 Barcelona workshop series into three lectures. Their arXiv document starts with polynomials, ideals, and matching rules in this max-plus world, linking them to geometry through bend relations.

The second lecture refines a classic limit theorem by relating Berkovich analytic views to the tropical version of a variety. The third turns from geometry to algebra, applying the tropical construction to symmetric, exterior, matrix, and Clifford algebras, with the exterior case completing the Plücker picture. Readers get an accessible entry to tropical ideals, matroid links, and open questions in the field.
arxiv-2602-08964:
What does it mean for a language-model agent to truly pursue a goal, rather than merely act as if it does? Raghu Arghal and eight co-authors build a framework that pairs behavioral tests with probes of the model's internal representations. Their case study sends an agent across a 2D grid world toward target states, varying size, obstacles, and goal layouts.

Behavior tracks task difficulty while resisting difficulty-preserving changes and multi-goal setups. Inside, probes reveal a coarse spatial map, nonlinearly encoded, with actions broadly matching the decoded positions and plans. Reasoning reshapes those codes, shifting emphasis from spatial cues to immediate choices. The authors argue introspection must join behavior in judging goal-directedness.
arxiv-2602-09264:
Splitting mirror-image bits with light is capped because twist forces are weak beside plain slope forces and heat jiggling. Guillermo Serrera and one co-author beat that trade-off with lengthwise Mie echoes in silicon nanodisks. They are lit by an azimuthally-radially polarized beam that picks out echoes with strong optical twist slopes and fairly even electric-field strength.

Magnet four-pole echoes split twist-picking forces from the plain backdrop, giving a heat-steady, keen trap. Full-wave sims plus Kramers escape-rate theory foretell pickiness above 100 for bits with Pasteur mark at least 0.03, and above 2 even for faintly twisty samples near 0.006. The rig offers gentle, all-light twist study and mirror-twin splitting.
arxiv-2602-09764:
Most guided learning methods learn smooth visual pictures by matching varied views of the same input, giving little control over how info is set across picture sides. Kawtar Zaher and three co-authors reframe guided learning as discrete talk between a teacher and a student network in their 2026 paper. Meaning moves through a fixed-size binary channel.

Rather than matching smooth marks, the student predicts binary notes made by the teacher. Discrete match is forced through a binary cross-entropy goal, while a coding-rate taming term pushes good use of the tight channel, aiding set pictures. Fresh mapping-head starts strengthen the effect, pushing vectors telling across discrete codes. Tests show steady gains over smooth match rivals on sorting, finding, and dense tasks, plus domain-shift tuning. Learned binary codes form a compact, rich discrete language holding meaning factors reusable across classes.
arxiv-2602-09864:
Grouping mixed linked data stays a challenge in graph learning, most when links involve more than two types. Benoît Hurpeau notes smooth modular goals such as DMoN enabled end-to-end group finding on even and two-part graphs, yet spreading these ways to higher linked forms stays hard. His 2026 paper offers a smooth form of three-part modular for graphs of three node types linked through go-between links.

Group structure is defined through weighted co-paths across the three-part graph, with factored math skipping open build of third-order tensors. Shape scaling at pivot nodes controls degree mix and ensures tuning. The final goal tunes with a graph neural network end-to-end while keeping cost in edges. Tests on large urban land data show settling and in-space tidy splits, setting smooth three-part modular as a block for free grouping of mixed graphs.
arxiv-2602-09964:
The Atlantic overturning circulation carries warm water north and cold water south, and its collapse is a feared climate tipping point. A 2026 paper led by René M. van Westen, with two co-authors, argues the danger depends less on a single warming threshold than on how fast forcing rises. A slow rise lets the ocean adjust in step.

In a slow carbon dioxide ramp, the circulation held steady up to five and a half degrees of warming, aided by stronger evaporation and shrinking sea ice. Under faster ramps it collapsed near two degrees. The lesson is rate-induced tipping. Limiting how fast greenhouse gases rise, not only how far, may cut the near-term risk of collapse.
arxiv-2602-10064:
Vibration spectra from the electron microscope reveal atomic shakes at tiny scales, but routine prediction has stayed out of reach. A 2026 paper led by Harrison A. Walker, with five co-authors, introduces PySlice, the first public code for the TACAW method. Users feed in atomic structures and get momentum- and energy-resolved vibration spectra through one automated workflow.

General machine-learned atomic potentials remove the need to build one potential per system. The workflow spans atom motion, GPU-sped electron scattering, and frequency analysis, yielding phonon maps, diffraction patterns, and spectrum images. The modular Python platform also runs standard microscopy simulations, turning rare prediction into routine screening.
arxiv-2602-10364:
Scans taken for one purpose often hold extra clues, yet open tools lack strict testing and commercial tools lack openness. A 2026 paper from a large team led by Adrit Rao reports Comp2Comp, an open-source package with two early open, FDA-cleared deep learning pipelines for opportunistic CT analysis. One pipeline segments the abdominal aorta to judge aneurysm size. The other gauges bone density and osteoporosis risk by segmenting vertebral bodies.

The team tested aortic diameters against radiologist measurements on two hundred fifty-eight patient scans from four outside institutions. Bone-density calls were tested against same-day DXA scans on three hundred seventy-one scans. Aortic error averaged about one and a half millimetres; bone-density calls reached about eighty-one percent sensitivity and about seventy-eight percent specificity. The authors judge both accurate enough for clinical use; open sourcing lets hospitals trial the tools before costly pilots.
arxiv-2602-10964:
Can a language model invent a Jamaican couscous dish that feels Jamaican? Florian Carichon and two co-authors test that question through recipes, where culture, habit, and invention meet. They pair human recipes across countries by cultural distance, using the GlobalFusion set, then ask several models to adapt recipes across the same pairs.

The models fail to match human patterns: unlike people, their recipe shifts do not track cultural distance. The authors trace the gap to weak cultural signals inside the models, a muddled sense of novelty and tradition, and a failure to tie dishes to their countries through key ingredients. The result warns against trusting current models for culturally sensitive writing and design.
arxiv-2602-11064:
Real motion data is scarce, yet wearables need robust activity models. Firas Darwish and three co-authors test built motion data for pretraining, built from motion-capture-derived forms. They train time-series models on built motion and check transfer to varied human activity tasks.

Built pretraining helps when mixed with real data or scaled up enough. By contrast, large-scale motion-capture pretraining alone adds little, since its signals mismatch wearable data. The paper clarifies sim-to-real limits for motion: built data is a useful lever, but only when its domain gap to deployment sensors is faced head-on.
arxiv-2602-11264:
Quasar light curves carry time delays that encode cosmic distances, but their variability is messy. Namu Kroupa and two co-authors build a fully Bayesian frame for delay inference and stationarity tests using marginalized Gaussian processes. A piecewise straight drift captures non-stationary trends, while stationary kernels capture random flicker.

Multiple lensed images are modelled jointly with per-image microlensing, and evidence is computed by nested sampling. Applied to three quasars, the frame finds strong non-stationarity in two and stationarity in the third. Time delays prove robust to model choices and match prior work. The authors also fix a likelihood pathology that biased delays upward, with a practical convergence protocol.
arxiv-2602-11764:
Shared low-orbit fleets carry sensitive traffic through mixed-trust networks, where traffic data alone can betray users. Nilesh Vyas and two co-authors enhance the Loopix mix-network for that volatile setting. Their design adds a multi-path transport method using erasure codes to survive link volatility and intermittent connectivity. It also adds a private lookup method for route discovery and adaptive delays based on hub scores.

The delays counter the topological bias of low-orbit networks and improve the privacy-to-latency trade-off. The design provably prevents traffic-data leakage at the user-provider directory, blocking profiling and correlation attacks. Packet-level simulations show near-zero message loss for the multi-path transport. Small tests confirm the lookup method is cheap enough for practical use. The result is a tested blueprint for high-privacy satellite communication that can ship.
arxiv-2602-11864:
The Chinese Space Station Survey Telescope is set for ten years of sharp, wide-field sky imaging, a program that needs strict calibration while in orbit. Chenxiaoji Ling and ten co-authors establish selection rules for stable celestial benchmark fields, including sky access, stellar number density, bright-star contamination, and interstellar dust dimming. Using the CSST survey planning tool and all-sky dust maps from Planck and SFD, they constrain allowed regions to high ecliptic and galactic latitudes.

From an initial sample of 29 possible clusters meeting the spatial constraints, six globular clusters are identified as optimal tuning fields, fulfilling all critical rules. Those clusters, including M13, M92, and NGC 104, are recommended as optimal tuning field choices for the on-orbit program. They are key to achieving record brightness sharpness in the space-based survey, giving CSST stable reference points for its decade of observations.
arxiv-2602-11964:
Most agent benchmarks freeze the world while the agent thinks, but real environments move on their own. Romain Froger and a large team introduce Gaia2, a benchmark for language model agents in realistic, asynchronous settings where scenes evolve apart from agent actions. Agents must work under time pressure, adapt to noisy and shifting events, resolve ambiguity, and collaborate with other agents, with each scenario paired with a write-action verifier for fine-grained, action-level scoring.

Tests of leading proprietary and open-source models show no model leads everywhere. GPT-5 scores highest overall at 42 percent pass at first try yet fails time-sensitive tasks. Claude-4 Sonnet trades accuracy and speed for cost, and Kimi-K2 leads open-source models at 21 percent. The results expose tradeoffs among reasoning, efficiency, and robustness, and a stubborn gap between simulation and reality. Gaia2 ships with an open platform designed for easy extension.
arxiv-2602-12064:
Top text-to-SQL models lean heavily on expert-written evidence clarifying schema and value linking, and collapse without it: execution accuracy drops by over 10 percent in real settings where experts are absent. Yafeng Nan and seven co-authors propose DIVER, a robust system automating evidence reasoning with dynamic interactive value linking. A compatible toolbox probes the database, while a structured workspace of thoughts and facts constrains reflection, guiding tool choice round by round.

Through that iterative process, DIVER finds schema and value linkings missed by existing methods, then infers correct SQL function and formula usage and generates high-quality evidence without expert help. Experiments show robustness gains across models, improving execution accuracy by up to about 11 percent and valid efficiency score by up to about 16 percent. Dynamic value linking, the authors conclude, is what makes text-to-SQL robust when experts are unavailable.
arxiv-2602-12164:
Language models can improve by checking their own work, but in science there is often no clean right answer to check against. Xiaohan He led this work with five co-authors, building Sci-CoE, a two-stage system where models grow as both solvers and checkers. It starts from a small set of labelled examples, then moves to learning without labels.

In stage one, those labels anchor basic judgement about what counts as correct. In stage two, a geometric reward blends agreement, trust, and variety, driving large-scale self-practice on unlabelled data. Tests on several science benchmarks show stronger complex reasoning and good scaling, pointing toward sturdier and more varied ways to judge scientific answers.
arxiv-2602-12364:
Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, only the third known visitor from beyond our solar system, passed through TESS view in January 2026. Jorge Martinez-Palomera led this work with one co-author, Amy Tuson, with the TESS Science Support Center also listed. NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite watched the comet from 15 to 22 January 2026, in Sector 1751, at rapid cadences of 200 and 20 seconds.

The team releases two high-level science products from official TESS data, both public at the Mikulski Archive. First, comet-centred image time series, corrected for scattered light and stars. Second, aperture light curves drawn from those corrected images. Near-continuous, high-precision photometry should reveal how the comet behaved after its closest approach to the Sun, aiding TESS and solar system researchers alike.
arxiv-2602-12764:
Feeling present in social virtual reality can mean feeling with others, feeling located in a place, or feeling like oneself. Each kind may feed basic human needs in different ways. Qijia Chen and two co-authors surveyed 301 social VR users and modelled links to autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Those three needs sit at the heart of self-determination theory. Social presence predicted all three needs, while self-presence predicted competence and relatedness, and spatial presence showed no direct effect.

Demographics shaped the pattern. Women gained more autonomy and relatedness from social presence. Men gained more competence and autonomy from self- and spatial presence. Younger users showed stronger links in several places. The findings cast presence as a motivational lever, not just a feeling, and suggest VR designers should tune social features with diverse users in mind.
arxiv-2602-12864:
Contact binaries are pairs of stars sharing a common envelope, and their energy transfer shapes how they evolve. Elham Sarvari and seven co-authors present detailed multi-band photometry of four W Ursae Majoris systems, adding TESS satellite data for DM Cir. They model light curves with the PHOEBE code and a Markov chain Monte Carlo approach, deriving new ephemerides and timing fits from eclipse minima.

In every system the two stars differ by less than 150 kelvin, confirming efficient heat sharing through the common envelope. Absolute parameters come from Gaia parallaxes, and the sample splits into two W-subtype and two A-subtype systems. Initial masses and energy transfer rates, set against a wider sample of 411 contact binaries, give a broad view of how energy moves through these systems across evolutionary stages.
arxiv-2602-12964:
Weak-force studies with argon-32 decay need beam shapes gauged to sub-mm sharpness inside a strong magnet. S. Lecanuet and team describe a small low-energy ion beam test built for the WISArD test at ISOLDE/CERN. The micro-channel-plate device, set in a Z-stack with an anode that senses place, was tested with stable and active beams.

The focus is image rebuild: fixing cushion warp from the square anode and weighing magnet-field effects on scores. The device hits sub-mm beam shape closeness while fitting the spatial limits and 4-tesla field of the test. Those powers meet WISArD's sharpness needs for pulling the beta-neutrino angular link factor to 0.1% doubt, a tough target for weak-force physics.
arxiv-2602-13264:
Trust in generative models depends on knowing when an output is shaky, yet many uncertainty tools lean on narrow rules that fail on new tasks or media. This paper proposes Directional Concentration Uncertainty, a method that reads the spread of a model's many outputs in embedding space through a directional statistics lens. When outputs cluster tightly in one direction, confidence is high; when they scatter, it is low.

The approach needs no task-specific tricks, and tests show it matches or beats prior tools such as semantic entropy on calibration, while also carrying over to multi-modal tasks. That breadth makes it a candidate for safety checks inside agentic systems, where a model must judge its own doubt before acting. Souradeep Chattopadhyay leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14664:
Speech machines learn from data, but human mouths impose hard physical limits. Parth Khadse, with Sunil Kumar Kopparapu as co-author, tests whether anatomy shapes end-to-end text-to-speech training. Some shifts between mouth shapes are simply hard to make or to mimic.

Two systems are tried, Tacotron-2 and VITS, under three setups: normal, fully reversed, and reversed text with normal speech. The reversed systems show that these models are purely data-driven, with no built-in sense of anatomy. Yet reversed speech still reveals traces of articulatory limits. The experiments separate what data teaches from what bodies impose.
arxiv-2602-14764:
J. Blunier, A. Neronov, and D. Semikoz probe the Fermi Large Area Telescope's point spread function using bright pulsars, aiming to sharpen searches for extended gamma-ray emission. Inaccurate point spread models can fake source extension, so the team compares analytical models from the telescope's instrument response functions against pulsar signals.

Fitting pulsar data with the same analytical form yields an improved parameter set, which the authors then apply to searches for extended sources. The work turns pulsars into calibration beacons, tightening the line between a true extended glow and a modelling artefact. Gamma-ray astronomy gains a cleaner lens.
arxiv-2602-15064:
Hou and Ji compare the social network of Moltbook, where AI agents and humans mix, with well-studied human communication networks. Large agent populations now live in online spaces, yet little is known about how their group interaction patterns stack up against human social systems. The team analyzes the full Moltbook interaction network and sets it beside human benchmarks.

Moltbook matches the node-edge scaling seen in human systems, suggesting similar global growth limits. Inside, it diverges sharply: extreme attention inequality, heavy-tailed and lopsided degree patterns, weak reciprocity, and too few connected triads. Communities form a modular structure with high modularity and relatively even community sizes against degree-preserving null models. Agent societies, the authors conclude, can mirror human global patterns while organizing themselves by quite different internal rules.
arxiv-2602-15464:
Cao and colleagues build the first fractional Skyrmions from light arranged in a vectorial superposition that carries non-integer orbital angular momentum. Skyrmion-shaped light patterns have lately drawn wide attention, and their integer Skyrmion number has proved sturdy when passing through complex media.

They unpack the map layout to show a new event, the sudden shift leaps in skyrmion number, which also acts to back the integer core of skyrmion shapes. Their lab demo matches simulation well and opens a fresh range of light patterns to explore, promising new uses for optical communication and sensing.
arxiv-2602-15564:
Wang and colleagues argue that text-to-SQL systems are held back by fixed pipelines. One static workflow cannot stretch across varied databases, odd distributions, and long-tail questions, yet users are left to pick methods by trial and error. The authors show, in theory and in tests, that an optimal dynamic policy beats the best static workflow, with gains driven by how much candidate workflows differ from each other.

Their SquRL frame uses reinforcement learning to let a language model build its workflow on the fly at inference time. A rule-based reward guides training, dynamic actor masking widens exploration, and pseudo rewards speed learning. Benchmark tests show dynamic construction beating the best static methods, with the largest gains on complex and out-of-distribution queries. Code is public.
arxiv-2602-15964:
Vombatkere and Terzi refuse the usual single answer to a trade off problem. In team building, recommendations, and influence campaigns, the goal is to pick a set that gains high utility at low cost. Standard methods fix a budget or blend the two aims into one score, then return one solution and hide the rest of the options.

The authors instead compute a small set of solutions that sketches the whole frontier between utility and cost. They define approximate Pareto frontiers with provable guarantees for several pairings of submodular utility and cost, plus an adaptive search that samples only the points needed to summarize the frontier. Tests across varied data sets show the method maps the trade off space efficiently, giving decision makers a menu rather than a single verdict.
arxiv-2602-16264:
Zixian Wu and coauthors develop a supervised classification framework with class-dependent rewards to predict major solar flares within a day. They construct multiple data sets covering knowledge features and line-of-sight magnetograms. Three deep learning models and three class-dependent reward counterparts are compared. They test parameter importance, compare data combinations, compare reward versus deep models, test reward sensitivity, use SHAP for interpretability, and compare against NASA and CCMC.

Findings show two line-of-sight feature combinations yielding the best results. The Transformer performs better with combined data than with either alone, and models using knowledge-informed features outperform those using magnetograms. The reward Transformer slightly beats its deep learning counterpart on knowledge features and achieves the best overall performance. Reward model performance is not overly sensitive to reward choices. Under identical prediction time and region count, the reward model beats NASA and CCMC.
arxiv-2602-16564:
Michael Lanier and Yevgeniy Vorobeychik introduce MetaDOAR, a lightweight meta-controller for solving simulation-based network security games at large scale. It augments the Double Oracle paradigm with a learned, partition-aware filter and Q-value caching, so a low-level actor searches only a small, well-chosen subset of devices on huge cyber networks. Candidate actions are scored in batches and cached, with conservative cache invalidation to keep decisions sound.

Tests on large network topologies show MetaDOAR earning higher player payoffs than state-of-the-art baselines without runaway memory or training time. Security and multi-agent researchers get a practical, theory-guided path to hierarchical policy learning where brute-force search over every device is simply too big to run.
arxiv-2602-16664:
Jiaming Liu and co-authors propose the Self-Supervised Semantic Bridge for unpaired image-to-image translation. Adversarial diffusion routes need target-domain adversarial loss in training, which can curb generalization. Diffusion-inversion routes often yield low-fidelity shifts from flawed inversion into noise latents. The bridge route weaves outside semantic priors into diffusion bridge models for spatially faithful shifts with no cross-domain supervision.

The key is self-supervised visual encoders that learn codes blind to looks but alive to geometry, forming a shared latent space that steers the bridges. Tests show the method beats strong prior routes for hard medical image synthesis, in-domain and out-of-domain alike. It also extends cleanly to high-quality text-guided editing, giving imagers a versatile translation tool.
arxiv-2602-16864:
Daniel Durstewitz and co-authors argue that time series modeling needs a dynamical systems view. The field has moved from early linear statistical methods to current foundation models. Hype and industrial demand are high, yet real progress is not always clear. Time series from natural or engineered systems almost always stem from some underlying dynamical system. Access to its governing laws would yield theoretically optimal forecasts.

That promise motivates dynamical systems reconstruction. It infers surrogate models of the underlying system from data. Beyond short-term forecasts, such models can predict long-term stats. Those stats are often the more relevant quantities in practice. Dynamical systems theory also gives domain-free insight into generation mechanisms, performance bounds, generalization to unseen regimes such as tipping points, and control plans. The position paper reviews core concepts and methods to make that case.
arxiv-2602-16964:
Prasham Titiya and co-authors propose SAGE, a structure-aware graph expansion frame for retrieval of heterogeneous data. Retrieval-augmented question answering over heterogeneous corpora needs connected evidence across text, tables, and graph nodes. Entity-level knowledge graphs support structured access but are costly to build and maintain and inefficient to traverse at query time. Standard retriever-reader pipelines use flat similarity search over independently chunked text, missing multi-hop evidence chains across modalities.

SAGE constructs a chunk-level graph offline using metadata-driven similarities with percentile-based pruning. Online retrieval runs an initial baseline retriever to obtain seed chunks, expands first-hop neighbors, and filters neighbors using dense plus sparse retrieval to select additional chunks. On OTT-QA and STaRK, SAGE improves retrieval recall by several points over baselines.
arxiv-2602-17064:
Yifan Bai led a four-author team putting two classic fixed-point algorithms on fully machine-checked footing. Krasnoselskii-Mann iteration and Halpern iteration approximate fixed points of nonexpansive operators in real Hilbert spaces, but their convergence proofs had not been formalized in the Lean4 theorem prover. The paper builds that formalization from the ground up.

Along the way the authors formalize weak convergence and topological facts for infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, the definition and properties of nonexpansive operators, and Fejer monotone sequences from convex analysis. On those foundations they verify convergence for both iteration schemes. The result is a reusable library of checked parts for future convergence proofs and convex analysis in Lean.
arxiv-2602-17264:
Michael Müller led a six-author team testing whether third-party ratings of conversational recommender systems can be trusted. User-centric evaluation aims to capture satisfaction, trust, and rapport, and scale pressures push researchers toward crowd workers or language models rating static dialogue logs. But the reliability of that practice had barely been examined. The paper runs a large study on static transcripts to measure it.

Over a thousand annotations from more than a hundred crowd workers on two hundred dialogues, scored on an eighteen-dimension framework, reveal a split. Practical dimensions like accuracy, usefulness, and satisfaction reach moderate reliability when aggregated, while social dimensions like humanness and rapport prove far less reliable. Many dimensions also collapse into one global quality signal, a halo effect. The findings challenge single-rater and model-based protocols and argue for multi-rater aggregation and dimension reduction.
arxiv-2602-17564:
Ting-Tung Wang led a six-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on faster observables for fractional quantum Hall systems. The team develops a hybrid Monte Carlo method for sampling the Laughlin and Moore-Read wave functions. Global updates and double stereographic projection on spherical geometry beat the widely used Metropolis scheme on speed. Systems with more than a thousand electrons become simulable on disk and sphere geometries.

The authors apply the method to the topological shift from the edge dipole moment, computed from disk density. They also compute non-Abelian braiding matrices for different braiding schemes of Moore-Read quasiholes on the sphere, reaching better quality than previous work. With thermodynamic limit results now easy to obtain, the paper discusses one open use for the method. It may clarify whether fractional quantum Hall states stay stable in an ideal Chern band setting or under quantum decoherence.
arxiv-2602-17664:
Aidar Myrzakhan and team rethink pruning for diffusion language models. Such models pay high inference costs from iterative denoising, so pruning matters. Prior heuristics, borrowed from autoregressive models, preserve attention sink tokens as stable global anchors. The authors show that assumption fails for diffusion models.

In diffusion models, the sink position shifts a lot across timesteps, so sinks are often transient and less structurally vital. Their method, Sink-Aware Pruning, finds and prunes unstable sinks on its own. With no retraining, it beats strong prior pruning baselines under matched compute and offers a better quality-efficiency trade-off. Code is public for reuse and checks.
arxiv-2602-17764:
Spencer Griffith and team build a generalized frame for minimal dark matter, a class of models prized for simplicity. Calculating freezeout abundance in such models is complicated by nonperturbative effects from Sommerfeld enhancement and bound-state formation. The paper asks a pointed question: if next-generation direct-detection tests find nothing, is minimal dark matter excluded?

For the simplest models, the answer is yes. It was unknown for the key extension of two multiplets coupled by Higgs interactions. The new frame calculates nonperturbative effects for those models and for single multiplets too, fixing gaps in the literature. For a mixed Majorana and Dirac combination, the 3M2D case, predicted signals can dip below the neutrino floor. Fully testing minimal dark matter will thus need more than direct detection alone.
arxiv-2602-17964:
X. Chu and team study ballooning mode saturation in realistic stellarators using the flux tube approach of Ham and colleagues. The method adapts to the lack of exact force balance in stellarator balance solvers that assume nested flux surfaces exist.

An energy-based approach for finding flux tube energy overcomes this force error problem in stellarator number equilibria. Settled flux tube states crossing ten to twenty percent of the plasma minor radius exist for linear bulging unstable profiles. Several features of the moved flux tube structure in a full nonlinear MHD run of Wendelstein 7X match the model. Settled states also appear in a compact stellarator balance close but below the marginal ballooning linear weakness, meaning the calm balance is metastable. That suggests Edge-Localized-Mode-like bursting MHD behavior may be possible in stellarators.
arxiv-2602-18064:
Ziyue Wang and team present 3DMedAgent, a unified agent letting 2D multimodal language models perform 3D CT analysis without 3D fine-tuning. CT analysis spans seeing to clinical insight. Current methods model single tasks alone or run end-to-end runs with one-hop outputs, blocking the steady buildup of sense evidence for later use. Recent models mix visual and textual information well, but their 2D designs limit volume analysis.

3DMedAgent mixes varied visual and textual tools, breaking complex analysis into subtasks: global to local views, volumes to telling slices, and visual evidence to text. A long-term structured memory gathers tool outputs for query-aware, evidence-driven multi-step reasoning. The authors present DeepChestVQA, a benchmark for unified perception-to-understanding in 3D chest imaging. Across more than forty tasks, 3DMedAgent beats general, medical, and 3D-only models, pointing toward general assistants.
arxiv-2602-18264:
David Mercier built a curated database that tracks thirty years of Ansys Granta use in the literature. His 2026 paper starts from a tracking headache: publication volume grows fast while software citation habits stay inconsistent, so evidence of real product use scatters. Granta tools serve materials teaching, materials and process choice, sustainability design, and enterprise materials data.

The framework ingests reference data semi-automatically through DOIs and citation files, then adds expert curation of product, context, domain, and technical depth, with links to authors and institutions. Python analytics, dashboards, and network visuals support repeatable queries and reports. As of September 2025 the base holds over eleven hundred records across journals, theses, books, patents, standards, conference papers, and reports. It turns scattered usage evidence into structured knowledge for scouting, reviews, and strategy.
arxiv-2602-18664:
Norbert Kaiser computes nucleon-nucleon forces from two-pion exchange. His notes follow a recent paper, calculating the spectral functions, or imaginary parts, of nucleon-nucleon potentials from two-pion exchange with single and double Roper excitation. Unlike the full one-loop calculation, spectral functions for isoscalar and isovector central and tensor potentials take simple analytical form.

The momentum-space potentials follow via subtracted dispersion relations. This form also admits a regulator function that tames high-momentum parts of the chiral two-pion exchange. The calculation extends to two-pion exchange with combined delta isobar and Roper resonance excitation. The compact analytical results give a usable handle on resonance inputs to nucleon-nucleon forces.
arxiv-2602-18764:
Two ways of letting language models use tools, schema-guided dialogue from 2019 and today's Model Context Protocol, may be two faces of one idea. Andreas Schlapbach, writing alone in 2026, argues that both encode more than tool signatures in schemas. They also encode operating rules and reasoning hints, making agent behaviour deterministic and auditable.

From that convergence he draws five design principles, from semantic completeness over syntactic precision to documenting failure modes and declaring relationships between tools. The analysis also finds gaps both frameworks leave open, above all failure modes and inter-tool relationships, and treats progressive disclosure as a key scaling insight under token limits. Concrete patterns for each principle aim at schema-driven oversight without inspecting proprietary systems.
arxiv-2602-18964:
Sarcasm turns on the gap between literal and intended meaning, and that gap is culture-bound. For Yorùbá, a tonal Niger-Congo language with over fifty million speakers, no gold-standard dataset existed. Toheeb Aduramomi Jimoh, with two co-authors, presents Yor-Sarc in 2026, the first such dataset for sarcasm detection in Yorùbá.

The dataset holds hundreds of instances marked by three native speakers of different dialects. Its protocol is designed specifically for Yorùbá sarcasm, taking culture into account, with context-sensitive interpretation and community-informed guidelines. Agreement ranges from substantial to almost perfect, with a large majority of unanimous consensus. Remaining majority-agreement cases are kept as soft labels for uncertainty-aware modelling. Yor-Sarc should aid research on meaning interpretation and culture-aware NLP for low-resource African languages.
arxiv-2602-19064:
Range-view LiDAR diffusion looks photographic, but its geometry often fails. Quan Liu, with three co-authors, designs L3DR in 2026 to fix that gap. Range-view methods neglect three-dimensional realism. They produce depth bleeding and wavy surfaces.

L3DR regresses and cancels range-view artefacts in three-dimensional space. It restores local geometry accurately. Theory and tests show three-dimensional models beat two-dimensional ones on sharp, authentic boundaries. A residual regression network predicts point-level offsets in space. A Welsch loss focuses on local geometry and ignores anomalous regions. Tests on KITTI, KITTI360, nuScenes, and Waymo show state-of-the-art generation with superior geometry realism. The frame transfers across LiDAR diffusion models at little extra cost.
arxiv-2602-19564:
Jilin Province, a key grain base in China with a cool-temperate inland monsoon climate, leans hard on heat levels for farming and eco safety. Xingyue Deng and Xuechen Liang note that most heat studies target country-wide or southeast coastal zones, with few tackling Jilin's own climate. Most models also miss local place-time shifts and yearly cycles, limiting how right they are.

Using 1 km by 1 km monthly mean heat grid data for 2000 to 2024, the authors map place-time shifts. They build a multi-model test rig. Four deep-learning entries (LSTM, GRU, BiLSTM, Transformer) join five old-school machine learning models in the test. They give Jilin-only tips on which methods predict monthly heat best.
arxiv-2602-19664:
The future Electron-Ion Collider needs a shared physics plan, and France's hadron-physics community met to shape one. The EIC-France Workshop's report, led by F. Arleo, sums up theory talks and discussions from its second meeting, held at IJCLab in Orsay on 1-3 December 2025. It opens with the collider's early running conditions and luminosity performance from the EIC Early Science Matrix.

Short overviews cover small-x, exclusive, semi-inclusive, inclusive, and heavy-flavor physics. Two early measurements stand out as fits for French strengths: inclusive diffraction and inclusive quarkonium production. They offer clean signals and a straight read on gluon saturation, heavy-quark behavior, and small-x structure. Longer-term prizes include the pion's three-dimensional structure via the Sullivan process and exclusive three-body final states.
arxiv-2602-19764:
Robots that handle objects with skill need more than vision: force and shape feedback matter when contact is delicate. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yirui Sun and seven co-authors presents DeMUSE, a framework that fuses colour, depth, and six-axis force into one stream for robot handling.

A diffusion transformer carries the fused stream, while a step that normalizes each sense on its own rebalances features so no sense dominates. Sparse expert modules add room for physical priors without slowing inference, which real-time control demands. A joint denoising objective generates scene evolution and action sequences together, keeping them true to physics. DeMUSE leads prior methods in both simulated and real-world trials, supporting the case for deep multi-sense integration.
arxiv-2602-21264:
Wormholes bend light in ways that mimic optical media, and Lorentz breach adds direction bias to the picture. Omar Mustafa, Semra Gurtas Dogan, Abdulkerim Karabulut, and Abdullah Guvendi study massless spin-one fields in a static round wormhole in this 2026 arXiv paper. The shape is horizon-free, complete along shortest paths, and flat in the limit, with below-zero bend packed near the throat.

A frame-free handling yields an exact radial rule with a bend-made field, recast as a working light-bending profile. Low-rate modes trap strongly while high-rate modes pass almost freely. A match with spiral sheets links Lorentz-breaching bend to shape twist, linking the model to twisted graphene nano-ribbons as analog-gravity platforms.
arxiv-2602-21364:
Giorgio Fabris and 21 co-authors show in a 2026 arXiv paper that granular aluminium can bring superconductivity into germanium for hole-spin hybrid devices. In such hybrids, superconductivity and spin effects fight each other, since magnetic fields break Cooper pairs. Past fixes worked poorly for small in-plane g-factors or out-of-plane fields.

Granular aluminium is made of nanometre-scale aluminium grains in an oxide matrix. Laid on germanium-silicon-germanium stacks, it produced a hard superconducting gap with peaks at 305 micro-electronvolts. The gap held up under fields in both directions, letting Zeeman splitting of Yu-Shiba-Rusinov states pass 50 micro-electronvolts. The authors use this toughness to reveal hole physics and sketch a way to drive Andreev spin qubits whatever the Rashba coupling strength.
arxiv-2602-21764:
William Wu and one co-author introduce a method to estimate the self-similarity index of a general H-self-similar process with steady or non-steady increments. The algorithm rests on a modified Lamperti transformation, which converts H-self-similar processes into steady ones. As applications, the team shows how to estimate the index for fractional, subfractional, bifractional, and trifractional Brownian motion.
