A simulation study supports the consistency of the estimators, and a Python implementation is shared publicly. The method is also applied to Nile river water level data from the years 900 to 1200 of the Common Era, estimating the self-similarity index of that long historical record.
arxiv-2602-21964:
Arnaud Casteigts, Matteo De Francesco, and Pierre Leone revisit a 1973 Scientific American puzzle by Martin Gardner, the Racetrack game, and turn it into serious mathematics. A vehicle moves on a grid, each step shifting position by a whole-number vector, with consecutive steps differing by at most one unit per dimension. The paper studies two tasks in any dimension: the cheapest move count between two states, and an explicit cheapest route.

The authors clarify earlier two-dimensional methods and prove both tasks solvable in constant time for any fixed dimension, despite routes growing arbitrarily long. The trick is that some optimal route always admits a compact form with only a handful of intermediate states and steady motion between them. As a bonus, routing through many points at set speeds in two or three dimensions drops to linear time in the point count.
arxiv-2602-22264:
The Dymnikova black hole is a regular spacetime that smooths the singular center into a de Sitter core while looking Schwarzschild far away. Faizuddin Ahmed and three co-authors generalize it further, surrounding it with perfect-fluid dark matter and immersing it in a cloud of strings. They ask how those two extra matter sources reshape the hole's thermodynamics, optics, and dynamics.

The team derives Hawking temperature and heat capacity, finding non-monotonic temperature behavior and parameter-dependent phase transitions. Photon-sphere and shadow calculations show both dark matter and string-cloud parameters strongly shift the shadow radius and strong-field structure. Orbits of massive test particles and their stability complete a portrait of a regular black hole in a richer environment.
arxiv-2602-22564:
Miriam Remshard and six co-authors test whether a tailored AI chat can correct mistaken beliefs about climate action. Even climate-concerned people often misjudge which steps cut emissions most, and that misjudgment shapes behaviour. The team recruited 1,201 climate-concerned volunteers and compared four groups: a personalized climate-knowledge chatbot, a web search, a generic chatbot, and no intervention.

Only the personalized climate chatbot raised both knowledge of action impacts and intentions to adopt high-impact, feasible habits. It did not beat web search at improving understanding of impacts alone, a limit the authors state plainly. Still, they argue that personal, actionable guidance may make chatbots stronger motivators of real behaviour change than search results that merely inform.
arxiv-2602-22764:
Jiahong Xiang and four co-authors bring repository-level issue resolution to Rust, a language whose steep learning curve makes automation valuable. LLM code agents shine on many software tasks, yet Rust lacked a large-scale benchmark. Rust-SWE-bench fills the gap with 500 real-world tasks from 34 popular Rust repositories.

A study with four agents and four leading language models sets the baseline. ReAct-style agents resolve up to about twenty-one percent of issues. They are blocked mainly by repository-wide structure and Rust's strict type and trait rules, with issue reproduction proving critical. The team's RUSTFORGER pairs automated test setup with metaprogramming-driven dynamic tracing. It resolves about twenty-nine percent with Claude Sonnet, a roughly thirty-five percent gain over the strongest baseline, uniquely solving 46 tasks.
arxiv-2602-22864:
Peter J. Cameron carries on work with Anatoly Vershik on mirror groups of two famed endless objects. The Rado graph, a highly mirror-like endless graph, gives its self-map group, while the Urysohn space, an all-embracing metric space, gives its shape-map group. Both groups have long charmed math minds for their size and structure.

The paper adds further thoughts on those groups, along with links to shape systems and filters on countable sets. For readers of endless counting and shape theory, it extends a team's line of thought, linking mirror groups of all-embracing objects with the fine structure of set shape theory.
arxiv-2602-22964:
Merijn Floren and one co-author make nonlinear state-space identification more reliable. Fitting such models from input-output data usually means solving a highly non-convex optimization problem, prone to slow convergence and poor local solutions. Their method splits the problem into a sequence of tractable subproblems.

Starting from a linear baseline model, nonlinear residual dynamics are first estimated with a guided residual search, then refined through multiple-shooting optimization. Tests on two benchmarks match state-of-the-art black-box methods while converging better than naive initialization, giving practitioners a steadier route to good fits.
arxiv-2602-23164:
Aviral Chawla and two co-authors probe how a single transformer organizes several conflicting world models at once. Most studies look at one game with one rule set. It is unclear whether a model splits its capacity into separate sub-models or shares one picture across tasks. MetaOthello, their test suite, mixes Othello variants that share notation but differ in rules or token schemes. Small GPT models train on the mix.

The models do not carve out isolated sub-models. Instead they converge on a mostly shared picture of board state that transfers across variants. Probes trained on one variant can steer another almost as well as matched probes. Games that differ only by token remapping line up under a single rotation. When rules partly overlap, early layers stay game-neutral, a middle layer tags the game, and later layers specialize.
arxiv-2602-23764:
Snehasis Bera and two co-authors build a broad new family of coherent states, the wave-like quantum states that behave most like classical waves. The 2026 paper takes a special function, the Fox-Wright function, as the rule that sets the size of each state.

The authors check that the states meet the core tests: they vary smoothly, they can be scaled to unit size, and they can rebuild any state from their parts. They then extend the work to states with a continuous range of values, and to a number system with two imaginary units, called bicomplex numbers. A generalized multi-parameter function plays the same sizing role in each setting. The result widens the toolkit for quantum optics and for math built on bicomplex numbers.
arxiv-2602-24064:
Zhidan Feng and four co-authors show how to determine factorial speed for graph classes quickly. The 2026 paper addresses the speed of a graph class, the count of labeled graphs it contains, a complexity function catalogued online where many classes still sit as unknown.

The authors prove that any graph class representable by a finite binary language has at most factorial speed. Its count grows like a factorial-scale function. They use that criterion to classify many previously unknown classes as factorial. As a consequence, several inclusions between graph classes are now seen to be proper, since classes with different speeds cannot coincide. They also prove that k-letter graphs have exponential speed, a slower growth class, giving a clean separation between language-based classes and letter graphs.
arxiv-2602-24264:
Arnas Uselis and two co-authors argue that compositional generalization in vision embedding models requires linear, orthogonal representations. The 2026 paper defines compositional generalization as recognizing familiar parts in novel combinations.

The authors formalize, for compositional generalization under standard training, three desiderata: divisibility, transferability, and stability. They show necessary geometric constraints follow: per-concept components must combine linearly to form representations. That result grounds the linear representation hypothesis. Tests across modern vision models find factors that are partly linear, low-rank, and near-orthogonal per concept. Dimension bounds link the number of composable concepts to embedding geometry.
arxiv-2603-00164: Graves introduces Reverse CAPTCHA, a benchmark testing whether language models obey invisible Unicode-encoded instructions hidden in normal-looking text. It exploits a perception gap: models can read Unicode control characters that human readers cannot see. Across 8,308 model outputs from five models, two providers, two encodings, four hint levels and two payload framings, tool use sharply raises compliance, with provider-specific encoding tastes. Explicit decoding instructions lift compliance within one model and encoding by up to 95 percentage points.
arxiv-2603-00464: Wilson, Reilly, and Holland derive a simple route to algebraic entanglement entropy between shared degrees of freedom, for links within particles and across particles. Permutation symmetry lets group blocks split reduced density matrices piece by piece, so results from a huge space emerge at polynomial cost. The method handles particles with two degrees at two levels each, such as atoms with two electronic and two momentum states. Such systems simulate exactly at polynomial scale while still holding rich entanglement.
arxiv-2603-00664: Shinde and Kadam study transversal coalitions in r-uniform hypergraphs, where the vertex set splits into two parts, neither of which alone hits every hyperedge, though their union does. They determine the transversal coalition number for complete r-uniform hypergraphs and for r-uniform stars. Complete bipartite and complete r-partite r-uniform hypergraphs get the same treatment, as do r-uniform linear paths and cycles. Together the results pin down the coalition number across these families.
arxiv-2603-00864: Dong and three colleagues clarify how Yukawa couplings and mass patterns arise for matter fields in heterotic string theory on smooth Calabi-Yau shapes. The shapes' topology yields textures no ordinary group symmetry can produce, including the Weinberg pattern for two generations. At special points in the multi-Higgs parameter space a U(2) flavor symmetry appears, and small shifts away from those points give semi-realistic quark masses and mixings.
arxiv-2603-00964: Das and Karmakar study how Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity changes waves in hot, sticky, churning solar plasma that follows a polytropic rule. Positive gravity tweaks lift wave frequencies and outward energy flow by about 10 percent, while faster sound speeds raise them up to 55 percent. Negative tweaks instead strengthen binding and damping. Matching four years of solar Doppler data yields the first solar limit on this gravity idea from helioseismology.
arxiv-2603-01064: Li and three colleagues replace old multigrid smoothers, which fail on integral equations, with learned neural operators trained offline. Level-wise losses with spectral filters teach each one a high-frequency band, echoing the multigrid band split. Once trained, the smoothers handle new right-hand sides with no new training, beating old solvers on speed with steady results across sizes and regularization weights, and the design extends to PDEs.
arxiv-2603-01464:
Finding facts about a protein often means searching text and also reading the protein code itself. Congying Liu, Taihao Li, Ming Huang, and colleagues built a search agent for that dual task in 2026. Older agents search once, use text only, and get scored only on the final answer, so errors in the search path slip past.

Their agent, ProtRLSearch, searches in rounds and uses both the protein sequence and text to guide each step. Training rewards judge the search path as well as the final report. To test it, the team built a set of three thousand choice questions in three grades of hardness. Scores rose sharply at all three grades, which matters for work on disease-linked protein changes.
arxiv-2603-01664:
D. D. Solnyshkov, V. Paquelier, C. Balmisse, and G. Malpuech simulate black hole mergers in a lab fluid in this 2026 work. Analogue gravity uses fluids to mimic effects like Hawking radiation, but past setups held the fake hole fixed in place. A fixed hole cannot move, gain mass, or merge with another hole.

Their setting uses polariton condensates, where loss tied to speed makes each quantum vortex act like a small black hole. Such vortices can move through the fluid, so mergers enter reach at last. Two vortices alone cannot form a shared horizon, the edge past which flow cannot escape. Four or more can, and the shared edge size follows a simple geometric law. The team also clarifies how the true horizon differs from the apparent one here.
arxiv-2603-01864:
Alexander Prutsch, David Schinagl, and Horst Possegger predict traffic paths in a continuous stream, not as lone snapshots. Their 2026 work serves self-driving cars, which must forecast nearby road users with low delay. Snapshot methods treat each scene alone and waste what prior forecasts already learned.

Their lightweight method carries context forward from one time step to the next. Endpoints of prior forecasts act as anchors that guide the scene encoder to key context. That targeted encoding skips refinement rounds and segment-wise decoding, which cuts latency a lot. Tests show the context relay works as planned across consecutive steps. On a leading traffic benchmark, the method sets top streaming scores for both single and multi-agent cases. It does so while using far fewer resources than refinement-heavy rivals.
arxiv-2603-02064:
Tom Jacobs, Chao Zhou, and Rebekka Burkholz ask how the choice of trainer shapes learning in this 2026 theory paper. Trainers such as Adam update model weights in set ways. The authors group steep update rules under one flow model. That lens shows how update shape steers what a model learns and what it ignores.

In simple test networks, steep updates escaped stuck points and learned features well. Plain gradient steps needed huge step sizes to escape the same points. Such sizes are rare in real fine-tuning work. Tests backed the claim that escaping stuck points is a core hurdle. The authors also show that split weight decay, as in AdamW, steadies feature learning.
arxiv-2603-02164:
Sami Abuzakuk, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Rafael Pires, and colleagues speed up vector search in this 2026 systems paper. Vector search finds the stored items closest to a query. Graph indexes do this well, but each query walks the same graph from set starts. Real query streams cluster, so much of that walk repeats past work.

Their add-on, CatapultDB, learns from that clustering and adds shortcut links. Each shortcut jumps a query from its region to a node that past queries visited often. The base graph and search code stay unchanged, so key features still work. In tests, speed rose up to about two and a half times at equal recall. The shortcuts also adapted well when query patterns shifted.
arxiv-2603-02364:
Kirill Borodin, Vasiliy Kudryavtsev, and colleagues test fake-speech detectors across languages in this 2026 paper. Synthetic speech can mimic real voices, and detectors are meant to catch it. Most detectors are built and tested on a few major languages. The team built a huge corpus to check whether they hold up worldwide.

Their corpus holds thousands of hours of fake speech in sixty-six languages. Twenty-four open text-to-speech systems generated the audio. Forty-five of the languages count as low-resource in their setup. Eleven public detectors were tested with thresholds set on outside data, so no local real speech was needed. Rejection rates varied sharply by language, even under controlled conditions. Language itself acts as a source of domain shift, they conclude.
arxiv-2603-02864:
Oktay Cebecioğlu and Salih Kibaroğlu derive cosmic expansion laws inside a gravity theory with built-in twist. Their 2026 paper uses AdS-gauged gravity, a gauge-style extension of general relativity with extra symmetry generators. The extra gauge field creates torsion, a twisting of spacetime geometry beyond ordinary curvature.

For a uniform, direction-free universe, they work out the modified Friedmann equations, the rules linking expansion to contents. The new terms allow steady de Sitter-like acceleration driven purely by the theory's structure, with no exotic matter added. The gauge field's moving parts act like an effective cosmological constant source. One regime mimics cosmic-string-like behavior, tying spacetime twist to a known cosmic defect picture.
arxiv-2603-03064:
Kiminad Mamo proposes a new way to read a hadron's gravitational properties from its entanglement. His 2026 paper defines the radius flow of a ball-shaped region's entropy inside a single hadron state, with the empty-space contribution subtracted. On a lattice, this quantity can in principle be measured, making it a practical observable rather than a formal curiosity.

In the continuum limit, changing the ball's radius acts like a rescaling, so the flow isolates the trace part of the energy-momentum response. Mamo organizes the flow into a surface term plus a remainder fitted by templates built from gravitational form factors. For sample nucleon inputs, the spin-zero and spin-two templates peak at clearly different radii. Lattice data could thus reveal which contribution controls the hadron's interior.
arxiv-2603-03364:
Jasem Hamoud, of the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology, works out formulas for a graph measure called the Sombor index. Introduced in 2021, the index sums a degree-based score over every edge of a graph and is used to describe molecular and network structure. Simple shapes like paths and stars have known formulas, but layered hierarchical trees with uneven branching did not.

Hamoud derives a general recursive formula for a family of trees built on a central spine path, with pendant branches attached level after level. Branches on odd and even spine vertices follow different rules, one with a plain replication factor and one with an offset that propagates upward. The result pushes the theory of degree-based descriptors toward the complex, repeatedly built graphs where closed forms were missing.
arxiv-2603-03664: Xiangyu Liu and others formalize learning-to-communicate in partially observable multi-agent settings, bridging deep multi-agent reinforcement learning and decentralized random control. They show non-standard learning-to-communicate problems are computationally intractable in general, focusing on quasi-standard cases. They propose terms under which quasi-standard problems preserve their information structure after sharing, whereas violations can cause hardness. They develop provable planning and learning methods with quasi-polynomial time and sample complexities for cases satisfying the terms.
arxiv-2603-03764:
Maximilian Weber, Daiki Suenaga, and Masayasu Harada dissect an exotic four-quark particle and find its energy budget upside down. The Tcc tetraquark is modeled as a heavy diquark bound to a light antidiquark. Intuition says exciting the motion between those two clusters should cost less than exciting the light pair inside the antidiquark. Solving the Schrödinger equation with a standard potential and a Gaussian expansion method, their 2026 paper finds the opposite.

The between-cluster excitation costs more, not less. The inversion traces to centrifugal force acting on the light degree of freedom, which inflates the wider motion's price. The same framework applied to the bottom-quark sibling and to two heavy baryons shows the identical behavior, marking the mechanism as robust rather than a fluke of one system. The result reshapes how modelers should budget mass in exotic hadrons.
arxiv-2603-03964: Hengquan Guo presents BLOCK, a two-stage open-source pipeline turning arbitrary character concepts into pixel-perfect Minecraft skins. A second stage then decodes skins with a fine-tuned FLUX-2 model, converting the preview into a skin atlas image. The author further proposes EvolveLoRA, a progressive LoRA curriculum moving from text-to-image through image-to-image to preview-to-skin, initializing each phase from its predecessor to boost stability and efficiency.
arxiv-2603-04064: Chen and colleagues study lightweight backdoors on multi-encoder diffusion models, focusing on Stable Diffusion 3. Prior backdoor work largely targeted single-encoder models, leaving multi-encoder models with large-scale encoders underexplored despite many trainable parameters. The authors define four attack-target categories and pinpoint minimal encoder sets needed per objective. They then propose Multi-Encoder Lightweight aTtacks, training only low-rank adapters with pretrained encoder weights frozen. Tuning a tiny fraction of total encoder parameters suffices for successful backdoors on Stable Diffusion 3, revealing underexplored multi-encoder vulnerabilities.
arxiv-2603-04164: Kulczycki and Ryznar obtain sharp figures for harmonic functions on balls for x-linked rectilinear stable steps. They study functions harmonic with respect to such steps in balls, assuming Dirichlet exterior data radial about the center. The proof's main idea builds global barrier functions for that operator in balls. The figures are sharp.
arxiv-2603-04264: The KM3NeT team tests Lorentz invariance, a symmetry behind the Standard Model and general relativity, with atmospheric neutrinos. A partial detector with six units supplied 1.4 years of data for a search for isotropic violations near the Planck scale. No violation appears, so the team sets competitive limits on some coefficients for isotropic violation. Those limits complement and extend earlier experimental constraints. The search thus probes physics beyond current theory.
arxiv-2603-04464: Jiao and colleagues trace how conflicting examples mislead in-context learning. Few shot examples let models infer rules, but noisy examples make that skill fragile. One corrupted rule example causes large degradation. Probes show models encode both correct and incorrect rules early, gaining confidence only late. Early vulnerability heads show positional bias, while late susceptible heads cut support for correct predictions. Masking a few heads improves performance by over 10 percent.
arxiv-2603-04564: Joshi and colleagues show noise adapted quantum error correction at break-even on IBM hardware. Standard schemes carry high costs and strict thresholds. Present day use is therefore hard. A new noise adapted 3-qubit scheme faces native amplitude damping noise. It uses tuned circuits for lean write and read steps, with non-unitary fix steps built by block encoding, making the scheme chance based. Logical qubit lives beat bare qubit lives across multiple fix rounds, and readout quality now limits results, with better chips likely to bring gains.
arxiv-2603-04664: Nath surveys 50 years of SUSY and SUGRA, circa 1974 to 2024, and future prospects. Early seventies SUSY, mid-seventies gauge SUSY and SUGRA, and early eighties gravity mediated breaking plus SUGRA grand unification drove union progress. They also linked particle physics, cosmology, and strings. In the low-energy superstring limit below Planck scale, tests bear on superstring validity. Decades of collider, precision, astro, and cosmos searches followed. SUSY and SUGRA models also deeply shaped inflation, dark matter, and dark energy theories.
arxiv-2603-04864: Bright, Mende, and Zelek present wide injury-risk screening for baseball pitching from broadcast video. Precise body motion usually needs expensive stadium systems missing outside pro venues. Their one-eye pipeline finds 18 medical key metrics from broadcast footage for injury models. A drift-controlled global lifting module finds pelvis path through speed-based tuning and sliding-window guesses. A motion polish pipeline using bone-length limits, joint-limited inverse solving, and balance rules ensures stable motion. On 13 professional pitchers, 16 of 18 metrics reach sub-degree match, aiding injury calls from video.
arxiv-2603-04964: Suhas Kotha and Percy Liang find that replaying generic pre-training data during fine-tuning improves target-task performance, contrary to the practice of mixing it in only to prevent forgetting. In a setting with 150M parameter models, 4M target tokens, and 4B total tokens, generic replay markedly raises target data efficiency for fine-tuning and mid-training. Replay helps more when less target data appears in pre-training. In practice, fine-tuning 8B models with replay improves agentic web navigation success by 4.5% and Basque question-answering accuracy by 2%.
arxiv-2603-05164: A. Ustyuzhanin and team train machine learning models to infer the entanglement structure of disordered quantum spin chains from the strong disorder renormalization group method. A graph neural network on the interaction graph learns a bond-ranking rule like the decimation policy, beating a Random Forest older model. It reaches near-perfect pairing accuracy on disorder average and reproduces entropy across subsystem sizes and interaction exponents. Finite-temperature acts come out with no retraining by feeding the zero-temperature flow into a two-stage thermal sampling scheme.
arxiv-2603-05264: Anders G Frøseth reads proportional wealth taxation at market value, its return, portfolio, and pricing effects. The tax is a proportional government stake, sharing risk so wealth and risk fall by the same factor while return per share stays unchanged. Results: wealth's number of change is tax-invariant, weights are tax-independent, Sharpe ratios survive homothetic shrink, and investors pay the same price per share. Modigliani-Miller analysis confirms pricing neutrality and corrects a Fama (2021) discount-rate error. Book-value taxation, liquidity frictions, or dividend extraction break neutrality.
arxiv-2603-05364: Vincent Astier and Thomas Unger prove a signature trace formula for hermitian forms over Azumaya algebras with involution. The result extends Knebusch's symmetric-bilinear-form work over finite étale commutative extensions. For semilocal base rings, the authors obtain an exact total-signature sequence tied to Pfister's local-global principle and stability index.
arxiv-2603-05564: The BESIII Collaboration reports the first multi-channel joint analysis identifying properties of the exotic charmonium-like state Tccbar(4020) via electron-positron annihilation. The spin-parity of the Tccbar(4020) is determined for the first time to be 1+ with 11.7 sigma significance. A partial wave analysis runs simultaneously in three decay channels, using data samples collected with the BESIII detector on the BEPCII collider. Pole positions are extracted on Riemann sheets with three branch points, and relative branching fractions are obtained.
arxiv-2603-05764: Pinchuk introduces TML-Bench for data science agents on Kaggle-style tasks. Autonomous coding agents produce strong baselines quickly, but value depends on correctness. The paper evaluates 10 open-source models on four Kaggle competitions at 240, 600, and 1200 seconds. Each model runs five times per task and budget. A run succeeds with a valid submission plus a private-holdout score. Results report median performance, success rates, and variability. MiniMax-M2.1 achieves the best aggregate score. Average performance improves with larger budgets, though scaling is noisy.
arxiv-2603-05864: Barja and Brehmer blend view and screen widgets both ways over mirrored partner video, like a pane of glass, for distant joint view. Video-call data talks usually rely on screen sharing, skipping wordless talk, yet choice making, talks, and teaching benefit when folks see each other. Both sides move shared parts through two-hand moves. The authors show the approach with several screens spanning those use cases, and test it with 16 folks against mouse-based video calls. Findings suggest the approach promotes presence and mutual sense of study intent.
arxiv-2603-06264: Shankar and his team audit cultural alignment of current language models across India, East Asia, and Southeast Asia, with religion as a lens for wider alignment. Weighing model views against ground truth public attitudes through log probabilities and logits, they find popular models largely line up on broad social issues. They still misrepresent religious views, most of all minority ones, often feeding negative stereotypes. Light fixes such as demographic priming and native language prompting ease but do not erase these gaps. Later bias benchmark tests show harm that lasts.
arxiv-2603-06364: Elflein and his team present the first score based diffusion models making monoscopic gamma ray and proton shower images with nearly 2000 pixels. Tests use Wasserstein GANs on HESS simulations. Air shower simulations for instrument response are heavy and repetitive under varying conditions. Such models speed such work and provide a smooth device surrogate. Their use in gamma ray astronomy has been limited, especially for hadronic showers filling the background. Quality is checked with low level parameters and shower shape signs, while GAN methods remake gamma ray showers well.
arxiv-2603-06464: Hall-Smith and team model nucleosynthesis from an accretion disk around a neutron star in a common-envelope phase. Earlier work centred on low-angular-momentum material and turbulent outflows. This study shows angular momentum shaping falling material into a disk, changing nuclear burning conditions. Material from a disk around a 1.5 solar-mass neutron star with a 15 solar-mass companion heats on infall. Large rapid-proton-process products are made, giving another galactic boost; later helium infall yields alpha-rich making with titanium-44 and nickel-56.
arxiv-2603-06564: Tussa and Heredia explore episodic wearable AI use, where assistance is invoked for short activity, then set aside when unneeded, with a take-off-between-sessions form factor. They present The Pen, an ear-worn pen-like device for episodic cognitive assistance through short sessions using voice and visual context, with start and end boundaries and processing. A study reports how activation boundaries shape agency, cognitive flow, and social comfort for users.
arxiv-2603-06664: Yuan and Li address Diffusion Transformer video bottlenecks for long synthesis and real-time inference: full spatiotemporal attention causes O(N^2) memory use and high first-frame latency. They adapt Self-Forcing to sequence parallel inference for a causal autoregressive pipeline. Causal-RoPE SP, a sequence-parallel causal rotary position embedding variant, enables localized computation and less cross-rank communication. On an eight-GPU A800 cluster, quality stays comparable with first-frame latency under a second and near real-time speed, achieving a 1.58x speedup for five-second 480P videos.
arxiv-2603-06764: Kuyanov and Kissinger present a ZX-calculus technique for contracting diagrams whose cost scales with rank-width, a graph parameter that behaves well under rewrites. Given a rank-decomposition of width R, their routine runs a graph ZX-diagram in time scaling like four to the power R. For quantum circuits, it never trails state-vector simulation or stabilizer decompositions at the threshold, and often runs far faster. Heuristics supply good decompositions, since optimal ones are NP-hard. Benchmarks against Quimb show cuts in floating-point work.
arxiv-2603-07064: Moriya and colleagues trace a rare supernova type, like SN 2021yfj, back to two white dwarfs merging. A carbon-oxygen white dwarf pulls helium from a companion star, and a burning front moving inward builds a shell rich in silicon and sulfur. Once the companion also becomes a white dwarf, the pair merges, and tidal stripping sheds that shell as dense circumstellar matter. A blast inside it then matches the observed event type.
arxiv-2603-07164: Gao and colleagues show that strain alone can steer both topological order and functional response in a technetium-coated penta-hexa silicon sheet. Biaxial strain drives a full pathway from Chern number 1 through 0 and minus 1 to a metal state. The driver is motion-space orbital-picked tuning of technetium-d and silicon-p mixing. Two states stand out. A key yet useful optimal state at minus 2 strain has a direct bandgap. An odd state at minus 4 strain has a piezoelectric response three times that of MoS2.
arxiv-2603-07364: Hodossy and Farina build a virtual human that learns hand movements through a muscle-driven simulation plus a neural interface. Simply replaying recorded signals cannot capture the flexibility and causal structure of real control, so their model couples forward musculoskeletal simulation with reinforcement learning and online muscle-signal synthesis. The virtual user adapts its policy through feedback and feedforward control. A gesturing task shows the approach can test neural controllers and grow training data.
arxiv-2603-07764: Brix and colleagues extend gradient-descent ideas for nonlinear real arithmetic problems by combining language models and GPU acceleration. Solving such problems is computationally hard, and prior work proposed a gradient-descent approach. They implement their technique in the novel SMT solver GANRA for GPU-accelerated nonlinear real arithmetic solving. On two NRA benchmarks, GANRA significantly improves over the previous state of the art. On the Sturm-MBO benchmark, it proves satisfiability for over five times as many instances in under one twentieth of the previous runtime.
arxiv-2603-07864: Martinez offers an interpretable generative tool for spotting breaks and odd points in high-dimensional finance time series. The model, ReGEN-TAD, joins forecasting with reconstruction in a refined convolution-transformer design and pools four signals: forecast mismatch, rebuild decay, latent shift and volatility change. A robust calibration turns them into one score with no labelled data. Tests on synthetic and real finance panels show sturdier detection of structured shifts, with factor-level reasons for each flag.
arxiv-2603-08064: Jia and colleagues argue that standard checks of generative models throw away cues that matter for perceptual quality. Metrics like FID run on continuous recognition features trained to ignore appearance variation, so they miss signals viewers notice. The authors instead judge models in the space of discrete visual tokens, where one-dimensional tokenizers pack semantic and perceptual detail. Quality there shows up as predictable token statistics. They introduce Codebook Histogram Distance, a training-free metric in token space, plus Code Mixture Model Score, a no-reference quality metric.
arxiv-2603-08164: Mathur and colleagues study how older adults perceive explanations from voice assistants based on large language models. Such assistants can support aging in place with proactive reminders, health information, and everyday help, but as they grow more conversational, explanation design matters more. In a mixed-design study with 140 older adults, the authors vary two dimensions: evidential grounding, or the source of information, and the assistant's conversational personality in agreeableness and extraversion. Both dimensions shaped perceptions in distinct but linked ways.
arxiv-2603-08764: Faizuddin Ahmed and colleagues study charged black holes wrapped in a string cloud under bumblebee gravity, where Lorentz symmetry breaks on its own. They map mass, temperature, and entropy shifts, then trace photon spheres, shadows, and light bending as possible signs of the break. Finally they test Solar System checks, such as perihelion advance, to bound the Lorentz-breaking parameters.
arxiv-2603-09064: Kun Li and colleagues study mode-picked laser travel and absorption in strongly magnetized patchy plasma. Field-aligned travel and crash absorption of inbound laser light give cutoff rules, absorption rates, and scaling laws for right-hand and left-hand polar waves. Left waves reflect at cutoff density with absorption climbing with magnet field. Right waves travel as whistler modes without cutoff once the normalized electron orbit rate exceeds unity, letting deep energy settle in overdense plasma.
arxiv-2603-09364: Ahmed Tedjani and Boubakeur Khantoul study a two-dimensional Dunkl-Pauli oscillator threaded by an Aharonov-Bohm flux. Reflection symmetry through Dunkl operators plus the flux's gauge field constrain which quantum states are allowed: radial regularity and matching at the flux tube force a lowest angular quantum number. So the flux restricts angular sectors rather than merely shifting energies. From the exact spectrum they derive the partition function and closed forms for internal energy, entropy, and heat capacity.
arxiv-2603-09564: Lionel Yelibi scales the Triangulated Maximally Filtered Graph method, whose need to store a dense correlation matrix caps it at small and medium datasets. The approximate version, a-TMFG, starts from a k-nearest neighbors graph and estimates missing correlations on the fly, under a memory plan that curbs combinatorial blow-up. Tests probe robustness to parameters and noise on datasets with millions of rows. The aim is a lean graph for learning tasks where no natural graph exists.
arxiv-2603-09864: Oktay Günlük and coauthors replace heavy semidefinite relaxations with sparse linear cuts for nonconvex quadratic problems. The cuts outer approximate the positive semidefinite cone but touch only variable products that appear in the problem. They prove the resulting linear relaxation gives the same bound as the semidefinite one. A separation routine finds the cuts, and tests show branch and bound solvers run faster with them.
arxiv-2603-10064: Shaideman, Arias H and Golubnichiy obtain a still solution of Einstein's empty space laws for N spinning masses. The solution, built by the Euclidon method, is axially symmetric throughout. With no spin it gives N arbitrary axially symmetric still masses, such as Zipoy masses placed on the symmetry axis. With no distortion, the same family gives N Kerr NUT solutions, linking several known cases in one form.
arxiv-2603-10264: Diane Jung and co-authors design a robot-assisted system for chemical dialysis, a slow purification step used in polymer and protein synthesis. Manual lab work is tedious, so the team took a user-centered route, running two usability studies and revising the design from participant feedback. The final system aims to meet working scientists' needs in the wet lab, cut the load of long procedures, and offer a model for automating other experimental workflows.
arxiv-2603-10664: Alexandre De Masi argues that the terminal, not the graphical interface, is the design model for human-AI agent collaboration. Agent research chases GUI control, yet the tools agents use most, and use best, are terminal-based. He traces that to three properties: a shared representation between agent and interface, actions that stay transparent in the medium, and a low barrier for humans to join. Each is grounded in HCI theory, and terminals meet all three by default. Other modalities must be engineered to match them.
arxiv-2603-11164: David Shih presents a self-supervised way to simplify symbolic expressions. He makes training data by scrambling simple ones and records the inverse steps. A permutation-equivariant transformer policy learns to predict the next oracle action for a given one, step by step. Applied to dilogarithm reduction and scattering amplitude simplification in high-energy physics, the policy reaches near-perfect solve rates at all levels. It beats reinforcement learning and end-to-end regression methods. It works through a set of five-point gluon amplitudes.
arxiv-2603-11364: Rokuto Nagata and coauthors attack LiDAR-based localization with nothing but a mirror. Plain reflection can corrupt the point clouds scan matching trusts. Earlier spoofing injects signals and needs sensor-specific timing, and defenses increasingly block it. Their MirrorDrift instead aims an actuated planar mirror to seed ghost points. These points systematically bias scan-matching correspondences. Optimized mirror placement multiplies pose error several-fold over random placement in simulation. Real-world trials against a modern hardened LiDAR still force localization errors of several meters.
arxiv-2603-11464: Dans and co-authors press the semimetal YPtBi and track how its quantum traits shift. YPtBi draws interest because its Cooper pairs may carry higher angular momentum than singlet or triplet pairs. The team takes Shubnikov-de Haas and transport readings at pressures up to 2.08 GPa. Under pressure, the material turns more insulating at low temperature, and quantum oscillations fade. The upper critical field drops while the Dingle temperature climbs sharply. The shifts point to weaker band inversion and a topology that pressure can tune.
arxiv-2603-11664: Huang and co-authors present BackdoorIDS, a zero-shot way to catch backdoored images in pretrained vision encoders. The method rests on two signs seen under gradual masking. A backdoored image first locks attention onto its trigger; once masking passes the trigger's limit, attention jumps to clean content. That jump bends the image embedding sharply, while clean images drift in a smooth path. BackdoorIDS clusters the embedding path and flags any input whose path forms more than one cluster.
arxiv-2603-11864: Calinescu and co-authors tackle a gap in AI agent design: turning broad social, legal, ethical, empathetic, and cultural norms into concrete, checkable requirements. High-level frameworks state the principles, but builders lack a path to code. The authors propose a step-by-step process to pin down, validate, build, and verify such requirements for agents. They also survey the methods and tools that support each step. Open challenges and a research agenda round out the work, aimed at agents that provably respect human norms.
arxiv-2603-12064: Sun, Artan, Mielle, Lilienthal, and Magnusson rebuild moving scenes in 3D from several free cameras. Many observers may film one shared event, each from a shifting viewpoint. Prior tools take one camera or demand fixed, pre-calibrated rigs. Their two-stage method first tracks cameras through a spatiotemporal graph that links time and space views. Wide-baseline flow then refines depth and poses for dense consistency. A new motion-capture dataset helps show clear gains over feed-forward models.
arxiv-2603-12664: Lehui Li and co-authors bridge text and numbers for time-series forecasting with event-driven shifts. Text states impacts in vague, qualitative terms, while forecast models need explicit signals. Tests showed older methods over-attend to redundant tokens and fail to turn meaning into cues. Their TESS builds a middle space from four temporal primitives: lag, shape, volatility, and mean shift. A language model extracts them with confidence gating. Across four real datasets, error fell by up to 29 percent.
arxiv-2603-12964: Pawandeep Kaur and co-authors show that glasses near failure behave in two unlike ways set by stress triaxiality. That ratio weighs dilatational stress against shear-like stress. At high triaxiality, glasses turn strongly hyperelastic with very little plasticity, whatever their quench rate. Disorder still drives reversible nonaffine motion and forms micro-cavities. A small share of those cavities survive unloading and can seed large-scale cavitation. At low triaxiality the picture differs, and the split holds across glass formers.
arxiv-2603-13064: Sanket Jantre and co-authors build a data-efficient Gaussian process surrogate for spectral functions in a hole-in-antiferromagnet model. Full spectra hold rich many-body data, yet they cost a lot to compute. Many learning surrogates also demand huge training sets. Their deep-kernel model trains on just 10% of the spectra on hand. It beat a neural network trained on the same small subset. Its errors stayed in the same range as a network fed all the data.
arxiv-2603-13264: Fernando Spadea and Oshani Seneviratne present FedTREK-LM, a way to personalize recommendations without pooling private data. It joins lightweight language models with personal knowledge graphs that evolve over time. Federated learning keeps user data on local devices while models still learn. Structured graphs prompt the models for context-aware picks, like movies and recipes. Across three small Qwen3 models, it beat graph completion and federated baselines by a wide margin. Real user data proved key, since synthetic data cut scores a lot.
arxiv-2603-13764: Shigehiro Yasui, Su Houng Lee, Pok Man Lo, and Chihiro Sasaki propose a new nonet scheme for scalar mesons. The nonet joins f0(980), a0(980), K0*(1430), and f0(1770) as quark-antiquark P-wave states under SU(3) flavor symmetry. They investigate production of these states in relativistic heavy ion collisions. Yields are estimated with the statistical model and the quark coalescence model. In contrast, f0(1500) is treated as a glueball outside the nonet. Comparing yields across internal structures strongly suggests f0(1500) is a glueball, they argue.
arxiv-2603-13864: Li, Chen, and Chen show that lossy compression can quietly break hidden backdoor triggers in poisoned images. Once images are stored as JPEG-like bitstreams, triggers placed in RGB pixels often vanish. The authors argue that attacks must plan for compression from the start. They use region-of-interest coding, which protects chosen image areas during compression. Two attack designs follow: one revives trigger data in learned compression, and one writes trigger data into the bitstream with custom masks.
arxiv-2603-14064: Scheppe and Pak study finite-time braiding in topological nanowire qubits built on Majorana edge modes. Most past work treats braiding as slow and adiabatic, which leaves real gate timing unclear. The authors track two ways to shuttle bound Majoranas along one nanowire with space- and time-varying controls. They then recast the setup as a T-qubit to get finite-time gate forms. The results aim to guide real experiments toward fault-tolerant, scalable designs.
arxiv-2603-14564: Pereira, Costa and Rocha thin dense networks with distance backbones. Dense graphs slow simulations of social and biological systems. Distance backbones drop edges that break a broad triangle inequality rule. All shortest paths survive the cut. The team adds backbone synthesis, a sweep across nested backbones by degree of thinning. Tests then track what sparsification keeps or loses. Backbones best preserve node centrality ranks, they find. Local and global spreading dynamics also hold up best under backbones.
arxiv-2603-14664: Baciak, Cellucci and Falkowski read AI progress through punctuated equilibria from evolutionary biology. Smooth growth stories assume capability climbs steadily with model size. Their account finds long stasis broken by fast phase shifts. Five eras since 1943 and four epochs in the generative era structure the tale. A fitness manifold scores systems on capability, trust, cost and sovereign compliance. The Institutional Scaling Law then shows fitness is non-monotonic in scale. Past an optimum, more size hurts, they argue.
arxiv-2603-14764: Laudari and Baek keep polygon labels valid under geometric augmentation for segmentation. Crops and clips can cut bridge vertices in a single chained polygon. One region with an inner void then splits into stray parts. Floorplan analysis shows this failure mode in practice. Their fix repairs lost adjacency links in index space. Vertex order stays as drawn, and overhead stays tiny. The method drops into standard preprocessing flows with ease. Near-perfect cyclic adjacency preservation holds across common transforms, they report.
arxiv-2603-14864: Yu and co-authors benchmark shopping agents on long-horizon taste memory with Shopping Companion Bench. E-commerce agents must hold user tastes across long chats. Two tasks demand cross-session preference recall over 1.2 million real products. Failure scans blame hallucinated tastes and weak attribute checks. Tool-wise rewards give step-level training signal without hand labels. Even GPT-5 clears under 70% success on the bench. A fine-tuned 4B model beats strong baselines on both tasks, they report. Preference grounding stays the hard core of shopping help.
arxiv-2603-15064: Yu and co-authors study what happens when key numbers in a rotating fluid model reach extreme limits. The fluid can be compressed, and its heat content is not fixed. They add surface-tension-like effects to the flow equations in two settings, split by a parameter value. One case uses a spread estimate for the sound wave equation. The other uses direct error bounds. In both, the three-dimensional flow settles into flat Euler flow that cannot be compressed.
arxiv-2603-15164: Jiang introduces HindSight, a way to grade AI-generated research ideas by their real future impact. An idea system is limited to literature before a cutoff date. Its ideas are then matched against papers from the next 30 months and scored by citations and venue acceptance. Across ten AI topics, language-model judges saw no gap between retrieval-augmented and plain generation. HindSight found the retrieval system scored two and a half times higher. Its scores even ran against judge-rated novelty, which suggests judges overvalue ideas that merely sound new.
arxiv-2603-15464: Blumer and Quadrelli build two families of pro-p groups that cannot serve as absolute Galois groups of fields. The groups are variants of Demushkin groups with simple presentations. They fail to complete into 1-cyclotomic oriented pro-p groups, which bars them from being maximal pro-p Galois groups of fields holding a p-th root of unity. Other standard tests do not rule them out. Both the triple Massey vanishing property and quadratic cohomology hold, so the new examples pass those screens.
arxiv-2603-15664: Kirke tests quantum amplitude estimation on catastrophe insurance pricing. Classical Monte Carlo settles slowly, so tail percentiles stay blurry. Sparse tail data then trains weak risk models where losses hurt most. Quantum estimation promises a quadratic speedup in oracle queries. He built a full pipeline on a Qiskit Aer simulator. Fitted lognormal loss curves were coded into quantum oracles. Tests used synthetic data and 58,028 NOAA storm records. Discretization, not estimation, proved the main bottleneck, he finds.
arxiv-2603-15764: Ettengruber and Kühnel map how micro black hole dark matter could be observed. Extra dimensions or many species can make tiny primordial holes stable. A memory-burden effect can also slow their Hawking evaporation. Such holes differ in mass-radius links, heat, entropy, and lifetime. Neutron star survival gives the firmest limits so far. One narrow region also fits the missing-pulsar puzzle near the Galactic center. Neutrino telescopes help mainly in extra-dimension cases. Merger bursts may add a further probe.
arxiv-2603-15964: Bayona unifies finite differences and semi-Lagrangian schemes through local matrix exponentials. Global spectral methods trade accuracy against sparse method speed. His Local Matrix Exponential Propagator works inside a small stencil. Weights harvested there carry high-order time corrections for free. The scheme proves equal to optimal semi-Lagrangian transport for advection. Mixed-physics runs gain exact coupled evolution with no splitting error. A localized augmented matrix extends the idea to semi-linear systems. Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries, and Allen-Cahn tests keep high time accuracy.
arxiv-2603-16264: Mu and co-authors give language model agents an adaptive sense of theory of mind. Agents reason about what partners think, and partners do the same back. When reasoning depths mismatch, coordination suffers. Their A-ToM agent estimates a partner's likely depth from past exchanges. It then predicts the partner's next action. Tests spanned a matrix game, grid navigation, and an Overcooked task. Matched depths improved coordination across the tasks.
arxiv-2603-16464: Kanodia and co-authors probe the air of a giant planet around an M-dwarf star. The planet, TOI-5293Ab, circles its star in about three days. Two JWST transits supplied the data. The star's patchy surface spoiled the first visit's spectrum. The second visit could be cleaned of that contamination. Cleaned data show air poorer in metals than the Sun's mix. Methane shows strong evidence in the retrieval. The planet's radius looks inflated past theory.
arxiv-2603-17264: Kaneko argues that systems biology needs two lenses at once: the complex and the merely complicated. A complicated approach builds a detailed model with many parameters to match one system. A complex approach seeks universal traits shared across systems, captured by a simple model that names a universality class. Pulling out such traits is backed by evolutionary robustness and by shrinking dimension in high dimensional states. He argues that joining data driven omics with the universality approach is a key step for the field.
arxiv-2603-17364: Laliberte and Toriumi apply matrix bootstrap methods to matrix and tensor models at finite N. They use a Gaussian model with a quartic term as their test case. For matrix models, bounds seem to hinge on multi-trace values, not on N itself. For tensor models, the equations let bounds shift with N. That opens a wider scan and gives new bounds on the two-point function, they report.
arxiv-2603-17464: Xiao, Zhang, and Lazarian probe the spectrum of turbulence in the Galactic interstellar medium. They use multi-frequency radio polarization surveys and a variance-based method called PFA. Cross-checks with a classic power spectrum method and a second survey back the results. The disk slope runs steeper than the classic Kolmogorov value, they find. The halo slope matches Kolmogorov instead. Disk and halo turbulence likely cascade in distinct ways.
arxiv-2603-17564: Chen, Barbero, Preuss, and Soydaner add a trust module to AI agents in shared-resource games. Each agent keeps a small internal trust state. That state steers memory, exploration, and action choice. The module needs only local rewards and observations, at near-zero cost. In a grid resource world, trust cut conflicts and stopped long-term depletion, they report. Cooperation also returned after long forced-greed phases in a tower test.
arxiv-2603-17864: Senar and co-authors model how to spot leftover cancer after surgery from blood DNA. Liquid biopsies read methylation patterns in cell-free DNA, but tumor signal can fade near zero. Their bivariate deconvolution model links samples taken before and after surgery. It splits each profile into tumor and background parts, mixed by the tumor share. A grid approximation keeps maximum likelihood estimation fast. They test forecasts against mutation-based measures and one-year outcomes.
arxiv-2603-17964: Armatol and co-authors report the first direct test of neutron damage as a source of low-energy phonon bursts. They compare detectors exposed to fast neutrons with control detectors. The exposed and control samples differ in spectral shape and in how rates track thermal history. Rates also scale with neutron exposure in a telling way. They conclude that neutron damage bursts do not dominate the low-energy excess seen in these calorimeters.
arxiv-2603-18164: Ghiba, Giang, and Ureche derive nonlinear Kirchhoff-Love shell models from the Ciarlet-Geymonat energy. Starting from a 3D model for compressible isotropic materials, the shell energy uses all three fundamental forms. Coefficients depend on Lamé values, shell thickness, and the reference surface curvatures. A quadrature step keeps lower semicontinuity clear for the reduced functionals. They prove coercivity and existence of minimizers in fitting Sobolev spaces, with thickness rules varying by model.
arxiv-2603-18364: Jang, Teranishi, and Kim develop robust optimal control for differentially private dynamical systems. A plant can outsource control computation to an untrusted server if its state stays private. Noise added to outputs gives privacy, but the server knows only a set of possible noise laws. The server then minimizes worst-case cost over that set. A KL divergence ball relaxation makes the problem convex with a closed-form solution.
arxiv-2603-18464: Lu and co-authors present AcceRL, a distributed asynchronous framework for training vision-language-action models with world models. Synchronous training wastes hardware on synchronization barriers and costly environment data. AcceRL isolates rollouts, inference, and gradient updates so none waits on the others. Plug-and-play world models join the pipeline in a modular way. It runs 2.4 times faster than synchronous baselines and, with a pretrained world model, uses up to 200 times fewer online samples.
arxiv-2603-18764: Zheng, Zhang, Wang, and Chau present ProCal for source-free domain adaptation. Such methods adapt a trained model to a new domain with no source data. Neighbor-based methods can over-trust look-alike predictions, which erodes source knowledge. ProCal pairs the frozen source model's first guesses with the live model's outputs. Their blend calibrates neighbor probabilities step by step. A joint loss adds soft supervision plus a diversity term. Theory shows the method settles where source and target knowledge fuse. Tests span 31 cross-domain tasks on four datasets.
arxiv-2603-18964: Pandit and co-authors read the terms of use of six generative AI services through EU consumer eyes. Users must accept these terms to get access, yet few grasp what they sign. The team builds a codebook and codes each term set with it. All six drop any promise on quality, uptime, or fit for use, paid or free. Users bear sole blame for outputs that break provider norms. They also face account loss, with little say over how models work or how outputs may be used.
arxiv-2603-19064: Jiang and co-authors study short quantum links, where photon travel time is close to the emitter lifetime. Few-mode models fail here, as delay and many modes matter. They use delay differential equations with exact solutions, from one cavity mode to a full waveguide. They show emitters lock into self-synchronized Rabi oscillations driven by coherent photon echoes. This yields lasting quasi-dark states and vacuum Rabi splitting, even under superstrong coupling. Testing three transfer protocols, they find STIRAP uses that structure best, beating SWAP and wavepacket methods.
arxiv-2603-19164: Marín and Salerno probe shape rules for two quantities tied to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator. They study torsional rigidity and the first eigenvalue on convex sets. Counterexamples show that neither quantity is concave or convex in general. Log versions of those traits fail too. For balls centered at the origin, one power of the rigidity does turn out convex. They also give a negative answer to a known question on the eigenvalue. The symmetric case still breaks the hoped-for rules.
arxiv-2603-19264: Ramakrishnan and co-authors cut the cost of building test sets for question answering models. Labels from experts are dear, above all in fields like health care. Their GAT method uses language models as stand-ins to judge which unlabeled items are most unsure. A module first rewrites open tasks into a pseudo-choice form. That form lets the method score doubt for each candidate item. In zero-shot tests, error in score estimates drops by about 40 percent. The gain holds against classic sampling baselines.
arxiv-2603-19364: Khan and co-authors build one model that handles many ultrasound tasks across organs and scanners. Ultrasound images shift a lot with device, operator, and body target. Their AURORA uses a transformer encoder from the Qwen3-VL family. Token features are fused across scales, then split to small heads for each task. Task-aware sampling and loss balance keep the mixed training fair. Scores rise from 67 to 85 percent on validation data. The test score averages 81.84 percent across all tasks.
arxiv-2603-19464: Yang and co-authors test whether language models can prove robot path planners optimal. Such proofs need geometric insight and strict multi-step math. Their benchmark holds 34 research-grade proof tasks across planner types. Each task gives the algorithm, its constraints, and the claimed bound. Even top models fail to write fully valid proofs alone. Adding task-specific lemmas in context lifts proof quality a lot. That help beats plain chain-of-thought and giving the true ratio. A fine error study sorts where proofs break.
arxiv-2603-19564: Wu and co-authors argue that wearable foundation models must move past static encoders. Current models map short sensor windows to fixed labels and do well on narrow tasks. They fail on chronic conditions that unfold over months or years. Three shifts are needed, the authors say. Data must become rich, long-term, and multimodal. Models must reason over long personal histories, not snapshots. Inference must become agentic, supporting plans and interventions under uncertainty. The goal is anticipatory health support.
arxiv-2603-19664: Qasim and co-authors argue that the key-value cache in transformer inference is fully redundant. Keys and values at each layer are fixed projections of the residual stream, they show. Rebuilding them from one residual vector per token is exact, not approximate. They verify this on six models from four architecture families. Their KV-Direct scheme stores small residual checkpoints instead of full cache pairs. Over long chats it holds memory flat while the standard cache grows. It keeps perfect token match where eviction baselines degrade sharply.
arxiv-2603-19764: Meier and co-authors add a material strength model to the pkdgrav3 simulation code. Strength effects matter even in planet-scale collisions, yet modelers often skip them. The new model adds elastic stresses and pressure-based yield strength. It also adds thermal softening, all on the GPU framework. Tests against lab cliff collapse runs matched very well. Strength raised the disruption threshold for low-mass bodies. The fluid limit appeared only at far larger sizes.
arxiv-2603-19864: Simon and co-authors present NASimJax, a fast simulator for training agents to test network security. Penetration testing is a step-by-step task with partial views and many possible actions. Older simulators run on CPUs and cover narrow scenarios. NASimJax is built in JAX and makes diverse, solvable network tasks. It runs up to 80 times faster than earlier tools. Baselines include PPO and PQN agents. Training on sparser networks gave a natural curriculum and better transfer to denser ones.
arxiv-2603-20264: Egolf, Zhou, and Tripakis ask whether language models can do program synthesis as well as symbolic tools. They test four domains, from reactive synthesis to recursive functions. Each domain pits a top symbolic tool against two language models. The open Qwen model loops with a symbolic verifier until success or timeout. GPT-5 gets one run per benchmark, with its output checked afterwards. Symbolic tools solved more benchmarks in every domain. They also ran faster than GPT-5 everywhere, despite weaker hardware. Against Qwen they were faster or close in speed.
arxiv-2603-20464: Baiardi and co-authors build a double machine learning estimator for panel data with instruments. Causal inference gets hard when treatments are endogenous and controls are many. Standard two-stage least squares can fail under flexible covariate adjustment. Their panel IV estimator adds weak-identification diagnostics for safety. They revisit three influential migration studies using shift-share instruments. In one case, results broadly confirmed the older findings. In others, flexible adjustment weakened the instruments sharply. Simulations support more cautious inference in those weak cases.
arxiv-2603-20764: Darnige and co-authors track single swimming microorganisms in 3D with deep learning help. Most microscopes lose motile cells fast, since the view is small. Lagrangian tracking follows one cell by moving the stage to keep it in focus. Old methods need fluorescence, which can harm cells over long runs. Their method reads the cell's 3D position with a learned model instead. It works with brightfield views too, as shown with magnetotactic bacteria. Tests gave faster and more accurate tracks in complex media.
arxiv-2603-20964: Morys-Magiera and co-authors compare ways to generate realistic small road networks with built in redundancy. They test an evolutionary method against Wave Function Collapse and two swarm methods. The networks are judged on connectivity, cycles, intersections, dead ends, and cut edges, with physical plausibility enforced. An extended method uses MAP-Elites to keep elite variants. Fitness design choices shape the networks strongly. They also show a practical use: synthetic maps built from tiles of a Duckietown lab model, with matching segmentation masks.
arxiv-2603-21064: Jeong and co-authors split geometry and appearance in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. Pose-free methods build 3D Gaussians from uncalibrated images in one pass. Most use one network for both camera poses and appearance, which entangles the two tasks. Their 2Xplat uses two experts instead. A geometry expert first predicts camera poses. An appearance expert then synthesizes the Gaussians. With fewer than five thousand training steps, it beats prior pose-free methods. It also matches leading posed methods, which supports modular design for 3D tasks.
arxiv-2603-21164: Qiao and co-authors study how light nuclei and hypernuclei are produced in gold-gold collisions. They start from nucleons and hyperons at kinetic freeze-out in a quark combination model. In a coalescence picture, they give analytic formulas for two-body and three-body nucleus momentum distributions. The formulas explain measured spectra of deuterons, tritons, helium-3, and hypertritons from the RHIC Beam Energy Scan. They also predict spectra for several omega hypernuclei. Production correlations between species show notable patterns as collision energy varies.
arxiv-2603-21464: Fulman and Röllin study Eulerian numbers, which count permutations by their number of descents. Earlier work asked how evenly descent counts spread across congruence classes modulo b, a question with cryptographic motives. They give two proofs of explicit error bounds for this spread. One proof uses Stein's method with translated Poisson approximation and gives polynomial decay. The other uses Fourier analysis and gives exponential decay for fixed b, but leans on a special representation from 1973.
arxiv-2603-21564: Talebirad and co-authors propose a shared theory for hierarchical memory in language agents. Many systems already split memory into extracted units, grouped summaries, and budget-aware retrieval, but designs are hard to compare. The theory uses three operators: extraction, coarsening, and traversal. Coarsening groups units and assigns each group a representative, whose self-sufficiency can vary along a spectrum. They show this choice constrains which retrieval strategies can work. They then map eleven existing systems, from document hierarchies to agent traces, onto the same three operators.
arxiv-2603-21664: Bai and co-authors tackle a hard video task: who said what, and when, in multi-person scenes. Omni-modal models often cheat here, leaning on visual bias in test sets instead of true sound-vision links. Sparse frame sampling also erases lip motion. Their test setup removes visual shortcuts and forces real identity binding from plain language queries. Their model samples video at 25 frames per second and squeezes motion into six tokens per frame. It can lip-read and locate speakers with no cropping, they report.
arxiv-2603-22064: Gu and co-authors prove that minimum-weight decoding is NP-hard in three basic quantum code settings. Decoding is a core task in fault-tolerant quantum computing. The hard cases cover the color code with Pauli Z errors. They also cover the surface code with Pauli X, Y, and Z errors. The third case adds a transversal CNOT gate and measurement errors to the surface code. The authors note a sharp split between exact decoding and its approximations. Approximate decoders can still run well in practice.
arxiv-2603-22864: Inan and Kisselev study the hunt for heavy axion-like particles at a future collider. The setting is light-by-light scattering at the FCC-hh, a planned 100 TeV machine. They compute cross sections for proton and lead collision modes. They then derive exclusion and discovery limits for the particle's coupling across mass values. The strongest coupling limit lands near a mass of 250 GeV for lead collisions. For proton modes it lands near 1 TeV. The authors conclude FCC-hh has strong reach for such particles.
arxiv-2603-22964: Rodriguez-Grasa and co-authors derive PAC-Bayesian bounds for generalization in quantum models. Standard bounds for quantum models depend on total capacity and can be loose. They also ignore what the model actually learned. The new bounds are non-uniform and data-dependent. They rest on channel perturbation analysis for layered circuits with general quantum channels. The bounds depend on the norms of learned parameter matrices. Extensions cover symmetry-constrained equivariant models. Numeric tests support the theory, and design lessons follow.
arxiv-2603-23064: Zhang and co-authors identify a memory pollution risk in personal AI agents with background execution. In Claw-style agents, background heartbeat work shares a session with user chat. Content from email, feeds, or social platforms can enter the same memory. The authors trace an exposure to memory to behavior path. In a controlled social replica, perceived consensus drove short-term influence most. Routine memory saving turned much of that pollution durable. It then shaped later behavior across sessions. No prompt injection was needed, they report.
arxiv-2603-23264: Fattasse and four co-authors study how Dirac fermions cross a barrier in silicene. They track the Goos-Hänchen shift, a sideways beam jump, and the group delay time. Both depend on entry angle, barrier height and width, and particle energy. The shift oscillates as waves interfere inside the barrier. More energy, width, or angle brings more peaks and larger displacement. Delay time peaks where quasi-bound states form in the barrier. The results point to barriers as tuning knobs for Dirac transport.
arxiv-2603-23364: Riabov and Kryvyi isolate the byte encoding layer that ring-based cryptosystems need before encryption starts. Their base-m codec maps byte strings shorter than 2 to the 64 into residue lists modulo m. The design adapts Duda's rANS system, and decoding stays exact under stated bounds. The length sits in a fixed-width header, so stray valid suffix digits do not break decoding. The work ships with a Rust implementation and a Lean 4 formalization. Machine-checked proofs cover roundtrip correctness and residue validity.
arxiv-2603-23564: Hashimoto, Bamba, and Mandal test energy conditions in bouncing universes built from quadratic gravity. Their cosmos skips the singularity by bouncing, plus a scalar field. They check the null, weak, strong, and dominant conditions along the history. With the scalar tensor, three conditions hold and the strong one must break at the bounce. That break is what lets the bounce dodge the singularity. With an effective tensor that folds in curvature terms, all four break near the bounce. The split exposes the non-Einsteinian dynamics.
arxiv-2603-23964: Luo and co-authors map how reinforcement learning environments have changed, using data from over 2,000 papers. Environments shape what agents can learn, yet past reviews were mostly qualitative. Their automated study sorts benchmarks by domain and by the cognitive skills they demand. They find the field splitting in two. One part centers on language models and semantic priors. The other centers on domain-specific generalization. They describe the skill profile of each part and draw lessons for future simulator design.
arxiv-2603-24364: Kakoti extends a left-right symmetric theory by adding one sterile neutrino for each generation, and that new particle serves as a dark matter candidate. The model is built with A4 modular symmetry. Kakoti studies how giving different modular weights to the particles changes the results. The focus is on the dark matter relic abundance and on leptogenesis, the process that may explain the matter excess in the early universe.
arxiv-2603-24664: Cutrona and co-authors build a realistic model based on classical scale invariance. In such theories, scales arise through dimensional transmutation, symmetries break radiatively, and first-order phase transitions always follow. The flat potentials that result also suit inflation. Their model accounts for all observational hints of new physics. It also fits the latest inflation limits from Planck, BICEP/Keck, and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. Scale invariance here yields a two-stage inflation: a slow-roll stage and a thermal stage, split by a radiation era.
arxiv-2603-24864: Pierce and Rajapakse model quantum billiards with the finite element method to hunt for quantum scarring candidates. Confined electrons have discrete spectra set by the Schrödinger equation for each shape. Closed-form spectra exist for boxes, circles, and triangles, but complex shapes need numerical methods. Their Mathematica implementation covers varied geometries. Checks include the many-sided polygon limit, known analytical solutions, and a standard convergence test, all matching well. At high energy index, scarring may appear for certain geometries, and the computed states are inspected for it qualitatively.
arxiv-2603-25064: Kheto and co-authors simulate how electron beams break apart a tungsten compound used in nano-printing. The molecule W(CO)6 is a standard feed gas for focused electron beam deposition. Their dynamics runs vary gas density and beam dose. The molecules shed carbon monoxide step by step, forming species with fewer CO groups. Tungsten atoms then gather into small metal clusters. Denser gas and higher dose push the breakup further. Some runs settle into a near-steady mix. Scaling rules link dose and density to the fragment mix.
arxiv-2603-25164: Wang and co-authors attack systems that pair a language model with a search database. Such RAG systems can be poisoned by bad passages planted in the store. Older attacks need to know the user's question first. PIDP-Attack joins prompt injection with poisoning, so it needs no such knowledge. Odd marks added to any query at run time steer the model toward planted text. Across three question sets and eight models, it beats the prior PoisonedRAG method. Success rates rise by 4 to 16 points while retrieval stays sharp.
arxiv-2603-25464: Hu and co-authors teach a four-legged robot new skills on the spot, with no reward hints and no retraining. Zero-shot methods learn from a fixed dataset, but a canned set can miss what real tasks need. Their FB-MEBE explores live, chasing the widest spread of behaviors it can reach. A critic then bends the recovered gaits toward natural, body-safe forms. In sim tests it beats other exploration plans on later tasks. Best of all, its policies walk on real hardware straight from training.
arxiv-2603-25764: Mehta studies whether coding agents can be trusted, not just whether they finish tasks. He runs four frontier models over 1,750 runs on 50 SWE-bench Verified tasks. GPT-5 submitted a patch every time but solved only 44 percent of tasks. Gemini submitted least often, at 70 percent, yet solved 50 percent. The main failure mode is what Mehta calls silent semantic failure. The agent repeats the same wrong reading of the task with full confidence. This mode covers most failing runs and stays hidden from simple monitoring.
arxiv-2603-25864: Yang and co-authors present GUIDE, a benchmark for AI help in open-ended software tasks. Most GUI agents just automate clicks, which ignores what the user wants to explore. GUIDE asks whether a model can read behavior, infer intent, and offer help at the right time. It holds 67.5 hours of screen recordings from 120 novice users across 10 programs. Think-aloud narration comes with the recordings. Eight top multimodal models were tested. All struggled, reaching 44.6 percent on behavior detection and 55.0 percent on help prediction. User context raised help scores a lot.
arxiv-2603-26164: Liang and co-authors present DataFlex, a single framework for data-centric training of language models. Data-centric methods tune which samples are picked, mixed, or weighted during training. Past tools for each trick live in separate codebases with clashing interfaces. DataFlex unifies selection, mixture adjustment, and reweighting on top of LLaMA-Factory. It keeps the standard workflow and adds shared support for embeddings and gradients. In tests, dynamic selection beats full-data training on MMLU for two models. Mixture methods also improve scores when pretraining on SlimPajama.
arxiv-2603-26264: Gao and co-authors build a learning controller for battery storage in power distribution networks. The controller must cut costs and guard voltage as loads and network shape change. It pairs the TD3 algorithm with graph neural networks that read the network layout. They compare three graph variants on 34-bus and 69-bus systems, under layout changes and transfer between systems. Graph-based controllers cut voltage breaches, with the clearest gains on the 69-bus system.
arxiv-2603-26664: Li, Xu, Tan, Cao, and Liu argue that coding agents fail code review not on logic but on fit with a project's habits. Their Learning to Commit framework builds an online memory from a repository's own history. The agent first retries past issues blind, then compares its attempt with the true fix. Gaps are distilled into reusable skills about style, internal APIs, and design constraints. New pull requests are then drafted under those skills, grounding the code in how the project itself evolved.
arxiv-2603-26964: Rigas and co-authors introduce VoroFields, a neural way to approximate generalized Voronoi diagrams. Building such diagrams exactly grows combinatorially hard as sites and metrics vary. VoroFields instead learns a smooth field whose peak regions form the cells. Borders appear where two sites give equal field responses. A hierarchy refines only near those transition zones, cutting the work. Experiments across site families and distance rules recovered cells and boundaries well. The approach needs no shape-specific construction for each new case.
arxiv-2603-27064: Kondic and co-authors introduce ChartNet, a million-scale dataset for teaching models to read charts. Chart reading mixes visual patterns, numeric tables, and language in one task. A code-guided pipeline synthesized 1.5 million chart samples across 24 chart types. Each sample aligns plotting code, the rendered image, its data table, a summary, and questions. Extra subsets add human annotations, real-world charts, safety, and grounding cases. A strict filtering pipeline guards visual and semantic quality. Fine-tuning on ChartNet improved chart benchmark results consistently.
arxiv-2603-27164: Qin and co-authors present daVinci-LLM, a fully open project on the science of language model pretraining. Pretraining sets a model's ceiling, yet its details stay hidden by business secrecy. The team shares its data flows, training runs, and findings in full.
