The model hits about 99 percent right on same-day tests and about 62 percent with 150 senders, beating CNN and Transformer base models. A phase step at the input helps most.
arxiv-2605-30664: Tuero and colleagues improve policy tree search guided by a learned policy, which pays heavy overhead for explicit subgoal generation. They replace explicit subgoals with a learned rerooter inside the introduced square-root Levin tree search algorithm, which implicitly splits problems into soft subtasks. Three rerooters are proposed: one clustering by global state structure, one using learned cost-to-go estimates, and a hybrid of both. Avoiding explicit subgoal reconstruction enables scalable search with far lower overhead, reaching environments where subgoal-based search fails with strong online training efficiency.
arxiv-2605-31164: Yuanjian Xu and colleagues schedule language-model training data by modelling how samples influence one another. Most schedulers adjust the overall data mix while ignoring directional effects between samples, yet training order matters when samples push each other in specific directions. Their D3 framework builds a dynamic influence graph from loss-based dependencies and solves a constrained optimisation over it to order the data. The method improves on existing schedulers in both pretraining and post-training, with modest extra cost.
arxiv-2605-31464: Khan and colleagues study language models as selective stand-ins for GPU kernel runtime tuning. Tuning a kernel normally needs repeated on-device measurement, and each run is costly since it needs compiling and rerunning. A good stand-in should forecast relative speed well, and know when it might be wrong, deferring to the GPU then. The team finds models can forecast relative kernel speed accurately. Reinforcement learning sharpens both forecasts and confidence, and the stand-in lets a search test several times more candidates on the same GPU budget.
arxiv-2606-00164:
Hayes and co-authors make the case for a boost to the Hubble Space Telescope. A higher orbit could keep Hubble at work into the 2030s. Their plea, a nod to a famed 1946 report, centers on gas that wraps round galaxies. This halo gas holds clues to how galaxies trade mass and heat.

Hubble alone can map glow lines from hot metals and hydrogen in these halos. No scope now flying or planned can match that reach. Such maps would give the first broad count of warm-hot halo gas. They would also hone the science plan for the next big scope. Target picks for its deep gaze would gain from this groundwork.
arxiv-2606-00464:
Markert and co-authors test if broad reach is the key spice in research-style physics labs. Such labs aim to give class folk a true taste of lab craft. Full CURE labs wrap that taste in real, wide-reach quests. They cost much and need a stream of fresh quests to run.

The team run two twin labs side by side for one term. One uses muon tools with reach past the class room. One uses stock intro gear with no such reach. Thought skill and views on labs are scored for both groups. Rank-fit math sets the two groups side by side. Both labs yield like gains in skill and views. Broad reach, on its own, adds no clear lift.
arxiv-2606-00764:
Zikkos settles an open question on Gabor systems in this 2026 maths paper. A Gabor system builds a set of functions from shifts and modulations of one fixed function. Here that function is a Gaussian. The system sits at the critical density, the tightest packing of its kind.

Zikkos proves the system is a weighted lower semi frame at that density. The result fills a gap left by recent work on the same system. That work showed it is not a weighted frame and has no reproducing partner. Zikkos adds a sharp extra fact. Remove any one atom from the system, and fit weights can be found for what is left. The rest then forms a complete Riesz Fischer sequence and a lower semi frame. The paper gives specialists a firm place for this borderline system in frame theory.
arxiv-2606-00864:
Zhang and Shao fix a flaw in bandwidth-free tests in this 2026 econometrics paper. Such tests judge a multi-part claim about time series data. They are loved for ease: no tuning knob, and size closer to the nominal level than classic methods. But with small or mid samples, size can warp badly. Strong time links and many parameters make the warp worse.

Their cure is sample splitting plus self-normalization. Splitting cuts the parameter down to one dimension for the final test. They build two test forms, one based on the max gap and one on squared gaps. Limit laws are derived under both the null and other cases. Simulations show the size warp shrinks a lot. The trick fits many jobs: mean tests, zero-autocorrelation tests, regression claims, and change-point tests for multivariate means. The pair present it as a broad patch, not a one-case fix.
arxiv-2606-00964:
Székelyhidi constructs a surgical flow for a wide class of surfaces in this 2026 maths paper. Mean curvature flow moves a surface by its curvature, like a film shrinking. Mean convex surfaces keep a sign on that curvature. Surgery versions cut and cap the surface where it pinches, so the flow can go on.

Past surgery flows needed a stricter 2-convex rule. His construction starts from any compact mean convex hypersurface in Euclidean space. That widens the reach past the Huisken-Sinestrari and Haslhofer-Kleiner lines of work. One novelty stands out: the flow does its own topology work. Nondegenerate cylindrical singularities perform the surgeries from inside the flow. The flow does need slight adjustment at a few smooth times. The result gives geometers a surgery tool for the full mean convex class, a setting where singularities are the rule, not the exception.
arxiv-2606-01264:
Sato and co-authors share a huge dataset of Japanese speech signals. It holds 1,020 hours of records from three speakers. Brain waves, face muscle signals, and audio were caught at once. All three speakers are healthy native Japanese speakers. They spoke with an open vocabulary, not fixed scripts. Three EEG systems were used across many sessions. Sessions ran over several months in total.

Channel counts span 62 to 128 per system. Each session adds synced signals, event notes, and transcripts. Checks show the expected spectral profile in the data. Task-linked alpha drops and timed responses also appear. The set is free in BIDS format on OpenNeuro. It aids speech decoding and broader brain signal work.
arxiv-2606-01364:
Bommarito ranks Windows functions to guide vulnerability research at scale. A modern OS is a haystack of signed binaries. It holds millions of functions, most of them irrelevant. Analysts must pick which function to read first. At whole-OS scope, target choice is the binding constraint. His pipeline, Symbolicate-Enrich-Sample, builds a ranked research queue. It works in cheap batches over production binaries.

Public symbol files restore function names for stripped binaries. Those names join to a recovered call graph. Cheap structural features attach to each named function. A low-cost language model assigns risk tiers and bug-class guesses. From 7 point 2 million functions, filters leave about 22,000 candidates. The dataset itself is withheld for legal and dual-use reasons.
arxiv-2606-01464:
Elhady, Agirre, and Artetxe boost multilingual reasoning via cross-lingual consistency. Advanced reasoning in LLMs clusters in a few rich languages. English dominates that small set of languages. Their principle is simple: equivalent problems should get the same answer. The answer should not depend on the problem's language. An unsupervised reinforcement learning approach enforces that consistency. It needs neither gold answers nor parallel data. Scarcity of multilingual reasoning data limits past methods.

Gains reach up to 21 point 7 percent on MGSM. That benchmark spans 10 languages in their tests. Unseen languages improve by 18 point 2 percent on average. Three out-of-distribution benchmarks gain up to 6 point 2 percent. Consistency-based training thus lifts multilingual skill without supervision.
arxiv-2606-01664:
Han proves spectral convergence for polynomials in Ginibre matrices. Fix a polynomial in n non-commuting variables, of any degree. Apply it to n independent complex Ginibre matrices of size N. The empirical spectral distribution of the result is his object. As N grows, it converges to the Brown measure. That measure is evaluated at free circular variables. For degree at most 2, the result was known from Cook, Guionnet, and Husson. Han extends it to polynomials of arbitrary degree.

A least singular value bound is the main proof step. It covers the polynomial shifted by almost any complex value. A wider bound for tensorized Ginibre matrices supports that step. The convergence also holds beyond Gaussian entries. Mean zero, variance one, and finite moments suffice.
arxiv-2606-01964:
Deng and co-authors model how eyes move during reading, in full detail. Eye movements reveal both reader cognition and text traits. Fixation data help improve language models and reader profiling. But large eye-tracking data sets are hard to collect. Recording sessions are costly and resource heavy.

Their Eyettention II model generates realistic scanpaths end to end. Each fixation carries location, landing spot, and duration. Those attributes arrive in chronological order as a sequence. The model is lightweight by design choice. It trains well on limited GPU resources. That trait suits the scarce-data setting directly. Generated paths can stand in for real recordings. Downstream language and reading tools gain training material.
arxiv-2606-02064:
Breiten and co-authors speed up optimal control for transport-dominated systems. Reduced-order models act as cheap surrogates for PDEs. The Kolmogorov barrier blocks efficient models for transport cases. Optimal control needs many full PDE solves. Surrogates could cut that cost a great deal.

Their framework optimizes first, then reduces the system. An optimality system is built for the full problem. Reduced models then approximate that system directly. The reduction uses shifted proper orthogonal decomposition. That method suits transport structure better than plain POD. The team explore how well the pairing works. Speed and accuracy trade-offs are the focus. The approach targets control problems with moving fronts.
arxiv-2606-02464:
Hassin and Ravner study how to admit customers to a queue they cannot see. The queue is a standard M/M/1 system. A memoryless controller can only thin arrivals at random. The authors compare that rule to a gated admission rule. Gated admission blocks new arrivals for a fixed time after each entry. At equal throughput, the gated rule wins.

The win is stochastic dominance over random routing. Social welfare rises under any cost tied to time spent in the system. The authors find the welfare-maximizing threshold for the gate. They also define the Price of Forgetting. That ratio compares gated welfare to memoryless welfare. The ratio has no upper bound. Yet the absolute welfare gain stays bounded. The result shows memory can matter greatly in relative terms, even when the absolute gain stays small.
arxiv-2606-02564:
Cheng and co-authors recast vision-language models as teachers for video reasoning. Video generation models make coherent visual paths for reasoning tasks. They often miss task rules, though. Logical failures follow. Past work uses vision-language models as pre-solvers. Their text guidance loses fine spatiotemporal detail. Generators also fail to follow long-tail instructions.

The teacher role plays to a different strength. Vision-language models judge process constraints and goal success well. The teacher extracts task rules as differentiable rewards. A lightweight LoRA module on the generator is tuned at test time. The rewards guide that tuning online. Tests span symbolic and general video reasoning benchmarks. The method gains 16.7 points on average. The solver paradigm gains only 0.4 points. Best-of-N scaling gains 2.2 points at similar cost. The findings frame test-time teaching as a path to general video reasoning.
arxiv-2606-02764:
Hsu and Moortgat test how well satellite depth maps of shallow seas transfer across regions. Satellite-derived bathymetry is cheap but scales poorly. Optically complex coasts are the hard cases. Sentinel-2 imagery covers the 0 to 20 meter depth range. A Random Forest baseline competes with four convolutional networks. Training regions are Pratas Island and parts of the Great Barrier Reef. Test areas are independent, within and across regions.

Keeping contiguous reef blocks in training is the single most impactful design choice. A smooth weight function loss emphasizes near-surface depths. Within regions, error runs from 1.15 meters up to 1.92 meters. For depths under 3 meters, error drops to about a quarter meter. Random Forest degrades sharply across regions. Deep models stay more robust. On the MagicBathyNet benchmark, the networks reach about a fifth of a meter of error. Multi-temporal imagery broadens training diversity. Median aggregation across passes cuts noise at inference.
arxiv-2606-02864:
Levit and Silman prove a theorem about the ends of stationary random spaces. The spaces are metric measure spaces with a random but statistically steady structure. The class covers random graphs, manifolds, and discrete subgroups. An end is, roughly, a distinct way for a space to run off to infinity.

The pair prove that such a space can have zero, one, or two ends. The only other option is a Cantor space of ends. For surfaces, they go further and list all possible homeomorphism types. This mirrors earlier work by Biringer and Raimbault on unimodular Riemannian manifolds. Their method rests on a general principle they call no geometric core. It also uses a study of finite versus infinite expected return times. The result gives a firm shape to a broad class of random geometries. It tells researchers which end structures can occur and which cannot.
arxiv-2606-03064:
Fan, Li, and Liu study the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on a half-space with nonhomogeneous boundary conditions. The team treats the initial-boundary value problem. For the matching linear problem, they derive endpoint Strichartz estimates.

For the nonlinear problem, they prove local well-posedness in Sobolev spaces up to regularity below five halves. The power of the nonlinearity must stay below a bound that depends on dimension and regularity. Global well-posedness follows in the same range. For higher regularity, they extend a one-dimensional global theory to the higher-dimensional half-space. For lower regularity, they obtain global solutions for the first time. The case of zero regularity is notable. Nonzero boundary data breaks mass conservation, yet the key estimates still follow. The work widens the well-posedness map for this equation.
arxiv-2606-03164:
Debele, Goytom, and Misbah test a phone-based score of human focus. The Focus Performance Score comes from Pulse Focus, a mobile Stroop app. In a Stroop task, a word names one color but is printed in another, and the user must fight the clash. The team asks if the score truly tracks attentional control.

Three checks support the score. In behavior data from 466 people and over 111,000 trials, the score caught the Stroop clash effect and tracked each person's control level. It also held steady across repeat tests. Brain data from 55 people in a known fMRI set tied the score's main part, mean reaction time on clash trials, to activity in the anterior cingulate cortex. A formula check fixed overlap inside the scoring frame and backed its weights. The authors offer the score as a firm behavioral signal for attention-aware AI.
arxiv-2606-03264:
Zhang and a large team upgrade a compact model for document parsing. PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 builds on a 0.9-billion-parameter baseline. The old model's errors cluster in weak regions: places where behavior is unstable, data is sparse, or labels are unreliable. Widening the corpus at random would waste effort on strong regions.

The new version uses a region-aware data plan. Weak regions of the old model are found and enhanced with care. The trust in supervision signals is raised at the same time. A staged post-training recipe then applies curated data choice and reinforcement learning in steps. The model scores about 96 percent on OmniDocBench, a new state of the art for the task. It also stands well against top vision-language models. The authors offer the recipe as a practical path for the model series. The lesson is to fix the weak spots, not to add data blindly.
arxiv-2606-03464:
Nurdin, Liu, Mccreadie, and Thamsen measure how much lakehouse query times vary in the cloud. Lakehouse systems now run much analytics work on shared platforms. Predicting query time helps balance money, resource, and carbon costs. Yet the same query can run at very different speeds from run to run. That variance had not been studied in a systematic way for lakehouses.

The team ran Kubernetes setups on three public clouds and one private cloud. Multiple data scales and three benchmarks were covered. Repeated runs of one query differed by nearly twofold in time. A factor study probes causes like data locality, neighbor load, and caching. Prediction models suffer under this variance. Fixing key sources of it cuts prediction error by up to 80 percent. A low-carbon scheduling test shows real savings when variance is counted in. Operators get hard numbers for a cost they often ignore.
arxiv-2606-03764:
Abel, Lee, Campbell, and Choudhary map crystal structures to Raman spectra and back with RamanGPT. Raman spectroscopy is a handy vibrational probe in materials labs. Predicting a spectrum from a structure usually needs costly perturbation theory. Reading a structure from a spectrum usually needs curated reference matching. Their framework tackles both directions for inorganic crystals.

A line graph neural network predicts spectra from structures. It trains on a database of about 5,100 materials. Output covers 200 bins across the standard wavenumber range. Many predictions capture the target spectrum's main features. A tuned language model runs the inverse direction from spectrum plus formula prompts. It recovers lattice values with small errors on held-out materials. Formula consistency reaches about 87 percent. A matcher and a consistency loop are live on a public site. Materials teams get fast two-way Raman tools.
arxiv-2606-03864:
Maillart and co-authors forecast scientific breakthroughs from how concept networks change. Breakthroughs show up as new or stronger links between research concepts. OpenAlex concept networks supply the evolving map. Fifty-nine semantic and topological features describe each concept pair. A two-stage LightGBM model predicts link formation first. A regression stage then estimates the future weight of the link.

Four technology and biomedical domains validate the approach. ROC-AUC lands between about 0.954 and 0.967 at all horizons, with no re-tuning. Prior models sat near 0.90. Forecasts rest on structural, auditable features, not opaque embeddings. Regression error stays stable from one to five years out. Adamic-Adar similarity and degree-based measures drive most of the accuracy. Two expert-checked cases match specialist expectations on convergence. A three-layer plan turns forecasts into research strategy.
arxiv-2606-03964:
Ghai and Mitra study how fully a quantum measurement reveals an unknown state. A measurement is informationally complete when its outcome rates pin down that state. Such tools matter for state and process tomography. The pair build a faithful measure of that completeness. They also ask how well channels keep this trait intact.

They work out the measure for symmetric qubit measurements of this kind. That value caps all minimal qubit measurements of the same class. Their channel measure links to a channel's least output coherence. That link holds for any choice of incoherent basis. A light-matter example shows the ideas at work. Readers get a shared frame for completeness, preservation, and coherence.
arxiv-2606-04064:
Fiedler, Greve, and Zalieckas propose a quantum sensing concept for liquid analysis. It joins NV centre magnetometry with magnetic nanoparticles tied to a diamond surface. DNA strands anchor the particles as tiny mechanical oscillators. Heat drives their motion, and the liquid around them shapes it. The moving particles make time-varying magnetic fields.

Near-surface NV centres pick up those fields through resonance or coherence shifts. The diamond surface is patterned with tether types of varied length and chemistry. One liquid thus maps to a high-dimensional response vector, not one number. Shifts in viscosity or surface binding change each region in its own way. The team sets out the physics, scaling rules, and feasibility. Label-free, parallel liquid checks are the goal.
arxiv-2606-04164:
Sotirios Vavaroutas, Yu Yvonne Wu, Ali Etemad, and Cecilia Mascolo propose ADAPTOOD in 2026, a way to fine-tune heart-signal models when deployment data drift away from training data. Electrocardiogram models meet new sensors, new populations, and new tasks, and standard adaptation treats every shift as equally severe.

Their framework measures data uncertainty to grade how far the new data sit from the pretraining distribution, then lets that severity score steer low-rank updates and automatic tuning of training settings. The result adapts hard when the shift demands it and gently when it does not. In out-of-distribution tests, the method gained up to seven percent accuracy and nearly thirteen percent precision over existing approaches, and held up as shift severity grew.
arxiv-2606-04264:
Zeyuan Yang and a team of co-authors propose UniCanvas in 2026, a diffusion model that generates images with real text drawn inside them, rather than emitting text as separate tokens. Unified models usually must choose: autoregressive systems reason well but draw poorly, while diffusion models draw beautifully and garble words.

UniCanvas treats the image as a shared pixel canvas, a kind of world model of visual change, and learns language as visual patterns on that canvas. The model therefore paints words as naturally as it paints objects, interleaving them in one synthesis pass. Experiments showed it improving over previous unified models on mixed text-and-image generation. The authors position text-in-image diffusion as a promising route to a single model that both understands and creates across modalities.
arxiv-2606-04364:
Dhanesh Ramachandram proposes in 2026 a concept bottleneck model whose named concepts must look at the right body parts. Such models predict interpretable attributes before the final label. But a concept head for the wing is usually free to peek at the beak. It can then answer correctly for the wrong reason.

His part-factorized design ties each part query to one body region by construction. A learned spatial prior, seeded from average keypoint positions, guides the tie. A small alignment loss nudges each query toward its keypoint. Aligning on well under one percent of training images moved pointing accuracy from near chance to about three quarters of full supervision. Bird classification accuracy barely moved across the whole range.
arxiv-2606-04564:
Böhm, Purucker, Hutter, and Schlosser teach a tabular foundation model to predict when an event will happen, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Standard models predict what class an example belongs to. It must handle censored data, where follow-up ends before the event occurs. Standard foundation models cannot do this natively. Their predictions get biased. Their model, SurvPFN, is a prior-data fitted network. It is pretrained on millions of synthetic survival tasks. It can then answer new datasets without fitting each one.

The synthetic tasks use Weibull-distributed event times. Training uses a censored negative log-likelihood. So the model learns survival as continuous-time distributional regression. On SurvSet, a collection of real-world survival tasks, SurvPFN proved competitive with classical and deep survival baselines. It needed no per-dataset fitting. It needed no survival-specific architecture or feature engineering. The trick is treating censoring inside the loss itself.
arxiv-2606-04864:
Zhou, Fu, and Chung present a preconditioner that makes very large sparse linear systems solvable in practice, in a 2026 arXiv numerical mathematics paper. Symmetric positive definite systems from elliptic problems with varying coefficients are notoriously slow for iterative solvers, because low-energy modes converge slowly. Their two-grid algebraic multiscale preconditioner builds a coarse space directly from the system matrix, using graph partitioning and local generalized eigenvalue problems to create basis functions capturing exactly those troublesome modes.

The method needs no geometric information, so it suits unstructured, matrix-only settings, and its construction parallelizes naturally. On heterogeneous Darcy flow problems, numerical results show robustness to coefficient contrast and problem size, better performance than standard algebraic multigrid on challenging large-scale cases, and good parallel scalability.
arxiv-2606-05464:
Nicolas Astorga, Nabeel Seedat, and Mihaela van der Schaar introduce OPT-star in this 2026 arXiv paper, a family of optimization-style tasks for training and evaluating step-by-step reasoning in language models. Training with verifiable rewards has improved math and coding reasoning. But real decisions are wider: the challenge is finding a high-value feasible plan among many valid options.

Each OPT-star task ships with a feasibility checker and an evaluator. A complexity parameter expands the search space without new human labels. The authors study two training regimes. One uses a classical solver as a value oracle for partial states, shaping rewards by rank. The other uses search-based offline reinforcement learning when no solver exists. They link success in large search spaces to the information a reasoner extracts per unit of search budget. Training on OPT-star improved step-by-step optimization-like reasoning.
arxiv-2606-05664:
Gideon Lee links fault tolerance and gauge theory by a single construction in a 2026 arXiv paper. The spacetime code views a quantum circuit's whole history as one error-correcting code. Dynamical phase research, meanwhile, treats fault tolerance as a stable process over time. Lee gauges the spacetime code, a standard move that turns global rules into local ones. The result is a lattice gauge theory that inherits the circuit's fault tolerance.

In the new theory, Gauss laws encode when two error patterns count as equivalent. Wilson loops play the role of detectors, the checks that flag errors. Three applications follow. The theory covers layered computation, yielding a gauge view of measurement-based quantum computing. It also describes the classical memory of certain mixed topological states. Its detector observables match exactly what can be learned about circuit noise. One construction thus serves error correction, condensed matter, and learning theory.
arxiv-2606-05764:
Qiliang Lin, Qian, and Zhou prove lasting solutions for a magnetized fluid with partial damping in a 2026 arXiv paper. Magnetohydrodynamics couples a conducting fluid to a magnetic field, as in fusion devices and the Sun. Their three-dimensional system damps motion only horizontally and the field in one direction. A steady background field points sideways. Prior proofs needed every part of the starting state to be small.

The new result drops that demand for the vertical parts. Only the horizontal parts of velocity and field must start small. The vertical parts may be arbitrarily large, in a standard smoothness measure. New energy estimates, split by component, tame the dangerous cross terms. The background field's structure does quiet work throughout the proof. The theorem breaks the full-smallness barrier that limited earlier work. It widens the proven-safe starting states for anisotropic plasma models.
arxiv-2606-06064:
Mahajan and Chopra settle how many regions lollipops can carve from the plane, for most small counts in a 2026 arXiv paper. A lollipop is a circle with a ray stuck on it. Overlap many, and the plane fragments into regions. Paulsen's argument used two obstructions, one about stem directions, one about circles meeting at obtuse angles. The authors recast it as a weighted problem on two graphs.

One graph tracks stem pairs that stay apart; the other tracks circle pairs that fail to intrigue. Paulsen had bounded their overlap by one graph alone. Keeping the overlap term explicit and studying near-extremal configurations sharpens everything. All gaps close up to seventeen lollipops, and the nineteen case falls too. Eighteen and twenty lollipops narrow to a single missing region each. A recreational-looking problem turns out to hide extremal combinatorics. The two-graph bookkeeping is the paper's reusable tool.
arxiv-2606-06464:
Mandana Samiei and co-authors compare human and machine scientists in this 2026 arXiv paper on causal learning. Adults are famously bad at conjunctive rules, where an effect needs several causes present together, while handling either or rules well. Most evidence comes from passive tasks where learners just watch limited data. The team asked whether the handicap survives when people can run their own experiments, using a modified blicket detector task where objects may or may not activate a machine.

Letting adults intervene freely improved their conjunctive reasoning a lot, though such rules still took more tests than disjunctive ones. Language models in the same setup told a different story. Some top models neared human accuracy at naming the rule, but explored less efficiently and showed the same conjunctive gap. The authors conclude that choosing informative tests, not just receiving data, is where human causal learning shines.
arxiv-2606-06564:
Kehan Wang adds one well chosen summary to a transformer's memory of itself in this 2026 arXiv paper. Deep transformers route information through residual streams. Block level routing methods compress each block's many updates into a single cumulative vector. That summary forgets the block's internal trajectory. HAARES keeps it and adds a second basis vector: the difference between the block's first half and second half updates, a coarse early versus late contrast, scaled to match and updated online.

Experiments on OpenWebText and character level benchmarks show a depth dependent pattern. Gains are small or mixed in shallow models but reliable at forty eight layers. In the two hundred one million parameter setting, HAARES beat the baseline on all three random seeds. A larger probe pointed the same way. Ablations rule out trivial explanations like extra sources or random details. The cost is modest extra memory.
arxiv-2606-06764:
This companion study asks the same generalization question for the most common network shape. Junyu Zhou, Wang, Lei, Ying, and Zhou focus on deep ReLU networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. ReLU is the standard activation that passes positive values and blocks negative ones. Earlier optimal results covered mainly shallow networks.

The authors give a full generalization analysis for gradient based training. Both plain and stochastic gradient descent are covered. They prove the first minimax optimal rates for deep ReLU networks. Minimax optimal means no method can promise better worst case rates. The conditions involve width growing with depth and sample size. Under those conditions, gradient methods match kernel methods on new data. The conclusion section restates the rate in formula form. It frames the work as closing a clear gap in deep learning theory.
arxiv-2606-06964:
Quivers are directed graphs whose representations form a rich algebraic world. Liu measures one family of those representations in this 2026 arXiv paper. The stage is the covering tree of the generalized Kronecker quiver. That quiver has two vertices joined by n arrows. Its module category splits into components, some of them regular.

For each regular Auslander-Reiten component, Liu defines two numbers. The width counts how broad the component runs. The second counts its flow modules, a special distinguished kind. He proves the width is at least half of that count, plus a half. A clean consequence follows at once. Every positive integer occurs as the width of some component. So the set of possible widths is exactly all natural numbers. The result gives a complete answer for this invariant, in a setting where classifying all modules is hopeless for three or more arrows.
arxiv-2606-07064:
Can boundary measurements reveal an unknown source hidden inside a curved region? Cârstea and Ghosh answer yes for a famous nonlinear equation in this 2026 arXiv paper. The equation is Monge-Ampère, where the determinant of second derivatives equals an unknown positive source. Solutions are convex functions pinned to prescribed boundary values. The slope at the edge is what an observer can measure.

The authors study the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, which sends boundary values to those edge slopes. Their theorem says this map determines the source uniquely. The proof cleverly uses very large boundary data. Big boundary values straighten the problem until it reduces to the X-ray transform. That classical tool recovers a function from its line integrals, and it is known to be injective. Inverse problems for fully nonlinear equations rarely yield such clean uniqueness.
arxiv-2606-07464:
Liang and a team compress a self-driving system's memory without discarding what decisions need, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-action driving models consume token sequences that balloon when they encode temporal context, breaching real-time budgets. Existing compression uses fixed heuristics like temporal decay, which can drop decision-critical moments. Their framework, COMPACT-VA, compresses context through a conditional vector-quantized autoencoder guided by planning intent: a latent summary of what the driver plans to do, distilled from trajectories.

A prior encoder predicts that intent from the compressed observations, and the policy plans using the bounded memory plus predicted intent. Evaluation focused on scenarios where history matters most, such as stopping, yielding, and proceeding at interactions. Under comparable token budgets, success rates improved by over 6 percent relative to heuristic compression, reaching about 68 percent. Closed-loop driving kept performance while running over 3 times faster and using under half the memory.
arxiv-2606-07564:
Young documents a design exercise for the next particle collider's detector, run as a long dialogue with an AI assistant, in this 2026 arXiv report. The Future Circular Collider's electron-positron mode would run a 15-year precision physics program in a 91 kilometer tunnel near Geneva. The AI proposed detector concepts from its assumptions; the physicist challenged subsystems in turn, from beam pipe to luminosity monitor, forcing revisions grounded in calibration, stability, and simplicity rather than headline performance.

The design evolved from the starting concepts through that exchange. Young is clear about the report's purpose: what a resulting concept could do remains unexplored, and the value lies in the process. The account is offered as a lesson on the promise and the limits of human-AI collaboration in experimental design. There, an assistant's first guesses need expert pushback to become engineering sense. It reads as a case study in machine creativity.
arxiv-2606-07864:
Dong and Song answer a question of S. T. Yau about when a curved three-dimensional space must really be flat, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is an asymptotically flat manifold, a space that looks Euclidean far away, with non-negative scalar curvature and curvature energy normalised to at most one. The positive mass theorem says such a space has non-negative mass, zero only for flat space. Yau asked whether small mass forces flatness in a strong, quantitative sense.

The answer is yes. Building on their previous work, the authors prove small mass yields a bilipschitz diffeomorphism to Euclidean three-space. That is an identification distorting distances by at most a fixed factor in both directions, far stronger than sharing a topology. The result quantifies the stability of the positive mass theorem's rigidity: near-zero mass cannot hide a very different geometry when curvature energy is controlled.
arxiv-2606-08164:
Jiangshuan Pang and co-authors ask a question every medical imaging lab pays for but rarely examines: how much preprocessing brain MRI scans need before pretraining, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Preprocessing pipelines define what a foundation model sees, yet are treated as routine cleaning rather than a modelling choice with a price.

Holding the corpus of twenty thousand brain MRI volumes, backbone, and protocol fixed, they compared eight graded preprocessing levels, P0 through P7, for two self-supervised methods. They then transferred the encoders to four downstream tasks. The lightest levels proved numerically unstable, making P2 the cheapest feasible choice. Beyond P2, picking the best level bought only about three point four points of aggregate utility for one method and one point eight for the other. Most gains were statistically unresolved. Stronger preprocessing helped mainly one task, and its edge could largely be recovered by preprocessing harder at transfer.
arxiv-2606-08464:
Lianyu Hu and colleagues let multimodal models look back at the image while they think, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chain-of-thought reasoning, where a model spells out intermediate steps, helps language models solve problems. But in multimodal models the reasoning happens entirely in text. After the image is first encoded, its visual features become inaccessible. The authors call this vision-blind reasoning, and it limits fine-grained visual extraction and error checking.

Their framework, TVI-CoT, interleaves textual reasoning with fresh visual feature access through learnable control tokens. Special tokens signal when the model should think in words, when it should look again at the image, and when it should answer. This switching lets the model re-examine the picture mid-argument, verifying a claim against the pixels rather than its memory of them.
arxiv-2606-08664:
Majumdar reports on particle detectors built in India for imaging with cosmic rays, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Muography is a passive imaging technique. It uses cosmic-ray muons to map the density inside large or hard-to-reach objects, from pyramids to cargo containers. Majumdar's group is developing a small prototype system that identifies materials by how muons scatter in matter. The tracking device is the Thick-GEM detector, a scaled-up, robust version of gas electron multiplier technology.

Several prototypes a few centimeters across were built by a local industry partner, with small changes in design from one to the next. After conditioning, each underwent detailed tests to check its fitness for the task. Domestic fabrication matters here: imported detectors are costly and supply-constrained. A robust local design could put muon imaging within reach of Indian laboratories and security uses.
arxiv-2606-08764:
Bob Osano tackles the backreaction problem in cosmology in this 2026 arXiv paper, asking whether the lumpiness of the real universe changes its expansion. Backreaction is the effect that clumped matter might have on the smooth expansion of the standard Friedmann model. Using a method that averages the universe over cells, he derives three results from the matter power spectrum, a curve showing how strongly matter clumps at each scale.

First, he proves a floor under the backreaction term: it cannot drop below the value simple linear theory gives, however clumpy matter becomes. Second, he shows the usual step-by-step approximation breaks down exactly where clumping turns strongly nonlinear. Third, he gives an exact formula for the information neighboring cells share, finding a value near one tenth for nearest neighbors at a scale of fifty megaparsecs. That shared information also measures the correction backreaction makes to the expansion energy budget.
arxiv-2606-08964:
An, Kim, and Ling ask how few coordinates it takes to embed an error-correcting code into a self-orthogonal one, over the integers modulo four, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-orthogonal codes, whose codewords are mutually orthogonal, are prized because they yield quantum codes. Embedding adds columns until self-orthogonality holds, and the shortest extension is the target quantity. The authors work with linear codes over Z4, the integers mod four, tied to nonlinear binary codes.

They prove tight bounds on the shortest embedding length, determined exactly under conditions including the quaternary Preparata codes. Along the way they classify the shortest doubly even self-orthogonal embedding length for binary codes in every case. When the two lengths coincide, their algorithm constructs all shortest embeddings. Running it produced 12 Z4 codes whose minimum Lee distances beat every comparable entry in Aydin's database.
arxiv-2606-09064:
Wang and colleagues teach video question-answering models to gather more visual evidence and double-check their answers against it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Long videos hide evidence in a few segments, and most models use one search intent and one answer. Their framework, CoVER, expands the query into pseudo-queries and retrieves zoomed-in evidence widely. It drafts an answer and extracts a clue from the draft, then verifies the answer against the visual record with it.

The design shifts long-video understanding from answer-centric to evidence-centric reasoning. Results backed the approach. CoVER beat its baseline across benchmarks, with gains of 3.9 percent on MLVU and 4.6 percent on LVBench, plus smaller gains elsewhere. The 7-billion-parameter CoVER model outperformed same-scale models and surpassed closed-source systems on some metrics. Seeing more and thinking deeper complement each other: broader evidence helps only if conclusions are interrogated against it.
arxiv-2606-09264:
Sofia-Eirini Kotti and colleagues untangle overlapping brain signals in ultrasound movies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Functional ultrasound images brain activity indirectly, measuring blood volume changes that follow neural firing through neurovascular coupling. The task is blind separation, unmixing signals without knowing them, while undoing each source's hemodynamic response, the slow blood-flow echo blurring timing.

Their model treats multi-trial ultrasound data as a tensor decomposed into blocks. Each source is represented spatiotemporally: a low-rank spatial map plus a piecewise-constant firing signal convolved with that response, plausible in shape but varying by trial and source. A constrained optimization framework computes the split via projected gradient descent. In tests it recovered the maps and activation time courses across noise levels. Estimating that response proved the hardest part, marking where future work should aim. For a cheap modality, such unmixing turns blood-flow movies into neuroscience.
arxiv-2606-09364:
Martí Bosch checks whether cheap temperature sensors can be trusted for tracking city heat in this 2026 arXiv paper. Swiss cities such as Bern, Lausanne, Neuchâtel, and Zurich now run dense networks of low-cost devices that map heat street by street. Their weakness is radiative overheating: sunlight warms the sensor itself, inflating readings when shielding is poor.

Bosch builds a statistical correction based on incoming short-wave radiation, fitted with a generalised additive model, a flexible curve-fitting method. The correction was calibrated by placing each sensor model beside a professional MeteoSwiss weather station near Bern. He then asks how corrections change two heat indices, counts of tropical nights and official heat warnings. Official stations outside the cities underestimated heat warnings, while some cheap sensors overestimated them before correction. Even uncorrected, though, the city sensors described urban temperatures better than the rural reference stations did.
arxiv-2606-09464:
Parkosidis and his co-authors confront a long-standing puzzle in binary star evolution in this 2026 arXiv paper. Classical theory says tides should circularise a star's orbit before it starts transferring mass to its companion. Yet wide binaries that have already interacted commonly keep eccentric, oval orbits, and the eccentricity grows with orbital period.

Their general mass-transfer model, GeMT, is the first complete framework handling mass transfer in orbits of arbitrary eccentricity. They confront it with observations of hot subdwarf B stars, stripped stars whose formation histories are tightly constrained, paired with main-sequence companions. The model reproduced all observed orbital parameters without any fine-tuning, and oval orbits emerged from the transfer process itself. The final ovalness also depends on measurable quantities such as transferred mass and accretion efficiency.
arxiv-2606-09664:
Tuan Vu, Harri Lähdesmäki, and Julien Martinelli tune a tabular foundation model for a special search task in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bayesian optimization is a thrifty way to hunt for the best design with few tests. In latent space, the hunt runs over coded forms of things like molecules. Tabular foundation models now lead at regression and serve as stand-ins inside such hunts.

Their quirk is the training mix: these models learn their Bayesian habits from huge fake task sets. Latent-space hunts warp the map from code to score, so the habits fit poorly. The team adds fake hunt tasks, drawn from a molecule coder's latent space, to the pretraining stage. A regularizer anchors the model to its first form, so broad skill is kept. On held-out molecule hunts, the tuned model scored strongly.
arxiv-2606-09764:
Lawrence Jang, Mareks Woodside, and Geronimo Carom build a phone-agent test that is personal by design in this 2026 arXiv paper. A good phone agent should know its owner: their past orders, trips, contacts, and tastes, all stored on the device. Past tests use blank sandboxes with no such past. iOSWorld instead seeds one fixed persona across twenty-six fresh iOS apps.

The set holds one hundred thirty-three tasks in three grades. Single-app tasks test one app at a time. Multi-app tasks span two to eight apps. Memory tasks ask the agent to infer habits from the stored past. The best setup passed fifty-two percent overall, but just thirty-seven percent on multi-app work. Extra screen-tree access helped top models by up to twenty-six points, while small models gained nothing.
arxiv-2606-10064:
Bansal and colleagues argue that competitive agent arenas can manufacture the training data small models need, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Post-training agents requires multi-turn trajectories with per-trajectory judgments. Synthetic data from frontier models inherits their biases and loses the long tail, while raw production logs are unjudged and contaminated by shortcuts. Their testbed is a Bittensor subnet running ShoppingBench, an agentic commerce benchmark, as a scored competition.

The arena's race mechanism, language-model judge, and rotating problem suite produce incentive-aligned diversity with held-out evaluation guarded against memorization. Post-training Qwen3-4B on the filtered corpus lifted its success rate from eighteen percent to about forty-three percent on held-out tasks. That lands within noise of a synthetic-data baseline trained only with supervised fine-tuning, showing arena traces are a viable substrate.
arxiv-2606-10364:
Wang benchmarks the steps needed to turn Mars rover photos into printable 3D terrain models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer vision. Her pipeline finds stereo depth from NASA Curiosity images, completes the missing shape, and exports watertight meshes in OBJ format for printing. On the standard Middlebury stereo benchmark, a learned matcher clearly beats classical block matching on disparity error and coverage.

On Curiosity imagery, however, the learned matcher's denser depth maps show weaker edge alignment and higher reprojection error, hinting benchmark accuracy does not transfer to Martian terrain. Shape completion involves trade-offs. Alpha shapes preserve accurate but broken-up structure, and Poisson reconstruction yields coherent meshes but adds surfaces not in the data. A fixed diffusion-fill baseline sits between, sensitive to stereo quality. Standard methods can produce printable models, she concludes, but reliable rebuilding needs stronger domain checks.
arxiv-2606-10464:
Balaji and colleagues tackle a weakness of speech recognition in this 2026 arXiv paper: models trained on typical speech stumble on noisy rooms, phone-quality audio, dialects, or children's voices. Their fix, GC-LoRA, adapts a pretrained model cheaply with small trainable parts, following LoRA's low-rank update idea. It also inserts short-range convolutional processing, borrowed from Conformer models, so the adapter can hear local sound patterns that global attention misses.

Across test sets covering degraded, band-limited, dialectal, and child speech, GC-LoRA cuts the word error rate by up to 10.9 percent relative to compared baselines. It beats standard LoRA while using fewer trainable parameters. The authors read this as evidence that a small amount of local structure, placed inside the attention output, is an efficient route to acoustic adaptation.
arxiv-2606-10564:
Song, Lee, and Pickett analyse the electronic structure of a new nickelate in this 2026 arXiv paper in condensed matter theory. Nickelates are nickel oxide compounds, cousins of the cuprate superconductors. The material, La3Ni2O5F, has formally monovalent nickel and an almost perfectly two-dimensional character. Band calculations reveal an electron band from no atomic orbital: it is built from interstitial density, charge in the crystal's empty spaces, forming a cylindrical Fermi surface.

This band coexists with the conventional nickel-oxygen band, and the two behave oppositely, one electron-like and one hole-like. The authors call this a dichotomous electronic system. The band also partners with nickel d bands to form an incipient Dirac point. The authors predict the split should carry into the superconducting state.
arxiv-2606-10664:
Chiappori and colleagues test how much spouses can commit in this 2026 arXiv paper on household economics. In the collective model, partners bargain toward efficient outcomes, but the force of the bargain depends on commitment. Full commitment binds future behaviour; none renegotiates everything; limited commitment binds only until a partner prefers to walk away. The authors derive tests separating all three regimes from the dynamic effect of wage shocks on labour supply, using sign restrictions from theory to reject limited commitment too.

Applied to EU-SILC data from 15 European countries over 2005 to 2019, the tests find the bargaining weight rises after a favourable wage shock, the empowerment effect limited commitment predicts. Full and zero commitment are rejected in all but 4 countries; limited commitment survives everywhere. Household promises are real but conditional: a pay rise today shifts bargaining power, and who works how much, for years.
arxiv-2606-11264:
Zhaohui Wang, Huang, and Bian propose OmniBioTwin in a 2026 arXiv paper, a framework for health digital twins. A health digital twin is a dynamic, patient-specific model of health and disease. Current twins are fragmented: single-organ models lack cross-scale fidelity, while system-level twins lack a general architecture. OmniBioTwin treats twins as modular entities coupled through explicit interaction operators.

It, called a System-of-Twinned-Systems, organizes the twins in seven coordinated layers. They span data integration, autonomous twin modeling, cross-scale coupling, temporal synchronization, and human-in-the-loop decision support. The authors demonstrate it with a multiscale twin for GLP-1 signaling pathways in Alzheimer's disease. There, molecular, cellular, and organ-level twins are composed and coupled inside one system. They present the design as a scalable, readable foundation for precision medicine.
arxiv-2606-11364:
Ahmad studies anomaly-driven transport in pseudospin-1 Weyl semimetals in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. Positive longitudinal magnetoconductance and planar Hall conductance are hallmark signs of the chiral anomaly in Weyl semimetals. Theory now extends Weyl fermions to multifold systems with higher-pseudospin quasiparticles. Ahmad asks how their anomaly-driven transport behaves.

He uses semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory with momentum-linked scattering and orbital moment terms. The planar Hall response needs broken azimuthal symmetry, supplied two ways: a tilt of the dispersion, and misaligned electric and magnetic fields. Untilted, the response is positive and quadratic in field strength. More scattering drives a sign reversal to negative values. Tilt changes the angular response into sine and cosine forms along each axis, giving strong anisotropy and a nonmonotonic tilt effect.
arxiv-2606-11764:
Huachao Zhang and Chang-An Zhao construct special error-correcting codes from algebraic curves in this 2026 arXiv paper. Linear complementary pairs and complementary dual codes matter for protecting hardware against side-channel and fault injection attacks. Recent constructions build them from function fields, but depend on non-special divisors, certain configurations on a curve with the right numerical properties.

The authors study Kummer extensions, a broad family of function fields defined by a simple power equation. They characterise non-special divisors whose support may include places that are not totally ramified, a widened class earlier work excluded. Using it, they explicitly build such divisors of the two key degrees on the famous GK curve and on general Kummer extensions, exploiting pure gaps. A general framework for complementary pairs of algebraic geometry codes follows, with security parameters determined inside it, plus a route to complementary dual codes.
arxiv-2606-11964:
Apashanka Das, Souvik Ghose and Tapas K Das study gas falling into a black hole in this 2026 arXiv paper. The flow is the Michel solution: spherical, steady accretion that passes from subsonic to supersonic speed. Real accreting gas mixes components, so the authors let the adiabatic index, which measures how pressure responds to compression, vary with radius.

They construct the stationary transonic solutions and draw phase portraits of Mach number against radius. A dynamical systems analysis sorts the transonic points; the relevant ones are saddle type, as expected for inviscid flow. Shaking the steady flow slightly shows it is stable. That analysis yields something striking: sound waves inside the flow obey an effective acoustic spacetime, with a horizon where the flow turns supersonic. Carter-Penrose diagrams display this emergent geometry's causal structure. Accretion thus doubles as a laboratory for analogue gravity.
arxiv-2606-12164:
Klein and co-authors build a statistical method that judges which influences on extreme pollution are straight and which are curved, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Regulators care about threshold breaches, which live in the upper quantiles, the high slices of a pollutant's distribution. Quantile regression models those slices, and additive forms let each factor bend freely. The catch is telling a factor's straight-line part from its curved part, which standard spline tools blur.

Their method, QDReSS, uses a Demmler-Reinsch basis splitting each effect into linear and nonlinear parts at right angles. Spike-and-slab priors, settings that can switch each part off, then select what matters via a Gibbs sampler. Simulations show both parts are estimated consistently and beat the standard mixed-model approach. Applied to Madrid air data, extreme nitrogen dioxide levels are driven differently by weather and by traffic-shaped spatial patterns.
arxiv-2606-12364:
Anamaria-Roberta Hartl and co-authors run a head-to-head race among the architectures challenging the Transformer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Transformers pay quadratic attention cost as sequences grow. Subquadratic rivals, recurrent, state-space, and linear-attention designs, promise cheaper scaling. Three leaders, xLSTM, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet, anchor hybrid models. Standard language benchmarks barely separate them, so the authors test on complex domains: code and time series, where long-range structured dependencies expose architectural biases.

Each backbone is trained from scratch and also distilled from a Transformer teacher. Broad reasoning and commonsense tests prove insensitive to backbone choice. Code generation separates them much more sharply. Mixing experiments vary how many subquadratic layers replace attention layers. One xLSTM-heavy mix leads on a mixed corpus at twenty billion tokens, while a leaner ratio leads on pure code. The paper distills principles for choosing operators by domain.
arxiv-2606-12464:
Bhoi and co-authors test a modified-gravity cosmos with a neutral measuring tape, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The VCDM model tweaks gravity minimally so the vacuum energy can drift with time, adding no new particles. A reported transition feature in its expansion history had raised interest. But features can be artifacts of how data are fitted. The authors instead use cosmography: describing expansion through its kinematic series, fitted with a Padé approximation that stays well-behaved.

They constrain the model with cosmic chronometers, DESI baryon acoustic data, and three supernova compilations in a Bayesian analysis. Parameters come out tight and consistent across dataset combinations. The jerk parameter, the expansion's third derivative, sits near its standard-model value of one. Critically, the transition feature vanishes under the Padé reconstruction. It was a creature of parametrization, not a demand of the data. VCDM thus mimics the standard cosmos at background level.
arxiv-2606-12564:
Pizarro and co-authors model how substance use spreads through a high school, and find first use and addiction obey different rules, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their SCAR model sorts students into susceptible, casual users, addicted or problematic users, and resistant students shielded by protective environments. Peer influence drives initiation and escalation, while problematic use pushes students out of school, with some returning after recovery.

Three findings stand out. First, the return rate after disengagement splits the dynamics: when every leaver returns, total population is conserved and endemic states are meaningful. When some never return, schools lose students, changing what equilibria mean. Second, initiation and escalation have distinct thresholds, so they are dynamically separate processes. Third, the model is bistable: identical conditions can end substance-free or in high use, depending on start. Policy should be layered: universal prevention, early help for casual users, and strong re-engagement paths.
arxiv-2606-12764:
Meeus and colleagues show that code language models can memorise the functional logic of their training data, not just its text, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Privacy audits of code models usually measure textual overlap between training examples and generated output. But code can behave identically while looking different, so verbatim checks can miss real leakage of proprietary logic.

The authors build a counterfactual setup around Olmo-3-32B, comparing a midtrained model that was exposed to code against a pretrained reference that never saw it. Both models are prompted with Python function signatures, and their completions are scored for textual similarity and for functional similarity, using an LLM judge and actual execution. The exposed model reproduces the target functions' behaviour well beyond what textual metrics detect. The authors conclude there is evidence of functional memorisation, and that auditing code models requires behaviour-based metrics alongside overlap checks.
arxiv-2606-12964:
Cuenin and colleagues prove sharp, logarithmically improved spectral cluster bounds for orthonormal systems on closed Riemannian manifolds with nonpositive sectional curvature, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spectral cluster bounds control the size of eigenfunctions concentrated in a narrow frequency window. Orthonormal versions bound whole families of eigenfunctions at once, in the spirit of the Lieb-Thirring principle that orthogonality needs space. On general manifolds the universal Frank-Sabin bounds are sharp, but negative curvature should allow gains.

For spectral windows of size 1 over log lambda, the authors obtain the orthonormal analogue of the sharper L q estimates of Hassell and Tacy, in the supercritical range. Their proof joins the field-wide orthonormal spectral cluster bounds of Frank and Sabin with Berard-type kernel bounds. Those bounds exploit how waves spread on nonpositively curved manifolds. The proof also carries the Bourgain-Shao-Sogge-Yao multiplier estimate into the orthonormal setting.
arxiv-2606-13864:
Archakov and Hansen study a tool for drawing sound conclusions from correlation matrices. Fisher's classic transformation tames the single correlation coefficient, making its sampling behavior nearly Gaussian. Extending that trick to whole matrices has long been elusive. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes the Generalized Fisher Transformation: the matrix logarithm of a correlation matrix, stacked into coordinates. They focus on finite samples, the small datasets economists actually have.

For elliptical data, the new values sit close to Gaussian, as Fisher's do for one coefficient. More strikingly, the values are nearly uncorrelated with each other. Their spread barely changes with the true matrix, unlike rival approaches. That stability makes errors nearly pivotal, so tests behave well in small samples. The pattern held in simulations and real data: macroeconomic series, industry returns, and high-frequency financial data. Strongly non-Gaussian data remain a weak spot.
arxiv-2606-13964:
Wang, Chen, and Song fix a clash that ruins AI-drawn caricatures. A caricature must exaggerate a sketch's shapes while keeping the person recognizable. Inside diffusion models, identity and shape instructions contaminate each other, collapsing output toward bland portraits or unreadable distortions. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents CaricHarmony, a training-free method running three diffusion paths: pure identity, pure shape, and a harmonized output.

Energy functions on cross-attention features guide the harmonized path. One enforces sketch fidelity; another matches identity tokens under extreme distortion. CaricHarmony accepts any sketch format and finishes in under sixteen seconds. Rivals need about seventy seconds of fine-tuning per identity. On benchmarks it scored zero point eight six one five on shape agreement against zero point eight four five zero for the comparison. Users preferred its results, scoring seven point eight one against six point zero six overall.
arxiv-2606-14164:
Qian and colleagues use language models to give fuzz drivers a sense of right and wrong beyond crashing. Greybox fuzzing feeds random inputs to a driver harness, but most drivers treat only crashes as failures, ignoring whether results are correct. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies metamorphic oracle enhancement: metamorphic relations state how outputs should change when inputs change in known ways, catching functional bugs. Their framework, MetaFOE, has language models write and integrate such oracles automatically.

Of one thousand sixty-eight OSS-Fuzz drivers analyzed, eighty-one point one percent lacked any functional oracle. Across three language models and five prompting strategies, MetaFOE generated 3,475 metamorphic relations, seventy-seven point three percent applicable, and built 6,228 valid enhanced drivers. After three hours of fuzzing, these improved edge coverage by eighteen point seven percent on average and triggered 1,528 unique crashes.
arxiv-2606-14264:
Ye, Wang, and Pan approximate high-dimensional functions by voting: estimate each coefficient many times, then trust the median. The task is L2 approximation of non-periodic functions on the unit cube, needed in finance and uncertainty quantification, where grids fail as dimension grows. Their method adapts median lattice algorithms to digital nets. It needs no smoothness or weight parameters, only a large enough candidate set of Walsh indices.

It runs in three stages: digital-net samples estimate each Walsh coefficient repeatedly; medians of estimates and their absolute values are taken; dominant coefficients are kept and a truncated series returned. For functions whose mixed partial derivatives have finite fractional Vitali variation, the error decays just below the sum of the smoothness and variation orders, with high probability. The constant grows at most polynomially in dimension under decay conditions on the ANOVA components. Experiments confirm it works in high dimensions.
arxiv-2606-14364:
Braudo, Michaelis, Akashi, and Soker explode a star with three pairs of tilted jets, and get back the mirror-symmetric shapes seen in real remnants. The jittering jets mechanism proposes such supernovae are blown apart by opposite jet pairs in changing directions, not neutrinos. In their 2026 arXiv paper, two 3D simulations launch three pairs of inclined jets into a stripped core within about a second, following the ejecta past shock breakout.

Although the jets are choked deep inside the star, they imprinted a multipolar, point-symmetric shape on the ejecta, with clumps and filaments from instabilities. In one run the strongest jet blew a large blowout ahead of the ejecta, like the Cygnus Loop; the inner ejecta showed two symmetry axes. Dense blocks between the jet axes carried a tilted Doppler-shifted outflow, as in remnants W49B and G292, supporting jittering jets as the primary mechanism.
arxiv-2606-14764:
Shanu speeds up submodular minimization on distributive lattices in a 2026 arXiv paper. Submodular functions model gains that shrink as sets grow. They are minimized across vision and machine learning. Many uses define them on a distributive lattice, a structured set of combos. The standard workaround stretches the function to the matching Boolean lattice. That blows the work space up hugely in set size.

Shanu proposes a generic scheme that works wholly inside the distributive lattice. It still runs proven Boolean-lattice minimizers. That avoids the huge growth making older pipelines wasteful. Tests show a huge gain in running time over classic methods. The result makes submodular tools practical for lattice-structured problems. Their Boolean stretches were simply too large to attempt before.
arxiv-2606-14864:
Silvetti presents state-of-the-art event generation for deep-inelastic scattering in a 2026 arXiv contribution. Deep-inelastic scattering, or DIS, probes matter by smashing electrons into protons or nuclei. Predictions are needed at hadron level, once quarks dress into visible particles. Targets are future colliders: the Electron-Ion Collider planned at Brookhaven, the proposed LHeC, and a DIS phase of the Future Circular Collider.

The predictions reach next-to-leading-order precision. Several jet multiplicities are computed and merged into one sample. The MEPS@NLO scheme stitches the multiplicities without double counting. One merged sample lets analysts study many final states with a single coherent simulation. The contribution is catalogued as CERN-TH-2026-140. The authors show momentum transfer distributions for the merged samples. The MC@NLO corrections to the leading-order shape are rather small. The merged leading-order sample shows the expected corrections at small momentum transfer.
arxiv-2606-15064:
Bedi reports a negative result on filtering robot demonstrations phase by phase in a 2026 study. Behavior cloning learns from demonstrations, so curators score and drop examples. A defect usually corrupts one phase of a task, such as the lift in pick-and-place. Scoring each phase with its best metric sounds like the right fix.

The test uses three contact-rich LIBERO tasks with an early-release defect, over five seeds each. Phase-gated curation is never the best of three strategies. It ranks worst on two tasks, trailing both uniform scoring and one global metric. The cause is dilution: rank aggregation mixes the informative phase's signal with noise from clean phases. The winning metric changes from task to task, so per-phase choices cannot transfer. Bedi advises spending effort on finding one defect-informative metric instead. Code, metrics, and per-seed results are released with the study.
arxiv-2606-15364:
Kar and coauthor construct the hydrodynamics of a perfect spin-1 fluid in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Hydrodynamics describes matter as a flowing continuum, and spin hydrodynamics adds the particles' internal rotation, measured in heavy-ion collisions through polarization. Earlier work built the theory for spin-1 particles under Boltzmann statistics, the classical counting rule. This paper extends it to Bose-Einstein statistics, the quantum rule for particles that can share states.

Working from the Wigner function, a quantum phase-space description, the authors derive the energy-momentum and spin tensors for the fluid. The resulting currents match the Boltzmann and spin-half results up to second order in polarization, whichever statistics or spin value is used. The equations also form a divergence-type theory, which guarantees they stay causal and stable. The message is universality: at small polarization, spin behaves as a classical trait, simplifying models of spinning quark-gluon matter.
arxiv-2606-15664:
Guo and Jing introduce stochastic Floquet engineering in 2026, a scheme for building a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with a periodic drive whose amplitude is noisy. Conventional Floquet engineering uses a perfectly periodic field, and non-Hermitian physics usually needs engineered loss or gain. Here noise itself is the resource: Hermitian dynamics plus a fluctuating drive yields the target's effective behaviour.

The team applies the scheme to a cavity with dissipative coupling between Fock states, and to preparing a chosen quantum state starting from an arbitrary one. The method also yields non-unitary quantum gates, which can beat unitary gates at some tasks, without ancilla qubits or updates. Because the construction starts from Hermitian dynamics, it sidesteps the hardware burden of building loss and gain directly. Noise, normally the enemy of quantum control, becomes a design ingredient for Hamiltonians previously hard to synthesize.
arxiv-2606-15764:
Lamoria and colleagues simulate shock waves in a dusty plasma monolayer in 2026, closing a gap between experiments and earlier computations. Dusty plasmas, gases seeded with charged microparticles, form two-dimensional crystals that a piston can shock-compress. Previous molecular dynamics work forced the particles into a flat plane, and so missed the out-of-plane buckling that experiments see under compression.

The new simulations run in three dimensions, with finite vertical confinement, fixed boundaries, Epstein drag, and a particle size distribution matched to the experiments. They recover the observed linear scaling between the shock's Mach number and the piston's. Crucially, they reproduce the shock-induced buckling of the monolayer, the first time molecular dynamics has captured it. The framework now lets researchers probe out-of-plane and wake-mediated shock physics in strongly coupled systems. Letting the crystal move in the third dimension was the missing ingredient all along.
arxiv-2606-16264:
Ma and co-authors present Tropical in 2026, a scheduler that helps large language model serving meet its latency targets. Serving splits into prefill, timed by time to first token, and decode, timed by time per output token. Disaggregated serving splits the two phases onto separate workers, which cuts interference between them. It also leaves requests waiting in queues, which hurts the first-token target.

Keeping both phases on one worker cuts the queues but lets prefill work disturb decode. Tropical instead multiplexes the phases with the service-level objectives in mind, weighing queue time against interference for each request. The design is a multi-worker scheduler built after a root-cause study of both layouts. In the reported tests, Tropical attains high rates on both latency targets at once, which neither plain layout manages. Scheduling policy, not just hardware layout, decides whether split serving pays off.
arxiv-2606-16564:
Papatheodorou and co-authors build in 2026 a robot optimizer that keeps working when the math problem it must solve has no valid answer at all. Robotic systems face conflicting goals, model errors, and degenerate contact cases that make their quadratic programs infeasible. Most solvers assume feasibility and break down exactly when constraints clash. Elastic Odyn is a primal-dual, non-interior-point QP solver that absorbs infeasibility through smooth squared elastic relaxations.

The relaxed problem stays well posed under ill-conditioning, supports warm starting, and settles on the closest-to-feasible answer when no feasible point exists. A lightweight polish stage then restores meaningful dual values from the elastic answer. Elastic OdynLayer is a differentiable QP layer whose gradients stay stable under infeasibility. Elastic OdynSQP handles nonlinear optimal control, resolving inconsistent subproblems and infeasible tasks through selective relaxation.
arxiv-2606-16664:
Chakraborty proves a dilation result in a 2026 paper on operator algebras. A dilation rewrites a simple operator action as the shadow of a richer one on a larger space, a trick behind many classic theorems. The objects here are semigroups, sets with a combined operation but no undo step, and the ways they can act as operators.

For a broad class of cancellative semigroups, Chakraborty shows an action dilates to the reduced boundary quotient algebra exactly when it extends, in a contractive way, to the semigroup operator algebra. That property holds for all constructible cases from amenable semigroups and for a very large further class. The test also extends the von Neumann inequality beyond simple power semigroups. For Ore semigroups the result fully settles which actions admit unitary dilations. The theorem unifies and extends the classic dilation theorems of Sz.-Nagy and Ando.
arxiv-2606-16764:
Ahmadi and colleagues design a quantum battery charger in a 2026 quantum physics paper. A quantum battery stores energy in quantum degrees of freedom for later extraction as work. The hard part is charging it so that unavoidable noise fluctuations become useful stored energy rather than waste.

Their charger is a driven bosonic Kitaev chain, a line of coupled oscillators with pairing terms. Chiral squeezing sends fluctuations both ways along the chain, squeezing them into opposite quadratures at the two ends, where batteries sit. Unlike ordinary amplifiers, which preserve phase and waste much of the gain as noise, the scheme stores mostly extractable energy. Its work-like signal-to-noise ratio stays near one even with thermal noise and moderate disorder that respects the chain's symmetry. The design turns the charger's own fluctuations from a liability into the main charging resource.
arxiv-2606-16964:
Neha Kukreti and Amol Holkundkar show control over free electron states in a 2026 atomic physics paper. Photoionization with extreme ultraviolet light ejects electrons from hydrogen atoms into a wide spread of possible momenta. Steering that spread, rather than bound states, would give a new handle on ultrafast electron dynamics.

By tailoring the light's polarization and its carrier-envelope phase, the team creates two distinct momentum-space states for the ejected electrons. One knob, the polarization mixing, sets how much population each state holds. The other knob, the phase, sets their relative phase on its own. Interference patterns in measured momentum maps confirm coherence, with visibility near the maximum possible. A two-color field extends the scheme to a four-state space, where states differ in both emission pattern and radial momentum, with the same independent control kept. The engineered states are directly visible in momentum-resolved spectra.
arxiv-2606-17264:
Mena and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on coupled-mode equations for superconducting travelling-wave devices, such as microwave amplifiers and frequency multipliers. The equations work well in nonlinear optics, but microwave devices face stronger losses, and each process has usually needed its own derivation. The authors revisit the theory to include losses and to derive the equations in a set way for any mix of travelling waves a device might carry.

Worked examples show how unwanted harmonics and mixing products can drag device results far from the ideal case when ignored. Testing used a superconducting line built on a coplanar waveguide, with its key nonlinear constant measured on its own. That constant came out near its theoretical pair-breaking scale rather than the much smaller critical current. Predicted multi-harmonic output then matched measurements up to the highest harmonic checked, with no free parameters.
arxiv-2606-17664:
Kim and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on teaching search systems the time dimension without labelled data, through a method called temporal preference optimisation. A query about a president in a past year should retrieve documents from that year, yet ordinary retrievers match meaning and ignore dates, returning well-written pages from the wrong era. Time-stamped supervision is the usual fix, but it is often unavailable. The proposed approach recasts preference learning so the retriever learns to favour documents aligned in time with the query's context.

A learned time embedding, interpolated smoothly, lets the system handle periods never seen in training. On temporal retrieval benchmarks, the method beat both unsupervised and supervised rivals. One variant, far smaller than a leading embedding model, still gained clearly on both explicit and implicit time queries. The work shows temporal sense can be trained in, not bolted on with labels.
arxiv-2606-17764:
Romero Jorge and colleagues present a 2026 article in the Journal of Subatomic Particles and Cosmology on dileptons as probes of the phase structure of strongly interacting matter. When heavy nuclei collide, the fireball passes through quark-gluon plasma and back, and lepton pairs emitted along the way escape untouched, carrying news of each stage. The authors model the plasma with a quasiparticle picture fitted to lattice results, then evolve whole collisions with an off-shell transport code that follows partons and hadrons together through the event.

A small deconfined core already forms at surprisingly low collision energy, their simulations indicate.
