For the first time in this framework, they trace how thermal plasma radiation shifts with baryon chemical potential, growing stronger toward lower energies. At the lowest energies, thermal radiation can outshine the charm-decay background that usually buries it. That makes planned facilities prime hunting grounds for direct plasma light.
arxiv-2606-17864:
Dimitrov and Shapiro compare two ways to stretch a classic class of entire functions, in a 2026 analysis paper. The Laguerre-Pólya class collects limits of real-rooted polynomials and sits at the heart of work on the Riemann hypothesis. A q-analog can be built from the coefficient side, through a q-Borel transform, or from the zero side, by demanding that zeros stay spaced in a logarithmic q pattern.

The authors prove the q-Borel transform sends the classical class, and its type-I subclass, into themselves, which yields a q version of the Jensen polynomial criterion. The coefficient-side class turns out to strictly contain the classical one. On the zero side they prove a genus-zero product form, showing no stray exponential factor can appear. The two classes form strict chains, and the paper ends with open questions on limits and special functions.
arxiv-2606-18064:
Gao and colleagues explain why the Aptos blockchain does not trust its own safety checks just once, in a 2026 systems paper. Move, its smart contract language, runs as typed bytecode in a sandbox, and a static verifier proves type and reference safety when code loads. That verifier is intricate and keeps evolving, so a single missed rule on a live chain could mean lost assets or forged authority.

Aptos therefore adds a second, independent layer: runtime safety checks that re-verify the critical invariants while transactions execute. The paper motivates and describes those checks, which guard against latent verifier bugs and hostile bytecode alike. The authors contrast the pairing with other virtual machines: the JVM and CLR verify statically but trust execution, while the Ethereum and Solana machines lack a typed verifier altogether. Aptos, unusually, refuses to choose.
arxiv-2606-18464:
Gómez-Vargas and colleagues use deep learning to pull the tiny Doppler shifts caused by small planets out of real stellar spectra, in a 2026 astronomy paper. An Earth-mass planet tugs its star by mere centimeters per second, and restless stellar activity produces similar-looking signals, so many methods that shine on simulated data falter on observations.

The team trains neural networks on HARPS-N solar spectra with planetary signals injected. Each spectrum is represented by shells organized by flux and by the temperature where spectral lines form, together with velocity gradients. The best model reliably recovered injected signals with amplitudes down to about a quarter meter per second across periods from ten days to well over a year. The recovered signals matched the strongest peaks in period searches. Temperature-based shells consistently beat flux-based ones, especially on unseen data.
arxiv-2606-18964:
Sorn and colleagues study altermagnets in 2026. These are magnetic materials with no net pull, yet their bands split by spin in a way set by crystal shape. Most past work looks at the bulk crystal. Real samples, though, have surfaces and thin films that break that shape. The authors ask how such breaks change the spin split near a surface.

When a surface matches a bulk symmetry plane, the bands lose their split and look like a plain antiferromagnet. Other cuts keep a changed split instead. In one thin-film cut of a g-wave case, a d-wave split appears where the bulk has none. That split can drive a useful spin-splitter effect, as in chromium antimonide. Surface tests may show a different symmetry than the bulk, and film shape can be used as a tuning tool.
arxiv-2606-19264:
Choi and colleagues propose Large Language Gibbs in 2026, a scheme for structured probabilistic inference with language models. A model's knowledge could serve as a base for reasoning over variables that describe a complex world. Accessing that knowledge in a coherent way is hard, though. Single-pass generation is order-dependent, so early choices bias everything that follows in the chain.

The method uses the model's conditional distributions as transition operators in a Gibbs sampler. It resamples one variable at a time, conditioned on the others, over many rounds. The stationary distribution then reflects a compromise among all local conditionals, not one arbitrary order. The team applies the scheme to sampling from synthetic distributions, to consistent reasoning tasks, and to Bayesian structure learning. Results suggest language model conditionals inside Markov chain Monte Carlo are a practical alternative to one-pass generation. Structured inference becomes far more stable.
arxiv-2606-19564:
Andreas Goudelis and three colleagues map freeze-in dark matter at strong couplings in 2026. Freeze-in builds dark matter slowly from the hot early universe bath, never reaching full equilibrium. Their model uses a charged parent particle that feeds the dark sector.

Focus falls on universes that reheat only to temperatures near or below the theory's mass scales. There, production is Boltzmann-suppressed, so stronger couplings can still yield the observed dark matter amount. Reheating temperature, mediator mass, dark matter mass, and coupling strength trade off in tangled ways. Tracking both dark matter and mediator densities proves essential for sound predictions. One surprise is a mediator that never equilibrates because it decays too fast. Updated bounds from LHC searches and lepton flavour-violating decays close the study. The two search types probe complementary parts of the viable parameter space.
arxiv-2606-20064:
Alexander Wuttke, Max Melchior Lang, Christopher Klamm, Quirin Würschinger, and Frauke Kreuter test AI-led conversational interviewing for public opinion research in 2026. Standard surveys scale but force answers into preset categories, while human interviews probe deeply yet stay small. The study pairs an AI interview with a standard survey on migration policy for 571 respondents recruited through online panels, comparing voice, chat, and free-choice modes.

Transcripts surface reasoning and mental models that a thorough fixed questionnaire misses, including sharply different views among people with similar attitude scores. Completers rate the AI interview at or above the survey across modes, though completion varies by condition. Open data and pipeline materials accompany the study. Survey methodology gains a scalable route to open-ended depth.
arxiv-2606-20364:
Ali Asaria, Tony Salomone, and Deep Gandhi turn a vision-language model that judges 3D meshes into a training signal for improving them. Their 2026 paper companions an earlier study that built a de-biased VLM judge for single-image-to-3D generation. Here they ask whether that judge's preferences can specialize a strong open generator, TRELLIS, on furniture, cheaply and with no human labels. Moving the judge into the optimization loop exposed failures ranking never triggered.

The hardened protocol keeps the training judge strictly separate from the evaluation judge to break circularity, and corrects position bias by swapping. Three failure modes are documented with fixes: image overload collapsing the judge into position answers, splat renders hiding geometry defects, and reference-free judging rewarding clean but wrong outputs. Under this independent evaluation, their methods match the strong base model rather than beating it, an honestly reported null.
arxiv-2606-20464:
Caroline Dorn, Aaron Werlen, and Sean Jordan model how formation ingredients shape sub-Neptune atmospheres. Their 2026 paper follows JWST detections of methane and carbon dioxide in sub-Neptune skies. The detections hint that air composition records what the planet was built from: rock, water, or refractory carbon, called soot.

Planets are assembled from varying proportions of the three ingredients, and the team computes global chemical balance plus the structure of the air above. Water-poor material yields atmospheres strongly depleted in carbon compounds. Interior and atmosphere are solved together, so outgassing and chemistry stay consistent. The results give observers a way to read a sub-Neptune's spectrum backward into its building blocks.
arxiv-2606-20564:
Jerônimo Menezes and five colleagues benchmark how well cloud language models translate network intents into vendor configurations. Their 2026 paper presents a reproducible semantic benchmark for DSM-to-CLI translation, where syntactically valid output can still violate the intended operational state.

The benchmark covers five cloud LLMs, three vendors, five representative use cases, and ten repeated runs per cell, under fixed judges and an explicit failure taxonomy. Results separate semantic quality from operational correctness across models and vendors. Reproducibility is the point: fixed judges and repeated runs make cross-vendor claims checkable. Network automation gains the rigorous yardstick it has lacked.
arxiv-2606-20864:
Mayank Raj and three colleagues compare two methods in 2026 for generating synthetic network packets to train intrusion detection for Internet of Things devices. Such systems need large labeled data sets with realistic benign and malicious traffic. Public data sets have fixed mixes and extreme class imbalance. Deep generative models offer no way to force packets to stay in valid ranges.

Both proposed methods enforce hard limits inside the synthesis pipeline. One uses statistical learning, with latent sampling and two anomaly detectors as gates. The other uses a genetic algorithm. It treats packet generation as a multi-goal search with fitness scores for acceptance and for matching real distributions. Feature ranges are clamped, and outputs are validated separately. Constraint-first generation matters because invalid synthetic traffic can teach a detector patterns that never occur on a real network.
arxiv-2606-20964:
Grant Mathews, the only author named in the hosted text, develops a loss-cone framework in 2026 for dark matter capture by early black hole seeds. Supermassive black holes appear surprisingly early in cosmic history. Non-baryonic growth channels deserve a fresh look. Dark matter particles on certain orbits fall into a loss cone and are captured. That phase space can deplete, so refilling controls the long-term rate.

The halo is modeled from a standard density profile through Eddington inversion. Capture uses a relativistic angular momentum boundary. Rates are computed with a one-dimensional Fokker-Planck equation averaged over orbits. Refilling by massive perturbers, especially primordial black holes, depends on a granularity parameter. Ordinary stellar relaxation gives negligible growth for the seeds studied. Granular refilling can yield meaningful growth. The result bounds whether dark matter alone could help explain the earliest giant black holes.
arxiv-2606-21264:
Priyanka Surve, Asaf Shabtai, and Yuval Elovici present RogueRover in 2026, a quadruped robot that hunts rogue wireless access points inside buildings. Such devices can open a covert path into a network, but finding one physically usually needs dense sensors, site-specific radio maps, or a person walking around with a meter. RogueRover patrols on its own, logging signal strength with a standard Wi-Fi interface as it moves.

Across eleven patrol runs with six planted devices, a single patrol located devices with a median error of 1.62 meters, with no prior radio knowledge. Combining runs put five of six devices within one meter, and a blind trial picked the rogue devices out of 73 observed networks. Simple weighted-centroid estimates matched or beat path-loss models, so patrol coverage mattered most.
arxiv-2606-21764:
Prithvi Raj Singh and Satyendra Singh teach a reinforcement-learning agent to nudge bounding boxes onto moving objects in 2026. One-shot detectors cannot correct a slightly-off box; their MARLNet agent refines proposals step by step. It sees a 268-dimensional state: the current box, a constant-velocity motion prediction, its previous action, and image features, and it outputs coordinate adjustments plus a stop-or-continue trigger, trained with PPO.

On Pascal VOC 2012 and VisDrone 2019, the motion prior stops the overshooting that makes plain PPO regress, yielding consistent small gains in detection success. The ablations are the interesting part: one reward pairing causes trigger collapse, fixed by an action smoothness penalty instead. A ceiling also emerges: refinement agents sharing a backbone with their base detector can only polish so far, a representational limit future designs must route around.
arxiv-2606-22464:
The Khai Nguyen and Ebrahim Bedeer propose a transmitter trick for a next-generation wireless waveform in this 2026 paper. The waveform, affine frequency division multiplexing, suits fast-moving receivers, but its signals suffer high peak-to-average power ratio. Peaks force amplifiers to back off, wasting energy and distorting the signal.

Their method circularly shifts the transmit signal in the affine domain and sends whichever shifted version has the lowest peak ratio. Unlike earlier schemes, it needs no side information, the extra data that tells the receiver what was done. They derive a maximum-likelihood receiver that detects the shift from the position of the pilot signal and guard band. Simulations show a reduction of roughly two and a half to four decibels compared with the original waveform and existing schemes. Depending on amplifier quality, that reduction translates into a significantly lower error rate.
arxiv-2606-22864:
Yanhang Li, Zhichao Fan, and Zexin Zhuang warn that a near-perfect detection score can mislead in this 2026 workshop paper. Their subject is hidden-state probing, a linear classifier trained on a vision-language model's internal activations. Such probes flag indirect prompt injection, malicious instructions hidden in content, before a computer-use agent acts on them.

The authors present a single-model case study, using Qwen2.5-VL-7B on the Mind2Web benchmark with teacher-forced replay. A probe scoring an AUC of 0.998 on a clean-versus-attack split looks decisive. Two follow-up diagnostics complicate that reading: a paired baseline on text-side injections, and nuisance-matched visual controls on the same overlay surface. Neither diagnostic licenses an unqualified claim that the probe detects malicious content, though partly semantic readings remain possible. The authors package the diagnostics as a candidate control set with reporting heuristics.
arxiv-2606-23164:
William Guey and colleagues show that the language of a question steers who gets credit for inventions in a 2026 paper. Many discoveries have rival national claimants: Popov or Marconi for radio, Bell or Meucci for the telephone, Bi Sheng or Gutenberg for printing. As language models become a default gateway to history, their framing of such disputes matters. The team queries eleven widely used models about twenty-one disputed inventions and discoveries. They ask in twelve languages and gather over seventy-five thousand responses.

Guey and colleagues find that models usually admit the credit is contested. Still, asking in a claimant's national language makes that figure significantly more likely to appear as the inventor. Russian prompts surface Popov. Chinese prompts raise Bi Sheng. Portuguese prompts strengthen Santos-Dumont. Dominant Anglophone figures stay stable across all languages. The patterns survive adjustments for answer length, model differences, and claimant prominence.
arxiv-2606-23264:
C. Quesne solves a quantum mechanics problem about the Scarf I potential in a 2026 mathematical physics paper. The Scarf I potential is a classic exactly solvable well. Quesne studies it when the particle's mass varies with position, following a profile set by one parameter. A change of variables maps the varying-mass equation onto the constant-mass Scarf I equation, which is already solved. Running the map backward yields exactly solvable rational extensions of the potential in the varying-mass setting.

Quesne links those extensions to exceptional Jacobi polynomials, modern generalizations that skip some degrees in the sequence. The extensions come in three types. The varying-mass problem also shows a deformed shape invariance, a symmetry linking neighboring potentials. A simple worked example illustrates the results.
arxiv-2606-23564:
Kovacevic and colleagues detect slow brightness changes in Seyfert 2 galaxies, in a 2026 astrophysics paper testing how active galaxies are oriented. Active galactic nuclei are bright centers powered by black holes feeding on gas. The unification model says Seyfert 2 galaxies differ from Seyfert 1 galaxies only by viewing angle. A dusty torus, a doughnut-shaped cloud, blocks our view of the center in type 2 systems, so their light should look steady.

Using survey data from ASAS-SN, TESS, and Swift, the team finds that nearby Seyfert 2 galaxies do vary, weakly but clearly, over months to years. Scattered light explains it. Light from the hidden center bounces off a region around the torus, which smears out fast flickers. Matching the damped flicker against Seyfert 1 behavior lets the authors estimate the scattering region's size. The sizes agree with torus sizes measured from emitted light, supporting the unification picture.
arxiv-2606-23764:
Ji and colleagues test whether a classic pattern of Chinese rural society can emerge in simulated societies of language model agents, in a 2026 paper on computational social science. Fei Xiaotong's Differential Order Pattern describes society as circles around each person, with trust and cooperation fading as social distance grows. The authors build CAREB-MAS, a multi agent framework where agents reason through emotion, ethics, and belief, grounded in affect control theory and social identity theory.

Across long simulations, the agents spontaneously reproduce five hallmarks of differential order. They settle into stable labor specialization and connection based economic ethics. Cooperation decays with relational distance, relational authority emerges, and clan based stratification forms. The authors read this as evidence that differential order is a general outcome of social mechanisms.
arxiv-2606-23964:
Kardoost, Gleiter, Peng, and Marr show that teaching AI on full three dimensional microscope volumes, rather than flattened pictures, produces better internal models of cells, in a 2026 paper on computational biology. Fluorescence microscopy images cells in stacks of slices, yet most self supervised methods collapse those stacks into flat projections. Masked autoencoders learn by hiding random patches and reconstructing them. The authors compare two and three dimensional versions under matched training.

The 3D model wins consistently on single cell tasks. Aligning its features with a pretrained protein language model adds further gains, larger for the volumetric model than for flat rivals. Channel cross attention and frequency domain regularization prove critical. On protein interaction prediction the 3D model sets the best score, and on localization it reaches state of the art accuracy.
arxiv-2606-24064:
Shi and colleagues argue that teaching a weaker language model by copying a stronger one's answers teaches the wrong lesson. Imitating full solution paths transfers what to answer, step by memorised step, rather than how to reason on new problems. Their 2026 method, Strategy-Guided Policy Optimization, replaces copied paths with reusable strategy descriptions drawn from strong-model responses, written as general problem-solving guidance.

For each problem the student model produces attempts both alone and with strategy guidance, allowing direct comparison. A token-level objective then transfers only the shift that guidance causes into the unguided policy, with safeguards keeping updates stable. Weighting adapts per problem: guidance counts more where the student struggles alone and fades as its own skill grows. Across four mathematics benchmarks and two model families, the approach beats supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and hybrid baselines, gaining ground on the strongest rival.
arxiv-2606-24764:
Ratirat Suntharawirat, Nongnaphat Ponkhuha, and Daris Samart compute a radiative decay between two pentaquark states. Pentaquarks are exotic particles built from five quarks. The two states here, labelled Pc 4457 and Pc 4312, are treated as hadronic molecules. They arise dynamically in the chiral unitary approach, using heavy quark spin symmetry and a local hidden gauge interaction. The transition is a pure magnetic dipole one.

Nineteen triangle loop diagrams make up the full calculation. Each loop is reduced to one numerical integral, and a closed analytic form is given. Unknown electromagnetic vertices are estimated with a naive quark model plus spin symmetry. The main coupling is normalised to a known charm meson decay, with a cross check on another. The central decay width comes out at 6.7 kilo electronvolts. A cautious range runs from about 2 to 9. The photon energy is 143 mega electronvolts, and one loop dominates the result.
arxiv-2606-24864:
Subhadeep Patra, Paolo Comaron, and Arko Roy study the pattern of defects formed when two coupled Bose gases condense out of equilibrium. Cooling through the transition breaks symmetry and nucleates point like vortices in each condensate. The Kibble Zurek mechanism predicts the average density of those defects. It says little about how defects are arranged in space. Elementary vortices can also merge across the two components into composite defects called full quantum vortices.

Simulations use the stochastic projected Gross Pitaevskii equation under a linear quench of the chemical potential. Both elementary and composite defect positions turn out to follow a Poisson point process. Voronoi tessellation of the defect pattern matches Poisson Voronoi predictions. A new spatial form factor reveals a dip, ramp, and plateau structure in the configurations. Patra and colleagues present this stochastic geometry as a basic feature of condensation in coupled Bose gases.
arxiv-2606-24964:
Francisco Ferreira da Silva and Stefan Heimersheim test a prediction about how large language models compute. Models are assumed to use superposition, packing more features than they have dimensions. Theory says computing in superposition needs error correction that favours feature directions over generic ones. That prediction had never been tested. The authors perturb residual stream activations and watch the response. Activations prove robust to small nudges, forming plateaus that fit error correction.

The asymmetry: models are less robust along feature directions, built from contrastive prompt pairs, than along blends of two such directions. The directions are privileged, as the theory wants. Fitting the response with an Lp norm split sharpens the picture. For contrastive, MELBO, and SAE decoder directions the fitted exponent exceeds two, matching feature specific error correction. Random and PCA control directions sit near two. It replicates across six models, including Gemma, Qwen, Llama, and Mistral.
arxiv-2606-25064:
Koorosh Sadri and Mikael Rechtsman show that quantum geometry governs how solitons behave in shallow lattices, even away from flat bands. Quantum geometry measures the distance in Hilbert space between Bloch states at nearby momenta. In flat band systems it controls superfluidity and superconductivity where ordinary transport vanishes. For dispersive bands its effects are entangled with, and masked by, the band's dispersion. The authors study weakly coupled bosons in two dimensions, the critical case for Kerr media. There the masking lifts.

The deviation from critical behaviour caused by the lattice turns out to be governed by it, and is directly proportional to the fourth order dispersion. The authors identify the lattice potentials that saturate the bound on the quantum metric for an effective mass tensor. Sadri and Rechtsman thereby connect an abstract quantity to a measurable effect in nonlinear wave physics.
arxiv-2606-25164:
How active galactic nuclei accelerate their massive gas outflows is still unsettled. Luke R. Holden and five colleagues use deep spectroscopy of the nearby active galaxy NGC 1068. They read the ratios of coronal forbidden lines from neon and iron to trace dust and gas in the disk and in the outflow above it.

The contrast is sharp. Gas sitting in the disk, not outflowing, shows heavy depletion of refractory elements onto dust grains. The gas outflowing just above the disk is largely free of dust, and denser than the disk gas by a factor between nineteen and one hundred ten. Lower ionisation line ratios tell the same story. Together the results point to fast shocks doing the accelerating: shocks that compress the gas and destroy much of its dust on the way out.
arxiv-2606-25964:
Chengheng Li Chen, Zhiqian Zhou, Hao Chen, and Nicolas Chauvin work on GUI grounding, teaching small vision-language models to point at the right screen element. Models near two billion parameters suit phones and cheap hardware, but training data with accurate boxes is costly to label by hand. The team also asks how supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning should be sequenced at this scale.

WinDOM is their corpus of more than fifty-four thousand records. It is harvested by driving a Windows 11 web recreation under a headless browser. Boxes are read straight from the page structure, with no human labelling. Self-Family Distillation then cold-starts training by rejection sampling, either from the student's own moving average or a larger sibling model. A deliberately under-trained cold start proves the better launchpad for reinforcement learning, lifting out-of-distribution scores across three grounding benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-26064:
Mark Whitmeyer, an economist, studies labels: grades, credentials, scores, and stars. Labels do two jobs at once. They inform whoever reads them. They also give people something costly to chase. His model makes an institution commit to a classification rule first. Agents then spend effort to land on the good side of the line. A receiver sees only the public label, nothing more.

Exact certification turns out wasteful. Certifying every fine difference forces heavy signalling costs for tiny decision gains. Pooling a small interval at the bottom saves first-order costs. The information lost is only higher-order by comparison. Whitmeyer gives conditions where lower censorship, hiding the bottom distinctions, maximizes efficiency. Other conditions guarantee that every optimal classification uses finitely many categories. The design question becomes which rungs of the ladder are worth building. Fewer, coarser rungs often beat a fine ladder once chasing costs count.
arxiv-2606-26164:
Ira Wolfson introduces ChiSao, a graphics-processor optimizer that hunts every peak of a rugged function. Many problems in science and inference need all modes of a black-box function, not just the best one. Classic tools like basin-hopping and CMA-ES work one search at a time. Modern GPUs reward the opposite style. ChiSao runs a whole population at once and cycles it between convergence and anti-convergence. Samples that reach true peaks freeze in place. The rest keep roaming with momentum and smoothed gradients.

Two reseeding tricks guard diversity. Repulse Monkey and Golden Rooster restock the wandering population. Tests span all forty-two functions of a standard benchmark suite, in dimensions up to sixty-four. ChiSao recovers every mode where CPU rivals collapse on the hardest cases. Speedups reach dozens of times over basin-hopping. Mode detection stays perfect even under heavy likelihood noise.
arxiv-2606-26264:
Laura DeGroot, Swara Ravindaranath, Karmellah Buttler, and Taliah Lansing measure how disk galaxies grew from the inside out. In inside-out growth, a galaxy's centre forms first and its outskirts keep building later. Ultraviolet light traces young outer stars, while optical light traces the older body. Comparing the two sizes tests the story. Webb and Hubble images of the Extended Groth Strip supply galaxies across a wide redshift range, at matched resolution.

Ultraviolet sizes beat optical sizes on average at every redshift examined. Dust could have faked that gap in older Hubble work. Webb's sharper imaging survives the dust correction, and the gap persists. Clumpy galaxies show the size gap most strongly, since their star formation is scattered across clumps and mergers. Size grows with mass in both colours, as earlier work found. The optical size-mass slope comes out shallower under Webb's cleaner measurements.
arxiv-2606-26364:
Omar Khan and colleagues at Drexel University and Virginia Tech study what makes virtual dog ears feel like part of your own body in virtual reality. A survey of social VR users chose animal ears as a popular non-human feature worth testing.

Twenty-eight users then touched their avatar's ears under four conditions, mixing vibrating gloves (active touch) with a physical headband (passive touch). Passive touch alone produced the strongest feeling of ownership, and combining both kinds actually reduced that benefit. Feeling ownership of the ears also tracked feeling ownership of the whole avatar, which matters for people who express identity through non-human features online.
arxiv-2606-26564:
Shravan Luckraz studies when finite games have pure strategy Nash equilibria. In game theory, a Nash equilibrium is a set of choices where no player gains by changing alone. Nash proved every finite game has an equilibrium when players may randomise their choices. Pure equilibria, where nobody randomises, are not guaranteed. When they exist, and why, is the open territory here.

Luckraz builds on the best-response structure of finite games. The best response is a player's optimal reply to the others' choices. He derives new sufficient conditions, guarantees that ensure a pure equilibrium exists. Several broad game classes are introduced. One generalises unilaterally competitive games, where one player's gain is another's loss. Another rests on a single profile maximising the aggregate payoff over an ordered set. The results clarify how acyclicity and aggregation produce pure equilibria, uniting earlier scattered conditions.
arxiv-2606-26864:
Muhittin Evren Aydin and Rafael López study plane curves under a nonstandard rule for measuring bending. A linear connection tells geometers how directions change along a curve. The standard connection used here differs from the classical one. The authors split curvature into two notions: tangential curvature and geodesic curvature, each capturing part of how a curve bends in this setting.

They prove existence and uniqueness results for curves with prescribed curvatures. Given either curvature function in advance, exactly one curve realises it, up to rigid motion. All curves of constant curvature are found explicitly. Curves whose curvatures are linear functions of arc length are also generalised from earlier work. The results extend classic curve theory into this wider connection setting.
arxiv-2606-27064:
Nusair, DeVries, and Toro-Gonzalez measure how long four tin isotopes survive before half of a sample decays. That span, the half-life, anchors calibration work, medical dose planning, and star-process modelling. All four forms were made by photon activation, blasting natural tin with high-energy light in an accelerator. A high-purity germanium detector then watched gamma rays from the samples over several months. Peak fitting on four chosen gamma lines gave separate decay curves for each tin form.

Three results agree with evaluated Nuclear Data Sheets values within combined uncertainty. Those three cover the ground states of tin-110 and tin-113 plus the excited state tin-123m. The excited state tin-117m stands apart, landing clearly away from its evaluated value beyond expected chance wobble. Such a gap hints at a systematic measurement difference worth chasing.
arxiv-2606-27164:
Afeltra, Ho, and Pinamonti construct a case where a geometric flow refuses to settle down. The CR Yamabe flow evolves a contact form on a three-dimensional CR manifold, a space mixing complex and contact geometry. Known results say the flow converges when a certain mass quantity stays positive. Their example lives on small Rossi deformations of the standard CR three-sphere. In the 2026 construction, the shape develops a one-bubble concentration regime instead of converging along the flow.

Negative pseudohermitian mass on the Rossi spheres drives the failure. Mass positivity is therefore not a mere technical convenience in earlier convergence theorems. It genuinely connects to how the flow behaves at large times. Remove it, and bubbling can block convergence outright. The example sharpens the boundary between flows that solve the CR Yamabe problem and flows that stall. Geometric analysts gain a concrete test case for future convergence criteria.
arxiv-2606-27264:
Malik and colleagues build CORTEX, a benchmark that grades the reasoning of medical image models, not just their answers. Multimodal models reading chest CT scans usually explain themselves in free-form text, judged only by the final answer. Existing question datasets strip reports down to answer-only pairs, losing that chain. CORTEX restores it as a four-stage diagnostic trace mirroring radiologist workflow in this benchmark paper from 2026.

Stages cover task understanding, visual observation, diagnostic reasoning, and answer synthesis. Frontier language models draft the traces, which are then filtered by rubric scoring and expert radiologist review. Rubrics and structure were designed with clinicians. Built on the public CT-RATE dataset, the collection holds over seventy-six thousand validated traces. Question answering and report generation tasks are both covered. Trustworthy three-dimensional chest CT reasoning finally gets training material and a checking protocol.
arxiv-2606-27764:
Constrained optimisation must balance three pressures at once. Solutions must be feasible, good, and cheap to find under a fixed evaluation budget. Dikshit Chauhan and Anupam Trivedi propose DE-2LS in 2026. It is a differential evolution variant built on the RDEx framework. All RDEx components are preserved, from mutation and crossover to archive handling and constraint rules. One component is added.

The addition is a lightweight coordinate-pattern local search. It polishes the current best solution late in the run. A small evaluation budget guards it, and acceptance uses a feasibility-aware comparison. Ablation tests compare variants with earlier or stronger local search. The final configuration scored best, showing that controlled late refinement beats aggressive or premature search. Against RDEx itself, the U-score rose by about five and a half percent. In a four-algorithm comparison, DE-2LS took the highest overall U-score and the best total rank.
arxiv-2606-27864:
Vision transformers dominate image recognition. But they ignore planar symmetry. Many image domains have such symmetries built in. Tīkun Ông and Georg Bökman introduce a unified family in 2026. Their transformers respect any discrete subgroup of the planar symmetry group. Earlier flipping and D4 designs become special cases of the framework.

One guarantee concerns nested groups. When one symmetry group sits inside another, the larger group's model class embeds in the smaller group's class. In the single-head case, their equivariant attention is fully general. It realises every equivariant attention map that ordinary attention can represent. A D6-equivariant model uses hexagonal patches for six-fold symmetry. Tests use the PatternNet aerial dataset, where data are scarce by design. Several subgroups of the square and hexagonal symmetry groups are compared. Early results under matched budgets suggest equivariance improves accuracy.
arxiv-2606-28064:
Software projects produce design documents, models, and code. Links between these artifacts matter for maintenance and consistency checks. Recovering the links automatically is hard to deploy, though. Jan Keim and five colleagues present the ARDoCo tool landscape in 2026 to make traceability usable. A REST API exposes four link-recovery pipelines over HTTP, with caching and asynchronous execution. TraceView, the browser frontend, offers a guided wizard. TraceViz is a VS Code extension.

TraceViz overlays trace links directly onto documents inside the editor. A developer can jump from a document line to linked code at once. A preliminary study tested that in-IDE view. Seven developers took part. Six of the seven found the view improved their comprehension during software understanding tasks. All three tools are publicly deployed. The landscape targets architects, developers, and tool builders who need modern traceability without building it themselves.
arxiv-2606-28364:
Subhankar Chattoraj and Karuna Pande Joshi automate a painful chore for medical device makers: proving compliance with United States food and drug regulations. The rules sit in long, cross-referenced federal documents that people must parse by hand, which drives up cost and slows products on their way to market.

Chattoraj and Joshi extract regulatory knowledge into a formal knowledge graph written in a web ontology language. A seven-billion-parameter language model then generates database queries on the fly, reasons over the graph, and produces structured compliance reports. The system classifies devices into the federal risk classes and evaluates them in real time. Validated on real-world cases, it cut manual review effort substantially while making each verdict easier to inspect and explain.
arxiv-2606-28464:
Kathlén Kohn, Giovanni Luca Marchetti, Farhan Shabir, Vahid Shahverdi, and Weisheng Wang explain a quiet bias of deep learning: trained networks tend toward simpler functions than they could express. Singular learning theory locates the cause at critical points where the model's Jacobian loses rank, points baked in by the architecture itself.

Focusing on deep fully connected networks whose activation functions are monomials, pure powers, the team brings polynomial algebra to bear, including Mason's theorem from the theory of polynomial equations. They show that once the activation degree is large enough, criticality occurs precisely at subnetworks, configurations where some neurons are switched off or redundant. Gradient descent is thus funneled toward effectively smaller networks, a mathematical account of Occam's razor inside deep learning.
arxiv-2606-28864:
Sammani, Chamiti and Deligiannis ask whether tricks that make text models think longer also help vision-language models, which answer questions about images. Test-time scaling means spending extra computing effort during use, without retraining, to get better answers. It is well studied for text models but barely analysed for models that also see, so the team ran the first broad study of its kind.

Their tests spanned several models and sizes, nine scaling methods and six benchmarks. Small, strong models gained the most, improving by up to around thirty percent and often matching or beating much larger models. Giving a model more compute than it needed backfired, because the models lost focus. They also found that visual information enters early in the reasoning chain. After that the chain runs mostly on text, and the image's contribution fades sharply, a pattern with direct lessons for deployment.
arxiv-2606-28964:
Shchetinin, Shevchuk and Salpagarov lay the analytic foundations for diffusion that is both noncommutative and direction-dependent inside an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. Their reference state is a Gaussian measure. The anisotropy varies with position and need not commute with the base covariance. That noncommutation forces a corrected energy form, different from the naive expression one might write first.

They prove the fixed form can be closed and the forward dynamics are well-posed. Galerkin approximations on finite grids converge to the true solution. Stability of a log Sobolev inequality under a Mosco limit is established, along with an entropy chain rule and a weak-bridge theorem. The main theorem gives conditions under which a backward weak drift exists and an entropy estimate holds. A 3D tensor class of anisotropies and a homogenisation rate estimate round out Part I.
arxiv-2606-29064:
Wang and Ge design an attack that makes recommender systems more unfair, to expose how easily their fairness can be gamed. Recommenders rank items for users, and attackers can inject fake users to promote or demote chosen items. Fairness attacks, which aim to widen unfair treatment between user groups, had barely been studied compared with attacks on raw accuracy.

Their method learns by reinforcement learning, improving through trial and feedback. A graph-based encoder captures how fake user-item links relate to real ones. A recurrent network models the order in which fake items are injected. Two policies are learned jointly: one attentively picks the next fake item, and one picks the gender of the whole fake profile, since target systems may train with sensitive attributes in view. On four kinds of model and two real datasets, the attack clearly worsened unfairness.
arxiv-2606-29164:
Malarkkan, Roy Choudhury, Byahut, Charde, Gupta and Fu investigate the hidden paths that latent models trace while thinking. Such models reason directly in hidden-state space over multiple steps, but the structure of those trajectories is poorly understood. Comparing stronger and weaker trajectories, the team find the useful signals concentrate in a low-rank structure, a few stable directions. Unconstrained updates wobble with paraphrases, checkpoints and perturbations.

Their framework, TILR, learns that low-rank stable subspace from contrastive trajectory differences. It restricts latent interventions to the subspace and suppresses poorly aligned updates through an adaptive gate, without retraining. Across six benchmarks, a small number of latent directions explained most of the variation between strong and weak trajectories. Intervening there made answers agree more under paraphrase, by about ten percent, and cut trajectory variance by up to half, while preserving accuracy.
arxiv-2606-29264:
Wu and five colleagues test a proposed origin for an unusual supernova, SN 2021yfj. This exploding star shows narrow lines of silicon, sulphur and argon, signs that the material around it was rich in those elements before the blast. One idea says a silicon-rich white dwarf merged with a heavier one, shedding silicon-rich material that the explosion later struck.

For that story to work, the silicon-rich dwarf must form when a carbon-oxygen white dwarf gains helium-rich gas from a companion star and carbon burns off-centre inside it. The team simulated this build-up with time-dependent accretion rates. Off-centre carbon burning did produce large amounts of silicon and sulphur. The resulting mix depended strongly on how much carbon the dwarf started with. They conclude the double white dwarf merger route remains a viable origin for events like SN 2021yfj.
arxiv-2606-30064:
L. Abdullaev, F. Herrera, U. Rozikov, and M. Velasco recast machine learning as statistical physics on trees. Standard training picks one best parameter set by minimizing loss. Their framework turns the loss from data into an interaction potential instead. A Gibbs law then describes a family of balanced learning states. Data generate the landscape; they do not select a single point.

The authors state consistency conditions for the finite-volume laws involved. Integral fixed-point equations pick out the allowed learning states. For shift-invariant solutions, positive compact operators take over the analysis. Existence and uniqueness results follow in the one-dimensional setting. Phase transitions appear for certain data-based kernels on Cayley trees. Beyond a critical temperature, several Gibbs measures coexist as distinct prediction regimes. Numerical tests with non-separable kernels show multiple solution branches. Learning states can therefore coexist, like phases of a physical system.
arxiv-2606-30564:
Kevin Mayer maps out a young investigative field in his 2026 synthesis: digital vehicle forensics, the recovery of digital evidence from modern cars. Today's vehicles are networked, computer-driven systems whose traces can matter in crash reconstruction, crime inquiries, warranty disputes and security incidents. Unlike computer or phone forensics, the field has no settled playbook, since evidence spreads across the car, phones, manufacturer servers and outside services.

Mayer builds his account from academic literature, standards and practitioner sources. He defines the field's stages, from identifying evidence to reporting it, under safety, legal and privacy limits. He then frames triage, the choice of which sources to pursue first, as a balance of volatility, access, safety and authorisation. Eight characteristics organise the analysis, including multiple users, heavy networking and safety implications. A final section adds an attacker's viewpoint and a triage procedure for planning real investigations.
arxiv-2606-30664:
Deddy Jobson studies whether the moment a coupon arrives changes how well it works. Marketers court users with coupons throughout the customer life cycle, and Jobson hypothesises that a coupon lands hardest at critical journey moments, right when a user is actively engaging. Testing that idea normally needs real-time, event-triggered delivery software, which many firms find too costly to build.

Jobson's framework sidesteps the expense. It applies causal inference, methods for extracting cause-and-effect from data, to natural randomised experiments, quirks of existing systems that already randomised users by accident. He demonstrates the framework on his company's user onboarding coupon campaign, showing it supports sound business decisions. To test generalisability and reproducibility, he also runs it on a public dataset from a user retention campaign. The paper argues that timing effects can be measured credibly without commissioning a dedicated A/B test.
arxiv-2606-30764:
Filippo D'Ammando reviews the case that active galactic nuclei, the cores of galaxies powered by accreting black holes, produce high-energy neutrinos. Since the IceCube observatory first detected cosmic neutrinos, finding their sources has been a major astrophysics goal. Active nuclei shine in gamma rays and are prime suspects, yet population studies suggest gamma-ray blazars supply only a small share of the total neutrino flux.

D'Ammando discusses recent searches for correlations between neutrino events and both gamma-ray-bright and radio-bright active nuclei. Two sources stand out in the literature: the radio-loud blazar TXS 0506+056 and the radio-quiet galaxy NGC 1068, each linked to IceCube events. Other claimed blazar associations remain controversial. The review compares the sources' properties and the production mechanisms proposed for each, from proton interactions in jets to coronae. It closes with open questions and prospects for upcoming neutrino facilities in the multi-messenger era.
arxiv-2606-30964:
Arvind Rajaraman, Chao-Hsiang Sheu and Alexander Stewart revisit whether fermions can bind to a baby Skyrmion, a swirling topological texture in two spatial dimensions. The Skyrmion here is stabilised by Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and Skyrme interactions under a quadratic potential, a setup that interpolates between the magnetic Skyrmion of chiral magnets and the classic baby-Skyrme limit. A coupled fermion obeys the Dirac equation in this background. The team study it two ways: an analytic non-relativistic reduction, and full numerical solution of the relativistic spectrum, mapping the parameter region where bound states exist.

Bound states turned up only for electrically charged fermions, and only with positive charge and negative angular momentum; neutral fermions had none. In each angular momentum sector, the lowest bound state was charted against fermion mass, charge and coupling, and compared across magnetic, baby and mixed backgrounds.
arxiv-2606-31264:
Bardhan and Saikia prove new identities and congruences for the SOME partition functions. These functions take a partition of a whole number, a way of writing it as a sum, and subtract the even parts from the odd parts. Variants cover ordinary partitions, distinct partitions, and overpartitions, where the first copy of a part may be marked.

Building on work by Andrews and Dastidar and by Gireesh and Hemanthkumar, the pair add congruences and monotonicity results for all three functions. They also define a general analogue for any family of partitions and a colour partition analogue, the version where parts come in types. For both new functions they prove divisibility properties, widening the arithmetic picture of these odd-minus-even sums.
arxiv-2606-31464:
Hwang and three colleagues, as Team MKC, build a language model pipeline that tracks mental health change across a person's social media timeline. Early detection and steady monitoring could widen care where professionals are scarce. Single-post classifiers miss how a user's state moves over time, which is often the signal that matters.

Entered in the CLPsych 2026 shared task, their pipeline joins two levels of analysis. Each post is assessed on its own, and the sequence of posts is modelled at user level to capture temporal change. The unified design aims at a full picture of well-being rather than isolated flags. The work shows how large language models can be shaped for careful, timeline-based mental health analysis of real posting histories.
arxiv-2606-31664:
Koutsianos, Mošner, Panagakis and Stafylakis propose Q-Margin, a training loss for biometric verification, the task of confirming identity from a face or voice. Standard margin losses such as ArcFace and CosFace push identities apart by bending geometric angles in the output scores. The newer alpha-divergence losses instead produce sparse probability outputs, which help accuracy, but geometric margins do not fit their framework.

Q-Margin places the margin inside the reference measure, the prior probabilities of the loss, rather than in the scores. Against ArcFace and CosFace trained with an identical recipe, it performs competitively or better on the IJB-B and IJB-C face benchmarks. The same holds on VoxCeleb speaker verification, with consistent gains at low false acceptance rates. Its extremely sparse outputs also allow exact, memory-efficient training on millions of identities.
arxiv-2608-00164:
Siegel and co-authors measure the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect around DESI red galaxies. Interpreting tSZ data for cluster gas is hard. Foreground contamination and uncertain halo masses cloud the picture. Weak lensing data join their tSZ measurements here. That pairing allows a like-with-like comparison with hydrodynamical simulations.

They model dust and radio emission of the target galaxies directly. That step isolates the tSZ signal robustly. Across halo masses and redshifts, the FLAMINGO simulation overpredicts the observed signal. Even its strongest gas-expulsion version overpredicts thermal pressure. That version already matches gas density from kinetic SZ data. The gap points to missing non-thermal pressure support, they argue. Simulations may overstate group thermal pressure by a factor of two.
arxiv-2608-00264:
Książek and co-authors prune attention heads in vision Transformers with insight as a guide. Models like DINOv2 learn rich visual codes. Their builds are huge and opaque, with heavy compute and memory needs. The team first studies single heads with a spectral lens. A new view uses Laplacian eigenvectors of attention maps.

Heads are grouped by meaning, which exposes spare copies among them. Their SAPER tool turns those insights into soft pruning. It trains end to end and rests on a LapSum soft top-K rule. On ImageNet-1K, SAPER cut FLOPs past the RAPTOR baseline. Class scores stayed strong through the pruning. The accuracy-cost trade-off was highly favorable, they report.
arxiv-2608-00464:
Hanai and co-authors teach robots to predict contact force distributions from vision. Humans forecast forces roughly from sight and past experience, then adjust handling. Their data pairs come from a rigid-body simulator used in robotics. Simulators output noisy point forces, unlike consistent human prediction. They hypothesize that smooth force distributions are the better target.

Their model predicts 3D force distributions from one RGB image of piled daily objects. Targets come from statistical smoothing of simulator point forces. Object geometry guides that smoothing to handle varied contact states. Tests run in both simulation and real settings. Prediction accuracy and downstream task performance both improve with smoothing. Geometry-guided smoothing adds further gains. The model generalizes to real scenes despite simulation-only training.
beltane-the-smith-pg10064:
Jeffery Farnol's romance of 1915 stands here in its Project Gutenberg text, matching the printing issued the same year with Arthur E. Becher's pictures. Beltane, the greenwood smith, leaves his forge and his foster-father Ambrose to challenge Duke Ivo, called Black Ivo. The contents promise his comrades in order: Giles Brabblecombe the learned archer, a black friar, the philosophy of folly, and Black Roger the hangman turned brother-in-arms.

Three mighty men swear fealty to Beltane as the rising gathers. In the market crowd at Belsaye, two tall fellows in millers' hooded smocks shoulder through the press. They aim for Sir Gui's file of heavy-armed pikemen, eager to see the grim post of punishment near. Farnol's tale mixes disguise, a wronged heir, and Helen the Proud's grief into a full-blooded revenge romance, told in mock-old English throughout.
burton-mission-gelele-vol1-1864:
Richard Burton went to Dahomey in West Africa in 1863 as Britain's envoy to King Gelele. Volume One of A Mission to Gelele, published in 1864, tells of the trip and the court. Burton was already famed for his pilgrimage to Mecca in disguise.

His orders were to press Gelele to end human sacrifice and the slave trade. Burton records the Fon kingdom's army, its famous women soldiers, the Amazons of Abomey, and court rites in close detail. He is frank, curious, and often harsh in judgment. The volume is firsthand ethnography from a kingdom few Europeans had entered.
burton-mission-gelele-vol2-1864:
Volume Two of Burton's Mission to Gelele completes his 1864 account of Dahomey. Burton had spent months at Gelele's court at Abomey, delivering Britain's message. What he saw there changed few British minds but filled two vivid volumes.

This volume treats the customs of the Fon people: festivals, sacrifices, oaths, and the palace guard of women. Burton adds notes on language, trade, and the slave ports of the coast. His mission failed in its aims, as he admits with dry irritation. The ethnography survived the diplomacy, and historians still mine his close, if biased, reporting. A route map and word lists support the main narrative.
bury-st-edmonds-tryal-witches-1664:
Amy Duny and Rose Cullender, two widows of Lowestoft, were tried at Bury St Edmunds in 1664 for bewitching children. A Tryal of Witches, printed in 1682, preserves the court record of their case. Judge Matthew Hale, one of the age's most prized legal minds, sat on the bench.

The report sets out the girls' fits, the toads and other signs, and the proof the jury heard. Hale let the case go to the jury, and the women were hanged. Lawyers and historians have argued over the trial ever since. It remains the most cited witch trial in English law.
busk-pithecoid-gibraltar-1864:
George Busk, an English surgeon and man of science, sent this short letter on a Gibraltar skull in July 1864. The skull had been dug from a quarry at Gibraltar in 1848 and left unheard of for years. Busk saw that it matched the famed Neanderthal skull from Germany.

He named the Gibraltar find ape like, or pithecoid, in the terms of his day. Its match with Neanderthal showed that odd skull was no freak or sick man, but a race. The letter is short, yet it gave the Neanderthal claim its key second proof.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-1400-1:
Martin, Benedictine abbot of Vienna's Schottenkloster, was born about 1400 and died 28 July 1464. Son of wealthy farmers at Leibitz in Zips, Hungary, he studied at Krakow and Vienna and taught arts at Vienna. On pilgrimage to Italy with his mother he visited Subiaco and took Benedict's habit about 1425.

Climate and discipline proved too harsh for his weak health, so he moved to Vienna's Schottenkloster. Sent to Basle council in 1428, he became prior on return and abbot on 19 October 1446 after John IV died. He laboured for abbey and order, building a library few of his day matched. Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa named him visitor of Salzburg diocese Benedictine abbeys in 1451, with reform powers. By Nicholas V's authority he confirmed Melk's abbot election, finding no canonical flaw. His Senatorium alone reached print.
cia-0000012364:
Through the summer of 1962 the Helms memos to the Director of Central Intelligence kept coming, this one dated July 2. The Penkovsky summit correspondence now ran toward the autumn of crisis. Paper flowed in both directions across the Potomac, questions down and answers up, while the colonel's fate hung over every page the file accumulated.

The two-way traffic shows a top fully engaged in a single case. Few sources in the agency's history held the summit's attention so long. For readers, the memo is one more proof of the channel's weight in the months before Cuba.
cia-0000013864: Someone saw a captured American officer in Phu Ly City, and a CIA note dated July 2, 1967, passes the sighting on. Phu Ly sits in Ha Nam Province, south of Hanoi. Sighting reports helped prove that a missing man was alive and in enemy hands. Each one gave his family and his service a fresh point on the map.
cia-0000014664: Reports from the field said Communists were capitalizing on something, in a CIA file dated November 1, 1952. The copy is marked poor, and the title itself is cut off. Even broken files were kept, since a scrap could matter later. This fragment shows the raw state of much Cold War reporting as it reached Washington desks.
cia-0000015264: Flying objects were seen in the Shakhty area, in a CIA report dated July 2, 1955. Shakhty was a coal town in the Soviet south. More than one object is claimed, which set the report apart from single light tales. The file adds a coal town's sky to the map of Soviet sightings.
cia-0000015464: East Germany had its own flying saucer reports, kept in a CIA record dated in 1952. The German Democratic Republic lay behind the Iron Curtain, where news was tightly held. Reports still leaked west and were filed in Washington. The entry shows the saucer wave crossing a hard border, with officials on one side trying to judge stories from the other.
cia-0000022364: Norway involuntarily became a party to American spy activity, a Soviet line kept in a CIA record dated in 1960. The heading adds a family angle that the catalog cuts short. Norway had been a planned landing ground in U-2 flight plans, which embarrassed Oslo. Moscow pressed that soreness hard, hoping to loosen a Western ally over the spy flights.
cia-0000022664: Photo comparison case number 12,769 has its results kept in a CIA record dated in 1971. The case sits one number below another result filed the same year. Numbered in the twelve thousands, these cases show the sheer scale of the picture matching effort. Behind each number stood a missing man, a family, and a folder of faces.
cia-0000028764: The situation and prospects in Cuba are judged in National Intelligence Estimate 85-2-62, dated in 1962. An NIE spoke for the whole intelligence community at the highest level. Cuba in 1962 meant Castro's state, Soviet ties, and, by autumn, the missile crisis. An estimate with that number is a landmark paper, read then by the men who faced the crisis.
cia-0000037164:
A group of American pilots was allegedly held prisoner in a house, according to a CIA record dated May 1, 1983. The house stood near a place the title leaves cut short in the catalog. Most prisoner claims involved camps, which made a house an unusual detail.

Inside, the claim is recorded with the detail that made it stand out from the rest. Odd details could help a report, since a strange fact is harder to invent well. They could also hurt it, and analysts had to judge which way this one cut before the file could move forward.
cia-0000042864:
A communique was issued on the killings in El Salvador, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. A communique states an official position in set, careful words. The killings then at issue were those shaking the country that autumn.

Inside, the official wording is preserved exactly as released. Governments write such texts for foreign ears as much as for home ones. The file lets readers study the chosen phrases up close. What a communique leaves out can matter as much as what it says, and this one was read that way in every capital that received it.
cia-0000049064: El Salvador's minister of defense was reluctant to prosecute military officers, and a CIA item from 1983 records the reluctance. Prosecution was the one tool that could have broken the forces' habit of impunity, and the minister would not use it. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, naming the block at the top.
cia-0000049364: Central American Monthly Report number three appears as declassified CIA document 0000049364, dated September 6, 1983. With a Truth Commission note, it continues the monthly series begun earlier that year. Readers get one more dated installment of routine regional reporting. It is useful chiefly as a marker of the series itself. It also marks the agency's steady watch on Central America.
cia-0000094964: Dated June 2, 1959, declassified CIA document 0000094964 is another copy of the Third Report to the President by the President's Board of Consultants on Foreign Intelligence Activities. The catalog holds more than one version of this board report. Readers get a dated advisory report record, notable here chiefly for its place among duplicate board filings.
cia-0000100064: National foreign intelligence community support for assessment of the Persian Gulf, in shortened heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000100064, dated May 4, 1991. The title concerns community backing for a Gulf assessment. The brief file is a support record rather than the assessment itself, preserved as an institutional item in the catalog.
cia-0000100164: West Europe problems of verifying the Biological Weapons Convention reviewed, in the heading's strained wording, is declassified CIA document 0000100164, dated August 3, 1989. Conventioned appears where convention belongs in the title. Readers get a short verification review record, companion in subject to the needle-in-a-haystack monitoring paper filed two years later.
cia-0000109064: Normality of Cuba-ussr Economic Relations and Western European Misgivings Con are two numbered headings in declassified CIA document 0000109064, dated November 3, 1967. The first item calls Cuba-USSR economic relations normal, in its own wording. The second item, on Western European misgivings, breaks off at Con. The brief record pairs an official sounding claim with outside doubt, as released there.
cia-0000112364: Conduct Offensive Strategic Counterintelligence Operations In is the heading, cut off mid-phrase, on declassified CIA document 0000112364, dated May 1, 1986. The title opens with an order-like verb: conduct. Where the operations were to run breaks off at the word In in the heading. The brief record preserves the hanging ending exactly as released in the files as kept there.
cia-0000119764: An October 1956 CIA report surveys reaction to the Hungarian revolt around the world. Governments, parties, and publics were taking sides on Soviet power. The report collects those responses as they arrived in Washington during the uprising. World opinion carried weight in 1956 because both blocs courted the new nations of Asia and Africa, whose delegates now filled the United Nations hall.
cia-0000124264: A January 1960 CIA report covers the space vehicles of the Soviet space research program. Rockets were the visible muscle of the space race, and every launch was watched from the West. The paper assesses Moscow's fleet of boosters and craft as the contest entered a new decade. By 1960 the vehicle question had shifted from whether the Soviets could orbit a craft to how heavy, how often, and toward which farther targets.
cia-0000126864: A November 1968 CIA report describes the current disorder in Zanzibar. Four years after the islands' revolution and their union with Tanganyika, the place was still unsettled. The report surveys the confusion as the agency saw it at that date. Disarray reports from the islands reflected a union still young and strained, where mainland and island leaders read the same events in sharply different ways.
cia-0000126964: A January 1967 CIA report describes the situation in Panama. The Canal Zone made the country a lasting American concern, and Panamanian national feeling was rising against the enclave. The paper gives the state of affairs as the agency found it that winter. Situation reports on Panama recurred through the decade as treaty talks, riots, and elections kept the canal question warm in Washington year after year.
cia-0000132264: European reactions share situation report 571, from January 1991, with its political developments, the heading breaking off. Europe's capitals stood together on the crisis while differing on details of the response. The report collects those reactions for the daily watch. European reaction roundups measured the coalition's second pillar, since public consent in Paris, London, and Bonn shaped how long governments could sustain the effort.
cia-0000132564: Leftists in Guatemala heartened by a coup in El Salvador fill a CIA paper dated October 3, 1960. A change of power in one capital lifted the hopes of foes of the regime next door. Central America's chain of states shook together in those years, link by link. The short paper reports how the Salvadoran coup played among Guatemala's left.
cia-0000134264: Two short items share a CIA paper dated March 1, 1960. Item 8 covers plans for a Cuban May Day rally in Havana. Item 9 turns to opinion in Brazil, though its headline breaks off mid-word. One item shows the revolution on parade. The other takes the region's largest state as its subject. The short paper covers both as filed.
cia-0000136264: With a date of 6 May 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with views of the situation joined to a request for authority. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136364: Attitudes inside the CALLIGERIS group, as summarized by the officer WELLBANK and passed on by LINCOLN in June 1954, fill this fragmentary cable. The surviving text complains that others let the group down, that someone was an Arbenz tool, and names unscrupulous politicians among its grievances. Much of the page is too garbled in transcription to recover more, but the resentment is unmistakable. The victors were already quarrelling as the fighting ended.
cia-0000136564: One of the Spanish documents of Brigade 2506 is dated 2 November 1960, a date shared by several records in this release. The exile brigade was in its training period, run in secret by the CIA. The catalog gives this item no distinguishing subject. It survives in the original Spanish, a single dated piece of the brigade's fall 1960 paperwork, held for readers to place and interpret from the text itself.
cia-0000136764: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade documents, cataloged at 1 January 1961 with the date flagged as estimated. The brigade was drilling that winter under CIA direction for the Cuba landing. The record states no subject for this item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, grouped with the other estimated New Year records in the exile force's files.
cia-0000136864: No action will be taken on the referenced themes themselves, headquarters reports to LINCOLN in this February 1954 cable, but it proposes a covert alternative. Send the Guatemala station ten propaganda envelopes, already stamped, with two sheets of white paper bearing a rubber-stamped seal. The station would prepare a press release announcing the president plans to break with the communists, mail twenty letters to key newspapers and ten to foreign correspondents, and pouch the rest. A forged announcement, mailed from inside, was the plan.
cia-0000136964: Daily press conferences are suggested in this May 1954 cable to LINCOLN. A spokesman would meet the press twice a day in Tegucigalpa. He would stress the indigenous nature of the revolt. He would stress the hopes of the CALLIGERIS group. News of the liberation struggle would follow. So would comment on government statements and atrocities. A daily press release is also proposed. It would go out in the liberation army's name. Sympathetic papers across the region would receive it by cable.
cia-0000137464: Security Conditions in Costa Rica, Special National Intelligence Estimate 83.4-63 of February 1963, judges President Kennedy's planned visit likely a great popular success, with any sizable demonstration against him highly unlikely. Should large-scale disorder occur, Costa Rican security forces probably could not handle it, and no guarantee can be given against violence by a fanatical individual or small group. An unconfirmed report of a Castroist plot to assassinate Kennedy in Costa Rica is under investigation. Costa Rica's politics are relatively stable under President Orlich.
cia-0000141164: Rosters of Cuban air crew fill these declassified CIA pages from 1961, the year of the Bay of Pigs operation against Cuba. Each line gives a file number, a job, and a name. Most men are listed as pilots. Others appear as radio operators, engineer crew, or support staff. At least one name carries a stark note beside it: KIA, killed in action.
cia-03000964:
Syria leads the Current Intelligence Bulletin of 1 October 1955. The Soviet minister in Damascus, it reports, offered arms on 27 September. Two or three years of credit were proposed, payable in cotton and other exports. President Quwatli's government was taking the offer under consideration. Both the American ambassador and the British chargé got evasive answers when they asked.

The comment judges Syrian arms antiquated and armoured vehicles scarce. It also reports Egypt advising Syria to copy its own barter deal for bloc munitions. An Israeli protest is expected if Syria accepts. Other items treat Nenni's mission to Peiping and Moscow, Greek-Turkish repairs after riots, and Bonn's fears for the next Geneva meeting. A Pathet Lao chief balking at a meeting closes the issue.
cia-03007364:
Geneva's stalled nuclear test talks open the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 22 December 1959. Soviet spokesmen, the brief reports, seek to blame Washington for the impasse. The technical experts had failed to agree on detecting underground explosions. Moscow fears the West will press for a limited treaty excluding underground tests. Delegate Tsarapkin, before the Christmas recess, tried to discount the disagreements.

Nehru's flat rejection of Peiping's latest note leaves the Sino-Indian border dispute deadlocked in the second item. He declined Chou's invitation to meet on 26 December as premature. Iranian artillery movement near Abadan keeps tension with Iraq over Shatt-al-Arab navigation alive. Moroccan friction between king and leftists eases. Brazil proposes that Latin American chiefs of state attend the April dedication of its new capital.
cia-03177764:
France opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 26 November 1957, with a firm decision to build an intermediate-range ballistic missile. Defence Minister Chaban-Delmas has given the project top priority, the item reports. An atomic warhead is presumed. French officials ask American help, admitting they are at the earliest stage. Retaliatory capability, they argue, now outranks pure defence.

An Atomic Energy Commission official has admitted atomic weapons work outright. A bomb could probably be produced in 1958. Britain's defence review may damage NATO, in the next item. A Soviet-Egyptian economic agreement follows. Hanoi moves to keep its grip on the Pathet Lao. South Korean equipment and uniforms bound for the North are seized at sea. A pro-Communist mayor on Okinawa faces ouster. Strikes continue in Ceylon, and Spain fears American arms deliveries to Morocco.
cia-03178364:
Suez opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 7 September 1956. Eden recalls Parliament for 12 September, seeking renewed support under heavy criticism. Even the Times, usually supportive, faulted his earlier refusal of a special session. The cabinet expects Nasr to reject the London proposals before Parliament sits. British military build-up against Egypt is to complete by 15 September.

French public opinion, especially outside Paris, opposes war over Suez, an Interior Ministry poll finds. Soviet bloc military leaves are reportedly cancelled. Lebanese Christians fear a Nasr victory would inflame Moslem fanaticism. A British Communist back from Moscow reports the anti-Stalin campaign in detail, secret speech included. Liberalisation continues in Hungary. The break between Italian Communists and Nenni's Socialists may take four or five months. The Arab-Israeli situation follows in its standing section.
cia-06485464:
Cable from April 1968, sent to Bonn among other addressees, reports continued American anti-Vietnam war activity in West Berlin. The cable states that members of the US Campaign kept up what they called action night life. That meant entering GI bars and passing out leaflets that encouraged and offered help for desertion.

The cable names campaign members Keith Chamberlain and Peter Standish as invited speakers at a 23 March Vietnam rally. Their chosen theme is given as the history of American involvement in Vietnam. Their remarks were coordinated with campaign leader Francis Fuller, according to the cable. It also reports Chamberlain traveling to Prague in late March for a meeting of the Third Christian Peace Conference. Other plans listed include a meeting with local Fulbright scholars.
cia-06520164:
Letter dated 30 December 2004, sent by secure facsimile to Dan Levin at the Justice Department, encloses a paper on interrogation. Levin is addressed as Acting Assistant Attorney General in the Office of Legal Counsel. The sender's name is sanitized in the record title, and the signature block reads Associate General Counsel. Markings include Top Secret, ORCON, and NOFORN.

The letter states the enclosed paper describes a generic interrogation process using approved measures, alone and in sequence. It asks for advice that following that process would not break 18 U.S.C. 2340A. The background paper then covers combined use of techniques on high-value detainees. Its stated aim is to win threat information in time to disrupt terrorist plots. Middle pages detail single methods, such as walling and water dousing, and their stated limits.
cieza-travels-peru-markham-part-1-1864:
Pedro Cieza de León came to the Americas as a teenage soldier and spent years walking Peru with a notebook. His Crónica del Perú of 1553, in Clements R Markham's Hakluyt Society translation of 1864, forms Part One of The Travels of Pedro de Cieza de León. The travels themselves cover 1532 to 1550, from first landfalls to the wars of the conquerors.

Cieza describes the Inca road system, cities, and peoples as the first European to survey them with care. He asked questions everywhere and wrote down what the Andean world told him. His chronicle became the great eyewitness record of the Inca conquest. Few sources bring a reader so close to Peru at the moment of its fall.
civil-rights-act-1964:
The 88th Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 after fierce debate. All eleven titles of the full text stand in this record. Segregation in public places is banned outright by its terms.

Hiring bias is outlawed across the land in the act's strong clauses. Hotels, theaters, lunch counters, and schools must open on equal terms. The law broke the legal back of Jim Crow in the South. Long filibusters and street marches both stand behind its hard passage. The century's greatest legislative win for equality reshaped daily American life at once. Its enforcement clauses gave the paper rights real teeth in court.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-26-january-:
A gift opens Volume 26 of Pepys's Diary, January and February 1664, and it is the best New Year's gift he ever had. Mr. Deering sends a bill of exchange for fifty pounds, drawn for Pepys's use, with a letter of compliment. Pepys records the pleasure and then the problem: he is not resolved what to do about it. Fifty pounds is a bribe in any honest ledger, and the diarist is building his career on being the honest man. The shorthand argues both ways.

Winter runs on such tests. Suitors court him; Tangier money passes near his hands. At home there are feasts, music, and his wife's growing wardrobe to match his purple gown. Readers get Pepys at the exact point where Restoration officialdom greased every palm. His diary lets us watch a capable man decide how much grease his own palm would take.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-27-march-16:
March 1664 opens Volume 27 of Pepys's Diary with business on the Exchange and family news of a narrow escape. His uncle Wight reports that Mr. Maes was nearly trapped the day before and forced to run for it. Pepys takes Creed and his wife down to Deptford in most pleasant weather. They talk ships and yards till night. Spring is coming, and with it the navy's busiest season in years. Dutch war rumors now reach London weekly.

The month holds a private anniversary too. On March 26th Pepys keeps the feast of his cutting for the stone, six years past and celebrated yearly with friends. Health, ships, and credit are his three accounts, and he audits each in shorthand. Readers get a month of balance in this volume. The plague is a year away, the war mere months. Pepys walks his yards in fine weather, not knowing either.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-28-april-ma:
Complaints open Volume 28 of Pepys's Diary, April and May 1664. On the Exchange, merchants are preparing their grievances against the Dutch for a committee of Parliament that afternoon. Seizures, insults, and forts in Africa head the list. Pepys hears the talk, dines, and sets his wife down at the New Exchange on his way to Whitehall. There the Tangier Committee waits. Coming too early, he walks to Mr. Blagrave's for a song. War is approaching at walking pace, with music in the intervals.

Spring entries show the machine stirring: ships commissioned, stores bought, and the diarist's own value rising with every list he masters.
