His Tangier treasurer's work begins to take shape this season. Readers get the run-up to the Second Dutch War from inside the office that would have to pay for it. Pepys hears the merchants' anger, sings his song, and goes back to the arithmetic.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-29-june-jul:
Fear opens Volume 29 of Pepys's Diary, June and July 1664. The surgeon Hollyard calls, and against all his past assurances he tells Pepys he fears the stone has returned. He brings a medicine to dissolve it. Pepys is very much troubled and prays God to ease him. Six years after the operation that made his fortune in health, the old pain governs his summer. He goes down by water to Woolwich and Deptford and works through the fear, because the yards cannot wait.

The navy is fitting for war. Dutch and English ships are already skirmishing on distant coasts, and every stores account is urgent. Pepys audits guns, cordage, and men with a stone in his thoughts. Readers get the Diary under strain in this volume. Pain, duty, and ambition share the shorthand, and none of the three is allowed to win the day.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-30-august-s:
A light mind opens Volume 30 of Pepys's Diary, August and September 1664. The last night's accounts please him. He rides to St. James's with Minnes, Batten, and Penn for a scheme prepared in secret: Mr. Coventry will move the Duke, this morning and no sooner, to reform the clerks under the Clerk of the Acts. The conspirators fear the clerks will talk among themselves if warned. Pepys is inside the plot, which tells us where he now stands. The clerk of 1660 has become a manager of other clerks.

Autumn hardens around the intrigue. English ships seize the Dutch colony in America, and New Amsterdam becomes New York in the news. The war still has no declaration and already has prizes. Readers get office politics at their most Restoration in this volume: reform drafted like a coup, executed at a levee, and recorded by its beneficiary in satisfied shorthand.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-31-october-:
Pleasure in work opens Volume 31 of Pepys's Diary, October and November 1664. He is at the office forenoon and afternoon, very busy, and glad of the work. The navy is arming for the Dutch war everyone now expects. Mrs. Lane, now Mrs. Martin, tests the pleasure. She sends a sealed note to the Horseshoe tavern asking him to come. Pepys refuses the tavern and grants her Westminster instead. The entry is a small masterpiece of caution and appetite in one breath.

Autumn business crowds the rest. There are prizes taken at sea, stores to find, and Tangier money to move. His wife keeps house; his shorthand keeps everything. Readers get Pepys on the edge of the great war years in this volume. The fleet he serves is about to fight, the plague is months away, and the diarist is enjoying his powers at their freshest.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-32-december:
Early rising opens Volume 32 of Pepys's Diary, December 1664. He is up betimes for a Tangier Committee at Whitehall. Then home to hard business, office till noon, dinner, office again, and a sitting that lasts past one in the morning. The navy is building toward a war that Parliament has voted money for and nobody has declared. Christmas week brings no rest to the Clerk of the Acts. Pepys works through the feast days like a man possessed by lists, and records, with satisfaction, that he does.

Between sittings come the season's dinners and his wife's company. He closes the year with his accounts, his health in his thoughts, and his Tangier treasurership settling onto his shoulders. Readers get the Diary's work ethic at its purest in this volume. December 1664 is all desk and candlelight: the unglamorous month in which the fleet of 1665 was actually created, one order at a time.
europmc-pmc10184764:
Kurwadkar and co-authors critically review PFAS chemicals in water and wastewater in a 2022 paper. PFAS are a large family of man-made chemicals prized for resisting heat, water, and grease. They persist in nature for very long periods, build up in living tissue, and have been tied to health risks.

The review maps where PFAS appear around the world and in what amounts. It covers how they spread through water systems and how treatment plants handle them. It also weighs removal methods. The paper is a full guide to the forever chemicals problem.
europmc-pmc10196664:
De Coster and Rademakers present NanoPack2, tools for checking and processing long-read DNA sequencing data at large scale, in a 2023 paper. Long-read machines from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio can read very long DNA stretches. As study groups grow to thousands of samples, scientists need faster software to judge data quality.

The paper describes new tools that summarize experiments and filter reads efficiently. The authors show the tools handle population-scale data with modest computing power. The work supports the quality control that big genome projects depend on. It is freely available to labs.
europmc-pmc10767964:
The CNCB-NGDC Members and Partners gave the 2024 update of the National Genomics Data Center of China. The centre runs a family of data banks for gene research world-wide. Data from many omics fields pour in at a record pace. The centre archives that flood, merges it, and adds curated value.

Fresh banks headline this round, the report notes. New sets cover protists, bacteria, and plants, from soy to a plant pan-genome. Trait and disease banks grew too, with sets on fatty liver and virus parts in human DNA. Staff also upgraded core banks and kept smooth data swaps with world partners. All sets sit free at the centre's public site.
europmc-pmc11332364:
He and colleagues show that a stress protein protects against liver cancer by blocking iron-driven cell death in this 2023 study. Liver cancer is a leading cause of cancer death, tied to viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, and alcohol damage. All three stress the cell's protein-folding compartment and trigger cell death and inflammation. One stress effector, ATF4, had an unknown role in this cancer.

In stress-prone mice fed a high-fat diet, removing ATF4 from liver cells worsened fatty liver cancer, they found. ATF4 switches on a transporter called SLC7A11, also known as xCT. That transporter blocks ferroptosis, the iron-driven death path. Restoring the transporter in ATF4-deficient liver cells restored protection. The authors conclude ATF4 suppresses liver tumour formation through this axis. The work names a concrete stress-to-death pathway in the liver.
europmc-pmc11351064:
Lam and a large panel of Canadian experts update clinical guidelines for treating major depression in adults in this 2024 document. Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, and treatment evidence has advanced since the network's 2016 guidelines. CANMAT, Canada's national network for mood and anxiety treatments, convened academic clinicians and patient partners to revise the advice.

The editorial group ran a systematic review focused on reviews and meta-analyses published since 2016. Recommendations are organised by lines of treatment, meaning the order in which options should be tried. Each rests on graded evidence plus expert consensus on safety, tolerability, and feasibility. The guidelines span eight topics in question-and-answer format. They map a care journey from assessment through treatment choice to preventing recurrence. Patient partners and peer reviewers revised the drafts.
europmc-pmc1241864:
Pope and co-authors studied air particles, heart rhythm, and inflammation in 2004. Eighty-eight elderly subjects lived in three Utah communities. Each wore heart monitors for 24-hour sessions and gave blood. Fine particle levels were matched to each session.

A rise of 100 micrograms per cubic meter in fine particles brought a clear change. A key heart rhythm variability measure fell by about 35 milliseconds. Blood markers of inflammation were tested alongside the rhythm data. Pope probes two suspected paths from dirty air to heart harm. Autonomic control shifts and body-wide inflammation are the candidates.
europmc-pmc1277864:
Barr and co-authors charted urine creatinine across the United States population in 2005. Creatinine adjustment corrects urine tests for sample dilution. The practice assumed fairly uniform creatinine levels. Diverse national samples broke that assumption.

Data covered 22,245 participants in a national health survey. Creatinine ranges differed across demographic groups. Those differences can misclassify exposure status for individuals. The authors show how adjustment choices shift study results. Barr recommends regression-based adjustment over simple division. Their ranges give body monitoring studies a firmer footing. The data came from a big national health survey of the late 1980s and 1990s. Men and women of all ages and groups took part in the count.
europmc-pmc1332664:
Alonso-Magdalena and co-authors showed bisphenol A disrupts insulin control in mice in 2006. Pancreatic beta cells store and release insulin to manage blood sugar. BPA mimics the hormone estradiol in the body. Adult mice got a single low dose of either compound.

A dose of 10 micrograms per kilogram rapidly lowered blood sugar. Plasma insulin rose at the same time. Longer exposure raised beta-cell insulin content within two days. After four days, mice showed chronic high insulin and altered tolerance tests. Alonso-Magdalena links environmental estrogens to insulin resistance and diabetes risk.
europmc-pmc1413964:
Shaky RNA samples can ruin gene tests before they start. Schroeder and co-authors built a fair grading method in 2006. Labs had long judged RNA quality by eye, using a rough ratio of two RNA bands. That old check proved patchy and hard to repeat between users.

The team fed a large set of machine traces into a learning method. It picked the trace traits that best foretold decay. The result is a single score, the RNA integrity number, or RIN. Schroeder shows the score is steady and free of user bias. It gives labs one shared yardstick for sample quality.
europmc-pmc1783664:
Friedrich, Adhikari and Beyene tackled in 2007 a quiet inconsistency in how study results are pooled. A meta-analysis combines many trials into one overall estimate. Trials with zero events in both the treated and the control group are kept when effects are stated as a risk difference, but dropped for relative risk or odds ratios.

The authors reran three published meta-analyses with and without those zero-event trials. Adding them pulled the pooled effect closer to no effect, narrowed its confidence interval, and reduced differences between studies. For relative risk and odds ratios the shifts stayed small, even when such trials were most of the set. For risk difference the shifts grew large. They urge reviewers to include the trials whatever measure is used.
europmc-pmc1865564:
Grönke, Kühnlein and co-authors showed in 2007 that fruit flies run two fat-burning systems in parallel. Storage fat sits in droplets inside cells, and the machinery that moves it is shared between insects and mammals. The team knocked out the receptor for adipokinetic hormone, the fly's main fat-mobilizing signal.

Flies lacking that receptor built up fat over time and could not release it quickly when needed. The defect matched loss of Brummer, a fat-cutting enzyme akin to the main mammalian one. Losing both systems at once caused extreme obesity and fully blocked fast fat release. Either system alone could partly cover for the other. The dual control keeps body fat steady across the fly's life and lets it respond to sudden energy demand.
europmc-pmc1885964:
Reznick, Shulman and co-authors reported in 2007 that aging dulls a key energy sensor in rat muscle. The sensor is AMPK, a protein kinase that boosts fat burning and orders new mitochondria, the cell's power plants. Aging already brings weaker mitochondria, messy fat handling inside cells, and insulin resistance.

In old rats, a drug that switches AMPK on, and exercise itself, both activated the muscle sensor far less than in young rats. Long-term stimulation through diet also built fewer new mitochondria in old muscle. The blunted response centered on the alpha2 form of the enzyme. The authors argue that fading AMPK activity helps explain why mitochondria falter with age. Restoring that signal is a candidate route to protect muscle metabolism in older animals and perhaps in people.
europmc-pmc2124964:
Charles F. Craig and Henry J. Nichols, both captains in the Army Medical Corps, tested syphilis antigens at the Army Medical School in Washington in 1912. Their question was whether antigens made from pure cultures of the actual spirochetes could serve in the complement fixation test. They prepared them from the syphilis, yaws, and a mouth species, and ran the same sera against the routine Wassermann antigen.

That routine antigen was an alcoholic extract of syphilitic fetal liver. The authors accept the standing view that the Wassermann reaction is no true antigen-and-antibody meeting. Their case list runs through primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary disease, with durations from two weeks to six years. Readers get a wartime laboratory weighing a more specific test against a working but indirect one.
europmc-pmc2125164:
Howard T. Karsner and W. Denis studied nitrogen retention in experimental acute kidney inflammation in 1914. Their preface is a warning: no one can make a purely glomerular or purely tubular nephritis, so every result mixes the kidney's two working parts. They compare arsenic poisoning and diphtheria toxin as their two models.

Early on, the pair split oddly. Diphtheria nephritis marks the glomeruli heavily yet behaves as a tubular form, also with little early retention. Later, both models converge: the kidney's excreting power gives out and nitrogen piles up in the blood. The pile-up is far smaller in arsenic cases, with less tubular change, than in diphtheria cases, with severe tubular decay. Readers get retention tied to failing tubules, argued through two poisons that disagree in every other way.
europmc-pmc2128064:
Peyton Rous and Philip D. McMaster asked why bile pent up in blocked ducts takes such different forms. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. Some blocked ducts fill with a watery, colorless fluid that surgeons call white bile. Others fill with dark, thickened true bile. The authors traced the difference to the gall bladder and ducts pulling in opposite directions.

The ducts do not concentrate bile as the bladder does. They dilute it with a thin secretion of their own, colorless and free of bile salts even in deep jaundice. Rous and McMaster collected this fluid from an isolated duct segment into a rubber bag. It formed against real pressure and ran clear and almost watery. In ducts cut off from a working bladder, this fluid slowly replaces the pent bile. With a sound bladder attached, stasis bile stays dark and thick.
europmc-pmc2128464:
Lloyd D. Felton and Katharine M. Dougherty restored a weakened pneumococcus strain to full virulence by growing it in an automatic feeding apparatus. Their paper is the second in a virulence series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. The device supplies fresh food to growing germs at any set interval, transferring the culture on schedule without hands.

A Type I strain that had gone harmless for mice regained virulence of the highest degree in the apparatus. The medium was skimmed milk sterilized in an Arnold sterilizer, and transfers every eight hours suited the germ best, with four and two hours following in that order. Milk from the same dairy on different days varied in effect, raising, lowering, or holding virulence steady. Heating the milk longer steadily ruined it for the purpose, in proportion to the heating time. Virulence, the work shows, can be farmed as well as lost.
europmc-pmc2128564:
Hugh J. Morgan and James M. Neill showed that sterile filtrates of pneumococcus cultures can turn oxyhemoglobin into methemoglobin, the unusable form of the blood pigment. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. The filtrates carried no living germs, so the chemistry belonged to substances the germs had left behind.

In solutions of pure crystalline hemoglobin with no catalase present, the change depends on the peroxide in the filtrates. Blood catalase, the enzyme that destroys peroxide, blocks it. In solutions from burst red cells, which do contain catalase, a second system appears: a fragile substance inside the bacterial cell does the work. That substance is itself easily ruined by peroxide and similar agents before it ever meets hemoglobin. A filtrate works, then, only when germ contents have escaped into the medium and have been shielded from the culture's own oxidizing products.
europmc-pmc2131164:
Charles Doan and Florence Sabin reported in 1927 on tuberculosis of the bone marrow in rabbits, in The Journal of Experimental Medicine. They injected bovine tubercle bacilli into the veins of rabbits and then followed both the marrow and the blood. Their aim was to link changes in the blood picture with what the marrow was doing at each stage.

Rabbits dying in the first month showed heavy lung tuberculosis and deep marrow disease, with anemia and a sharp fall in platelets and white cells. In rabbits that lived past three to four weeks, platelets rose first, then hemoglobin and red cells, as the marrow healed on its own. By the third month the blood counts ran above normal.
europmc-pmc2131464:
Richard Shope and John Gowen, at the Department of Animal Pathology of The Rockefeller Institute in Princeton, measured cholesterol in cow colostrum in a 1928 paper. Colostrum is the first milk a cow gives after calving, richer than later milk in proteins and salts. The pair tracked total cholesterol and the share bound as cholesterol ester as milk secretion settled in.

Cholesterol in colostrum and milk is fairly low overall. The colostrum level fell from the start, at a slowing rate, until by forty-eight hours it nearly matched milk taken three or seven months after calving. Morning and evening milk differed in one respect: the morning milk held more of its cholesterol bound as ester.
europmc-pmc2131764:
Russell Haden and Thomas Orr, at the University of Kansas Medical School, measured tissue chloride in dogs in a 1926 paper. Blood chloride was known to fall after blockage of the stomach outlet or upper gut. The pair asked whether the tissues share that fall. They compared chloride in blood, liver, and muscle after blockages at three points of the upper digestive tract.

After blockage of the pylorus, the stomach outlet, liver chloride fell markedly and muscle chloride fell slightly. Blockage of the jejunum, the upper small gut, gave much the same changes. Blockage at the cardiac end of the stomach, where food enters, gave no change at all. Vomiting can explain part of the loss in outlet blockage, but not all cases.
europmc-pmc2180264:
Herpes virus hides inside infected nerve tissue, and Hans Zinsser and Fei-Fang Tang probe how immunity works against it. Their 1926 study examines whether serum from immunized animals can neutralize the virus and whether that protection can be passed to animals not yet infected.

Serum from actively immunized animals does neutralize herpes virus, and the pair explain why earlier results varied so much. Brain extracts neutralize weakly, far less than serum. Giving neutralizing serum ahead of infection protects no animals, even when placed near the brain 12 to 24 hours before. Lasting immunity, they find, comes only after some reaction to living virus; animals shielded by serum-virus mixes gain none.
europmc-pmc2363864:
Fallowfield, Ratcliffe, Jenkins, and Saul measured how often cancer doctors miss mental illness in 2001. Depression and anxiety are common in cancer and, untreated, tend to persist. The team wanted a hard number for how much of this suffering goes unseen in clinics.

Across 34 UK cancer centres, 2,297 patients filled in a short mental health questionnaire before their appointment. Doctors then rated each patient's distress. The questionnaires flagged likely psychiatric problems in 36.4% of patients, but doctors spotted only about 29% of those cases, while correctly clearing about 85% of healthy patients. Overall, the wrong call was probably made for 797 patients. The authors said doctors need communication training to draw problems out, plus clear routes to refer patients for psychological help.
europmc-pmc2495064:
Elliott and colleagues measured how common disease-causing mitochondrial DNA changes are in the general population in this 2008 study. Mitochondria are the cell's energy producers, and faults in their small loop of DNA cause genetic disease. The team screened newborn cord blood for ten known harmful point mutations.

They tested 3,168 samples from consecutive live births, plus matched blood from the mothers. Fifteen babies, which is 0.54 percent of the sample, carried one of the mutations, and nearly all had inherited it rather than gaining it fresh. The commonest fault was the change known as m.3243A to G. The authors conclude that at least one in 200 healthy people carries a mutation that could cause disease in the children of female carriers.
europmc-pmc2557064:
Baird and colleagues introduced in 2008 a cheap way to find DNA differences and map genes by sequencing short DNA tags. Genetic mapping needs many markers called SNPs, single-letter DNA differences, but finding them was slow and costly. Their method, RAD sequencing, cuts DNA at fixed points with enzymes and reads only the DNA beside each cut.

With less than half of one run on a sequencing machine, they found more than 13,000 SNPs. They also mapped three traits in two model organisms. One mapping pinpointed the gene behind lost armour plates in stickleback fish, using barcoded samples pooled together. They also mapped a pelvic reduction in fish and a mutation in a fungus. Choosing different cutting enzymes lets users tune how dense their markers are.
europmc-pmc2584664:
Bihari and colleagues worked out in 2008 a reliable recipe for dispersing nanoparticles in the salty, protein-rich fluids used in biology experiments. Nanoparticles clump into coarse agglomerates in such solutions, which ruins toxicity and imaging studies. The team used titanium dioxide particles and varied the ultrasound energy, the preparation order, and which stabiliser to add, checking sizes by light scattering and electron microscopy.

A specific ultrasound dose broke the clumps apart, and more energy gained nothing. The winning order was to sonicate in water first, add the stabiliser second, and add buffered salt solution last. About 1.5 milligrams per millilitre of serum albumin, from human, cow, or mouse, kept dispersions stable for at least a week. The method also worked for zinc oxide, silver, silica, carbon nanotubes, and diesel particles.
europmc-pmc2634664:
Muirhead and co-authors published in 2009 the third large analysis of deaths and cancers among British radiation workers. The group followed more than 174,000 people listed in a national registry, with records running to 2001. For the first time, the analysis also used cancer registration data, not deaths alone.

Overall, the workers died less often than the general public, a pattern the authors call a healthy worker effect. Within the group, though, deaths and new cases rose as the radiation dose rose. This held for leukemia other than one slow type, and for cancers as a whole. The size of the rise matched estimates drawn from Japanese atomic bomb survivors. A weaker rise in deaths from heart and circulation disease might reflect smoking instead of radiation.
europmc-pmc2649164:
Smedley and co-authors presented in 2009 BioMart, a single doorway to many biological databases. Biologists often need to ask complex questions across several data stores at once. Each store had its own search page to learn, and copying results between sites by hand wasted hours.

BioMart lets users build a rich query once and run it across stores held in different countries as if they were one. A query can then be saved and rerun with one click, which suits large routine jobs. The system plugs into tools scientists already use, such as R-based analysis packs and pathway drawing software. Big projects including Ensembl and UniProt run on it. The paper walks through real tasks, like picking gene variants for a screening study.
europmc-pmc2654964:
Hughes and co-authors compared in 2009 the daily gene rhythms of mouse liver with those of cells grown in dishes. The body clock switches genes on and off in roughly 24-hour cycles in most tissues. The team sampled gene activity at very fine time intervals, far denser than earlier studies, to catch rhythms others might have missed.

The liver showed a surprise: besides the daily cycle, many genes rose and fell every 12 or 8 hours, at the second and third harmonics of the day. These faster waves appeared in heart, kidney, and lung too. Dish-grown cells showed almost none of them, and far fewer cycling genes overall, by about a hundred-fold. Restricting feeding times wiped the harmonics out. Clock studies based only on cells, the authors warn, miss much of what the clock does in a living animal.
europmc-pmc2661364:
Hidalgo and colleagues built in 2009 a network of human diseases from the medical histories of more than 30 million patients. Diseases that often strike the same people are linked, forming a map of how illnesses cluster and follow one another. The team released the map, called the Phenotypic Disease Network, as a public resource.

Clear patterns emerged from the map. Patients tended to develop new diseases close to ones they already had. The paths of spread differed between men and women, and between ethnic groups. People whose diseases sat at busy hubs of the map tended to die sooner than those with lonely, rarely linked diseases. Diseases that usually came late in a chain were also more connected and more deadly. Disease, the authors argue, advances along this map like traffic along roads.
europmc-pmc2717464:
Dubin and co-authors tested in 2009 whether raising blood pressure with norepinephrine, a drug that tightens blood vessels, improves tiny-vessel flow in septic shock. Septic shock is a severe infection state where pressure falls and organs starve despite a strong heartbeat. Doctors often aim above a mean pressure of sixty-five, assuming higher pressure means better flow to tissues.

In twenty ventilated patients, raising mean pressure in steps to seventy-five and then eighty-five raised heart workload but did not improve flow under the tongue. The share of open capillaries, the smallest vessels, stayed flat, and perfused capillary density trended down. Patients who started worst tended to worsen most, which warns that higher targets may harm some.
europmc-pmc2725864:
N'Guessan, Corbel, Akogbéto, and Rowland tested in 2007 whether treated mosquito nets and indoor spraying still control malaria in a pyrethroid-resistant area of Benin. Pyrethroids are the insecticide class used on nets and for wall spraying across Africa. Resistance through the kdr mechanism, a nerve mutation, had become common in the local Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes.

In experimental hut trials against the resistant population, both nets and spraying performed poorly compared with their known effect on sensitive mosquitoes. Mosquito survival was high and malaria control was weakened, which suggests these tools may no longer work well in such areas. The results argue for new insecticide classes where kdr resistance is widespread.
europmc-pmc2731764:
Henderson and co-authors tested in 2009 AC-1202, a ketogenic compound taken by mouth, in a ninety-day trial for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease. Brains in Alzheimer's use glucose poorly in specific regions early on. Ketone bodies, made when glucose is scarce, offer the brain an alternate fuel that it can still burn.

In one hundred fifty-two patients on normal diets and usual Alzheimer's drugs, the compound raised a blood ketone marker within hours. Thinking scores favored the compound over placebo at day forty-five in all analysis groups. Among patients without the APOE4 risk gene form, the benefit was larger and still present at day ninety. A stronger ketone response also tracked with better scores.
europmc-pmc2763764:
Surjushe, Vasani, and Saple gave in 2008 a short review of Aloe vera, a plant long used for health, beauty, and skin care and now common in cosmetics. The plant has served medicine for millennia across Greece, Egypt, India, Mexico, Japan, and China, from royal beauty routines to treating soldiers' wounds. Its gel, latex, and rind layers carry distinct active compounds.

They summarize the plant's properties, how its compounds are thought to act, and its clinical uses in dermatology and beyond. Controlled trial evidence, though, is thin for many claimed uses. They note plainly that rigorous trials must still test whether it truly works, rather than relying on tradition. The review also traces the plant's history and its anatomy, including the water-rich inner gel that holds most active ingredients.
europmc-pmc2784464:
Stommel and Schoenborn examined in 2009 how accurate body mass index values are when they rest on self-reported height and weight. They used the national NHANES and NHIS surveys from 2001 to 2006. Interviews gather such figures cheaply, but people misreport them, so the error pattern needed mapping. They compared self-reported values against physical measurements and hunted for traits that predict the gaps.

Self-reported BMI ran too high at the low end of the scale, below about twenty-two. It ran too low at the high end, especially above twenty-eight. Errors also varied with age, sex, and ethnic background. Adjusting for those traits narrowed the mistakes but still misclassified some obese people as merely overweight. Health risk estimates, however, came out virtually the same from self-reported and measured values. Corrected self-reports, they conclude, can serve risk estimation well.
europmc-pmc2827364:
Tan, Cang, Ma, Petrillo, and Liu reviewed in 2010 a new family of cancer drugs that block enzymes called histone deacetylases, or HDACs. These enzymes remove small chemical tags from the proteins that spool DNA, which can silence tumor suppressor genes, the genes that hold cancer back. Blocking them can switch those genes back on.

One blocker, vorinostat, had already won United States approval for a skin lymphoma after standard treatments failed. More than eleven agents were in at least eighty clinical trials, covering blood cancers and solid tumors, alone and in drug combinations. Early results showed real promise in several cancers, and the review maps which agents reached which trial stage.
europmc-pmc2846864:
Daley, Abbott, Doyle, Nader, and Larson pulled together three decades of research in 2010 comparing beef from grass-fed and grain-fed cattle. Consumer interest in grass-fed beef had grown fast, raising questions about whether its fat profile and antioxidant content truly differ. The review weighs measured fatty acid and nutrient differences alongside taste and cooking trade-offs.

Grass-based diets clearly raised conjugated linoleic acid, its precursor trans vaccenic acid, and omega-3 fats per gram of fat. Total saturated fat matched grain-fed beef, but grass-fed carried more harmless stearic acid and less of the cholesterol-raising kinds. Grass-fed beef also packed more vitamin A and E precursors plus protective enzymes, ran leaner overall, and brought a distinct grass flavor and yellowish fat.
europmc-pmc2874364:
Mugnier, Poirel, Naas, and Nordmann traced in 2010 how a resistance gene that defeats last-resort antibiotics spread around the world. The gene, blaOXA-23, makes an enzyme that breaks carbapenems, drugs kept for the worst infections. Its carrier, Acinetobacter baumannii, haunts intensive care units with pneumonia and blood infections that resist many drugs.

First found in Scotland, the gene has since been reported on every inhabited continent. It travels inside a mobile DNA package flanked by insertion sequences that also switch it on strongly, and a harmless relative species appears to be its original source. Hospital clones carrying it match across countries, which shows patients and equipment move it. Stopping the spread will be hard, the authors warn plainly.
europmc-pmc2898064:
Wu, Feng, and Stein built in 2010 a human protein interaction network based on functional links and showed it can spotlight cancer genes. Rather than physical contacts alone, their network connects proteins that work in the same pathways, drawn from curated pathway knowledge and expanded by prediction. Projecting gene lists onto such a network lets patterns emerge that single-gene ranking misses.

Applied to cancer datasets, the network pulled out candidate driver genes that sit amid known cancer players, even when the candidates' own signals were modest. Network neighbors of a suspicious gene proved strong evidence in its favor. The resource and its cancer workflow were released for other analysts, offering a route to interpret the flood of tumor sequencing results gene by gene.
europmc-pmc3144464:
David Habier and colleagues extended a family of statistical methods for predicting breeding value from DNA in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Breeders now score animals at tens of thousands of DNA markers, most with no effect, and the methods must guess how many markers matter. Two new variants learn that share from the data instead of fixing it beforehand.

In simulations and in records from North American Holstein bulls, one variant gave steadier guesses about how many trait genes exist, and it ran faster than its sibling. Milk and fat yield appeared driven by larger-effect genes than protein yield or cell counts. Prediction accuracy was similar across all variants, so the authors recommend the faster, self-tuning one for routine breeding work.
europmc-pmc3185064:
Ewan Gibb and colleagues compiled the first atlas of long non-coding RNAs across human tissues and cancers in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. These long RNA copies make no protein and were once dismissed as genome dark matter, yet mounting work gives them real jobs in cell control. Nobody had charted them comprehensively, so the team mined hundreds of gene-tag libraries.

Parsing tens of millions of short tags, they profiled the RNAs across more than two dozen normal tissues and nearly twenty cancers. Normal tissues each ran a distinctive, tightly tissue-specific pattern. Cancers broke those patterns extensively, with widespread abnormal levels. The atlas gives cancer researchers a first map of where these RNAs act and which ones go wrong.
europmc-pmc3219664:
Denny Borsboom and colleagues proposed a network view of mental disorders in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. People with one disorder often have another, and the usual explanation, a single hidden cause for each diagnosis, struggles with that overlap. The team instead modeled symptoms themselves as a connected web, using the symptom lists of the DSM-IV diagnostic manual.

Half of all listed symptoms turned out to be connected, and the web had a small-world shape: tight local clusters linked by short paths. Distances between disorders in the web predicted real-world comorbidity rates. Simulations of depression and generalized anxiety reproduced population statistics well. The authors argue disorders are inherently complex systems, which may explain why simple genetic or brain-based explanations keep falling short.
europmc-pmc3222064:
Lucienne Cardoso and colleagues examined whether waiting for an intensive care bed harms critically ill patients, in this 2011 cohort study in Critical Care. When demand exceeds beds, patients wait in other wards, and delay had been blamed for worse outcomes. The team followed adults admitted to one Brazilian unit through 2005, comparing immediate admissions with delayed ones.

Of four hundred and one patients, about two-thirds waited for a bed. Mortality rose significantly with delay, and the authors estimate roughly three in ten intensive care deaths were attributable to the wait. Each additional hour of waiting was independently linked to a higher risk of death, even after accounting for age, diagnosis, and severity scores. The findings argue that getting patients into intensive care early saves lives.
europmc-pmc3234264:
Martin Ganal and a large consortium built a high-density genotyping array for maize in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Such arrays, which read tens of thousands of single-letter DNA differences at once, power genetic mapping and breeding. The team selected markers mainly from genes, spread evenly across the maize genome, and tested the array on diverse breeding material.

Nearly fifty thousand markers proved reliable, with low failure rates across North American and European inbred lines, crosses, and wild teosinte relatives. The team then genotyped two mapping populations to build dense linkage maps carrying tens of thousands of markers. Comparing those maps with the reference genome assembly exposed several regions where the assembly's order looks wrong, and placed markers missing from it. The array is offered as a durable resource for maize genetics and breeding.
europmc-pmc3241564:
Antoine Lecharpentier and colleagues searched the blood of lung cancer patients for circulating tumor cells caught mid-transition, in this 2011 paper in the British Journal of Cancer. Tumor cells that shed into the blood drive metastasis and carry prognostic information. A process called epithelial-mesenchymal transition is thought to prepare them, but direct evidence in patients' circulating cells was scarce.

Using a filtration method that traps tumor cells by size, the team stained cells from six patients. All had non-small cell lung cancer that had already spread. Every patient carried tumor cells, singly and in clusters, that strongly displayed both an epithelial marker and the mesenchymal marker vimentin. Cells bearing only the mesenchymal marker were rarer, and none bore only the epithelial one. The authors present these hybrid cells as the first direct evidence of the transition in this disease.
europmc-pmc3254664:
Anna Protasio and a large team delivered a thoroughly rebuilt genome for the human blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Biology. The parasite causes schistosomiasis, a disease affecting millions in poorer countries, and its earlier draft genome was highly fragmented. Using two sequencing technologies on clonal worms, the team upgraded the assembly and re-examined its genes.

The new assembly collapsed the sequence into under nine hundred scaffolds, with most bases placed on chromosomes. Sequencing the parasite's RNA at four life stages refined the gene catalog, cutting the predicted gene count while extensively revising nearly half of the genes. The team mapped expression changes for more than nine thousand genes across the life cycle and found a splicing trick, trans-splicing, at work in at least a tenth of genes. All data feed two public databases for parasite researchers.
europmc-pmc3314964:
Scheres set out a cleaner statistical way to build three dimensional structures from electron microscope images, in a 2012 paper. The method, called cryo-EM, photographs huge numbers of frozen particles and averages them into a structure. The images are extremely noisy, so the math can accidentally sculpt noise into fake detail, especially near the sharpness limit.

Traditionally, researchers filtered their maps by hand picked rules, which let personal judgment creep in. Scheres instead frames the whole task in Bayesian terms, a style of statistics that weighs the data against prior expectations in a principled way. The approach builds in smoothing automatically and gives an honest estimate of sharpness. Tested on real data, it produced more trustworthy structures than standard methods and could even spot small hidden groups of differing particles.
europmc-pmc3315464:
Sun and colleagues worked out how warm weather makes young plant stems stretch, in a 2012 genetics study. Seedlings of the small plant arabidopsis grow tall, thin stems in heat, a change thought to help the plant cope. Two players were already suspected, a gene switching protein called PIF4 and the growth hormone auxin, but how they connected was unclear.

The team showed that heat raises the activity of both PIF4 and a hormone making gene named YUCCA8. PIF4 binds directly to that gene's control region and switches it on, raising hormone levels in the plant. Plants with a broken YUCCA8 gene barely stretched in heat, even when PIF4 was overactive. A second mutation that blocks hormone signaling did the same. The results draw a straight line from temperature sensing to hormone production.
europmc-pmc3317864:
Wiltsey Stirman and colleagues reviewed what research says about keeping new health programs alive after their launch, in a 2012 article. Getting proven practices into clinics has drawn heavy study, but far less is known about whether those practices survive once the launch support ends. The team gathered one hundred twenty five studies that followed programs past their first rollout.

Most studies looked backward rather than following programs forward, and about half relied on what staff said about themselves. Few checked quality or faithfulness to the original program with hard measures, and among those that did, only a small number found full survival. Programs also quietly changed over time, a topic barely studied. Workplace setting, staff capacity, everyday processes, and the design of the program itself all shaped survival. The authors call for clearer definitions and studies planned from the start.
europmc-pmc3318764:
Yeung and Summerfield reviewed how people judge their own decisions, in a 2012 article on the science of self monitoring. People often sense their confidence in a choice and notice their own mistakes, even with nobody telling them the right answer. This self knowledge, called metacognition, helps people avoid repeating errors and stops them wasting effort on shaky choices.

The review brings together two research lines that grew up apart, one on confidence judgments and one on error spotting. Both, the authors argue, rest on extra processing that happens after a decision, inside the same systems that made it. That shared machinery explains why confidence and accuracy usually rise and fall together. The authors note that nearly all the evidence comes from quick, simple lab choices, and question how well the ideas stretch to long, real world decisions.
europmc-pmc3323564:
Waldenström, Gennebäck, Hellman, and Ronquist showed that heart muscle cells send out tiny parcels carrying genetic messages, in a 2012 study. Many cells release such membrane wrapped parcels, which can influence the cells that receive them. The team collected parcels shed by mouse heart cells grown in the lab and examined them under powerful microscopes and by sorting instruments.

Inside, they found hundreds of kinds of RNA messages forming a connected biological network, plus hundreds of distinct stretches of chromosomal DNA. The parcels could deliver DNA into connective tissue cells, reaching even the cell nucleus. Receiving cells changed the activity of hundreds of genes afterward. The authors propose that heart cells use these parcels, which they nickname cardiosomes, to coordinate metabolism with their neighbors.
europmc-pmc3384264:
Stuhrmann, Suslow, and Dannlowski reviewed brain-scan studies in 2011 on how people with major depression read emotion on faces. Theories of depression predict a bias toward sad or threatening expressions. The team gathered twenty-five functional MRI studies comparing acutely depressed patients with healthy controls.

Patients showed a shared pattern of overreaction to negative faces and underreaction to happy ones. The amygdala and several face and feeling regions drove the effect, with further changes in cingulate and frontal areas. Results varied in some frontal regions, likely because tasks and patient groups differed. Whether the pattern marks a passing state or a lasting trait, they say, needs studies of recovered patients.
europmc-pmc3393664:
Eaton led twelve modeling teams in 2012 to compare forecasts of how HIV treatment itself could prevent new infections in South Africa. Each model had tackled slightly different questions before, making their answers hard to compare. Here all twelve ran the same standard treatment scenarios and reported the same measures.

Under an ambitious scenario, the models agreed new infections would fall by roughly a third to a half within eight years. Long-range forecasts spread much wider, leaving deep doubt about wiping HIV out with treatment alone over four decades. Seven models judged that today's real rollout already cuts incidence meaningfully below the no-treatment path. The exercise shows where modelers agree and where honest uncertainty remains.
europmc-pmc3428864:
Nik-Zainal and a large team reconstructed the life histories of twenty-one breast cancers in 2012 from the mutations written into their genomes. A cancer evolves as cell families replace one another under shifting pressures, and the genome keeps the diary. The team built algorithms to read that diary in order.

Mutational processes, they found, change across a cancer's lifespan, with several switching on late yet adding huge variation. Most mutations sit in only a fraction of tumor cells, showing rich branching, but every tumor kept one dominant family making up over half its cells. That family's takeoff seems to need hundreds or thousands of mutations first, and its expansion may be the final step that brings the cancer to notice.
europmc-pmc3443064:
French and colleagues demonstrated a systematic way in 2012 to build behavior-change programs that push medical evidence into everyday practice. The gap between what studies prove and what clinics do is notorious, yet intervention design lacked a standard recipe. Their four-step method leans on a framework cataloguing the domains that drive professional behavior.

The steps ask who must act differently, which barriers and enablers theory points to, which techniques and delivery modes could shift them, and how change will be measured. They illustrate with a program to improve back-pain care in primary practice, delivered through two interactive workshops plus a DVD. Outcome measures were chosen to expose the mechanisms of change. Other teams, they argue, can reuse the scaffold.
europmc-pmc3499364:
Oil-rich marine algae could supply biofuel without farmland, and Astrid Vieler leads a very large team presenting the genome of one candidate in 2012. Nannochloropsis oceanica strain CCMP1779 belongs to the heterokonts, naturally stores much oil, and already serves industry for high-value lipids.

The assembled genome spans 28.7 million bases. RNA data from nitrogen-rich and nitrogen-starved growth support 11,973 genes, including over 100 tied to lipid metabolism and more than 200 transcription factors and regulators. Comparison with Nannochloropsis gaditana finds 2,649 genes likely specific to this species. The team also demonstrates nuclear transformation, inserting DNA into the nucleus, giving engineers a working genetic toolkit for the alga.
europmc-pmc350664:
Tiny RNAs guide gene silencing, and Gyorgy Hutvagner, Martin J. Simard, Craig C. Mello, and Phillip D. Zamore report a chemical off-switch for them in 2004. Hundreds of microRNAs and small interfering RNAs were known, but their jobs were hard to probe without a blocker.

A modified building block, 2'-O-methyl, turns a matching strand into a stubborn inhibitor that binds the small RNA essentially irreversibly. It blocks messenger RNA cutting in fly embryo extract and human cell extract, and in worms it mimics loss of the let-7 microRNA. Fixed to a support, the same strand fishes out the Argonaute proteins ALG-1 and ALG-2 riding with let-7, naming parts of the silencing machinery.
europmc-pmc3527464:
Huntington's disease mouse models were too gentle, and Liliana B. Menalled leads a large team introducing a stronger one in 2012: the zQ175 knock-in mouse. Huntington's stems from an expanded CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene; longer repeats mean earlier illness. The new line arose when a colony's repeat expanded spontaneously to about 188 copies.

Knock-in mice carry the mutation in its proper genetic setting, mimicking patients best, but older lines showed late, mild signs. The zQ175 characterization covers behavior and molecular measures in depth, showing earlier and more robust phenotypes. The team presents the line as a better test bed for pathogenesis studies and for trialing candidate therapies before human studies.
europmc-pmc3583064:
Rolf Barth and colleagues reviewed boron neutron capture therapy in Radiation Oncology in 2012. The treatment loads tumor cells with boron-10, a harmless isotope, then bathes the area in slow neutrons. Boron atoms that catch a neutron split into particles that travel only about one cell's width, killing from inside while sparing neighbors. Interest has centered on aggressive brain gliomas, returned head and neck cancers, and melanoma.

Two boron drugs, BPA and BSH, carry the clinical record so far. The sticking points are plain. The drug must pile into tumor at around twenty micrograms per gram while clearing normal tissue. Neutron sources, meanwhile, have meant special nuclear reactors found in only a handful of countries. Machines that make neutrons with accelerators are under development, with the first Japanese unit expected for treatment in 2013. The review weighs trial results and what must improve before wider use.
europmc-pmc3594764:
José Soares and colleagues wrote a beginner's roadmap to diffusion tensor imaging in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2013. The method, a form of MRI, infers the direction of brain wiring from how water drifts along fibers, giving maps of network connections no other scan can show in living people. Its popularity among doctors and researchers has outrun shared know-how, and every stage of a study hides choices that can spoil the result.

Chapters walk the whole workflow in order: designing the scan, shaking out artifacts, checking data quality, rebuilding the fiber directions, and choosing how to display and measure them. Software options for each stage are compared, with their trade-offs stated plainly. The guide's aim is practical: help newcomers steer around the standard roadblocks rather than discover them in print. Experienced users get a checklist for auditing their own pipelines.
europmc-pmc3607064:
Anthony Gregory, Richard Titball, and Diane Williamson reviewed nanoparticle vaccine delivery in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2013. Vaccines have tamed many infections, yet some diseases resist because the candidate stirs the wrong kind of immune response, a weakness growing sharper as designs shift to purified sub-unit ingredients. Particles under a thousand nanometers, from virus-like shells and liposomes to plastic spheres, can protect the cargo and coach the response, acting as adjuvants in their own right.

Different particles enter the immune system's presenting cells by different doors, which can tilt the response toward the cell-killing arm needed against germs that hide inside cells. Small size also suits delivery through the nose or gut lining and into the skin. The review compares each system's strengths across target pathogens and judges where nano-delivery could crack vaccines that have stayed out of reach.
europmc-pmc3615964:
Claudia Simões-Pires and colleagues asked what sets one enzyme, HDAC6, apart as a drug target in Molecular Neurodegeneration in 2013. Drugs blocking histone deacetylases, enzymes that tighten how DNA is packed, protect nerve cells in animal models of degeneration. Most family members work on DNA packaging, but HDAC6 works in the cell body on transport machinery instead. Inhibiting it improves the axonal shipping that fails in Alzheimer, Parkinson, and Huntington diseases.

A puzzle runs through the review: boosting HDAC6 might instead help clear the protein clumps that mark those same diseases, so whether to block it or raise it is contested. Computer, dish, and animal results on HDAC6 and its relatives are gathered and compared, along with where each family member sits inside cells. The authors chart a path toward inhibitors selective enough to test the blocking strategy cleanly.
europmc-pmc3621664:
Leigh Johnson and colleagues estimated how long South Africans starting HIV treatment can expect to live, in PLoS Medicine in 2013. Life expectancy on antiretroviral therapy was well charted in rich countries but barely measured in poorer ones, where late starts and patients lost to follow-up cloud the records. Six South African treatment programs pooled data from 2001 to 2010, correcting for deaths hidden among patients who vanished from care.

Survival depended strongly on how healthy patients were when they started, and on age and sex, with women faring better than men. Patients starting early, before deep immune damage, could expect life spans approaching those of HIV-negative adults. Late starters lost many of those years. The authors warn that poor immune recovery and drug resistance still threaten the gains, and that services must start people earlier.
europmc-pmc3627464:
Ryan Donnelly and colleagues described swelling microneedle patches for drug delivery in Advanced Functional Materials in 2012. Microneedles pierce the skin's outer layer painlessly, but loading drug inside tiny needles caps the dose. Their arrays invert the design: the needles carry no drug at all. Made from crosslinked polymer, they drink in skin fluid on insertion and swell into gel channels. These link a drug reservoir patch on the surface to the blood-rich dermis below, and the channels cannot clog.

Because delivery is governed by the gel's crosslink density rather than the skin barrier, large molecules become deliverable, and an electric current can modulate the flow. Arrays can be made in varied sizes and needle shapes, sterilized, resist the hole closing that defeats hollow needles, and peel out whole, leaving nothing behind. The authors present the platform as a route past the dose ceiling that limited earlier microneedle designs.
europmc-pmc3629564:
Kathi Zarnack and colleagues uncovered a guard that keeps stray genetic text out of human messages in Cell in 2013. Scattered through our genes sit about 650,000 Alu elements, short repeats carrying hidden splice sites. If the splicing machinery mistook one for a real exon, the message would break. Something had to be policing them constantly.

Genome-wide binding maps showed the protein hnRNP C sitting on those danger sites, directly competing with a genuine splicing factor, U2AF65, for the same spots. Remove hnRNP C and Alu exons flood into messages, wrecking their function. Disease mutations in Alu elements turn out to work by weakening the guard's grip. The authors cast hnRNP C as a sentinel whose quiet competition protects the whole transcriptome, with lessons for both evolution and disease.
europmc-pmc3637064:
Gene lists that need a meaning check meet a new tool in a 2013 BMC Bioinformatics article by Edward Y. Chen, Christopher M. Tan, Yan Kou and five colleagues. Labs that profile genes or proteins end up with long lists of changed genes and no clear story. Enrichr, the tool they built, tests such a list against many ready-made gene sets drawn from past work.

Enrichr runs on the web and on phones, adds new gene-set banks, ranks matched terms in a fresh way, and shows results as live charts. It can also sit inside other tools that study gene lists. Put to work on nine cancer cell lines, it found a shared rise of a gene-silencing group and its mark on packing proteins across the lines, set against matched normal tissue.
europmc-pmc3655264:
A cell's cargo catcher changes shape to open for business, Jackson and eight colleagues show in a 2010 Cell study. The catcher, the AP2 complex, links the cell's clathrin web to membranes and to cargo proteins that need pulling inside. In its resting form, parts of the complex block both cargo grip sites. Using protein crystallography, a method that reads shape from crystal patterns, the team caught it open.

On opening, one grip part swings to a fresh face of the complex, freeing both cargo sites at once. A loose strap on the same part folds into a helix and locks back onto the body. All four membrane grip sites and both cargo sites end up in one flat plane. Bench tests show the membrane grip drives cargo binding.
europmc-pmc368164:
A parasite bacterium of fruit flies carries a genome overrun by mobile DNA, Wu and a large team report in a 2004 PLoS Biology study. The bacterium, Wolbachia pipientis strain wMel, lives inside the cells of its fly host and passes through eggs. Kin strains range from reproductive parasites to helpful partners across many invertebrates. The team read the full genome, about 1.27 million letters, and compared it with other inside-cell bacteria.

For a streamlined genome, mobile DNA is strikingly plentiful, a sign selection weans it out only weakly, perhaps through repeated population bottlenecks. Unlike its kin Rickettsia, the bacterium keeps full sugar-burning and purine-making paths, making up for its inability to steal host energy. No signs of recent gene swapping with the fly were found.
europmc-pmc3794764:
Hye Jin Jin and nine co-authors reported a comparison study in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2013. They compared mesenchymal stem cells from three human sources: bone marrow, fat tissue, and umbilical cord blood. All three are candidates for cell therapy, but bone marrow and fat require invasive harvesting and donor age limits them.

The sources matched on surface markers, immune calming, and the ability to form bone, fat, and cartilage. Cord blood cells grew and cloned fastest and showed much lower levels of aging markers p53, p21, and p16. In co-culture with inflamed rat lung macrophages, cord blood cells cut inflammatory cytokines, an effect traced in part to a secreted factor, angiopoietin-1. The authors present cord blood cells as a biologically advantaged source for therapy.
europmc-pmc3904164:
Rebecca M. Leech, Sarah A. McNaughton, and Anna Timperio review behavior clustering in youth in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity, with the record dated 2014. Diet, movement, and sitting time each sway child obesity risk. Kids rarely carry just one bad habit, so studies hunt for habit bundles.

The team kept studies that used data-driven grouping methods on children and teens. Most were one-time snapshots of older children. A mixed bundle, pairing some activity with much sitting, showed up most often. Fully healthy and fully unhealthy bundles appeared too, and bundles tied to social background and weight in varied ways. The patchwork picture argues for programs that shift whole bundles, not single habits.
europmc-pmc3920964:
P. Nigro, G. Pompilio, and M. C. Capogrossi review cyclophilin A in Cell Death and Disease in 2013, presenting a common cell protein as a player in many human diseases. Cyclophilin A helps other proteins fold and move through the cell. Though long treated as an inside-only protein, it can also be released by cells when inflammation strikes, and there it acts as a signal.

High levels of the protein track with poor outcomes in inflammatory disease, and it is often overproduced in cancer, where it supports tumor change and spread. The review covers its roles in heart and vessel disease, viral infection and replication, brain degeneration, rheumatoid arthritis, sepsis, asthma, gum disease, and aging. Blocking it is raised as a possible shared drug strategy.
europmc-pmc3937164:
Alpha A. Fowler and colleagues run a first safety trial of intravenous vitamin C in severe sepsis, in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2014. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, often ends in organ failure, and animal work suggested infused ascorbic acid could calm the inflammation and clotting problems behind it. Twenty-four patients in a medical intensive care unit were randomized to a low dose, a high dose, or a placebo infusion, given every six hours for four days.

Blood vitamin C levels, low at entry, rose fast with treatment. No safety events were linked to the infusions. Organ failure scores fell promptly in the vitamin C groups but not on placebo, and two inflammation markers dropped, while a marker of vessel injury stayed flat instead of rising. The authors call the treatment safe here and worth larger trials.
europmc-pmc3938664:
Dylan P. Smith and Kabir G. Peay ask a budget question for DNA-based ecology. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Is it better to repeat the DNA copying step? Or is it better to sequence each sample more deeply? They worked with soil fungi from pine forests in North America. Three soil samples were sequenced on two platforms. The team varied how many copy rounds were pooled each time.

Pooling more copy rounds changed little. Measures of diversity within and between samples stayed put. Deeper sequencing helped a lot. It cut the false gaps seen when one sample was read twice. The newer platform also found far more species. Diversity patterns from the two platforms still agreed well. The authors advise labs to spend on depth, not on copy repeats.
europmc-pmc3947164:
James E. Ussher and colleagues find which T cells answer a two-signal alarm. Their paper appeared in the European Journal of Immunology in 2014. The signals are IL-12 and IL-18. Both are released during infection. Together they can make immune cells release interferon-gamma. They do this without the usual antigen trigger. The responding cells form a group with very high CD161 levels. MAIT cells dominate that group in adult blood. MAIT cells patrol tissues such as the gut and liver.

Both MAIT cells and their non-MAIT neighbors responded to the pair. So the trigger is the CD161-high state, not MAIT identity alone. Bacteria set off the same response by an indirect route. They cause IL-12 and IL-18 release first. The findings widen the likely role of MAIT cells. Viral infection and wider inflammation may call on them too.
europmc-pmc3962364:
Martin J. Sergeant and colleagues take a deep census of the microbes in the chicken's ceca in PLoS ONE in 2014. Chickens are a major world protein source, and how well they turn feed into growth depends heavily on gut microbes, above all in the paired ceca where plant fiber ferments. The team profiled twenty cecal samples by a marker gene and sequenced one sample's whole community DNA in depth.

They recovered 699 microbe types, over half apparently new to science, and more than 648,000 gene tags, most from unknown species, sortable into over two dozen draft genomes, including two known pathogens. The genes were rich in enzymes for breaking down plant sugars, organized into coordinated uptake systems, and in pathways that ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids, some with novel features.
europmc-pmc3962464:
Harold Kwok, Kyle Briggs, and Vincent Tabard-Cossa describe a simple way to make a nanopore. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. A nanopore is a hole a few atoms wide in a thin film. DNA threaded through it can be read base by base. Drilling such holes used to need costly beam tools. Few labs own those tools. This method needs only a voltage supply and a current meter. It works with the film already in liquid.

The user raises the voltage across the film. The electric field grows until the film breaks at one weak spot. Watching the leak current shows when to stop. Pore size can be set with sub-nanometer care. The team made single pores down to two nanometers wide. The pores gave clean signals from passing DNA. The authors see a path to cheap mass production.
europmc-pmc3999464:
V. V. Makarov and six co-authors review plant-based ways to make metal nanoparticles, in Acta Naturae in 2014. Such tiny metal particles find wide use across industry. The usual chemical and physical routes to make them can cost a lot and can harm the environment.

Plant extracts offer a cheaper, safer route. Natural compounds in plants can turn dissolved metal salts into solid particles, a step called bioreduction. The review sorts out what shapes the size, form, and yield of the particles, from extract strength to heat and acidity. It gives weight to the plant molecules that do the reducing work. Added templates such as peptides, proteins, and virus parts can guide particle form in the extracts. Food industry plant waste could serve as cheap raw stock, cutting cost to little more than the metal salts alone.
europmc-pmc4048464:
Neil P. Blackledge and a large team overturn the assumed order of two gene-silencing complexes, in Cell in 2014. Polycomb complexes switch off genes that must stay off for body plans and cell identity. Textbooks held that one complex, PRC2, arrives first and lays a mark that calls in PRC1.

Using a fresh targeting test in mouse stem cells, the team saw the reverse. A variant form of PRC1 placed its own mark on the packaging proteins of DNA. That mark then recruited PRC2, which laid its silencing mark and sealed a repressed domain. Only variant PRC1 complexes could start the chain. A targeting protein steers the key variant to CpG islands, the usual polycomb landing pads. Mice lacking that steering develop poorly. The finding rewrites the entry logic of a system often broken in cancer.
europmc-pmc4051964:
Tim P. Morris, Ian R. White, and Patrick Royston tune two shortcut methods for filling gaps in data, in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. Multiple imputation guesses missing values from a model. When the model is off, the guesses can mislead. Two fixes borrow from real records instead: one takes a whole observed value from a similar donor case, the other takes only the donor's leftover error.

The team reviewed the variants of both methods and tested them in simulations, first with a correct model and then with a wrong one. One warning stands out: never draw from a single donor, a default in some software. A pool of about ten donors behaved far better.  The shortcuts help when the model is slightly wrong. Nothing replaces building it with care.
europmc-pmc4053864:
Carola Ingrid Weidner and eleven colleagues show that blood aging can be read from just three DNA sites, in Genome Biology in 2014. Methylation at certain genome sites shifts steadily with age. A small, cheap test of that shift could serve forensics and studies of biological aging.

The team first sifted methylation profiles down to about a hundred age-linked sites. Most of those changes reversed in reprogrammed stem cells, showing they mark age, not fixed identity. Three sites, in three named genes, were then tested by a targeted method in over a hundred and fifty blood samples. Age estimates from the trio landed within about five years of true age on average, beating telomere length as a clock. Patients with bone marrow failure read as older than their years, matching their worn cell pools.
europmc-pmc4105164:
Hui Huang, Chao Shi, Yuan Liu, Shu-Yan Mao, and Li-Zhi Gao sequenced the chloroplast genomes of thirteen Camellia species, the genus of tea and ornamental camellias. Their study appeared in BMC Evolutionary Biology in 2014. Frequent hybridising and genome doubling make Camellia one of the hardest plant groups to classify.

Eight genomes were completed and five drafted using high-throughput sequencing, mixing fresh assembly with reference guidance. All showed the typical circular form with a conserved structure and gene order. Comparing five complete genomes exposed differences in repeats, insertions, and single changes. Fifteen stretches varied enough to serve as molecular markers for identifying species and tracing relationships. Wider family-tree analysis supported one disputed placement of a species within the tea section.
europmc-pmc4141964:
Ali Eatemadi, Sang Woo Joo, and colleagues reviewed carbon nanotubes, hollow cylinders of carbon a few atoms wide. Their review appeared in Nanoscale Research Letters in 2014. New forms of carbon nanostructure have drawn wide interest, and nanotubes hold particular promise for medicine, gene delivery, and drug delivery.

The authors cover how nanotubes are made, purified, and chemically altered, including filling, doping, and surface treatment. Handling and characterising single tubes is now possible. Traits such as structure, surface charge, size spread, and purity strongly affect how reactive a sample is. Their strength and flexibility also suit them to organising other nanoscale structures. The review weighs medical uses against open questions, including toxicity and safe handling.
europmc-pmc4192464:
Andrew W. Foster, Deenah Osman, and Nigel J. Robinson explained how proteins end up holding the right metal in the Journal of Biological Chemistry in 2014. About a third of enzymes need a metal atom to work, yet most proteins grab metals by a fixed pecking order that does not match what they need. Left alone, many would seize the wrong metal and fail.

Cells solve the puzzle in layers. Delivery proteins hand metals to about 30 percent of these enzymes, and a quarter get ready-made metal clusters. The rest compete from pools the cell keeps carefully rationed, holding scarce metals at far lower free levels than common ones. Zinc, for instance, is kept at least a million-fold below magnesium. Sensors and buffers tune the pools so each protein's odds favour the metal it truly needs.
europmc-pmc4222664:
Seyed-Mahdi Khaligh-Razavi and Nikolaus Kriegeskorte tested computer vision models against the brain in PLoS Computational Biology in 2014. The inferior temporal cortex is where primates recognize objects, and its activity patterns cluster objects by kind. Many computer models claim to mimic that area, with little direct comparison.

The team compared a shelf of models, from classic neuroscience designs to a deep neural network, against brain data from human scans and monkey cell recordings for the same images. Models that categorized images better also matched the brain's pattern geometry better. Unsupervised models, though, missed the brain's strong clustering by category. The deep network, trained with supervision on over a million labelled images, came closest to the brain while still falling short, hinting that category training shapes brain-like representations.
europmc-pmc4240164:
Reuben Saba, Debra L. Sorensen, and Stephanie A. Booth reviewed a brake pedal of the immune system in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. MicroRNA-146a is a tiny RNA that rises sharply when cells meet bacterial endotoxin. Rather than attacking germs itself, it reins in the alarm signals that endotoxin sets off.

Its best-known targets are two relay proteins, IRAK1 and TRAF6, in the Toll-like receptor pathway; trimming them keeps inflammation from overshooting and helps produce endotoxin tolerance when exposure lingers. The same small RNA shapes blood cell development, adaptive immunity, and some cancers. When it is mis-set, autoimmune disease can follow. The review weighs microRNA-146a as both a marker and a possible drug lever in inflammatory disorders.
europmc-pmc4256164:
Richard M. Dodds, Rachel Cooper, and ten co-authors charted grip strength across the British life course in PLoS ONE in 2014. Handgrip strength predicts disability and death in old age, but doctors lacked one chart showing normal values from childhood to old age, measured the same way.

Pooling twelve population studies gave 60,803 measurements from 49,964 people aged 4 to 90. Strength rose to a peak in early adulthood, held through midlife, then declined. Men's median peak reached 51 kilograms at ages 29 to 39, against 31 kilograms for women at 26 to 42. Weak grip, defined against the peak, reached 23 percent of men and 27 percent of women by age 80. The curves were steady across grip devices and test positions.
europmc-pmc4335664:
Panagiotis F Christopoulos, Pavlos Msaouel, and Michael Koutsilieris review the insulin-like growth factor system and its place in breast cancer. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer in 2015. IGF-1 is a strong growth signal for breast tissue, and when it locks onto its receptor it sets off chains that push cells to divide and resist death.

Several major cancer pathways meet at this system, which helps explain its weight in how breast tumors start, grow, and spread. The review covers how the signal is regulated, including the binding proteins that hold it in check, and its cross talk with estrogen signaling. It closes on why blocking the receptor has proved harder in trials than the biology first promised.
europmc-pmc4346664:
Oliver Baumann and eleven co-authors gather expert consensus on the cerebellum's role in perception. Their paper appeared in Cerebellum in 2015. The cerebellum, a dense structure at the back of the brain, was long treated as a pure movement controller, yet thirty years of evidence tie it to sensing as well.

Contributions span the structure's wiring, its evolution, and its part in vision, hearing, body motion sense, pain, timing, and predicting what a sense signal will do next. No single theory yet covers all the findings, and the authors mark where views agree and where they split. The paper is a reference point for a shift in how the cerebellum is understood.
europmc-pmc4383964:
Faviel González-Galarza and co-authors updated the Allele Frequency Net Database in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Launched 12 years earlier, the database stores how often immune gene variants occur in populations worldwide. Its most used section covers HLA tissue types, KIR immune receptors, related MIC genes, and cytokine variants. By then it held more than 1,400 populations drawn from over 10 million healthy people, serving transplant, immunogenetics, drug-response, and anthropology research.

New sections record how often HLA epitopes, the exact fragments immune cells recognize, occur in populations. Another gathers studies linking HLA types to adverse drug reactions. A third covers links between KIR variants and infectious and autoimmune diseases. Stricter quality criteria for incoming data were also introduced. Population frequencies turn single-patient results into sound clinical and evolutionary judgments.
europmc-pmc4392164:
Bruno Vergès reviewed the disordered blood lipids of type 2 diabetes in Diabetologia in 2015, asking where understanding stands. Heart and vessel disease kills most people with type 2 diabetes, whose risk runs two to four times that of others. Their lipid pattern is a major reason. It goes beyond amounts: triglycerides are high and protective HDL cholesterol low, but particle quality and handling are also off, making the whole profile more artery-clogging.

Large triglyceride-rich particles are overproduced and cleared slowly, small dense LDL particles multiply, and HDL is broken down faster. Even with normal LDL cholesterol levels, LDL particles linger longer than they should. Insulin resistance and relative insulin lack likely drive much of this, since insulin steers lipid handling. Signals from fat tissue add further influence. The review maps each defect to its mechanism.
europmc-pmc4396364:
Matthew Hong and a team of co-authors traced how prostate cancer spreads, clone by clone, in Nature Communications in 2015. Primary prostate tumors hold many subclones, but how that mix changes during spread and treatment was poorly known. The team sequenced whole genomes and deeply re-read key regions in primary and metastatic tumors collected over time from four men with lethal disease, plus end-stage blood samples.

One case showed spread back into the surgical bed, causing local return; another showed metastases seeding each other, with subclone mixes reshaped by therapy. Blood carried DNA from both primary and metastatic clones years after the prostate was removed. Mutations in the TP53 gene were enriched in spread, and in 19 more patients, gaining TP53 mutations tracked with clones gaining metastatic power. Blood tests might catch that shift.
europmc-pmc4406164:
Per Nilsen sorted the theories, models, and frameworks of implementation science, in Implementation Science in 2015, in a solo article. Implementation science studies how research becomes practice, and it increasingly leans on theory to explain why putting evidence to work succeeds or fails. Its vocabulary is muddled, though: similar labels hide different jobs. Nilsen proposes a taxonomy of five categories, grouped by three aims, to help researchers pick the right tool and talk across fields.

Process models describe or guide the steps of translation. Determinant frameworks, classic theories, and implementation theories explain what drives outcomes. Evaluation frameworks judge how an implementation went. Nilsen warns that most determinant frameworks name barriers too generically to guide action. Clear categories, he argues, are a precondition for cumulative progress in a young field.
europmc-pmc4470864:
Anna Stincone and a team of co-authors reviewed the pentose phosphate pathway in Biological Reviews in 2015, calling their article the return of metabolism. The pathway is a branch of sugar processing found in nearly all cells. It keeps carbon balance, supplies building blocks for DNA and amino acids, produces reducing power for growth, and helps cells withstand oxidative stress.

One branch burns sugar to make NADPH, a reducing agent vital when cells grow fast, age, or face stress, and exploited by cancer cells in the Warburg effect. The other branch rearranges sugar fragments to make ribose for nucleic acids and precursors for amino acids, and runs almost everywhere. Long treated as background housekeeping, the pathway, the authors argue, sits at the center of how cells grow and cope, and its study has revived with new tools and cancer interest.
europmc-pmc4472464:
Phillip Low and a large team of co-authors followed the course of multiple system atrophy in The Lancet Neurology in 2015. Theirs was the first forward-looking study of the disease in North America. Multiple system atrophy is a rare, fatal brain disorder combining parkinson-like movement problems or balance failure with failure of automatic body functions such as blood pressure control.

Patients with probable disease were recruited at centers across the continent and checked every six months for up to five years with symptom, movement, and autonomic scales. Survival from first symptoms ran to roughly a decade at the median. The study compared the parkinsonian and cerebellar forms and tested which features, including severity of autonomic failure, predict decline and death. Such a natural history baseline is essential for judging future treatments, since trials need to know how fast untreated patients worsen.
europmc-pmc4490364:
Xing Huang and eleven co-authors built a flat copper polymer with record electrical conductivity in Nature Communications in 2015. Two-dimensional organic materials promise unusual electronic properties, but most conduct poorly. Their material, Cu-BHT, links copper atoms with a sulfur-rich ring molecule, benzenehexathiol, into sheets with a regular lattice, grown as a thin film where two liquids meet.
