Measurements with a four-probe method gave the highest conductivity then reported for a coordination polymer, far above typical organic conductors. Under an electric field the film carried both positive and negative charge carriers well, a rare ambipolar behavior, with high mobilities for each. Quantum simulations supported the proposed sheet structure. The authors present such conjugated coordination polymers as a new platform for flexible electronics and for studying charge transport in two dimensions.
europmc-pmc4579264:
Albert Hofman leads a twelve-author team reporting the state of the Rotterdam Study, a long-running Dutch health cohort, in the European Journal of Epidemiology. Running since 1990 in the city of Rotterdam, the study follows aging residents to find the causes of diseases that cluster late in life. Its scope spans heart, hormone, liver, brain, eye, mental, skin, ear, joint, and lung disease.

As of 2008 the cohort held 14,926 people aged 45 and over, and its findings had filled over 1,200 articles and reports. The update restates why the study exists, how participants are examined, and what has been found so far, then sets objectives and methods for the next phase, whose title looks toward 2016. It serves as the reference design paper for the cohort.
europmc-pmc4619264:
A team led by Katelyn Godin published a 2015 methods paper on searching grey literature systematically. Grey literature covers reports and guidelines outside journals, which are hard to search in an orderly way. Their test case gathered Canadian guidelines for school breakfast programs. The work appeared in Systematic Reviews.

The team combined four routes: grey literature databases, tailored Google searches, targeted websites, and asking experts. Screening used summaries or contents pages where abstracts were missing. The four routes produced 302 items to screen, and the authors judge the plan manageable, thorough, and easy to follow. Reviewers who need policy documents can adopt this search plan instead of improvising, which makes later updates and checks possible.
europmc-pmc4623764:
Patrick M. Bossuyt and colleagues, with the STARD Group, published the 2015 update of the STARD reporting list for diagnostic accuracy studies. Such studies judge how well a test finds disease. Poor reporting wastes research money because readers cannot appraise or repeat the work. The update appeared in BMJ.

STARD 2015 lists thirty essential items that every report of a diagnostic accuracy study should include. The revision folds in newer evidence about bias and variation in test performance. It is designed to be easier to use than the earlier version. Journals and authors who follow the list should produce clearer, more complete reports, which helps clinicians and policy makers judge whether a test is ready for practice.
europmc-pmc4662664:
V. Vijaya Padma wrote a solo 2015 overview of targeted cancer therapy. Cancer grows from a mix of genes, life habits, and strain from the world around us. Standard drug care can work, but it harms healthy cells too and tumours learn to resist it.

Targeted care aims drugs at cancer cells alone, sparing the rest of the body. The review covers lab-made antibodies, drugs that wake up only at the tumour, small drugs that block key proteins, and tiny fat balls that carry antibodies to their mark. It also notes ways to beat resistance, such as new drug forms and add-on drugs. Padma argues that this aim is why targeted care is gaining ground over broad drug care.
europmc-pmc4682164:
Russell A. Poldrack, Timothy O. Laumann, Oluwasanmi Koyejo, and a large team reported the MyConnectome project in Nature Communications in 2015. Psychiatric illness swings over weeks and months, yet almost nothing was known about how a healthy brain changes over that span. So one healthy volunteer, Poldrack himself, was measured in depth for eighteen months. The project paired brain scans with tests of mood, health, gene activity, and blood chemistry.

The data and tools were posted openly, with a web browser for exploring results. Brain connection patterns shifted across days and months, and some shifts tracked gene activity and chemical levels in the blood. The authors present the project as a test bed for studying brain and body together over time. They argue that this kind of dense tracking is what personal medicine for brain disorders will need.
europmc-pmc4735864:
Charles D. Cox, Chilman Bae, Lynn Ziegler, and seven colleagues tested how the touch channel PIEZO1 senses force, in Nature Communications in 2016. Force-sensitive channels might be pulled open by tethers to the cell skeleton, or pushed open directly by tension in the membrane itself, and telling these apart is hard inside a living cell. The team grew membrane blebs, bubbles of membrane largely stripped of skeleton, and tested the channel there.

A bacterial channel with a known threshold calibrated the tension scale, and it behaved in blebs exactly as in pure membranes. PIEZO1 opened under membrane tension in the blebs, at lower pressures than in intact cells, showing the skeleton normally shields it. The evidence says PIEzo1 reads force straight from the lipid bilayer. That settles the channel's basic mechanism and reframes its roles in blood, vessels, and touch.
europmc-pmc4756464:
Grainne O'Donoghue leads ten authors in a BMC Public Health review from 2016 on why adults sit so much. Long sitting harms heart and metabolic health even in people who exercise. To cut sitting, health planners first need to know what drives it.

The team searched five databases for studies of adults of working age and kept 74 that fit. Most tracked self-reported screen time or total sitting. Age, activity level, body weight, income level, and mood each tracked with sitting time. Having children meant less total sitting, while marriage or living with a partner meant more screen leisure. Green space nearby, safe streets, and weather also mattered. Most studies were snapshots, so cause and effect stay open.
europmc-pmc4762164:
Rachel Rosenthal and four co-authors present a software method in Genome Biology in 2016 for reading the mutational history of one tumor at a time. Each process that damages DNA, from smoke to faulty repair, leaves a pattern of changes called a signature. Until now, pulling signatures out took large groups of tumors, which left single patients out of reach.

Their tool, deconstructSigs, fits a single tumor's mutation list against the known signature set and reports the mix. Applied to throat and gullet cancers, it flagged tumors with broken DNA repair and showed the two cancer types carry distinct, shifting mixes over time. The authors argue that reading one tumor's mix could steer care, since repair faults hint at which drugs may work.
europmc-pmc4763064:
Nasser Sewelam, Kemal Kazan, and Peer M. Schenk review stress signaling in plants in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2016. Plants cannot flee drought, salt, heat, or attack, so they rely on inner alarm networks to react. Those networks are dense and cross-wired, which makes them hard to map branch by branch.

The review takes the meeting points as the way in. Bursts of reactive oxygen species, reactive forms of oxygen made under strain, appear in nearly every stress reply and act as a shared hub. The authors trace how this hub talks with calcium signals, hormone lines, protein switches, and gene switches. Grasping that hub, they argue, could guide crops that hold yield as field conditions grow harsher.
europmc-pmc4792964:
Takehito Ono and six co-authors report an immune assist for bone repair in Nature Communications in 2016. Broken bone heals through swelling, a bridging callus, and slow reshaping, and immune cells crowd the break from the first hours. Which of them help, and how, was partly open.

The team found that a T cell type called gamma delta settles at breaks and releases IL-17A, a signal better known for driving swelling diseases. Mice without IL-17A healed poorly because their bone-building ran weak. The signal pushed early bone stem cells to multiply and mature into builders. The finding adds a repair role for these T cells and names a signal that fracture care might one day borrow.
europmc-pmc4815064:
Ashley E. Thompson and five co-authors study who seeks medical care in Canada, in BMC Family Practice in 2016. The data come from a 2013 survey of over seven thousand patients across ten provinces, part of an international primary care study. The team built a care-seeking score over eleven conditions and asked which patient traits predict using it.

Women reported seeking care more than men, for body and mind complaints alike, and everyone sought less for mental health than for physical trouble. For mental health visits, age, trust in the doctor, prevention habits, and chronic illness each predicted seeking in both sexes. The patterns for physical complaints were weaker. The authors say the findings can help clinics spot who stays away and design outreach to draw them in.
europmc-pmc4816164:
F. Gao and eight co-authors review mesenchymal stem cells as immune calmers in Cell Death & Disease in 2016. These stem cells, drawn from marrow, fat, and cord tissue, can mute an overactive immune system: they stall attacking T cells, soften inflammation signals, and coax regulatory cells up. That talent has made them candidates for graft-versus-host disease, lupus, and other immune disorders.

The review sums the state of the field: the signals the cells release, the immune cell types they touch, and the trial record so far. It also faces the gaps. Cell batches vary by source and handling, dosing is unsettled, and manufacturing standards are still forming. The authors set out what must be standardized before these cells can move from promising trials to routine therapy.
europmc-pmc4817264:
Ming-liang Chen leads nine authors in mBio in 2016 testing whether a grape compound fights artery disease through gut microbes. Resveratrol, found in grape skins, protects arteries in animal studies by unknown means. The suspect on the other side is TMAO, a blood chemical made when gut microbes process certain foods, which promotes artery clogging.

In mice prone to artery disease, resveratrol blunted the clogging that TMAO feeding caused. It reshaped the gut mix, cutting the microbes' output of TMAO's raw material and raising two helpful genera. That shift also sped bile acid exit from the body and fresh bile making in the liver. Wiping out gut microbes with antibiotics erased every benefit. The work ties the compound's protection firmly to the gut community it cultivates.
europmc-pmc4850464:
Jingyu Zhang, Xiao-Jun Tian, and Jianhua Xing reviewed three signal pathways that drive a cell change called EMT, in the Journal of Clinical Medicine in 2016. In EMT, sheet-like epithelial cells loosen and gain the roaming traits of mesenchymal cells. The switch aids embryo growth and wound repair, and cancers hijack it to spread. Three pathways, named TGF-beta, SHH, and WNT, each push the switch.

The pathways talk to each other and meet at shared switch proteins such as SNAIL1, which start and hold the change. The review maps those links as a network. It also surveys drugs in development that aim at each pathway, a guide for blocking cancer spread at its signaling roots.
europmc-pmc4879264:
Eri H. Kobayashi and co-authors showed in Nature Communications in 2016 how Nrf2, a stress defense switch, also mutes inflammatory gene reading in macrophages. Nrf2 guards cells against chemical and oxidative harm and was known to calm inflammation, by unknown steps. In macrophages hit with a bacterial trigger, Nrf2 blocked the switch-on of two key inflammatory signal genes, IL-6 and IL-1 beta.

Mapping showed Nrf2 parked near those genes and stopped the gene-reading machine from being recruited. The block did not need Nrf2's usual DNA docking motif, a fresh mechanism. Stress defense and inflammation control thus share one hand on the gene switch, which may guide drugs for chronic inflammation.
europmc-pmc4906164:
Sarah Holliday and co-authors built a high-performing plastic solar cell in 2016 around a new non-fullerene acceptor. Organic solar cells promise cheap, light, green power. Top cells paired pricey low-bandgap donors with fullerene acceptors, both with stability and cost flaws. Their acceptor was designed to partner P3HT, a donor prized for scale-up and toughness.

The pair's matched light and shape traits gave 6.4 percent efficiency, the best yet reported for fullerene-free P3HT cells. Air stability also jumped against rival high-efficiency cells. A mass-friendly donor finally has a worthy partner, which moves plastic solar closer to roofs and chargers made by printing presses rather than clean rooms.
europmc-pmc4931664:
Mi Hee Park and Jin Tae Hong review NF-kappaB, a gene switch at the heart of inflammation and cancer. Their review appeared in Cells in 2016. NF-kappaB is a transcription factor, a protein that turns genes on. It steers immune responses, inflammation, cell growth, and cell survival. When it stays on at the wrong time, it feeds autoimmune disease, chronic inflammation, and tumors.

The review maps the factor's two main signaling routes and its five building blocks. It lists diseases tied to faulty activation, from rheumatoid arthritis and atherosclerosis to bowel disease, multiple sclerosis, and cancers. Because the switch touches so many genes, blocking it looks like a broad treatment strategy. The authors survey drug approaches aimed at the pathway. They also note the risk that comes with muting a switch healthy cells need.
europmc-pmc5007264:
Natalia Davidenko and six co-authors test how cells stick to collagen and gelatin in the Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Medicine in 2016. Both proteins are used to build medical materials, from thin coatings to sponge-like scaffolds. The team varied the mix, a hardening treatment, and the flat versus three-dimensional form, then watched which cell grip proteins did the holding.

Cell lines with known grip proteins showed that adding gelatin and hardening the mix changed which binding motifs were free to use. The hardening step wiped out true grip-based sticking on both flat and three-dimensional forms. Yet the sponge form still trapped cells in its pores, which could be misread as sticking. Cell spreading confirmed that real grip-driven contact drives later cell activity. The study gives material makers a simple way to split the effects of chemistry, shape, and form.
europmc-pmc5012864:
Kelly D. Sullivan and eleven co-authors report in eLife in 2016 that an extra copy of chromosome 21 steadily switches on the interferon response. Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome, but the chain of events below the extra chromosome was unclear. Interferons are alarm signals of the immune system. The team compared gene activity in cells from people with and without the trisomy.

Across skin cells, blood cell lines, and circulating immune cells, the interferon program stood out as switched on everywhere. Genes answering interferon rose, while genes for building proteins fell. A gene-silencing screen showed that two interferon-driven enzymes held back the growth of trisomy cells, and a drug blocking them restored growth. Since chromosome 21 carries four interferon receptor genes, extra dosage likely drives the effect, and calming it might ease some features of Down syndrome.
europmc-pmc5028964:
Josephine Kang, Sandra Demaria, and Silvia Formenti review trials pairing immunotherapy with radiotherapy in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer in 2016. Radiation was long used only to kill tumor cells where it is aimed. Newer evidence shows it can also wake the immune system, sometimes shrinking tumors far outside the beam, a pattern called the abscopal effect.

The review explains why the pairing might work: radiation can turn a treated tumor into a kind of vaccine, exposing it to immune attack. It then surveys trial results and the many studies still running, which combine radiation with checkpoint drugs and other immune agents. Open questions include the best order of the two treatments, the right radiation dose, and how to judge success. Marker tests that predict who will respond are a further need the authors highlight.
europmc-pmc5070064:
D. S. Quintana, G. A. Alvares, and J. A. J. Heathers propose reporting guidelines for heart rate variability research in psychiatry, in Translational Psychiatry. Studies of HRV, the beat-to-beat wobble set by the autonomic nervous system, have multiplied in psychiatry, where reduced variability marks several disorders. Yet methods are reported so unevenly that results are hard to judge, repeat, or combine.

Their GRAPH checklist covers four domains: how participants were selected, how the intervals between heartbeats were collected, how the data were prepared, and how variability was calculated. Each domain gets a rationale for why standard reporting matters. The authors are plain that the checklist judges communication, not study quality: its aim is clear reporting so findings can be interpreted, reproduced, and pooled in meta-analyses. Adopted widely, they argue, it could help HRV mature into a usable psychiatric biomarker.
europmc-pmc5082564:
Courtenay Frazier Norbury and seven co-authors measure language disorder at school entry in a population study, in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry in 2016. Diagnosis once required normal nonverbal IQ, which kept many children from services; DSM-5 dropped that rule. The team screened 7,267 children aged four to five across Surrey reception classrooms and assessed a subsample in depth, to see what the wider rule does to prevalence and presentation.

They estimate language disorder in 9.92 percent of children, about 7.58 percent unexplained and 2.34 percent tied to intellectual disability or a known medical condition. Affected children showed more social, emotional, and behaviour problems, and 88 percent fell behind expected school progress. Crucially, children with low-average nonverbal scores looked no different from those with average scores in severity or school outcome. The authors back the DSM-5 change and note that the old ICD-10 rules would count at least seven times fewer children.
europmc-pmc5183164:
R. McCarrison reported on endemic cretinism in the Chitral and Gilgit valleys in The Indian Medical Gazette in December 1908, in a paper read to the Royal Society of Medicine. McCarrison, agency surgeon in Gilgit, based the study on 203 cases. They made up the whole cretinous population of the Gilgit and Mastuj districts. He gathered them by house-to-house checks of nearly every goitrous village, across some 500 miles of Himalayan country.

He organizes the study around the link between cretinism and goitre, in the child, in the mother, and in the district at large. Where goitre is only beginning, he notes, no cretinism appears. He could not trace a single case where a child's own goitre gave rise to cretinism. That points suspicion toward the mother's condition. He warns that his conclusions apply to these races and conditions and must be adjusted elsewhere.
europmc-pmc5193064:
Shishira Bharadwaj and seven co-authors ask how malnutrition should actually be diagnosed. The condition raises illness, death, and hospital costs, yet it lacks a single agreed definition. Reported prevalence runs from 30 to 50 percent of patients, and as high as 85 percent in long-term care. Doctors have long leaned on serum proteins such as albumin and prealbumin. The review finds those markers unreliable on their own, because inflammation distorts them.

The authors give the central role to a nutrition-focused physical examination. Lab values can support that examination but cannot replace it. They estimate the malnutrition tied to eight major diseases costs about 157 billion dollars, and malnourished patients stay in hospital about 11 days longer. Future work, they argue, should hunt for blood biomarkers that inflammation does not disturb.
europmc-pmc5226664:
Waqas Nasir Chaudhry and six colleagues tested phages and antibiotics together against Pseudomonas biofilms in PLoS ONE in 2017. Bacteria living in biofilms, slimy surface communities, resist both antibiotics and bacteria-killing viruses called phages when each is used alone. Since the two kill in very different ways, the team asked whether combining them works better, and whether the order of treatment matters.

Biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa were treated with two phages and antibiotics from five classes, alone and in combination. Single treatments usually killed modestly, but some pairs cut bacterial numbers far below the best single agent, sometimes below what independent action would predict, a true synergy. Order mattered strongly in some cases, with phages first and drugs second killing most. Combinations also worked well on biofilms grown over cultured skin-like cells and held down the rise of antibiotic-resistant minorities.
europmc-pmc5236064:
Vikram Patel and many colleagues tested the Healthy Activity Program for severe depression in The Lancet in 2017. Structured talking treatments are a first-line care for depression, yet few people worldwide can get them in routine primary care. The program trains lay counsellors, people without formal mental health qualifications, to deliver a brief form of behavioral therapy.

The trial enrolled 495 adults with moderately severe to severe depression at ten primary health centres in Goa, India. It split them between enhanced usual care alone and the same care plus the program. At three months, the program group had clearly lower symptom scores and a 64 percent remission rate against 39 percent with usual care alone. Disability, days off work, and suicidal thoughts also improved, and the added cost per healthy year gained suggested good value in that setting. Serious harms were rare and similar in both groups.
europmc-pmc5314464:
Pramudita R. Prasetyanti and Jan Paul Medema reviewed tumor diversity in Molecular Cancer in 2017. No two cells in a tumor are quite alike. They differ in growth rate, surface marks, gene flaws, and response to drugs. That mix helps tumors grow back after treatment. Cancer stem cells, rare cells that can renew the tumor, are one source of the mix.

The review adds a twist: the stem-like state is not fixed. A tumor cell can gain stem traits through gene changes or through signals from the tissue around it. So the pool of stem-like cells shifts over time. The authors sort the forces that build this shifting mix, from gene and mark changes to cues from nearby support cells. They close with what this means for therapy: drugs must face a moving target, not a fixed cell type.
europmc-pmc5332864:
Karin Roelofs reviewed the freezing response to threat in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2017. When danger grows, animals switch between set defense modes. Freezing halts motion and slows the heart under calm-branch control. Fight or flight speeds the heart under the alarm branch. Human freezing had been little studied, despite its weight for stress coping.

Rat work ties freezing to paths from the amygdala, the brain's alarm hub, down to a brainstem zone. Brain scans in people point to the same zones at work. Shifting out of freeze into action leans on links between the front brain and the amygdala. Roelofs argues freezing is no passive state. It is a brake on a primed motor system that sharpens sensing and readies action. Grasping it may help treat stress illnesses marked by stiff responses.
europmc-pmc5337964:
Norbert Pardi and co-authors delivered an antibody by mRNA in mice, in Nature Communications in 2017. Antibody drugs are a fast-growing class, but they are costly to make in factories. The team instead sent the body's own cells the instructions. Their test case was VRC01, a rare antibody that blocks a wide range of HIV strains.

They built mRNA for both halves of the antibody, tweaked its letters for safety and yield, and packed it into fat bubbles. One shot into the blood of mice brought high antibody levels in the blood within a day. Weekly shots in mice with weak immune systems held the level up week after week. Best of all, mice fitted with human immune cells were shielded from an HIV challenge after one shot. The work backs mRNA as a cheaper path to passive immune care.
europmc-pmc5453364:
Kołodziejczak-Radzimska and Jesionowski review zinc oxide from making to use. Their review appeared in Materials. Zinc oxide is a material with many talents. It stays stable under light and heat. Its wide band gap suits electronics and lasers. It can sense pressure and turn it into signals. It is low in toxicity. Its tiny forms include rods, wires, tubes, and flowers.

The review first sorts the ways to make it. One group roasts zinc ore. A second group builds it by wet chemistry. Those paths include sol-gel, precipitation, and heat-and-water routes. The next part covers surface changes. Organic coatings use fatty acids and silanes. Other metal oxides can join the surface. Plastic hosts can hold the grains as well. Uses close the survey. Rubber, drugs, and cosmetics lead the list. Cloth, electronics, and light-driven chemistry follow.
europmc-pmc5473464:
Nowicka and co-authors present an updated workflow paper in F1000Research. It gives steps for analyzing data from mass and flow cytometry tests. These tests measure many proteins on single cells at high speed. The data are large and hard to compare across groups. The authors offer an R-based pipeline built on Bioconductor packages.

The pipeline first groups cells with FlowSOM clustering. It then tests which cell types or signals differ between sample groups. Mixed models handle batch effects and paired designs. Plots support checks at each stage, from quality control to final results. Researchers who study immune cell profiles can follow it step by step.
europmc-pmc5516164:
Stirnemann and the INTERGROWTH-21st consortium present fetal weight standards in Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology. Clinicians screen unborn babies for growth problems with ultrasound. A single weight estimate often drives those calls. No shared international standard for that estimate existed. The project followed healthy pregnancies across eight cities worldwide with scans every five weeks.

Birth weight was predicted best from belly and head size alone, they report. Femur length added nothing to the formula. The team built weight centile tables for 22 to 40 weeks of pregnancy. Term values matched their newborn size standards well. Preterm babies grow slower after birth than fetuses do inside.
europmc-pmc5529664:
Liu and co-authors present a review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity on oxidative stress in brain disease. Reactive oxygen species arise naturally inside cells. Neurons are unusually exposed to their damage. Their membranes are fat-rich, their oxygen use high, their defenses weak. Many brain disorders show signs of this chemical strain.

The review walks through Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's diseases. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spinocerebellar ataxia get chapters too. Clumped proteins and failing mitochondria feed the stress in each case. Antioxidant drugs like vitamins C and E show mixed results so far. Better delivery may be the missing piece.
europmc-pmc5589764:
Toyofuku and co-authors watch bacteria shed vesicles in Nature Communications. Bacteria release membrane vesicles that ferry cargo between cells. How Gram-positive bacteria do it was a puzzle. Their thick cell wall should block vesicles many times wider than its pores.

Live imaging and electron cryo-tomography solved it. A dormant virus inside Bacillus subtilis makes an enzyme, endolysin. In a few cells, that enzyme switches on. It chews holes in the peptidoglycan wall. Membrane bulges out through the holes and pinches off as vesicles. The producing cells lose integrity and die. Released endolysin then triggers neighbors to do the same. Readers get a death-linked mechanism for vesicle release, with uses in medicine and nanotechnology.
europmc-pmc5710964:
Filley and co-authors assess a failed immunotherapy trial in recurrent glioma. Their review appeared in Oncotarget. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive adult brain tumour. Survival is often under two years. Recurrence is nearly universal. The trial, CheckMate-143, tested the drug nivolumab. It blocks the PD-1 pathway.

Early results showed no survival gain. Nivolumab did not beat bevacizumab. That trial arm closed early. The authors explain why PD blockade was tried. They weigh reasons for the failure. Brain tumours pose special immune barriers. The review looks ahead as well. Checkpoint drugs may still help some patients. Better combinations and patient selection are discussed.
europmc-pmc5735564:
Steggerda and co-authors test a drug that blocks arginase, an enzyme in tumor linked immune cells. Those cells drain arginine, a nutrient T cells need to multiply. The drug, CB-1158, is taken by mouth. The team tested it in cell cultures and in mouse tumors.

They report the drug freed T cells from myeloid cell suppression. Mouse tumors grew less, alone and with other treatments. Treated tumors gained more killer T cells and natural killer cells. Human tumor samples held many arginase rich myeloid cells. Patient blood also showed high arginase and low arginine levels.
europmc-pmc5739464:
Friedland, Chapman, and Bliska review how amyloid proteins made by gut microbes may affect the brain. Gut bacteria shape metabolism, immunity, and even brain function. Brain diseases such as Parkinson and Alzheimer involve misfolded proteins that spread like prions. The review asks whether microbial amyloid helps start that spread.

Bacterial amyloids might push human proteins to clump, the authors propose. They might also stoke inflammation around nerve cell amyloid. The team coins the term mapranosis for this joint process. The field is young, they stress. Changing gut microbes offers many possible routes to treatment.
europmc-pmc5806364:
Groveman and co-authors sharpen a test for rogue alpha-synuclein seeds. Clumps of this protein mark Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia. Finding their seeds in spinal fluid could aid early diagnosis. Older tests took five to thirteen days.

Their new RT-QuIC test copies the seeds and reads them in one to two days. Blinded checks used fluid from 29 patients and 31 controls. The test caught 93 percent of cases and flagged no controls. Tiny volumes, down to 0.2 microliters, still gave a signal. Readers get a faster, countable route to spotting these diseases early.
europmc-pmc5826964:
Tedesco and co-authors ask whether THP-1 cells can stand in for real macrophages. Labs grow macrophages from blood monocytes, a slow and costly route. The THP-1 cell line offers a handy shortcut. Its replies to polarization cues were in doubt.

The team polarized both cell types toward M1 and M2 states. Blood-derived cells changed their gene markers more strongly. Of 41 released proteins, only 12 drew matching trends. Seventeen answers differed markedly between the pair. One key M2 marker never appeared in THP-1 cells. Feeding and movement tests split further. Readers get a caution: the shortcut cell is no full substitute.
europmc-pmc5835664:
Gupta and co-authors measure HIV drug resistance present before treatment starts in poorer nations. Their systematic review appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. Resistance to NNRTI drugs can doom first-line therapy from day one. The team pooled data from 63 countries.

Across 358 datasets and 56,044 adults, resistance kept climbing each year. By 2016 it stood near 11 percent in southern Africa and 10 percent in eastern Africa. Latin America and the Caribbean sat close behind. Those levels brush the WHO threshold for switching first-line regimens. The authors call for routine national resistance surveys.
europmc-pmc5859264:
Cheng and co-authors study how liver cancer fibroblasts change neutrophils. Their article appeared in Cell Death and Disease. Fibroblasts around a tumour can reshape its local environment. Neutrophils are immune cells that often gather inside solid tumours. The team tested fluid from fibroblasts taken from liver cancers. They measured how that fluid affected fresh neutrophils.

The team reports that the fluid drew neutrophils in and kept them alive. Treated cells raised PDL1, a protein that can mute T cells. Those neutrophils then weakened T-cell function in lab tests. A signal chain ran from IL6 through STAT3 to PDL1. Blocking that chain could offer a new treatment angle for liver cancer.
europmc-pmc5862964:
Wang and co-authors trace the global spread of the colistin resistance gene mcr-1. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Colistin is a last-resort drug for hard-to-treat infections. The mcr-1 gene sits on plasmids, so it can jump between bacteria. The team studied 457 sequenced isolates that carried the gene. They compared the gene's setting across many plasmid types.

The authors report one shared background behind all mcr-1 copies. All copies seem to descend from a single gene capture event. They date that event to the mid-2000s. A fast expansion then carried the gene worldwide. The study gives the first full tree of this gene's origin. Global tracking of such genes is vital, they stress.
europmc-pmc5869864:
Rabanal-Ruiz and co-authors review mTORC1 as the main gateway to autophagy. Their article appeared in Essays in Biochemistry. Cells must grow only when conditions favour growth. The protein complex mTORC1 sits at the centre of nutrient sensing. When nutrients abound, it drives building of proteins and lipids. It also shuts down autophagy, the cell's recycling pathway. Its interplay with the energy sensor AMPK sets the balance.

Amino acids are the key cues for mTORC1, the authors stress. No other signal can stand in for them. The review covers current models of amino acid sensing. It links those models to mTORC1 signalling and recycling control. Faults in this hub tie to metabolic disease and cancer.
europmc-pmc5876064:
Kelly and co-authors adapt variant classification rules for the MYH7 gene. Their article appeared in Genetics in Medicine. A standard framework guides how labs judge genetic variants. Expert panels tailor that framework to single genes and diseases. The panel chose MYH7, a key gene in inherited heart muscle disease. Two reviewers each checked 60 variants under draft rules. Final rules were set through repeated group discussion.

Twelve changes tailored rules to this gene and disease. Five more adjusted the strength of existing rules. Nine rules were dropped as not applicable. Early agreement between experts reached 93 percent. Shared lab data changed one fifth of the calls. The rules now guide MYH7 testing with expert review.
europmc-pmc5877064:
Basner and McGuire review how environmental noise affects sleep. Their systematic review supported the WHO noise guidelines for Europe. They searched six databases for field studies published from 2000 onward. Seventy-four studies met their rules. Most were run between 2000 and 2015. Evidence quality was judged with GRADE criteria.

Traffic noise raised self-reported sleep disturbance, they report. The link was clearest when survey questions named noise itself. Lab sleep recordings also showed more awakenings as noise rose. That held for aircraft, road, and rail noise alike. Evidence for wind turbine and hospital noise was weaker or mixed. Readers get a graded summary of what noise does to sleep.
europmc-pmc5956964:
van Leeuwen and co-authors review alpha and beta values of the linear-quadratic model for human tumours. Their review appeared in Radiation Oncology. The linear-quadratic model predicts how tissue responds to radiation. Its alpha, beta, and alpha/beta values must be chosen with care. Wrong values spoil estimates of dose and tumour control. The team searched the literature for clinical values. They found 64 studies that reported these parameters.

Values varied a lot within and between studies, they report. Histology explained part of the spread for one tumour site. Epithelial tumours held higher alpha/beta values than adenocarcinomas. Stage, model type, and endpoint also drove the differences. Careful selection by site and histology is urged.
europmc-pmc5991564:
Grady and co-authors test which tissue measures best track disease burden in m.3243A>G mitochondrial disease. Their study appeared in EMBO Molecular Medicine. This variant causes a common, varied neurogenetic disorder. Mutation load can be read in blood, urine, or muscle. The team modelled which reading links most tightly to burden. Blood samples numbered 231 and urine 235. Muscle samples numbered 77.

Mutation levels correlated across the three tissues, they report. Blood levels fall by about 2.3 percent per year. Age-corrected blood values were the handiest reliable measure. In muscle, copy number added more signal about burden. Urine values needed a sex adjustment formula.
europmc-pmc6006764:
Leone and Emens review targeting adenosine for cancer immunotherapy. Their review appeared in the Journal for Immunotherapy of Cancer. Checkpoint drugs produce durable gains in several cancers. More patients need help than those drugs reach. Adenosine builds up heavily inside the tumour environment. It strongly damps immune responses through one receptor. Low oxygen and rapid cell turnover drive its production. Two surface enzymes, CD39 and CD73, help make it.

Blocking this pathway could extend immunotherapy's reach, the authors argue. Each target in the chain has preclinical support. Early clinical activity is now under way. Rational drug combinations look most promising.
europmc-pmc6031064:
Rodrigues and co-authors present DynaMut, a mutation analysis web server. Their article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Proteins move constantly, and motion shapes their function. Most mutation tools still judge effects from static structures. Simulating motion for every mutant is costly.

DynaMut uses two normal mode approaches instead. These sample protein motions at low cost. It adds graph-based signatures of the local structure. A consensus model then predicts stability change. Blind tests reached a correlation up to 0.70. The authors report it beat rival methods. The server also visualizes flexibility and motion. Readers get a free tool for judging mutations. It covers both disease and drug resistance settings.
europmc-pmc6043964:
Grgic and co-authors scope studies that swap time between daily behaviors. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. Each day splits among sleep, sitting, and activity. Studying each behavior alone ignores that fixed total. Swapping models estimate what a trade would do.

The search covered ten databases in total. Fifty-six studies met the inclusion rules. Most swapped thirty minutes per day in models. Trading sitting time for activity linked to lower death risk. Gains grew when the activity was more vigorous. Body fat measures also tended to improve. Heart and metabolic markers showed similar patterns in adults. Evidence for children and older adults was thinner. Many studies ignored sleep time entirely.
europmc-pmc6057964:
Wang and co-authors build glowing nanoprobes that assemble inside tumors. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The goal is better surgery for spread ovarian cancer. Tiny leftover tumors often cause the disease to return. Surgeons still rely mostly on touch and sight.

The probes shine in a deep-penetrating infrared band. They carry DNA and targeting peptides on their surface. Inside tumors, the probes join into larger structures. That assembly keeps them in place for six hours. Images beat the standard clinical dye in quality. Tumor outlines stood out sharply from normal tissue. Spread spots of one millimeter could be removed fully. The team verified removal with tissue analysis afterward. Readers get a new tool for precise cancer surgery.
europmc-pmc6117964:
Wevers and co-authors present a methods article in Fluids and Barriers of the CNS on a human blood-brain barrier built on a chip. The barrier guards the brain from most large drugs. Testing whether antibody drugs cross it is slow work. The team built a tiny, flowing model of the barrier for high-throughput tests.

The chips hold human brain vessel cells with astrocytes and pericytes. Up to 96 chips fit in one plate. The model formed tight seals and blocked a dye well. An antibody aimed at the transferrin receptor crossed more than a control antibody. The authors say the setup suits drug screening work.
europmc-pmc6120664:
Riley and co-authors present a research article in The EMBO Journal on how mitochondrial DNA escapes during cell death. When a cell dies by apoptosis, proteins called BAX and BAK open its mitochondria. That step is seen as a point of no return. DNA from inside mitochondria can then trigger inflammation. How it crosses the inner membrane was not clear.

The team used super-resolution imaging to watch the process. Pores in the outer membrane widen over time. The inner membrane then bulges out into the cell body. It breaks open and frees the DNA. That release drives the immune effects of this form of cell death.
europmc-pmc6132564:
Smith and co-authors wrote a review in Current Environmental Health Reports on microplastics in seafood. Tiny plastic bits now spread through the oceans. Fish and shellfish swallow them. People then eat those animals, shellfish often whole. What that means for human health is not yet known.

The review gathers evidence on exposure through seafood. Any harm likely depends on dose, plastic type, and particle size. Plastics can also carry chemicals picked up from seawater. The authors point out large gaps in toxicity data. They suggest fixes across the plastic life cycle. They also urge more research, given how much nutrition seafood provides.
europmc-pmc6188564:
Flouri and co-authors present a practical guide in Molecular Biology and Evolution to inferring species trees with the program BPP. Different genes can tell different evolutionary stories. The multispecies coalescent model handles that, since ancestral variation makes gene trees differ. BPP implements the model in a Bayesian framework.

The guide shows how to run BPP on multilocus genomic sequence data. The program weighs competing species trees and reports their probabilities. It accounts for gene tree differences in shape and branch length, plus uncertainty at each locus. Settings such as priors are explained step by step. The protocol helps researchers move from raw sequences to a defensible species tree on any major operating system.
europmc-pmc6200764:
Kirchdoerfer and co-authors present a research article in Scientific Reports on stabilized coronavirus spikes. The SARS coronavirus enters cells using its spike protein, which locks onto the ACE2 receptor and fuses the viral and cell membranes. During entry the spike is cut by host enzymes and changes shape. Those shifts are central to infection.

The team had earlier designed mutations that lock spikes in their pre-fusion shape. Here they used cryo-electron microscopy to test the locked spikes. The stabilized proteins resisted the shape changes normally triggered by receptor binding and by cutting. They still bound ACE2 about as well as normal spikes. Locked spikes of this kind are valued as vaccine antigens and study tools.
europmc-pmc6219764:
Zech and co-authors tested a deep learning model for pneumonia. The model reads chest X-rays. Such models may not work as well on new hospitals' data. The team checked this across three hospital systems. The study appeared in PLoS Medicine.

The dataset held 158,323 chest images. Images came from NIH, Mount Sinai, and Indiana sites. Pneumonia rates differed sharply by site. At Mount Sinai the rate was about 34 percent. At the other sites it was near 1 percent. Merely sorting by hospital gave a strong score. Models trained at one site did worse at another. They did as well on the third site as local models. The authors warn that site traits can inflate results.
europmc-pmc6259264:
Cartea and co-authors review the phenolic compounds in Brassica vegetables. Their review appeared in Molecules. Brassicas include cabbage, kale, broccoli, and their kin. They are eaten worldwide and carry economic weight. Phenolics are plant chemicals that may guard against cancer and heart disease. Their antioxidant strength drives much of that interest.

Profiles for the main Brassica species are now well established. The review groups the compounds by structure, from simple acids to flavonoids. It then asks what shapes those profiles. Weather, soil, and growing method all play a part. Cooking and processing change levels further. Readers learn which vegetables carry which compounds. The account also weighs how much of the benefit survives the trip to the plate. That link matters for honest diet advice.
europmc-pmc6323964:
Cunningham and co-authors report the 2019 state of the Ensembl genome resource. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Ensembl gives genomic data to all scientists without restriction. It builds reference annotation and comparative resources. This year its gene and variant tools expanded. Vertebrate genomes supported rose by half.

Human variants in the system doubled in number. Regulatory regions were added for many mouse cell types. Developmental stages gained mouse coverage too. A new method speeds gene annotation for new species. Unusual genomes like hagfish were annotated this way. Pairwise whole-genome alignments also doubled. Data flow through the website, an interface, and downloads. Quarterly updates keep the resource current.
europmc-pmc6324064:
Burley and co-authors describe the RCSB Protein Data Bank and its reach. Their report appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The RCSB is the United States center for the global archive. It takes structure deposits from the Americas and Oceania. It shares the data free, with no use limits. Over a million users visit its main site each year.

Depositors use crystallography, magnetic resonance, and electron microscopy. Readers include researchers, teachers, and students worldwide. A sister site serves classroom users in large numbers. The center reorganized its work into four linked services. New tools joined the web portals over two years. They support what the authors call a structural view of biology. The paper explains each service and recent addition.
europmc-pmc6325164:
Giraldo and co-authors review the tumor microenvironment in solid cancers. Their review appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. A tumor is not just cancer cells alone. Blood vessel cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells live there too. These neighbors shape how the tumor grows and spreads. Anti-tumor immunity is a key hurdle for any tumor.

Studies in melanoma and bowel and ovarian cancers guide the field. Tumors rich in killer T cells often fare better. In kidney cancer, the type of T cell matters for early relapse. Vessel and fibroblast cells also sway immune impact. The review pulls together these parts of the ecosystem. It weighs how the setting predicts outcome and drug response. That helps doctors read a tumor beyond its cancer cells.
europmc-pmc6359764:
France and co-authors present reporting guidance in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Their subject is meta-ethnography, a way to join findings from many studies of people's experience. The method is used a lot in health research, but reports often leave key steps unclear.

Weak reporting makes readers doubt the findings. The team built the eMERGe guidance through a mixed-methods study. It sets out what a report should state at each of the seven phases of the method. Clearer reports should help policy makers trust and use this kind of evidence. The guidance is aimed at authors, reviewers, and editors.
europmc-pmc6361464:
Garud and co-authors present a research article in PLoS Biology on how gut bacteria evolve inside people. They built a model-based method to track genetic change within one host and across many hosts. They applied it to metagenomic samples for about forty common gut species.

Within hosts, they find resident strains usually change in place over six months. New variants or gained and lost genes sweep to high frequency, rather than outside strains taking over. Some sweeps seem seeded by recombination between strains. Twin data suggest replacement wins over decades, which limits local adaptation. The work shows gut bacteria evolve on human timescales.
europmc-pmc6372664:
Yang and co-authors present a review in Cell Death and Disease on the NLRP3 inflammasome. This protein complex triggers inflammatory cell death and releases the cytokines IL-1 beta and IL-18. Faulty control of it is linked to Alzheimer's disease, type 2 diabetes, prion diseases, and infections.

Activation needs two steps: a priming signal, then a trigger from danger or pathogen patterns. The review gathers what is known about each control point, from potassium flow to the NEK7 partner protein. It then surveys drugs that block NLRP3 itself rather than its neighbors. The authors frame these inhibitors as candidate treatments for many inflammatory diseases.
europmc-pmc6379264:
Almeida and co-authors present a perspective article in Frontiers in Microbiology on the neglected burden of fungal disease. Fungi kill an estimated 1.6 million people each year, and over a billion people suffer severe fungal illness. Yet reporting is rarely required, so the true counts are likely higher.

Few antifungal drugs exist, and none wholly new has been approved since 2002. Funding lags far behind malaria and tuberculosis relative to deaths caused. Fungi also destroy about a third of food crops and drive some animal species toward extinction. Warming climates are raising case counts. The authors demand dedicated research funding and better surveillance.
europmc-pmc6437964:
Ménétrier-Caux and co-authors review lymphopenia, the shortage of lymphocytes common in cancer patients, and its growing importance in the immunotherapy era. Low lymphocyte counts predict poor prognosis and survival, yet clinics rarely track them when choosing treatment. Checkpoint inhibitors have changed that calculus by making immune status a likely marker of response.

Sections cover how often lymphopenia occurs, what it signals, and how it may blunt checkpoint therapy alongside tumor infiltration by CD8 cells. Strategies to restore lymphocyte numbers, including cytokine combinations, are weighed as ways to rescue responses. The authors argue lymphocyte counts deserve routine attention next to neutrophils and platelets.
europmc-pmc6478664:
Tomova and co-authors review how vegetarian and vegan diets reshape the gut microbes, the roughly 3 × 10^13 germs each person carries. Plant-based eaters host richer and steadier mixes than meat eaters, with clearly different Bacteroidetes-related groups. The drivers are parts of food that animals never supply.

Fiber feeds lactic acid makers such as Ruminococcus, Eubacterium rectale, and Roseburia, while trimming Clostridium and Enterococcus. When germs ferment fiber they yield acetate, propionate, and butyrate, short fatty acids that fuel the colon lining and back immunity. Polyphenols push Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus upward, calming inflammation and guarding the heart. The papers support plant diets as a way of gardening the gut, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc6492164:
Morris and co-authors write the manual simulation studies always needed. Simulation studies are the lab bench of statistics, spinning data from a known truth to measure a method's bias or error. Yet they are too often designed, analyzed, and reported badly. The tutorial's scaffold is ADEMP: state the Aims, the Data-generating mechanisms, the Estimands, the Methods, and the Performance measures before running anything.

Coding practice gets detailed treatment. So do how to estimate these measures and their error bars, plus honest tables and graphics. Worked warnings show, for one, how root mean square error comparisons flip with sample size. To ground the advice, the authors audited 100 simulation papers from one journal volume and named the recurring failures.
europmc-pmc6492564:
Liu and co-authors portray cancer-associated fibroblasts as the builders and security guards of the tumor microenvironment. Solid tumors are ecosystems, and fibroblasts, abundant and genetically stable unlike the cancer cells, lay down the desmoplastic matrix, run much of the local signaling, and decide how deeply drugs penetrate.

Therapies keep aiming at the fast-growing seed while ignoring this soil, one reason resistance blooms within months. The review details how fibroblast products, matrix proteins, enzymes, growth factors, and chemokine signals such as the CXCR4 axis, feed tumor growth and shield it. It also weighs early attempts to block those channels. Anti-tumor faces of fibroblasts exist too, complicating any plan to simply destroy them.
europmc-pmc6507064:
Marra, Viale and Curigliano review new immune treatments for triple-negative breast cancer. Their review appeared in BMC Medicine. This cancer type lacks hormone and HER2 targets, so drug choices stay narrow. It tends to strike younger patients and grow fast.

The review centres on the IMpassion130 trial. Adding atezolizumab to chemotherapy helped patients whose tumours showed PD-L1. Gains in the wider trial group were less clear. The authors weigh how to test PD-L1 and find better markers. They discuss which chemotherapy drug pairs best with immune therapy. They also look at single-drug use and trials in early disease. The piece maps open questions for the next trials.
europmc-pmc6514564:
Singh and co-authors review oxidative stress in neurodegenerative disease. Their review appeared in Molecules. Oxidative stress arises when oxidants overwhelm antioxidant defences. Reactive oxygen species then damage DNA, lipids and proteins. The brain is prone to this harm. It uses much oxygen and holds many fragile fats.

Mitochondria sit at the centre of the account. Faulty energy production there can raise reactive species. The authors cover sensors and biomarkers of stress. They also cover heavy metals, ferroptosis, and cell ageing or death. Later sections take Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and other diseases in turn. Each section asks how oxidative stress shapes the illness.
europmc-pmc6548764:
The Global Burden of Disease Health Financing Collaborator Network tracks health spending for 195 countries, writing in The Lancet. The team rebuilt spending from 1995 to 2016 across government, out-of-pocket, prepaid private and aid sources, then projected every stream forward to 2050.

Global spending hit $8.0 trillion in 2016, yet the gaps were stark. High-income countries spent $5,252 per person against $40 in low-income ones, a 130-fold gap. Poor countries held a tenth of world population but only 0.4% of the spending. Growth is set to slow, reaching $15 trillion by 2050 with the gap near intact. Aid leaned most toward HIV/AIDS. Stronger government effort, the authors show, could more than double per-person spending where it is now lowest.
europmc-pmc6693264:
Kokorelias and co-authors scope existing models of family centered care toward a shared model for all. Their scoping review appears in BMC Health Services Research. Families carry much of the care burden. Unsupported caregiving damages their own health. The team searched four databases across decades. Fourteen thousand papers narrowed to 55 models. Child-focused care dominated the model landscape. Forty of the models targeted children. Every model built care plans within family context.

Four parts recurred across models. Joint work between families and providers came first. Regard for family contexts followed. Policies and procedures formed the third pillar. Education for all parties completed the set. Few models had outcome evaluations. Privacy and decision-making gaps need work.
europmc-pmc6744664:
Xu and co-authors review the role of collagen in cancer, from lab bench to bedside. Collagen is the main part of the tissue around tumors. Cancer cells steer its production through changed genes and signal paths. Collagen in turn steers tumor behavior through receptors on the cell surface.

Low oxygen, common in collagen-rich tissue, speeds cancer along. Other matrix parts interact with collagen to sway cancer cell activity. Immune cells and fibroblasts join collagen in shaping growth and spread. Together they form a feedback loop that affects outlook, return of disease, and drug resistance. The review also covers nanoparticle treatments aimed at collagen. Its double role offers promising treatment options.
europmc-pmc6767464:
Ong and MacGregor give a practitioner's guide to two pleiotropy checks in Mendelian randomization. The method uses genes to test whether a risk factor truly causes a disease. Huge genome studies now supply hundreds of genetic instruments. Some instruments affect the outcome through other paths, a flaw called pleiotropy. Two tools, MR-PRESSO and GCTA-GSMR, hunt those flaws.

MR-PRESSO runs a global test of whether removing suspect instruments changes the causal estimate. GSMR instead filters outlier instruments one at a time. In their test example, 10,000 simulation runs took about six minutes. The commentary also covers the genetic layouts now being found for risk factors. Design choices should reflect those layouts.
europmc-pmc6827364:
Baillo and co-authors review stress-control genes in crops, in the journal Genes. Field crops face drought, cold, salt, and heat, plus pests and germs. Such stress can cut yields sharply, and climate change adds pressure. Plants switch on defence genes through master regulators called transcription factors. Those regulators are prime targets for breeding tougher crops.

More than 80 families of these factors exist in plants. A few, such as NAC, MYB, WRKY, bZIP, and ERF/DREB, do much of the stress work. The review gives cases where raising or lowering one factor changed a plant's tolerance. It also flags how much remains unknown about the rest.
europmc-pmc6847864:
Donath and co-authors tackle a quiet problem in genome science, in Nucleic Acids Research. Animals carry a small second genome in their mitochondria. Its protein-coding genes are easy to locate roughly. Pinning down exactly where each gene starts and stops is surprisingly hard, because mitochondrial transcripts are processed in odd ways. Manual checking cannot keep pace with new sequences.

The team studied annotated start and stop positions across many genomes. They measured which codons appear, how long genes run, and how the genetic code variant in use changes the picture. A new prediction method built on those patterns follows. It is not perfect, they note, but it sharpens automatic annotation of new mitochondrial genomes.
europmc-pmc6927964:
Sun and co-authors review PROTACs, a drug strategy that destroys target proteins instead of blocking them. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Drug resistance limits many current therapies. Only a small share of protein targets can be drugged at all. Most drugs also ignore what a protein does as a scaffold.

A PROTAC links two parts: one grabs the target protein, the other recruits the cell's disposal machinery. The joined pair marks the target for degradation. Results show sharper selectivity than classic inhibitors, and effects on hard, drug-resistant targets. Uses span cancer, immune disorders, viral infections, and brain disease. The authors call for more work on safety and on finding new target binders.
europmc-pmc6964864:
Prodan and co-authors compare software pipelines that turn raw microbial DNA reads into counts. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. Surveys of the 16S rRNA gene illuminate ecosystems from soil to the human gut. Software choices shape the results, yet users often miss each pipeline's biases.

Six pipelines faced off: three that cluster reads into operational units, and three that resolve exact sequence variants. The team tested them on a mock community of known makeup. They also ran a large set of 2170 stool samples from a multi-ethnic health study. One pipeline, DADA2, caught the most true variants but let more false ones through. Another, USEARCH-UNOISE3, balanced sharpness and accuracy best. One older tool produced many fake units and inflated diversity, and should be avoided, the authors say.
europmc-pmc7033564:
The GBD 2017 Stomach Cancer Collaborators profile stomach cancer worldwide in The Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology. Stomach cancer remains a major health problem in many countries, and its trends differ sharply by location. Prevention planning needs those differences mapped, so the collaborators report cases, deaths, and disability for 195 countries and 21 regions from 1990 to 2017.

In 2017, more than 1.22 million new stomach cancer cases occurred worldwide and nearly 865,000 people died of the disease, adding up to 19.1 million disability-adjusted life-years. The highest age-standardised incidence rates appeared in high-income Asia Pacific and east Asia, and nearly half of all new cases occurred in China. Rates fell in most regions over the period, yet total case numbers still grew as populations aged and expanded.
europmc-pmc7034864:
Jenkins and Quintana-Ascencio tackle a practical statistics problem in PLOS ONE. Regressions are used everywhere to find patterns, yet many studies run them on small samples, which feeds reproducibility worries. Power analysis is the usual guide to sample size, but the authors argue model selection should come first: find the most plausible model, then ask how much data it needs.

They simulated null, straight-line, and curved data sets with different variances and effect sizes, then sampled them repeatedly. With very low variance, the true pattern was always clear at a sample size of 8 or more. With high variance, stable inference needed at least 25. Akaike information criterion weights separated the models cleanly, while R-squared values did not. The authors warn that small samples judged by R-squared invite false findings.
europmc-pmc7054964:
Chen and co-authors link virus in the blood to worse COVID-19 outcomes in Emerging Microbes and Infections. Diagnosis of the new coronavirus relied on throat swabs. The team looked back at laboratory results from patients whose pharyngeal swabs, blood, and anal swabs were tested by real-time PCR. They wanted to know where else the viral RNA turns up, and whether it predicts how sick a patient becomes.

Viral RNA was found in blood in 6 of 57 patients and in anal swabs in 11 of 28 patients. Every patient with detectable RNA in the blood went on to reach the severe stage, a strong statistical link with later severity. Most patients with positive anal swabs were also severe. Viral levels in anal swabs ran higher than in blood in one tracked patient, hinting the virus may replicate in the digestive tract. The authors propose blood testing as a warning sign.
europmc-pmc7068164:
Spiteri and co-authors document Europe's first COVID-19 cases in Eurosurveillance. Surveillance for the new disease began in the WHO European Region on 27 January 2020. The authors detail what the earliest cases looked like and how they were found, using reports gathered through 21 February 2020.

By that date, nine European countries had reported 47 cases. Of 38 cases studied closely, 21 belonged to two clusters in Germany and France, and 14 patients had been infected in China. The median age was 42 years, and 25 were male. Slow recognition of the clusters' first cases delayed isolation of later local ones, a lesson the authors underline. Most hospitalised patients recovered smoothly, though four had a harder course. By 5 March the regional total had jumped to 4,250 cases. The report freezes the moment a local problem became a continental one.
europmc-pmc7073164:
Kao and co-authors review lipids in Alzheimer's disease in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Lipids build every cell membrane, and the brain is unusually rich in them. When lipid balance breaks down, neurological disease can follow. Alzheimer's is the commonest dementia: about 46.8 million people lived with dementia worldwide in 2015, with an estimated 9.9 million new cases each year.

Ageing itself shifts the brain's lipid mix. Changes in fatty acids inside membrane rafts and oxidation of brain lipids appear early in Alzheimer's. Genes for apolipoprotein and lipid transporters alter risk, and so does the fat content of the diet. New analytical methods have opened lipidomics, the full census of lipids, as a hunting ground for markers that predict, diagnose, or help prevent the disease. The review gathers what is known about each lipid family in Alzheimer's, from membrane phospholipids to signalling fats, aiming toward new therapeutics.
europmc-pmc7081964:
Rosen and co-authors present a new reference genome for cattle, ARS-UCD1.2, in GigaScience. The older cattle genome, built with outdated methods, had gaps and errors that limited research. Their team rebuilt it from the same animal using single-molecule sequencing and other modern tools.

The new assembly spans 2.7 billion bases and is far more continuous than the old one. Added RNA data support a count of 30,396 total genes, including 21,039 that code for proteins. Because the same animal was used, results from the old genome carry over. Readers get the case for adopting this assembly as the standard cattle reference.
europmc-pmc7144564:
Breijyeh, Jubeh, and Karaman review resistance in Gram-negative bacteria and the ways being tried to defeat it, in Molecules. These bacteria resist drugs more readily than Gram-positive ones because of their extra outer membrane. Most of the World Health Organization's 2017 priority pathogen list is Gram-negative.

Plans surveyed include helper compounds that switch off resistance enzymes, such as beta-lactamase blockers, reshaping existing antibiotics, and hunting entirely new targets. Natural products feature too, from bacteria-eating phages to membrane attackers like DCAP and new peptide families. The review's message is that no single fix suffices; several lines must advance together against a global health crisis.
europmc-pmc7199464:
Yap and co-authors critically review electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve through the skin. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Implanted vagus nerve stimulators are approved for severe depression and epilepsy. Surgery limits them to the toughest cases. The skin-based version, tVNS, uses surface electrodes instead.

Electrodes usually target the nerve's branch in the ear or in the neck. Studies report effects similar to the implanted device. Yet stimulation settings vary wildly between studies. Frequencies from 1 to 30 hertz have all been tried, with differing results. That inconsistency blocks clinical adoption, the authors argue. They call for standard settings and stronger trials. The review maps what must be fixed before tVNS reaches routine care.
europmc-pmc7256664:
Rossi and co-authors surveyed mental health among health care workers in Italy during COVID-19. Their cross-sectional study appeared in JAMA Network Open. Data were gathered online from March 27 to 31, 2020, just before the national peak. Workers were asked if they treated COVID-19 patients directly. Standard scales measured trauma symptoms, depression, anxiety, insomnia and stress.

A total of 1,379 workers replied. About half reported trauma symptoms. About one in four reported depression symptoms, and one in five reported anxiety. Younger workers and women scored worse on most measures. Frontline work raised trauma risk. Losing a colleague was linked to several harms. The authors urge ongoing support for staff.
europmc-pmc7278864:
Scarmozzino and Visioli report how lockdown changed what people in Italy ate, based on an online survey. Italy shut down on March 9, 2020. People in the sample told the team what they ate in the weeks spent at home, and whether their weight had changed.

About half said their diet stayed much the same. But close to half said they ate more than before, and about one in five said they gained weight. Comfort foods rose a lot, above all chocolate, ice cream, and desserts, and salty snacks rose too. Many blamed stress and worry. Fresh fruit and greens rose for about one in five, while buys of ready-made meals fell by close to half. Home life pushed diets both ways at once.
europmc-pmc7294764:
Bokolo Anthony Jnr., a solo author, reviews how telemedicine and virtual care were used to treat patients remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic. The rapid literature review appeared in the Journal of Medical Systems. Hospitals strained under pandemic demand needed ways to diagnose, treat, monitor, and follow up patients without bringing them in.

The review draws on 35 research studies published from 2019 to May 2020. Telemedicine delivered timely care while limiting exposure for both patients and medical staff, using ordinary communication technology. The article doubles as a practical guide to running remote care during an emergency. Its author argues the experience shows virtual care should be consolidated into normal health systems after the pandemic, not abandoned when the crisis passes.
europmc-pmc7296164:
Chew, Solomon and Fonteh argue that lipids, the fatty molecules of the brain, sit at the center of Alzheimer's disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. Lipids make up most of the brain's dry mass. The strongest genetic risk factor for the disease, the APOE epsilon4 variant, is itself involved in lipid transport and metabolism.

Under healthy conditions, balanced lipids support the blood-brain barrier, membrane upkeep, signaling, and energy balance. When that balance breaks, many disease processes follow: faulty processing of amyloid precursor protein, poor insulation of nerve fibers, disturbed inflammation and oxidation, and failing energy supply. The authors examine each link and point to therapies aimed at lipid pathways as a promising direction for a disease short on options.
europmc-pmc7296264:
Peixoto da Silva and co-authors explain cancer cachexia, the wasting syndrome that accompanies many cancers. Their review appeared in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle. Cachexia progressively strips skeletal muscle and fat, drives body-wide inflammation and metabolic disorder, and cannot be fully reversed by normal feeding. It directly worsens quality of life and outcomes.

Related conditions share some of its features: sarcopenia, the muscle loss of aging; anorexia, loss of appetite; and asthenia, weakness and fatigue. Telling them apart matters, because mixing them up slows research and muddies diagnosis. The authors map the mechanisms driving cachexia and compare it point by point with its neighbors, aiming to sharpen both basic research and the search for effective therapies.
europmc-pmc7314664:
Fong, Li and Yu review whether reshaping the gut microbiota can prevent or treat colorectal cancer. Their review appeared in Oncogene. Colorectal cancer is the third most commonly diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death, with 1.8 million new cases and 881,000 deaths worldwide in 2018. Gut microbes out of balance, called dysbiosis, are now part of the disease picture.

Strategies include probiotics, prebiotics, postbiotics, antibiotics, and transplanting fecal microbiota from donors. In studies they correct microbial composition, calm or tune innate immunity, strengthen the gut barrier, block pathogens, and even kill tumor cells selectively. Risks and controversies travel with the promise, so benefit and harm must be weighed patient by patient. Personalized microbiome therapy may be the key to success.
europmc-pmc7323564:
Dong and Bouey describe a mental health crisis in China that grew with the COVID-19 outbreak. Their article notes that China was hit first. Old memories of the 2003 SARS outbreak fed fear. Early downplaying of the threat hurt trust in the state. Huge quarantines then kept whole cities at home for weeks.

Word of shortages in masks, staff, and hospital beds spread worry through the land. A flood of news and false claims, an infodemic, made things worse. China did set up emergency teams to help minds in crisis, but the help was made up on the fly. The team's advice is plain: mental health work should be built into health plans for the next emergency from the start.
europmc-pmc7417164:
KC and co-authors study childbirth care in Nepal before and during the national COVID-19 lockdown, in The Lancet Global Health. Data came from nine hospitals between January and May 2020, covering 12.5 weeks before lockdown and 9.5 weeks during it. In all, 21,763 women were enrolled and 20,354 gave birth.

Institutional births fell by 52.4 percent, from about 1,261 to 651 per week, as women stayed away. Stillbirths rose from 14 to 21 per 1,000 births, and newborn deaths from 13 to 40 per 1,000 live births. Fetal heart monitoring and early breastfeeding slipped, though hand hygiene and skin-to-skin care improved. Lockdown's indirect toll on mothers and babies, the authors warn, demands urgent protection of maternity access.
europmc-pmc7473764:
Son and co-authors survey how COVID-19 affected the mental health of college students in the United States. Student mental health was already a rising concern. The team ran interview surveys at a large public university.

Of 195 students, 138, or 71%, reported more stress and anxiety from the outbreak. Worry about their own health and that of loved ones hit hardest. Trouble focusing, broken sleep, and lost social contact were common strains. Concern over grades also weighed on students. To cope, students sought support from others. Some used healthy habits, others harmful ones. The authors urge quick action to build support and prevention for students. Long lockdowns, they note, deepen the strain on higher education.
europmc-pmc7532964:
Nocera and Jacob review Schwann cell plasticity after peripheral nerve injury. Schwann cells make myelin in the peripheral nervous system. Their ability to change state drives nerve repair.

After injury, Schwann cells switch to a repair form. They clear myelin and shed mature traits. They turn on genes from their immature state. They also turn on new genes for repair. These steps help axons survive, regrow and find targets. Repair cells then remyelinate the new axons. The review details signals and gene controls behind each step. Readers learn why peripheral nerves heal better than central ones.
europmc-pmc7547664:
Andersson and co-authors present a method to infer cell type layout from spatial transcript data. Spatial assays capture gene activity across tissue spots. Each spot may hold a mix of cell types.

Their model uses single-cell data to split those mixtures. It gives probabilities for cell types at each spot. Tests used mouse brain and developing heart data. Mapped cell types arranged as expected in both tissues. The method works across different lab platforms. It helps put gene expression into tissue context. Readers get a model for a common spatial data problem. Full expression depth is kept while cell identity is recovered.
europmc-pmc7561164:
Haischer and co-authors observe mask wearing among shoppers in the United States. Masks can slow COVID-19 spread in public places. Who wears them had not been studied by observation.

The team watched 9935 shoppers entering retail stores. Observations ran across June, July and August of that year. About 41% of the June sample wore a mask. Odds of masking rose with age. Women were 1.5 times as likely to wear one. Urban and suburban shoppers masked far more than rural ones. Mandates later pushed compliance above 90% in all groups. A small share of shoppers still resisted after mandates.
europmc-pmc7643364:
Tang and co-authors show that TM4SF1 drives shape change and stemness in colorectal cancer. The protein is raised in several epithelial cancers. High levels link to poor outlook for patients.

Levels were far higher in tumor than in normal tissue. That pattern held across databases and lab tests. Lowering TM4SF1 cut cell migration and invasion in vitro. It also cut tumor sphere formation in two cell lines. Raising it had the opposite effect on those traits. Silencing blocked shape change driven by TGF-β1 signals. The pathway ran through Wnt, beta-catenin and SOX2. A gene called c-Myc linked into that chain. Removing TM4SF1 slowed spread and growth in mice. The axis may sustain recurrence in this cancer.
europmc-pmc7684964:
France and co-authors present a standard tool for sorting vaginal microbe communities. Such communities fall into a few types, called community state types. Past sorting used clustering within each dataset. That made results hard to compare across studies, since each set gave unlike groups.

The new tool, VALENCIA, matches each sample to fixed reference profiles. The references rest on 13,160 profiles from 1975 women in the USA. Tests on three unlike datasets, from Africa and from postmenopausal women, went well. The tool should make vaginal microbe studies robust and repeatable. The authors also link the types to pH, clinical scores, and demographics.
europmc-pmc7721364:
Suárez-Calvet and co-authors test new tau markers for the earliest stage of Alzheimer disease. Tau protein changes in the brain leak into spinal fluid and blood. The team measured tau changed at three sites: T181, T217, and T231. They compared new tests with a standard automated tau assay.

The new markers rose sharply in the preclinical stage, when amyloid change was still subtle. They split amyloid-positive from amyloid-negative people with sharp accuracy, though those people had no symptoms. A blood version also rose, though mildly, at this early point. The authors say early tau change, likely sparked by amyloid, can now be caught with these tests.
europmc-pmc7730664:
Bush and co-authors review how quinolone antibiotics kill bacteria and breed resistance. Fluoroquinolones have served in clinics for over 30 years. They trap two bacterial enzymes on cut DNA, which blocks copying and kills the cell. This trap makes them potent against many infections.

Resistance is now rising and new drugs are needed with care. The authors trace the paths by which bacteria survive these drugs. They also show how quinolone use can raise resistance to other drug classes. Low-level exposure can drive this wider effect. The review links lab mechanism to a clinical threat that cuts across antibiotic families.
europmc-pmc7812564:
Kotlar and co-authors review how the COVID-19 pandemic affected maternal and newborn health. Effects run both direct and indirect. The two kinds twist together in practice. The team ran a scoping review for a fast, broad picture.

The search found 396 publications, and 95 were included. Work covered January 1 to September 11, 2020. Pregnant people faced higher risk of severe symptoms. Passing the virus to the baby seemed unlikely. Care rules for labor and breastfeeding varied widely. Reports showed sharp rises in anxiety and depression among mothers. Domestic violence appeared to spike. Prenatal visits dropped during the same months.
europmc-pmc7841464:
Bellan and co-authors check COVID-19 patients four months after leaving hospital. The cohort held 238 patients from one hospital in Northern Italy.
