The team asked what lung, body, and mind effects linger. Tests covered lung gas transfer and daily function. Mood and trauma symptoms were screened too.

More than half of the patients showed real impairment. Lung gas transfer was cut, or daily function was measurably worse. About one-fifth showed signs of posttraumatic stress. These effects came despite full recovery from the virus itself. The authors warn that discharge is not the end of illness. Follow-up care should screen lungs, function, and mental health together.
europmc-pmc7887664:
Tennison and co-authors report a carbon footprint assessment of the NHS in England. Health care protects public health, but it also produces large greenhouse gas emissions. The NHS has tracked and tried to cut its footprint since 2008. This account updates that record through 2019.

The team used a hybrid model that blends broad economic data with detailed local figures. In 2019 the service's emissions totalled 25 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. That was a reduction of 26% since 1990. Of the 2019 total, 62% came from the supply chain. Direct care made up 24%, and travel by staff, patients, and visitors made up 10%. The authors call the work the longest national accounting of its kind. It shows other health systems where their own cuts can bite hardest.
europmc-pmc7920964:
Lozano and co-authors report an experiment on how microplastics change soil and plant growth. Microplastics reach soil in many shapes and polymer types. Little was known about how those traits alter soil traits or plant performance. The team set out to test shape, polymer, and dose together.

They mixed 12 microplastics into soil at four low concentrations. The shapes were fibers, films, foams, and fragments. Carrots grew in each pot for 4 weeks. All shapes raised plant biomass. Shoot mass rose by about 27% with fibers and about 60% with films. The shapes work in different ways, such as holding water or loosening the soil. Yet all shapes cut soil aggregation by about 25%. The study shows that the form of a microplastic matters as much as its amount.
europmc-pmc7934264:
Han and co-authors present a review of the hurdles facing multicellular tumour spheroids in early drug research. Spheroids are balls of tumour cells grown in three dimensions. They sit between flat cell cultures and real tumours in how complex they are. In shape, gradients, and growth pace they mimic solid tumours well. That makes them a hopeful platform for drug screening.

Cells in a spheroid touch neighbours and matrix much as they do in the body. Oxygen and nutrient levels fall toward the centre, as in a real mass. Yet the model is still little used in preclinical work. The review sets out why. Making uniform spheroids, reading results, and scaling up all pose problems. The authors survey the fixes now being tried. Their aim is to move a strong model from promise into routine use.
europmc-pmc7946264:
Wile presents a study of the worship of Asklepios, the Greek god of healing. The paper was read at Athens in August 1925. The cult began with a man and ended with a god, Wile writes. One estimate counts more than 300 shrines, with solid references for 207 of them. Centres of the cult included Tricca, Cos, Pergamos, Epidaurus, and Rome.

Two buildings draw his special attention: the tholos and the theater. Both stood within the great healing sanctuaries. The paper links them to the rites by which the sick sought cures in sleep. Homer knew Asklepios only as a Thessalian chief, father of two army doctors. From that start the cult spread across the ancient world. Wile traces its growth and its meaning at each stage.
europmc-pmc7999964:
Jacob and co-authors present a review of hydrogels in drug delivery, tissue building, and wound care. Hydrogels are water-rich gels whose traits can be tuned with care. They can hold small drugs and large protein drugs alike. They flex, hold water, and break down at a set pace. Those gifts have made them a favourite base material across medicine. The review maps how far their role has spread.

Ways to improve plain gels lead the account, including DNA-based gels. Cross-linking methods are compared in tables of strengths and flaws. Delivery through the cheek, mouth, and skin gets full cover. Composite gels built for wound dressings follow. Gel nanoparticles that aim drugs inside cells are explained as well. Tissue building and contact lenses round out the uses, with shop products named.
europmc-pmc8271064:
Liu and co-authors review metal- and metal oxide-based nanozymes, their traits, and their uses. Nanozymes are built materials that act like enzymes. Natural enzymes catalyse with great speed and precision, but they are fragile.

The review sorts nanozyme designs and their built-in properties. It explains the catalytic routes each type follows. Uses in biological analysis lead the applications. Others include easing inflammation and fighting bacteria. Cancer therapy with nanozymes also appears. Their toughness and low cost drive the interest. The authors weigh what still limits these enzyme stand-ins. Design choices set how strong and selective each nanozyme is.
europmc-pmc8356364:
Honorato and co-authors describe the WeNMR-EOSC ecosystem for structural biology computing. Structural biology reads the shapes of biological molecules at atomic detail. Those shapes explain most cell processes.

Since 2010, the WeNMR project has run web services for the field. They ride on European high-throughput computing grids. Later projects folded the services into the European Open Science Cloud. Users run advanced tools through a browser, not local clusters. Health and food science both draw on the platform. The paper maps the services and their shared base. Access, not hardware, is the point.
europmc-pmc8481764:
Galea reviews the blood-brain barrier in body-wide infection and inflammation. This barrier is a tightly run interface between blood and brain. It shields neurons while still signaling illness to the brain. That signal drives the protective sickness response.

As inflammation grows stronger or lasts longer, the barrier leaks more. Lymphocytes cross in greater numbers, and innate immune cells move in. Vessel lining damage can occur, and brain function then falters into encephalopathy. Many moderators shape the response, from sex and genes to gut imbalance. Galea argues that naming these factors is key to explaining varied study results.
europmc-pmc8544364:
Saginala and co-authors review the epidemiology of melanoma, a serious skin cancer. Melanoma makes up a small share of world cancer cases but kills at high rates when caught late. Its incidence climbs in rich, fair-skinned countries. Sun exposure without protection is the chief risk factor.

Death rates in the United States fell over the past decade as new drugs arrived. Ten targeted or immune agents won approval since 2011, per the authors. Half of cases carry a BRAF mutation that oral drug pairs can strike. Most patients are white, older men, with a mean diagnosis age of 65 years. Sun safety campaigns in Australia curbed rates there.
europmc-pmc8648564:
van Rheenen and co-authors report a genome-wide study of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a fatal nerve disease. The study held 29,612 patients and 122,656 controls across ancestry groups. It aimed to find gene regions that raise risk. Lifestyle risk claims from past work were also tested with gene-based methods.

The study found 15 risk regions. Extra data from whole-genome sequencing helped pin down likely genes. Risk regions overlapped with other brain diseases but in distinct patterns. Gene tests pointed to a causal role for high cholesterol. All signals together implicate transport of vesicles and cell cleanup paths. The authors argue the disease may start inside glutamate-using nerve cells.
europmc-pmc8658264:
Roger, Tomas, and Gire review how cells enter senescence, a lasting stop in cell division. Senescent cells stay alive and active. They release inflammatory and tissue-cutting factors. Many DNA damage signals can push a cell into this state.

Such cells build up in tissues with age and in disease. Each cell type reaches the state by a distinct path. Still, all must survive without dividing and mute their damage alarms. The review traces how their gene programs, metabolism, and structure change over time. Shared traits define the state across cell types. The authors link this knowledge to cancer control and healthy aging.
europmc-pmc8769664:
Wolter and co-authors assess the clinical severity of Omicron infections in South Africa through linked national data. Omicron was identified there in November 2021 as cases rose. A gene test failure served as a proxy for the variant. The team linked case, lab, genome, and hospital data for the country.

From October to early December 2021, 161,328 cases were reported. The proxy marker rose from 3.2 percent to 97.9 percent of tested cases in weeks. People with proxy infections had far lower odds of hospital admission. Their odds were 0.2 times those of other infections at the time. Once in hospital, severity odds looked similar.
europmc-pmc8831564:
Liu and co-authors build a risk score for colorectal cancer from immune-linked long noncoding RNAs. These RNA molecules shape immune behavior in tumors. Their clinical value, though, was largely untested. The team used machine learning to combine many candidate RNAs. The result is a consensus signature called IRLS. They checked it against survival and treatment response.

IRLS predicted overall survival on its own. It beat standard clinical measures and 109 published signatures in accuracy. High-risk patients gained more from fluorouracil-based chemotherapy. Low-risk patients gained more from bevacizumab. The low-risk group also showed rich lymphocyte infiltration. Its tumors expressed more CD8A and PD-L1, and answered pembrolizumab. The authors offer IRLS as a tool for personal care.
europmc-pmc8834764:
Edú-Valsania, Laguía, and Moriano review the theory and measurement of burnout. Burnout grows out of chronic stress at work. Interest in workplace health rose sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic. The review first traces how the burnout concept developed. It sets out the syndrome's dimensions. It then asks what conditions trigger it.

The authors sort triggers into job factors and personal factors. They list effects on workers and on organizations. Prevention and reduction strategies follow. A large section covers tools built to measure burnout. Some tools suit any job; others fit one occupation. The review also sums up a special journal issue on the topic. Readers get both the science and the practical state of the field.
europmc-pmc8938264:
Pérez-Then and co-authors measure antibody responses after a mixed vaccine schedule against COVID-19 variants. Participants first got two doses of CoronaVac, an inactivated vaccine. A Pfizer mRNA booster followed. The team checked neutralization against three virus forms. The ancestral strain, Delta, and Omicron were tested. Two CoronaVac doses alone left Omicron neutralization undetectable. The booster changed the picture sharply.

After boosting, antibody levels and neutralization jumped. Titers against the ancestral virus and Delta matched two-dose mRNA results. Omicron neutralization rose 1.4-fold above the two-dose mRNA level. Even so, Omicron titers stayed 7.1-fold below ancestral ones. They sat 3.6-fold below Delta. The authors draw a clear policy line. Countries that used CoronaVac need boosters. Variant escape makes them urgent, not optional.
europmc-pmc8963864:
Naik and co-authors ask who bears responsibility when artificial intelligence errs in healthcare. AI now supports diagnosis, research, and drug work. Errors in care can devastate patients. Yet no clear rules assign blame for AI mistakes. Privacy, surveillance, and bias worries compound the problem. Data breaches add a security layer. The review works through these legal and ethical knots. It highlights transparency as a recurring demand.

The authors survey AI uses in health research first. Drug development applications follow. Ethical challenges get a full section. Global legislation is compared across regions. A central section asks why responsibility is necessary. The next asks who should bear it. Developers, doctors, and institutions all face claims. Bias in AI systems is treated separately. The authors call for defined regulation. Patients meet doctors at their most vulnerable, they remind readers.
europmc-pmc9122264:
Gideon and co-authors profile lung granulomas in macaques to find what marks control of tuberculosis. Granulomas are mixed cell clusters that form around the TB bacterium in the lung. Some clear the bacteria, while others let them persist and grow. The team matched imaging, single-cell RNA data, and measures of bacterial clearance.

Granulomas that failed were rich in mast, endothelial, fibroblast, and plasma cells. Their signals favored type 2 immunity and wound healing. Granulomas that won held more type 1 and type 17 T cells and killer T cells. Later granulomas tended to be more restrictive. The results point to host targets for new TB vaccines and drugs.
europmc-pmc9266664:
Ho and co-authors review microRNA-based diagnosis and therapy. MicroRNAs are small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression. Shifts in their levels change many gene profiles and contribute to human disorders. They are stable in body fluids, which suits them as biomarkers.

The review explains how microRNAs move inside and outside cells. It then covers how circulating microRNAs are measured, plus technical pitfalls that skew levels. Panels already available for clinical use are highlighted. A second half turns to microRNAs as drugs themselves. Clinical trials of such therapies are updated in detail. The authors see strong potential for breakthroughs in treating many diseases through this route.
europmc-pmc9341364:
Ahmed and co-authors review how gut microbe metabolites drive talks between gut and brain. Microbes reshape food and host molecules into many small products. These travel through immune, nerve, and hormone routes to reach the brain. Changes in gut microbes are tied to developmental, degenerative, and mental disorders.

Single metabolites may act as key messengers on this axis. The review covers products under 1,600 daltons with known nerve effects. Some calm or stir inflammation; others feed cells or tune transmitters. Roles in barrier strength and brain development are detailed. The authors ask whether diet or microbe treatments could prevent brain disease. They stress that the exact molecular paths still need proof. Human trials remain the missing step.
europmc-pmc9428564:
Pathak and co-authors present a broad review of pesticide effects and greener ways to clean them up. Pesticides are natural or synthetic compounds used against pests in farming, forestry, and fish work. Their toxicity reaches far past the target pests. Global use leaves traces in soil and water.

The review first sorts pesticides by type and toxicity grade. It then traces their move through ecosystems. Chapters cover harm to soil life, fish, and plant growth. Human health effects include gene damage, cancer, allergies, and asthma. The last part turns to bioremediation as a fix. Bacteria, fungi, plants, and microalgae can break pesticides down. The authors urge work on strong microbes and new genes for waste cleanup.
europmc-pmc9792464:
Yang and co-authors build GatorTron, a large language model trained for electronic health records. Clinical notes hold rich patient detail in loose text form. Few language models are trained on that kind of writing. The largest clinical model before held just 110 million parameters.

GatorTron trained from scratch on over 90 billion words. More than 82 billion of those words were de-identified clinical text. The model scaled up to billions of parameters in size. The team tested it on five clinical language tasks. Finding concepts and relations in notes were two of them. Judging text likeness and logical inference came next. Answering medical questions rounded out the task set. Bigger models and bigger training sets both lifted scores. Accuracy on inference and question tasks rose by about a tenth. The models were released for other teams to use.
europmc-pmc9801064:
Zheng and co-authors upgrade SynergyFinder, a tool for reading drug combination screening data. Drug pairs are proposed to lift cancer treatment results. Screens test many pairs across cell models at once. Reading which pairs truly synergize takes careful math.

The Plus update adds five main advances to the package. Models now handle combinations of three or more drugs. Dimension cutting gives clear maps of synergy landscapes. Statistics now come with confidence ranges and P values. A synergy barometer blends scoring methods into one consensus. The tool also judges clinical promise without bias. Fast notes on drugs and cell lines were added. Those notes carry chemical and target details for each entry. A web server makes the package easy to reach. The authors aim for clearer hits from combo screens.
europmc-pmc9805564:
Fang, Liu, and Peltz present GSEApy, a Python package for gene set enrichment analysis. The method checks if gene groups shift together in data. Existing tools struggle with very large data sets. Single-cell studies produce exactly that kind of bulk.

GSEApy runs from the command line or inside Python code. Its core is rewritten in Rust for speed gains. The Rust build runs threefold faster than the older build. It also uses over fourfold less memory per run. Scores match the reference method's enrichment statistic. The package links Python to the Enrichr web service. That link adds over-representation tests for gene lists. A BioMart bridge widens the annotation reach further. Several sub-tools each serve one analysis style. The authors aim to make big gene studies routine.
europmc-pmc9834364:
Eisenberg and co-authors issue the 2022 joint indications for metabolic and bariatric surgery. Two surgical societies wrote the statement together. It replaces guidance that dated back three decades. The old rules set surgery bars that no longer fit evidence.

Surgery is now recommended above a BMI of 35 outright. That holds whether or not other illnesses are present. Patients with metabolic disease at lower BMI should be considered. Cutoffs drop further for Asian patients in the update. Long term data show the surgery is safe and effective. Chosen children and teens may also qualify now. The statement covers surgery as a bridge to other care. Joint replacement and transplant paths get attention too. High risk patients, including the very heavy, are addressed. Cancer risk and death rate gains are reviewed. Lifelong follow up after surgery remains a firm rule.
europmc-pmc9977964:
Wang and co-authors survey p53 pathways as targets for cancer therapy. The TP53 gene is the most often altered gene in human cancers. Its protein, p53, switches on genes that guard the genome. It controls cell cycle, apoptosis, and genomic stability.

New work shows p53 also steers metabolism, ferroptosis, and autophagy. It shapes the tumor microenvironment as well. Mutations can strip its protective role and add cancer-driving traits. For years p53 was called undruggable, and progress stayed slow. The review covers pathway mechanisms and key protein structures. It shows how mutations inactivate the protein. Past therapy efforts and their clinical hurdles are weighed. The authors map where p53 drug work stands now.
experiments-and-considerations-touching-:
Boyle's Experiments and Considerations Touching Colours opens his experimental history of colors. Robert Boyle, a Fellow of the Royal Society, wrote it first as essays to a friend. The London title page is dated MDCLXIV, or 1664. Its motto from Bacon urges finding what nature does, not inventing schemes.

In the preface Boyle defends giving facts without a full theory. He calls his design historical rather than dogmatical. New trials and observations make up the body of the treatise. Speculative hints are added, but they serve the record of experiments. Boyle hoped they might help frame a solid hypothesis later. The book models his broader program for experimental natural philosophy.
five-years-in-new-zealand-1859-to-1864:
Booth recalls a young man's emigration in Five Years in New Zealand, printed in 1912. Robert B. Booth was an engineer who sailed in 1859 and stayed to 1864. His contents promise a full colonial tale: rats on board, a white squall, a shark harpooned, twins buried at sea, and icebergs on the way to Port Lyttelton.

On land he and a friend went as cadets on a sheep run near Nelson, then worked as shepherds. He joined a survey party to the Ashburton, hunted wild pigs, rode stock, and took work with a bush contractor before turning south to the gold diggings. The sampled pages find the party at a rough bush inn. They sup on boiled mutton and damper at a table of boxes, sleep on the floor, and cross the Waitaki in the morning to reach Dunedin by ten.
fossil-man-abbeville-again-1864:
An unsigned piece in the Anthropological Review took up the Abbeville fossil man row once more in 1864. Its blunt title ends with the word 'Again.' The row dealt with a jaw found at Moulin-Quignon, near Abbeville in France, the year past.

Fresh bones kept turning up, and each new find fed the fight on both sides. The piece tells where the row stood, what was claimed, and what was doubted or charged as fraud. It shows a key case of man's deep age stuck in doubt, in the words of its own time.
french-art-of-distillation-1664:
John French teaches distillation in The Art of Distillation, from 1664, a great English manual of the craft. Stills draw out the virtues of plants, minerals, and animals drop by drop. Waters, oils, and spirits for medicine fill his practical, workmanlike pages of recipes and furnace lore for the laboratory.

French writes for the working chemist of the seventeenth century here. Herbs for the sick, metals for the seeker, all pass through his alembics. The book blends alchemy's aims with a tradesman's plain method throughout. It served as the chemist's handbook before chemistry had the name, a bridge between the spagyric art of Paracelsus and the science that followed.
frus-1861-d164:
William Preston wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 May 1861. Preston had lately held the Madrid post for the United States. The dispatch is document 164 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Preston's letter comes from the handover season in Spain, as Schurz came to take the post. An outgoing envoy's report could still guide the new chief at home. His May page adds a Kentucky voice to the Spanish file of 1861. Preston, a Kentuckian of the old school, knew Spain from his years at its court. A clear thread in the whole volume runs through the hands of such aides.
frus-1861-d264:
30 October 1861 brought James Shepherd Pike a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 264 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the autumn of the war's first year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d64:
From Washington on 29 July 1861, William H. Seward addressed a letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 64 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A week after Bull Run, Seward's aim abroad was plain: no panic, no threats, no open door. This late July letter carries that aim to London. It shows a Secretary chastened by defeat at home but steady in his handling of the most risky front of the war. A week of such letters rebuilt abroad the calm that Bull Run had broken at home. Calm rebuilt abroad was worth regiments to a cause that had lost its first battle.
frus-1862-d164:
Dated 20 October 1862, Document 164 is a Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the State Department's yearly account of its work abroad during the Civil War.

The tempo of the London mail tells its own story: letters every few days, each one short and businesslike. Through them Washington tracked British shipyards building warships for the South, a sore point Adams raised again and again. This dispatch belongs to that grinding, vital strand of the wartime correspondence. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d264:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, opened April with a dispatch to William L. Dayton in Paris dated 1 April 1862, printed as Document 264 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

April 1862 would bring Shiloh's slaughter and the fall of New Orleans. Events that cut both ways in foreign eyes: proof of Union power and proof of the war's cost. Seward wrote at the month's start with his usual aim, to keep France from giving the South the one thing it lacked, a great-power friend. The letter starts the spring run of the Paris file. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d364:
Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 May 1862, in a letter printed as Document 364 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mercier wrote three weeks after his return from Richmond, where his April visit had stirred Union anger and Confederate hope. Relations between the minister and the Department were strained that spring. A letter from his hand in mid-May belongs to the repair and testing that followed. Both men were sounding out how much trust the channel still held. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862.
frus-1862-d464:
On 25 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to George Perkins Marsh, the American minister to Italy at Turin. The instruction is Document 464 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Marsh had spent the summer reporting Italian goodwill, and Seward's late-August order reached him as Union armies fell back in Virginia. Italy's government, still securing its new unity, had every reason to wish the Union well and little power to help it. Instructions to friendly but minor courts still mattered: they kept sympathy alive and denied Confederate agents any opening. The dispatch shows Seward tending the whole map of Europe, not just its great capitals, in a hard month.
frus-1862-d564:
On 14 January 1862 Henry Shelton Sanford reported from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward, five days after his previous dispatch. The report is Document 564 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Sanford's quick second letter of the year is characteristic: he wrote when he had something, not on a fixed day. Brussels gave him early word of moves in London and Paris, and January 1862 was full of moves, as Europe digested the Trent settlement. His reports fed Seward's sense of where the real dangers lay. The Belgian file's value lies in this flow of well-placed observation, offered by a minister who treated information as the whole of his job.
frus-1862-d64:
15 May 1862 is the date on a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 64 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d664:
On 1 August 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote straight to the ministers for foreign affairs of Japan. Most letters in this file went through the American legation; this one speaks government to government. It is document 664 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Direct notes like this one carried the formal voice of the United States to the shogun's court. They dealt in the courtesies and claims that held the young tie between the two lands in place. The letter is a rare formal piece in a file of working mail. It shows Washington treating Japan as a full partner in talks, not a mere port of call.
frus-1863p1-d164:
On 22 April 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 164 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a late-April letter held the day's last point for the London brief. Seward's pairs, all through this file, let each claim stand on its own page. This one closes both the pair and the three-day run behind it. Read in line, the run shows a secretary who treated the British file as the war's second front. He staffed it with paper as others staffed forts.
frus-1863p1-d264:
On 20 August 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 264 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Mail crossed the Atlantic by steamship, taking roughly ten days or more each way. News in a dispatch like this one was already old when Seward read it, yet it guided his next orders. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d364:
The British minister in Washington, Lord Lyons, took up his pen on 17 January 1863 to write Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is document 364 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The channel between Lyons and Seward was the main safety valve of Anglo-American relations in the war. Papers like this one are the valve at work. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d464:
Dated 16 April 1863, document 464 is a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d564:
Writing on 15 June 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington in an official letter. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d64:
From the State Department on 26 January 1863 went this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 64 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, answering the thick mail Adams had sent that month.

Seward's letters did more than reply. They set the claims Adams was to press and the tone he was to use with Lord Russell. By early 1863 the two men had a rhythm: reports in by steamer, orders out by the next. This letter is one turn of that wheel, sent in the depths of a war winter.
frus-1863p1-d664:
Document 664, dated 14 November 1863, records a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d164: The British delegation to the Moscow Conference set down a memorandum dated October 24, 1943, preserved as Document 164 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Delegations traded such papers to state a position in writing where speeches might blur it, and the American editors kept this British text among their own files. The record gives the source and the date. The memorandum is printed in the Foreign Relations series' Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d264: A luncheon meeting at Cairo on 24 November 1943 between General Marshall and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek left no official record, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. Later that afternoon Marshall reported to the Combined Chiefs of Staff on a discussion with Chiang about proposed operations in the Southeast Asia Command. The editors presume that discussion took place at this luncheon. The Stilwell Papers show that Stilwell and Madame Chiang were also present. Where the luncheon was held is not indicated.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d364:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Tehran on 29 November 1943, at half past ten in the morning, record the first three-power military session. General Sir Alan Brooke leads, running through the war as the British see it, with General Marshall invited to interrupt where he disagrees.

Brooke's theme is keeping German divisions pinned down during the five or six months before Overlord can sail, at the earliest on 1 May. In Italy, amphibious hooks around the flanks should drive the Germans north of Rome and wreck the eleven or twelve divisions in the south. In Yugoslavia, where he counts twenty-one German and eight Bulgarian divisions, the Partisans should get arms and air help to deepen German troubles. Turkey's entry, he adds, holds great military advantage, whatever the politics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d464:
John J. McCloy, the Assistant Secretary of War, wrote to John Gilbert Winant, the American ambassador in London, on December 2, 1943. The letter falls between the Tehran Conference, which had ended the day before, and the Second Cairo Conference, which opened on December 4. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

McCloy was one of the War Department's central fixers, and Winant was Washington's man at the center of the British war effort. Their exchange belongs to the back-channel traffic that kept the alliance running while the leaders traveled. Readers see how business moved between Washington and London even at the height of summit season.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d564:
Harry Dexter White, assistant to the Secretary of the Treasury, wrote this memorandum on August 13, 1944. White was the Treasury's chief technical mind and a main designer of the postwar monetary system agreed at Bretton Woods that summer. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

White's papers matter because the peace was being designed in economic offices while armies fought. Questions of money, trade, and Germany's economic future ran from Tehran's discussions into the Quebec Conference that autumn. For readers, this memorandum shows the Treasury's hand in that design work, written by the official who more than any other shaped America's postwar financial plans.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d64: On October 27, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek, less than a month before the two men were to meet at Cairo. The letter is Document 64 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Keeping China's leader close was a steady task for Washington that fall. The record supplies the date and the names and leaves the subject to the text. It is part of the Foreign Relations series' road to the Cairo Conference.
frus-1944-quebec-d164:
Abbot Moffat, chief of the Division of Southwest Pacific Affairs, sent Hull a short covering note on September 8, 1944. It introduces the attached memorandum for the president on Indochina and Southeast Asia, the long paper that follows it in the volume. Moffat explains why policies toward Indochina appear inside a broader Southeast Asia paper.

The policies, he writes, were included to stress correlating Indochina with the other regions of Southeast Asia. They stated the objectives the department's European, Far Eastern, and Near Eastern offices agreed were most desirable. If Churchill raised the subject at Quebec, the president would have them before him. The department also hoped for basic guidance to develop its own policies and procedures.
frus-1944-quebec-d264:
One sentence kept the Octagon basic policies from full agreement, and the secretaries' note C.C.S. 654/8 of September 12, 1944, isolates it. Every other policy for the final report to Roosevelt and Churchill had been settled informally before the conference. The exception was paragraph 6(i), on reorienting forces from Europe to the Pacific as a matter of highest priority.

The British text spoke of regard to other inescapable commitments. The American text said agreed commitments instead. The difference mattered. Britain feared being trapped by promises; America feared unilateral excuses. The Combined Chiefs were asked to decide. Their eventual compromise kept both words: agreed and/or inescapable.
frus-1944-quebec-d64:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on September 12, 1944, the opening day of the Second Quebec Conference. The two men were in the same city, yet the written habit held. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Letters exchanged inside a conference fixed points between sessions and carried proposals too formal for talk. Churchill, installed at the Citadel with Roosevelt, used paper as he always did. For readers, an opening-day message shows the conference starting in the leaders' own words, at the summit remembered for the Morgenthau Plan and the final division of the war's work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d164:
A telegram from the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy) reached President Truman on 21 August 1946. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 164, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Replies in the same file show the exchange from both sides. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d264:
Dated 31 March 1948, this memorandum runs from the Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs (Allen) to Acting Secretary of State Lovett. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 264 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d364:
Dated 9 February 1949, this memorandum runs from the Chief of the Intelligence Coordinating and Planning Staff (Childs) to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. It survives in print as document 364 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d64:
Sidney Souers, deputy director of naval intelligence, wrote to Clark Clifford on 27 December 1945. Clifford was then a naval aide and adviser at the White House, close to President Truman. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

This letter is a hinge in the volume. Within weeks, Souers would become the first director of central intelligence, and Clifford one of the new system's architects. A paper between them, days before the January directive, shows the settlement being readied by the men who would run it. Readers should mark the names: the volume's story turns here from tearing down the wartime service to staffing the peacetime one that replaced it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d164:
The Polish ambassador brought his government's latest terms to Washington on 22 January 1945. Acting Secretary Grew sent them to the President the next day with a cool judgment. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, finds no real basis for an approach to Moscow in them.

The London Poles would rather leave frontiers until the war ends. But they will talk now, if gains in the north and west make up for losses in the east. They seek an alliance with Moscow inside the new world body. They refuse one-sided solutions and claim the right to order their own home life. If Moscow will not negotiate, they propose an inter-allied military commission to run local rule in Poland for those loyal to London.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d264:
The Joint Staff Planners sent the chiefs a fresh report on Russia and Japan on 18 January 1945. Their paper, J. C. S. 1176/6, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It was drawn up on the planners' own initiative, and a memorandum by General Arnold rides with it as an enclosure.

The coming allied staff conference at Malta, the report begins, offers a favorable chance to advance American planning. That planning rests on Russian participation in the war against Japan. General Deane's recent talks in Moscow had aimed at the information and agreements the planners need. They had not yet been able to win them. The report therefore goes to the Joint Chiefs for their consideration, days before the President's party sails for the Crimea.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d364: The Joint Chiefs asked the President to intervene in person in this short memorandum of February 6, 1945. They judged it necessary to win Stalin's approval for a meeting with the Soviet staff. The subject was details of possible Soviet participation in the war against Japan. They suggested Roosevelt speak to Stalin to obtain his agreement. An endorsement on the paper records that Admiral Leahy delivered it to the President that afternoon, at 4:15. The few lines trace how a staff question became a leader's errand.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d464:
Hiss's notes of the final foreign ministers' meeting, February 11, 1945, return to the question of credit. Bridges reported on the communiqué text. Molotov relayed Stalin's view: the communiqué should say what was agreed on voting, not that the President's proposal had been adopted. No other place, Molotov noted, said on whose initiative a step was taken.

Stettinius answered that the point had been discussed that morning with Stalin and the President present. It would be very hard for him to agree to strike the reference. Molotov replied there had been no agreement on this special point. The notes break off mid-bargain, with the wording — and the credit — still contested.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d64:
President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin on 22 January 1945 to settle press rules for the conference code-named Argonaut. His short top secret telegram is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It carries the plan already agreed with Churchill.

Roosevelt says he has decided to have no press representatives at the meeting. Only a small group of uniformed photographers from the American Navy will take the pictures the leaders want. He notes that Churchill agrees. Stalin's reply, quoted in the editors' note, raised no objections and said the same answer had gone to the Prime Minister.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d164:
Secretary Stettinius commented on the draft American agenda from San Francisco on June 22, 1945. His telegram to Grew is document 164 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It works through the items in Noyes's list of June 20, point by point.

Stettinius asks whether free access for foreign correspondents in places like Yugoslavia, Poland, and Czechoslovakia has been considered. On Italy, he wants the item on joining the United Nations moved to last place, and asks whether abolishing the Advisory Council for Italy should be raised. On international bases, he advises that the United States not take the lead in proposing discussion, though the delegation should be ready if others raise it. The comments show the agenda being sharpened at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d264:
A briefing paper traced the long history of international control of the Danube, dated July 6, 1945. The paper is document 264 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It gave Truman's staff the legal background for a question the settlement would raise: who governs Europe's greatest river.

The principles began with the Treaty of Vienna in 1815: navigation free to all nations, no charges beyond the cost of upkeep, and rules set by common consent of the river states. The Treaty of Paris in 1856 applied them to the Danube and created a European Commission to run its maritime section. After the First World War the Danube was declared an international river. By 1945 the Soviet Union held both banks of the lower river and meant to run it alone, which the West resisted.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d364:
Frustration boils over in Pauley's letter of July 3, 1945, to Maisky, chairman of the Reparations Commission in Moscow. For the third time, Pauley writes, Maisky had put off the Commission's full meeting. The meeting was to discuss the Soviet proposal set out in Maisky's own Memorandum No. 2, the plan named in the Crimea Protocol.

The American delegation, Pauley notes, had now waited twenty-two days in Moscow. It had not received a single figure to support the Soviet proposal. Nor had Moscow tried to explain the plan's basis to the Americans or, so far as he knew, the British. The letter is a formal protest against allied stalling.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d464:
Italy is redefined as an American interest in an undated briefing book paper on policy toward that country. The objective, it states, is to strengthen Italy economically and politically. A stronger Italy could withstand the forces that threaten to sweep her into a new totalitarianism. The paper lists those forces one by one.

They include economic distress and national humiliation. They include doubt about British intentions, and about America's readiness to carry out a friendly policy. They include Soviet power, shown in Tito's nearly successful move in Venezia Giulia, a well organized Communist party, and no real experience of democratic government. American troops, it notes, are being withdrawn, and with them a sense of protection.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d564:
A secret priority wire from Belgrade charge Harold Shantz reached Washington on June 21, 1945. It is document 564 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports the signing of the Duino military deals and the gap left in them.

Shantz cites a British colonel who said the deals were signed without article 3 of the Belgrade agreement. The Yugoslavs meant to raise that point again at government level. They hoped to have their liberation committee named the sole agency under Allied military government. Shantz adds that the Yugoslav press twists the U.S. stand, since the Belgrade text was never published there. He suggests Washington and London issue a joint statement of facts and broadcast it into Yugoslavia.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d64:
Churchill proposed a royal visit to Berlin in telegram number 92 to President Truman, sent June 15, 1945. It is document 64 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. King George VI would be in France and Germany inspecting his troops while the Big Three met, and he wished to spend a day in Berlin.

Churchill's plan has the King take no part in the talks. He would lunch with the Russians if Stalin agreed, then dine in the British sector with Truman and Stalin as fellow heads of state, and leave early the next day. The King would also hand out decorations to Allied officers. Churchill says he has sent the same news to Stalin and asks Truman's view so he can advise the King.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d664:
Ambassador Caffery described a British bid to read Soviet motives on Tangier from Paris on July 4, 1945. His secret wire is document 664 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports a talk with Peake, head of the British team at the talks.

Peake read out a private letter he had sent to the Foreign Office. In it he guessed that Moscow wanted above all to embarrass Franco's Spain. A foothold at Tangier, he thought, would aid a subversive campaign against Franco. The U.S. team found that reading plausible, but framed the issue more widely. They saw an expanding Russian interest in the Mediterranean at work. As a way out, they proposed a Soviet observer, drawn from the Paris embassy, to follow the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1064:
Soviet delegates presented this proposal on Greece to the foreign ministers on July 20, 1945. It is framed under the Yalta Declaration on Liberated Europe. The printed text gives extracts only; the remaining paragraphs appear elsewhere in the volume. Greece, the paper charges, still lacks due order, and law goes unrespected there.

Terror, it says, rages against the democratic elements who bore the main burden of fighting the German invaders. The Greek government is also accused of breaking the peace with its neighbors, threatening Albania and Bulgaria. The Soviets urge urgent measures. One is to press Greece's Regent to build a democratic government at once, in the spirit of the Varkiza Agreement of February 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1164:
Nikolai Novikov, secretary of the Soviet team at Potsdam, wrote to Assistant Secretary Dunn on 23 July 1945. Team secretaries handled the daily traffic between the three staffs. They passed papers, set up meetings, and smoothed the small frictions that summits breed.

A note from one team's office to another's is backstage work. No speeches ride on it, but the talks could not run without it. This one shows the Soviet staff writing to the American staff in the ordinary way of business. Readers rarely see this layer of a summit. Here it survives in the record, dated and signed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1264:
On 21 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Behind each choice the leaders made stood staff work of this kind. The chiefs' papers turned the services' knowledge into advice the team could weigh at the table.

By the end of the first week the chiefs had a full file running at Potsdam. Their notes covered the fronts and the forces that would hold the peace. This memorandum is one entry in that file. It shows the staff-level writing under the headline choices, done by the men who would have to make those choices work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1364:
The State, War, and Navy Coordinating Committee sent a paper to its own panel at Babelsberg on 18 July 1945. Babelsberg was the suburb of Potsdam where the American delegation lived and worked during the conference. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A committee in Washington writing to its forward panel shows how the summit was staffed. Men at Babelsberg needed questions answered and positions cleared by the home machinery, and this paper is part of that flow. It gives readers a rare look at the plumbing of a summit. The staffs pass paper between Germany and Washington to keep the talks fed, far from the leaders' photograph.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-164:
A second set of State Department minutes records further business on August 1, 1945. The closing day held more than one meeting, and staff minuted each. This set joins the other records of the final day in the second Potsdam volume. Together they cover the conference's last working hours.

Two formal records for one day show the end's density. As one session closed, another took up the next task. Readers can follow the handoffs in sequence. The minutes preserve the order in which the last business was cleared. They give the conference a fully written finish, not a fade.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-64:
Truman and Churchill conferred for an hour at Truman's quarters on July 22, 1945, beginning at 12:15. No official record of the talk's substance has been found. An editorial note in volume two covers the meeting, resting its account on the President's log.

The editors connect the talk to the atomic report Churchill had read that morning. They quote his memoir account of inviting the President to confer with him forthwith. General Marshall and Admiral Leahy were with Truman at the meeting, Churchill writes. The editors also quote Truman's own memoirs on the decision at stake. The final decision of where and when to use the atomic bomb was up to me, Truman writes. He regarded the bomb as a military weapon and never doubted it should be used. Churchill, he adds, unhesitatingly favored its use if it might aid in ending the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d764:
Kirk wrote again from Rome on July 29, 1945, in document 764. The ambassador in Italy kept the Acting Secretary supplied as Potsdam neared its end. Two reports in three days suggest pressing business. This one joined the second Potsdam volume beside its fellow.

Repeat reports let readers watch a situation move. Kirk could update facts and shift his advice as news arrived. The letter shows the tempo of an embassy in a fast week. It also shows Italy's stake in Potsdam: a beaten ally of Germany, now pleading its case through men like Kirk.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d864:
American advisers at Potsdam drafted this undated working paper to suggest edits to the proposed agreement on Germany. The agreement covered the political and economic principles for the first period of Allied control. The paper responds to the text sent to the foreign secretaries by the Economic Sub-Committee.

The paper proposes new wording for paragraph 13, on treating Germany as a single economic unit. It would add finance, transport, and communications to the fields needing common policy. It also asks to strike or rewrite a clause on foreign grants and credits to Germany. Readers can watch American drafters tighten the deal line by line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d964:
William Clayton sent the Secretary of State a joint memorandum on art objects on July 30, 1945. The enclosure, signed by Clayton and Edwin Pauley, gives their views to General Clay. It sorts looted and stored art in the American zone into three classes, from clearly stolen public works to German-owned pieces stored for safety.

Clayton and Pauley back quick return of the first two classes to their countries of origin. The third class, true German property, may be shipped to America for care by museums. They insist no final fate be promised for it now. Any such move must be announced as safekeeping only, pending later Allied decisions.
frus-1951-54Iran-d164: The State Department cabled the Embassy in Iran on February 27, 1953, in this short top secret message. The Shah seemed set on leaving Iran, and Mosadeq held that he should go. Washington saw little it could usefully do to stop the departure. The Department asked the Embassy for its reading of the crisis. It planned to play down the event to the press. Still, it feared headlines would say the Shah had fled, as Farouk had.
frus-1955-57v16-d264: An editorial note in the Suez volume fills a gap in the record. No formal memo of Harold Macmillan's White House talk with President Eisenhower has been found. At 11:20 a.m., Secretary Dulles phoned the President to ask what was said. Eisenhower reported that Macmillan spoke in a mild tone. The issue, Macmillan granted, was Nasser more than the Canal. The two also weighed the Users' Association as a way to keep the Canal open.
frus-1969-76v32-d264: An editorial note in Volume XXXII of the 1969-1976 series prints sharp messages of April 23, 1972, from Kissinger's secret Moscow trip. Haig relays Nixon's worry that Rogers and Smith had matched Kissinger's arms gains in Vienna. Kissinger replies that the Washington view is absurd. He says the Soviets gave firm terms only through his channel. Nixon's own message warns that the summit will be judged on Vietnam. The note shows credit for the arms breakthrough fought over before it was announced.
gao-gaoreports-b-295764:
Mathews Associates, Inc., brought the protest in GAO files B-295764 and B-295764.2, decided on April 20, 2005. The Army had cut the firm's offer from the competitive range in a buy of lithium manganese dioxide batteries. The award was to be made on a best value basis, with up to two contracts in prospect. The firm said its offer had been misjudged. GAO denied the protest. The digest states the ground in short form: the agency fairly found the offer technically unacceptable. That finding followed the terms of the solicitation.

A technically unacceptable offer has no claim to stay in the range, whatever its price.
gao-gaoreports-b-298864:
Barnes Aerospace Group protested an Air Force sole-source award to Ferrotherm Corporation. The contract covered repair of certain F100 engine parts. The firm sought approved source status in the same field. GAO decided B-298864 and B-298864.2 on December 26, 2006.

GAO split its ruling across the claims. The claimed delay in the firm's source review was not shown to be unfair. But the sole-source award could not stand as made. A notice had drawn a second firm close to approval. The agency skipped that firm's prospects in its sole-source case. It also held the firm to rules it waived for the winner. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299864:
Harris Corporation protested a Space and Naval Warfare Systems Command award to Raytheon Company. The contest was a downselect for a naval satellite communications terminal. The terminal links ships, shore sites, and submarines to satellite systems. GAO decided the B-299864 series on September 14, 2007.

Tests of the two prototypes drove the result. The winner's unit met nearly all hardware and software bars. The firm's unit missed many of those bars. Much work set for the first phase stayed undone. That gap marked the firm's path as a medium to high risk. GAO found the pick fair on the test record. The contrast in results was stark. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-305864:
A shuttle bus for Capitol Police staff is the subject of this GAO decision, B-305864, dated January 5, 2006. The force asked about a bus from its parking lot to the Fairchild Building. Staff would ride the bus to finish their trips to work. The force also asked about a bus from its main building.

GAO held that funds may not pay for a bus whose aim is the commute. Trips to work are a personal cost. Funds do not cover personal costs without a law that allows it. A bus that serves a real work need is fine. Staff may ride it as part of a commute by chance. That use must add no extra cost.
gao-gaoreports-b-309964:
ITT Industries Space Systems, LLC lost its protest. GAO ruled in B-309964 on November 9, 2007. NASA sought space gear under a call for offers. The award went to Ball Aerospace & Technologies Corp. ITT fought the scoring of offers and the source pick. It also flagged a caveat in an audit of the winner's cost plan.

GAO denied the protest. The file showed a fair review in line with the call. ITT's claims read as a clash of views, not proof of error. The audit caveat did no harm in the end. NASA showed the winner's cost quirk would add no cost to the government.
gao-gaoreports-b-310564:
Gap Solutions, Inc. lost its protest — GAO decision B-310564, dated January 4, 2008. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention sought tech and pro services. The award went to Total Solutions, Inc. GAP said the point scheme was too blunt. It said point gaps hid real gaps in bid worth. It also faulted the price review of the winner.

GAO denied the protest. The pick rested on rich prose notes, not points alone. Those notes set out plus and minus points of each bid. GAP made no real attack on the facts found. Point scores are mere guides to a wise pick. A guide cannot be faulted when the facts stand.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-264:
Maritime Administration, GAO-05-264 of March 7, 2005, tracks a fleet of old ships that rot at anchor and risk the waters near them. More than 100 worn-out ships wait for scrap. Congress told the agency in 2000 to clear them by September 30, 2006. Each path out, from scrap to reef sink, snags on law, cash, or rules.

GAO asks if the date will be met, and if not, why not. It asks how far paths past scrap have been used. It grades how scrap work is bought. It weighs how foreign yards and price shifts move the bill.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-464:
Police use of Taser weapons is described in GAO-05-464, a report GAO issued on May 26, 2005. A Taser fires two barbs that deliver an electric shock and disable a person. The maker said more than 7,000 of the nation's 18,000 law agencies used the weapons. GAO studied the rules, training, handling, and safety steps at seven agencies. It also surveyed laws that speak to Tasers.

All seven agencies folded Taser use into their general force policies rather than writing Taser-only rules. Training was required for officers who carry the weapons. Daily checks of the weapons were standard, and some agencies tested them each shift. Safety rules barred use on children and pregnant suspects. They also required a doctor's check for people hit in the neck or face. Laws varied widely by place. Some treated Tasers like firearms for private buyers, while others barred them from certain sites.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-764:
Nuclear waste cleanup gets a progress check in GAO-05-764, a report from July 29, 2005. In February 2002, the Energy Department promised a faster cleanup. It pledged to cut costs by $50 billion and shorten the work by 35 years. GAO checked progress so far. It judged the odds of hitting the savings pledge. And it tested whether reports show progress clearly.

GAO found mixed progress by March 2005. The department was on track or ahead on many of its 16 tracked tasks. It lagged on three hard, costly ones, among them tank waste and tank closures. The full $50 billion saving looks unlikely, GAO said. The math behind it likely overstated what could be saved. Many assumed gains are far from sure.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-264:
State veterans' nursing homes and the data gaps around them fill GAO-06-264, a report issued on March 31, 2006. The Department of Veterans Affairs pays for nursing care in three settings. It runs its own homes, buys beds in private homes, and helps fund state-run homes for veterans. For state homes it repays part of the care cost, issues guidance, and oversees operations. GAO asked how much the department knows about the veterans in state homes and their care.

Thin data hamper the department's planning, GAO found. Without a full picture of who lives in state homes and what care they get, leaders cannot plan capacity well. Oversight suffers for the same reason. States lean on varied income sources to keep the homes running. The report presses the department to close its data gaps. Aging veterans make long-term care planning too important to fly blind.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-364:
Sharing fighter jet secrets with partner nations takes many permits. Report GAO-06-364 of March 14, 2006, turns to the Joint Strike Fighter technology transfer process. The program is the Defense Department's largest joint effort with other nations to build a weapon system. The permits needed to share data, seek bids, and sign contracts would far exceed past transfers.

In July 2003 GAO urged tools to plan disclosure and transfer timing. This report checks the department's response to that advice. It names practices used to speed license work and avoid delays. Readers learn how export control can slow a weapon program. They also see how managers tried to keep pace.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-664:
Food program costs are examined in GAO report GAO-06-664, released on July 28, 2006. The WIC program gives food benefits to low-income women, infants, and children through retail grocers. Some states saw growth in WIC-only stores, which stock only WIC food and take only WIC vouchers. Both store types trade vouchers for cash payment from the program. GAO compared prices and practices at the two kinds of stores.

GAO found that WIC-only vendors grew in number from fiscal years 1999 through 2004, though their market share stayed small. Their pricing and service practices differed from regular grocers in clear ways. GAO said the Agriculture Department could judge program spending better with more detailed price and quantity data. The report shows how store type affects food benefit costs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-764:
Design work on a new Coast Guard cutter is tracked in GAO-06-764 of June 23, 2006. The cutter is part of the Deepwater program, which renews the service's aging fleet. All 49 of the Coast Guard's 110-foot patrol boats were first to be stretched to 123 feet as a bridge. A new 140-foot Fast Response Cutter would then enter service, starting in 2018. GAO reported on the state of the design effort for that replacement boat.

GAO noted that the Deepwater system integrator chose composite materials for the cutter's hull. The choice promised a lighter boat, but it carried design and testing risks. Early conversion work on the older boats had also run into trouble. The report captures a program at a decision point, where material choices could shape cost and performance for decades.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-164:
Soldiers on the move sleep in military lodging that works like a hotel chain. GAO reviewed those lodging programs in GAO-07-164, issued December 15, 2006. The Defense Department runs about 82,000 rooms worldwide. Running them cost about $860 million in fiscal year 2005. The Army planned to privatize its U.S. lodging. GAO asked how each service runs and funds its program. It also tested whether privatization would save money.

Each service runs lodging its own way, GAO found. The department had a strategic plan but no measures to judge success. Only one program, Navy family lodging, checked customer views across all its sites. Privatization would refresh Army rooms faster, GAO agreed. A developer could rebuild them in 7 years instead of over 20. But GAO's analysis showed fees would likely raise government costs by about $75 million a year. The Army's own upgrade path would cost about $1.1 billion.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-264:
The State Department flies 357 aircraft in the drug war, worth over $340 million. GAO checked how the fleet is run in GAO-07-264, issued February 2, 2007. The narcotics bureau owns the planes and helicopters. Contractors help maintain and fly them. Most serve crop spraying and support work in Colombia. GAO compared bureau practice with budget office fleet rules. It also reviewed oversight of support contracts.

The bureau had no systematic fleet process, GAO found. It never sized the fleet against long-term needs. Big purchases went ahead without formal cost studies. Fleet costs and use went largely untracked. In October 2006 the bureau began to centralize fleet control. A full fleet study was due in fiscal year 2007. Because reforms were under way, GAO made no recommendations. It promised to follow up on the fixes. The department noted its own reforms in reply.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-364:
Two-thirds of the tax agency's known computer security flaws from the last audit are still open. GAO reported the backlog in GAO-07-364, dated March 30, 2007. The agency collected about $2.5 trillion in fiscal year 2006. It paid about $277 billion in refunds. GAO tested controls on five key systems at three sites. The audit supports GAO's review of the agency's financial statements.

The agency fixed or eased 25 of 73 old weaknesses, GAO found. Password rules and access approvals improved in places. But 48 weaknesses, 66 percent, remain unresolved. Access controls still fail to block or spot intruders well. Duties are not always split to prevent abuse. Media disposal and staff screening also lag. The root cause is an unfinished security program, GAO said. Taxpayer data stays at risk of misuse or loss.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-564:
A master blueprint for the security department's computers is reviewed in GAO-07-564, dated May 9, 2007. An enterprise architecture maps how an agency's systems should fit together. Congress required the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to send its blueprint plus a funding plan. GAO was told to judge both. DHS filed its report in June 2006. Its overhaul has been a GAO high-risk area since 2003.

The 2006 blueprint is the third version, and it beats the earlier ones. It meets part of GAO's past advice. But content is still missing, and many user comments went unresolved. The funding plan also has limits. GAO found the step-by-step release method sound for so vast a shop. It urged DHS to finish the missing parts and give users real time to weigh in on each draft. A blueprint no one can use, it warns, guides nothing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-64:
Cheap loans for campus building at Black colleges are underused, and GAO-07-64, a GAO report dated October 18, 2006, asks why. About 100 Historically Black Colleges and Universities run aging plants with thin funds. Congress built the HBCU Capital Financing Program in 1992. It lends at rates near the government's own cost of borrowing. GAO spoke with officials at 34 of the schools.

Demand for building money is large, the study found. Yet only about half the loan funds on offer have been drawn. Some schools find even better terms in the open market. Others are too weak to borrow safely. Loan terms and slow, murky approvals put off more. A June 2006 law added special loan terms for hurricane-hit schools, and GAO checked the rollout. It urged the Education Department to run the program with clearer word and to set goals that show whether the aid works.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-764:
Timber sale records at the Forest Service are faulted in GAO-07-764, dated June 27, 2007. Ranger districts run most timber sales on national forests. For years, GAO has warned the agency cannot track what it spends on each sale. This report checks how the Forest Service logs its costs and revenue. It compares that with the Bureau of Land Management, which also sells timber.

The agency logs costs by funding program, not by sale. It stopped logging them at the district level, where sales occur. It now rolls them up to the forest level. Headquarters called the broad data "good enough" and cheaper to keep. Field managers disagreed. Without per-sale costs, they cannot compare sales or shift funds wisely. GAO urged steps to give field staff the detail they need. The Forest Service largely agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-264:
A new Navy readiness model is graded in GAO report GAO-08-264 (February 1, 2008). The Fleet Response Plan began in March 2003. It reshapes training, upkeep, and crewing so more ships can surge on short notice. The Navy vows to do this within a steady upkeep budget of about $40 billion a year for 5 years. GAO had earlier faulted the plan's management base.

The Navy has made progress in putting the plan to work, GAO finds. Yet its goals and measures remain half-built. The resource needs behind the plan are also unclear. Long-term risks and trade-offs have not been fully weighed. The report shows a bold shift still missing its scorecard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-364:
Tax-exempt bonds are examined in GAO report GAO-08-364, issued February 15, 2008. Interest on these state and local bonds escapes federal tax, costing the Treasury billions of dollars in revenue each year. GAO tracked bond trends, the projects they fund, and the costs of issuing them.

New bond volume had hit historic highs, with education the largest category of governmental bonds and nonprofits the largest issuers of private activity bonds. Past law barred such bonds for sites like stadiums, hotels, and golf courses, yet many such sites still get tax-exempt funding through other bond types. Some issuers also seemed to breach limits on paying issuance costs from bond proceeds. GAO asked Congress to rethink the tax break for private-use sites and told the Internal Revenue Service to clarify cost reporting. The acting commissioner agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-564:
Information security at the deposit insurance agency is audited in GAO report GAO-08-564, dated May 30, 2008. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation guards bank data and depositor funds. GAO checked its controls as part of the audit of its 2007 financial statements.

The corporation has fixed or eased 16 of 21 weaknesses left from the 2006 audit. It tightened physical access at its Virginia Square site and secured accounting data sent by e-mail. Five old flaws remain open, and new ones appeared in access and configuration controls. Staff shared login IDs and passwords, source code access was wide open, and system change records were incomplete. GAO made 10 recommendations. The corporation agreed with one and partly agreed with nine.
grant-walk-across-africa-1864:
James Augustus Grant, Speke's companion on the Nile expedition, published A Walk Across Africa with Blackwood in 1864. His subtitle calls it domestic scenes from his Nile journal. Where Speke's journal argues the great discovery, Grant's book lingers on the daily life of the march.

Grant, often sick and once left behind for months, records camps, carriers, food, sickness, and the peoples along the route. His sketches and notes cover the first full traverse from Zanzibar to Egypt by Europeans. The book is the expedition's human companion piece: less glory, more ground truth. Grant's modesty made it a favorite with readers then and now.
heydon-theomagia-1664:
John Heydon published Theomagia, or the Temple of Wisdom, in London in 1664. Three parts raise the temple in turn: spiritual, celestial, and elemental magic, hall upon hall. The work is the culminating system of Heydon's Rosicrucian writings, the grandest book he built with his pen.

Astrology fills much of the temple, with the natures of spirits and the arts of divination around it. Heydon compiles at his usual vast scale, adapting older authors into his structure. The Theomagia aims to house all occult learning under one roof. Its confidence is Restoration confidence, system-building after civil war. Readers who finish it have walked the whole circuit of Heydon's wisdom, room by room.
hotten-slang-1864:
John Camden Hotten issued his Slang Dictionary in 1864, the fullest record of Victorian street language. Hotten was a London publisher with a taste for the city's low life and its speech. He built the book on Grose's earlier slang dictionary and added the new words of his own century.

Inside are the cant of thieves, the patter of street sellers, and slang from schools, barracks, and music halls. Hotten explains terms that polite print of the day left out, often with notes on where a word came from. The result catches the English that Dickens put in his characters' mouths. For historians of speech and of city life, the dictionary is a first-hand record of a vanished London.
huxley-further-remarks-neanderthal-1864:
Huxley answered William King on the Neanderthal skull in 1864. King had just named the fossil a separate species, Homo neanderthalensis. Writing in the Natural History Review, Huxley pushed back firmly.

He argues the Neanderthal skull falls within the range of human variation. In his view it is an ancient human, not a separate kind. The exchange became a classic statement of the Darwinian position on fossil people. Later science sided more with King on the species question. Huxley's reasoning, though, still shows comparative anatomy being used with great skill. It is short, sharp, and well worth a close read.
institutiones-chimicae-prodromae-i-e-ioa:
Johann Joachim Becher of Speyer, doctor of mathematics and medicine, printed his Institutiones Chimicae Prodromae at Frankfurt in 1664. Its second title, Oedipus Chimicus, promises to open the mysteries of dark chemical terms and principles. Becher dedicated the work to Franciscus de le Boe, called Sylvius, at Leiden. The text is in Latin.

Cures are matched to principles in the middle pages. A mercurial disease, Becher argues, must be cured by a mercurial medicine made saline. Like treats like through opposed qualities, in his scheme. The little work was offered as needful reading for students of medicine and chemistry.
institutiones-chimicae-prodromae-id-est-:
Johann Joachim Becher's Institutiones Chimicae Prodromae appears here in an Amsterdam printing of 1664. Weyerstraten was the publisher, where the Frankfurt issue names another house. The Oedipus Chimicus subtitle is the same, promising to resolve obscure chemical terms. The dedication to Sylvius of Leiden is also the same.

Latin pages argue that names of salts do not cure the sick. Causes of inflammation and putrid blood must be sought in first principles, Becher insists. Unknown causes are too often blamed on a hidden quality, he complains. This issue is the Amsterdam twin of Becher's early chemical primer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ha-levi-b:
