Aaron ha-Levi ben Moses of Staroselye was a Talmudic scholar and cabalist active in Poland in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century. He was a devoted disciple of Senior Salman, rabbi of Lozhne and Lody. Aaron urged Salman to publish his work "Tanya," which came out in 1796.

When Salman was jailed in 1798, Aaron went from town to town raising money to ransom him, or at least to win access for his followers. After Salman's death in 1812, Aaron served as rabbi at Staroselye, and his followers formed a school known as the Ḥasidim of Staroselye. His "Sha'are 'Abodah," printed in 1820-21, treats the unity of God, souls, service, the Law, and repentance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abbahu-164:
Abbahu was a famed Palestinian amora of the third generation, about 279-320, often cited as Abbahu of Caesarea. He learned mainly at Tiberias, in the academy of Johanan, who treated him almost as a son. He was an authority on weights and measures. He learned Greek to be of use to his people under the Roman proconsuls, and taught Greek to his daughters too.

Wise, handsome, and wealthy, Abbahu became rector of the academy at Caesarea and won trust with the Roman power as well. One rule of his, on the sounding of the shofar, has been kept ever since. It is still cited by its own name, the Enactment of Abbahu. He traveled widely, taught in many towns, and gathered so many rulings that scholars turned to him on hard points.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-sam:
Abraham ben Samuel Cohen of Lask, called the Hasid of Amsterdam, was a Jewish ascetic of the late eighteenth century. He went to live at Jerusalem in 1785. Later he traveled in Europe raising funds for Polish Jews in Palestine, with Amsterdam as his base.

He fasted six days a week, then feasted well on the Sabbath. He studied Torah standing for whole days and nights, and broke river ice in winter for his morning washing. Turkish officials once beat him in prison to squeeze out money. He died as hakam at Safed during a riot. Four Cabala books by him appeared between 1784 and 1797.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-testame:
The Testament of Abraham is an apocryphal book telling the story of Abraham's death. It first came out in print in 1892, in two versions, from a Greek original. Ethiopic, Slavonic, and Rumanian versions have also been found.

God sends the archangel Michael to prepare Abraham, famed for kindness and hospitality, for his end. Abraham resists, wins a ride in a heavenly chariot, and views the whole world and the judgment of souls. At last Death comes in disguise, shows his true and dreadful faces, and God takes Abraham's soul as in a dream. The entry argues the book is Jewish in origin and very early.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adamantius-764: Adamantius was a Jewish doctor, author, and student of nature. He lived in Alexandria in the fourth century. He made a short form, in two books, of a work on faces and character by Polemon. An Arabic form of it rests in script at Leyden. Prints came out at Paris in 1540 and at Basel in 1544. He also wrote a work on the winds. In it he says he used the method of Aristotle more than any other. Doctors of his day cite drugs he brought in.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adullam-864: Adullam was an old Canaanite capital in west Judah. Genesis xxxviii. 1 and Joshua name it. Rehoboam walled it, as II Chronicles xi. 7 tells. It stayed a lived-in town to the end of Old Testament times. The modern Id-el-Miyeh holds its site. Its famed cave sheltered David in his outlaw days. Custom puts that cave six miles southeast of Bethlehem. The entry warns the word cave may rest on a false reading. Stronghold may be the true word in the tale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahali-taurat-pe: Ahali-Taurat, "People of the Torah," is the name used by the Persian Jews of Hamadan, Demavend, and Teheran. Jews in other Persian districts use it as well. The name sets them apart from Persian Jews of Indian origin. Those Jews are called "Israeli" instead. The entry adds a dry note: despite the name, these Jews are not remarkable for their knowledge of the Torah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alatri-giacomo-:
Giacomo Alatri was an Italian banker and philanthropist. He was a son of Samuel Alatri, born at Rome in 1833. He died there on March 9, 1889. For years he served as president of the Banca Romana. He resigned in 1881, when his plans to rebuild the bank were turned down. The bank's later fall in 1893 proved his stand right.

His giving went chiefly to one cause. He worked to set up kindergartens for the Jewish poor, and he gave that work all his energy. His own plan for reforming Italy's banks of issue came out at Rome in 1888. He died at fifty-six, just two months before his father.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexandra-1164: Alexandra was a daughter of King Aristobulus II. Pompey brought her to Rome in 63 B.C., with her parents and brothers, as a prisoner of war. The senate freed her in 56 B.C., keeping Aristobulus alone. Her father was poisoned in 49 B.C. by the partisans of Pompey. She then found shelter, with her mother and her brother Antigonus, at the court of Ptolemy, prince of Chalcis. She married Ptolemy's son, Philippion. Her father-in-law was smitten by her beauty. He had his son killed, and married the widow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alliance-israel:
Alliance Israélite Universelle is a society founded in Paris in 1860. Six Paris Jews set it up that year. Its aim was to guard and lift Jews as a whole. Its chief care went to Jews in the east. North Africa and Asia Minor drew much of its work. Two shocks helped bring it to birth.

One shock was a blood charge at Damascus in 1840. The other was the forced baptism of a child in 1858. The entry traces its aid work land by land. Schools form a large part of that work. Reports from 1885 and 1896 sum up the gains. The society spoke for Jews who had no voice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amasa-1364:
Amasa was a nephew of King David. Two books give his father's name in two forms. Absalom made him chief of the host that rose against David. When Absalom fell, David meant to keep Amasa in that post. Amasa was sent to crush a new revolt under Sheba. Joab met him on the march and killed him.

A second part gives rabbinic tales of Amasa. One tale shows him defying Saul over a death order. He threw down his belt and cloak rather than kill priests. Sages say he put study of the Law first. For that delay Joab struck him down. The entry holds that Joab did wrong in that act.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anschel-solomon: Solomon Anschel was a German author who lived in southern Germany at the end of the eighteenth century and the start of the nineteenth. His first listed work, on commerce between soul and body, was a translation from the Hebrew. It came out at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1788. His Thanatologia, on the nature of death, followed at Gottingen in 1795. A primer of natural science, with pictures, appeared at Mayence in 1801. The entry rests on Furst's Bibliotheca Judaica.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-appeal-1664:
Appeal, the carrying of a case from a lower court to a higher one for a fresh hearing, is practically unknown to Jewish law, the entry states. A paragraph in Deuteronomy, chapters 16 and 17, has led some to think appeals existed in Bible times. The entry reads it otherwise.

That passage tells judges who doubt the law to refer the case to the High Court at Jerusalem and take its opinion. A judge who dissents uses the same path. The answer binds the court that asked, but no party has appealed a judgment. Biblical law, the entry argues, treats a lawful court's judgment as the judgment of God, and so as final. Courts thus did not stand in a ladder of appeal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aristeas-the-hi:
Aristeas the historian was a writer on Jewish history known only from a fragment. Eusebius quotes it from Alexander Polyhistor's collection. His work, called On the Jews, told the history of Job much as the Bible does, but with fresh matter on names.

Aristeas held that Job's first name was Jobab, matching him to the Jobab of Genesis, chapter 36, verse 33, a great-grandson of Esau. He rested the match on shared names: Eliphaz, the Temanite title, the land of Uz, and Zophar all turn up in that Genesis chapter. The entry points out that the Job author had simply borrowed the names from Genesis. It also shows the same changes standing in the Septuagint's additions to Job.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-eliez:
Eliezer ben Solomon Ashkenazi, a rabbinical scholar, was born in Poland about the start of the nineteenth century and later lived in Tunis. At Metz in 1845 he published Dibre Hakamim, The Words of the Wise. The book rescues eleven old manuscripts in one volume. Among them stand a Midrash on the Pentateuch. Joseph Caro on Lamentations stands there too. So does Maimonides on the intercalary month.

The rest range just as wide. Moses Narboni writes on free will. A prose poem praises the pen. David ben Yom-Tob sets out thirteen articles of belief. A letter from Palestine to Ferrara, dated 1438, closes the set. Salomon Munk wrote the introduction. Ashkenazi also issued Ta'am Zekenim, The Taste of Old Men, another gathering of old texts on Jewish literature and history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asufot-2064:
Asufot means Collection. It is the name of a medieval book of Jewish laws, customs, and religious practice. The work survives in one manuscript, No. 115, in the Montefiore College Library at Ramsgate, England. Its author lived at the start of the fourteenth century. He drew on many named sources.

The book covers slaughter rules, Passover and the Seder, the feasts and fasts, and the Sabbath. It also gives marriage and divorce rules, mourning customs, charms, and forms for contracts. Its writer noted local customs and even superstitions with care. That habit makes the book a rich record of Jewish daily life in the Rhine country in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. German glosses in the text, and full vowel signs, add to its value for language study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-averroism-2164:
Averroism is the teaching of Averroes, the great reader of Aristotle. The entry sets him beside his fellow thinker Maimonides. Both were strict followers of Aristotle. They split on faith. Maimonides would bend or soften Aristotle where he clashed with religion. Averroes backed him to the full, even where the Koran taught otherwise.

Averroes held that the universe is eternal, and matter with it. He also hemmed in man's free will, since acts shaped by outer forces cannot be free creations. Against Avicenna he argued that every being, having a cause, exists by need. The entry's second half turns to the Jews who kept his work alive. Through their translations and comments, kept up for four centuries, his books passed to the Christian world. Translators at Marseilles, Arles, and Tortosa all get their due.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baalis-2264: Baalis was king of the Ammonites. Jeremiah names him as the leading spirit behind the murder of Gedaliah, the governor set over Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. The first part of his name is plainly Baal. The second part is a puzzle. No good account of it had yet been offered when the entry was written, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bahur-plural-ba:
Baḥur, plural Baḥurim, means "a youth," and above all a Talmud student among the Ashkenazic Jews. In Biblical Hebrew the word marks an adult but unmarried young man. From the end of the fourteenth century it became the standard term for students of the Talmud, who were mostly young. The entry builds a full picture of their life from responsa and other sources.

After the Black Death of 1348, many schools closed and parents could no longer fund study. The baḥur then wandered from town to town, poor and at risk on the road, sitting at the feet of one rabbi after another. Baḥurim-houses lodged them on gifts from the community. Later the center of study shifted to Poland, where stipends, meals, and marriages into wealthy families changed the baḥur's place, as the entry describes from an eyewitness account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bar-kokba-and-b:
Bar Kokba and his war stand at the center of this long entry, which opens with the revolt's background. The risings in Cyrene, Cyprus, and Egypt under Trajan were still burning when Hadrian took power in 118. The war shifted to Palestine. At Lydda the Romans executed masses of Jews, and the patriarch Gamaliel II. died shut up in the town. The entry weighs Talmudic praise for the "slain of Lydda."

Coins of the war are pictured and read, one bearing Simon's name and "The Deliverance of Jerusalem." The entry then takes up the name Koziba in Jewish tradition and the years claimed for Bar Kokba and his sons. Governor Tinnius Rufus is blamed for goading the Jews in their most sacred ties. A Talmudic tale ties the war's spark to an insult offered by Romans to a bridal couple. The account runs on through the war's course and fall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-apocalyp:
Apocalypse of Baruch, in its Syriac form, is a pseudepigraphic work in which Baruch narrates his experiences before and after the Temple's destruction. He also reports revelations about the future. With one small fragment, the work became known only recently. Ceriani published a Latin translation of the Syriac text in 1866, the Syriac itself in 1871, and a facsimile in 1883.

God first reveals Jerusalem's coming destruction and bids the pious leave the city. Angels fire the walls only after the sacred vessels are given to the earth, which swallows them until the latter days. The long entry outlines every section in turn. Its eschatology joins national hopes (Jerusalem rebuilt, the Ten Tribes gathered, the heathen doomed) with individual reward and punishment. Its resurrection teaching matches the rabbis: the earth gives up her dead as she received them, to show the living that the departed have returned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-b-jacob-:
Baruch b. Jacob of Shklov, Talmudist, physician, and scientist, was born at Shklov about 1740 and died about 1812. Ordained in 1764, he became dayyan in Minsk, then left to study medicine in England. At Berlin in 1777 he published "'Ammude Shamayim," on astronomy, with an appendix on anatomy. His "Derek Yesharah," on hygiene, appeared at The Hague in 1779, and his Hebrew Euclid the next year. His trigonometry, "Ḳeneh ha-Middah," came in 1784.

In later days he kept a chemical laboratory at Joshua Zeitlin's palace in Ustye and made scientific experiments there. He ended at Sluzk as physician to Prince Radziwil and dayyan of the town. Though ahead of most early maskilim in secular learning, he stayed strictly conservative. He bitterly attacked Azariah dei Rossi's radical views on the calendar. He admired the Gaon of Wilna, who held that works on science should be translated into Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-batlanim-litera:
Batlanim, literally men without work, were ten men of leisure who gave all their time to communal affairs. A town counted as a true town only if it had ten such men to keep daily synagogue service going. Rashi says the community supported them for that work.

The entry reports debate over whether the town truly paid them. Benjamin of Tudela still found ten Batlanim in twelfth century Bagdad, leading its colleges and judging cases. In modern times, the entry adds, paid minyan men fill the same need in strict synagogues. Levy links the Batlanim to the men of the synagogue named in another tractate of the Mishnah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-b-ihi-: Benjamin ben Ihi, also called Minyamin, was a Babylonian scholar of the third century. He was a brother of Abbahu ben Ihi, a pupil of Samuel. Both brothers kept apart and had no dealings with Gentiles, the entry says. Yet both were kind to their servants. One set a single dish from his table for them, while the other shared every dish. Legend held that the second brother was deemed worthy of visits from the prophet Elijah for that kindness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bergel-yom-tob-: Yom-Tob Bergel was a merchant and communal worker of Gibraltar, born in 1812. He died there on Oct. 14, 1894. Counted among the richest and most respected merchants of its Jewish community, he held the post of its president for thirty years. He set the Hebrew Poor Fund back on firm ground when it stood in a shaky state. As a trustee he gained valuable holdings for the poor. He also served on the health board and helped run relief in the cholera year of 1865.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bersohn-mathias: Mathias Bersohn was a Polish bibliographer and art writer. He was born at Warsaw in 1826. He owned a choice private library. It held rare books and manuscripts. His best known work is "Tobias Kohn" from 1872. It tells the life of a Jewish physician. Kohn lived in the seventeenth century. A supplement adds key documents. They concern the Jews of Poland. Bersohn also wrote on W. Stosie. He wrote on Marcin Teofil Polak too. Another pamphlet covers old South-Russian synagogues.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bischofsheim-on:
Bischofsheim-on-the-Tauber is a city in Baden. Its Jewish history is a record of persecutions. In 1235 seven Jews were burned on a murder charge. Rindfleisch's hordes nearly wiped out the community in 1298. Armleder's men struck again in 1337. The Black Death brought more martyrdoms in 1348.

Documents then trace taxes and rabbis for centuries. The poll-tax stood at 20 kreutzer in 1724. The city belonged to the Mayence electorate. Its Jews answered to the Aschaffenburg rabbinate. Jacob Löwenstein served as rabbi from 1851 to 1869. In 1902 the community numbered 40 families, and it stood under the rabbinate of Morbach, in the wider district of Mosbach in Baden.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bleibtreu-phili: Philip Johann Bleibtreu was a Jewish convert to Christianity. He was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main in the seventeenth century. He died there in 1702. His Jewish name was Meïr. He published a German work called "Meïr Naor." It means The Enlightened Meïr. The book tells of his conversion. It also notices Jewish festivals and prayers. The entry cites Wolf and Fürst as its sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-borchardt-bruno: Bruno Borchardt was a German physicist and author born at Bromberg on Nov. 17, 1859. He studied at Berlin and took his doctorate there. He was made a high-school teacher, then forced to resign for his socialistic views. He turned to journalism and wrote much for the daily press. His pieces made physics and chemistry plain and reported new finds. He also published three scientific treatises. One, a physics outline of 1892, reached a second edition in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brass-15264:
Brass is a composition of copper and zinc. Its use in the Bible is uncertain, the entry warns. Instruments of copper and bronze were often meant where brass is named in translation.

Copper and bronze were known to Egyptians before the Exodus. The altar of burnt offering was overlaid with brass, Exodus says. Moses made a serpent of brass in the wilderness account. Goliath wore armor of brass, and David took much brass as spoil. Singers sounded cymbals of brass in Chronicles. The word also works as an image: a heaven of brass means no rain, and flesh of brass means hardness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breach-of-trust:
Breach of trust is the violation, by fraud or neglect, of a duty laid on a trustee or guardian. The entry treats it as a branch of criminal law. Its moral base lies in verses against stealing, lying, and defrauding a neighbor.

Biblical law on the subject covers bailees in the main. A guardian of orphans could not be forced to render a full account. Instead he swore an oath that he had not touched the goods wrongly. That appeal to conscience, the entry says, guarded orphans' estates well in practice. A bailee who falsely denied holding goods lost the right to act as witness or to take an oath thereafter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brull-ignaz-376:
Ignaz Brüll was an Austrian composer born at Prossnitz, Moravia, on Nov. 7, 1846. His family moved to Vienna in 1848, where he studied piano, composition, and instrumentation. Epstein played a piano concerto by the young Brüll in 1861. Tours through Germany and England followed, and in 1872 he became professor at Vienna's Horak Institute.

His first opera was never played, but Das Goldene Kreuz, given at Berlin in 1875, became very popular at home and abroad. Emperor William I praised him in person at the first Berlin performance. More operas followed over two decades, along with concertos, serenades, and chamber works. The entry praises his chamber music and notes his close friendship with Brahms, whose works he played well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buxtorf-johanne: Johannes Rudolphus Buxtorf was a great grandson of Johannes Buxtorf the first, born at Basel on Oct. 24, 1747. After study in his home city he worked as a private tutor in the family of the count of Schaumburg-Lippe. Back in Basel, he became professor of rhetoric and theology at the university in 1793. He also lectured and wrote on Biblical archaeology. He died in 1815. The entry is brief and names no single book of his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-candlestick-heb:
Candlestick, or menorah, appears as a household object only once in the Bible, in Second Kings. In the Temple it appears often, though early facts about its shape stay thin. At Shiloh a lamp, not a menorah, is named. First Kings speaks of ten golden candlesticks in Solomon's Temple, five on each side. Critics, the entry notes, doubt those verses.

The heart of the piece is the seven branched candlestick of the tabernacle, told in Exodus. Critics assign that account to post exile times and match it to the Second Temple lampstand. It was chased from pure gold. Josephus says three lamps burned by day and all seven by night. Later rabbis held the lamp burned only at night. Copying Temple vessels was banned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caro-jacob-4064:
Jacob Caro, a German historian, was born at Gnesen, in Posen, on Feb. 2, 1836. He was a son of Joseph Ḥayyim Caro. Study at Berlin and Leipsic led to his 1861 book on the Polish interregnum of 1586. That work won him the task of continuing Röppel's history of Poland.

Caro wrote volumes two through five of that history, issued from 1863 to 1888. Research trips took him through Galicia and southern Russia. He taught at Jena, traveled in the suite of Grand Duchess Helena, and moved to Breslau in 1869. From 1882 he held a full chair there. His fame rests chiefly on Polish history. Other books treat the Polish royal chancery, Lessing and Swift, and Catherine II of Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cedar-4164:
Cedar is a tree of the pine family named often in the Old Testament. The cedar of Lebanon is usually meant. It grows best in high, dry, sandy ground, and found that ground in the Lebanon district. Trees there reach a girth of forty-two feet and a height of ninety feet. The tree spreads wide, with dark green evergreen leaves about an inch long.

Cedar wood resists dry rot and worms, thanks to its oil. Solomon used it throughout the Temple, for walls, court, and altar. It later served in the Second Temple and in ship masts. In ritual it was used in cleansing a leper and in the rite of the Red Heifer. Bible writers use the cedar as a figure for strength and flourishing. A strong nation, a lover, and the righteous are all compared to it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-christiani-mori: Moritz Wilhelm Christiani was an author and a Jewish convert to Christianity. He was born at Altorf late in the seventeenth century. He died at Prague about 1740. He claimed he had been a rabbi at Schleusingen before his baptism in 1715. He may have belonged to the Keyser family of Schleusingen in Bavaria. The entry lists five of his writings. One from 1723 describes a Jewish synagogue and its customs. Another from 1720 tells the story of his own conversion. A third, from 1733, renders the Sefer ha-Minhagim into German.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-benjamin-:
Benjamin Louis Cohen, an English politician and communal worker, was born in London in 1844. He sat in Parliament for East Islington from 1892. Educated in private, he joined his father's firm, Louis Cohen and Sons, as a young man. From early on he gave his time to charity work, Jewish and general, with a strong bent toward technical education.

His posts pile up across the entry. He governed three hospitals and led the Jewish Board of Guardians from 1887 to June, 1900, moving it to new quarters in Middlesex street. He sat on the London County Council from 1888 as a Moderate. He also helped found the Russo-Jewish committee and kept its funds until 1887.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-council-of-four:
Council of Four Lands was the central body of Jewish self-rule in Poland. It lasted nearly two centuries, from the middle of the sixteenth to the middle of the eighteenth. Each Polish Jewish community, or ḳahal, ran its own affairs. Elders handled taxes and charity. Rabbis held charge of religion and the courts. A body above them all grew out of meetings at the Lublin fair.

The council's work mixed law-making with daily management. It set fair rules for courts across the land. It also guarded the general welfare of Polish Jews. Its agents went to Warsaw during the Polish Seim. There they pled, paid, and presented gifts to win and keep Jewish privileges.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dampierre-hebr-: Dampierre is a village of Champagne, in the department of the Aube, France. In the Middle Ages it held an important Jewish community. In 1206 King Philippe-Auguste ordered its Jews to set a special seal on their loan papers. He also barred loans on holy vessels or Church lands. Local lords and the abbey of Saint-Loup stood among Jewish debtors in 1212, 1220, and 1225. Five rabbis of the village are listed. The first is Isaac ben Samuel the Elder, called the Saint (1120-95).
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-duport-adrien-5:
Adrien Duport was a French lawyer and friend of the Jews, born in 1758. He became a deputy to the States-General in 1789. At first he sat with the Jacobin party. After the king's arrest in June 1791, he turned royalist. He died in exile in 1798.

The constitution of September 1791 said nothing for the Jews of France. On Sept. 27, 1791, Duport moved that Jews receive full citizenship rights. The Assembly adopted his motion against slight opposition. It then struck down every special law against the Jews. The entry credits that single proposal with the legal freeing of French Jewry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ebiasaph-or-abi: Ebiasaph, also read Abiasaph, was a Levite of the line of Kohath. The entry makes him an ancestor of the prophet Samuel and of Heman the singer. In Exodus and in parts of Chronicles he stands as a son of Korah. There he is brother to Assir and Elkanah. But another Chronicles passage places him a step lower, as a son of Elkanah and grandson of Assir. The entry simply sets the two placements side by side and leaves them there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ehrlich-meshull: Meshullam Ehrlich was a Polish philologist born at Lublin in 1818. He died at Paris in 1861. The entry calls him a leading Talmudic scholar of his time. He also mastered Oriental and modern languages. Nearly all his many works stayed in manuscript. One alone was printed, on Hebrew philology, at Paris in 1868. The entry gives no titles for the lost manuscripts and no account of his teaching. His name survives through that single printed study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elhanan-god-is-: Elhanan is a name borne by two men in the Bible. The first Elhanan came from Bethlehem, a son of Jaareoregim. Second Samuel credits him with killing Goliath at Gob. There he is a son of Jair who killed Lahmi, brother of Goliath. The entry explains the clash in plain terms. An older tale gave the kill to Elhanan. When David grew to be the hero, the deed passed to him. The second Elhanan was a son of Dodo. He ranked among the thirty men of David.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-ben-mord: Elijah ben Mordecai was a prayer poet of the eleventh century. He may have been a native of Italy. Only one of his poems is still in hand. It is a kerobah for the afternoon service of the Day of Atonement. That poem stands in the German and Polish liturgy. Eliezer ben Nathan wrote a commentary on his poems. The entry gives no facts of his life at all. His fame rests on that single surviving piece.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-england-5764:
England is treated here through the Jews who lived in it. Most of their tale in that land centers on London. The entry takes up the bonds between Jews and the state. It falls into three spans of time by its plan. The first runs to the great expulsion of old. The last runs from the return of the Jews on.

No proof shows Jews in England before the Norman Conquest. Church laws of Saxon times speak of rites, not residents. Slave traders may have passed through with their wares. William of Malmesbury states the source of the first flock. William the Conqueror brought the Jews from Rouen, he says. The entry finds no cause to doubt that claim. Domesday shows what the king gained by the move.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-esra-elia-5864: Elia Esra was a giver to charity born at Calcutta on February 20, 1830, son of David Joseph Esra. He died in March 1886. The entry calls him one of India's richest merchants, nicknamed the Indian Rothschild. He is said to have given 10,000 francs to the poor every month. At Calcutta he built a large synagogue and named it Magen Dawid after his father. His will ordered a large Talmudic school built at Jerusalem at his estate's cost. No business or family details beyond those gifts are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-exilarch-aramai:
Exilarch was the title of the head of the Babylonian Jews, the golah or exile community. The office carried state-backed honors and rights, and it passed by birth in a house claiming descent from King David. Its start is unknown, the entry admits. First firm records come from Parthian times. The office lasted through Sassanid rule and for centuries under the Arabs.

A chronicle from about 800 names Jehoiachin, the captive king, as the first exilarch. His rise at Evil-merodach's court is read as the office's seed. The entry lists his supposed heirs and follows the office into Egypt, where it ended with David ben Daniel in 1094. Later sections map how the exilarchate was run, before and after Arab rule began.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezobi-eliezer-b: Eliezer ben Hanan Ezobi was a Provencal poet who lived at Beziers in the thirteenth century. He was brother of Joseph Ezobi. He was also a peer of Abraham Bedersi, and the two exchanged poems. His known work is a teaching poem of thirty stanzas on man. In it he took the form of Ibn Ezra's poem Ben Adamah. The entry gives no other works, dates, or life events for him. Its sources are Carmoly, Renan and Neubauer on the French rabbis, and Gross's Gallia Judaica.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-feldman-wilhelm:
Wilhelm Feldman was a Polish author born at Warsaw in 1868 who argued for Jews blending into the peoples around them. His books, in Polish, press that case and study Mickiewicz's tie to the Jews. He served as secretary of the Baron de Hirsch Fund at Cracow from 1891 to 1894. He helped found Ognisko, a journal for progressive Polish youth.

In 1895 he studied social science at Berlin, but charges of pushing a Great Poland plan forced him out that year. At Cracow he founded a freethinkers' daily that lasted eighteen months. He then settled at Lemberg as a journalist. His plays and novels include a drama staged at Warsaw in 1890 and a run of fiction through Ananke in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-flaccus-l-pompo: L. Pomponius Flaccus was a Roman governor of Syria, dated in the entry by a questioned 32-35. The entry is very short. It says plainly that no particulars of his life are known. His one recorded link is with Agrippa, later King Agrippa I. Agrippa was then poor and in distress. His brother-in-law Herod Antipas had insulted him. So Agrippa turned to Flaccus for help. The two men had formed a friendship earlier at Rome. Three source lines close the brief notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frances-jacob-b:
Jacob ben David Frances was an Italian scholar and poet born at Mantua in 1615. He died at Florence in 1667. His father grounded him in the Talmud, and he studied further at Venice. His fame as a poet rests chiefly on his satires. They attacked Shabbethai Ẓebi and his following with great heat. They also warned against the false Messiah's agents. With his brother Immanuel he called on the rabbis of Smyrna to act.

The Shabbethaians answered with pamphlets that branded Frances a heretic. His house was attacked, and attempts were made on his life. He traced the sect's errors to cabalistic guessing about the Messiah's kingdom. His poem against untrained study of Cabala roused the Mantua rabbis. They demanded that the poem be burned. His death cut the quarrel short, and his brother carried on his defense.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedenthal-kar:
Karl Rudolph Friedenthal was a Prussian statesman born at Breslau on September 15, 1827. He died on his estate near Neisse on March 7, 1890. He was a nephew of the author Markus Bär Friedenthal and later became a Christian. He studied law at Breslau, Heidelberg, and Berlin. In 1854 he entered the court service. In 1856 he was chosen a district deputy, and in 1857 a deputy to the Prussian Landtag.

In 1867 Friedenthal was elected to the North German Reichstag. He took part in talks at Versailles on the new empire's frame during the war with France. In 1874 he became minister of farming. Five years later the domains and forests also came under him. For some months he headed the home office as well. In 1879 he could not accept Bismarck's new trade policy, so he resigned. He gave up his seat in the Upper House in 1881 and retired to his estate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gai-solomon-646: Solomon Gai, an Italian scholar and Hebraist born at Mantua in 1600, died there in August 1638. He is known chiefly as a friend and letter partner of Johannes Buxtorf the Younger. War drove him to Botzen in Tyrol, where he tutored two sons of a rich man. There he learned German. After five and a half years he went back to Mantua. His letters to Buxtorf praise a Latin version of Maimonides Guide and point out Hebrew books Buxtorf had missed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geldern-simon-v: Simon von Geldern, a traveler and author born in 1720, died in 1774. He was a great-uncle of Heinrich Heine, who calls him an adventurer and a dreamer of utopias. Long trips in eastern lands won him the name the Oriental. He spent years in North African ports and learned the armorer trade there. A desert tribe chose him as sheik. He later fled to England after a scandal with a lady of high birth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gideon-6664:
Gideon, son of Joash the Abiezrite and also called Jerubbaal, ranks among the great judges of Israel. His tale fills Judges vi to viii. Midian raiders had stripped Israel at harvest for seven years. An angel calls Gideon as he beats out wheat in a wine press. He doubts the call, then gains a sign of fire that eats his food gift.

That night he tears down his father Baal altar and earns his new name. He then tests God with a fleece, wet then dry. God cuts his host from 32,000 men to 300. With horns, jars, and torches those 300 rout the Midian camp at night. Gideon takes two kings captive and kills them to avenge his brothers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldschmiedt-gu:
Guido Goldschmiedt was an Austrian chemist. He was born in Triest on Oct. 5, 1850. He studied at Vienna and Heidelberg. At Vienna University's chemical laboratory he rose from assistant to associate professor. His papers on organic chemistry won him the Lieben prize more than once.

After a short post at Vienna's agriculture school, Prague called him as professor in 1892. His best-known feat was proving the constitution of papaverin. He had studied that substance thoroughly. Many treatises on pyridin and quinolin compounds followed. Prague made him dean of its philosophical faculty in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-graziani-august: Augusto Graziani was an Italian economist. He was born at Modena on Jan. 6, 1865. His home university trained him in law and economics. He took his law doctorate in 1886. He rose at Modena from privat-docent to assistant professor by 1890. In 1894 Sienna made him professor of financial science. In 1899 Naples gave him its political economy chair. He still held it when the entry closed. The Lincei academy counted him a corresponding member. His books treat profit, value theory in Italy, stock operations, and interest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guttmann-paul-6:
Paul Guttmann was a German physician and medical author. He was born at Ratibor, Prussian Silesia, on Sept. 9, 1833. He died in Berlin on May 24, 1893. He studied at Ratibor's gymnasium and at Berlin, Vienna, and Würzburg. He took his medical degree at Würzburg in 1858. In 1859 he began practice in Berlin. He became a privat-docent in 1867 and chief physician of the Moabit hospital in 1879.

His fame as a clinician spread widely. He wrote about eighty essays on medical topics. His book with Albert Eulenburg on the sympathetic nervous system won the Astley-Cooper prize in London. His textbook of clinical examination methods appeared in 1884. From 1885 to 1893 he edited the "Journal für Practische Aerzte."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hakam-aramaic-a:
Ḥakam is a word for a wise or skillful man, used for a cultured and learned person. Even a non-Jew who says a wise thing is called ḥakam in the Talmud. Wise men of the nations earn the title too. As an office, ḥakam appears in the rebuilt Sanhedrin beside the nasi and the ab bet din.

What the office holder did is not clear. Scholars guess he weighed cases from all sides, broke ties between nasi and ab bet din, or headed a school. The post seems tied to Palestine and its academy. Among Spanish-Portuguese Jews, ḥakam became the set title of the local rabbi, though how old that use is stays unproven.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hana-huna-b-biz: Ḥana b. Bizna was a Babylonian scholar of the third and fourth centuries who served as judge at Pumbedita. He worked above all in Haggadah and won fame in that field. R. Sheshet once tried to fault his homilies, was beaten, and owned, "I can not contend with Ḥana in the field of the Haggadah." As a halakist he thought for himself: despite criticism he used pagan barber-shops in Nehardea's suburbs. He also saved the name and teachings of Simon Ḥasida from being lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harod-7264: Harod was a well in the valley of Jezreel, south of the Hill of Moreh. In the Book of Judges, Gideon and his army camped beside it on the morning of their fight with the Midianites. The entry says the test of the men by how they drank water took place there. The Midianites camped nearby, and the day ended in their rout. The well is now called Ain Jalud. The entry gives no other facts about the site.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henochs-moses-7: Moses Henochs was a Talmudist who lived at Jerusalem about 1570. The entry names him as author of a devotional work. That work was translated into Judæo-German by Phinehas b. Judah Heilprin. The translation appeared at Basel in 1602 under the title given in the entry. The entry is very short. It gives no birth or death dates, no teachers, and no other writings. Its facts rest on a single cited source, Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heyman-elias-76:
Elias Heyman, born at Göteborg in 1829, was a Swedish physician. He studied medicine at Lund and at Stockholm. He practiced at Göteborg from 1862 to 1878. There he helped start the Gothenburg temperance system and founded health bodies.

In 1878 Heyman became professor of hygiene at Stockholm. He edited a medical journal, led a hygiene society, and directed its museum. He built up hygiene teaching across Sweden. He died suddenly in 1889 while giving an address on that subject. His many writings covered vital statistics, sanitation, air flow, workers' housing, temperance, and school hygiene.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirschler-ignaz:
Ignaz Hirschler, born at Presburg in 1823, was a Hungarian eye doctor and leader in Jewish affairs. He studied medicine at Vienna and practiced two years at Paris. At Budapest he won fame as an eye specialist. His works treat alcohol and nicotine effects on sight, eye care, and retina pigments.

From 1860 until death Hirschler led Hungarian Jewish affairs in thought, the entry says. He presided over Pest's Jewish community for some years. As a friend of Baron Eötvös, he advised him closely. He chaired the 1868 Budapest Jewish congress on communal rules. Bitter splits later led him to retire. He died at Budapest on Nov. 11, 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hor-hagidgad-78: Hor-hagidgad was a place in the desert where the Israelites camped during their journey. The entry places it between Bene-jaakan and Jotbathah, citing Numbers. In Deuteronomy the name appears in a changed form, Gudgodah. The short article adds one modern suggestion. Robinson mentioned a Wadi al-Ghudaghid on the west side of the Arabah as a possible match for the site. Beyond those points, the entry offers no further history of the camp or its people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hyena-7964:
Hyena in this entry is a Bible word puzzle. The Septuagint renders a Hebrew word in Jeremiah as hyena. The Vulgate gives a tinted bird, and English versions give a speckled bird. Most commentators side with the Greek. Arabic kinship and a nearby verse about a fierce beast back them.

The striped hyena was common across Palestine, and a place name, Zeboim, may keep its memory. Rabbinic lore gives the animal three more names. Tales say the male hyena changes form every seven years, passing from bat to nettle to thistle to evil spirit. Law ranks its danger with the wolf, lion, bear, and serpent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-iglau-8064:
Iglau is a mining town in Moravia, Austria. Town records first name its Jews in 1250. Charles the Fourth brought Jews in to spur trade, and families settled in the Judengasse, building a synagogue in 1345. Peace lasted near a century. In 1426 Margrave Albert expelled them for alleged league with the Taborites.

Iglau was the first royal town in Moravia to expel its Jews. Exiles could later enter one at a time, and a rule of 1709 let them in by one gate for a fee of fifteen kreuzer. Full relief came only in 1848. A congregation formed in 1861 and dedicated a Moorish-style synagogue in 1863. In 1900 about 1,450 Jews lived among 24,387 people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-inspiration-326:
Inspiration is the state of being prompted by or filled with the spirit of God. Bezaleel was filled with it to plan the Tabernacle. It came on Balaam, on the seventy men chosen by Moses, on Saul, on Elisha and on Daniel, and it let Micah tell Jacob his transgression. The prophet is therefore called "the man of the spirit," the inspired one.

Rabbinic teaching treats the Holy Spirit and the spirit of prophecy as one. Every letter of the Torah was fixed and counted, and even the Masoretic signs grounded laws in Akiba's system. The entry ends with the modern view: prophet and writer spoke under the Divine Spirit, yet as children of their age, their human element not extinguished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-eliak: Isaac ben Eliakim of Posen was a German moralist and author of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. His one named work is "Leb Tob," an ethical book in Judaeo-German in twenty chapters, printed at Prague in 1620. The entry judges its popularity from its many reprintings. Criticism of it appeared in the anonymous "Hassagot," printed at Amsterdam, perhaps, about 1707. That is the whole record the entry gives: no birth or death dates, no teachers, no other writings and no account of his life beyond the book and its reception.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-islami-abd-al-h: Abd al-Hakk al-Islami was a Jewish convert to Islam who lived at Ceuta, in Morocco, in the first half of the fourteenth century. The short entry records one work of his. It is an Arabic book written against the Jews. In it, the Bible passages he quotes are given in Hebrew, spelled out in Arabic letters. Manuscripts of the work are kept in the British Museum. The entry names no other facts about his life, family, or career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-hayyim-a: Hayyim Abraham Israel was an Italian rabbi of the eighteenth century who lived at Candia and Ancona. He wrote two casuistical commentaries, both printed at Leghorn. "Bet Abraham," from 1786, treats the Tur Hoshen Mishpat and the Bet Yosef on it, and ends with a treatise on the laws of government. "Amarot Tehorot," from 1787, does the same work for the Tur Eben ha-Ezer. Mattithiah Terni quotes him in the "Sefat Emet," the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jaazer-or-jazer:
Jaazer, or Jazer, was a city east of the Jordan, in or near Gilead, held by the Amorites. A special force sent by Moses took it, and the Septuagint puts it on Ammon's border. So strong was it that the whole country around bore its name, and Jeremiah even speaks of a sea of Jaazer. The land was rich for cattle, and its vineyards were praised by Isaiah and Jeremiah.

The tribe of Gad held the city and gave it to the Merarite Levites. In David's day Hebronites lived there, and David's census officers used it as a station. Josephus says Judas Maccabeus later captured and burned it. Eusebius and Jerome set it 8 or 10 Roman miles west of Philadelphia and 15 miles north of Heshbon, at the source of a river running to the Jordan. Some name the modern Khurbat Sar as its site; Cheyne rejected that match.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jehoram-joram-8:
Jehoram, also called Joram, is the name of two kings treated in one entry. The first ruled Israel from 852 to 842 B.C. as son of Ahab and Jezebel. He kept up Baal worship, warred with Moab and Syria, and clashed with the prophet Elisha. Wounded at Ramoth-gilead, he was killed by Jehu's arrow at Jezreel, and the house of Omri ended with him.

The second Jehoram was the fifth king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat. He killed his six brothers, married Ahab's daughter Athaliah, and walked in Israel's ways. Edom and Libnah revolted under him, foes sacked Jerusalem, and a warning letter came from Elijah. After two years of painful sickness he died unmourned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonathan-nathan: Jonathan, or Nathan, ben Amram was a near-teacher of the second and third centuries. He would not make learning a way to gain goods, a rule the rabbis pressed hard. In a famine Judah offered food to needy people who had some learning. Driven by want, Jonathan applied but hid who he was. Asked his claim, he said he was only an animal that felt hunger. His plea was let in, and when the trick came out, Judah dropped the learning test for all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-mord: Joseph ben Mordecai ha-Kohen was a Turkish rabbi and hymn writer of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, born in Jerusalem. He studied under Moses Galante the younger. He carried that teacher's book Zebah ha-Shelamim to Amsterdam, where it was printed in 1708. His own book Dibre Yosef, a set of sermons, came out at Venice in 1751. His Sha'are Yerushalayim, printed in 1707, gathers weekday hymns in praise of Jerusalem. Some of those songs are his own work and some are by other hands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ii-8964:
Judah II was a patriarch, son of Gamaliel III and grandson of Judah I, who lived at Tiberias in the middle of the third century. Sources call both him and Judah III by the name Judah Nesiah, so the two are hard to tell apart. In law he is known for three decrees made with his academy. One eased the rules of divorce.

His famed decree let Jews use oil made by pagans, wiping out an old ban. Samuel in Babylonia accepted it as binding. Simlai pressed him to lift the ban on pagan bread as well, but Judah refused. He would not, he said, have his court called the loosing court. His learning drew less awe from great peers than his grandfather's had.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kallir-eleazar-: Eleazar b. Eleazar Kallir was a Hungarian rabbi and author. He died at Kolin, in Bohemia, in 1805. His grandfather was Meïr Eisenstadt, author of "Panim Me'irot." Kallir served as rabbi of Rechnitz and of Kolin. His chief work, "Or Ḥadash," has three parts. One part comments on the Pentateuch. The other two give new notes on two Talmud tractates. He also printed sermons and a volume of responsa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klatzko-mordeca:
Mordecai ben Asher Klatzko was a Russian rabbi and author. He was born in Wilna in 1797 and died at Lida on July 2, 1883. He descended from Rabbi Mayer Katzenellenbogen of Padua. Klatzko was known for his keen mind and retentive memory. In 1831 he became chief teacher at a newly founded yeshibah in Wilna. In 1844 he was chosen dayyan of Wilna.

Klatzko later held the rabbinate at Kalvariya and then at Lida. The entry counts him among the most eminent rabbis of Russia. He probably ordained more young rabbis than any of his contemporaries. His novellæ on the Talmud were partly published after his death. His son issued them as "Tekelet Mordekai" in 1889. A pupil had written them down from Klatzko's oral teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kutner-joshua-h: Joshua Höschel Kutner, preacher at Lissa in the middle of the nineteenth century, wrote a work on faith and inquiry. Printed at Breslau in 1847, it builds out the thirteen articles of belief of Maimonides. Extracts from the Haggadah and from old philosophers support the argument. Three parts treat belief, prophecy and revelation, and last things. An added essay treats the religious state of his own day. A second book, dated 1853, treats the precepts tied to the Decalogue, with a German translation alongside.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lamp-sabbath-12:
Sabbath Lamp is the special lamp or chandelier lit in Jewish homes on Sabbath eve. Early teachers treat the lighting as a known and binding duty. The housewife bears the duty first, and neglect draws a stated penalty. If no woman is in the house, the man must light.

Rules fill most of the entry. Fit wicks are flax, linen, or cotton, while pitch, wax, and fat are barred as fuel. Olive oil is praised most. Two lights match the two forms of the Sabbath command, and some homes hung a lamp of seven or eight branches. Early Karaites barred all Sabbath lights, while later Karaites lit candles on Sabbath eve.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lauchheimer-cha: Charles Henry Lauchheimer, an American naval officer born at Baltimore on Sept. 22, 1859, graduated from the Naval Academy at Annapolis in 1881. A law degree from Columbia followed in 1884. He made first lieutenant in 1890 and captain in 1898. For the last three years he has been a major in the Marine Corps. His two books, both dated 1896, cover naval courts and naval law, with procedure forms revised and enlarged in 1902. The entry gives no family facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-liebermann-libe:
Eliezer Liebermann was a Talmudist of the first half of the nineteenth century. Sources split on his origin. Wolf calls him a native of Austria. Jost says he claimed to be a Hungarian rabbi. In his own preface he signs as a son of Zeeb Wolf, rabbi of Hennegau.

Liebermann acted for the backers of the Reform Temple at Hamburg. In its defense he printed "Nogah ha-Zedek," a set of views from Italian and Hungarian rabbis. One endorsement in it was later declared fake. His "Or Nogah" of 1818 sets out his own long case for Reform. The Hamburg rabbinate answered with a book of Orthodox views in 1819. In 1819 he toured Austria to spread Reform ideas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lob-mokiah-of-p: Mokiah Löb of Polonnoye was a Polish preacher and Hasidic leader of the late eighteenth century. He was a pupil of Israel Ba'al Shem-Tob and of Bär of Meseritz. Tales in a book about the Ba'al Shem tell of wonders linked to him. He wrote Kol Aryeh, sermon notes on the Pentateuch, printed at Korzec in 1802. The entry is brief and gives two source references on Hasidic history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lubarsky-hesche:
Heschel Abramovich Lubarsky, a Russian writer born at Balta in September 1878, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and J. L. Lait. Raised in a Hasidic family, he studied at the Odessa Commercial School and the Riga Polytechnical Institute. As a student in 1897 he joined the Zionist movement.

Lubarsky soon traveled to Palestine and wrote about the Jewish farm colonies he visited there. Back in Odessa in 1898, he wrote “Palestina” (Warsaw, 1900), describing the land and the condition of its Jews. He graduated as an engineer in 1900, kept writing for Russo-Jewish periodicals, and in 1903 published a pamphlet on the Sixth Zionist Congress. His father, the article notes, was a well-known Zionist too. The entry captures a young engineer whose reporting linked Russian readers to the early Zionist settlements.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magic-10264:
Magic, the pretended art of producing unnatural effects, is surveyed at length in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The article defines it beside its twin, divination, within the occult. Its effects may be physical, like storms or sudden death, or mental, like love or hate raised by a spell. Its tools are acts, incantations, and formulas.

The entry traces magic through the Bible first. Deuteronomy names and forbids many kinds of diviners and exorcists as idolatrous. Scripture never doubts that magic works, so the magician is feared and hated. The death law in Exodus speaks of the witch, not the wizard. The Talmud read that as proof that women practiced magic most. Love charms were the commonest form, often tied to illicit affairs. The article then turns to the Babylonian Talmud, rich in magic passages. It shows a practice that law condemned but daily life kept using.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-masliansky-zebi:
Zebi Hirsch Masliansky, a Russian preacher who became a famous orator in America, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik. Born at Slutsk, in the Minsk region, on June 6, 1856, he had a thorough rabbinical schooling, including two years at the yeshivah of Mir. He then taught at Pinsk for about fourteen years, preaching on the side.

Odessa changed his course in 1891: his preaching talent caught the eye of the Zionist leader Lilienblum, who urged him to preach full time. After three years touring Russia with Zionist speeches, he reached the United States in 1895 and was soon counted a leading Yiddish and Hebrew speaker. From 1898 he lectured every Friday evening at the Educational Alliance in New York, and in 1902 he founded a Yiddish daily there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-baruch:
Meir ben Baruch ha-Levi, rabbi of Vienna from 1360 to 1390, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn. A native of Fulda, he was honored across Germany and even by Spanish rabbis. His fame rests on one reform: he brought the formal ordination of rabbis into Germany. Persecution had thinned the ranks of competent rabbis, and unqualified men were being installed, so Meir decreed that no one should serve as rabbi without ordination and the title "morenu."

At first colleagues accused him of wanting to rule them, then accepted the rule; later he extended his authority to France, sending an envoy to appoint rabbis there. The entry closes with a paradox: this powerful organizer left no book, and is known through the custom-book of Jacob Mölln and two prayers ascribed to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendelson-moses:
Moses Mendelson of Hamburg was a German Hebraist. He is not the philosopher of the same name. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A relative of Samson Raphael Hirsch, he lived in his native city as a private scholar. He died there at an advanced age in 1861. His first publication put Campe's discovery of America into Hebrew, printed at Altona in 1807. He also wrote a poem for the installation of Hakam Isaac Bernays. He issued an anonymous devotional work too.

His life's labor was the "Shushan Edut." It explains the Five Books of Moses. Issued at Stuttgart from 1840 to 1842, it represents, by his own account, thirty years' work. Its long Hebrew introduction amuses itself, the entry notes, by scourging preachers old and new. A pamphlet on the Hamburg synagogue, as it was and as it should be, completes the portrait.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-victor-10:
Victor Meyer, born in Berlin on September 8, 1848, was a German chemist of the first rank, profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and J. G. Lipman. Drawn first to literature and the stage, he turned to chemistry after visiting his brother at Heidelberg. There he studied under Bunsen, who made him his private assistant.

At twenty-three Meyer was teaching at Stuttgart, and in 1872 he took a chair at Zurich, then Göttingen, then Heidelberg itself, succeeding Bunsen. He discovered the thiophene group and the oxime type, measured vapor densities, and co-wrote a leading textbook of organic chemistry. The entry ends grimly: unceasing work wrecked his nerves, and in 1897 he took his own life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minters-10864:
Minters are the men licensed to strike a government's coinage. They form a small, sharp Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs, published in 1906. Jews held the office remarkably early. A Priscus was striking coins at Châlons in 555. A Gideon was minter at Milan in the tenth century. England, Germany, and Austria supply the medieval roll.

Three Jews at Winchester were apparently fined for minting in 1181, though the document is ambiguous. The names on short-cross pennies may or may not be Jewish. They are David of London, Isaac of York, and Solomon of Canterbury. In Germany the evidence is firmer. Coins of Bishop Otto of Würzburg name a Jewish mint-master, Jehiel. Schlom, mint-master to Leopold V of Austria, was murdered in the Third Crusade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nadab-lit-liber:
Nadab is the name of four men in the Bible, and the Jewish Encyclopedia article sorts them out. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote it. The first Nadab is Aaron's eldest son, who went up Sinai with Moses and saw the God of Israel. Consecrated priest, he died with his brother Abihu for offering strange fire.

The second Nadab was a king of Israel, Jeroboam's son, who kept his father's idolatry. Baasha assassinated him at the siege of Gibbethon and wiped out his whole house. The remaining two Nadabs are names in genealogies, a Jerahmeelite and a Benjamite of Gibeon. The entry keeps the four apart, as the sources name them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-ben-mach:
Nathan ben Machir was a French Talmud scholar. His entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and A. S. Waldstein for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the eleventh century and studied under Rashi. Rashi prized his learning in Bible and Talmud alike. His brother Menahem was a liturgical poet.

Nathan compiled Ha-Orah, a book of Rashi's decisions. He also wrote parts of the work called Ha-Pardes. He explained some liturgical poems and some prayers as well. An Aramaic poem of his survives as an acrostic. It spells his name and treats a Talmudic legend. The entry shows a scholar shaped by his great teacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neugebauer-ladi:
Ladislaus Neugebauer was a Hungarian bank officer and translator. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Budapest on Feb. 22, 1845. He studied at Budapest and at Vienna. In 1870 he joined the Austro-Hungarian Bank at Vienna.

His first work turned a Jókai novel into German. Poets urged him to translate Petöfi next. The Petöfi Society elected him a member in 1871. The Kisfaludy Society followed eleven years later. Honors came: a gold cross, then a grand cross. In 1892 the king raised him to Hungarian nobility. He took the surname Aszódi with that rank. His versions carried many Hungarian poets to German readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-niter-hebrew-ne:
Niter was the alkaline salt of the ancient world. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Immanuel Benzinger for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was carbonate of soda, not modern saltpeter. Egypt held it in great quantities then. Natron Lake and Natron Valley take their names from it.

Egyptians used much of it to embalm their dead. Smelters found it quickened the flux of ore. Scripture names it as a cleansing agent in Jeremiah. Healers also used it often for medicine. Proverbs likens songs on a heavy heart to vinegar on niter. The salt fizzes when acid touches it, the note explains. The Greek text instead reads, vinegar on a wound.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oesterreichisch:
The Oesterreichische Wochenschrift was an Austrian weekly paper in Vienna. The board and Isidore Singer wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Dr. Josef S. Bloch founded it to fight hate of Jews. It came out each Friday from October 1884 on. Its full name spoke for all needs of Judaism.

In its pages Bloch struck hard at foes of the Jews. He took on Professor Rohling and Pastor Deckert by name. The paper helped unmask Aaron Brimanus and Paulus Meyer. Both men were found guilty in court in time. Known rabbis and scholars wrote for the paper. Chief Rabbi Güdemann of Vienna was one such voice. Theodor Herzl placed his first Zionist pieces in its columns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paleography-118:
Paleography is the study of old script and old carved texts. Crawford Howell Toy, Seymour de Ricci, Joseph Jacobs, and Isaac Broydé wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. About 500 Jewish texts of old are known to men. More texts of pagans name Jewish affairs in part.

Those 500 texts have been found through the old world. Most of them come from the land of Italy. Great Jewish grave caves have been found in that land. No one book holds all such texts in one place yet. A French group gave this task to one of the authors. He made lists of the texts in four set heads. One head lists the lands where each text was found. One lists the kinds of carved texts on stone. One lists their stock phrases and forms of words.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peace-11964:
Peace, in Hebrew shalom, carries more meaning than quiet alone. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Adolf Guttmacher wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word first means wholeness, health, and prosperity. It serves as the common greeting.

The article traces each sense of the word in turn. Shalom can mean friendship between people. It can mean the end of war between nations. It can also mean calm of heart for one person. The prophets looked ahead to a world at peace. Isaiah called the coming ruler the Prince of Peace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pines-elijah-b-: Elijah Pines was a rabbi at Shklov in Russia. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He taught there in the eighteenth century. He descended from Jacob Polak and Judah Puchowitzer. His book Tanna debe Eliyahu came out at Zolkiev in 1753. It treats religion and ethics in seven parts. The parts follow the seven days of the week. An appendix adds notes on the tractate Berakot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pompey-the-grea:
Pompey the Great was the Roman general who brought Judea under Rome. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 65 B.C. he sent his officer Scaurus into Syria. Two years later Pompey came to Syria himself. The land was torn by a fight between two royal brothers.

The brothers were Aristobulus the Second and Hyrcanus the Second. Each sent Pompey rich gifts to win his help. At Damascus all three claims were laid before him. A third party spoke for the people, who wanted no king at all. Pompey put off his choice for a time. He beat down small rulers as he drew near Judea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ranschburg-paul:
Paul Ranschburg was a Hungarian psychiatrist born on January 3, 1870. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Raab. He took his medical degree at Budapest in 1894.

The article says he then joined the psychiatric clinic at Budapest. In 1899 he set up a laboratory for mind and body studies. His writings cover hysteria, old age, and memory. Later books treat weak school children and child psychology. The list runs from 1894 to 1904. Readers see a young doctor building a new field by tests and notes. The entry is short but packed with titles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reines-isaac-ja:
Isaac Jacob Reines was a Russian rabbi born on October 27, 1839. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He founded the Mizrahi, the Orthodox branch of Zionism. He was born in Karlin, in Minsk province.

The article says his father gave him a thorough rabbinical schooling. He also studied logic, mathematics, and medieval philosophy. He learned Russian and German, rare for older Russian rabbis. He studied at the Volozhin yeshivah from 1855. Later posts took him to Shukian and Shwentsian. His book Hotem Toknit proposed a logical Talmud method. Some ultra Orthodox called that plan a dangerous novelty. Only his learning and piety shielded him, they say.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rimos-remos-mos:
Moses Rimos was a physician, poet, and martyr born about 1406. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Palma on Majorca. He died at Palermo in 1430.

The article says he mastered philosophy and several languages. He left home young and lived at Rome in Italy. He finally settled in Palermo and practiced medicine there. A Christian patient died, and poisoning was charged against him. He was imprisoned and sentenced to death for it. Baptism was offered as a way to save his life. He chose death by the hangman instead. Before dying he wrote a metrical poem on his attainments. He also left a wedding poem and a liturgical poem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-eliez:
Eliezer Rosenthal was a German bibliographer born at Nasielsk, in Russian Poland, on April 13, 1794. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His private library at Hanover was famed across Germany for its size.

Rosenthal's shelves held what many called Germany's largest Hebrew library at the time. His own Yodea Sefer lists 2,530 works printed up to 1857. After his death in 1868, M. Roest catalogued the Hebrew part at Amsterdam. That two-volume catalogue, from 1875, prints Rosenthal's list in full. The library itself now rests in Amsterdam's university library.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samek-13064: Samek is the fifteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its name may connect with samek, meaning a prop or support. Samek belongs to the sibilant group and sounds like the English s. It occurs only as a root letter, never as a formative element in words. As a numeral in the later period, samek carries the value of sixty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-san-millan-de-l:
Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on San Millán de la Cogolla. The Spanish village, near Najera, holds a famous old convent. Jews lived there from an early date. They suffered badly in the civil war between Pedro and Henry de Trastamara. The entry rests on two royal orders.

On October 15, 1369, Henry II of Castile acted for the small Jewish community. Its leaders had asked for his help. He ordered Christians and Moors to pay their debts to the Jews at once. That way the Jews could pay their taxes more promptly. On September 10, 1371, he reversed course in part. He freed the abbot and monks of San Millán from their debts to Jews. The two orders show how royal favor shifted with royal needs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shababo-jeshua-:
Jeshua Shababo was an Egyptian scribe and rabbi of the late seventeenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lazarus Grünhut wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His teachers included Abraham ha-Levi of Cairo. Joseph Nazir, another teacher, later became his father-in-law.

Abraham printed some of his pupil's essays in his own book. Where the two men disagreed, Shababo answered in a work printed in 1732. He wrote other books, including a large two-part set of responsa. For a time he worked as a scribe, then left that post on religious grounds. He ended as a judge in Cairo, and the entry preserves his path.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shephatiah-1356:
Shephatiah is a name borne by several persons in the Old Testament. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the name. One Shephatiah was a son of David and Abital. He was David's fifth child, born at Hebron.

Another Shephatiah joined David's guard of thirty at Ziklag. A third led the fighting men of Simeon's tribe. Others head families that returned from exile with Zerubbabel. One was likely a young son of King Jehoshaphat. Still another's descendants came back with Ezra in a group of eighty. The entry lists nine such men, keeping each in his own book and generation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silva-francisco:
Francisco Maldonado de Silva was a Peruvian physician, writer, and martyr for Judaism. Cyrus Adler and George Alexander Kohut wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was born about 1592 at San Miguel in Tucuman. Lima burned him at the stake in 1639.

His father and brother were New Christians reconciled by the Inquisition. Francisco himself was baptized and raised a devout Catholic. He attended mass faithfully until age eighteen. Visiting his father at Callao changed everything for him. There he read a defense of scripture by Paul of Burgos. His father then confessed his own secret Mosaic faith. Francisco embraced Judaism while outwardly keeping Catholic rites. His zeal grew fast, and the entry follows his path to martyrdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sin-offering-13:
The sin-offering was a sacrifice brought to atone for a sin done without intent. Joseph Jacobs, George A Barton, M Seligsohn, and Emil G Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The offering could be a beast or a fowl. Its form changed with the rank of the sinner. A priest or the whole congregation brought a young bullock.

A ruler brought a male kid without blemish. A private person brought a female kid or lamb. The poor could bring a turtle-dove instead. Sin-offerings also marked the Day of Atonement and times of dedication. The entry sets out the full rite of slaughter and blood use on the altar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-jer:
Solomon ben Jeroham, in Arabic Sulaim ibn Ruhaim, was a Karaite exegete. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He flourished at Jerusalem between 940 and 960. Karaites counted him among their greatest authorities on Scripture. They call him the Wise in their prayers for dead teachers.

Like other Karaite leaders, he was a zealous propagandist. His Milhamot Adonai attacked the Rabbinites in verse. He aimed many harsh epithets at Saadia in particular. He tried to refute Saadia's defense of oral tradition. His Bible commentaries breathe deep hatred of foreign nations. He even barred Karaites from studying foreign languages at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spinoza-baruch-:
Baruch Spinoza, or Benedict de Spinoza, was a Dutch philosopher and Bible critic. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Amsterdam on November 24, 1632. His family name came from Espinosa, a town in Leon. His grandfather led the Sephardic community of Amsterdam as president.

Spinoza trained at the communal school and Pereira yeshivah. There he studied Hebrew, Bible, Talmud, and Jewish philosophers. He learned Latin from Franz van den Ende after school. Descartes led him toward a philosophy based on reason alone. Such ideas soon brought rumors of heresy against the young thinker. He died at The Hague on February 21, 1677.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strack-hermann-:
Hermann Leberecht Strack was a German Protestant theologian born in Berlin in 1848. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on May 6 of that year. Since 1877 he taught Old Testament and Semitic languages at Berlin. He studied rabbinics under Moritz Steinschneider.

Strack became Germany's foremost Christian authority on rabbinic literature. When anti-Semitism rose again, he defended the Jews in print. He answered attacks by men like Stöcker and Röhling. In 1883 he founded an institute aimed at converting Jews. He also edited a journal for church work among Israel. Prussia sent him to St. Petersburg to study Bible manuscripts. There he exposed the Firkovich antiquities as forgeries. The entry honors a scholar who fought prejudice with learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theophilus-1436: Theophilus was a high priest, son of Anan and brother of Jonathan. Wilhelm Bacher and Samuel Krauss wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Vitellius deposed Jonathan in 37 C.E. and raised Theophilus in his place. He served about three years before Simon Cantheras succeeded him. Theophilus was probably the father of the high priest Matthias. Büchler identified him with Hananeel the Egyptian, named in the Mishnah. His name also appears in the Seder Olam chronicle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-touro-judah-144:
Judah Touro was an American merchant famed for giving across all creeds. Joseph Jacobs and L. Hühner wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Newport in 1775 and died at New Orleans in 1854. His father ministered to Newport's Jewish congregation. The Revolution scattered that community to Jamaica.

An uncle in Boston raised the orphaned boy. At twenty-two Touro sailed as supercargo to the Mediterranean. The trip proved his sharp business mind. He settled at New Orleans in 1802 and opened a store. Ships and real estate made him a leading merchant. In 1815 he fought as a common soldier for the city. A friend's bravery saved his wounded life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-waley-jacob-147:
Jacob Waley was an English lawyer and professor. He was born in London on March 17, 1819. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died in London in June 1873. At the University of London he took first place in math and classics. He was called to the bar in 1842.

Waley became a leading expert on property transfers. He served as counsel for the Bedford estates. In 1867 the queen named him to a royal commission. That body studied the law on transferring real property. Its report shaped a major bill in 1874. Waley also led the Jews' Orphan Asylum. He was the first president of the Anglo Jewish Association.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-werner-abraham-:
Abraham Werner was a Polish rabbi who led congregations abroad. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Tels, in Kovno province, in 1837. His father was the government rabbi of Tels. Abraham mastered Talmudic literature by age thirteen. Eminent rabbis ordained him in 1856.

Werner served as rabbi at Weger, then as judge at Tels. He rose to chief rabbi of his home town. Next he led all Finland as chief rabbi at Helsingfors. In 1891 London's Mahazike Hadath congregation elected him rabbi. He served there for ten years. In 1901 he settled in the Holy Land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wittmann-franz-:
Franz Wittmann (born 1860) was a Hungarian physicist who led his land on electric tech. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Budapest and then in five more cities in Europe. In 1892 he became a physics professor at the Budapest polytechnic.

Five years later he joined the royal patent bureau. He also served as secretary of the board that tests teachers. His books deal with hard problems in strong currents. One treats the electric lighting of Budapest. Others treat tests of currents from jars and coils. He wrote on sound tests as well. The entry shows a scholar who tied lab work to city needs. His name stood high in Hungarian science at the time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yarmouth-15064:
Yarmouth is a sea town in Norfolk, England, with an old Jewish past. Joseph Jacobs and Victor Rousseau Emanuel wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived in the town at an early date. A deed of 1280 names one Isaac of that town.

One street there was long known as Jews' Row. A synagogue stood on that row for many years. A new one was opened there in the year 1847. It took the place of an old house worn out. In 1877 that house shut for lack of Jews. It serves as a church hall for the poor now. In 1801 the town gave land for a Jew grave yard. The first man laid there was a smith in silver. He had lived in the town for forty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zante-15164:
Zante is an island in the Aegean Sea with a late Jewish past. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Caimi wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews did not form a group there till 1498. That date rests on a study not yet in print then.

In that year Venice held out rights to new settlers there. The isle had lost folk to oft Turkish raids in past years. Jews of Corfu, Patras, and Lepanto took the chance at once. Two kin names stand in the first writs of the isle. In 1527 the Jews of the isle stood at two hundred forty. By 1555 that count had sunk to one hundred forty. By 1809 it had rose to three hundred souls once more. The Jews there have always spoke Greek in daily life.
john-cross-dark-night-soul-lewis-1864:
John of the Cross was a Spanish Carmelite friar who was jailed by his own order for backing reform. In prison he began the poem that his Dark Night of the Soul, in Lewis's 1864 translation, explains line by line. The poem and its commentary treat the soul's purgation, its cleansing by loss.

John describes two nights: one strips the senses of their cravings, the other strips the spirit of its false comforts. The dryness believers fear, he argues, is often growth disguised as abandonment by God. Few books map the hard middle of the spiritual life with such precision and mercy.
joly-dialogue-aux-enfers-1864:
Maurice Joly, a French lawyer, wrote this sly book in Brussels in 1864. Its title means a talk in hell between Machiavel and Montesquieu, in French. Joly aimed his wit at Napoleon III, whose rule he held to be a despot's craft in a new dress.

In twenty five talks, Machiavel lays out how a modern despot can rule by law, press, and fear. Montesquieu makes the case for free rule, and is beat down point by point in the game. The book gained a dark fame when the fake Protocols stole its lines years later.
king-reputed-fossil-man-neanderthal-1864:
William King, an Irish geologist, read his paper on the Neanderthal fossil in 1864. He took a bolder step than his peers dared. King declared the Neanderthal remains a separate human species.

He proposed the name Homo neanderthalensis, which science still uses today. King based his case on the skull's shape and its differences from modern humans.
