They asked whether the playing surface, grass or artificial turf, shapes match results and the formations coaches choose. Many MLS stadiums use turf, so the question affects a large share of games.

Johnson and his co-authors compared outcomes and team shapes across surfaces. Patterns of that kind tell whether turf quietly aids home teams or pushes coaches toward certain lineups. Clubs deciding on stadium surfaces, and leagues weighing fairness, can use such evidence instead of anecdote. Players, too, have a stake in how surface affects play and injury risk.
plos-pone-0358464:
Adrien Le Guillou leads a team of five with a lesson for everyone training image models on small maps, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their task was spotting invasive cordgrass in aerial photographs of tidal marsh, where labeled examples are inherently scarce. Three respected segmentation architectures were each trained under twelve configurations, varying how the training itself was run, for many runs judged by cross validation.

Training strategy crushed architecture. The spread between the best and worst training recipes was about ten points of overlap accuracy; the spread between the three architectures was under one point. Two popular tricks, freezing the encoder and a fashionable loss function, hurt every architecture they touched. The winning recipe mapped the whole Bay of Brest, estimating some forty-four hectares of cordgrass. Elevation data, assumed precious, contributed little beside the color imagery. Data scarce fields should tune their teaching before shopping for bigger models.
plos-pone-0358764: Hussain and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on measuring how body weight spreads across the feet. Their setup uses a grid of force-sensitive resistors, thin sensors that react to pressure, plus foot data analysis. The goal was a shared standard way to record and read such maps. Standard foot pressure records help shoe design, sports science, and care for people with foot risk.
plos-pone-0358864:
Jun Chen, Xun Wan, and Yu Zhou follow three trainee teachers through a year of change in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rural schools in China struggle to recruit and keep teachers, and a beginner's professional identity, how they see themselves as a teacher, shapes whether they stay. The case study examines an English teaching course at a university in western China that wove theory, practice teaching in miniature, and guided reflection into one design.

At the start, the three trainees doubted themselves and pictured teaching as drilling grammar and vocabulary. By year's end their outlook had widened to whole lesson design, and fear had given way to confidence and commitment. Interviews and reflective journals traced the shift to discussion rich practice, where rehearsing, talking, and belonging to a learning community rebuilt identity. The study offers teacher programs a concrete model for growing rural teachers who intend to remain.
plos-pone-0358964:
Jae Shin Song and Min Seok Kim ask whether smoking changes the thickness of the choroid, the blood vessel layer feeding the retina, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their data come from a national Korean health survey spanning 2017 to 2021. Over twenty-two thousand adults with clean eye scans and no eye disease were divided into never, former, and current smokers, and the layer under the central retina was measured for each group.

Thickness rose in steps across the three groups in both eyes. Never smokers measured thinnest, former smokers sat in the middle, and current smokers measured thickest, a gap that survived adjustment for age, sex, eye length, and heart disease. The authors read the pattern as a fingerprint of smoking on the eye's circulation, visible in ordinary population data. Whether the thickening harms or merely marks exposure is a question they leave for follow up studies.
plos-pone-0359164:
Shuai Yan, Qingzhi Yu, Wenfeng Dai, and Xiang Cheng published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents a dual-head transformer model, called GP-DHT, for single-cell gene regulatory network prediction, mapping which genes switch others on and off in individual cells. Pretraining uses shared genes and supervised contrastive learning.

Gene regulatory networks explain how the same DNA produces many cell types. Predicting them from single-cell data is a central problem in genomics, and pretraining on shared genes aims to make the model work across datasets. Computational biologists building cell atlases are the readers who would test this model's predictions.
plos-pone-0359564:
Abdullah Shaker and Muawia Dafalla characterized in 2026 the expansive soils of a region and how their mineral makeup governs their swelling when treated with lime. Expansive soils swell when wet and shrink when dry, cracking roads, pipelines, and building foundations. Adding lime is a standard treatment that tames the swelling, but how well it works depends on the minerals in the soil.

The authors describe the region's soils and test how mineralogy influences the swelling of the treated ground. Regional characterization matters because soil recipes do not travel: what works on one clay may fail on another. Engineers planning foundations and highways in such terrain need exactly this local evidence before they build.
plos-pone-0359864:
Pizhao Hu and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies how people look at book covers, using atlas covers as the test case. The authors connect aesthetic preference, which designs people like, with gaze-based visual attention, where the eyes actually go.

The evidence comes from an eye-tracking study, which records eye movements as people view the covers. Comparing what people say they like with where they look can reveal gaps between taste and attention. Cover designers and publishers can use that pairing to make designs that both attract the eye and please it.
plos-pone-0359964:
Solène Neyret, Julien Pellet, Julien Ryard, Mickaël Campo, and Jean-Rémy Chardonnet wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about professional rugby players. The players were immersed in an interactive virtual environment. The authors work on inducing and measuring identity levels, how strongly players feel merged with their virtual presence.

Virtual training and analysis tools only work if athletes take the simulation seriously as themselves. Measuring identity inside the environment tells designers whether players engage as competitors or as detached viewers. Sports scientists building virtual reality training for contact sports are the audience for methods that create and verify that sense of presence.
plos-pone-0360164:
Mohamed El-Tanani and colleagues reported in 2026 a two front strategy against lung cancers that have learned to resist the drug gefitinib. The cancer type is non-small cell lung cancer, and gefitinib works by blocking EGFR, a growth signal receptor many of these tumors depend on. Resistance to it is a common and deadly turning point.

The team combined EGFR blockade with a second attack on microtubules, the cell's internal scaffolding needed for division. Together, the two pressures raised the stress tied to copying DNA and suppressed tumor growth in their models. Combination strategies of this kind try to close the escape routes that single drugs leave open, and this study tests one pairing in detail.
pmc-10654564:
Omar Y. Mady and co-authors reformulated the antiviral drug acyclovir in 2023 so more of it crosses the intestinal wall. Acyclovir works, but the gut absorbs it poorly, forcing high doses given often. The team used a factory, pilot-scale procedure with span 60, a sorbitan ester, as a granulating agent at several concentrations. They then characterized the granules' flow, drug content, crystallinity, and how the drug partitions between oil and water.

The process trapped drug in the polar part of the span 60, shifting its partition actions. Release tests showed rapid, complete drug release. In a changed non-everted sac test using rabbit intestine, permeability boosted greatly across several calculated measures. Histological checks accompanied the transport work. A manufacturing-friendly method that raises absorption could eventually mean smaller, less frequent doses for patients with herpes infections.
pmc-10655664:
Tahir Qadri and twelve co-authors report a chemistry and cell study from 2023 on a new compound called TAJ1. They made the compound in the lab, checked its shape with light-based tests and crystal analysis, and tested how it affects human cells grown in dishes. The work links the compound to a family of enzymes tied to cell growth.

Computer models showed that TAJ1 binds strongly to one such enzyme, NEK2, which is often active in cancers. The compound also slowed growth in some test cell lines. The authors present TAJ1 as a lead for more work, not as a proven drug, and call for further tests of how stable the binding is.
pmc-10656064:
Ararat Ablooglu and co-authors (2023) tested an antibody that switches on a vessel-protecting receptor, as a treatment for Clarkson disease. The disease causes repeated episodes where fluid leaks from blood vessels. Blood pressure drops dangerously; a third of patients die in a flare, and no effective therapy exists. The antibody, called 4E2, activates the Tie2 receptor without needing its natural trigger. In vessel cells grown from patients, it tightened the barrier and resisted inflammatory damage.

In a mouse model of the disease, the antibody cut deaths and leakage after histamine challenge and flu infection. The authors read this as proof that Tie2 failure sits near the heart of the disease. They present 4E2 as a treatment candidate for a catastrophic orphan disorder. The work matters beyond one rare disease: leaky vessels drive harm in sepsis and severe inflammation, so a switch that seals them could find wider use.
pmc-10656564:
A research team studied why some trees die in long droughts while neighbors survive. Their 2023 paper covers the California drought of twenty twelve to twenty sixteen. They tracked over one million trees and how stand structure shaped death rates. Forest shape, not just dryness, seemed to steer which trees were lost.

Death rates rose and fell with tree height in a wave-like pattern. Trees shaded by taller neighbors died less often, whatever their own height. Shade likely cut sun load and water loss for the sheltered trees. The authors suggest rebuilding varied canopy layers to harden forests against drought. New remote sensing tools could help plan such mixed stands.
pmc-10657464:
Amirhossein Hajiaghajani and co-authors report a body-worn network that moves data and power on land and underwater in this 2023 paper. The body runs many spread-out processes worth tracking. Health tools, virtual reality, and prosthetics all want that data. Sensors stuck on skin must work in air and in water alike. Battery-free wearables draw power through the body-area link itself. An artificial near-field channel across the skin carries both power and signals.

The system kept working from dry settings to fully wet ones. Uninterrupted function across that range is the paper's claim to novelty. Swimmers and divers are among the imagined users. So are patients whose monitors must not drop out. The work is a device ecosystem report. It blends materials, circuits, and body channel physics.
pmc-10674564:
Amanda Fortes Francisco and co-authors test a mouse model of Chagas heart disease in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. The disease follows infection with the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi and scars the heart over years. A good lab model should mirror the human range of damage.

One mouse strain paired with one parasite strain already showed widely varying heart scarring, like patients. Heart tracings in infected mice now revealed early warning signs: slow sinus rhythm, a right bundle branch block, and stretched intervals. Inflamed hearts and a raised enzyme marker appeared in the acute stage, while nerve loss seemed uninvolved. The authors offer the pairing for drug screening.
pmc-10675564:
Yanan Wang and five co-authors trace a gene circuit that controls how long flower stalks grow in a small plant, in a study published in twenty twenty-three. The stalk, called the filament, holds the pollen parts, and its growth matters for plant breeding. The circuit centers on a switch gene named MYB21.

Plants missing that switch grew filaments with shorter cells. In those plants, a second gene ran much hotter than normal. That gene makes an enzyme that cuts the cell's inner scaffolding. Lab tests showed the switch protein grips the second gene's control region and damps its activity. The pair forms a fine-tuning module: the switch holds the cutter gene in check so filament cells reach full length.
pmc-10687464:
Vinit Gilvaz and Anthony Reginato review how artificial intelligence could help care for rheumatoid arthritis in a 2023 paper. This common autoimmune disease makes the immune system attack the joints. At the same time, digital health records and advanced tests have created a flood of patient data, too large for any team to mine by hand.

The authors survey how machine learning and deep learning can read that data: doctor notes, lab tests, and scans alike. Such tools could help spot the disease earlier, forecast its course, and pick treatments that fit each patient. They weigh the proof so far and the gaps that remain, such as data quality and trust. The review closes with what AI may change in the daily care of this disease.
pmc-10691264:
Bo Liao and colleagues describe yak hair follicles and grow their cells in the lab. Their study from twenty twenty-three uses yak skin from the plateau. Yaks evolved thick coats for extreme cold and altitude. Their follicles offer a model for hair growth in harsh climates.

Skin structure was mapped across the hair growth cycle phases. Three follicle-related cell types were cultured successfully. A simplified method sped up isolating the key signalling cells. Fat precursor and support cells also grew in the models. No such yak cell models existed before this work. Hair biology and livestock breeding both gain tools. The models support tests of growth factors without animal trials.
pmc-10693064:
Ziqian Song and co-authors present a 2023 study building a survival chart for small cell lung cancer. This cancer grows fast and carries a poor outlook. A chart that sorts patients by risk could guide treatment choices and follow-up intensity.

The team gathered records for 2,309 patients from hospitals in fifteen cities in Shandong province, treated from 2010 to 2014. Earlier years built the model and the final year tested it. Regression analysis found the traits that independently shaped survival. The chart's sorting power and accuracy were checked with standard curves and compared against the usual stage system. Added tests measured how much the chart improved on staging alone for clinical decisions.
pmc-10694964:
Laura D'Adamo and five co-authors measure a little-known eating disorder in users of an online screening tool, in a 2023 study. The disorder, ARFID, involves avoiding or restricting food without body image concerns, driven by fear, sensory dislike, or low interest in eating. Over fifty thousand adults completed the National Eating Disorders Association screen between January 2022 and January 2023. The team validated screen items for the disorder and counted positive screens.

They compared those who screened positive with others on demographics, eating attitudes, suicidal thoughts, and treatment status and intentions. ARFID is under-researched next to anorexia or bulimia, yet it can starve the body just as surely. Numbers from a sample this large give clinics and researchers a first map of who is affected.
pmc-10698964:
Fifiya Biluala and co-authors present a 2023 study on repeat sexual violence against adolescent girls and young women in Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Survivors of one assault face raised risk of another, yet data outside conflict zones are scarce. The team reviewed records from several centers covering 2015 to 2020.

Of 241 survivors in the records, 74, about thirty-one percent, had been assaulted more than once. Repeat victimization clustered with being over nineteen, being sexually active, and living in a single-parent home. The type of attacker mattered too, with intimate partners among the linked profiles. The authors argue that follow-up protection should focus on these higher-risk survivors.
pmc-10700464:
Sekiko Taneda and six co-authors compare a scarring pattern in transplanted kidneys under four different conditions, in a study published in twenty twenty-three. The pattern, called focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, scars parts of the kidney's tiny filters. It can come back after transplant, or arise from drug harm, rejection, or other disease.

The team sorted two hundred fifty-eight cases from kidney grafts by the condition that came with the scars. Returning disease struck earliest and often showed a collapsed form of the filters. Drug-linked cases mostly showed a plain form with heavy vessel harm. Rejection cases had the worst kidney function and most inflammation. Most of the rest had other clear causes, such as reflux or immune attack. The patterns may help doctors find the true cause.
pmc-10701964:
Yiran Hao and seven colleagues published a 2023 study that checks a quick test for dry eye disease. The phenol red thread test uses a small thread that changes color when wet with tears. It is fast and easy, but its accuracy in Chinese patients needed a firm check.

The study enrolled 108 eyes, split into groups with and without dry eye disease. Each eye got a full set of tests, from symptom scores to tear film checks and the Schirmer test. The authors measured how steady the thread test was across repeats and readers. They also checked how well it matched other tests and flagged disease on its own. The aim is a clear verdict on its use in clinic.
pmc-10704664:
José Ramón Martínez-Riera published this editorial in 2023. It previews two major nursing gatherings held in Spain in the same week of October, in Madrid and Granada. The first is the seventh international congress of the Community Nursing Association, an organization with almost thirty-five years of history. Its theme is vulnerability and community health, with a focus on the social determinants that shape health. The editorial stresses care for vulnerable populations through a comprehensive, integrated approach.

The second event is the seventeenth Ibero-American nursing education conference, run by an association of nursing schools with a similar history. Its theme is research in nursing education and building an Ibero-American context for care. Martínez-Riera argues the two meetings complement each other. They push nursing knowledge across the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking world, centered on people, families, and communities rather than on nations.
pmc-10707764:
Ajna Hamidovic, Shahd Smadi, and John Davis study food craving across the menstrual cycle in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Craving is a tangled behavior tied to weight. The team asked whether it swings with cycle phase, and whether obesity or a severe premenstrual mood disorder changes the pattern. Women of reproductive age were sorted into four groups by abdominal obesity and by the mood disorder's presence. Group sizes ran from thirteen to sixteen women.

Participants used self-reports and urine hormone tests over two to three cycles. Craving stayed flat across most of the cycle. In the final days before bleeding, women with both obesity and the mood disorder craved more strongly. Their craving also tracked mood symptoms. The finding may help time weight-loss support to the riskiest days.
pmc-10712864:
Shevchenko and five co-authors checked in twenty twenty-three how long stress shifts gut germs in rats bred for calm or jumpy nerves. Gut germs talk to the brain and may shape stress ills like low mood. They gave rats long sore and felt stress and read stool germs at set times.

The calm-bred rats held a more wide range of gut germs than the jumpy line. Under long stress the calm line gained two germ groups in their stool. Both lines lost a milk germ group after stress in the same way. Breed thus shapes how stress moves the gut, they find.
pmc-10714564:
Inui and a large team reported in twenty twenty-three on a knee swap that keeps both cross cords in the joint. The goal is a knee that moves more like a real knee. Past results with this swap have been mixed, so the team used a fit tuned to each person.

They checked fifty such swaps and matched them with fifty-eight part swaps of the knee. X-rays showed the joint line and gaps stayed close to plan across bend angles. At about two years, scores for the full swap were as good as or a bit better than the part swap. Folks also had a bit more bend at full stretch.
pmc-10716164:
Shu Yang and colleagues finger a sugar-burning enzyme as the switch that turns kidney scarring on, in this study from twenty twenty-three. Chronic kidney disease rewires tubule cells toward glycolysis, and the platelet form of phosphofructokinase, PFKP, is its rate limiter. In mice with a blocked ureter, forcing extra PFKP into tubules widened them, fed glycolysis, and spread fibrosis; silencing it did the opposite.

The upstream hand was the scarring signal TGF-beta, which docks a SMAD3-SP1 protein complex onto the PFKP gene to raise its output, confirmed in human tubule cells. A plant flavonoid, isorhamnetin, dialled the enzyme's elevation back and eased both glycolysis and fibrosis in the animals. The authors propose PFKP as a metabolic drug target for kidney fibrosis, a disease with few.
pmc-10716664:
Loranzie Rogers and co-authors show a fish's swim bladder doubles as a sound maker and a sound receiver in this 2023 study. The plainfin midshipman is a vocal fish that hums to court. Its bladder vibrates to produce those calls. The same organ can also help the fish hear. Male bladders change shape with breeding state. Breeding males grow horn-like extensions at the bladder's front.

Shape, electrical, and modeling methods were combined in the study. The extensions boost low-frequency sound handling in season. One organ thus serves both sides of the conversation. That flexibility is called functional plasticity in the title. The work links body change to communication success. It is a study in animal bioacoustics.
pmc-10717764:
Xiaoyun Wu and co-authors check the safety of stem cells grown in a serum-free defined medium, in work published in 2023. The cells come from umbilical cords and are candidates for therapy. The team's defined medium avoids animal serum, and cells grown in it had earlier shown stronger therapeutic effects than serum-grown cells.

Before clinical use, they compared the two cell types in rats after injection into the abdomen. They tracked vital signs, blood tests, immune cell mixes, organ tissue, and antibody production, plus tumour risk in mice. The defined-medium cells caused no significant changes in the rats and produced no antibodies, while serum-grown cells triggered high antibody levels. Neither type promoted tumours. The authors judge the defined-medium product to have the better safety profile.
pmc-10717864:
Lun Huang and five co-authors present a 2023 study on predicting breathing trouble after a ventilator tube comes out in elderly patients. The patients, one hundred nine analyzed, were recovering in an anesthesia intensive care unit after bowel cancer surgery. Nineteen suffered critical respiratory events after extubation. The team combined ultrasound measures of the diaphragm's movement and thickening with a monitor reading of remaining muscle relaxation.

The event group was older, more often female, and more often had prior lung disease; their diaphragm and relaxation measures all ran lower. Three measures independently predicted trouble. Combined, they forecast events with an accuracy score of about zero point nine five, beating any single measure. The authors recommend the paired bedside checks before pulling the tube in older patients.
pmc-10719864:
Anne Hokstad and co-authors study how the early pandemic changed activity and quality of life for stroke survivors in Norway, in a survey study from 2023. The group was already enrolled in a long-term trial of life after stroke. The team sent a questionnaire between March and July 2021.

Of 150 invited patients, 118 answered. Two thirds said they moved less than before lockdown, and about two in five felt lonelier or reported worse quality of life. In simple checks, less activity, loneliness, and worse mental health all tracked with poorer quality of life. When factors were weighed together, only reduced activity kept a strong link, with fourfold odds. The authors flag activity support as a key need in crises.
pmc-10720164:
Oliver Rumle Hovmand and co-authors published a 2023 study testing a well-known mood questionnaire in Danish patients. The questionnaire, called PANAS, measures two traits: positive affect, such as feeling alert and keen, and negative affect, such as feeling upset or afraid. The team checked whether the Danish version works well for outpatients with depression or anxiety.

Scores from 256 patients were analyzed. Both halves of the questionnaire gave steady, consistent results. Statistical checks confirmed the expected two-part structure, one part for each kind of affect. The scores also lined up sensibly with other measures. Positive affect fell as detachment and depression rose. Negative affect rose with anxiety and depression scores. The authors conclude the Danish version is sound for this patient group. That gives clinics and researchers in Denmark a trusted tool for tracking mood traits.
pmc-10724364:
Liantao Ma and colleagues published a 2023 study building an artificial intelligence tool that predicts death risk for kidney patients on peritoneal dialysis. The system, called AICare, learns from electronic medical records gathered over many follow-up visits. Unlike many medical algorithms, it was designed so doctors can see which factors drive each prediction.

The training data covered hundreds of dialysis patients and thousands of visits across twelve years, with a second public dataset used for comparison. The tool beat standard deep learning models while showing how each factor's importance shifts over time. A companion display lets doctors view a patient's health path and risk signals together.
pmc-10724564:
van Balkum and coauthors compare two blood tests for Graves disease. Graves disease stems from antibodies that switch the thyroid on. Labs have long used a test that counts all such antibodies. That test counts both the ones that switch on and block.

A newer test counts just the switch-on type more sharply. The team checked both tests in real clinic use. Their set held 356 patients with Graves disease or eye signs. Tests took place at a large thyroid center. The team asks which test guides care best in daily practice.
pmc-10726364:
Swanson, Lau, and Tuttle study tiny peptoids, which are kin to peptides but with side chains moved to a new spot. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. That small change lets peptoids take more shapes than peptides can. Some short peptoids with ring-shaped side chains join up on their own into neat, ordered forms.

The team asks if the way a side chain moves inside one molecule can hint at whether it will build such forms. They build force field tools and run many checks. Even spread of shapes across key twists tracks well with good assembly. One short peptoid shares a shape theme with a known tube-forming peptide, which may mark a route to long, straight builds.
pmc-10730464:
Ningning Kang and five co-authors report a refined chest surgery for a collapsed lung in this two thousand twenty-three paper. The condition, primary spontaneous pneumothorax, strikes when a weak blister on the lung bursts. Surgery that removes the blister and part of the chest lining lowers the chance of relapse. The authors' center added a twist to this standard operation. They operate through a single small port with a camera.

Their method strips the upper lining but keeps it in the chest on a stalk. The kept lining then covers the lung stumps. The team reviewed eighty-six patients treated this way over three years. They report their early experience and how well relapse was prevented. The report offers other thoracic surgeons a technique worth testing.
pmc-10732664: Delphine Pedeboy gives a first-person account of contracting female genital schistosomiasis. The disease is a neglected tropical condition affecting some fifty-six million women worldwide. She describes her own illness and distills the experience into concrete recommendations for the global health community. Her asks aim at helping other women get diagnosed sooner and treated better. Personal testimony of this kind is rare in the medical literature for this condition. The piece uses it to press for practical change in outcomes for women living with or recovering from the illness.
pmc-10733764:
Rossella De Falco and co-authors wrote this 2023 paper on whether human rights law can rein in private health care. Private firms now help finance, run, and govern health systems in many countries, and their role feeds economic inequality. The authors review what international and regional rights bodies have said about that role.

They survey rulings and statements from United Nations treaty bodies and recent cases from the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights. The review weighs where current standards on the right to health are strong and where they leave gaps on private actors. It closes with recommendations to sharpen those standards. The paper serves lawyers and advocates working on health equity.
pmc-10735664:
Jee eun Kang and co-authors tracked day-by-day links between social life and objectively measured sleep in older adults, in a 2023 study. Volunteers in an aging study, 285 people averaging 77 years old, reported social interactions and physical contact four times daily for sixteen days by phone prompts. Wrist devices recorded their sleep at the same time.

On days with more social interaction than usual, participants fell asleep earlier, slept less overall at night, and spent less time awake mid-sleep, though sleep efficiency held steady. Extra physical contact days showed earlier and shorter sleep without the mid-sleep change. The models adjusted for health and living setup.
pmc-10735764:
Reed Bratches and co-authors survey family caregiver comfort with telehealth in this 2023 paper. During the COVID-19 pandemic, most patients needed help to join telehealth visits. Family caregivers often gave that help. Their comfort with computers, phones, and tablets varies, and the team asked whether it varies by race and ethnicity.

Survey data from 2020 covered 340 caregivers across the United States. Comfort was rated for each of the three device types. Models adjusted for other traits that might explain gaps. Asian caregivers reported higher odds of comfort with computers than White caregivers. Black and Hispanic caregivers reported lower odds on some measures. The gaps matter for fair access to remote care.
pmc-10736164:
Ashley Bryant and co-authors present a 2023 report on an oral health program for people with mild memory or thinking problems and their care partners. Failing cognition often brings dirty teeth, gum disease, and tooth loss, which feed wider illness. Care partners do much of the brushing help, so the program trained them.

The team studied coaching sessions from seventeen pairs, ten with mild cognitive impairment and seven with mild dementia. They cataloged which behavior change techniques the coaches actually used. Prompts and cues, direct instruction, goal review, and problem solving appeared often in both groups. Social support surfaced for the impairment group, and trusted expert voice for dementia. The overlap clarifies the program's active ingredients.
pmc-10736564:
Zhixuan Lin and Helene Fung ask in 2023 whether a varied daily life makes older adults happier. Two theories clash: one says aging well means focusing on fewer pursuits, the other says variety brings purpose. They tested the question in Hong Kong's hot summer, where going out more also means more heat.

A group of 344 adults aged 60 and over reported their activities and moods three times a day for ten days. More varied days went with less positive mood, less meaning, and more loneliness. Heat risk itself worsened mood but did not change the variety effect. The authors conclude that, in this setting, focused activity served older adults better than breadth.
pmc-10736664:
Katherine Supiano, Troy Andersen, Laura Bradbury, and Kimberly Ponce Gonzalez describe building a training program with nursing home social workers in two thousand twenty-three. The intervention at the center is PreLoss Group Support, a ten-session group program for family care partners of residents living with dementia. It aims to support healthy preparation for a loved one's death and better bereavement afterward. Earlier cohorts were led by research-team licensed social workers, with nursing home staff as trainees.

The new pragmatic trial tests whether telehealth-delivered PreLoss Group Support works when nursing home social workers run it themselves. Stakeholders helped design a full-day clinical education program, including scripted family characters played by professional actors. Trainees rated the training highly, with a satisfaction rate near ninety-five percent.
pmc-10737364:
Arden ODonnell mapped palliative care for homeless adults in a 2023 study of ten United States cities. The homeless population is aging, with a median age near 50, and street life brings the ills of old age decades early. Yet journal proof on end-of-life care for this group was tiny, just six intervention studies in a 2017 sweep.

ODonnell searched the grey literature of the ten cities with the largest homeless counts. Community programs that journals missed were the quarry. The map shows what care is emerging on the ground, from hospice beds to street teams. It gives funders a base for a long-neglected field.
pmc-10737464:
Narcissa Plummer, Aneeka Ratnayake, Chelsea Wong, and Brianne Olivieri-Mui published a 2023 study of whether historic redlining still shapes nursing home quality. Redlining was a 1930s practice that marked neighborhoods with many residents of color as risky, cutting off investment. The team mapped Massachusetts nursing homes from 2021 onto a 1934 redlining map and compared quality ratings and income growth across the old zones.

Most of the 63 homes sat in areas once labeled declining or hazardous, and only two sat in the best-rated zones. Both of those homes held top five-star ratings, while just one home in a hazardous zone did. Incomes had risen most in some hazardous areas, yet home quality there stayed low. The authors suggest that new money alone may not repair the old harm.
pmc-10738364:
Travonia Brown-Hughes, Alyssa Gamaldo, Corinne Pettigrew, and Roland J Thorpe studied thinking skills in highly educated African American adults, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. All took part in a memory and aging project and were tested by phone or online. None had dementia, and all were aged fifty or older.

Older age went with slower speed on attention tasks, even after other factors were counted. Age also hinted at weaker learning scores. Mood problems, metabolic conditions, and daily activity levels showed no clear link to test scores. The authors say more work is needed on how midlife strengths and risks shape thinking in later life for this group.
pmc-10738964:
Susan Saffel-Shrier, Amy Covington, and Jing Wang test, in a 2023 study, a fuller way to assess poor nutrition in older adults who live at home. Many older people enter hospital already malnourished, and those sent home with meal deliveries face the same risk. Yet little research guides nutrition care for this group. The team built an assessment that also weighs social and living conditions.

A pilot study enrolled 46 people from meal programs in northern Utah. A dietitian visited homes over six months and applied the new assessment in both the study and comparison groups. The group that received the fuller care improved more on a hands-on nutrition exam, ate more calories and protein, and moved better on a timed stand-and-walk test. The authors report that the approach lifted both nutrition and daily function.
pmc-10739364:
Ye Luo, Dandan Zhao, Xi Pan, and Lingling Zhang study how home conditions track with cognitive decline in China, in a research paper from 2023. Older adults spend much time at home, yet few studies weigh many home factors together. The team asks how social, economic, and physical home traits shape thinking over time.

Data cover more than sixteen thousand adults aged forty-five and older, across four survey waves from 2011 to 2018. Living with a spouse but not children, higher spending, better housing, and clean cooking fuel all tracked with slower decline. Effects split by sex and age. Housing policy may thus support brain health in later life.
pmc-10741664:
Doris Hansen and a team of co-authors review cell therapy for blood cancers given in clinic rather than in hospital, in two thousand twenty-three. These engineered cell therapies are usually delivered to inpatients. Giving them to outpatients is growing fast, but pooled evidence comparing the two settings was limited.

The review covered thirty-eight reports from twenty-one studies. Side effect rates looked alike in both settings, and response rates overlapped closely. Quality of life improved in both, while costs ran lower for outpatient care. Outpatients did face more unplanned hospital visits, yet used fewer health resources overall. The authors conclude outpatient delivery can match hospital care on key outcomes while easing cost.
pmc-10741964:
Riccardo Mastroianni and co-authors wrote a study from 2023 on life quality after bladder removal surgery for cancer. The operation, with its rerouted urine flow, is among the heaviest in urology, yet quality of life is often left unmeasured beside survival. The team enrolled patients facing the surgery and a healthy comparison group, then matched eighty-five pairs by age, other illness, and smoking. Patients answered a standard quality questionnaire before surgery and at six, twelve, and twenty-four months after.

Even before surgery, patients scored worse on mood, thinking, appetite, and money strain. Afterward, the surgical route split the recovery. Those opened the classic way hurt more across every window: more fatigue, nausea, pain, and appetite loss. The robot-assisted group, whose urine rerouting was done inside the body, tracked closer to healthy scores. The authors argue the gentler route buys a faster, fuller return to daily life.
pmc-10742064:
Bharati, Kumar, Kumar, Malhotra, and Singhal review microRNA-193a as a rising mediator of kidney glomerular diseases, in a review from twenty twenty-three. Small regulatory RNAs tune how much protein a cell makes from its messenger RNAs. This one proved directly harmful in a mouse model of a scarring disease of the glomeruli, the kidney's tiny filters. It switches off a factor that keeps the filter cells sound.

It also flips cells next door toward a filter-cell identity in lab dishes. Links reach to diabetic and membranous kidney diseases as well. Since good biomarkers are lacking, this mediator draws clinical interest. What drives its levels up shifts from disease to disease and stays unclear. The review maps how it acts and what use care might make of it.
pmc-10742164:
Yun, Cho, Jeon, Lim, and Kim wrote a review in twenty twenty-three on tracking stem cells inside the body with fluorescence. Stem therapies need watching to prove safety and reveal how they work. Glow-based imaging offers sharp detail and live monitoring. Several color tags can be followed at once. Label routes include glow genes, dyes, and nanoparticle uptake. Pairing glow with other scans covers single-method blind spots.

Partners include light-emission, nuclear, sound, and magnetic imaging. The review walks through each pairing's strengths. Efficient, precise detection strategies are the organizing thread. It suits readers designing cell-tracking experiments.
pmc-10744064:
Nephrotic syndrome, where kidneys leak protein and children swell with fluid, is the most common glomerular disease of childhood. Guillaume Mahamat Abderraman and co-authors describe cases from three hospitals in Chad in this 2023 study, a rare report from one of the world's poorest countries.

Twenty-four cases appeared among nearly seventeen thousand children seen over three years, mostly young boys with swelling. About nine in ten of the unexplained cases answered to steroid treatment. Biopsies in the stubborn cases mostly showed scarring disease. At last check, four in five unexplained cases were in full remission with healthy kidneys, and none had died.
pmc-10745764:
Hua Zhu leads a ten-author team optimizing how to extract medicinal polysaccharides from an orchid herb, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Dendrobium huoshanense is a valued plant, as food and as a drug. Its polysaccharides are the main active ingredient, and how they are drawn out shapes how they are built.

Three methods were tuned with response surface statistics: enzyme-assisted, ultrasound-microwave-assisted, and hot water extraction. The products looked unlike under the microscope. The enzyme product formed irregular granules, while the rest looked like a sponge. How they acted with heat also split by method. The team sets chemical properties and antioxidant activity side by side, so makers of herbal extracts can pick a process that fits their quality marks.
pmc-10746964:
Alexander Tacey and co-authors co-design a digital aid for patients waiting for bone specialist care. Public hospital waits for osteoarthritis consults run long and keep growing. Waits hit hardest for patients from poor and mixed-language areas who lean on public care. Patients, clinicians, experts, and hospital staff shaped the tool together in rounds.

Talks with sixteen clinicians and eleven patients set the needs list. Seven content modules were built and refined over the rounds. All content was rendered into Vietnamese, the top local tongue after English. Fifteen new patients tested the tool for two weeks at home. Usability scored in the excellent band, with a mean near eighty-three of one hundred.
pmc-10747064:
Aras Türkoğlu and co-authors present a 2023 study on how silver treatments affect wheat grown from cells in the lab. Silver nitrate and silver nanoparticles can steer callus growth, the lump of cells from which new plants regenerate, and can also alter DNA marking. The team wanted a clear model of those effects.

They treated wheat tissue, measured callus formation and plant regeneration, and read DNA profiles for changes. The treatment and molecule data then fed machine learning and mathematical models of the outcomes. Such models could help breeders pick doses that raise regeneration while limiting unwanted DNA change, speeding lab-grown wheat work.
pmc-10748264:
Trong-Dong Pham and colleagues improved face expression reading in 2023. Reading expressions helps machines grasp human emotion. Most past work redesigned the neural network itself. The scoring rule behind training got little attention. The team wrote a new scoring rule for training. It handles two kinds of variation at once. Faces of one emotion should cluster tightly together. Faces of different emotions should sit far apart. The rule pulls features toward their own class center. It pushes them away from other centers too.

Standard photo and video datasets tested the rule. Four well-known benchmark sets were used. Results beat existing scoring rules on those sets. The authors argue loss design matters as much as network shape. Their rule needs no new network hardware. Any similar classifier could adopt it in training. The work targets steadier emotion reading in real applications.
pmc-10749564:
Rita E Atalor, Blake W Dieckmann, John S Penn, and MD Imam Uddin describe a way to calm immune cells that drive eye vessel growth. Their methods paper, from twenty twenty-three, targets a gene called HIF-1 alpha. White blood cells called monocytes enter the retina when it is inflamed. In diabetes they switch on in the blood and may fuel harmful new vessels.

The team built a tiny hybrid carrier that brings gene-silencing strands to these cells. In lab tests it cut the target gene in mouse cells starved of oxygen. In mice with an eye disease model, shots cut new vessel growth. Gene levels in blood cells also fell toward normal.
pmc-10771864:
Yoshinori Maki and co-authors reported this surgery paper in 2023. Neck wear can squeeze both the spinal cord and the nerve roots that branch off it, causing pain, weakness, and trouble walking. Care often needs two staged operations, front and back. The team shows a one-session back route that mixes three moves to fit each patient's map of squeezes.

Two men are described. One had cord squeeze plus pinched roots on both sides at set levels; the other had cord squeeze plus pinches low in the neck. Each got a blend of bone-arch widening, bone removal, and root-hole widening in a single session. Both men's pain eased after surgery. The authors say fitting the mix to the case can spare patients a second operation.
pmc-10788564:
Jae-Gu Cho and six co-authors present a 2023 study on parathyroid glands removed by accident during thyroid surgery. These tiny glands control blood calcium, and losing them can cause lasting harm. Even careful surgeons sometimes take one out without knowing. Past work sorted the glands' hiding places into a few types. The team asked whether a partly buried gland, sunk partway into the thyroid, forms its own risky type.

Reviewing 743 thyroid operations, they found accidental removal in about one case in eight. Of 103 glands removed, most sat within the thyroid's capsule, and over half of those were fully or partly buried. The authors argue the partly buried gland is as risky as one fully inside the thyroid. New imaging methods that make glands glow may help surgeons spare them in future.
pmc-10811764:
Kayla Ann Jackson, Kate Eliza Collins, Te Yeun Kim, and Rebekah E Donaldson ask whether COVID-19 lockdowns changed bladder disease rates in cats. Their 2023 study reviews emergency visits at two Queensland hospitals across two years, split at the start of movement restrictions. The two feline conditions studied, a bladder inflammation of unknown cause and urethral blockage, are both tied to stress.

Cases were sorted by strict criteria, excluding infections and repeat sufferers. Incidence in the restriction year was compared with the year before using standard risk measures. Owners working from home changed cats' routines and stress in opposite directions at once, so the direction of any effect was genuinely open. The study gives vets data where anecdote had ruled.
pmc-10823364:
Lanbo Wang and co-authors wrote a cohort study, dated 2023 in its text, on a cholesterol ratio and stroke risk in older Chinese adults. The ratio weighs the harmful cholesterol classes against the protective one. Past work treated its link to stroke as a straight line. The team followed more than ten thousand middle-aged and older adults from a national aging study for about seven years.

About one in nine suffered a stroke. In the plain model, the ratio showed no clear link to stroke. A curved model told a different story: the link bent at a clear threshold. Below the bend, each step down in the ratio came with a notably lower stroke risk. Above the bend, the risk stopped moving with the ratio. Repeat checks under varied assumptions held the shape. The team urges doctors to read the ratio with its bend in mind.
pmc-10962664:
Yu-Te Yeh and four co-authors hunt the compounds in Chinese olive fruit that slow cancer cell growth, in a 2023 study. The fruit is rich in phenolic compounds, chemicals plants make that often carry health effects. Earlier work hinted at promise, but the active molecules were unnamed.

The team split the fruit extract into fractions and tested each on mouse colon cancer cells. A linked instrument chain then separated the winning fractions and read the structures of their contents in one flow. Thirteen phenolics were identified, including two never described before. Several purified compounds, among them derivatives of chebulic acid, showed strong growth-slowing power. Naming the actives is the first step toward any future drug or supplement claim.
pmc-11532364:
Ying Li and co-authors study how a ratio of thyroid hormones links to blood sugar swings in type 2 diabetes, in work published in 2024. The ratio reflects how sensitive the body's tissues are to thyroid hormones. Sugar swings, beyond average sugar level, may harm patients over time.

The study covered 468 hospital patients who wore continuous sugar monitors for six to fourteen days. Patients in the lowest quarter of the ratio had the worst sugar control on nearly every measure, including more time spent too high. The link between the ratio and several swing measures was curved, with turning points the team located. Below those points, a higher ratio meant steadier sugar. The authors suggest the ratio could help flag patients prone to unstable sugar.
pmc-11535064:
Naohide Shinohara and eight co-authors gauge COVID spread risk in the Tokyo Dome with fake spit drops. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Wind flow and drop spread were taped in the dome, which holds fifty-five thousand folks. Seats face one way in rows, and drops from cough play acts were read on the folks and seats in front.

Set face-first, drops did not reach the mouths of near folks. Masks cut drops laid on hair, neck, and seats by two to three spans of ten, but a nose-out mask cut seat drops far less. Bare a trace of fine mist was breathed in.
pmc-11536864:
Hairui Zhang and co-authors compare shoulder treatments for calcified rotator cuff tendons in a 2024 records study. Calcium deposits in the shoulder tendon cause pain and stiffness. Needling under ultrasound can break them up, and shock wave therapy is another standard option. The team compared needling alone with needling plus high- or low-energy shock waves.

Records covered 130 patients, split near evenly across the three groups. At three months, both shock wave groups hurt less than the needling-only group, and the gap held at six and twelve months. Shoulder function scores followed the same pattern. Scans showed the combined treatments cleared calcium faster and more fully. High and low energy waves did not differ clearly from each other.
pmc-11546364:
Ivana Šola and colleagues published a food science study in 2024 on microgreens from the cabbage family. They compared kohlrabi, Savoy cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, radish, and garden cress. Each was measured young, as a microgreen. The team tracked plant chemicals linked to antioxidant and blood sugar effects.

Lab methods measured phenols, glucosinolates, proteins, sugars, and vitamin C. Garden cress had the least soluble sugar. Savoy cabbage and Brussels sprouts carried the most glucosinolates. Brussels sprouts best blocked protein glycation, a process tied to diabetes damage. The team also ran the greens through simulated digestion. They checked which helpful compounds survived each stage and kept working.
pmc-11547564:
Iodine deficiency still harms health in poorer countries, and adding iodine to salt is the main defense. The authors pooled household survey data from forty-nine low and middle income countries, gathered between 2005 and 2021. They asked how many households use salt with enough iodine, and how that share varies with wealth, place, and education. A combined analysis put the overall share at about eighty-three percent.

The averages hide sharp gaps. East Asia and the Pacific and Europe and Central Asia both reached about eighty-eight percent. Latin America and the Caribbean lagged far behind at about thirty-one percent. Poorer and rural households were less likely to have adequately iodized salt. The authors call for stronger public health efforts aimed at access, education, and price, to protect groups at highest risk of deficiency, above all children and pregnant women.
pmc-11557364:
Jian-Gao Fan and co-authors issue, in a 2024 guideline, updated advice for preventing and treating fatty liver disease tied to metabolic trouble in China. With obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome rising, this liver condition is now the country's most common chronic liver disease. The update replaces a 2018 version and renames the disease to its modern term.

The guideline covers screening, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up in full. It stresses that the liver problem travels with heart and metabolic risks, so care teams should span specialties. Advice also speaks to patients carrying alcohol-related damage or hepatitis B at the same time. The authors frame the disease as a public health threat needing joint action.
pmc-11559964:
Rajani Brandsen and co-authors scan the central retina in sickle cell disease to see if early change warns of wider eye damage, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Scans of two hundred forty-nine eyes from one hundred thirty-seven patients measured thinning and vessel density at the macula. Eye exams graded the outer retina disease stage.

Thinning showed in about four in ten eyes and tracked with lower vessel density nearby. Age and female sex also tracked with lower density. Yet no link tied macular change to the stage or presence of outer retina disease, and vision was not impaired. The scan finds macular change well, the authors note, but does not flag who risks outer damage.
pmc-11565264:
Aya Olivia Nakitanda and four co-authors studied the safety of a common drug in pregnancy. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, looked at tetracycline use in the first three months. They asked if use at that stage raised the risk of major birth defects. The team used health records for babies born in Sweden over more than a decade.

Babies whose mothers took the drug were matched with babies whose mothers did not. The match used scores that made the two groups alike in other ways. Readers learn how large record based studies test drug safety when trials in pregnancy are not done. The work speaks to care choices for women who need this drug class early on.
pmc-11577664:
Dorothea Lindtke and her three co-authors, publishing in 2024, study what happens genetically when beef bulls are bred to dairy cows. Crossing promises meatier calves and a hybrid vigor boost. The risks are overlarge calves at birth and the loss of genes the dairy breed refined for its own setting. The team sequenced Brown Swiss cows, bulls from Angus, Limousin, and Simmental breeds, and 301 crossbred calves.

Inbreeding fell sharply in the crosses, with little difference between sire breeds. In the dairy cows, 585 genes showed signs of past selection, mostly tied to milk and production. Only a handful of genes differed sharply between the breeds. One cluster of four genes stood out: the dairy version tracked with lighter carcasses in the calves. The authors suggest picking mating pairs by markers could tune calf traits while keeping the inbreeding gains.
pmc-11580064:
Flavio Pinheiro Martins and co-authors review how climate change loads a double burden onto health systems, in a paper from 2024. Systems must treat climate-driven illness while their own buildings, staff, and budgets face the same storms and heat. The team scanned 179 studies for themes, trends, and gaps. Their lens was how systems can grow tougher without losing fairness.

Strong governance that bakes climate into planning stood out first. Money must be raised in fresh ways, since old budgets strain. Buildings, supply chains, and staff skills all need to adapt to new risks. Service delivery must bend during heat waves, floods, and disease shifts. The authors call for joint work across fields and for care that shields the most exposed. They map where proof is thin and new studies should aim.
pmc-11585064:
Christoph Königs and co-authors report a clinical study, published in 2024, on rescue treatment for people with severe haemophilia A. Some patients develop inhibitors, antibodies that block the factor VIII protein used to control bleeding. An earlier method called immune tolerance induction had already failed for these patients, so the team tested a long-acting form of the protein, given within a set period of sixty weeks.

Sixteen subjects took part, and nine finished the treatment period. One subject met all three marks of full success, two reached partial success, and one more cleared the inhibitor without full success. Blood tests also tracked antibody types and immune cells, and no new safety concerns appeared. The authors conclude that the rescue approach can help some hard-to-treat patients, though success was far from certain.
pmc-11593964:
Maoqin Xia and co-authors compare the chloroplast genomes of ginger family plants across China, in a study from 2024. The genus Zingiber holds herbs prized as medicine, food, and garden plants. Their family tree has stayed murky, since outward traits can mislead. The team assembled the full chloroplast genomes of twenty-nine samples to sort the branches.

The genomes proved close in size and layout, with size gaps traced to edge growth and repeat counts. Six stretchy regions stood out as handy markers for telling species apart. Many short repeat markers were also catalogued. The tree built from the genomes split the genus into three clear groups. Those groups match the classic sections of the genus fairly well. The data should help farms name, guard, and breed these plants with more care.
pmc-11596464:
Flu vaccines must be reformulated as the virus keeps changing, and Romania's low vaccine uptake makes tracking that change urgent. Ovidiu Vlaicu and co-authors analyze flu strains collected across three seasons, from 2021 to 2024, in this 2024 study, comparing their surface protein against each season's vaccine strain.

The first season's main virus had drifted widely from the vaccine, likely blunting its effect. The next season showed fewer changes, while the last season again brought a fast-varying clade. The authors argue that high viral diversity in a lightly vaccinated population argues for stronger uptake campaigns and better-matched vaccine choices.
pmc-11597364:
Cristian Sandoval and co-authors report a mouse study from two thousand twenty-four on beta-carotene and insulin under long-term alcohol exposure. Beta-carotene is an antioxidant linked to protection against diabetes and heart disease. The team asked whether it guards the pancreas, which makes insulin, when alcohol harms it over time.

Thirty-six mice were split into six groups: control, two alcohol doses, beta-carotene alone, and each alcohol dose with the supplement. After twenty-eight days, supplemented groups showed better insulin levels and larger insulin-making cell mass. An AI-assisted image measure of insulin staining confirmed the protection in the combined groups. Alcohol-clearing enzymes also fell with the supplement. The authors read the results as support for a protective role.
pmc-11599164:
Nancy Lightfoot and co-authors published this interview study in 2024 on rheumatoid arthritis care in Northern Ontario, Canada. The disease is a long-lasting joint condition that can disable, and it hits older adults and northern communities hardest. The team spoke with 18 patients, 6 family doctors, 6 pharmacists, and a group of specialist arthritis providers who treat northern patients.

Patients stressed acting on early symptoms, speaking up for themselves, and the need for more local specialists. They also said they were satisfied with their providers. Doctors wanted better training in the disease and a bigger role in starting treatment. Pharmacists described their work as educators who also watch for drug clashes and help with insurance. Across all groups, the study calls for more public education and closer teamwork among providers in the north.
pmc-11600964:
Patients who cannot speak English well risk poorer care unless an interpreter joins the visit. Hieke and co-authors survey 609 South Asian adults in England with limited English about using professional interpreters in family doctor care. Interviewers worked in several languages across four regions.

About 63 percent had used a professional interpreter at their practice. Face-to-face help was most common, then phone, then video. Uptake ran lower among Indian-background participants, in the Midlands, and where family or friends had interpreted in the past year. It ran higher among recent visitors who knew the service existed and were offered a choice of support. The authors say simple steps, telling patients the service exists and letting them choose its form, could lift use.
pmc-11602664:
Katarina Zeder and three co-authors reply to a critic of their past pooled study on a lung blood pressure measure. Their letter, from two thousand twenty-four, defends the top end of the normal range they found.

The measure shows pressure in the lung blood path when a small tube rests in place. The authors agree that even a one-point shift in this value can change care choices. Their pooled work used three data sets and nine hundred sixty healthy people, the most with this invasive test to date. They found a top normal value based on a high mark in the data. The letter argues that a bigger such set is not apt to be built, since the test is not seen as fair in healthy people now.
pmc-11603664:
Zhiyuan Yu and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on how diabetes affects patients after surgery for stomach cancer. Removing the stomach is the main cure, but diabetes could slow recovery or shorten survival. The team used hospital records from 2011 to 2015 to test that concern fairly.

From more than two thousand five hundred patients, about twelve percent had diabetes. To compare like with like, the team matched each diabetes patient with three similar patients without the disease. They then compared early recovery and long-term survival between the matched groups. They also searched for other traits that sway survival after this surgery. Fair matching matters, since diabetes patients often carry other risks that could be blamed on the disease itself.
pmc-11606164:
Yali Zhu, Weijia Yin, Jun Ma, and Lin Zhang studied anxious depression in hospital patients in China in 2024. Anxious depression is a common form of major depressive disorder and is linked to worse progress and outcomes. The team wanted to know how often it appeared at first hospital admission and which factors tracked with its presence and severity.

Nearly one thousand patients admitted for the first time were assessed for symptoms, illness severity, and basic health measures. About one in ten met the anxious depression pattern. That group scored higher on depression and psychosis measures and had higher blood sugar, cholesterol, blood pressure, and body mass. The authors suggest these features could help clinicians spot the condition early.
pmc-11608464:
Four authors present a study in two thousand twenty-four on what parents in northwestern Ethiopia know about worm infections and malaria. Both diseases thrive in developing countries, where they kill, stunt children's growth, and drag on productivity. Control programs work only when the affected communities know and practice the right measures.

Nearly four hundred parents of children at one elementary school were interviewed about their background, knowledge, and habits. The team then tested how those factors tracked with the child's infection risk. Children of mothers who answered had lower worm infection risk. Household income also played a role in the patterns reported.
pmc-11608564:
Mansor and co-authors map COVID-19 spread in a rural Malaysian district through social networks. How people mix within and between communities shaped how the virus moved. Contact patterns in villages differ from cities, so rural spread needs its own study rather than borrowed city models.

The team reviewed records of positive cases and contact tracing data from the district. Social network analysis charted who linked to whom among cases. Clusters and bridge persons who connect groups stood out in the maps. Such insight helps health teams target testing and isolation where spread is most likely to jump next.
pmc-11610164:
Shen and co-authors present HTAD, a tool that finds chromatin domains with human help. These domains, called TADs, are core units of genome folding that shape gene control and disease risk. Automated finders struggle with noisy backgrounds and domains nested inside larger domains.

HTAD mixes machine learning with expert guidance to raise accuracy. It first extracts features for candidate border pairs in the genome. An active learning loop then asks humans to label the most useful cases, refining the model step by step. The result is a supervised caller that learns from both data and expert judgment.
pmc-11610264:
Alba Rodriguez-Muñoz led a large team testing exercise and blood sugar in a 2024 trial. Healthy volunteers did aerobic or anaerobic sessions in the morning or afternoon, in a crossover design where each person tried several conditions. Blood was drawn before, right after, and two hours after each session to track sugar and related hormones.

Glucose rose more sharply after anaerobic than aerobic exercise. Insulin and a companion marker fell more after aerobic work. Time of day mattered too: the post-exercise glucose rise was higher in the morning than the afternoon. The authors conclude that both exercise type and body-clock timing shape short-term sugar control in healthy people.
pmc-11612164:
Hua and ten colleagues study Radix Astragali, a traditional herb, for allergic rhinitis in twenty twenty-four. The herb is known for potential benefit in this nasal allergy condition. Its pharmacological mechanisms were unclear. The team combined network pharmacology with lab validation.

They found hundreds of potential targets for the herb's key compounds. Intersecting those with disease targets gave a shared target set. Network analysis highlighted central inflammatory nodes, including TNF and NF-kB related proteins. Enrichment pointed to inflammatory and immune signaling pathways. Docking studies showed strong, stable binding to the central targets. In a nasal inflammation model, the herb reversed key inflammatory markers. The authors propose a multitarget anti inflammatory action.
pmc-11612664:
Inzoli and coauthors track surgery choices in women with BRCA gene faults. Faults in those genes raise ovarian cancer risk a great deal. Guide rules urge removal of tubes and ovaries to cut that risk. Yet many women decline or delay that surgery.

The team tracked carriers sent for first advice at a center in Monza, Italy. Records span from 2010 to 2023. Each woman was offered surgery or close checks based on her traits. The team logged who chose surgery and who chose checks. They also sought traits that swayed each choice. Facts may help staff counsel new carriers with more care.
pmc-11613364:
Khadijah Mukhtar, Mahnoor Mukhtar, Syed Abdullah Haider, and Sadia Iram ask how trust grows between medical mentors and their mentees, in a 2024 study. A mentor guides a less experienced person through training and career choices, and trust holds that bond together. The team interviewed ten mentees and studied their answers for the traits and habits that build trust.

Respect came first on the list the mentees gave. Keeping confidences mattered, as did empathy from the mentor's side. Humbleness, hard work, and good communication from both sides rounded out the picture. The authors say these traits strengthen the mentoring bond and help mentees grow. They present the short list as practical guidance for medical schools that pair senior doctors with trainees.
pmc-11615164:
Simon and five co-authors hunted for heart protection in a muscle disease in this study from twenty twenty-four. Myotubular myopathy devastates skeletal muscle, yet the heart seems spared. Using mice lacking the disease gene, the team sequenced RNA across muscles, heart, and liver. Organ function and structure were checked in living animals and in cells.

The liver showed no defects in form or function. Skeletal muscles shared a disease signature spanning development, inflammation, and energy pathways. The heart's gene shifts ran opposite in key pathways, hinting at compensation. Two molecular markers of the missing protein rose in skeletal muscle but stayed normal in heart. The authors say the heart's workaround may suggest therapies for skeletal muscle.
pmc-11615964:
Tao Wen, Yu-wang Chen, and Renaud Lambiotte model how groups settle on shared word rules, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Their test case is the past tense of English verbs. Most verbs take a regular ending, but some famous ones break the rule. The team used a naming game, in which agents swap words and adjust what they say.

Each agent learns in two ways: from neighbors, and on its own, with a lean toward rules it likes. Agents also forget, since memory is limited. On both made-up and real social networks, the shape of the network mattered a lot. Tight clusters and hubs could push a group to one shared usage, or split it into camps. Self-learning sped up the spread of regular rules, while forgetting changed little. The work links word change to network shape and social habits.
pmc-11616364:
Chaolu Meng and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study of a leaner method for classifying antioxidant proteins. Finding these proteins by computer helps biology, but heavy feature sets slow models down. Cutting features usually throws away useful information.

Their algorithm, called Rore, maps many features into a smaller hidden space instead. Nothing is simply discarded, so signal survives compression. On an antioxidant protein dataset it reached high accuracy with only fifteen features. Scores for balanced correctness were also strong. A public web tool hosts the method. Protein researchers get speed without the usual accuracy trade-off.
pmc-11616664:
Tomáš Scholz and co-authors present a 2024 report of a likely new focus of a fish tapeworm disease in Central Europe. The disease, diphyllobothriasis, spreads to people who eat raw or undercooked freshwater fish. Pike and perch, both prized sport fish, are known sources of the worm in the Northern Hemisphere.

The team documents a case with a local origin at a popular tourist spot in Central Europe. Local origin means the patient caught the worm there, not abroad. That fact points to fresh settlement of the parasite in local fish stocks. The report is brief and meant as an alert for clinicians and health officers. It adds the site to the map of known foci for the disease.
pmc-11618764: An author correction from 2024, issued by Hyunjin Rho and a team of co-authors, fixes a detail in their earlier article. That article covered a liver disease mechanism involving a protein called CHIP and the cell's recycling system. The only change is to one author's affiliation. Jaewhan Song's listing at Yonsei University in Seoul should also have named the university's Institute for Bio-medical Convergence Science and Technology. No data, results, or conclusions were altered. The original article has been corrected accordingly.
pmc-11619664:
Qian Zhao and co-authors test how a gum disease germ harms lung lining cells in the lab, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Gum disease is a known risk factor for chronic lung disease, and the germ can drift from mouth to lungs. Mouse lung cells were grown with rising doses of the germ.

Cell survival fell as dose and time rose, while self-eating and cell death both climbed. Blocking the self-eating path eased the harm and cut cell death. The results suggest the germ drives lung cell harm in part by pushing self-eating too far. Readers see one lab path that may link mouth health to lung decline, still to be proven in people.
pmc-11626664:
A cheap blood count may stand in for a dearer iron test in teens. Walaa Alsafi and five co-authors checked that swap in 2024 on three hundred seventy-four teens in eastern Sudan. One in six of them proved low on iron by the store test. Five plain marks from the count were weighed against that truth: the red protein level and four size and spread marks of red cells.

All five marks ran low in the iron-short teens. Each scored fair at the call, with the spread mark and the red protein at the top of the pack. None was sharp enough to rule alone, the team grant. Still, in clinics where the store test costs too much, the plain count can flag who needs a closer look.
pmc-11626764:
Ivo Petersen and co-authors compare in 2024 two ways to keep dogs free of fleas and ticks for a year. One is a single injection of fluralaner, sold as Bravecto, meant to end monthly owner dosing. The other is a monthly chewable, afoxolaner, sold as NexGard.

Clinics in Germany, France, and Spain enrolled 976 household dogs. At checks across the year, at least 95 percent of dogs in each group were tick-free and at least 93 percent flea-free. The single shot matched the monthly pills at every visit, cutting pest counts by over 99 percent. No unexpected side effects appeared, supporting the shot as a compliance-friendly option.
pmc-11626864:
Pleasants and eight co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on abortion access barriers shared on Reddit after a court leak. The twenty twenty-two leak and ruling threw United States abortion access into turmoil. The team code posts from a large abortion support community. Their sample spans May to December twenty twenty-two, with over five hundred posts. Coding blends known barrier types with new themes from the posts. State bans, cost, scarce appointments, and long travel dominate the structural barriers. Stigma and thin social support dominate the social ones.

New barriers emerge, like mail medication delays and distrust of online sellers. Legal risk fears also surface as a fresh theme. Harms most often hit mental health and delay care. Some posters self-manage abortion due to blocked access.
pmc-11628264:
Ngoc Chi Banh and three co-authors published a 2024 study of how verbal negations tax visual attention. Negated statements take more effort to process than plain claims, though repetition softens the cost. Using a formal model of visual attention, the team measured total capacity and how it splits between stimuli, while subjects judged time order under negated or plain instructions. Three experiments used the simplest binary negations.

Negations cut overall capacity. Repetition restored some of it, but it leveled off below the mark seen with plain claims. Negations also spread attention evenly between target and reference, while plain claims tilted it toward the target. The authors conclude negation carries a real, lasting processing cost for vision. The work speaks to interface and instruction design, where wording shapes what people can attend to.
pmc-11628864:
Paolo Beck-Peccoz and eight co-authors give final data from PATRO Adults, a large watch study of a copy growth hormone in adults who lack the hormone. Their report appeared in twenty twenty-four. The study ran in clinics across Europe in day-to-day care. Key fears to check were high blood sugar, new diabetes, and new cancers over long use.

More than fifteen hundred adults were tracked, most for years. Most side effects were mild, and joint pain was the most common drug-linked one. New diabetes and cancer counts gave no sign of raised risk from the drug. A key growth marker rose to a healthy range, weight held steady, and blood fats got better.
pmc-11629564:
Phyumar Soe and co-authors report, in a 2024 study, how children and teenagers in Canada fared in the week after mRNA COVID-19 vaccination. A national safety network actively surveyed families rather than waiting for reports, enrolling hundreds of thousands of vaccinated young people and a small unvaccinated comparison group across eight provinces and territories.

After the second dose, adolescents reported health events that disrupted daily life more often than unvaccinated peers did, though nearly all settled within a week. No such excess appeared after the first dose, nor in children under twelve after either dose. Heart inflammation cases were rare and clustered in male adolescents after dose two, more with one brand than the other. The authors conclude that the short-term burden is real but brief for teenagers, and indistinguishable from background for younger children.
pmc-11634064:
Bhanu Shrestha and colleagues mapped sour taste sensing inside the throat of fruit flies in 2024. Sour tastes, from acids at low pH, help animals separate appealing food from possibly harmful food. Many acids attract at natural levels but repel at higher strength, and sensing in the mouth has been studied more than sensing deeper inside.

Work focused on taste neurons in the pharynx and their ion-channel receptors. Responses to carboxylic acids depended on a set of receptors working together, beyond the pair already known from sweet-sensing cells. Switching two newly identified neuron types on with light drove eager feeding. The findings open study of how insects sense tastes internally, past the mouth.
pmc-11634364:
Carlucci and five co-authors reviewed trials of omega-3 supplements as add-on care for gum disease in twenty twenty-four. The disease, periodontitis, eats away the tissues that hold teeth, driven by inflammation. Omega-3 fatty acids can shift how the immune system reacts. That raised the idea of host modulation care on top of standard dental care.

The scoping review found seven randomized trials. They set omega-3 groups against control groups, or tracked the omega-3 groups over time. After the supplements, levels of key inflammation messengers fell. The list includes interleukin-1 beta, tumor necrosis factor alpha, interleukin-6, and RANKL. The shifts came with better scores for gum health. But the trials gauged distinct markers in distinct samples by distinct methods. That blocks straight comparison and pooling. The authors call for stronger trial designs, to pin down the effects on inflammation and the marker signs to watch.
pmc-11634464:
Laura Borkenhagen and Jonathan Runstadler published a machine learning study in twenty twenty-four on predicting which sugars an influenza A virus prefers to bind. That preference helps decide which hosts a virus can infect and how likely spillover is. Measuring it in the lab is slow and expensive.

They trained a convolutional neural network on the hemagglutinin protein sequence alone. On held-out data it called the preference correctly ninety-four percent of the time. It tolerated about ten percent missing sequence without losing accuracy and generalized to subtypes it had never seen. The team then mutated the protein spots the model relied on, using lab-made pseudoviruses. The checks supported the model's reasoning and its use in risk screening.
pmc-11634764:
