Cheng Chen and co-authors report, in twenty twenty-four, strong links between electrons and sound waves in a special form of graphene. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms. When two layers are twisted to a magic angle, the stack can conduct with no resistance. Why it does so is still unknown. Using a light-based method that maps electron energies, the team looked at the flat energy bands of this stack when it was not lined up with its base layer.

They found copies of the flat bands, spaced evenly in energy. Such copies signal strong coupling to a vibration of the lattice, a phonon. The copies were absent in stacks that do not conduct freely. Math checks point to one vibration mode at a key lattice point.
pmc-11635464:
Heating plant waste without oxygen, a process called pyrolysis, turns biomass into fuel and chemicals. Predicting how fast that breakdown runs at each stage usually takes slow lab work. Kai Xiao and Xianghui Zhu instead train neural networks to predict the energy barrier of the reaction from simple lab measures of the raw material.

They built three models using different input sets: full chemical analysis, quick burn-and-ash measures, and the shares of three plant fibers. The data covered 32 kinds of biomass and 270 kinetic data sets. The fiber-based model matched lab results best, with the largest error near 13 percent. Adding a swarm search method to tune the network cut that error to about 7 percent. The authors present the models as a faster way to screen waste feedstocks for fuel production.
pmc-11638064:
Pilar Álvarez Jerez and co-authors trace how an African-ancestry gene variant raises Parkinson disease risk, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The variant sits in a gene whose severe faults cause a storage disease. It is carried by about half of West African patients, yet is near absent in European and Asian groups.

Full-length RNA reads showed the variant lets a gene segment slip into the final message, breaking clean splicing. Editing tests proved that single change drives the effect. Enzyme activity fell in steps as variant copies rose. The team names splicing repair as a possible treatment path for an underserved group.
pmc-11638164:
Yu and seven co-authors present a case report from twenty twenty-four on a child whose white cell counts cycle, who then developed a dangerous immune overreaction. The child's gene mutation causes neutrophil counts to rise and fall in cycles. Severe mixed infections trigger the overreaction syndrome. Killer cell function tests show impaired release machinery. The pairing of this mutation with the syndrome was undocumented before. Inborn immunity errors are known to underlie some such cases.

The authors establish the new link for clinicians. The syndrome should be watched for in these patients. Infection control becomes doubly urgent in that light. The case widens the mutation's known risks.
pmc-11638364: Francisco Renero and Tania Martínez-Azmitia report a case where heat imaging flagged breast changes in a young woman, in a report from twenty twenty-four. A scan of a woman in her twenties showed a mean heat gap of about one degree. Sound imaging then found a plain cyst and swollen, blood rich lymph nodes in both armpits. The authors note that breast thermography may help find disease early in women under fifty.
pmc-11638764:
Wenxuan Huang and her four co-authors, publishing in 2024, map what happens inside a leukemia cell when a key housekeeping machine is switched off. The machine, an enzyme called p97, keeps proteins in order across the cell. A drug that blocks it, CB-5083, is of interest as a cancer treatment. Earlier work charted the drug's effects in colon cancer cells. This team repeated the experiment in a blood cancer line.

Their twist was location. They split the cells into compartments, the fluid body, the nucleus, and the stubborn membrane fraction, and measured thousands of proteins in each. The drug's impact differed sharply by compartment rather than shifting everything at once. The authors say this geography of response reveals how the enzyme's jobs are divided across the cell. It may also hint at where the drug will help or harm.
pmc-11638964:
Thilo Bender and Alois Fürstner report a nickel-catalyzed route to a useful class of chiral building blocks in a 2024 paper. The products join an amino group and an alcohol group on neighboring carbons, a pattern common in drugs and natural products. Their method couples aldehydes with protected amino diene esters under reducing conditions.

A special ligand, derived from a known chiral scaffold, flips the usual regiochemistry of the coupling. The products form in good yields with high optical purity and the opposite configuration to the usual pattern. A bench-stable nickel source and a boron promoter make the setup practical.
pmc-11640764:
Runliang Zhai and colleagues studied a tree frog in 2024 that changes its skin color to match its background. The frog turns light green on a white background and black on a black background within about two days. Matching the background helps cold-blooded animals hide and manage body heat, but which skin changes drive the shift was unclear. The team used single-cell gene sequencing to compare skin cells from light and dark frogs.

They found two kinds of pigment cells behind the color difference. The key change was in cell numbers, not in how hard each cell worked to make pigment. Frogs grew more pigment cells rather than turning existing ones up. Dark frogs also showed more energy-related activity in their pigment cells, while light frogs showed more immune-related activity. The work shows a cell-count route to camouflage in a wild frog species.
pmc-11641364:
Gemma Lombardi and a large team review blood tau markers that may predict decline in mild cognitive impairment. Their meta-analysis from twenty twenty-four covers three forms of phosphorylated tau. Blood tests are far less invasive than spinal or scan methods. Clinicians need markers that flag who will progress to Alzheimer dementia.

Studies had to measure blood tau at the start and follow patients for at least a year. Evidence was strongest for one form, with many studies included. That form separated future converters from stable patients fairly well. A second form looked even stronger, but from fewer studies. A third form rested on a single study. The authors urge caution before clinical use.
pmc-11642364:
Roxana Șipoș and co-authors study screen habits and social anxiety in teens with ADHD, in a paper from 2024. Screen use rose a great deal during the pandemic years. For teens with attention problems, heavy digital use may link to anxiety in ways that are not yet clear.

The study group was close to one hundred teens aged eleven to eighteen, all with an ADHD diagnosis. Teens filled in surveys on daily digital activity and anxiety, and caregivers added background facts. A learning method then searched for links among screen time, ADHD severity, and anxiety signs. Average screen time was high on both school days and weekends, with social media the top activity, above all for girls. Some anxiety traits, such as physical symptoms and fear of harm, predicted time on social media.
pmc-11643164:
Mishra and co-authors compute the magnetic ground state of a rare iron oxide phase in this 2024 study. The beta phase of Fe2O3 has a cubic structure where iron-iron couplings should all oppose each other. Such conflict can frustrate magnetism and hide the true ground state.

The team compared candidate orders from first principles: ferrimagnets, altermagnets, and Kramers antiferromagnets. The beta phase settles as a Kramers antiferromagnet, unlike its alpha and gamma relatives. A d-wave altermagnetic state sits close in energy. With realistic electron repulsion the material becomes a charge-transfer insulator with an indirect band gap of 1.5 electron volts. The detailed spin pattern runs in zigzag chains through the unit cell.
pmc-11643464:
Conventional grinding wheels scatter their abrasive grains at random, wasting grains and inviting heat damage. The seven authors fabricate a structured cubic boron nitride wheel by 3D printing with ultrasonic vibration, so grains sit in a planned pattern. They analyze how overlap rate, scanning path, and ultrasonic amplitude shape the printed layer, and they run orthogonal tests on laser power, scanning speed, and powder disk rotation.

A genetic algorithm neural network trained on those data yields optimal process parameters. Experiments then tune overlap and path, and the team checks how ultrasonic amplitude changes surface topography and microhardness. Wheels printed with the best settings and with vibration ground workpieces to a smaller surface roughness than wheels printed without it, giving a better finish.
pmc-11643564:
Mengjie You and seven co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on how sulfate attacks the gel that binds concrete. The gel, a hydrated calcium silicate, gives concrete its strength. Sulfate in soil and water eats it from the inside. The team builds a molecule level model of the gel in sodium sulfate baths at three strengths. Electron scans of worn samples back the model.

Stronger baths drew far more ions onto the gel. Sulfate sped the loss of calcium from the gel, which forms gypsum and a swollen mineral. Both chew the gel and speed ion flow, which deepens the attack. Sodium clung tight to pore walls. Water ran far ahead of the other ions, with sulfate in tow.
pmc-11644364:
Pedro Bezerra and five co-authors make a seaweed-based packaging film strengthened with orange waste, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. Plastic from oil pollutes, and juice making leaves piles of orange by-product. The team dried that waste into powder and mixed it into films of sodium alginate, a natural polymer, with glycerol.

Films with more powder held less water and pulled much stronger before breaking. Their surfaces also shed water better. Heat tests showed the filled films resist heat more, though their inner structure grew less orderly. The strongest mix used the highest powder share tested. The authors call the waste powder a promising filler that turns two problems, plastic and food waste, toward one answer.
pmc-11644764:
Yilin Zhang and co-authors built a vision system that lets robots recognize garments and rebuild them, plus their surroundings, in three dimensions, in a 2024 study. Robots are rare in garment work because cloth bends and folds in hard ways. Their system rests on object SLAM, a method that maps a scene and tracks the camera at the same time.

The team made two data sets: flat garment images to train a segmentation model, and fake 3D garments to sharpen a shape model. A second model finds planes such as tables and floors, which grounds the scene. Tests with a depth camera showed garments and planes detected and rebuilt together in real time.
pmc-11644964:
Reem Ibrahim Alkanhel leads a ten-author team forecasting blood sugar with a hybrid neural network wired into connected health devices, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Manual glucose checks are laborious and imprecise. Many variables push glucose around, making multi-step prediction genuinely hard.

The model pairs convolutional layers, which extract features from incoming data, with gated recurrent units that track sequences over time. It is designed for Internet of Things diabetes systems, processing data in real time at the edge. Forecasts several steps ahead could warn of highs and lows before they arrive. The framework targets the daily management burden: fewer fingersticks, earlier insulin decisions, and alarms a patient can actually act on.
pmc-11645464:
Beata Szabo and her team show that loss of links twixt ponds brings loss of life range in groups. Their 2024 test ran out doors for four months, with fake pond nets to pull link acts out from the rest of the acts of split-up ground.

In the wake of a first span with moves twixt ponds, moves were stopped, and ground size and states stayed the same. Loss of links raised deaths of kinds and cut range in zones near and far for small life with a core in its cells. Range for life with no such core stayed in the main as it was. Some signs of late death of kinds showed there too. Fair shares fell for the core group too, most like through shifts in links with tiny beasts that graze. The finds make a case to keep ground nets with good moves twixt home zones.
pmc-11645964:
Li and co-authors tie a blood share mark to ward death in long heart-fail hosts. Two stock blood marks, Hb and RDW, guess ends in such hosts. Their share, HRR, adds grade by hosts' wide traits in one mark. No past work had probed HRR in two big ward banks. Banks in view are MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD in the work. The team weighs HRR next to in-ward death in those banks.

Fit sums, split reads, and bend-line reads do the weigh work. In sum, 30,411 heart-fail hosts sat in the two banks. One bank gave 15,983 hosts, the next gave 14,428 hosts. HRR caps both marks in one cheap count for ward use. Its tie to death is the chief ask of the work.
pmc-11650264:
Anyu Zhang and co-authors report a 2024 food study on egg white gels, the firm whites used in many dishes. They added fiber from coconut flesh left over after oil and milk are taken out. Plain fiber holds water poorly, so the team first treated it with sound waves and enzymes, then added one of two chemical steps.

Treated fiber held more water and swelled more than plain fiber. Gels made with it were harder, chewier, and kept more water after freezing and thawing. The treated fiber helped more than the plain kind. Some mixes also held up better in tests that mimic the stomach and gut. The authors say more work is still needed to explain just how the fiber helps.
pmc-11650364:
Vandana Aggarwal and co-authors studied how setting changes the glow color of terbium compounds in two thousand twenty-four. Terbium ions can emit visible light, and the color and brightness depend on what is bound to them and where they sit. Such compounds matter for optoelectronic devices.

They made two kinds of complexes, single and paired, with a fluorinated ligand and with water or pyrazine partners. Light tests showed the single form glowed much more strongly than the paired form. Color also shifted between solid and solution and across solvents. Computer theory mapped the electron spread behind these effects. Color points in solution sat close to a television standard.
pmc-11651564:
Marie-Eve Bouthillier and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on what the public finds acceptable in rules for rationing intensive care during an overwhelming pandemic. Triage protocols decide who gets a ventilator when there are not enough, raising fears of judgments about worth, age, or frailty. The team ran structured online deliberations with forty-seven lay adults in Quebec and Ontario.

Participants broadly accepted prioritizing patients with the best prognosis, but attached conditions. They wanted extra considerations built in, transparency about criteria, and safeguards against discrimination. Three themes organized their views: the values behind the protocol, what it should weigh, and what would earn public trust. The findings aim to ground future protocols in public values, not just clinical logic.
pmc-11653064:
Andrzej Smereczyński, Grzegorz Goncerz, and Katarzyna Kołaczyk share their experience imaging a small bowel valve with ultrasound, in two thousand twenty-four. The valve sits where the small bowel meets the large bowel. It is rarely the first site of disease, but nearby bowel disease often spreads to it.

The authors describe how infections, Crohn's disease, and fatty growths look at the valve on a scan through the belly. They also cover cancers, with bowel cancer the most common at that site. Cancer cases showed uneven thickening and loss of the normal wall layers. The paper argues that the scan can serve as a first test for some of these problems.
pmc-11653964:
Wanlin Jiao and co-authors find the exact virus fragments that duck killer T cells recognize in bird flu, in this 2024 paper. Ducks with the B1 gene type fight H5N1 well, and their CD8 cells lead the defense. Which peptides those cells target was mostly unknown.

Infected ducks showed surging CD8 shares and defense gene activity a week in. From one hundred nine predicted fragments, twelve proved able to wake memory cells. Five were shared across H5N1 and four other flu strains. The catalog steers design of a universal T-cell vaccine for poultry. The catalog steers design of a universal T-cell vaccine for poultry flocks facing repeated flu threats.
pmc-11654664:
Haseeb Mehmood Qadri and co-authors review cases of a stress-linked heart condition in people with epilepsy, in a systematic review from 2024. The condition, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, weakens the left ventricle after physical or emotional stress. In epilepsy, seizures may trigger it and raise the risk of complications.

The review gathered sixteen studies from 2000 to 2023, covering 18 women with an average age near 57. Convulsive seizures were the most common trigger named. The authors trace the mechanism to a surge of stress hormones that stuns the heart muscle. Most patients had raised troponin, a heart damage marker, and scans showed weak pumping. Care mixed seizure drugs with heart drugs such as beta-blockers. Most patients' heart scans improved, and the authors stress early recognition.
pmc-11655664:
Ashish Kumar Tripathi and co-authors test a front line sickle cell drug for bone effects in mice in this 2024 paper. Sickle cell disease causes red cells to bend and block blood flow. Bone loss is common, especially in the spine, and leads to fractures. Whether hydroxyurea helps or harms bone was not established.

The team used Townes mice, a standard model of the disease. High resolution scans measured cortical and trabecular bone in vertebrae. Sick mice lost cortical bone at all ages, and adults also lost trabecular bone. The drug eased cortical loss in adults. It worsened trabecular loss in both age groups, though. Cell tests showed the drug blunted energy use in bone building and bone clearing cells.
pmc-11655964:
Letizia Vestito and eight co-authors describe a faster way to re-scan old genome cases with the Exomiser tool when new disease genes surface, in this 2024 paper. Most rare disease patients stay undiagnosed after first sequencing, yet knowledge grows monthly. Inside the 100,000 Genomes Project, reanalysis had already found answers for 463 of more than twenty-four thousand unsolved cases, at the price of heavy manual review.

The team tuned Exomiser's settings to spotlight only fresh candidates from new gene links or upgraded variant calls. The tuned pass caught eighty-two percent of known new answers while keeping eighty-eight percent of its flags real. Its built-in classifier also relabeled most mystery variants correctly. The authors present the recipe as ready for routine use.
pmc-11657264:
Damian Di Florio leads a large team sequencing heart tissue from virally infected male and female mice to find why myocarditis hits the sexes differently. Immune differences by sex are documented; upstream heart biology that might set them up is not. Mice received heart-passaged coxsackievirus B3 or a control injection, and bulk RNA sequencing charted the transcriptional landscape, with enrichment analysis and functional validation following.

As expected, infected hearts of both sexes lit up innate and adaptive immune pathways. Males, distinctively, were enriched for inflammatory pathways and gene changes reaching into mitochondrial function, the paper's title focus. The authors argue sex differences in disease begin partly in the heart's own energy machinery, upstream of the immune response itself.
pmc-11657364:
Hadis Barati and three co-authors model future cancer rates in Iran in a 2024 study. Cancer cases there have been rising, and planners need forecasts to prepare care. The team used a Bayesian age-period-cohort model, which separates the effects of age, calendar time, and birth generation.

Working from data for 2005 to 2017, the authors found that the overall yearly drift in rates was about 1.8 percent for men and 3.3 percent for women. Age patterns and generation effects helped explain the trend. They then projected rates forward to 2027 and expect the upward trend to continue. The forecast gives health officials a basis for planning screening, staff, and treatment capacity in the years ahead.
pmc-11657564:
Adeoye Oyebade and co-authors test whether feeding live microbes to dairy cows improves rumen fermentation and feed breakdown. The work uses rumen fluid from lactating Holstein cows in two experiments. The first mixes corn silage with pooled rumen fluid in lab vessels. Two microbial products, one with two strains and one with four, are added at three doses each. Gas output, acidity, and the breakdown of dry matter and fiber are tracked over 24 hours.

The second experiment feeds three cannulated cows in rotation through control and supplemented diets. Periods last 28 days, with products sprinkled on the feed daily. Rumen fluid from each period is then tested again in the lab. The design separates effects that come from the microbes themselves from effects carried by the cows' adapted rumen fluid.
pmc-11657864:
Ye and six co-authors published a 2024 study of how depression shapes self-harm in teens with mood disorders. They compared youths with unipolar depression and bipolar disorder, all aged 12 to 18, seen at one Chinese hospital from 2018 to 2023. Two specialists confirmed each case. The team compared self-harm patterns, severity, and mental state scores across the two groups.

Unipolar teens burned themselves with cigarettes more often and reported more unacted suicidal thoughts. Bipolar teens scored higher on suicide risk, and their anxiety strangely tracked with less self-harm. In both groups, higher suicide risk scores matched more frequent self-harm. The authors say prevention must differ by diagnosis, not treat all such harm as one pattern.
pmc-11658164:
Bianka Eperjesiova, Jessica Peterson, and Sriram describe setting up a robot assisted bronchoscopy program at a veterans hospital in a 2024 paper. Lung cancer is often found late, and robotic scope systems can reach and sample small, hard to reach lung nodules. The paper reports early outcomes and the hurdles of launching the program.

Building the program required new infrastructure, resource allocation, and a multidisciplinary team. Funding, technology integration, and logistics all posed challenges. Despite them, the program launched successfully and improved diagnostic precision in their early experience. Future plans include more procedure capacity, staff training, advanced imaging, and a training center for other veterans hospitals. The authors offer the effort as a blueprint.
pmc-11660964:
Bowen Chen and co-authors follow internet use and thinking skills in 2024 among older Chinese adults. Memory and thinking decline is a growing burden in China, the country with the most older adults. Internet access has spread fast, but its long-term effect on the aging mind was unclear.

The team used a national aging survey with close to thirteen thousand people aged forty-five and up, tracked for five years. Internet users scored higher on thinking tests than non-users, even after accounting for age, schooling, and health. Steady users also developed brain diseases at less than half the rate of non-users. More frequent use linked to better scores. The authors see the internet as a possible aid to healthy aging.
pmc-11663864:
A large team of co-authors presents a trial from two thousand twenty-four on a brief program for fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue. Both conditions involve heightened pain sensitivity, poor fitness, and intolerance of effort. The program, called Synchronize+, combined activity, nutrition, and body-clock advice.

One hundred forty-three patients in Catalan primary care, nearly all women, were assigned at random to the program or usual care. The group program ran briefly by design. Outcomes covered movement, sitting and sleep time, muscle strength, and heart-lung capacity, testing whether a light package can shift entrenched symptoms.
pmc-11664264:
Xiaoyan Xu, Zahyah Hanafi, and Shun Zhang study mothers in mainland China in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. They ask how parenting stress links to parental burnout. They also test whether marital satisfaction helps explain that link. A third test asks whether socioeconomic status changes the link.

The team collected data from 314 mothers and used Chinese versions of three scales. The scales measured burnout, stress, and marital satisfaction. Stress and burnout rose together, and marital satisfaction helped carry the link. Stress lowered marital satisfaction more for mothers with higher status. The authors say raising marital satisfaction could ease stress and cut the risk of burnout. The study matters as China's three-child policy can add parenting hours and costs.
pmc-11666964:
Jia Hao leads a team on bisphenol A and rabbit milk quality. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses lactating rabbits in two groups. One group got BPA by mouth for a short span.

Weight, feed intake, and milk yield did not change in a clear way. Blood marks for harm also stayed much the same. Yet milk make up shifted, with fat making impaired. Chem scans of milk built a profile of that change. Gene level paths for the harm are also probed. Short exposure can still hurt milk quality.
pmc-11668764:
Nardos Hailu, Benti Negero, Keno Melkamu, and Yawkal Tsega measure use of youth-friendly health services in Gambella, Ethiopia, in a 2024 study. Teenagers face high risks around pregnancy, unsafe abortion, and infections, and services designed for youth are meant to lower them. How much students in this town actually use such services was unknown. Three hundred ninety-four preparatory school students, chosen at random, answered questionnaires in June 2023.

The analysis searched for factors that track with using the services, from knowledge and attitudes to distance and privacy concerns. Naming those factors shows a town exactly where its program leaks: whether students never hear of the service, fear being seen there, or find the hours wrong. Similar towns across the region can read their own gaps in the list.
pmc-11670064:
Lei-Lei Li and seven co-authors report a gene edit in rice that boosts growth and pest defense at once, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Plants usually trade growth against defense: more of one means less of the other. The team edited a gene in the jasmonate signaling path, which steers defense in rice.

Most edits left standard signaling untouched. One edit, though, created a brand-new protein from a shifted reading frame. Plants carrying it grew faster and resisted brown planthopper attacks better. The new protein jams two partners: one that brakes growth hormone action, and one that brakes woody defense compounds. Field trials confirmed the double win. The authors see a route to higher yields without weaker defenses.
pmc-11671264:
Zijian Zheng and ten co-authors build a tool, in two thousand twenty-four, to predict sight recovery after pituitary adenoma surgery. These growths sit near the eyes, and doctors find it hard to say in advance who will see better. The study mixes past cases with new cases seen later.

The group drew on scans, eye tests, and field-of-vision tests for close to two hundred patients. Blindness, headache, and a long course of poor sight lowered the chance of recovery. The size of the growth and of the gland also mattered. A model built from five such signs scored high in both case groups. The authors say it could help guide talks with each patient before surgery.
pmc-11671964:
Yijun Cai leads a team on eye harm from contact lens use. Their study from twenty twenty-four looks back at cases at a large eye center. Lens linked keratitis can threaten sight if not caught.

UK rules now ask for a check of each case in two days. That loads a stretched health service, they note. Cases were graded by size of the surface wound. Risk traits, care, and results were checked by grade. The team aims to sort who needs fast review most. A new care plan based on proof is proposed.
pmc-11673264:
A research team tested whether deep learning methods that rebuild CT scan images help doctors see tumors more clearly, in this 2024 study. Sharper scans could raise confidence when staging cancer. The team compared two learning-based methods against two older ones on the same set of scans.

Thirty-three contrast-enhanced scans were rebuilt eight ways each, and more than twenty radiologists ranked and scored the results without knowing which was which. The deep learning method from the scanner maker scored best on image quality, tumor contrast, and reader confidence. The other learning method only matched a mid-level older setting. Junior and senior radiologists agreed closely. The authors say such methods could set a new standard for tumor staging scans.
pmc-11673564:
Mironov and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-four on wafer-scale ultrathin gold films made with graphene-inspired methods. Gold is a workhorse of modern electronics but usually thick. Their multistep process yields films that stay continuous at tiny thickness. The films show low electrical resistance and high light transparency. Two demos show off the material: smart contact lenses and thermal camouflage. Transfer to other surfaces works at wafer scale.

Flexible, see-through electrodes for photonics are the near-term prize. The authors claim a paradigm shift for two-dimensional materials. Quasi-flat forms of classic bulk materials become plausible. Production details fill the methods sections.
pmc-11673864:
Olimpia Pino and colleagues ask whether trauma changes how people with post-traumatic stress disorder respond to pleasant things, in a 2024 study. Most research on the disorder studies fear and threat. Yet a dulled response to rewards may matter just as much. The team tested this in a sample of refugees.

Forty-two people with probable PTSD and twenty-six trauma-exposed peers rated sixty standard emotional pictures. The pictures were pleasant, neutral, or unpleasant, and ratings covered arousal, pleasantness, and sense of control. The PTSD group showed a broad state of heightened arousal and poor emotional control. Crucially, the difference was not limited to unpleasant pictures. The authors argue that treatment should also rebuild how patients engage with positive experience, not only calm their fear responses.
pmc-11674264:
Yunhao Mei, Fei Chen, and Xiaoxiang Chen test how English skill shapes the way Chinese learners chop speech into events in this 2024 study. Listeners naturally segment a stream of speech at boundaries, and native listeners focus attention sharply there. The team asked whether learners do the same, or whether weak segmentation is part of the foreign accent of listening.

Fifty-six learners, split by test scores into stronger and weaker groups, listened to English sentences and pressed a key when they heard a probe syllable. Stronger learners showed a partly selective attention pattern at boundaries, nearer the native style. Weaker learners spread attention evenly, and for them attention at boundaries tied into how well they remembered the sentences. Both stronger learners and natives remembered more than the weaker group. The authors suggest drills aimed at segmentation could lift listening skill where language knowledge alone is not enough.
pmc-11674364:
Vuttinun Chatupos and a team of co-authors tested a numbing rinse for pain after wisdom tooth surgery. Their trial, from twenty twenty-four, deals with mesioangular impacted third molars. A wash with anesthetic is known to dull pain after a pull, but its span is short. They asked if lidocaine with epinephrine, a blood vessel tightener, keeps the calm for longer. Twenty-eight patients with like teeth on both sides took part.

Each patient had two sittings, one side per plan, in a blind split mouth trial. All had a nerve block shot as the base. Pain in the first hours was the key read. Readers who pull teeth get a read on a cheap add on for the worst pain window.
pmc-11674764:
Ceballos and co-authors study whether inbreeding raises gallbladder cancer risk in Chile, in this 2024 paper. Chile has some of the highest rates of this cancer in the world. Long stretches of matched DNA, a sign of shared ancestry, have been tied to several diseases but rarely to cancer in Latin America.

The team studied more than four thousand Chileans with mixed ancestry. They measured matched DNA stretches, Native American ancestry shares, body weight, and gene-based risk for gallstones. Models then weighed each factor against cancer risk. The design lets the authors separate the effect of inbreeding from ancestry and weight, two strong forces in this population.
pmc-11674864:
Sigal Eilat-Adar and co-authors test a year of extra physical education in disadvantaged schools, in a 2024 study. Children should move vigorously for an hour a day, yet many fall short. The team worked with fifth and sixth graders in a low-income neighborhood. One group took six weekly gym classes, with an athletic subgroup adding two more, while a control group kept the standard two.

Fitness tests ran before and after the year. Girls in the program group gained clearly on a flexibility test. The athletic subgroup improved on an endurance shuttle run, and the hardest-training children trended toward the largest gains overall. Daily activity, screen time, and school climate did not differ between groups. The authors urge daily 45-minute gym classes with a stronger athletic focus.
pmc-11675064:
Claude Beazley, Stefano Giannoni, and Silvio Ionta study, in twenty twenty-four, how seeing your own hand affects reaching accuracy. Many daily acts rely on sight to guide motion and cut errors. Reaching tasks offer a clean test bed for that link. Their task was to draw a line between two dots with a computer mouse. The setup could show or hide the cursor that marks hand position. It could also separate that hand cue from the task cue, the tip of the line being drawn.

Fifty-three healthy adults took part. When the hand cue was visible and split from the task cue, corrections to spatial distortions were less accurate than when the hand cue was absent. The authors link this to shifts between inner and outer focus, and to body-based frames.
pmc-11675364:
Daniela Amicizia leads a team on lung cancer care in Liguria, Italy. Their study from twenty twenty-four looks back at five years of data. Lung cancer is a top cancer threat in Italy and world wide.

New care models use networks of centers and team based care. Region data covered surgery, chemo access, and patient movement. Most surgeries were done at the hub center in the region. Most cases were in males aged sixty-five and up. Travel out of region for care fell in recent years. Near all chemo access came through day hospital care.
pmc-11675464:
Francisco Jahuey-Martínez and three co-authors mapped the trait gene zones of four farm species, in a study published in 2024. Such zones steer growth, milk, and meat traits that farms breed for. Their pool held more than 200,000 zones from a world bank, for cattle, pigs, sheep, and hens, logged through 2021. Cleaning steps cut duplicates and bad labels.

Zone density per span ran ten for cattle, four for pigs, three for hens, and one for sheep. Densities were lumpy: some spans teemed, and most were thin. Zone density tracked gene density and span size in each species. Rich zones often steered many traits at once and sat on known major genes. The team lists the rich spans per species as leads for breeding work.
pmc-11676064:
Matej Zrimsek and co-authors test blood products during plasma exchange in a 2024 pilot study. The treatment swaps a patient's plasma for clean fluid, but it also drains clotting factors. That loss can raise bleeding risk. The team compares three ways to refill one key clotting protein: a concentrated form, donor plasma, or plain albumin fluid.

Seventy-three treatments in patients with low-to-middling protein levels were split by bleeding risk. Standard clot tests and a spinning blood test ran before and after each swap. The concentrate held protein levels about as well as donor plasma. Some clot measures, though, looked a bit worse with the concentrate alone. The results guide safer refills for patients who bleed easily.
pmc-11676564:
Pedro Pablo Martínez-Vega and co-authors search for a parasite in opossums living in and around Mérida, Mexico, in a study from 2024. The parasite, called Trypanosoma cruzi, causes Chagas disease and is usually spread by biting insects. Opossums may also pass it in other ways, since they can carry its infectious form in scent glands.

The team caught just over one hundred Virginia opossums in the city area. They tested blood, scent gland fluid, and milk for the parasite with a gene test. About one in six animals tested positive in at least one sample type. The study weighs what that means for spread that does not involve insects, including possible passage from mother to young. Urban opossums, the authors argue, deserve a place in local disease planning.
pmc-11677464:
Bruna Raquel Fonseca and co-authors published this review in 2024. It gathers evidence on technology for preventing infections tied to urinary catheters. These infections are the second most common caught in hospitals, and catheter cases make up about forty percent of them.

Eight studies met the review's bar. The technologies ranged from reminder systems that prompt timely catheter removal to better diagnostic tools and monitoring devices. Across studies, they cut infection rates, shortened how long catheters stayed in, and improved patient safety and comfort. Shorter hospital stays followed in several reports. The authors stress that gadgets alone do not deliver these gains: teams across professions must adopt them, backed by staff education. They frame technology as an amplifier of good catheter practice, not a substitute for it. Hospitals planning purchases, they suggest, should budget for training in the same breath.
pmc-11677564:
Yue Wang and six co-authors sequence the genome of Irpex lacteus, a fungus eaten and used in medicine. Their 2024 study assembles and annotates the full genome for the first time. The fungus shows strong biological activity, yet knowledge of it stayed thin. A PacBio machine read its DNA end to end.

The genome spans about forty-two million bases with over thirteen thousand predicted genes. Most genes match known ones in public databases. The team found hundreds of enzymes for carbohydrate handling and many drug-making pathways. Fourteen terpene synthases and other synthase genes hint at rich secondary chemistry. A MYB gene family stands out in growth control. The map now grounds future work on this fungus.
pmc-11677764:
Renata Tobiasz-Salach and four co-authors published a plant physiology study in twenty twenty-four on spraying silicon onto wheat leaves to blunt salt stress. Salinity shrinks harvests worldwide, and silicon is a cheap candidate protectant. Wheat seedlings were grown in pots salted with sodium chloride, then sprayed at three silicon doses.

Salt depressed every measured function, from photosynthesis to chlorophyll fluorescence. Silicon-sprayed plants recovered significantly on gas exchange and fluorescence measures, and the benefit persisted across repeated measurements. The middle and high doses outperformed the lowest. The study also tracked epigenetic responses, the chemical marks that tune gene activity under stress. Foliar silicon, the authors conclude, is a practical shield for wheat on salty ground.
pmc-11678264:
Lukasz Gwozdzinski, Anna Pieniazek, and Krzysztof Gwozdzinski review how oxygen stress and red blood cells conspire in varicose veins in this 2024 paper. The condition is usually blamed on weak valves and standing pressure. This review pushes two quieter actors to center stage.

The authors survey where reactive oxygen species come from and how the body's enzyme and small-molecule defenses answer them. In varicose veins, low oxygen, inflammation, and a tired vessel lining feed each other. Red blood cells, trapped in sluggish flow, help clots form and leak hemoglobin, whose iron-rich core can damage proteins and fats nearby. The review ties these threads into one picture of the disease as a loop of oxygen shortage, inflammation, and oxidative harm, with red cells as active players rather than passengers.
pmc-11678664:
Anna Wójcicka and Marcin Mączyński review the antimicrobial activity of naphthyridine compounds, a family of ring-shaped molecules built from two fused pyridine rings. Six versions exist, differing in where the nitrogen atoms sit. As microbes grow resistant to standard drugs, new chemical families with fresh mechanisms are needed. Naphthyridines have shown a wide range of drug-like activity, with microbe-killing effects prominent among them.

The review gathers the literature on synthetic and natural members of the family that fight bacteria or fungi. It surveys which structures have been tried and how strongly they acted. The authors aim the survey at medicinal chemists searching for starting points. A family with many isomers offers many chances to tune strength and side effects. The paper does not report new experiments; its value is in organizing a scattered record into one map of what is known.
pmc-11679164:
David Ponce and co-authors compare three headset tools for testing short-term memory of place. One tool uses mixed reality, where users see the real room with digital objects added. The team built that app for a see-through headset and ran it with twenty-nine people. Scores were set against two past studies that used phone-based and full virtual tools.

All three tools gave like scores for right placements and total tries. The mixed tool took more time in both the learning and test phases. The authors blame its novelty for users and traits of the app build. Objects placed in the mixed app matched users' mental maps of the room. Ratings were good overall, though they dipped as computer experience rose.
pmc-11680264:
Carmina Gallardo and co-authors engineer, in a 2024 study, a tamer version of the African swine fever virus that still protects pigs. The virus devastates pig herds, and weakened live vaccines are the leading hope, but they must be safe. Starting from an already mild isolate, the team deleted three virulence-linked genes, singly and in pairs. They tested four engineered strains in pigs, tracking blood virus levels, shedding, antibodies, and survival after a deadly dose.

Deleting one gene alone made the virus nastier. Deleting two together, EP402R and EP153R, made it safer while keeping full protection: no shedding, strong antibodies, and every pig survived the deadly challenge. The double-deleted strain also carries a marker letting vets tell vaccinated pigs from infected ones. A stress test showed some risk of the virus regaining strength over many passages.
pmc-11683364:
Daan van der Veen and Menno Gerkema argue that fast biological rhythms, those shorter than a day, should not be judged by the standards of daily rhythms. Researchers often expect such rhythms to have discrete pacemakers, chemical buffering, and links to cycles outside the body. The authors note those hopes often fail. The failure itself, they suggest, may be adaptive.

They lay out questions the field should ask about these fast rhythms instead. Their case centers on metabolism and behavior. Coupled fast rhythms may help animals manage negative energy balance, when food intake cannot cover what the body spends. The article is a perspective piece. It proposes new definitions and expectations rather than reporting experiments.
pmc-11684464:
Soham Naik reports a rare case, published in 2024, in which dengue fever attacked the white matter of a young patient's brain. The condition, called ALERD for short, brings sudden confusion and loss of awareness. On MRI scans it shows a telling pattern: water movement is restricted in the deep white matter of the brain. The syndrome is usually tied to other viral infections, and its link with dengue is seldom recorded.

The report walks through the patient's signs, the brain images, the treatment given, and the outcome. Dengue is common in many warm regions, so doctors there may meet this complication without expecting it. Naik argues that dengue belongs on the list of causes to consider when a patient shows this picture. Quick recognition and prompt care, the report stresses, give the patient the best chance of a good recovery.
pmc-11686464:
Adam O'Donnell and five colleagues published a 2024 chemistry paper on plastics that can heal their own cracks. Their materials are polyurethane elastomers, stretchy plastics used in coatings. Special bonding units in the chains let broken parts link back together.

The team hung ring-shaped urea units along the plastic chains as side groups. These units pair up by hydrogen bonds and pull the material into ordered hard zones. A soft base block keeps the plastic flexible. They made two versions and studied how the parts assemble. Coatings that mend small damage could last longer on cars, floors, and gear. The paper lays out how to build and test such materials.
pmc-11688364:
Vogl and co-authors launch a new task set for flight-mind work in an Army lab. The lab is the U.S. Army aero-med lab, called USAARL. Its task set builds on the old MATB, used for 30 years. Four flight-like tasks form the heart of the old set. The new set keeps those four task types in place. It aims at fresh needs: mind load, act marks, and trust in code.

Fresh traits add task spins and live shifts in task load. Code hand-offs now bend with how well the host scores. Those shifts let labs probe trust and bend in hard drills. The text tells the set's past, chief traits, and use paths. It brings the set to peer labs for the first time.
pmc-11688764:
Traci Wilson maps what Area Agencies on Aging share and how they differ, in twenty twenty-four. These local agencies were set up under a nineteen seventy-three law. They plan and fund services that help older adults and people with disabilities stay at home. A common saying claims each agency is unlike all others. Wilson tests that claim with survey data.

She uses a twenty twenty-two national survey with a strong reply rate. All agencies gave a core set of funded services. Funds from states, towns, and health groups let some do more. Wilson sorts agencies into types by size, funds, and place. Each type, she finds, still finds new ways to serve.
pmc-11688864:
HwaJung Choi, Stephen Jivraj, and Stefan Fors compare, in twenty twenty-four, function at older working ages in the United States and eleven European countries. Their sample is adults aged fifty-five to sixty-four. They split people into low and high income groups within each country. Tests cover daily tasks, complex daily tasks, and word recall. The aim is to see if the income gap in function differs by place.

United States adults had more trouble with daily tasks than peers in nearly all the European countries. In the lowest income group, the gap was stark. High income Americans fared closer to peers on basic tasks. They still lagged on complex tasks in most countries.
pmc-11689964:
Evan Henricks and Pratima Gangupantula lead a session, in twenty twenty-four, on microlearning in geriatrics teaching. Microlearning means learning in small, short units. Health teachers praise it for gains in knowledge and trust. It often pairs with phone learning, so material is quick and easy to reach. That sets it apart from long online texts and lectures, which can be heavy and hard to access.

The session shows cases that use social media, podcasts, apps, and point-of-care web sites. It shares use data from one such site. Speakers weigh pros and cons of each form. They also show how to mix short units with classic teaching for best effect.
pmc-11690364:
Vanessa Fabbre, Austin Oswald, and Sarah Jen set out, in twenty twenty-four, five principles for a queer approach to the study of aging. The field now pays more heed to LGBTQ+ lives, they note. Some scholars call for a queer view of the life course itself. But no clear, practical statement of that view existed. The authors write from their own place as scholars in the field, across career stages.

Their principles call for lifting up hidden lives, and for using theories that question the status quo. They call for direct work against bias and unfair treatment. They also back many ways of knowing and asking. The talk traces the past of LGBTQ+ aging studies first.
pmc-11690464:
Hariom Yadav describes a multi-center study, the Microbiome in Aging Gut and Brain consortium, built to trace how gut microbes shape aging and memory, in this 2024 symposium report. Aging disorders keep rising with no strong prevention or cure, and the gut microbiome is emerging as one lever behind them. Several institutions joined to gather large linked datasets on microbes and their pathways.

The consortium layers microbe data with measures of metabolism, proteins, gene marks, and immune state. Yadav presents findings tying microbe shifts to leaky gut barriers, inflammation, and immune changes that track with fading cognition in older adults. He also asks whether correcting those microbe faults could ease aging disorders, the question the consortium was formed to answer.
pmc-11690964:
Jennifer Portz and Sara Czaja led a symposium in 2024 on lessons learned from user-centered design with older adults and caregivers. Digital health tools can address real care challenges, but only if people find them usable, acceptable, and inclusive. Designing with users, rather than only for them, is meant to ensure that fit.

The symposium shared findings from three projects. One designed a dyadic intervention for advanced dementia. One improved care coordination for rural older adults. One integrated social support into palliative care. A final presentation drew lessons from four remote co-design processes for dementia care partner interventions. Czaja then led a discussion of the benefits and limits of this way of working. The shared conclusion is that users need a genuine voice from the start of the design process.
pmc-11691064:
Asmus Cosmos Skovgaard and co-authors search for blood markers of heart disease in Swedish twins. Heart and vessel diseases are the world's leading cause of death, with artery disease of the heart and stroke the most common forms. Twins help because comparing pairs strips out much of the shared genetic and early-life background that can confuse such studies. The data cover 11,228 twins with metabolite measures and register records of new cases.

The team ran survival models both on individuals and within twin pairs, then used a selection method to pick the strongest independent markers. Different markers emerged for heart artery disease and for stroke, which suggests the two conditions partly run on different biology. Fat particles carrying one protein class tracked with artery disease, while those carrying another tracked against stroke. The authors present the markers as new leads for how each disease develops.
pmc-11691364:
Lindsey Smith, Eric Jutkowitz, and Kali Thomas ask what memory care in assisted living really means in two thousand twenty-four. Memory care is the most common specialty in assisted living, aimed at residents with dementia. What counts as memory care, though, shifts with who does the counting.

The team built a national list of large assisted living homes and read them through three lenses: state licenses, an industry data set, and business ads aimed at families. Shares classed as memory care ranged from about a quarter, under state and ad lenses, to three in five under the industry lens. The spread raises fair questions about how care varies behind the same label.
pmc-11692764:
Frailty creeps up with age, but how a body answers a stress may reveal where it stands on that path. LaDora Thompson and Lais Perazza classify older female mice as robust, prefrail, or frail using a vitality score built from strength, endurance, activity, walking speed, and health deficits. Downhill running then served as the stress, and the team measured muscle force and bone density as signs of resilience.

About a third of the mice fell into each class. Frail mice already showed weaker soleus muscle force, even per gram of muscle, hinting at poorer protein quality. Bone density in prefrail mice matched the frail group and lagged the robust, suggesting bone loss comes early. After the stress run, robust and prefrail mice lost muscle force, while frail mice did not change, because their muscles were already impaired. The authors conclude that resilience after stress depends on frailty status.
pmc-11693264:
Alisha Johnson, Amy Vogelsmeier, and Veronica Thompson wrote a 2024 study of advanced practice registered nurses who work full time inside nursing homes. Such nurses are known to cut hospital trips and raise satisfaction, yet few homes use the model. The authors asked how these nurses shape results for residents and for the home as a whole.

They compared two high-performing homes with two lower-performing ones, using eight years of data from a Missouri project in 16 homes. In stronger homes, the nurses acted early, mentored staff, and had real backing from managers. In weaker homes, work stayed reactive and support was weak. The study shows that nurse skill pays off only when the home's structure supports it.
pmc-11697764:
Maaike Noorman and colleagues survey engagement with HIV cure research in the Netherlands. Their study from twenty twenty-four questions affected community members. Inclusive cure development needs community involvement from the start. Awareness, interest, and active searching mark three engagement stages.

About five hundred people with HIV took part in the survey. A similar number of partners and at-risk men also joined. Interest scored higher than basic awareness of cure research. Active information seeking lagged well behind both measures. Statistical models linked personal traits to each engagement stage. Beliefs about the illness also shaped engagement levels. Research teams learn where outreach must work harder to include communities.
pmc-11702264: Justin Kuhlman and four co-authors review how immunotherapy is moving into curative treatment of lung cancer that has not yet spread, in this 2024 review. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs have shown clear benefit for locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer treated with surgery or with combined chemotherapy and radiation. The authors gather the key trial data, then take up the open practical questions: when around surgery the drugs should start, and how long they should run. They close by marking unmet needs and the directions trials are heading next.
pmc-11710364:
C Dirk Keene describes a new platform, published in 2025, for studying donated human brains in Alzheimer's disease research. New tools can map single cells and gene activity in tissue, but older ways of collecting brains were not built for them. Keene's team set out to collect and cut brain tissue in a way that keeps it in top shape.

Their method uses fast brain scans, careful slicing, and a mix of fixed and frozen samples taken from set brain areas. They applied it to eighty-four donor brains, from people with no memory loss to people with dementia. Tissue quality was high, and cell and gene tests worked well. The platform gives labs a shared, careful way to prepare brains for modern studies.
pmc-11710464:
James Pike and co-authors present a 2025 trial study of hearing care and brain shape change. Past work tied hearing loss to faster brain shrinkage in older adults. It was not known if hearing aids could slow that change, so the team used data from a large trial.

Adults in their seventies and early eighties with untreated hearing loss joined the trial. Half got hearing aids with counsel and training, and half got health classes. Brain scans were taken at start and three years later in a large sub-group. The hearing group showed a slightly slower loss of outer brain thickness. A few areas showed clear gains. The authors say hearing care may help guard brain structure.
pmc-11712264:
Becca Levy published this article in 2024, though the catalog lists it under 2025. It tells how Robert Butler fought ageism with science. Butler was a physician, scholar, and activist who spent his life seeking equal rights for older people. That drive led him to become the founding director of the National Institute on Aging. The article traces how his commitment took shape, and how he argued the case for such an institute.

Butler built the institute as a broad effort, drawing on research, training, and public policy at once. Levy shows how that base supported fifty years of work on aging. The piece closes with Butler's own later life. His active old age, she argues, embodied the chances he had worked to open for others.
pmc-11712364:
Claus Dethlefsen and Peter Johannsen write a methods paper on extra medication use inside Alzheimer's drug trials in a 2025 piece. Phase three trials run over eighteen months, and participants often start standard symptom drugs along the way. That extra use can blur the trial's main result, making the tested drug look better or worse than it is.

Guidelines disagree: one major trial paper backs counting all outcomes as they come, while the European regulator backs imagining outcomes without the extra drug. The authors propose a middle path using the estimand framework. The extra drug counts as an event with both a start and a stop date. Only readings taken while it could act are swapped for the imagined scenario. They say this sharpens what a trial result means.
pmc-11712564:
Patricio Riquelme Contreras and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on stress load and bright spots seen on brain scans of people who report memory trouble. The spots, in the brain's white matter, can mark small vessel disease. The team asked whether people with a higher load of long-term stress show more of these spots along key nerve tracts.

The study covered 135 adults in Chile, split by test scores into mild impairment and plain complaint groups. Stress load was built from fifteen body measures, from blood pressure to blood fats. Only in the mild impairment group did scan spots grow with stress load, and the clearest gap sat between the low and middle risk bands. The authors link long stress to early brain change.
pmc-11712664:
Geir Selbaek published a review paper in 2025 on treatments for the thinking symptoms of dementia, with a close look at the new anti-amyloid antibodies. Older drugs have eased symptoms modestly for three decades but do not change the disease. The new antibodies clear amyloid from the brain, yet how much that helps daily life is still debated.

Selbaek weighs trial results, expert views, and clinic reports. The older drugs are cheap, safe for most, and linked in long studies to lower death rates. The antibodies help a little on test scores but carry risks such as brain bleeding, and their costs are huge. Wider use would also demand earlier, marker-based diagnosis for many more patients.
pmc-11712964:
Amanda Annettesdotter and a large team of colleagues examined which disease proteins are linked to shrinkage of the amygdala, a small brain region involved in emotion and memory. Their study, published in twenty twenty-five, used brain scans and tissue scores from people who had died with or without degenerative brain disease. They measured the whole amygdala and some of its subregions, and they scored four abnormal proteins both inside the amygdala and in nearby memory regions.

One protein, TDP forty-three, was linked to smaller amygdala size when found inside the amygdala itself, pointing to a local effect. Tau protein showed a different pattern: tau in nearby memory regions, rather than in the amygdala, tracked with smaller size, pointing to a distant effect. Early links for another protein did not survive stricter statistical checks. The authors call the results preliminary and plan larger samples.
pmc-11713764:
Ye Zhang and co-authors follow loneliness over time in a large British study in a 2025 paper. Feeling lonely has been tied to memory loss and Alzheimer's risk. Most past work checked loneliness once, which misses people who recover or stay lonely for years. The team sorts people by how their loneliness changed across five years.

The study covers 5,346 adults who were about sixty-five years old at the start. Loneliness was rated at two points, years apart. Brain scans and thinking tests then tracked the groups for eight more years. People whose loneliness lasted showed faster decline and more brain shrinkage. The work suggests that lasting loneliness, not a brief spell, is the pattern that harms the brain.
pmc-11713964:
Sheelakumari Raghavan and ten co-authors compare scan measures of brain wiring for use in trials on vessel driven thinking loss, in a 2025 conference paper. Small vessel disease in the brain wears down white matter, the wiring that links areas. A scan method that maps water flow in tissue can catch this wear early.

The study held 718 adults over fifty from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, each with at least two such scans. The team computed four wiring measures, both for the whole brain and for single areas. They matched the measures to vessel risk and to thinking change over time. They also sized a mock trial for each measure. The aim is to pick the scan sign that trials can trust most.
pmc-11714664:
Patrizia Vannini and co-authors report a 2025 study that tracks fine brain change, amyloid, and thinking over time. All of the adults were thinking normally at the start. A scan method can gauge fine injury in the brain's outer layer. The team asked how that gauge and amyloid change together over years. Their group held more than one hundred and fifty older adults from a Harvard aging study.

pmc-11714864:

pmc-11716164:

pmc-11717064:

pmc-11723664:

pmc-11772164:

pmc-11789164:

pmc-11800364:

pmc-11821264:

pmc-11840964:

pmc-11870064:

pmc-11970164:

pmc-12039564:

pmc-12082664:

pmc-12088964:

pmc-12663164:

pmc-12663564:

pmc-12666164:

pmc-12687064:

pmc-12691164:

pmc-12692664:

pmc-12694864:

pmc-12712664:

pmc-12715064:

pmc-12733764:
