Hydrogen peroxide is a key clean oxidant, but it is hard to use well because materials break down and radicals escape unchecked. The team designed a sphere with a special surface layer to tame that reaction.

The hollow spheres were made in one step, with the peroxide itself serving as oxidant, template, and reactant. A coating of tannic acid bound with copper then formed a network on the surface. That layer raised reactive oxygen output by about half while keeping heat conversion steady under repeated light cycles. The authors present the design as a green platform linking chemical reaction control with energy use.
pmc-12737564:
Kazuyuki Terai and a team describe a young cat with body-wide lymph vessel disease causing fluid in the chest and belly. Their case report was published in twenty twenty-five. Systemic lymphatic disorders are well classified in people but almost unreported in animals.

The five-month-old male cat struggled to breathe. Milky fluid filled both chest and abdomen, and scans showed dye leaking from the main lymph duct plus widespread skin swelling. Human medicine splits such cases into generalized and central conducting anomalies; the cat's pattern was compared against those classes. The report imports the human framework into veterinary care, giving clinicians a language for a disease they may rarely see.
pmc-12738664:
Ruijie Sun and co-authors optimized a tunneling method for shallow tunnels under uneven pressure in two thousand twenty-five. Their case was a twin-tunnel project in Qinghai Province, where the vault of one portal sank by fourteen point eight centimeters. They modeled the full build in three dimensions.

The model showed that removing the middle partition wall triggered the sudden settlement. A dual-dose response curve fit the settlement history with very high precision. Comparing dig orders, starting from the deep-buried side cut settlement by about a fifth and support forces by over half. They propose that order, plus fast wall removal and live prediction, for the other portal.
pmc-12744864:
Zongyuan Che and eight colleagues published a prediction study in two thousand twenty-five on a deadly complication of pancreatitis. When the pancreas inflames badly, several organs can fail at once, with high risk of death. Spotting high-risk patients on day one guides intensive care.

The team used records of six hundred ninety-three patients admitted to one Chinese hospital. From twenty-nine early measures they picked seven that best predicted organ failure. Three machine learning models were built and compared. A chart-style tool called a nomogram, based on the simplest model, performed best. It separated high-risk and low-risk patients well in both the build and test groups. The authors offer it for early risk sorting.
pmc-12748464:
Fei Wang, Zhuyi Guo, Michael Carr, and Weifeng Shi review a family of enzymes called PARPs and the drugs that block them. These enzymes tag proteins to steer DNA repair, cell death, and stress responses. Their overdrive feeds genome chaos and helps tumors grow and dodge treatment.

Blocking drugs exploit a flaw in tumors that cannot fix DNA well, and four are in use for ovary, breast, prostate, and pancreas cancers. Early work hints at uses against viruses and in brain, heart, and metabolic disease. Resistance and side effects still limit reach. The review covers next-wave blockers, drug pairings, and tests to pick the right patients.
pmc-12748864:
Ron Yefet and co-authors report, in twenty twenty-five, strong antibodies that stop monkeypox virus by hitting one of its surface proteins. Monkeypox is the most harmful poxvirus now in spread, yet many of its proteins are still not well known. The protein, called A28, sits on mature virus bits. The team took anti-A28 antibodies from men who had got well after infection. They also took antibodies to two other viral proteins. In lab tests, the anti-A28 set stopped both monkeypox and a related virus.

They worked by calling in the complement system, a blood defense chain. Crystal views showed two antibodies bound to two distinct spots that stay the same across strains. Giving one antibody to sick mice eased disease by a small amount. Shots with A28 itself brought strong stopping responses and kept mice safe from a lethal challenge.
pmc-12749064:
Nobuaki Sekido, Tetsuya Saito, and Kyosuke Yoshimi seek a heat recipe that toughens a molybdenum alloy. Their 2025 study works on MoSiBTiC, a high-heat alloy whose weak point is room-temperature brittleness. Annealing can reshape its inner structure. The team compared three heat treatments to find the best balance.

Toughness rose as one phase grew larger and fell as that phase hardened. Very hot, long annealing coarsened the structure but hardened the key phase, hurting ductility. A cooler, longer bake kept the phase soft but grew it slowly. The authors propose a two-step bake that takes the best of both. The plan should lift fracture toughness for parts in extreme heat.
pmc-12749864:
Seven researchers simulate how sodium ions pass a heat and chili sensing channel in a paper from 2025. The channel, TRPV1, opens to heat, acid, and chemical triggers. Simulations used a near-complete human channel under a realistic membrane voltage. Sodium ions paused at three binding sites inside the pore on their way through. Energy analysis showed ions in the filter lowered the barrier at a greasy gate.

A residue before the gate proved important for smooth passage. Changing it cut the number of permeation events. Ions there interact through their water shells with moderate strength. The authors say this balance explains efficient conduction. The findings refine how the channel's gating is understood.
pmc-12751364:
Katherine Jones and co-authors map pooled proof on drugs to prevent or treat delirium in intensive care, in a review from two thousand twenty-five. Delirium lengthens stays and raises death and mind decline. The team gathered systematic reviews of drug trials in adults in intensive care and mapped effects with proof grades.

Fifty-six reviews were found, and a drug class led by dexmedetomidine held the largest proof base. That class likely cut delirium and shortened stays versus dummy care. Proof for other drugs was mixed, and no pooled work covered mind or distress outcomes. Sedative trimming plans also lacked pooled proof. Readers get the strongest drug lead and the gaps named.
pmc-12751664:
Sorayya Rezayi and six co-authors list what a phone app to train surgery tool use must hold. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The team pulled facts from books, guides, and live apps to set a least data set. A survey of experts and teachers then set which parts count most.

Top parts span tool sets, kit gear, an A-to-Z tool list, and guides on use, care, safe steps, wash, and fix, before, in, and past the cut. App build needs span sign-in, code gates, and links to lessons and more reads. The full spec is now set for build work with room students.
pmc-12751864:
Chia-Huei Chu and co-authors link a class of diabetes drugs to safer hearing in this 2025 study. Hearing loss in the inner ear is a quiet complication of type 2 diabetes. The drugs in view, SGLT2 inhibitors, already protect hearts and kidneys beyond sugar control; whether they touch hearing was unknown.

From Taiwan's national insurance records the team matched users of the drugs with non-users among more than 380,000 patients. Users developed confirmed hearing loss at a lower rate, with risk about sixteen percent lower overall. The pattern held across sex, age, town size, and illness groups. Long use mattered most: a year or more of therapy came with risk cut to about a third. The authors call hearing a part of full diabetes care and suggest the drugs may guard the ear as they guard other organs.
pmc-12752064:
Jacob Morgan and Kelly Williams published a field ecology study in twenty twenty-five tracking two sparrow species through Ohio winters. Wintering birds must balance food, warmth, and safety in landscapes carved up by people. Radio telemetry followed Slate-colored Juncos and American Tree Sparrows across two winters, including around a prescribed burn.

Juncos ranged over about seventeen hectares on average; tree sparrows over about twenty-seven. Both species favored edges and used yards and roadsides. Juncos avoided short fields, while tree sparrows used fields of both heights all winter. After the burn, tree sparrows shifted to the burnt fields and away from forest. The study shows two neighbors solving the same winter differently.
pmc-12752864:
Rodrigo Carrillo-Larco and co-authors sort in 2025 high blood pressure into four kinds with very different outlooks. Guidelines treat hypertension as one condition, but outcomes vary widely. Using pooled United States survey data on 4,084 adults with new or undiagnosed hypertension, they clustered patients by eight routine measures.

Four groups emerged: early-onset, late-onset, glucose-related, and lipid-related hypertension. The glucose-related group, marked by high weight and blood sugar, carried by far the highest death risk. Its all-cause risk ran over three times the early-onset group's, and its heart death risk over five times. The other groups' risks were close to the reference. The authors say such profiles could refine treatment choices.
pmc-12756764:
Tilen Berglez and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-five study of how metal ions stick to titanium dioxide nanoparticles. These particles meet alkaline earth ions in bodies and the environment. Ion size and water shells may decide who wins a spot on the surface.

Four ions, from magnesium to barium, competed in the tests. Surface analysis proved the ions adsorb, each to a different extent. Charge measurements showed heavier ions adsorb more and can even flip the particle's charge sign. Computer simulations mapped binding sites and energies. The results explain particle stability in salty, real-world fluids.
pmc-12757364:
Jia Qiu and six colleagues redesign an iron heart scaffold so it opens more evenly, in a study from twenty twenty-five. These scaffolds dissolve in the body over time. Uneven opening can crack coatings and leave gaps against the wall. The team tuned strut and crown sizes by computer model.

The new design kept recoil and shortening about the same. Peak strain dropped by about a fifth. Bench tests confirmed the more even opening. Its push-back strength beat magnesium and polymer rivals. It matched cobalt-chrome stents on that measure. Even opening lowers the risk of coating cracks. The authors say support stays strong enough for clinic use.
pmc-12766764:
Yang Fang and co-authors set out a trial plan for an immune drug given after artery and heat treatments for liver cancer, in work from 2025. Early to mid-stage liver cancer often returns after those local treatments. A short course of immune therapy might mop up what is left.

The phase two study takes thirty patients who first show a complete response on scans a week after treatment. All get the drug every three weeks for six months. There is no comparison arm. Follow-up runs until the cancer returns, death, or study end. Safety is watched alongside effect. The protocol answers a gap: proof for added immune therapy after curative local care is thin.
pmc-12771164:
Choi, Kim, and Oh reviewed world data in twenty twenty-five on loss of an upper arm or hand that comes after birth. Such loss brings a heavy load in body and mind, yet world counts are scarce. They sought the rate, the level of loss, and the main causes.

They searched large health data banks and kept nineteen studies that fit their rules. Loss below the elbow was the most common major level in the reports. Harm from wounds was the top cause, though illness played a large role for folks with a lasting health limit. Rates varied a lot by group and place, and good shared data were rare.
pmc-12772564:
Gregory Davies, Jason Wiles, Alison Walker, and Christopher Humphries describe a prehospital antidote service for sodium nitrite poisoning, in a service report from 2025. Sodium nitrite has become a known method of self-harm. It poisons blood by forming methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen well, so fast antidote access can save life.

A regional ambulance service in England built the service after a coroner request. A specialist response team carries methylene blue, the antidote, under a group direction for paramedics. Handheld meters check blood levels at the scene. Over four years, nine patients were attended and three got the antidote before hospital. The report weighs the impact of the service.
pmc-12780264:
Yuanming Liu and co-authors report a 2025 battery study on lithium metal cells. Anode-free cells start with no lithium layer, which lifts energy density. A weak surface film on the lithium causes uneven deposits. Uneven growth spawns side reactions and early failure. The team shows that standard steady-current charging builds a porous lithium layer. Pores invite the parasitic reactions that kill the cell.

Their fix is a charging protocol with a peak current in the middle of the charge. The peak guides dense, even lithium growth. The resulting surface film is stronger and conducts lithium ions better. Coin-type anode-free pouch cells then cycle stably in tests. Battery engineers get a software-side fix: no new materials, just a smarter charge curve. Protocol changes are cheap to deploy across factories, which gives this result unusual reach.
pmc-12785264:
Shuyi Zhou and co-authors measure how much of young Chinese adults' water intake comes from food, in this 2025 paper. Food water is easy to overlook in hydration advice, and its share in China was unclear. The study covered seven regions of the country.

Nine hundred forty-seven healthy adults aged eighteen to twenty-five took part in spring 2023. The team weighed duplicate portions of everything eaten over three days and logged drinks with a daily diary. Food supplied about thirty-eight percent of total water on average, more in the east than in the south. Energy, salt, and carbohydrate intake each tracked with higher food water.
pmc-12785364:
Paul Horton, Camilla Forsberg, and Ben Lohmeyer published a 2025 study on the harm of calling transgender and non-binary students by their birth names. The practice, called misnaming, is a form of bias-based bullying. It has been studied elsewhere, but little in Swedish schools. The authors set out to record how LGBTQ+ students there experience it.

They interviewed twenty-one young people aged fifteen to twenty-five from across Sweden. Students described feeling thrown off balance and hit by anger, sadness, anxiety, and hurt. The harm did not stop with the individual. Feelings built up across students and turned schools into tense places for the whole group. The authors argue that names are a basic matter of respect and safety in school. Their findings give Swedish educators testimony on a practice that policy often treats as minor.
pmc-12785864:
Dolaya Sadubsarn and Rattana Muangrat optimized a green method for extracting oil from crickets with pressurized carbon dioxide, in a 2025 study. Cricket oil is a valued product, and the supercritical method avoids harsh solvents. The team varied temperature, pressure, and extraction time, then used a response surface design to find the best mix.

Oil yield ran from about 9 to 16 percent across the runs. The best setting, the hottest temperature with mid pressure and the longest time, gave near 16 percent yield with good quality marks. The oil's main fats were palmitic, oleic, and linoleic acids. The authors then tested how well the oil keeps, with standard food antioxidants added.
pmc-12786464:
A Hungarian team led by Hermina Sánta published a 2025 real-world analysis of an all-oral drug combination for multiple myeloma that has returned or stopped responding. The three drugs, shortened to IRd, suit patients who are frail or cannot travel often. Records covered patients treated across Hungary from 2020 to mid-2025.

Patients starting treatment at the first chemical sign of relapse stayed progression-free for about 24 months, against 16 months for those starting at full clinical relapse. Survival averaged about 35 months overall. Side effects appeared in about two-thirds of patients, most often low blood counts, diarrhoea, and nerve tingling. Starting earlier, the authors conclude, gives the regimen its best chance.
pmc-12787164:
Anna Adamczak-Bugno, Sebastian Lipiec, and Jakub Adamczak test how heat changes prestressing steel, the stretched wire that strengthens concrete. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five, though cataloged in twenty twenty-six. Fire can quietly weaken such steel, and judging the damage after a blaze is hard.

Steel samples were heated up to seven hundred degrees and tested for strength. Listening sensors picked up tiny cracking sounds during loading, while computer models supplied stress and strain maps. Heat reshaped the steel's inner structure and cut its strength. Failure style shifted from near-brittle at room state to fully ductile at the highest heat. Sound signal traits were matched with local strain for the first time. The team proposes a combined score for judging fire-hit steel.
pmc-12795764:
Guganesan Krishnanmoorthy and co-authors present a 2025 trial of a nurse-led program to cut muscle and joint strain at work. Nurses face high rates of such strain from lifting and moving patients. The program joined teaching, workstation fixes, patient-lift devices, and muscle relaxation drills. Nurses helped design it, a step meant to boost uptake on real wards.

The trial split ward nurses into a program group of 45 and a control group of 30. Health checks ran at the start and at one, three, and six months. Neck, back, and shoulder pain fell more in the program group over time. Gains in work output showed only after fuller statistical checks. Sick leave shifts were less clear. The study shows that staff-shaped safety programs can ease pain in a high-strain job.
pmc-12801764:
Wala ELsharif and nine co-authors test AI chat models on pregnancy scan reading, in this twenty twenty-five study. Ultrasound scans are central to care before birth, and reading them well takes skill. Big vision-language models might help, but their limits in this task were unclear.

Nine scan images were shown to six advanced models through a public arena site. Each model answered plain prompts and custom prompts written by experts. Three expert scanners graded the answers on five points, from naming body parts to giving sound advice. Tailored prompts helped, but the study shows where the models still fall short of clinical use.
pmc-12804864:
Matisz and co-authors show that long-running gut inflammation rewires gene activity in the brain's emotion circuits, unevenly from region to region, in this 2025 study. Gut diseases often travel with depression and anxiety that linger even when the gut calms. Mice with chronic gut inflammation had their gene messages read in four brain areas.

Changes clustered in the hippocampus and the reward hub, less so in the cortex areas sampled. Genes for cell power plants and antioxidant defense moved most. One energy gene fell in two regions, hinting at weaker power output there. Gut inflammation levels also tracked with synapse and calming-signal genes in one cortex area. The authors frame the pattern as a route from bowel to mood.
pmc-12808464:
For lung cancer that can still be operated on, treatment before surgery aims to shrink the tumor and stop its return. Yanchi Shao and co-authors reviewed records of one hundred thirty-four patients with stage one to three non-small cell lung cancer. They compared chemotherapy alone with chemotherapy plus immunotherapy, given before surgery. The paper, published in 2025, weighs tumor response, survival without events, and side effects.

Adding immunotherapy nearly quadrupled the rate of complete tumor disappearance in the removed tissue, and it raised the share of patients whose scans improved. Survival without events stretched longer too, with the risk of progression roughly halved. Side effects did not climb clearly, and no treatment deaths occurred. Squamous type tumors were likelier to vanish completely. The authors also built a model to predict which patients fare best, using response and a blood inflammation ratio.
pmc-12810164:
Rajkumar and co-authors compare clove and ginger extracts against the main cavity germ in lab tests. The germ, Streptococcus mutans, drives most tooth decay worldwide. Spice extracts were made with ethanol and dosed into germ cultures in tiny wells. Growth was counted across a range of strengths for each spice.

Ginger held full growth block at a higher strength than clove did. At the same low strength, ginger left fewer live colonies than clove. That gap missed the mark for statistical certainty, though. Both extracts thus showed real anti-germ action in the dish. The authors see both spices as candidate natural agents for decay care.
pmc-12811164:
Tomoyuki Araya and colleagues describe a two thousand twenty-five case report of long remission in a rare vessel inflammation disease that began in adolescence. The disease, EGPA, usually strikes middle-aged adults. Teenage onset is seldom documented over long follow-up.

Their patient was eighteen, with asthma, fever, muscle pain, and breathing trouble. Blood counts showed extreme levels of eosinophil white cells. Lung biopsy confirmed the diagnosis. Steroids calmed the disease, but cells rose again during tapering. A targeted antibody then held remission for over five years, letting steroids stop entirely. The case supports durable control with modern therapy.
pmc-12816164:
Daendy Nova Setia, Tartila, and Yogi Prawira report a twenty-three-month-old boy who developed a cascade of problems after surgery to repair tetralogy of Fallot, a set of heart defects. His heart's output fell after the operation, marked by rising lactate, low blood oxygen in the veins, low pressure, and little urine. A fast, misplaced heart rhythm followed and resisted standard care.

Doctors treated the rhythm with several drugs and careful temperature control. A clot formed in the heart's upper chamber despite the chaos, and blood thinning cleared it, but a clot still reached the brain's vision area, causing temporary cortical blindness. By day thirty his sight was partly back, and he went home on day thirty-five with improving strength.
pmc-12816264:
Stefan Schob and co-authors published this study in 2025, though the catalog lists it under 2026. It gathers German experience with flow diversion for hard aneurysms outside the brain. Flow diverters are dense braided stents that reroute blood away from a bulge. They are proven in head arteries, but reports for belly and limb arteries are scattered. Ten vascular centers pooled their cases from 2022 to 2025.

Thirty-six patients were treated, one with two aneurysms. The spleen artery was the most common site, then liver and kidney arteries. The study reviews how the work was done, what blood thinners were used, and what follow-up showed. Side effects and complications are also covered. The aim is a shared picture of safety and feasibility, where until now only single case reports existed.
pmc-12817464:
Jonatan Dewulf and colleagues tested a combined cancer therapy in mice in 2025. One part is a tiny antibody that seeks the HER2 growth marker. It carries a radioactive payload to tumor cells. Treatment focus has widened to tumors with low marker levels. The team used two radioactive versions of the antibody. Cell tests used bowel cancer cells with low marker levels. Those cells also lacked a key repair gene. Mouse tumors grown from such cells tested the pairing. The partner drug blocks a DNA repair enzyme.

Both versions bound the target cells specifically. They damaged DNA and cut cell survival alone. Adding the repair blocker strengthened that effect. Tumors in mice took up the tracers as expected. Split-dose treatment shrank tumors versus control clearly. Pairing with the blocker extended survival further. The authors call the pairing synergistic. Low-marker tumors may thus join targeted radiation care.
pmc-12822264:
Godwill Acquah and co-authors pool studies on how well junior doctors read trauma X-rays on first look, in this 2025 review. In busy emergency rooms, junior staff often give the first read when no radiologist report is ready. Errors can steer care wrongly. The team searched five databases and combined seven studies with standard quality checks.

Across studies, junior doctors caught about two thirds of real injuries while correctly clearing most normal films. Accuracy was somewhat better for skeleton films than for limb films. Results varied a lot between studies, driven by body region and scoring method. No publication bias showed. The authors warn that missed injuries are likely and urge support tools, training, and backup systems for first reads.
pmc-12824164:
Zhihe Yang and eleven colleagues build an AI grading model for a common lung tumor using scans and tissue images together, in a twenty twenty-five study. Grading this tumor by eye is hard because its forms vary so much. The study covered 988 patients from several centers who had surgery with confirmed invasive lung adenocarcinoma. Features from CT scans and slide images were fused into one ensemble model.

The model graded tumors well in both home and outside test sets. Paired gene data tied the image patterns to two gene groups and hundreds of pathways. Paths covered signaling, cell growth, DNA repair, and spread. The authors say joint image reading beats either source alone for grading.
pmc-12827464:
Honghuan Cui, Wei Wan, Biao Ma, Hongyan Guo, and Huizhen Wu study how crack networks grow in worn mudstone as it wets and dries again and again, in work from 2025. Such rock sits shallow and breaks down fast, which threatens slopes and tunnels. The team ran lab cycles on samples and photographed the cracks at set points.

Image tools measured crack share and pattern complexity at two scales. Shear tests then gave strength under varied cycle counts. Both grip and friction fell in steps as cycles rose, with grip falling much faster after nine cycles. The team folded the crack measures into a damage model that joins wet-dry wear with load. The model aims to forecast rock failure in the field.
pmc-12828964:
Mubarak Patel, Mohammed Aadil Buchya, and Olalekan Uthman studied how ethnic group ties to well-being and heart disease. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, used data from the UK Biobank. The set held close to three hundred thousand people. They asked how group ties shape how people rate their own well-being. They also asked what traits best predict well-being and heart disease.

The team used path models to trace direct and side effects. They also used machine learning to rank key traits. Ethnic group showed a clear tie to both health outcomes. Readers learn which traits stand out as signs of risk. The work joins social and body health in one large data view.
pmc-12829064:
Junsheng Zhang and co-authors show how a chicken protein helps an avian flu virus copy itself, in a research paper from 2025. The virus, subtype H6N2, threatens poultry farms and human health. The protein, called PIAS2, tweaks other proteins by attaching a small tag.

The team cloned the chicken version and found it switches on during infection. Adding more of it sped up virus growth. The protein binds the virus's core protein in the cell nucleus and tags it at four spots. That tagging is what lifts replication. The finding exposes a host lever the virus leans on, and a possible target for control.
pmc-12837064:
Dan Xu and five co-authors pooled case-control studies to measure how often COVID-19 patients carry autoantibodies, in this 2025 review and meta-analysis. Reports had linked the infection to immune systems turning on the body, but no settled rate existed. The team gathered seventeen studies with 1,652 patients and 1,455 controls.

Patients proved far more likely than controls to test positive for several self-directed antibodies. The odds ran roughly three times higher for antinuclear antibodies and over three times for anti-cardiolipin. For one neutrophil-targeting type, the odds were over eight times higher. Study quality varied, and signs of publication bias appeared for one antibody family. The authors read the pattern as a real link between the infection and switched-on autoimmunity.
pmc-12837364:
Yao Zhang and co-authors (2025) built a machine learning tool that flags atrial fibrillation risk in people with fatty liver disease. The two conditions travel together, possibly through chronic inflammation, yet no risk tool existed for this group. The study enrolled 723 ultrasound-confirmed patients, 203 with the rhythm disorder and 520 without. Ten immune-inflammatory markers were computed from blood counts and lipids. Three selection methods narrowed the field, and ten learning algorithms competed under cross-validation.

Five markers survived as independent predictors. A support vector machine won the contest, scoring an area under the curve of 0.848 on held-out patients. Explanation analysis ranked age, one platelet ratio, and creatinine as the strongest inputs. The team packaged the model as an online calculator anyone can use. They present it as a practical screen: cheap blood markers, already collected, can point clinics toward the liver patients whose hearts most need checking.
pmc-12838464:
Epple leads a large team on tuberculosis in migrating populations, in work from twenty twenty-five. Tuberculosis can be fatal in patients with blood cancers or weakened immune systems. In low incidence countries, awareness of the disease is low, which delays diagnosis.

Migration from high incidence regions raises the need for vigilance in receiving countries. The article joins a case report with an epidemiologic analysis. The case shows how infection and malignancy can collide in one patient, complicating both diagnoses. The analysis frames the wider pattern, urging clinics to keep tuberculosis in mind for at risk newcomers.
pmc-12840764:
Jongkonnee Thanasai and nine co-authors pool travel-linked cases of melioidosis seen outside its home regions. Their 2026 systematic review covers a soil bacterium's imported infections. The disease thrives in Southeast Asia and northern Australia. Travelers carry it home to places where doctors rarely expect it.

One hundred four studies held one hundred forty-three cases. Most diagnoses landed in rich countries, led by the Netherlands and France. Thailand was the top source country. Patients averaged about fifty years old, and most were men. Diabetes was the commonest side condition. Lung illness led the presentations. The patterns help distant clinicians spot a disease they were never trained to expect.
pmc-12847864:
Haosen Yang and co-authors published a study in 2025 on a privacy-preserving way to warn of battery faults across massive fleets of electric vehicles, using heterogeneous data from charging stations. Timely fault warnings improve safety. Charging data, however, belong to many different owners, take many forms, and are closely guarded.

The proposed framework is a personalized form of federated learning, in which data owners cooperatively train fault detection models without sharing raw data. Each owner can also customize the model to its own fleet, keeping performance robust across different data distributions. Validation used a large real-world data set: charging sequences from more than ten thousand vehicles at thirty charging stations, spanning wide ranges of vehicle and battery types and power levels. The method outperformed earlier collaborative approaches at detecting faults. It also adapted easily to new stations and held up under mixed data.
pmc-12848064:
Meng and a large team show in twenty twenty-five that an enzyme that tags RNA drives the growth of glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain tumour. This tumour grows fast and kills quickly despite surgery, radiation, and chemo. The enzyme is the only known one of its kind for this tag, and it has been tied to several other cancers.

The team found the enzyme at high levels in tumour tissue, linked to worse features and poorer survival. In lab dishes it sped tumour growth, movement, and invasion, and animal tests agreed. It works by stabilising a partner gene's message, which fuels the cancer. Levels of the two tracked together in patients. The authors name the enzyme as a possible drug target.
pmc-12849464:
Kun Fang, Jiacheng Shen, Bangchuan Hu, Ziqiang Shao, and Li Li follow blood salt levels in sepsis in this two thousand twenty-five cohort study. Sepsis throws off the body's fluids and salts, and blood osmolality, the salt strength of the blood, shifts with it. A single reading was known to matter; the path over days was not. The team studied over twenty-two thousand sepsis patients from two databases, with a third group for checking, and grouped the first four days of readings into paths.

Three paths emerged: flat, rising, and falling. Both rising and falling groups died more within twenty-eight days than the flat group, with risk one point eight times higher for each. Kidney harm and excess fluid each explained about a tenth of the link. Simulations of fluid plans showed responses differed by path. The trend, not one reading, should guide care, the authors say.
pmc-12855964:
Mohammed Baafif, Hany Abdo, and Abdulmohsen Albedah test whether copper nanoparticles can protect a common plastic from sunlight, in a 2025 study. Polypropylene serves outdoors everywhere, but ultraviolet light slowly breaks it down. The team mixed copper particles into the plastic at levels up to ten percent by weight. They then measured flow, density, strength, stiffness, and heat behavior, and aged the samples for a thousand hours under harsh light.

Small doses worked best. At one to two percent, the plastic kept more of its strength, stretch, and stiffness after aging, and its crystals and heat resistance held up better. Heavy doses backfired, as clumped particles concentrated stress. The two percent mix gave the best balance of sun protection and toughness. The authors aim the result at outdoor and engineering uses.
pmc-12858964:
Kan Liao and a large team of co-authors report a light effect in an organic crystal in two thousand twenty-five. Optical heterostructures vary in optical traits across tiny distances and are prized for photonics. They are usually made by joining different materials, not within a single uniform material.

In their two-dimensional organic nanosheet, the inner zone glowed far more strongly than the outer zone. Analysis showed a solid-state change in the central top layer, which turned the crystal into a twin structure there. That change raised the efficiency of light emission. The shift came from a contest between molecule-surface and molecule-molecule forces. The authors offer the sheet as a platform for single-material optical structures.
pmc-12859964:
Zhengping Zhu, Yiting Shao, Jingwen Wang, and eleven colleagues map how illness drags down life quality in people with HIV in this two thousand twenty-five survey study. People with HIV face more long-term diseases, like heart and kidney problems, than the public, and their quality of life runs lower. How extra diseases, social support, and low mood fit together was not clear. The team surveyed two thousand six hundred twenty patients at seven HIV hospitals in Nanjing, China.

About twenty-eight percent had at least one long-term disease, and about forty-four percent screened positive for depression. In the team's model, the risk from diseases cut life quality directly and through paths that ran via weak support and low mood. Physical health scores ran higher than mental health scores. The authors argue care should treat body, mood, and social support as one problem.
pmc-12883764:

pmc-12960564:

pmc-12970564:
Ceri Jones, Stuart Noble, and Sylvia Delpratt evaluate a resettlement program for senior police officers near retirement, in work from twenty twenty-five. Senior officers carry years of trauma, stress, and public scrutiny. Retirement in midlife can shake identity, mental health, and job prospects.

pmc-13005364:

pmc-13081464:

pmc-13083964:

pmc-13087264:

pmc-13094564:
Natsinee Athinartrattanapong and co-authors test a training simulator for arterial puncture in this 2026 paper. Arterial puncture is a basic skill for medical trainees. Done poorly, it can cause serious harm. A part task trainer lets students practice the steps on a model first.

pmc-13128664:

pmc-13135564:

pmc-13136464:

pmc-13138664:

pmc-13150064:
Rishi Chowdhary and co-authors review how gut microbes shape cancers far beyond the gut, in a 2026 article. pmc-13150464:

pmc-13152064:

pmc-13156664:

pmc-13175964:

pmc-13215064:

pmc-13215664:

pmc-13216164:
Nayne Vieira da Silva and co-authors present a 2026 veterinary case report of a cancer never before documented in cattle. The tumour is a carcinoma of the rete testis, the network of tubules at the centre of the testicle. The patient was an eight-year-old Nellore bull referred for blood in its semen.

Ultrasound showed dilation of the central testicular tissue with fluid-filled cystic spaces. After surgical removal, microscopy revealed an infiltrative tumour confined to that central region, and staining tests showed the cells carried both vimentin and cytokeratin but not a blood vessel marker. On that combined evidence the team made the diagnosis. They advise adding this rare tumour to the list of possibilities when bulls show blood-stained semen or cystic changes.
pmc-13216264:
Tsumugi Shoji and co-authors present a 2026 cell biology study of how the immune sensor STING is switched off. After STING sounds the alarm over stray DNA, lysosomes swallow and destroy it; the hand-off step was not understood.

Working in cultured cells, the team shows that two lysosome components are indispensable for that swallowing step: a membrane fat called PI(3,5)P2 and CHMP4B, part of the ESCRT-III machinery. Binding tests place CHMP4B directly on that fat. A mutant CHMP4B that cannot bind it failed to restore STING destruction in cells missing the normal protein, and signalling stayed on. The authors present this pairing as the mechanism that ends the innate immune signal at the lysosome surface.
pmc-13216764:
Nihangma Patangwa and co-authors present a 2026 dental case series on fixing a gummy smile the gentle way. Two patients showed excessive gum display with small, spaced upper front teeth, traced to altered eruption patterns that leave crowns looking short.

Treatment combined surgical crown lengthening, by gum removal and bone reshaping, with a three-month wait for the gumline to settle. The teeth were then built up directly with a bioactive nano-hybrid composite rather than ground down for porcelain. Standardized pink and white aesthetic scores improved, tooth structure was preserved, and gum health held. At about two years, the team noted only minor chipping and mild plaque-related inflammation, with gum levels broadly stable, while flagging the lack of longer-term data.
pmc-13217164:
Keerthi Miryala and co-authors present a 2026 computational chemistry study of two closely related light-absorbing dyes built around a barbituric acid acceptor. The question is why near-identical structures behave so differently when excited by light.

Density functional calculations showed the first dye staying rigid and planar on excitation, its electron cloud barely reorganizing, a locally excited character with weak response to solvent. The second dye flexed along its donor-to-acceptor axis, shifting charge strongly toward the acceptor, polarizing further in polar solvents, and shrinking its energy gap. Photovoltaic descriptors followed the same split: the second dye aligned well for injecting electrons into titanium dioxide with strong light harvesting, while the first looked unsuitable. The authors frame rigidity versus charge transfer as the design lever.
pmc-13217664:
Shouxia Li and eight co-authors link low levels of the hormone DHEAS to diabetic eye disease in men, in this 2026 study. The records covered 796 hospitalized patients with type 2 diabetes. Three androgen measures were taken from blood, and the team compared them with retinal damage, separately by sex.

In men, the top third of DHEAS levels came with less than half the eye-disease risk of the bottom third, and the relation ran in a straight line. The other two hormones showed nothing solid in men. In women, an early hint for testosterone faded once other factors were counted. The authors suggest DHEAS may guard men's retinas, a lead for mechanism studies.
pmc-13218164:
Huazheng Cao and colleagues track how the back surface of the cornea shifts over five years after a laser procedure, in a 2026 retrospective study. Keratorefractive lenticule extraction reshapes the cornea by removing a lens of tissue. A bulge of the posterior cornea can signal instability and raise ectasia risk, a thinning disorder. Which tissue thicknesses predict that shift matters for screening before surgery.

The study followed 165 patients, measuring posterior central elevation at twenty-seven points across central and peripheral zones. Measurements ran from three months to five years. The cornea shifted forward, then returned to baseline by five years. The center moved backward while the periphery moved forward. A thinner cornea mattered most: patients below 500 micrometers faced roughly three to six times the raised-elevation risk. Residual bed and lenticule thickness correlated with the shift, while cap thickness did not, so the authors urge caution with thin corneas.
pmc-13218264:
Shasha Guo and four colleagues review fucosterol, a plant sterol from brown algae, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-six. Fucosterol is the dominant sterol in brown seaweeds. Reports credit it with balancing lipids, easing insulin resistance, and fighting inflammation, oxidation, and tumors.

Its effects run through metabolic and inflammatory pathways including LXR, PPAR-gamma, and NF-kappaB. Practical use faces real obstacles. The molecule hates water, dissolves poorly, and is absorbed at under ten percent orally. Processing and storage degrade it by oxidation. The review surveys its distribution across edible seaweeds and the mechanisms behind its benefits. It also covers recent food-grade delivery advances meant to rescue its bioavailability.
pmc-13218464:
Xinjuan Zhou, Xinrui Li, Haiyi Chen, and Jing Deng evaluate China's employee medical insurance outpatient pooling reform in a 2026 study. The reform pooled costs into shared funds, widening coverage for clinic visits once paid for alone. Using 2018 data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, the team asked whether the scheme changed outpatient use among people aged forty-five to sixty.

Three models examined visit chances, visit counts, and out-of-pocket spending. Residents of pooling regions had a five-percentage-point higher chance of an outpatient visit and higher visit frequency. Expected out-of-pocket spending was still about forty-eight percent higher in policy regions, a tension the authors report without resolving. Places offering richer outpatient benefits showed stronger responses, and people with several chronic conditions used more care. The authors read this as improved access to unmet needs, while flagging design questions.
pmc-13218564:
Katie M. Babbott and a large team report user experiences with a well-being app for young people with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 qualitative study. Young people with the condition face psychological distress, yet scalable support services are scarce. The Lift app, built for emotional well-being, had completed a twelve-week feasibility trial in New Zealand and the United States.

Thirteen from that trial, nine users and four support people such as parents and partners, joined focus groups or interviews about the app. Analysis followed a rating framework covering engagement, how well the app worked, its look, and its quality. Participants found Lift engaging, easy to use, and affecting, praising features like a well-being tree that grew with use and the calming design. Several described emotional or behavioral shifts, including connection, self-awareness, and better coping with diabetes. The feedback will guide refinement of the app.
pmc-13218664:
Ambrose Hon-Lam Chung, Yu Jun Wong, and ten co-authors tally the symptom burden of a liver disease. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, covers primary biliary cholangitis, a slow attack on the liver's bile ducts. Tiredness and itching can wear patients down for years. No past work had summed up how common and severe these symptoms are.

The team pools twenty-five studies with more than thirteen thousand patients. Fatigue hits about half of all patients, and itching about a third. Severe forms affect smaller shares. Women report worse fatigue than men. Rates also vary by place and study size. The numbers can help clinics plan symptom care, not just liver care.
pmc-13218764:
Aidan Shulkin and co-authors review facial reconstruction performed with the patient awake in a 2026 paper combining a literature review with cost analysis and practical guidance. General anesthesia has been the default for facial rebuilding, but it brings perioperative risks and resource use. Operating under local or regional anesthesia avoids those costs, yet the approach remains underreported and its best practices unsettled.

Thirty studies covering 1,249 patients and 1,262 flaps met the review's criteria, with forehead and nasolabial flaps the most common. Minor complications affected about ten percent of flaps and major ones under three percent, most patients reported little or no pain, satisfaction ran high, and nobody needed conversion to general anesthesia. A forehead flap done awake cost about 1,280 dollars against roughly 6,647 dollars under general anesthesia, a saving above five thousand dollars per case. The authors supply a guide to patient comfort and argue the technique deserves a wider role.
pmc-13218864:
Lei Yu and co-authors present a case report the catalog lists under 2026. A 63-year-old man had late-stage rectal cancer and a nerve-muscle disease. After urgent bowel surgery he caught two drug-hard germs in the lung and belly. One germ resists nearly all drugs. The first rescue drug mix failed to clear the infections.

Care then switched to a newer paired drug plus a second strong drug. Lab tests showed the germs were cleared from the body. The case is set against host health problems that cannot be reversed. Infection teams get a worked example of a new drug pair in a deep belly infection. Such cases matter because trial data for the hardest germs are still thin. The report shows both the drug result and the limits set by the patient's other diseases.
pmc-13220464:
Yufang Niu and colleagues show that a noncoding RNA in chickens encodes a small protein that steers growth in a 2026 study. Long noncoding RNAs were defined by not making proteins, yet ribosome profiling catches some of them in the act of translation. The team compared RNA production and ribosome activity between precursor cells that were multiplying and those that were maturing.

Of 178 noncoding RNAs that changed between states, three were differentially translated, and one, named lncMPD, carried coding potential and ran high in multiplying cells. It produces a seventy-four-amino-acid peptide, MPD-74aa, which the team confirmed by antibody detection and mass spectrometry. Adding the peptide pushed cells to keep dividing and held back maturation into muscle. The peptide binds CDK1, a cell-cycle protein, and raises its abundance. The authors present the finding as a new regulatory layer in muscle development, with relevance to poultry breeding.
pmc-13221064:
Donrawee Waeyeng and co-authors investigate plant foods and kidney health in a 2026 cross-sectional study from southern Thailand. Ninety-six residents aged fifty or older lived with environmental exposure to cadmium and lead, metals that can damage kidneys. The question was whether eating more plant foods still helped under that exposure.

Blood metal levels, diet scores, and several kidney markers were measured during routine screening in late 2024. People eating more plant foods showed lower levels of a urine marker for tubule cell injury. Nuts and seeds stood out most clearly. The authors also flag that urine marker as a possible early warning test for metal-related kidney damage.
pmc-13222364:
Eman S. Sabry and co-authors present a sensor-based smart driving test system meant to replace human judgment with measured results, in a 2026 engineering paper. Sensors and a control chip log how a test taker actually drives, producing steady scores. A working model demonstrates the concept, built for uniform, scalable license exams.

The paper weighs technology readiness, cost, rollout, and legal compliance, with a detailed cost model. Set against platforms abroad, the design's data links, modular hardware, and screens stand out. Planned upgrades include machine learning to predict outcomes, low-power radio links, and cloud dashboards. The authors frame automated testing as a route to fairer testing and stronger public trust.
pmc-13223064:
David Lasry and seven co-authors showed that antibiotics with no direct action on a tough germ can still teach it resistance, in twenty twenty-six. The germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, is famed for evolving drug resistance. Clinicians often favor drugs that spare it, assuming they exert no pressure. The team passaged three strains for fourteen days in low doses of three such drugs.

Resistance to the front-line drugs then rose sharply: up to twenty-nine-fold, thirty-one-fold, and twelve-fold for the three pairings. The raised resistance held after three drug-free days. Genome reads showed the same regulator mutations that direct pressure usually selects, in efflux and enzyme control genes. The authors say resistance can be selected without the drug ever engaging its target, a caution for prescribing.
pmc-13223964:
Kiana Kawarizadeh and co-authors describe a 2026 immunology study centred on VPS33B, a protein that helps compartments inside cells fuse. Earlier work linked faulty VPS33B to a rare syndrome affecting joints, kidneys, and bile flow. The new work asks what the protein does in dendritic cells, which show fragments of microbes to other immune cells.

Removing VPS33B from dendritic cells weakened their display of peptides on MHC class II molecules, and CD4 T cell responses fell as a result. Responses that depend on CD4 help also suffered, while direct CD8 priming stayed intact. The cells mainly displayed leftover pieces of the invariant chain, pointing to a loading fault.
pmc-13226064:
In vulvar cancer, whether the disease has reached the groin lymph nodes drives both prognosis and treatment. Giorgio Bogani and co-authors review a gentler way to check: sentinel lymph node biopsy, which samples only the first nodes a tumor drains to. For sixty years the standard was removing all groin nodes on both sides, an effective but punishing operation marked by wound problems and leg swelling.

Trials named GROINSS-V and GOG-173 showed that sentinel sampling works in patients with a single tumor under four centimeters and no sign of node spread, cutting complications while keeping cancer outcomes strong. The catch is misses: false negatives run up to seven to ten percent in some series. A missed node can mean a lost chance of cure, since groin relapse is fatal. The review weighs that risk against the gentler recovery, and stresses surgical skill, node examination, and close follow-up.
pmc-13226264:
Chongyang Zhu and five co-authors published a materials study in twenty twenty-six on a seaweed-of-the-land hydrogel designed to carry drugs past the stomach to the intestine. Konjac glucomannan, a plant gum, was oxidized to add acid groups, then crosslinked with its unmodified parent. Oxidation levels were tuned across a series.

One formulation formed the strongest network, while heavier oxidation traded strength for flexibility. The gels barely swelled in stomach-like acid but expanded strongly at intestinal pH, exactly the targeting behavior wanted. Drug release followed a swelling-driven transport model. Characterization by infrared spectroscopy, thermal analysis, and X-ray scattering backed the structure claims. The authors propose the family as biocompatible, tunable intestinal carriers.
pmc-13226864:
Figen Celebi Celik and seven co-authors compare two nasal sprays for teenagers with moderate to severe allergic rhinitis, the allergy-driven inflammation of the nose. Their study came out in 2026. One spray is a steroid alone; the other combines the steroid with an antihistamine in a single bottle.

Seventy-nine patients were followed for two months with symptom scores, quality of life questionnaires, and an adherence scale. Both sprays improved symptoms and quality of life similarly. The combination group stuck to treatment notably better, and better adherence went with better outcomes. Parents' education also tracked with adherence. The authors suggest the combination may suit stubborn cases, and could be offered first to teenagers whose symptoms persist, partly because one bottle is easier to keep using.
pmc-13230664:
Biachew Asmare and colleagues assess in 2026 drinking water quality in Debre Markos town in northwestern Ethiopia. Sixty-six samples came from boreholes, disinfection points, household taps, and storage containers in a 2024 study. Lab tests covered chemical traits such as acidity and nitrate, plus germ counts that signal fecal contamination.

Most chemical measures met World Health Organization guidance, aside from warm source water. Protective chlorine left in water fell below advised levels at sources, taps, and homes, though levels were fine right after disinfection. No harmful germ markers appeared at disinfection points, yet most tap and home samples carried coliform bacteria. Guarding sources, keeping disinfection steady, and treating water regularly are urged to close the gap.
pmc-13230864:
Omar Alkhazragi presents in 2026 an optical computing system that keeps memory and processing together using a laser array. Normal chips lose time and energy moving data between memory and processor, a snag known as the Von Neumann bottleneck. Tiny surface-emitting lasers can switch very fast and sip power, which suits small devices.

The array performs the repeated pattern-matching steps that image networks need, reaching hundreds of millions of convolutions each second in the demonstration. Reported accuracy was near ninety-eight percent for the computing tasks shown. Fast low-power optical math could help driverless cars and drones run vision models on board. Scaling the laser approach may prove easier than growing chip-based optical systems.
pmc-13231964:
Xiang Fang and co-authors present a microneedle patch for infected burn wounds in this 2026 paper. Severe burns heal poorly when biofilms, oxidative stress, immune upset, and low oxygen feed each other. Many microneedle designs are too weak, too slow to make, or too narrow in effect. The new patch aims to break all of those barriers at once.

The patch base mixes two polymers into a strong network. It carries three agents. One breaks up biofilms by silencing a bacterial gene. One mops up harmful oxygen species and releases oxygen. The third calms inflammation as an antioxidant. The paper also links the healing to a growth pathway in skin cells. The goal is faster, cleaner closure of hard burn wounds.
pmc-13232164:
Samantha Velazquez and colleagues use in 2026 magnetic floating to reveal that identical nanoparticles wear surprisingly different protein coats. Blood proteins coat any particle entering the body and decide how cells treat it. Standard tests blend millions of particles, which hides differences between single coats.

Their sensitive setup floats particles at heights set by tiny density gaps, sorting one batch into distinct layers. Protein checks across layers found more than five hundred proteins shifting in an orderly gradient. Top layers leaned toward blood and outside-cell proteins, while lower layers gained structural and energy proteins. Coat variety built into every batch could explain why some nanomedicines behave unevenly in the body.
pmc-13232864:
Habib ur Rehman and colleagues develop in 2026 a four-step iteration for finding points that two special mappings share unchanged. Fixed point results guarantee solutions to equations without always giving a way to compute them. The mappings here stretch distances in a controlled one-sided way, and pairs of them arise in shared-solution problems.

The new scheme builds a sequence from both mappings at once and is shown to settle toward a common fixed point. Weak and strong convergence results cover different space conditions, backed by worked examples. The method is then applied to nonlinear integral equations of a specific class in Banach spaces, with an example validating the approach. Iterative schemes like this turn existence claims into numbers engineers can use.
pmc-13233064:
Evangelia Baka and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study on how human factors shape artificial intelligence in health care across low- and middle-income countries. Most guidance on AI ethics comes from wealthy settings, leaving local realities understudied. The team interviewed 21 AI researchers and innovators working across Latin America, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East with North Africa.

Five themes ran through the interviews. Oversight needs people who are ready and trained to provide it. Ethics training is scarce, and systems built elsewhere often fit local conditions poorly. Governance should center human needs, and multidisciplinary teams help bridge the gaps. The authors call for investment in AI education and inclusive governance so these tools narrow health gaps instead of widening them.
pmc-13233564:
Wugui Chen and colleagues reported a 2026 study testing a cancer drug, KPT-330, against osteoarthritis in mice. The drug blocks exportin-1, a protein that ferries molecules out of the cell nucleus. In osteoarthritis, bone-eating osteoclast cells under the cartilage help drive joint damage. The team used mice with surgically triggered joint disease and cultured osteoclasts in dishes.

Treated mice kept more of their under-cartilage bone, preserved cartilage, and formed fewer osteoclasts. In dishes, low doses blocked osteoclast formation and bone resorption without poisoning cells. The drug quieted two signaling routes, NF-kB and MAPK, and lowered the master osteoclast genes they control. The authors propose exportin-1 blockade as a two-way strategy against bone and cartilage damage.
pmc-13233664:
Jayco Cheng and colleagues published a 2026 rapid review of how to teach palliative care to oncology residents. Adding palliative skills to cancer care improves how doctors talk with patients, control symptoms, and make decisions, yet resident training varies widely. Searching literature from 2000 to 2025, the team found twenty studies of training programs for residents in cancer care.

Half the programs were immersive rotations inside specialist palliative services, usually lasting four to eight weeks. These rotations steadily improved how trainees talk with patients, control symptoms, and feel about the work, with no clear gain from going longer. Required rotations beat optional ones, producing broader gains and more change in real clinical behavior. Short courses and workshops formed the other half. The review feeds into work on shared training standards across Europe.
pmc-13234064:
Elisabeth Stöttinger, Beate Priewasser, and Eva Rafetseder published a 2026 developmental psychology study on why children cling to first impressions. When a picture slowly morphs from a rabbit into a duck, children keep calling it a rabbit long after adults switch. Three experiments with children aged three to eleven probed the reasons, replicating the earlier finding.

Away from the morphing sequence, children named the same images as readily as adults, so perception itself was not the problem. Only children aged nine and older matched adult timing in the gradual condition, and a focus on the whole picture rather than details helped. Telling younger children both possible answers in advance improved their switching, though not fully. The authors suggest younger children struggle to picture the alternative, while older ones explore less efficiently.
pmc-13234364:
Marwa O. Abd El-Halim and colleagues surveyed in 2026 how common Staphylococcus aureus is in horses, donkeys, and mules in Egypt. The bacterium normally lives on skin and in noses, yet it can cause serious infection. Resistant forms, known as MRSA, limit treatment choices for animals and people. Nasal samples were tested, and owners' management and animal history were examined for risk patterns.

Colonization appeared in a substantial share of nasal samples, while gene-based testing gave a lower rate. Horses carried the bacterium more often than donkeys or mules. Higher rates linked to young age, poor body condition, breathing signs, and earlier antibiotic treatment. Resistant isolates often withstood several important antibiotics. The authors call for better hygiene, careful management, and more prudent antibiotic use in equine care.
pmc-13234764:
Cristina Emilia Ursu and co-authors reported in 2026 heart surgery in a 64-year-old man with a bleeding disorder, severe haemophilia A. He needed a new aortic valve and repair of a widened ascending aorta, the large vessel leaving the heart. Such surgery is especially demanding in haemophilia because blood thinning, bypass machines, and surgical injury all raise bleeding risk. A multidisciplinary team planned factor replacement and laboratory monitoring in detail.

Surgeons implanted a biological valve and reduced the aorta to a much narrower, even tube. The patient left intensive care after two days and went home after ten days. Later protection combined clotting factor treatment with blood-thinning medicines in a staged plan. No bleeding, clotting, or other complications appeared in follow-up described. The authors stress that continuous laboratory checks made personal dosing possible.
pmc-13236164:
Vargas-Moreno and colleagues report outcomes for a nose-based operation on tumours at the base of the skull. The clival region sits deep in the midline, wrapped in vital nerves and vessels, which makes it one of surgery's hardest targets. The extended endoscopic endonasal approach reaches it through the nose, a direct and less invasive corridor.

The team reviews how their patients fared after surgery by this route. Outcomes in such series guide a hard balance: removing enough of a lesion against the risk of harming nearby structures. Their results add one centre's experience to a technique that has shifted skull base surgery away from large open operations.
pmc-13236564:
Peng Zheng and co-authors validated in 2026 a combined model for predicting lymph node spread in rectal cancer before surgery. Node status guides whether patients should receive treatment before an operation. Their main group held more than one hundred patients, with a smaller external group from two other centres. A previously built image algorithm read the magnetic resonance scans alongside two human radiologists.

The algorithm alone predicted node spread more accurately than either radiologist in the main group. Agreement between the two human readers was low, highlighting the judgement problem the tool addresses. A blood tumour marker above a set level and poor tumour differentiation independently raised spread risk. Combining the algorithm with those two clinical factors lifted accuracy substantially in both patient groups. The authors see the fusion model as support for choosing pre-surgery treatment.
pmc-13236664:
Anna Michalska-Falkowska and Karine Sargsyan reviewed in 2026 why biological samples and their digital data stay disconnected in poorer countries' biobanks. Samples are collected locally, yet the systems to store, link, and share their data often lag behind. That divide shuts local populations out of genomic medicine gains and invites extractive data practices by richer partners. More than one hundred fifty studies and policy papers informed their synthesis.

Four gaps underpin the divide in their analysis of the literature. Weak physical infrastructure, incompatible data systems, scarce staff with joint lab and data skills, and thin governance each play a role. Their proposed model, named DIGS, treats infrastructure, interoperability, governance, and skills as one cycle needing joint investment. Partnerships should centre local leadership over data decisions, the authors argue. Sustainability means growing local capability rather than only buying equipment.
pmc-13236964:
Uriel Gomez-Ramirez and colleagues sequenced microbes from the middle ears of children with cholesteatomatous chronic otitis media in 2026, a stubborn ear disease that often returns after surgery. Samples came from healthy ears and from diseased ears before and after dissection assisted by the chemical MESNA. The analysis treated the microbe community as an ecological network rather than a list of germs.

Healthy ears showed a richly connected network, while diseased ears collapsed to almost no connections, with one bacterium, Cutibacterium, standing isolated as a possible keystone troublemaker. MESNA broke up the disease community but recovery brought sameness and, in several children, a bloom of Pseudomonas. The authors argue for restoring a healthy ear ecology, not just killing germs.
pmc-13238664:
Tanaka and colleagues close a patient's chest with plastic cables after emergency heart surgery, because metal was not an option. The patient had a torn aorta, a Stanford type A dissection, needing urgent repair through the breastbone. A suspected metal allergy ruled out the usual steel wires for holding the breastbone shut afterwards, and there was no time for allergy testing.

Cables made of ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene, a very strong plastic fibre, did the job instead. The team reports the closure held. Their case gives surgeons a tested fallback for a rare bind: emergency chest surgery in a patient whose body may reject the standard metal hardware.
pmc-13239064:
Alexander A Huang and Samuel Y Huang reviewed in 2026 how machine learning is changing sleep medicine. Their survey covers automated sleep stage scoring, treatment tuning for apnea and insomnia, and wearable devices that watch sleep outside the laboratory. Sleep disorders burden a large share of the population, and traditional scoring by hand is slow and scarce.

Machine learning has sharpened the accuracy and speed of stage classification and enabled treatments tailored to individual patients. Wearables add continuous, noninvasive monitoring at home. Against the gains stand data privacy worries, ethical questions, and the need for clinicians and engineers to work together. The authors conclude that clearing those barriers will decide whether the promised personalization reaches ordinary care.
pmc-13239764:
Hiroyuki Fujii and colleagues report a 2026 case of lung artery hypertension caused by old blood clots in a teenager. A 16-year-old boy had already suffered deep vein thrombosis, and testing showed severe deficiency of protein S, a natural clot brake, caused by a newly found frameshift fault in the PROS1 gene.

Blood thinners and a drug called riociguat did not clear the pressure problem, and imaging showed organised clots in outer lung arteries. Doctors therefore widened the narrowed vessels with balloon angioplasty in staged sessions at sixteen, seventeen, and again at twenty-two. Every procedure went smoothly, and circulation plus exercise capacity stayed improved over long follow-up.
pmc-13239864:
Samuel Deakin and a large Canadian team map the genetic structure of woodland caribou across western Canada in a 2026 study. Ice age advances and retreats, plus modern habitat damage, have layered the animals' ancestry at several scales, and conservation units need to reflect that history.

Genotypes at roughly thirty-three thousand DNA positions came from 759 animals in forty-five subpopulations. Clustering revealed groupings at multiple levels that do not match the management units currently recognised. Genetic diversity peaked at mid-latitudes, a signature of mixing when separated herds met again after the glaciers withdrew. The authors urge planners to protect diversity at every level of the hierarchy.
pmc-13239964:
Tomoki Ishida and a large team of co-authors report an adrenal cancer in a woman with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, an inherited condition that raises cancer risk. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-six. The syndrome's usual cancers strike the gut, pancreas, and breast; adrenal cancer is almost unheard of.

The forty-year-old patient came in with uncontrolled diabetes and low potassium. Scans found a twelve-centimeter adrenal mass and swollen lymph nodes. Dark patches on her lips and fingers, plus gut polyps, fit the syndrome. Surgery removed the gland, a kidney, and part of the liver. Cancer later spread to lungs and liver, then held stable for two years on drug treatment. Gene testing found a rare inherited variant.
pmc-13240064:
Minoo Moghimani and co-authors gather published case reports of foodborne Campylobacter infection in a 2026 systematic review. These bacteria, mostly from poultry, are the leading bacterial cause of food-related gut illness worldwide, and individual case stories reveal the range of harm they can do.

From more than nine thousand papers, sixty-three reports covering sixty-six cases between 2000 and 2024 qualified. The United States and Japan contributed the most cases, men outnumbered women roughly three to one, and diarrhoea dominated the symptoms. Severe complications such as heart inflammation and bloodstream infection appeared mainly in people with weakened immunity. The authors call for stronger surveillance and food safety.
pmc-13240264:
Yuxia Hao and co-authors test a compound from a medicinal food plant against liver cancer in a 2026 study. Ophiopogonin D comes from Mai Dong, the tuber of Ophiopogon japonicus, and liver cancer urgently needs options beyond toxic chemotherapy and drugs that tumours learn to resist.

The compound slowed three liver cancer cell lines, pushed them into programmed death, and curbed their movement, while barely harming normal liver cells. Network analysis and experiments converged on a target protein whose suppression raised damaging oxygen radicals and triggered an iron-driven death called ferroptosis. A major growth pathway also quieted. In mice, doses of the compound shrank implanted tumours in a dose-dependent way.
pmc-13240364:
Chengfang Sun and eight colleagues examine a dangerous pregnancy complication pairing, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Severe preeclampsia can progress to HELLP syndrome, where blood breaks down, liver enzymes climb, and platelets fall. Outcomes for mother and baby worsen sharply.

Records covered 170 patients with severe preeclampsia at a Wuxi hospital, plus thirty healthy pregnant controls. Thirty of the patients had HELLP syndrome. Clinical and laboratory data were compared among the three groups. Regression identified risk factors, and prediction curves tested their accuracy. Mothers with HELLP showed distinctive markers, including clotting and liver measures. The authors aim at earlier recognition of the patients headed for the syndrome.
pmc-13240764:
Saumik Sarkar and co-authors present a 2026 trauma case from Sylhet, Bangladesh, involving three fishing spears lodged in one patient. The 34-year-old man arrived six hours after an assault. Spears pierced his cheek, lower back region, and foot, and his abdomen was swollen.

Scans confirmed deep penetration into soft tissue and internal organs. Emergency abdominal surgery found holes in the large and small bowel, which surgeons repaired, adding a temporary bowel opening because of the delay and tissue swelling. All three spears were removed at the same hospital, and recovery passed without major problems. The authors highlight careful sequencing and teamwork in hospitals with limited resources.
pmc-13240864:
Küçüksönmez and co-authors at Selçuk University surveyed why young people in Türkiye still go to the cinema. Streaming has made films cheap at home, yet theaters charge premium prices. The sample covered one thousand one hundred eighty-three students at twelve universities. Questions probed habits, motivations, and socioeconomic background.

Socializing ranked as the strongest reason for attending, not escaping loneliness. Screen and sound quality also pulled students in. Attendance rose with socioeconomic standing, and motivations differed by class position. The authors caution that a student-only convenience sample limits how far the findings travel.
pmc-13240964:
Marn Joon Park and co-authors publish a 2026 narrative review of depemokimab, an antibody drug for chronic sinus disease with nasal polyps. The drug targets interleukin-5, a signal that drives allergy-type inflammation. Its design allows dosing only twice a year.

Two large phase three trials in severe adult patients supply the core evidence. After a year, polyp scores and nasal blockage ratings improved more with the drug than with placebo. Blood levels of the inflammatory cell type the drug targets stayed suppressed between doses. Side effects looked similar to placebo. The authors call for work on patient-selection markers, cost-effectiveness, and long-term safety and adherence data.
pmc-13241064:

pmc-13241464:
Dousset's team at James Cook surveyed 2,317 Great Barrier Reef neighbors about stewardship. State plans lean on coastal towns to ease pressures on the reef. pmc-13242464:

pmc-13243264:

pmc-13244464:

pmc-13245064:

pmc-13245564:

pmc-13246064:

pmc-13246564:

pmc-13246764:

pmc-13247564:

pmc-13247764:

pmc-13248664:

pmc-13248764:

pmc-13248964:

pmc-13249164:

pmc-13249764:

pmc-13250164:

pmc-13250864:

pmc-13254564:

pmc-13254764:

pmc-13255764:

pmc-13259664:

pmc-13264864:

pmc-13265264:

pmc-13266564:

pmc-13267564:

pmc-13268464:

pmc-13268764:

pmc-13269264:

pmc-13272464:

pmc-13272564:

pmc-13272664:

pmc-13275064:

pmc-13276764:

pmc-13279664:

pmc-13279764:

pmc-13280664:

pmc-13281064:

pmc-13281364:
Patrick Krastman and colleagues published a 2026 register study measuring what share of Dutch general practice consultations concern musculoskeletal disorders, aches and injuries of muscles, bones, and joints. Using a national database holding records for over 2.5 million patients from 2017 to 2023, they classified consultations by chapter and broke the musculoskeletal share down by age, sex, and body region.

Musculoskeletal problems accounted for 11.3 to 12.6 percent of all consultations across the period, making them the leading reason for visiting a Dutch general practitioner. Lower limb complaints led the regions, followed by back and upper limb problems. Women generated about 60 percent of these consultations, and the heaviest concentration sat in the 55 to 64 and over-75 age bands. With population aging advancing, the authors expect the share to grow. They frame the numbers as planning evidence for workforce capacity and for care models that keep musculoskeletal work from crowding out everything else in general practice.
pmc-13281464:
Ameer Hohlfeld and colleagues surveyed trial leaders in sub-Saharan Africa on publishing results in a 2026 study. Trials that never reach print can skew what doctors think works. The team emailed more than six thousand leaders found in a global trial registry. Four hundred nine took part in the web survey. They were asked about duty to publish, delays, and blocks they had met.

Most agreed trial leaders must publish all results, and most within two years. Bias in what gets printed was rated high for the region. Close to two thirds had printed at least one trial within two years. Yet about one in four had a finished trial they could not print. Top blocks were journal rejection, lack of time, and dull results. Three in four had no training in writing trial papers. The authors urge training and support for African teams.
pmc-13281764:
Emanuela Foglia and colleagues assessed full automation in an Italian germ lab in a 2026 study. Germ labs face rising sample counts with flat staffing. Machines that run the whole chain, from check-in to plate reading, promise relief. The team took a broad health technology view at one hospital lab. They compared hand work and machine work on urine samples and on blood cultures that had turned positive. Costs, staff time, and staff views were all weighed.

Automation cut check-in time by about two thirds. Seeding plates by hand all but vanished, and plate reading time fell steeply. Yearly staff costs for the tracked work fell by about two thirds too. Total handling time dropped by a like share. Staff reported safer work and a lighter load. The authors say the case rests on more than speed: freed hands can shift to harder tasks.
pmc-13281864:
Jun Zou and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a woman with a deadly fungal infection. She was thirty-nine and had just learned she carried both HIV and hepatitis C. The fungus spreads through the body in people with weak immunity and kills up to three in ten treated patients. Blood tests and cultures confirmed it had spread widely. She began a strong fungal drug at once. Her liver and kidneys then failed, and confusion set in as the liver faltered.

She was moved to intensive care in grave shape. Teams added a machine that does the liver's cleaning work from outside. A second machine took over the kidneys' filtering. The authors present the paired support as a rescue that pulled her through. They note that organ failure often caps drug doses in such cases. Their report adds rare guidance for this exact crisis.
pmc-13282164:
Taifu Huang and co-authors published a 2026 study modelling how climate change is shrinking habitat for the dhole in China. The dhole is a wild dog and top predator, listed as endangered worldwide and given the highest protection class in China. The team combined sighting records with climate projections in an ensemble model, a blend of several models, to map suitable habitat in past, current, and future periods.

Suitable habitat now covers about one million four hundred thousand square kilometres, mainly around the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. That area has fallen by nearly half since the past period studied. Future climate scenarios project a further fall of roughly twelve to thirteen percent. Cold-month temperature, height above sea level, and slope shaped past habitat most. The authors name mountain ranges, including the Qilian and Hengduan ranges, as future refuges, and call for larger protected areas.
pmc-13282264:
Mojtaba Aghaei and co-authors wrote a 2026 narrative review on two small genetic variants in a gene linked to leukaemia. Leukaemia is a group of blood cancers shaped by both genes and environment. The gene, BMI1, helps blood stem cells renew themselves and is tied to cancer growth. The review examines two single-letter DNA changes, named rs1042059 and rs11591377, and their possible effect on leukaemia risk.
