Reports covering January 2020 through December 2025 came from the national reporting system. The team classed events as common reactions, rare reactions, or coincidental. Patterns by age, dose, season, and region were examined.

In total, 12,597 events were reported, a rate of 213.15 per 100,000 doses in their figures. Most cases involved children aged one year or younger, at 76.49 percent of the reports. Fever led the symptoms at 70.75 percent, followed by rash and irritability. Sixty-eight severe events occurred, and 95.49 percent of all cases improved without treatment. Giving MMR alongside other vaccines raised high fever and rash rates. The authors judge the safety profile sound.
pmc-13319864:
Pedro Giorgetti Montagner and co-authors fire dental ceramic discs again and again in a 2026 lab study of crown materials. Machine made crowns often need extra firings to fix shade or shape, yet heat rounds may change surface feel and strength. Two glass ceramic types in wide use were fired two, three, or five times and then tested side by side.

Sixty discs were split evenly between the two materials and across the firing counts. One type grew smoother and stronger with more firings, while the other grew weaker at five firings. Hardness fell at five firings for both, and one type showed tiny surface flaws at that count. Extra firings help one material more than the other, so lab plans should differ by type.
pmc-13320664:
Jan Hojný and colleagues write a 2026 letter on the mixed nature of high-grade womb stromal sarcomas. They respond to a study by Hartwich and others that used whole genome, exome, and RNA reading on 80 such tumours and flagged a gene gain tied to worse survival. These cancers are aggressive, hard to classify, and short on treatment options.

The writers note that similar looking tumours can stem from quite different gene faults. Some are driven by gene fusions, with fairly few added mutations, while tumours lacking fusions more often show a mutation driven pattern. Sorting those groups apart matters for prognosis and for finding drug targets, including rare repair fault cases.
pmc-13321564:
Iwasaki and co-authors ask if time before hospital arrival affects early death after severe torso trauma. City centers have short transport times, so patients often arrive before cardiac arrest. Yet chest, belly, or pelvis bleeding can worsen fast on the way.

The team reviewed past cases at an urban emergency and critical care center. They linked total prehospital time to early death in patients with severe torso injury. The aim was to see if longer times still matter even where distances are short. Findings may guide how fast crews move and what care they give en route.
pmc-13321864:
Arnold Fredrick D'Souza and an international expert panel build, in 2026, a home exercise programme for balance and mobility in Parkinson's disease that can run with remote support in low-resource settings. Centre-based physiotherapy is ideal but rarely feasible long term, and existing remote programmes seldom target this disease or poorer settings.

The team pooled 473 candidate exercises from literature and expert suggestions. After removing duplicates, ninety-nine exercises in six domains entered three rounds of structured online consensus voting. The final programme kept forty-two exercises, each with dosage, progression steps and safety notes. Participants spanned several professions and countries. The authors present the protocol as adaptable worldwide, giving clinicians a ready framework for tele-assisted home rehabilitation where clinic access is limited.
pmc-13322864:
Manar Abdelazeem Gomaa and colleagues report real-world use of anti-CGRP drugs for migraine in Egypt, in a 2026 study of patients prescribed these newer treatments. Clinicians followed headache diaries and disability scores at the start of care and again at one and three months.

The cohort held 80 patients, 62 with chronic migraine and 18 with episodic migraine, treated with erenumab, galcanezumab or rimegepant. About two thirds reached at least a halving of migraine burden, with gains in monthly migraine days, pain level, attack length and disability scores. Stopping treatment, seen in 35 patients, often reflected cost, good improvement or poor response, and relapse followed in a large share of those who stopped.
pmc-13323164:
Robert N D'Angelo and Natalia C Berry argue in a 2026 commentary that care for the left atrial appendage in atrial fibrillation needs one joined strategy. The appendage triggers rhythm trouble and supplies most clots in this disease, so isolating it electrically and closing it mechanically are often discussed apart.

Trials pull in mixed directions: isolation cut recurrence in the BELIEF trial, device closure matched drug care in OPTION and CHAMPION-AF, yet CLOSURE-AF missed its target in older, higher-risk patients. Stroke risk after isolation, from weak appendage contraction, pushes many clinicians toward closure anyway. The authors weigh why results differ, including leftover patency, and propose treating isolation and closure as one planned package.
pmc-13323464:
Yang Wu leads a review of CRISPR tools for tracking mosquito-borne viruses, published in 2026, across detection, tracing and discovery support. Surveillance must catch many co-circulating pathogens, types and lineages quickly at clinics and mosquito sampling sites.

Detection is the most mature use, with Cas12 and Cas13 assays for Zika, dengue, West Nile virus, chikungunya, Japanese encephalitis and kin reporting sub-hour runs and portable readouts. Tracing still leans on portable sequencing, while CRISPR sample preparation tricks remain transferable ideas rather than field standards. Multiplex systems such as CARMEN can screen known viruses, but finding truly new ones still needs metagenomic sequencing. Field proof in pooled mosquito samples stays thin.
pmc-13324664:
Fei Ye and co-authors test whether a yellowing step can soften the bitter taste of Qianlin cha in a 2026 food study. The herbal tea comes from Camellia cuspidata and is valued for health uses, yet its harsh flavor limits appeal.

Sensory panels, color checks, and two gas chromatography methods compared plain and yellowed tea. Yellowing lifted panel scores, moved color toward yellow, and raised amino acids and soluble sugars for a sweeter sip. Bitter ester catechins fell at the same time. Four scent-active compounds stood out: linalool, nonanal, sulcatone, and (E,E)-2,4-heptadienal. The shift from herbal and bitter toward sweet and floral gives makers a route to premium products.
pmc-13325364:
Cándida Pastor-Ramírez and co-authors build copper cluster compounds with three, four, and eight metal centers in a 2026 chemistry study. One product holds the first cubane-like core built from a Cu4O3N unit.

A Schiff base ligand, sodium azide, and copper salts combined into three structures read by X-ray diffraction. The four-copper compound forms a distorted cube, the eight-copper one a double cube with azide bridges, and the third a chain polymer. Magnetic tests from 2.9 to 300 K showed mixed friendly and opposed spin coupling in the first compound. The larger two showed opposed coupling throughout, tied to their wide copper-oxygen-copper angles.
pmc-13326064:
Fernán González Bernaldo de Quirós and Alejandro Macchia question a national dengue estimate built from blood donors in a 2026 letter. The study under discussion found rising dengue antibodies in donors and virus RNA during the 2022-23 outbreak in Argentina.

From those data came a claim of about 10.2 million new infections nationwide. The letter argues donors from 12 urban centers cannot stand in for the whole country without calibration by age, sex, and region. Reweighting to an older donor mix fixes survey comparability, not population reach. A Buenos Aires household study with careful weights found adult rates of 8.1 percent before and 18.6 percent after a later outbreak, on a stated base.
pmc-13326464:
Ramazan Başaran and co-authors follow blood pressure around the clock in adults over 80 during Ramadan fasting in a 2026 study. Daytime fasting shifts fluid and meal timing, and evidence in the oldest old was thin.

Sixty-nine community-dwelling adults were checked in fasting and non-fasting periods with 24-hour monitors and function tests. Average pressure rose slightly while fasting, to 132.5 over 70.2 mmHg from 129.8 over 68.0 mmHg in the comparison period. Hydration markers and mobility scores did not shift. Fall risk scores, though, rose by a mean of 0.44 points during fasting. The afternoon near 15:00 showed the widest gap between periods. Careful fall watchfulness seems wise.
pmc-13327164:
Marie-Joelle Beaudoin and co-authors published a 2026 study on spotting dementia in adults with intellectual disability. Early signs are hard to judge when thinking skills were already limited, so carers often complete a screening questionnaire. The team checked how questionnaire scores related to age, background, and thinking test results.

Data came from 322 adults, including 55 people with Down syndrome, who also took tests of severe impairment, practical skills, and word fluency. Older age and Down syndrome both went with higher questionnaire scores, while disability severity did not. Higher scores also tracked with stronger verbal fluency, hinting that carers notice change more easily in people who speak well. Closer watching is urged for adults with weaker speech.
pmc-13327364:
Haya A. Alnafisah and colleagues report topical treatment of recurrent conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia. Their 2026 case paper follows a 64-year-old man with a recurrent mass in the right eye causing irritation, a decade after excision of a similar lesion there. Examination found a 6 by 7 mm raised, gelatinous lesion on the nasal conjunctiva, extending from the caruncle to the limbus with about 2 mm of corneal involvement.

Rather than repeat surgery, the team treated the lesion with topical mitomycin C 0.02% in a cyclic regimen. Marked regression appeared after four weeks, and a second course for a small residual lesion achieved complete regression with mild scarring. Treatment was well tolerated, with only mild transient discomfort, injection, and tearing, and no recurrence over more than one year of follow-up. The authors present topical mitomycin as an effective conservative option for selected recurrent cases, pending larger studies.
pmc-13327564:
Wong, Bénard, and Perrin load DNA strands with metal tags in a set way for the first time in this twenty twenty-six study. Tagged DNA could serve as a probe that finds and treats sick tissue in one build. The trick is to place each metal at a known spot on the strand.

Inside, the team uses a DNA-copying enzyme to build strands from tagged blocks on a guide strand. Five metals were placed this way, and two unlike tags shared one strand in some builds. Checks by mass tools and film tests proved the ray-active metals sat where planned. The route could make probes whose mix is set by the DNA code itself.
pmc-13328364:
Sharmake Gaiye Bashir and a large team review artificial intelligence for forecasting pregnancy complications in a 2026 article. Models now predict preeclampsia, preterm birth, gestational diabetes, and growth restriction, yet reported accuracy swings widely, with AUC values from about 0.73 to 0.97 across studies. The authors focus on bias and the road to clinic.

Eight bias routes are named, from sampling and measurement bias to deployment and access bias, each able to warp performance and widen gaps in maternal care, above all in poorer countries. Outside validation, real impact trials, and cost studies remain scarce, and rules for accountability are still forming. Careful bias control must precede bedside use, they argue.
pmc-13328464:
Julie Toby Thomas and co-authors test saliva markers in prediabetes with gum disease in a 2026 study. Eighty-four adults aged 25 to 55 were split into four groups crossing prediabetes and periodontitis status, and saliva was assayed for three molecules: total MMP-8, adiponectin, and resistin. Clinical, body, and metabolic measures accompanied the sampling.

Total MMP-8 ran highest in prediabetic patients with periodontitis, while adiponectin ran lower in prediabetic groups than in healthy controls, and MMP-8 rose alongside body mass, HbA1c, pocket depth, and attachment loss. A combined profile separated the groups in pattern analysis. A spit test joining metabolic and gum signals could flag patients needing joint medical and dental care.
pmc-13329564:
Robert Lundberg and co-authors detail a method for gathering airborne chemicals over time in a 2026 article. Metal discs coated with sorbent collect volatile compounds, which are then moved onto a fibre for gas chromatography and mass checks. Steps cover disc making, cleaning, exposure, heating, and transfer in a repeatable routine.

Each disc of 3.6 cm held about 0.2 g of sorbent, and sampling lasted 60 minutes in the described setup. Across standard tests, discs gave larger signals than direct fibre sampling for most compounds, though very volatile ones such as acetone gave lower signals. The authors explain the pattern with a model that weighs trapped mass against transfer success. The routine uses no solvents and discs can be reused.
pmc-13329664:
Rena Conti and team weighed the United States public-private CARB-X drive against antibiotic resistance. Their 2026 study notes that building new antibiotics to replace dead ones is a top policy goal. CARB-X is the biggest world public-private drive chasing that goal, having pledged over one billion dollars through 2028 to innovators through competitive bids with money and tech backing. The team weighed all bids from the drive's start in 2016 through 2019, with results tracked through February 2024.

Seventy-seven bids won funds and 59 did not. Holding funding scores steady, funded projects were likelier to move ahead in clinic testing, while other results were positive but not firmly tied to CARB-X backing. No bids reached regulator approval or market launch. The team holds that CARB-X tracks with some middle-stage results, while later-stage results still need a look.
pmc-13330164:
Xinyuan Zhang and team studied Er:YAG laser debonding of cement-retained zirconia implant crowns. Their 2026 study notes that erbium laser debonding is used for natural tooth restorations and matters for implant repair. Yet research on its safety and how well it works remains thin. The team tested how crown and abutment type affect temperature rise and debonding time.

Four groups of eight crowns each, mixing titanium or zirconia abutments with 3Y or 4Y/5Y zirconia, were taken off with an Er:YAG laser, with heat measured at three points. All 32 came off. With the same abutment, peak temperature rise was lower in 3Y groups than in 4Y/5Y groups, though 3Y crowns took longer to remove. With the same crown kind, titanium groups showed lower temperature rise and shorter removal time, neither significant, and microscopy found no microcracks. Crown type, not abutment type, drives temperature rise and debonding time.
pmc-13330364:
Valeriia Fil and co-authors present a 2026 paper on fairer ways to grade computer programs that generate new drug-like molecules. Generators can dream up vast numbers of compounds, but common grades reward mere validity and novelty. The real goal is finding structures that could act in the body, and those grades miss it.

Their new scores judge a generator by the scaffolds, the core frames of molecules, that it can recover or supply. One score tracks recovery of known active frames left out of training, and others track the range of frames produced. They graded four known generators with the scores and released the tools openly for drug library design.
pmc-13331764:
Thomas W Kuhn offers a 2026 narrative review of ambient scribe tools, the software that drafts clinic notes from spoken visits. Kuhn stresses that a draft note is not a direct record of the visit. It comes from a staged process in which sound is captured, turned into digital data, rendered as text, and reshaped into a note.

The review searched PubMed, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv, Google Scholar, and other sources for work from November 2025 through May 2026. It turns that technical account into hands-on guidance and weighs privacy, consent, remote transfer of data, and legal risk. Its core advice is the 3C approach: choose wisely before the visit, capture with care during it, and check the draft closely after. The clinician stays responsible for the final note.
pmc-13332264:
Alizée Gerard and colleagues describe a 2026 cat case in which a stone lodged deep in a lung airway needed open surgery to remove. A 3-year-old spayed domestic shorthair arrived with sudden cough and breathing difficulty. Chest X-rays showed a dense object in the right caudal main bronchus. Attempts to pull it out with a flexible scope failed, as the object slid further down into the lobe bronchus, beyond the scope's reach.

Surgeons then opened the chest through the fifth rib space on the right and cut directly into the bronchus to retrieve the small stone. The airway was closed in a single layer with simple interrupted monofilament stitches. Pain relief, antibiotics, and restricted activity followed, and recovery was smooth. By day fifteen, signs had cleared and the cat was in good general shape. The case shows when direct bronchotomy beats repeated scope attempts.
pmc-13333364:
Amr El-Nile and co-authors tested a trace mineral cocktail in drinking water for growing rabbits in a 2026 feeding study, asking whether it improves organ health, immunity, antioxidant defenses, and gut bacteria. Minerals such as iron, zinc, and copper run many enzymes, and shortfalls quietly cap farm animal performance.

Seventy-two seven-week-old male V-line rabbits were split into four groups of 18: plain water or water carrying the mineral mix at 0.5, 1.0, or 1.5 mL per liter. At the two higher doses, the liver enzyme alkaline phosphatase rose while alanine aminotransferase fell, hinting at friendlier liver readings, and blood antioxidant capacity increased across treated groups. Total gut bacterial counts dropped with supplementation, and the top dose cut E. coli counts below every other group. The authors conclude the mix benefits liver and kidney markers, antioxidant and immune status, and gut balance, most clearly at 1 and 1.5 mL per liter.
pmc-13333764:
Hamid Ullah, Muhammad Adil, and Chong Zhang wrote a 2026 lab study of Fingerhuthia africana, a perennial grass used in folk healing for gut disorders and wound care. Its chemistry and safety had barely been studied.

Gas chromatography with mass spectrometry profiled the methanol extract and found 35 metabolites, while atomic absorption measured minerals such as calcium at 12.4 mg per gram and potassium at 9.8 mg per gram in the plant matter. The extract scavenged DPPH radicals in step with dose, reaching 79.5 percent at the top strength tested. A comet assay in human white blood cells probed gene damage risk, and a charcoal meal test in mice measured effects on gut transit. The package gives this folk remedy its first broad chemical and safety profile.
pmc-13333964:
Ramzan leads a large team finding hearing loss genes in Pakistani families, in work from twenty twenty-six. Recessive hearing loss of moderate to severe degree links to at least twenty-seven known genes. Families where parents are related, common in Pakistan, are powerful for finding such variants.

Fifty-four consanguineous families were ascertained for genetic study. Both known and novel variants were identified, the title reports. Each solved family gains a precise diagnosis, recurrence risk figures, and carrier testing options. The work also expands the global catalog of hearing loss variants, which is still biased toward European ancestry samples.
pmc-13334064:
Derick Rodriguez-Reyes and colleagues review 2026 decision fatigue in the senior surgeon across a surgery day. Decision fatigue means growing worsening in choice quality from the piled-up mental burden of many choices. Senior surgeons navigate hundreds of micro-choices daily, covering instrument choice, tissue handling, and real-time changes in surgical approach. Surprise surgery findings demanding immediate adaptive thinking also draw on finite neural resources.

The review pulls together evidence on neural workings behind surgeon decision fatigue, with emphasis on prefrontal cortex drain, neurotransmitter shifts, and metabolic limits. It sorts operative micro-choices by type: big-picture or tactical, sense-based or idea-based, time-critical or slow, and undoable or one-way. Evidence shows fatigue shows in measurable performance drops detailed in the full paper. The work offers a frame for scheduling, support, and safety nets against late-day decision erosion.
pmc-13336364:
Keyi Chen and co-authors found a new antibiotic candidate by predicting it from a genome and then building it in the lab in a 2026 natural products study. Most microbes resist culturing and many antibiotic genes stay silent, so the team used a synthetic gene-data approach instead of growing the producer.

A gene cluster from Rhodococcus erythropolis D-1 pointed to a nonribosomal peptide scaffold, which the chemists built and refined through four rounds of structure-activity work, yielding 37 analogs. One, ZURJC28, killed multiple Gram-positive bacteria, among them two drug-resistant strains. Mechanism studies and metabolomics showed it disrupts membranes rich in phosphatidylglycerol, wrecking cell chemistry along the way. The pipeline shows genome mining plus lab building can surface antibiotics that fermentation never reveals.
pmc-13336564:
Lina Gao and co-authors link copper imbalance to depression in a 2026 study spanning patients and stressed mice. Copper was high in the blood of people with major depression and in a mood-related brain area of the mice. Inside star-shaped support cells called astrocytes, the protein FDX1 rose as copper built up.

Extra FDX1 in astrocytes tracked with fewer, simpler support cells, weaker calcium signals, and faulty excitatory connections between neurons. Targeted cell changes and recordings showed FDX1 carried much of the harm. Exercise in mice restored copper balance, calmed FDX1, and eased depression-like behavior. The work names a cell-level path that lifestyle steps might help correct.
pmc-13336764:
Qiaoli Wu and colleagues map how a brain lymphoma feeds in a 2026 single-cell study. Primary central nervous system lymphoma grows in a setting low in oxygen and short on glucose in spinal fluid. Starved of glucose, tumor cells instead leaned on fructose, imported through a carrier called SLC2A5.

Low oxygen also switched on that carrier in macrophages that support the tumor, through a HIF-driven route. Blocking fructose uptake, by gene or drug means, sharply slowed lymphoma growth in lab and animal tests. Because both tumor cells and their helper macrophages share the habit, fructose handling stands out as a weak point worth targeting in this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13336864:
Abin Nas Nalakath and a large team test an ultrathin chiral layer for spin-selective electronics in a 2026 study. When electrons pass through twisted molecules, their spin tends to align with the twist, an effect called chiral-induced spin selectivity. Most test systems use long, fragile biomolecules, so the team tried a small, sturdy acid instead.

Calcium stood out, boosting both reactions, with the best transfer efficiency at middle-range doses. Molecular dynamics movies showed why: the ion barely moves the overall shape of the enzyme but stiffens the loops around its working pocket, seating the reacting parts more precisely. Binding energy checks backed the picture. The authors offer calcium dosing as a cheap lever for greener sugar chemistry.
pmc-13377864:
Yaniv Grosskopf and co-authors give a spare math tale for trauma stress in a 2026 paper. Just one to two in ten folk struck by trauma stay ill for long, while the rest heal at a spread of paces. Why that split falls was not clear in past frames.

Their tale has one driver that feeds its own growth, held by a clear-out pull. One trait, grit, sets who tips to the ill state. At mid grit, heal times spread wide, which fits true logs from many groups. Care must pass a bar to hold, the sums say. Spare tales can still guide who gets what care, and when.
pmc-13379764:
Krzysztof Kaczmarek and colleagues report a 2026 case where a heart device stopped working well and heart failure worsened as a result. The device, called cardiac contractility modulation, sends gentle signals that strengthen the heartbeat without using extra oxygen. It suits patients who cannot have another common device therapy.

Their patient, a 58-year-old man with a weak, enlarged heart, improved greatly after the device was fitted. Years later he declined, and checks showed the device was delivering its signals only sometimes. Surgery found worn insulation on all three leads. Replacing the leads restored the therapy, and his exercise ability and heart function improved again over long-term follow-up.
pmc-13379864:
Loukas Rentifis and co-authors report a 2026 study of bacteria growing on bile duct stents placed before major pancreas surgery. Such stents drain bile to reduce complications, but germs can colonise them and affect later care. Records covered 313 patients who had the surgery for tumours between 2010 and 2022.

Of 171 patients who had stents, 115 stents were tested for germs. Most tested positive, with gut-type bacteria most common and fungi found in over a third of samples. Some bacteria resisted many antibiotics. Longer waits between stent placement and surgery were linked with positive cultures. The findings matter for choosing preventive antibiotics around surgery.
pmc-13380664:
Ala Bala Babiker Abdalla and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of a blood test used to diagnose acute heart failure in emergency departments. Breathlessness in the emergency room has many causes, and sorting them quickly is hard. The test measures a marker called NT-proBNP, which rises when the heart is stretched.

Following standard review guidance, the authors searched four databases for studies from 2021 to 2026 in adults with suspected heart failure. Eight studies were included, and their quality was assessed with a standard tool. A low marker level proved strong for ruling the condition out across the prospective studies. The review also examines which cut-off levels work best and how performance varies between patient groups.
pmc-13382764:
Shoushun Chen and co-authors review how solid-state NMR helps reveal the inner structure of metal-organic frameworks in a 2027 article. These porous crystals, built from metal nodes and organic links, now number in huge variety and serve many uses. Their range also makes it hard to link local structure to how a material behaves.

The review covers probes of metal centers and linkers, plus studies of guest molecules held inside the pores. New hardware and pulse methods that sharpen what the technique can show receive close attention. For labs designing frameworks for real use, the piece maps where NMR can guide choices and where limits still remain.
pmc-13384564:
Emine Teke Öner, Melis Irmak Aydın, Merve Nida Dursunoğlu, and Ayşe Bayrakçeken present a 2026 study of catalyst supports for fuel cells that run on hydrogen. The cells need platinum particles spread on a support to speed their reactions. A foam like form of graphene offers a large, light scaffold for those particles.

The team made the catalysts by two routes. One mixed the graphene foam with carbon black in set ratios, then added platinum with microwave heating. The other made platinum on carbon black first, then grew the foam in with hot water treatment. They checked the products with several tools and tested how well each worked in a cell.
pmc-13386564:
Khalil Kargar Shooroki and colleagues report wrist masses that first revealed systemic amyloidosis in a 2026 case report. A 75-year-old man had swelling at both wrists with weak, numb hands and a history of repeated carpal tunnel syndrome. MRI showed the bilateral masses behind the returning symptoms.

Surgery removed the masses, and tissue testing confirmed amyloid deposits of the wild-type transthyretin kind. He stayed free of symptoms through four years of follow-up, the authors report. The case argues for biopsy and body-wide checks when wrist masses accompany repeating carpal tunnel problems.
pmc-13386964:
Germán Ortuño-Hernández's team hunted for the genetic regions behind healthy compounds in apricot fruit, working with two crosses that shared the parent variety Currot. They tracked flavonoids, phenolic acids, and glycosides. These plant chemicals link to antioxidant activity, flavour, and aroma. High-detail chemical profiling of parents and seedlings mapped them.

Mapping turned up linked regions for epicatechin on one chromosome group, and for myricitrin and rutin on another. Vanilloyl glucose linked to a third group, while one glycoside showed a scattered pattern across several groups. Breeders could use these markers to select seedlings richer in the valued compounds, aiming for apricots with stronger nutritional and eating quality.
pmc-13387664:
Hussein and coauthors screen for irritable bowel in diabetes patients in Jeddah. Type 2 diabetes is a major health issue in Saudi Arabia. Irritable bowel is the most often diagnosed gut disorder. Overlap of the two may add burden for patients.

The study held 245 diabetes patients at private clinics. A survey form logged personal and diabetes facts. It also held bowel screening and family history items. Just over 37 percent screened as probable bowel cases. A small share, just over one percent, were classed as likely to have it. Traits that tracked with bowel signs were weighed. Joint screening may help clinics plan gut care.
pmc-13388364:
Casper Grønlund and six co-authors track the long-run money and welfare costs of Ménière disease in Denmark. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The disease affects the inner ear and can drive fits of vertigo and hearing loss. They match each patient with like controls and follow both groups for years around the first hospital record.

Health costs were higher for patients, with a peak in the year of diagnosis. Pay fell and stayed lower than for controls. More patients moved to sickness benefits, disability pension, and flexible job schemes over time. The study shows a heavy, lasting load on both the health system and the lives of patients.
pmc-13389464:
S. P. Zimmerman's team asked how seven different gene fusions can cause the same childhood muscle cancer, fusion-positive rhabdomyosarcoma. All seven share a PAX3 or PAX7 DNA-binding head fused to different partners, yet they drive a common disease.

The fusions proved functionally interchangeable, binding overlapping genes through a shared protein network the team calls the common interactome, which even contained a newly found translocation partner. Knocking out interactome members hurt the cancer. Screening flagged thymidylate synthase as a shared weakness, with the antifolate pralatrexate suppressing growth across all seven fusions, in cell lines and a patient-derived graft.
pmc-13390364:
Wei Wang's team used shape and working MRI to tell apart the brain marks of lung disease grade from those of mental damage in chronic blocking lung disease. Thirty-three patients with mild mental damage, thirty cognitively normal patients, and thirty-four healthy controls underwent multi-mode scanning.

All patients shared sense-move network shrinking and weaker links that tracked disease length and set patients apart from controls. The impaired subgroup alone showed focal deep-brain wasting and visual-network split. These separated the two patient groups well and tracked with Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores, pointing to own brain markers for each side.
pmc-13390464:
Hongmei Dai and co-authors compare surgery safety across three treatment plans for cancer at the stomach-esophagus junction, in a research paper from 2026. Patients may go straight to surgery, or get chemotherapy first, or get chemo plus radiation first. Proof on which path is safest around surgery has been thin.

The study followed 276 patients treated at one Beijing cancer center from 2012 to 2018. After weighting to balance patient mix, the chemo-radiation group had far more post-surgery complications than the other two groups. Major complications also ran higher on that path. The results can help teams weigh tumor control gains against surgical risk.
pmc-13391664:
Marie Gudmundsson and colleagues build, in 2026, a grounded theory of how people using mental health services experience recovery through a nature-based programme. Nature-based interventions support recovery-oriented care, yet how users themselves live the recovery process inside them was little known.

Twenty participants took part in a newly developed programme at a farm-based rehabilitation centre, including horse-assisted therapy in groups. In-depth interviews, gathered by purposeful sampling, were analysed with constructivist grounded theory into an account the authors frame as an embodied journey. Mental health practitioners gain a user-voiced process model that can shape how farm and nature programmes are designed and paced.
pmc-13391964:
Hasan Alchalabi and colleagues pool, in 2026, evidence on shrinking the prostate's blood supply before shaving it from inside for men with very large glands. Large-volume benign prostate enlargement makes transurethral resection harder, with more bleeding, longer operations, and more complications.

The review pools the two paths. One path blocks gland blood flow first, then resects. The other resects at once. The pooled data cover time in theatre, blood loss, and harm rates. Urologists gain a joint estimate of a key trade. Does the extra step pay for itself in a smoother, safer cut? The doubt is greatest for the largest glands.
pmc-13392664:
Nuraini Nuraini and colleagues fermented cassava peel with an oyster mushroom fungus, then fed the product to broiler chickens at five rates up to a fifth of the diet. Raw cassava peel is a cheap farm residue but a poor feed, and fermentation was meant to upgrade it. The trial ran thirty-five days and tracked growth, carcass traits, gut shape and germs, blood fats, and meat quality.

Birds on fermented peel grew faster and heavier, most clearly at the highest rate, without eating more or wasting feed. Carcass share rose, the thymus immune organ grew, gut villi lengthened, harmful Escherichia coli fell while friendly lactic bacteria rose, and blood fats shifted in a healthier direction. Meat carried more of the prized omega fatty acids, though its cholesterol stayed put. The authors rate fermented peel as a working functional feed.
pmc-13392764:
Mohammad Jamir Ahemad's team built a room-heat CH2O sensor from a tungsten oxide and carrying metal-organic system layered build, aimed at trace indoor pollution that is cancer-causing even at low levels. Single sensor chips had struggled to combine ultra-low spotting with focus at ambient heat.

Edge orbital mixing between tungsten and oxygen orbitals tuned electronic structure and charge transport, with CH2O preferring phenol oxygen sites and oxygen-gap sites. The sensor reached about forty-eight parts per billion spotting, with fast response and recovery, minimal wander, and strong focus in mixed gases.
pmc-13393064:
Mohammed Mosharraf Hossain Khandaker and four colleagues describe a 60-year-old man who developed clots in the brain's venous drainage channels just after finishing treatment for pneumococcal meningitis. The infection itself had settled on two weeks of intravenous ceftriaxone, with blood tests back to normal and no weakness or focal signs. A lasting headache and neck stiffness refused to fit that tidy recovery.

Fresh brain imaging explained the mismatch: widespread cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, a rare but known complication most often tied to this meningitis germ. Blood-thinning treatment cleared the clots on later scans, although headaches hung on even after the channels reopened. The authors warn that a headache outlasting meningitis recovery should trigger venous imaging, not calm words.
pmc-13393264:
Donghyeon Han leads a eighteen-author team building probabilistic bits, hardware elements that flicker randomly between zero and one, from magnetic trilayers steered by two crossing spin currents. Probabilistic computing uses such flickering bits to attack hard problems with some of the flavour of quantum machines but without extreme cooling. Earlier versions relied on tiny magnets whose randomness swung wildly with temperature and size.

The new device stacks iron, titanium, and a cobalt alloy so that paired spin currents with perpendicular twists set the switching odds of the top magnetic layer. Odds can be dialled by a magnetic field or by the driving current itself, giving controlled randomness in a micron-sized, room-friendly device. The team wired the bits into a reversible logic gate and a small stochastic neural network, reporting gains in energy and area over prior designs.
pmc-13393664:
Tianyi Yang and nine colleagues restored the tumour suppressor STAG2 in human cancer cells and watched the genome's three-dimensional loops shrink rapidly across the board. STAG2, part of the cohesin ring that folds chromosomes, is lost in many cancers including bladder tumours, brain tumours, and leukaemias, yet how its loss drives cancer has stayed murky. Acute reconstitution offered a clean before-and-after view.

Despite the global loop change, few genes changed expression early, and most of those switched on. One gene, encoding the growth-suppressing matrix protein fibulin-3, rose in every model. The most robust responders sat inside intense loops whose anchors and strength did not budge, a puzzle the authors note. They propose that losing STAG2 removes a size limit on loops, widening chromatin contacts until the tumour-suppressive programme can no longer hold.
pmc-13393864:
Reza Khademi and Saeed Shoar review whether two diabetes drug families should be combined in heart failure, a major harm of type 2 diabetes. The families work differently: SGLT2 inhibitors act through fluid, pressure, and kidney pathways, while GLP-1 receptor agonists work through metabolism, inflammation, and artery protection. That contrast makes pairing them appealing on paper.

The evidence splits by family. SGLT2 inhibitors reliably cut heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death across the pumping-strength spectrum, by roughly a third. GLP-1 drugs trim hospitalisation only modestly while excelling against atherosclerotic events and weight. Meta-analyses and routine-care data hint at additive benefit from combining, with no major safety excess beyond known class effects, but almost none of it comes from dedicated heart failure trials. The authors hold the combination plausible yet unproven.
pmc-13394064:
Wang and colleagues report, in 2026, a mouse model carrying a working sheep immune system, built to study diseases that affect sheep but not ordinary lab mice. They transplanted spleen lymphocytes from sheep into severely immunodeficient NBSGW mice, then checked where the sheep cells settled and how long they survived. Finally, they infected the reconstituted mice with Brucella melitensis, the bacterium behind brucellosis, a serious livestock and human disease.

Sheep immune cells, including CD4 and CD8 T cells, remained detectable in the mice's blood for up to 13 weeks after transplant. The cells also populated the spleen, liver, and bone marrow of the recipient animals. After Brucella infection, the mice developed characteristic tissue damage and bacterial colonization, showing the model can host a real sheep pathogen. The authors offer the system as a platform for studying sheep diseases and testing prevention strategies, while noting the rebuilt immune system remains incomplete.
pmc-13394464:
Marlus S. Pedrosa leads a 2026 study of gut bacteria that worsen Crohn's disease, a chronic bowel illness. One group of E. coli makes a compound named yersiniabactin, which unsettles iron balance in immune cells. That switch turns on a protein, HIF-1 alpha, tied to scarring of the bowel wall. The team asked whether the cells must burn sugar fast for the switch to work.

Blocking sugar use cut the signal path that builds the protein and kept it out of the cell core. Extra bacteria alone did not explain the effect. The authors suggest that drugs which slow sugar use could curb scarring. Such drugs would target the host cells, not the germs.
pmc-13394664:
B. Ryan Davis and colleagues compare, in 2026, three ways of cycling to learn how each loads one leg. Twelve active adults rode with both legs, with one leg, and with one leg doing most work while the other helped lightly. Each style was tried at three set power levels. The team tracked breath gases, leg blood flow, and felt effort.

The mixed style burned more sugar and drew more leg blood flow than two-leg riding. It still stayed below pure one-leg riding on both counts. Felt effort matched two-leg riding at each level. The authors suggest the mixed style could stress one leg more during rehab without taxing the whole body.
pmc-13394764:
Yanxia Gao and colleagues study, in 2026, a tiny RNA that may flag kidney damage from diabetes early. The RNA, named miR-224-5p, runs high in the blood of patients with diabetic kidney disease. The team measured it in patients and compared levels with later kidney outcomes. Cell tests then probed how the RNA harms the filter cells of the kidney.

High levels marked patients more likely to lose kidney function over two years. The RNA targets a guard gene named PTEN, and easing the RNA let that guard recover. Blocking the guard wiped out the gain. The authors urge wider tests before clinic use, since the work is early and the patient pool was small.
pmc-13394864:
Martin Ruddock and co-authors review, in 2026, how patients use digital self-care tools for asthma and COPD. Such tools promise feedback and support for daily lung care. The team screened studies that reported who patients were, health outcomes, and hard usage counts. Twenty-seven studies passed all screens. Patient and public panels helped read the findings.

Only four usage measures could be compared fairly across tools. Studies reported two usage measures on average, which limits fair judging. Age, sex, and illness severity were the traits most often logged. Layered hardships, such as low income plus poor access, were rarely traced. The authors urge fuller reporting so tools serve all patients.
pmc-13395064:
Honggang Shen and co-authors review, in 2026, how tiny tech could make light-based gene control work in cancer care. Optogenetics uses light to switch cell behaviour with fine timing and aim. Two walls block clinic use: tools reach tumours poorly, and light fades fast in tissue. Nano carriers can ferry the tools, and nano materials can shift light to deeper forms.

The blend also allows living drugs, such as tuned immune cells and bacteria that attack tumours under light. Early results in animals look strong. Safety over years, immune reactions, and exact light dosing still worry the field. The authors call for joint work across materials, protein design, and AI.
pmc-13395964:
Yeonwoo Kim and colleagues used a long-running United States survey to ask whether hard events in adult life raise the chance of later pain among older people. Their 2026 analysis drew on the Health and Retirement Study, which follows adults aged 50 and older.

The sample held 6,724 people who reported no pain in the prior ten years, and pain was tracked over six years. Those who had lived through two or more adult traumatic events faced a higher risk of new pain, with an odds ratio of 1.34, even after childhood trauma and health factors were counted. One event alone showed no clear link, so repeated adult trauma stood out.
pmc-13396064:
Cheng and co-authors analyze, in 2026, real-world use of botulinum toxin type A injections for cervical dystonia, a painful neck muscle disorder, in United States insurance claims. From the Optum Clinformatics database covering 2016 to 2024, they identified 1,756 adults starting toxin therapy with at least a year of enrollment before and after. The study compared the three marketed toxins on switching rates, health care use, and costs over the first year and beyond.

OnabotulinumtoxinA dominated practice, starting 88.6 percent of patients, against 9.3 percent for incobotulinumtoxinA and 2.2 percent for abobotulinumtoxinA in the cohort. Switching within the first year was comparable between the two main products. Over the full follow-up, however, only 2.6 percent of onabotulinumtoxinA starters ever switched, versus 6.8 percent of incobotulinumtoxinA starters, a significant difference. pmc-13396364:

Tests showed HELZ binds BRCA2 directly and works as an unwinding enzyme specific to these knots. BRCA2 boosts HELZ activity and brings it to R-loops at DNA breaks, clearing the way for the end trimming that homologous recombination repair requires, especially in busy gene regions. The authors also show HELZ matters most in cancers where heavy gene activity creates many such knots.
pmc-13396664:
Ashton Williamson and others score language AIs at pulling bone surgery steps from op notes in a 2026 study. Hand coding of op notes is slow, dear, and patchy, yet these notes hold key facts for surgery files and study.

Fourteen free and paid AI models were tried cold on 800 true op notes, marked by a bone surgeon and a clerk across 74 step kinds. AI reads were scored for rightness, with size, thought, and prompt effects probed. Across models, AIs beat old baselines time and again, backing auto file growth for surgery study.
pmc-13396864:
Raffaele Falsaperla and co-authors write to the editors in 2026 about a review by Thompson and colleagues on seizure medicines for newborns. The review framed a dilemma with a classical image: drugs that boost the calming signal GABA might backfire in the newborn brain, yet leaving seizures untreated harms that same brain.

The letter writers agree the dilemma is real. In immature brains, chloride handling differs, so switching on GABA receptors can excite rather than calm nerve cells. They push back, though, on letting the metaphor settle practice, and argue the evidence deserves a more careful weighing before clinicians either lean on these drugs or abandon them in neonatal units.
pmc-13397464:
The EFSA Panel on Nutrition, Novel Foods and Food Allergens delivered a 2026 safety opinion on roasted sacha inchi seeds, a traditional Peruvian food proposed for sale in the European Union. The seeds, from the plant Plukenetia volubilis, have been eaten in Peru for more than 25 years.

Under the European Union's novel food law, long use abroad counts toward safety, but an earlier notification of the seeds had stalled over uncertainty about alkaloids, plant chemicals that can be toxic. The panel weighed the new evidence on composition and consumption to judge whether whole roasted seeds can be sold as a snack food. Its opinion guides the Commission's decision.
pmc-13397764:
Subham Preetam and others review gut bug roles in cancer tuning in a 2026 paper. Gut bugs deeply affect host body work, defenses, and disease weakness, with growing proof tying them to cancer start, growth, and therapy response.

Bug imbalance and bug-made outputs drive cancer start through lining signals, immune control, and whole-body swelling, via paths including NF-kB, STAT3, Wnt, and inflammasome firing. Patterns track with risk and growth across colon, gastric, liver, breast, female, and lung cancers, and shape chemo, radio, and immuno results. The review gauges gut-bug-aimed therapy plans.
pmc-13398164:
Lasya P Marla and co-authors compare results when forehead sinus fractures are repaired by plastic surgeons versus ear, nose and throat surgeons. Their 2026 study uses the national ACS NSQIP surgical database. The frontal sinus sits between two specialties' turf, and whether the operating surgeon's field shapes outcomes had not been tallied at national scale.

In all, 111 patients were analysed, 85.6 percent of them male, with a mean age near 30 years across the group. Ear, nose and throat surgeons treated 70 patients (63.1 percent) and plastic surgeons treated 41 in the series. Median operating time ran 131 minutes for the first group against 115 minutes for the second, with complications and patient mixes compared by standard tests.
pmc-13398664:
Davide Benedetto Tiz, Massimo Catania and David C Magri review molecules that answer questions with white light. Their 2026 survey covers white-light emitting materials, prized for displays and lighting because their glow spans 380 to 700 nm of the spectrum. Making one molecule shine white defies the usual rule that emission comes from the lowest excited state, so clever photophysics must bend it.

Designs exploiting proton transfer, twisted charge transfer, vibration-born emission and aggregation effects are catalogued. Rarest of all are sensors that emit white light while running logic, answering two or more chemical inputs like a tiny gate. The review teaches the Boolean basics alongside the chemistry, aiming to grow this small but striking field.
pmc-13398764:
Matteo Arnaudi and team interpreted DNA polymerase variants at the structural level for two repair enzymes, POLE and POLD1. Their 2026 work addresses genetic changes that can alter protein stability, catalytic action, DNA binding, and partner links. Variant reading matters in clinics, yet many reported changes lack a clear structural explanation.

Using the MAVISp framework and molecular dynamics, the team analyzed over 60,000 missense variants and joined folding and binding energy changes with effects near active and phosphorylation sites. Their catalog classified 364 variants of uncertain significance as supporting pathogenicity and 323 as supporting benign status under medical genetics rules. They also flagged variants that tilt catalytic residues or weaken DNA binding. The resource aids future variant classification, pending lab proof.
pmc-13398964:
Tâmara Taynah Medeiros da Silva and eight co-authors reviewed care for skin damage caused by radiation therapy in head and neck cancer, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. The damage, called radiodermatitis, ranges from redness to open sores. It is common in this treatment and can force breaks in therapy.

The team searched eight databases and kept a final set of studies spanning more than a decade. Trials were the most common design, and standard grading scales were widely used. Tested options included medicated creams, light-based therapy, and various dressings. China produced the most studies. The authors judge the evidence too thin and uneven to endorse or reject any single product for wide use.
pmc-13400164:
Constanza Rodriguez and colleagues, with senior author Rosa Nguyen, show that a targeted radioactive drug can supercharge CAR T cell therapy against neuroblastoma, in a 2026 preclinical study. The radiopharmaceutical, copper-67 attached to LLP2A, homes to the VLA-4 integrin found on neuroblastoma. It delivers a short-range beta radiation dose over about two and a half days, timed to fade before the engineered T cells arrive.

In radiation-sensitive tumors, the drug killed cancer cells directly and fired up immune pathways, notably TNF-alpha signaling, that activated the T cells in a paracrine relay. In radiation-resistant tumors, killing was minimal, but the radiation remodeled the myeloid compartment of the tumor's surroundings. It fostered niches where cytotoxic CAR T cells, both CD8 and CD4 types bearing granzyme B, could gather and work. The authors present such preconditioning as a general strategy for solid-tumor cell therapy.
pmc-13400264:
Alesha Salby and colleagues report a 2026 case of a very large aneurysm, a weak bulging spot, in the inferior mesenteric artery of a 65-year-old man. The man came in with rectal bleeding and had several other health problems. Scans showed the bulge was 7 cm wide and linked to an abnormal join between an artery and a vein.

Doctors treated him through the blood vessels rather than with open surgery. They fed coils into the bulge, and final imaging showed both the aneurysm and the abnormal join fully blocked. The authors note that which problem came first is unclear, but coil treatment worked well for a high-risk patient.
pmc-13400464:
Brennan Delattre and colleagues introduce, in 2026, a new game task for studying how young people learn whom to trust. Adolescence is a key period for building social skills. Classic trust games measure choices but say little about how players react when partners vary in generosity.

Their Social Learning-Generosity task rebuilds the multi-round trust game with set gain, loss and mixed conditions, plus more realistic features. In a single online session, UK participants aged 18 to 24 played it and rated its acceptability. Play shifted with self-reported trust and with gender, much like older versions. The added generosity settings, the authors argue, make the task sharper for mental health research.
pmc-13400864:
Samuel Béliard and colleagues compare, in 2026, vein health in adults who do high-impact versus low-impact exercise, questioning advice that sports like running harm leg veins. Guidance has often favored cycling and swimming while warning against running and team sports, based more on tradition than proof. Varicose veins and faulty valves were the concern.

Within a sports cohort, 161 adults who met activity guidelines for at least six months had clinical and ultrasound examinations. Fifty-three did low-impact and 108 high-impact activities. Varicose vein prevalence did not differ significantly between groups, at about fifteen percent in the low-impact group. Symptoms, disease stage and vein diameters were also compared across the groups.
pmc-13401164:
Xuyong Chen and co-authors published a 2026 multicentre cohort study asking whether the total bilirubin-to-albumin ratio, a simple blood measure, predicts death in critically ill patients with gastrointestinal bleeding. The ratio reflects liver dysfunction and body-wide inflammation, but its value in bleeding patients was unclear.

Drawing on the MIMIC-IV database, with outside validation in the eICU database, the study covered 1,627 adults. Patients who died had worse organ function and much higher ratio values, and the ratio stayed linked to 28-day mortality after full adjustment in Cox models. The authors built a prediction nomogram, a scoring chart, using Boruta-selected variables and checked it with ROC curves, calibration, and decision curve analysis.
pmc-13401264:
Runhua Zhou and co-authors wrote a 2026 cost-effectiveness study comparing two operations for middle-aged patients whose knees bow inward from osteoarthritis. One is open-wedge high tibial osteotomy, which preserves the joint. The other is total knee replacement. Which strategy pays off over the long term has been debated.

Registry data from three Chinese university hospitals covered 825 patients aged 45 to 65 treated between 2005 and 2015, with follow-up through 2025. The team tracked pain and function scores, quality-of-life utilities, range of motion, leg alignment, muscle strength. Total health care costs from a societal angle, including lost productivity. Costs and results were discounted at 3 percent yearly, and 1,000 bootstrap simulations fed cost-effectiveness ratios judged against China's 2024 income-based willingness-to-pay range.
pmc-13401564:
Akira Imai, Patrice Revol, and Yves Rossetti revisit a touch illusion first reported by Cormack in 1973. Their 2026 experiment studies how the two hands conspire to distort felt size. When a disk held in one hand is turned end over end by the other, the turning hand feels the disk as longer than it is.

Twenty members rotated disks of 30 and 39 millimetres for one minute under three setups. One was ordinary two-handed use. In another, both hands worked through custom devices that separated holding from turning. In the third, one hand acted alone. The illusion reached Cormack's reported strength in the first two setups. With one hand only, the turning hand's illusion shrank to about a quarter of that size. The holding hand felt almost none, though recombining the one-hand values predicted a moderate illusion growing over time.
pmc-13402264:
Philip Stather and colleagues worked out, on cadaver models, how to place robot ports and control arteries for a groin bypass using the da Vinci Single Port system. Groin cuts carry high infection risk, so moving the entry point under the skin of the thigh could spare the wound. Earlier cadaver work had flagged two weak points: seeing the vessels well and clamping them safely.

Repeated sessions tested port spots across the thigh. One spot, on the front of the thigh and set 5 centimeters below the femoral split, gave a clear view of the femoral triangle. It also stopped the robot arms clashing with the leg and allowed vessel repair in every run. Clamping through the skin under robot vision worked as the main control method, with slings and balloon control as backups. The team offers the setup as groundwork for first patient trials.
pmc-13403164:
Andrea CALDERONE and colleagues profile long-term vulnerability in adults who made it home after severe traumatic brain injury, asking which early traits predict struggle five years on. Their secondary analysis drew 2835 adults who were living at home one year after injury, with linked five-year data. A latent class model sorted people by rehospitalization, depression and anxiety scores, and life satisfaction at year five.

Two profiles emerged: a lower-vulnerability majority of 2361 people and a multidomain vulnerability group of 474 marked by more symptoms, lower satisfaction, more rehospitalization, and worse functioning, participation, and work status. Better one-year global outcome protected against the vulnerable profile; female sex, preinjury illicit drug use, and living alone raised the odds. The authors argue discharge home should start surveillance, not end it.
pmc-13403464:
Hong Zeng and co-authors reviewed 2026 records from 9,372 fertility cycles to ask how long hormone stimulation should run. Clinics can adjust the number of stimulation days in these egg-growth cycles. The records came from one hospital and used fresh embryo transfer.

Egg maturity rose with each extra day up to about day nine, then leveled off. A span of eight to ten days tied to the best rates of pregnancy and live birth. Very low responders showed no clear link at all. The team favors plans that adapt to how each patient responds, rather than fixed day counts for all.
pmc-13403564:
Di Lu, Mingming Zhao, and Feng Yin recounted in 2026 a man with Parkinson's disease whose brain stimulator battery would not charge well. The 54-year-old also walked with growing unsteadiness. Device checks read normal, which made the charging fault hard to explain.

A chest X-ray showed the implanted pulse unit had flipped over inside its pocket under the skin. That turn had not appeared on older images. Surgeons opened the pocket, set the unit right, and charging worked well again. The case reminds clinics to picture the hardware when charging fails yet electronic checks pass.
pmc-13404564:
Osamah Al-qershi and team present AutoCumulus, an auto breast density gauge learned by artificial intelligence from semi-auto readings. Their 2026 work takes on mammographic density, a known breast cancer risk factor once gauged by varied quantitative, semi-auto, and auto methods. A steady auto gauge could lift risk prediction at screening scale.

Trained on mammograms from 9,057 women screened in the general population through the BRAIx program, the deep learning model matched human percent density gauges at 0.95. On a fresh dataset, AutoCumulus beat the LIBRA gauge on left-right breast agreement, at 0.95 versus 0.79, and on specificity at high sensitivity. The work offers a checked auto density tool for screening programs, while medical risk-model uptake still needs prospective testing.
pmc-13405064:
Laura Fertitta and co-authors standardise a way to measure skin tumours in mice bred to model neurofibromatosis type 1, in 2026 work. The tumours, called cutaneous neurofibromas, are common and burdensome in the human disease, and no drug is approved for them. Testing candidate drugs in mice needs measures that different labs can repeat.

Their mouse model switches off the Nf1 gene in Schwann cells, which also glow through a reporter so tumours can be tracked. The workflow counts tumours, measures glowing area and checks cell makeup under the microscope. Custom ImageJ scripts automate the analysis and matched manual scoring closely, with reproducibility reported as excellent.
pmc-13407064:
Na and colleagues built a machine learning model in 2026 to sort heart patients into risk groups before exercise training in cardiac rehabilitation, the supervised exercise care that follows heart disease. Risk sorting guides how hard each patient can train safely, but current rules differ between organizations. The team trained computer models to copy the risk labels that clinicians had already assigned.

The study used records from 1,163 patients at three hospitals and tested four methods, including logistic regression and random forests. The XGBoost method, a tree-based model that builds many small decision trees, matched clinician labels best, and accuracy rose further after a feature-selection step cut the data to key measures. Breathing efficiency during exercise, peak blood pressure, peak oxygen use, and body weight mattered most. The authors offer the model as decision support for safer, better-targeted exercise prescriptions.
pmc-13407664:
Marie-Soleil Dumont and co-authors count, in 2026, how often Quebec's mental health law sends people to emergency departments against their will. The P-38 Act lets police or crisis workers bring a person for assessment. The person must be judged a danger to self or others. How heavily the Act is used was poorly documented. The team reviewed five departments' records from 2020 and 2021.

Of 15,021 mental-health visits, 860, or 5.7 percent, involved the Act: roughly one visit in twenty. Those brought in were typically in early to middle adulthood, mostly arrived by ambulance, and nearly all had a recorded mental-health history, with material deprivation over-represented. Compared with voluntary patients, they faced far more restraint, preventive confinement, and hospitalisation. The authors urge stronger community crisis alternatives to coercion.
pmc-13408664:
Stéphane Sauvagère and co-authors review in 2026 what happens when hobbyist DNA databases, AI, and police work collide. Consumer ancestry testing has built databases holding tens of millions of genetic profiles. Police have begun, under set conditions, to search them for kin of unknown suspects. AI tools meanwhile help with kinship calls, mixture unravelling, and ranking leads.

The review ranges over six areas. They run from the state of forensic DNA methods to data oversight, split rules across countries, and the ethics of searching kin who never agreed to police use. Two points anchor the discussion. Family-tree and AI outputs should serve as leads, not as courtroom proof in themselves. Genetic data are also shared by nature across a family. French and European frameworks get close attention, and the authors close with advice on oversight.
pmc-13408764:
Yang Yuchun and Liang Jiayao measure in 2026 how efficiently forty resource-based cities in China's Yellow River Basin are turning their industries green. These cities grew on mining and heavy industry and now face carbon limits in an ecologically fragile basin. An efficiency model scored each city from 2010 to 2021, and a second model hunted for what drives the scores up or down.

Efficiency wobbled upward overall, with downstream cities ahead of those in the middle and upper reaches, and still-growing cities ahead of mature and declining ones. Across the basin, economic development and environmental regulation both lifted efficiency. For mature cities, upgrading industrial structure and clustering industry helped too, while technology and structure showed no clear effect in declining or regenerating cities. The authors tailor policy advice to each city type rather than prescribing one recipe.
pmc-13410664:
Tomoyuki Ikai and colleagues built ladder-shaped polymers in 2026 whose stiff, flat frames twist into ordered spirals. Unlike their loose linear forerunners, which gave almost no chiral light signal, the new chains lined up in a solvent mix and in films. There they gave both circular dichroism and circularly polarized light.

Breathing solvent vapor over the films boosted the polarized glow well past a dissymmetry mark of 0.1, and the effect held even when three quarters of the film was a non-chiral twin. Readers interested in light-based devices get a clear recipe for strong, tunable polarized emission from mixed films.
pmc-13413164:
Cătălin Prodan-Bărbulescu and co-authors gather in 2026 what is known about the many shapes of the splenic artery, a vessel surgeons meet in upper abdominal operations. Its origin, route, and branching vary widely, and scattered reports made the full picture hard to see. The systematic review searched four databases for dissection, imaging, and surgical studies describing those variations and their operative consequences.

Seventeen studies covering 4,301 subjects and specimens met the criteria. The artery most often springs from the celiac trunk and runs above the pancreas, yet origins from the aorta or a neighbouring artery, and paths behind or through the pancreas, recur often. Branching varies greatly, with a two-way split commonest. The authors urge detailed imaging before pancreatic, stomach, and spleen surgery.
pmc-13415564:
Dexin Qiu, Lee Chin, and Abdul Rahim Abdul Samad present a 2026 study of how people in Malaysia feel about electric vehicles. The government there is pushing adoption, and public mood shapes how fast it spreads. Past studies leaned on surveys, which can be small and shaped by the questions asked.

Instead, the team mined more than ninety-six hundred user comments posted on a major national car website between early 2023 and early 2024. Price was the most mentioned word, and main topics included market trends, state incentives, batteries and charging, and car features. Overall feeling was mildly positive or curious, which the authors offer as guidance for policy.
pmc-13416664:
Laveborn and co-authors used Swedish registry data on dialysis access fistulas. A fistula is a surgically created connection between an artery and a vein. They asked whether fistula location raises the risk of new heart failure. Clinicians had worried that upper arm fistulas, which carry faster blood flow than forearm fistulas, might strain the heart over time.

The study covered 6,579 patients with 11,238 accesses created between 2013 and 2022. Anyone with earlier heart failure or dialysis was excluded. Heart failure risk was comparable for upper arm and forearm fistulas, even though flow ran highest in the upper arm group. Risk instead followed a U-shaped pattern across flow rates, rising at both the lowest and the highest flows. Age, diabetes, valve disease, and ischemic heart disease mattered more than access type.
pmc-13417064:
Qian Ma and colleagues test a traditional herbal mixture against udder infection in nursing mice, in a 2026 animal study. The mixture, Danggui Buxue Decoction, was given to mice with mastitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus bacteria. Mastitis harms mammary health and cuts milk output on dairy farms, so gentler options are sought.

Treated mice carried fewer bacteria and showed less inflammation and tissue damage in the gland. The barrier between blood and milk held up better, gut microbe makeup shifted toward balance, and key inflammatory pathways quieted. The results mark the mixture as a candidate worth further study, not yet a proven farm treatment.
pmc-13417964:
Mengting Xu, Zili Zhang, Xiao Hu, and Rong Zheng study whether smoke free laws affect the illegal cigarette trade in China, in a 2026 longitudinal analysis. Critics often claim strict tobacco rules push smokers to black markets. Data covered nearly 300 cities from 2011 to 2016, with illegal trade measured from official seizure records.

Cities adopting smoke free laws saw illegal trade fall by about 27 percent on average. The effect was stronger in coastal and border cities than inland ones. Extra statistical checks supported the result. The authors argue such laws deter supply rather than fuel smuggling, though other settings need testing before global claims are made.
pmc-13418464:
Ye-Jin Jang and co-authors run a long term field test of modified zoysiagrass on non target arthropods in South Korea, published in 2026. The grass can survive a strong weed killer, and one line is male sterile. Two sites gave over half a million arthropods in all. The catch was sorted into pests, natural enemies, and other groups.

The mix of species changed a lot by place and by year. Models showed year and region drove counts and diversity. Modified and normal grass did not differ in a clear way. A few small gaps faded on closer checks. The field results back the grass as safe for arthropod life.
pmc-13419364:
Matthias Serger and colleagues add live motion tracking to two standard structural MRI scans so head movement can be corrected as the scan runs. Head motion blurs brain images and can force costly repeat scans. Their servo navigation system slips quick tracking modules into the scan before each preparation pulse, letting position estimates settle fast.

Extra reference trackers spread along the reading train allowed updates even mid-sequence in the tests. Volunteers made sharp, instructed head moves while scanning at high field strength, and the artifacts from those moves shrank clearly with correction on. Both scan types gained from the before-pulse correction scheme. Sharper first-time scans would spare patients repeat visits and keep research data cleaner.
pmc-13420264:
John N-yelbi and colleagues explore what worries basic school teachers in Ghana as retirement nears, using in-depth interviews rather than surveys. The study drew 24 teachers aged 50 to 55 years, all within sight of the statutory retirement age of 60 in their system. A qualitative design built for lived experience guided the work, with interviews read thematically.

Worries fell into three families. Psychological concerns covered anxiety and doubt about life after work ends. Social concerns tracked shifting family roles and friendships built around school. Financial concerns centered on insecurity, whether pensions and savings would stretch. Naming the three strands helps counselors and unions design preparation programs that speak to real fears rather than forms and dates alone.
pmc-13420764:
Lisa Schwartz and co-authors explore what shapes the professional identity of genetic counselors, meaning how they understand who they are and what they bring to their work. Their 2026 qualitative study uses social identity theory and interviews with fifty counselors sampled for diverse backgrounds, experience, and practice settings.

Four influences emerged from the interviews. Internal validation came from purpose, pride, and confidence, while external validation came from colleagues, employers, autonomy, and patients. Personal identities, including life experience and demographics, also shaped professional identity, as did connections such as peer support, role models, and mentoring others. When these factors aligned with the profession's collective identity, counselors felt they belonged; misalignment weakened that belonging. The authors say the findings can inform recruitment, training, and retention in the field.
pmc-13420864:
Rajat Anand and colleagues tune a CRISPR editing platform for a lactic acid bacterium, aiming to raise its output of natural antimicrobial compounds. Editing these bacteria is hard: thick walls block DNA entry, defense systems shred foreign DNA, and the cutting enzyme itself can kill the host. Their target was a brake gene in the network that controls plantaricin, the bacterium's own antibiotic.

Extensive tuning of delivery and editing steps let the team knock out the brake gene cleanly. Stronger, steadier bacteriocin output followed from the edit in their design. Such compounds attack germ membranes with a narrow resistance profile and kind handling of human tissue, making them attractive for food safety and medicine alike. A reliable editing recipe for this workhorse species widens what strain engineers can attempt.
pmc-13421264:
Kolodziejwski and colleagues present a 2026 protocol comparing two light therapies to prevent mouth sores during head and neck cancer radiotherapy. One group gets red light inside the mouth, the current standard. The other gets infrared light through the skin of the face and neck.

The randomized pilot will enroll 54 patients, split evenly between the two approaches. Light sessions run three times a week throughout radiotherapy. The main outcome is sore severity on a World Health Organization scale, with pain, ulcer size, and quality of life also tracked. The team tests whether the through-skin method is not worse than the in-mouth standard. A method that works from outside would help patients who cannot open their mouths wide.
pmc-13421464:
Naoya Itoh and co-workers set outcomes against each other in 2026 for cancer and non-cancer patients in Japan with tough gut germ cases. Tough cases threaten cancer patients most, yet their traits and outlook in Japan were unclear, so the team followed 167 patients prospectively from 2019 to 2022.

Thirty-day death rates and ward stays varied little between groups, yet after weighting, cancer patients faced clearly worse joint results of death or clinical worsening. The paper urges stronger blocking of tough cases in cancer wards, where the same case carries heavier harms for frail ward patients.
pmc-13422064:
Dana Ogaz and co-authors draw lessons from a large HIV prevention pill trial in England, in work published in two thousand twenty-five. The trial proved the pill program workable and effective, and fed into national rollout. The team now checks how delivery varied by region and clinic size.

Uptake of the pill ranged widely across clinic types, and was higher in London. HIV rates were far lower in trial members than in other clinic visitors in both regions. Many new infections arose in people with no clear risk markers. The authors back broader, less gated access and steady national data reporting.
pmc-13422664:
Kildegaard and colleagues tracked prescriptions for GLP-1 receptor agonists, the gut-hormone drugs widely used for weight loss, among Danes aged 12 to 24 years from 2018 through 2025. Drawing on nationwide prescription, hospital, and laboratory registries, they described who started treatment, who prescribed it, and how long young people stayed on it.

Use rose more than fiftyfold over the period, reaching 418 new users per 100,000 young people by 2025, driven mainly by semaglutide for weight management. Growth was steepest at ages 18 to 24, climbing from 13 to 686 per 100,000, while uptake among adolescents climbed from 1.7 to 72 per 100,000 across those years. Most users were women, and few had diabetes, and 33 percent had a psychiatric condition recorded. By 2025 general practitioners started 78 percent of treatments, yet only 38 percent of users still held a prescription after one year.
pmc-13422864:
Faith Logan leads an eight-author team describing, in a 2026 protocol, a pilot trial for teenagers with chronic muscle and joint pain. The trial treats teenagers' belief in their own coping as the lever for moving more. Adolescents with such pain often avoid activity, fearing flare-ups, and avoidance feeds disability into adulthood.

Their PREP-Y programme runs four virtual sessions building pain resilience, self-efficacy, motivation and flexible coping, wrapped around activity goals. Forty adolescents aged twelve to seventeen at a Columbus children's hospital will wear activity monitors and carry fitness watches, with questionnaires and physical tests before and after. As a single-group pilot, the study's job is feasibility and signal, preparing a later randomised trial.
pmc-13423064:
Anaïs Mons and colleagues report sixteen years of outcomes for very preterm infants in Switzerland, using the national neonatal network that covers every top-level intensive care unit. Their population study follows 12,453 babies born before 32 weeks of pregnancy across three periods, from 2006–2011 through 2017–2021, tracking survival and major complications by gestational age.

Overall survival rose from 85.4% in the first period to 89.7% in the last, with the largest gains among babies born before 26 weeks. Deaths both in the delivery room and in intensive care fell clearly. Survival free of major complications held steady near 72%, though lung disease and eye disease among survivors became more common over time.
pmc-13423164:
Liu and colleagues show in 2026 how myosin VI helps breast cancer turn its surroundings acidic and disarm immune attack. Myosin VI is a motor protein that hauls cargo inside cells. Acidic surroundings are known to suppress immunity, but this driver's role was not.

Analyzing large cancer datasets, the team linked high myosin VI levels to more M2 macrophages, a wound-healing immune state that shelters tumors, and to poorer patient outcomes. Inside the cell nucleus, the protein recruits the factor SP1 and the gene-reading machinery to switch on CA9, an enzyme that pumps acid outward. The acid then triggers a sensor on macrophages that flips them into the M2 state. A drug blocking myosin VI reduced acidification in mice, revived antitumor immunity, and made anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy work better.
pmc-13423364:
Alexa S. Podolsky and three colleagues analyse opioid prescribing after selective matrixectomy, a toenail operation for ingrown nails that usually needs only simple painkillers. Drawing on the TriNetX research network, they counted prescriptions written within three days of surgery and modelled which patient traits predicted receiving one.

Of 97,208 patients, 15.2% received an opioid, though the share fell from 24.3% in 2008–2018 to 12.8% in 2018–2025. Prescribing ran lower for women, older patients, and people with anxiety, depression, or chronic pain histories. Prior sedative or opioid use, fibromyalgia, Black or African American race, and Hispanic or Latino ethnicity predicted higher odds. The authors offer the patterns to guide post-operative counselling.
pmc-13423564:
Kyo Soung Koo and three colleagues challenge the rice-paddy image of the Suweon treefrog, a critically endangered frog found only on the Korean Peninsula. Because rice farming is recent in the frog's long history, strict dependence on paddies seemed doubtful, so the team surveyed a core site in Pyeongtaek before the 2024 breeding season.

They found 701 frogs at a density of 436 per square kilometre, and not one sat inside a rice paddy. Every frog rested on plants rising from streamside waterways, with 97% on common reed.
