Paddies still matter for breeding, the authors say, but reed beds are the essential non-breeding habitat, and protection plans that ignore them risk missing the species' ancestral home.
pmc-13424064:
Zhengyang Kong and nine colleagues engineer a soft ion-conducting gel. The gel is both tough and able to heal itself at room temperature. Those two traits usually trade off in materials for wearable electronics. Their gel, named ZESTI, builds strength from chains carrying both positive and negative charges on side groups.

Those twin charges create a web of ion and dipole attractions that reinforce the material, carry current efficiently, and re-form after a cut, restoring function without heat or glue. Sensors built from the gel kept sensing reliably and recovered after damage in the team's tests. The authors present the design as a route to self-sustaining iontronic devices, machines that move charge with ions rather than electrons.
pmc-13424364:
Angelica E. Lang and three colleagues show that neurons must ship old mitochondria back to the cell body to keep making new ones. Mitochondria far out in an axon sit a long way from the nucleus. The nucleus holds most of the genes for building them. How distant organelles prompt their own replacement was therefore a puzzle.

Live imaging in zebrafish neurons settled the point: blocking the return trip stalled production of fresh mitochondria, even in distant branches. A hormone-linked gene switch, an estrogen-related receptor, connected the transport signal to switching on mitochondrial genes in the nucleus. The authors describe a feedback loop in which axonal mitochondria report back and set the pace of their own renewal.
pmc-13424464:
Li and colleagues used Swedish national registers to test a safety question. Did COVID-19 infection or vaccination raise the risk of new type 1 diabetes? They followed everyone under 80 in the country from 2020 through 2023. The cohort held 2,650,492 children and 6,870,328 adults. Risk was tracked in windows after each infection and vaccine dose.

Infection was linked with higher diabetes incidence within two years. Hazard ratios were 1.22 in children and 1.10 in adults in the adjusted models. The increase concentrated in the first 30 days after infection. In that window, hazard ratios reached 5.41 in children and 3.33 in adults, before fading. Vaccination did not modify the infection-related risk. An early lower rate in children disappeared when only ages 12 to 17 were examined. The authors read the pattern as faster diagnosis rather than lasting causation.
pmc-13424664:
Maher and the ELEVATE IPF Investigators report a phase 2b trial of a reformulated lung drug. Their 2026 paper tests deupirfenidone, a chemically modified version of pirfenidone designed to keep its benefits with a kinder profile, in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive scarring lung disease. A total of 257 patients were randomised to two deupirfenidone doses, standard pirfenidone, or placebo for 26 weeks.

Lung capacity, measured as forced vital capacity, fell by about 111 millilitres on placebo but only about 48 millilitres across the combined deupirfenidone arms. The higher dose alone beat placebo by an adjusted margin of about 91 millilitres in the conventional analysis. Gastrointestinal side effects were the most common in every active arm. The authors conclude deupirfenidone slowed disease progression over the trial period.
pmc-13426464:
Pacheco Filho and colleagues surveyed dental students in Brazil in 2026 about syphilis and its mouth signs, comparing students early in the program with those near graduation. Of 171 students invited, 169 answered a sixteen-question test on the sexually transmitted infection, which dentists may first spot through oral lesions.

Knowledge was thin overall. Only about twenty-four percent answered correctly about the disease stages, about twenty-six percent about its oral manifestations, and about thirty-seven percent about look-alike diagnoses. Surprisingly, the direction ran backward: earlier-year students scored better than later-year students on the cause, symptoms, stages, oral signs, similar conditions, and drugs. The authors suggest knowledge fades without reinforcement in later clinical years, and they call for teaching that revisits the disease before graduation.
pmc-13427064:
Richter and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how large language model chatbots change communication between doctors and patients, pooling recent studies. Such tools are now drafted into clinics to answer questions and explain findings. Whether they make communication better, in empathy, clarity, and trust, had not been summed up.

Ten studies qualified from more than three hundred records. In head-to-head ratings, chatbot replies were judged more empathetic than doctors' replies in five of six comparisons, sometimes by wide margins. Simplified chatbot reports raised patient understanding scores and cut consultation time sharply in one study, though answers could run long or stay too hard for low-literacy readers. A pooled analysis of four studies found a large empathy gain. Satisfaction results were mixed, and no study tracked trust over time, a gap the authors flag.
pmc-13427564:
Ashley Hirons leads a 2026 study of a virus called HTLV-1c that stays in the body for life and harms the lungs. The team recruited 41 First Nations participants in Alice Springs, in Central Australia, where this subtype is common. Blood tests measured virus levels and sorted immune cells by surface markers. For six donors, the team read whole virus copies inserted into human DNA, one copy at a time.

All infected participants had extra lung-seeking immune cells, and those cells carried much of the virus. Many virus copies were broken yet kept a gene called hbz, which helps the virus persist. Virus material also turned up in sputum from people with lung disease. The findings name two possible drug targets for a neglected infection.
pmc-13427664:
Pei Ma and co-authors propose, in a 2026 study, a forecasting network modeled loosely on how the visual cortex fires. Predicting series that unfold over time, such as weather or prices, needs both accuracy and cheap computing. Their design, called BINN-ESN, keeps a fixed pool of pulsing units and trains only the output layer. A modified coupled neural network, drawn from mammalian vision, supplies the pool's units.

Across test systems, deep learning rivals often won on one-step-ahead accuracy. The new network held up better over long horizons on most systems and used far less computing than a leading rival in long runs. Code is shared openly for others to try. Engineers who must forecast far ahead on modest hardware gain an option worth benchmarking, with honest trade-offs stated.
pmc-13427764:
Sergei L Kosakovsky Pond and colleagues present B-STILL, a statistical method for finding genome sites that evolution has kept unchanged because change is harmful, not by chance. Standard tools cannot separate these two explanations at sites that never vary. Their 2026 paper applies the framework to viral and mammalian genomes.

The method models how much opportunity each site had to change, given the genetic code and mutation biases, and compares observed stillness against the gene's background rate. Sites passing the threshold are called evolutionary stasis anchors. In clinical and pathogen datasets, these anchors strongly predicted biological importance and disease relevance. Across the genomes studied, thousands of anchors clustered in known functional domains and in uncharacterised structural motifs. The authors present B-STILL as a scalable way to turn uninformative constant sites into precise markers of constraint.
pmc-13428164:
Shen and Xia used computer methods in 2026 to screen how berberine, a plant compound, might act against respiratory syncytial virus, a common cause of lung infection. They gathered predicted targets of berberine from drug databases and virus-related targets from gene databases, then looked for overlap. Network tools mapped how the shared target proteins interact, and docking software tested how tightly berberine might bind the core ones.

Shen found 72 shared targets out of hundreds on each side, and network analysis picked out core proteins such as the epidermal growth factor receptor, Src, and caspase-3. Enrichment checks tied the targets to kinase activity, the adding of phosphate tags that switch proteins on, and to 145 signalling pathways in total. Docking gave strong binding scores for the core targets. The authors present these as leads for lab work, not yet proof of a treatment.
pmc-13429564:
Yanjiao Hou and colleagues hunt across cancers for the value of SYNGR4, a synaptic vesicle protein known in motor neuron disease but unexplored as a cancer marker. In lung adenocarcinoma above all, its worth as a prognosis tool and drug target was unknown.

Pan-cancer multi-omics work tracked expression, outlook, prediction models, methylation, gene changes, pathways, immune infiltration, immunotherapy response, and drug sensitivity. Lab tests in lung cancer cells then probed growth and movement with viability, colony, and wound assays. Results point to SYNGR4 being raised in tumours, marking it as a candidate marker and target worth clinical testing.
pmc-13430064:
Eileen Willis and co-authors examine how nurses separated work from home to protect their families during the early, pre-vaccination phase of COVID-19. Their 2026 study draws on an online survey run between October 2020 and February 2021.

Sixty-nine nurses from hospitals, aged care, general practice, and community settings, aged 18 to 74, answered open-ended questions. The analysis found five themes, including stress from heavier workloads, confusion from fast-changing guidelines, and shortages of resources. Nurses also described anger toward colleagues who could work remotely, and deliberate routines they built at home to block infection. The authors argue that these unseen home rituals extended nursing work into family life and should inform future pandemic planning.
pmc-13430264:
Zhihui Dou and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, FLASH radiotherapy, a method that delivers radiation so fast it seems to spare healthy tissue. Conventional radiation trickles in over minutes; FLASH delivers its dose in bursts lasting less than a thousandth of a second, at rates above forty units per second. Animal studies keep showing the same pattern: tumors die as usual while normal tissue damage drops. That gap is called the FLASH effect.

The review walks through candidate explanations, from fleeting oxygen depletion in tissue to immune preservation and reshaped tumor surroundings. Physical settings that make or break the effect get a full accounting across organ systems. Early human trials have begun, and combinations with immunotherapy look especially attractive. What blocks routine use is honest: incomplete mechanism, machine limits, and dose planning that still needs proof.
pmc-13430764:
Anna K-J Macintyre and co-authors worked with parents and clinic staff in Oslo in 2026 to build a tool that helps immigrant parents use child health services with more ease. Parents from abroad can face language hurdles, new service layouts, and clashing views on child care. Strong skill in finding and using health facts guards child health, yet few tested tools serve this group.

Ideas came from 14 parents and 59 staff members across many fields, giving more than three hundred raw ideas. Sorting cut the list to a short set, and joint workshops ranked the top picks. One shared pick won out: clearer word on what the family clinic offers. The group then made short cartoon videos in several tongues about clinic follow-up visits. Five rounds of fixes with 43 users polished the result.
pmc-13432664:
Jonathan Daniel and co-authors tested a fast-track recovery plan in 2026 for robot throat surgery done through the mouth. Such plans have cut stays after many kinds of surgery, yet proof for this robot route stayed thin. The plan, set in place in 2021, adds a risk sort for throat leaks and full checks around surgery.

Forty cases split into care before and after the plan took hold. Patients on the plan followed its steps at a high rate. Their mid stay fell by three and a half days, a firm gain for such a small set. Costs per patient and time back to swallowing by mouth both trended down as well. The authors pitch the plan as easy to adopt, while large trials would firm up the claim.
pmc-13434664:
Zugai and colleagues interview former involuntary inpatients about working with mental health clinicians in this 2026 qualitative study. Collaboration is supposed to be a foundation of ethical mental healthcare, yet coercion and restrictive practices remain common on inpatient wards. The team held one-on-one interviews with twelve people who had experienced involuntary inpatient care and analyzed the transcripts for shared themes about partnership with staff.

Participants valued collaborative care. But their own views were rarely sought or taken seriously, they reported. Clinicians' default skepticism deepened the sense of being dismissed. Where staff built genuinely caring relationships, patients felt safer and collaboration became real, they said. The authors call for systemic reform of ward cultures, policies, and structures so that everyday practice is organized around interpersonal care rather than control.
pmc-13436264:
Andrew Hudson's team mapped liver natural killer cells in 2026 in rhesus macaques during lentivirus infection, a model for HIV. Liver-resident killer cells help guard liver balance and fight viruses, but their role in lentivirus infection was poorly defined. Across uninfected, acutely SIV-infected, and chronically SHIV-infected monkeys, the team separated liver-resident cells marked CD49a from circulating-type cells lacking it.

CD49a cells carried more activation and metabolic markers, divided less, and on stimulation gave strong multi-cytokine responses with less killing marker than their counterparts, regardless of infection stage. The paper defines a metabolically robust, cytokine-biased liver subset. HIV teams get a refined cell map that may inform liver immunity and vaccine thinking.
pmc-13436564:
Woo-Taek Jeon's team defined a brief root cap cuticle phase in 2026 that helps seedlings push into soil. Young roots face strong mechanical resistance, and a transient waxy cuticle forms on the root cap early, yet its job during soil entry was unclear. Mutants lacking the cuticle were tested on dense substrates and agar, tracking tip damage, cap layer shedding, and responses to gravity and water cues.

Cuticle-free seedlings crossed dense ground poorly with more tip damage, shed their outer cap layer too fast, and showed weak gravity response while water response stayed mostly normal. The early window faded with age, before the cuticle itself vanished. Plant scientists get a timed protection-plus-steering role for a fleeting structure at life's first push.
pmc-13437364:
Raquel Suriá-Martínez and colleagues studied online gambling among young Spaniards with motor disabilities. Easy phone and web access has raised worry about gambling harm in groups that may face extra barriers in daily life. Their 2026 study surveyed 135 members of major Spanish disability groups about their betting habits, their thinking errors around chance, and their level of gambling risk.

About sixty-one percent had gambled online. Two classic thinking errors, believing a losing streak must turn and believing one can steer random outcomes, tracked closely with worse gambling severity. Each error also predicted higher risk of problem gambling on its own, and together they sorted risk levels well. A deeper model showed the errors partly carry the effect of taking part in gambling into actual risk. Prevention and treatment targeting those beliefs directly, they argue, should sit at the center of efforts to protect this group.
pmc-13437464:
Yan Lu and co-authors describe a leukemia case sitting awkwardly between two disease classes. A 29-year-old man came in with swollen glands, severe fever, low white cell defenses, and a spreading infection. Lab work fitted an early T-cell precursor form of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, yet the cells oddly carried CD19, a marker of the rival B-cell line.

The blasts held an NPM1 mutation and a change in FLT3, both classic marks of myeloid leukemia rather than the T-cell kind. Such mixed signals can mislead teams, the authors warn. After the sepsis was controlled, he received three rounds of a combined drug regimen and then a half-matched stem cell transplant. He stayed in full remission seven months after the transplant. The 2026 report claims the first case of this subtype with this NPM1 change and urges strict use of classification rules when markers clash.
pmc-13438764:
Teruhisa Kinoshita and co-authors test whether pharmacists can lead the care of candidemia, a yeast infection of the blood, in a hospital with no full-time infection specialist. The team compared two eras at their tertiary hospital in Japan. From 2013 to 2018, care ran as usual. From 2018 to 2024, pharmacists on the antimicrobial stewardship team actively promoted a treatment bundle for every patient with Candida in a blood culture.

The two groups looked alike at baseline, with the same spread of Candida species. Bundle compliance jumped from 4.5% to 39.6% once pharmacists drove it. But 30-day mortality did not differ between the eras. The pharmacists helped most by recommending the right treatment course. The lesson is two-sided: pharmacists can lift process quality a long way in a specialist's absence, yet better checklists did not, here, translate into fewer deaths.
pmc-13439364:
Fangzheng Li's team built a personalized prediction model in 2026 for student progress in moral education, where individualized forecasts could guide timely help. Moral growth paths differ per student, yet schools lacked accurate, personal predictions for ethics learning. The hybrid method cleaned raw data, encoded each modality with auto-encoders, fused modalities by self-attention, and forecast outcomes with a random forest.

The fused model beat rival methods by about seven percent on accuracy and F-measure, suggesting modality fusion captures aspects single sources miss. Educators get a proof-of-concept for tailored ethics support, with clear limits: moral development is value-laden, and prediction must not become labeling. Human judgment must stay central in any school use.
pmc-13439564:
Tanya Pareek and John Vergis lead a team reading gene activity in the hippocampus of monkeys with chronic alcohol use, hunting the changes behind relapse. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Places and contexts trigger relapse in recovering drinkers. The hippocampus stores those contexts, yet its molecular scars from alcohol were unmapped in primates.

Sequencing found thousands of genes dialed up or down in drinkers. Synapse signaling and neuron development genes were turned down. Mitochondrial energy genes were turned up instead. Some altered genes matched human genetic risk hits for dependence. A drug-matching analysis surfaced existing medicines that might reverse the pattern. Growth factor blockers and calcium channel drugs appeared on that list. The authors offer the map as a target finder for relapse prevention. Primate data bring the findings closer to human biology.
pmc-13441764:
Mingfeng Zhao, Liang Chen, and Suiwen Hou review how plants tag their own proteins to survive cold, writing in 2026. Cold shapes where plants can grow and what yields they give. Beyond switching genes on, plants rapidly modify proteins already made, changing their stability, activity, and partnerships. The review covers the major tag types: phosphorylation, ubiquitin tagging, SUMO tagging, acetylation, crotonylation, and fat-based S-acylation, each mapped into cold signalling pathways.

Such tags let a plant answer cold within minutes while balancing defence against growth. The harder problem, the authors argue, is the crosstalk: tags compete, cooperate, and cascade, forming one regulatory web rather than parallel lines. Mapping when and where each tag lands during a cold spell remains incomplete. They urge time-and-place-resolved studies so breeders and engineers can borrow the logic for hardier crops.
pmc-13441964:
Agarwala and co-authors extended a major credit-rating methodology to show how biodiversity loss will raise borrowing costs for nations, putting numbers on nature risk for the 83 trillion dollar sovereign debt market. Their scenarios modeled partial collapse of tropical timber, wild pollination, and marine fisheries services across 23 countries home to 5.5 billion people.

Partial ecosystem collapse would add about 49 billion dollars a year to India's debt servicing costs, equal to 2.4 percent of median post-tax income there. China's added annual interest bill reached 70 billion dollars under the same scenario family in their modeling. Across all countries studied, extra interest payments could total 162 billion dollars yearly, approaching the 200 billion dollar annual conservation finance target. Angola, Bangladesh, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Madagascar each faced gross domestic product losses above 15 percent by 2030.
pmc-13442664:
Jiayuan Ye and colleagues test a two-step path to catch lung tuberculosis in a 2026 study. Chest CT scans screen for suspect cases first, then a fast gene read called nanopore targeted sequencing checks lung wash fluid. Records held 380 people from one center, seen from March 2023 to December 2024.

Three scan readers with varied skill took part, and the most seasoned reader missed the fewest true cases. Flags pooled from the three readers gave a missed-case rate as low as 9.09 percent in the shared pool. The gene read then faced off against older lab tests such as culture, smear, and Xpert. The authors argue that wide scan screening plus the gene read lifts catch rates. They frame reader teamwork as a cheap first gain for clinics.
pmc-13442864:
Yifang Qian and coauthors describe a 2026 clinical study that builds an early warning tool for children whose tics have just begun. Many go on to develop chronic tic disorders. The team followed 108 children with new-onset provisional tic disorder for a year, fitting a prediction model and checking it with resampling methods before turning it into a bedside aid.

Three factors predicted progression: longer tic duration, higher parent-rated vocal scores, and the presence of another condition. A two-cutoff scheme split children into low, middle, and high risk groups, with progression far more common at the top than at the bottom. The resulting chart, online calculator, and care pathway aim to focus follow-up where it helps most, though wider testing must confirm the tool beyond one cohort.
pmc-13443164:
W Zhao and colleagues map how drebrin grips and reshapes actin nets inside cells in a 2026 study. Drebrin guides nerve growth, synapse flex, virus entry, and cancer spread through those nets. Ice-cold microscope views show drebrin holds actin through two grip zones, ABD1 and ABD2.

The first grip zone takes two poses, and a loose loop lets the pair sit at varied spots along a strand. That loop also lets drebrin bundle strands in a light way. Both grips span many actin units and tweak the seam between them, which firms the strand. Rival grip proteins share the same actin patch, so drebrin can push them off. The map explains how one protein can steer so many cell tasks.
pmc-13443864:
K Asmiya Banu and coauthors develop a 2026 secure control scheme for nonlinear networked systems under deception attacks, where false signals threaten stability and bandwidth is scarce. Their interval type-2 fuzzy observer design widens the classic fuzzy model with upper and lower membership functions, and an observer-based event trigger fires only when needed.

Stability rules drawn from a Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional, solved as linear matrix inequalities, yield the observer and controller gains. Numerical examples showed the design holds stability while cutting needless transmissions. Engineers gain a sound defense for grids, vehicles, and process plants, though hardware trials must test the scheme against real attack traffic.
pmc-13444064:
Behnam Gheisary and colleagues report a 2026 study of a three-part natural blend that helps madder plants withstand salty soils in arid regions. The team optimized seaweed extract, willow bark, and gum arabic with a 14-run mixture design, tracking growth, water status, antioxidants, and pigment compounds under salt stress, plus antibacterial tests by computer docking.

The best blend, roughly half seaweed with smaller shares of willow bark and gum arabic, maximized fresh and dry yield alongside water retention, proline, and antioxidant enzymes. Root extracts also curbed two bacterial pathogens in lab tests. The formulation offers growers a natural salt-stress aid, though field trials across soils and seasons must confirm the greenhouse gains.
pmc-13444264:
Radhika Thagunna and colleagues report a 9-year-old boy whose fainting spells pointed to a pituitary fault in a 2026 case paper. The rare birth state, pituitary stalk interruption syndrome, starves the body of gland hormones, with growth hormone lack the most common face. Growth hormone helps hold blood sugar during fasts and stress.

The boy came for short stature checks, with a past of repeat fainting attacks. Brain MRI was run as part of the workup, since low sugar can flag growth hormone lack early. The classic trio for the state spans a thin or cut stalk, a tiny front gland, and a stray back gland. The authors urge doctors to treat repeat low sugar as a hormone clue, not a stray event, so scans and care start sooner.
pmc-13445364:
Zachary Butzin-Dozier and colleagues use health records to ask whether COVID-19 vaccination lowers the later risk of long COVID, and whether any shield fades with time, in a 2026 study. The records form a national group drawn from many care sites. Two comparisons run side by side: vaccinated against unvaccinated, and illness at set gaps after a shot.

In a group of more than half a million patients, those with two or more doses faced lower risk of long COVID and of death than those with none. A second group of over a million patients showed no clear change in long COVID risk across the seven months after vaccination. The authors read the pattern as a shield that holds through that window.
pmc-13445664:
Xiaoying Chen and coauthors investigate a 2026 survey of how coaches lead and shape burnout among 519 college players in China, testing whether toughness and emotion control carry the effect. The team used standard scales for coaching, burnout, toughness, and control difficulties, analyzing mediation with standard statistical tools.

Positive coaching linked to lower burnout both directly and through greater toughness and easier emotion control, with indirect paths carrying 41.65 percent of the total effect. Male players showed greater toughness and control and lower burnout than female players, while age and level did not matter. Coach training that builds toughness and control skills could cut burnout, the authors suggest.
pmc-13445764:
Yujing Huang and colleagues design a music program for children with cochlear implants, built on a positive psychology frame and the Orff approach of learning music by doing, in a 2026 study. Hearing implants restore sound, yet speech and social growth still need rich practice. The team sought expert agreement on a full program before wider testing.

Fifteen experts in medicine, rehabilitation, and nursing refined the draft over two rounds, with strong agreement on each item's worth. The final plan holds five main parts, each split into finer steps. A trial run with fifteen children over three months showed gains in hearing, speech, and social measures, with good acceptance by families. The authors offer the plan as a base for a full randomized trial.
pmc-13446364:
Taro Narumi and colleagues ask whether restoring a steady heart rhythm eases disordered breathing in sleep for patients with persistent atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 study. The patients had pulmonary vein isolation, a catheter procedure that seals off the lung veins driving the faulty rhythm. Breathing and rhythm were checked again three months on.

A standard breathing index improved in thirty-nine in a hundred patients, and just over half saw the severity of their sleep breathing disorder step down. Later return of the faulty rhythm ran far lower in patients whose breathing index had improved. The authors read the tie in both directions: calm rhythm may lighten sleep breathing, and that gain may help the rhythm hold.
pmc-13447264:
Zhonghai Dao and co-authors review plant flavonoids for fatty liver disease in 2026, weighing lab promise against weak human proof. No drug has yet won approval for the condition, which now ranks among the most common liver diseases. Flavonoids, a broad family of plant compounds, hit many targets at once in cell and animal tests.

Thirty-three well-defined compounds were graded by strength of evidence across models and early human trials. Reported actions include cutting fat production, burning fat faster, easing insulin resistance, calming inflammation and boosting cell clean-up. Certain named compounds engaged several pathways at once. Absorption by mouth stayed very poor, mainly due to low solubility and rapid processing in the body. New delivery forms such as tiny carriers show early promise for closing that gap.
pmc-13447564:
Daisy Hazarika leads a large team reporting two cases of slow-growing mycobacterial infection at keyhole surgery entry sites in northeast India in 2026 work, joined by a review of Indian reports. Such infections appear weeks after surgery, mimic tuberculosis, and resist many standard antibiotics, leaving no settled treatment guidance.

Both patients developed delayed wound infections that proved hard to diagnose and showed partial or full resistance to commonly used drugs. Prolonged combinations of antibiotics, including reserve agents in one case, were paired with surgical cleaning of infected tissue. Recovery required months of persistence from patients and teams alike. The accompanying review gathers prior Indian cases to guide recognition, since delayed entry-site infection after laparoscopy should prompt testing for these atypical organisms.
pmc-13448664:
Aydın Uzun and coauthors map a 2026 study of leaf shape, nutrient content, and bioactive richness in wild pear types from Central Anatolia and farmed pear kinds. The team took shape traits, nutrients, plant acids, plant pigments, and cell-guard action across types and farmed kinds, noting wild pear leaves had never been fully mapped.

Type spread proved large across every trait, with calcium, sulfur, P, and K leading nutrients and wild pear leaves richer in nutrients than farmed ones. Main parts cleanly split types and farmed kinds by their joint lists. The data support picking genetic stocks and valuing wild pear leaves as bioactive goods.
pmc-13448864:
Simon Cichosz, Kristine Færch, and Morten Jensen set out in 2026 to chart what continuous glucose monitor readings look like across the full range of glucose health. Standard labels rely on blood tests such as HbA1c and fasting glucose, yet sensors reveal daily patterns those tests miss. Reference ranges for sensor measures remain scarce, especially spanning people treated with insulin.

The team analyzed the AI-READI cohort, a multi-site study of 2,280 people gathered between 2023 and 2025. Participants had normal glucose, prediabetes, or type 2 diabetes, some on oral drugs and some on insulin. For each group they report distribution ranges for key sensor metrics drawn from standardized assessments. The result is a framework linking laboratory categories to real-world glucose patterns, meant to help clinicians judge an individual's readings, spot early loss of control, and design future studies.
pmc-13449064:
Agnieszka Czapska and colleagues review in 2026 how contrast-enhanced ultrasound has grown from a visual aid into a measuring tool for liver cancer care. Modern scanners now turn the wash of microbubble contrast through a tumor into numbers: peak intensity, time to peak, wash-in slope, and area under the curve. Three-dimensional and fusion imaging, increasingly steered by artificial intelligence, guide biopsies and ablation in real time.

The review weighs these clinical uses, especially judging liver lesions in chronic liver disease and checking whether viable tumor survives local therapy. It then looks ahead to targeted microbubbles that can image molecules and be burst on command to deliver treatment, a theranostic turn for the method. Persistent hurdles around standardization get a critical look, and the authors map where research is heading next.
pmc-13449464:
Juncheng Han and coauthors studied how often to feed young balsa trees during the rainy season, publishing in 2026. Ochroma lagopus grows fast and demands heavy nutrients, so the timing of water-soluble fertilizer could shape both growth and nutrient balance across organs. The team tested one-year-old trees under four schedules: no fertilizer and three different frequencies.

A medium schedule, 500 grams per plant every thirty days, produced the strongest height gains at sixty, ninety, and one hundred twenty days. A lower-frequency schedule, the same dose every forty-five days, gave the largest stem-diameter gain instead. The contrast suggests steady supply favors height while leaner nitrogen avoids holding back stem thickening. Plantation managers can match fertilizer timing to whether they want height or girth.
pmc-13449764:
Josephine Bicknell and co-authors announce in 2026 a new crystal form of uric acid, the waste product behind gout and many kidney stones. For two centuries, every attempt to grow its crystals from solution, hundreds in the senior author's laboratory alone, produced the same single water-free form. The new form, labeled Form III, never appears from solution at all; it emerges when ammonium urate hydrate is heated past 200 degrees Celsius and decomposes in the solid state.

The two forms stack molecules almost identically, differing mainly in one axis length by about two tenths of an angstrom, yet their X-ray powder patterns separate unambiguously. A structure model built by refinement, backed by quantum calculations, suggests Form III traps a mixture of molecular tautomers, alternate hydrogen arrangements that heat makes affordable. Form I, grown gently from water, holds only the lowest-energy tautomer, above ninety-nine percent pure.
pmc-13450064:
Sandra Carpenter and colleagues surveyed medical residents in 2026 about disability, support, and mistreatment at one teaching hospital. Little was known about trainees with disabilities, and better data were needed to build fair support systems in graduate medical training. The team ran an online survey across all residents between 2024 and 2025.

Only sixteen percent responded, with 91 replies from 558 residents. Twelve reported a disability, most often learning or neurodevelopmental conditions and chronic health conditions. A third had formal accommodations, a third reported disability-related mistreatment, and almost all were unaware of key support routes. The low response itself warns that stigma may hide the true picture.
pmc-13450364:
Runhua Li and colleagues developed a simpler way to isolate heart muscle cells from adult mice in 2026, removing the need for a Langendorff apparatus. Adult mouse heart cells are a key model for disease and drug testing, but current isolation relies on specialized equipment and gives uneven yields. A convenient, reliable protocol was needed.

After anesthesia, the team infused enzyme solution directly through the aortic root, using the coronary vessels to digest tissue. The method yielded viable heart muscle cells with intact shape, suitable for long-term culture, matching the standard technique. Cells still responded to low oxygen and to adrenaline-like drugs with expected changes in contraction and calcium handling. Heart fibroblasts were co-isolated in the same run. Labs gain a cheaper route to high-quality heart cells.
pmc-13450564:
Hiroki Nagasawa and colleagues tell in 2026 of a rare mild blood-vessel tumor in a man's belly wall that looked like a far worse cancer. Growths of this type, spindle cell hemangioma, most often sit in fingers or feet and are very rare on the trunk. Their patient, a man in his twenties, first felt the lump in early 2024.

Scans showed a firm mass about five centimeters wide under the skin, with no spread into deep tissue. Its size and cell shape made a skin cancer called dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans a real fear, so scans alone could not settle the label. The case shows why large trunk lumps of this cell type need tissue proof before treatment is set.
pmc-13451864:
Nadine Skoluda, Nida Ali, and Urs Nater pilot in 2026 a home version of a lab stress test that relies on speeches and math under judgment. The lab form needs a room, staff, and travel, which bars people who are old, far away, or limited in movement. Seventeen healthy young men each did both the home stress form and a calm control form, in random order, at their own homes.

Stress was read through felt strain, spit stress hormones, and heart rate. Most men crossed set stress marks under the home test, and all measures rose more than under the calm form. The authors say the home test stirs a true stress reply and can reach people labs cannot.
pmc-13452164:
Daniele Fabbri and co-authors scope in 2026 what is known about Europe's wood mice as hosts of germs that can jump to people. Finds on these Apodemus mice were scattered across many small studies. The team screened over 4,000 records and kept 166 pathogen-linked study records from 141 papers since 2000.

Proof ran strongest for hantaviruses and Leptospira, mid-grade for a few virus and germ kinds, and thin for many more. Host traits, seasons, food pulses, land use, and wet weather all shaped the finds. Since study styles clashed too much to pool, the authors cast the mice as likely holders in set systems and as bridge hosts at farm and town edges.
pmc-13452364:
Dongbin Wang and co-authors explain in 2026 why pairing ultrasound with low pressure makes a tin salt crystallize far better. Stannous sulfate serves plating, synthesis, and new energy work, yet plain drying runs slow, and low pressure alone sparks wild bursts of poor crystals. Their joint method was tuned across heat, sound rate, power, pressure, and stir speed.

At the best mix, yield hit near nine tenths, and the crystals came out as even rods of one size band. Fast cameras showed two bubble kinds at work: short-lived ones that sped mixing, and steady ones that seeded crystal births. The authors offer the pairing as a base for controlled crystal work.
pmc-13452864:
Gujarathi and colleagues charted results for appendix adenocarcinoma diagnosed before age 50. It is an early-onset form whose incidence is rising, while evidence about its course stays scarce. Of 181 patients treated from 2013 to 2024, 49, or 27.1 percent, had early-onset disease. Their median age was 42.1 years in that group.

Among patients whose disease stayed locoregional, 57.9 percent remained disease-free for at least two years after treatment in the combined cohort. Within those two-year survivors, early-onset patients relapsed sooner, with median recurrence-free survival of 49.5 months versus 83.3 months and a hazard ratio of 4.07, though the difference was borderline significant. Late recurrences were common, appearing in 60 percent of patients followed five years in the relevant subgroup. Early-onset patients received more experimental and bevacizumab-containing therapy, yet overall survival did not differ significantly between age groups.
pmc-13453464:
Arani K Ranasinghe, Lai Ming Lam, Kelly K Miller, and Brett A Bryan publish survey data on the strains and coping strength of smallholder farmers in Sri Lanka. Their 2026 data paper covers 300 farmers in 12 villages of the Galgamuwa area, in the dry zone's cascade tank farming system. Face to face surveys ran from June to September 2025 with a pre tested questionnaire.

Farmers were picked at random from official voter lists for each village. The data span farm and household traits, farming problems, coping strength, views on risk, and the steps farmers take when shocks hit. Files come as a spreadsheet with a codebook and six sheets that sort the answers by theme. The authors offer the set as a base line so later studies can judge whether support policies truly lift resilience over time.
pmc-13454064:
Xin Liu and Ang Ji mine the United States drug safety database for eye side effects tied to immune checkpoint inhibitors, the cancer drugs that release immune brakes. Their 2026 study covers reports from 2011 to mid 2025 across four regimens, from single drugs to two drug pairs. Three statistical signals cross check which eye problems show up more than chance would predict.

A total of 5,244 eye reports surfaced, led by inflammatory problems. Uveitis, inflammation inside the eye, carried the strongest broad signal, ahead of scleritis and optic nerve inflammation. Pairing two checkpoint drugs sharpened the signals sharply: uveitis reporting ran far above the single drug level. Melanoma cases made up over half the uveitis spectrum reports. The authors urge fast eye checks and joint care for patients on these drugs, above all on paired regimens.
pmc-13454564:
A. Ampuero leads a large team reconstructing, in 2026, how fast tropical South America warmed as the last ice age ended. Land temperature records from that era are scarce, which clouds forecasts of future warming. The team read temperature from a stalagmite in central-eastern South America using a precise droplet-based method.

Cave temperatures climbed about 5.8 degrees from the glacial peak to the early Holocene, tracking global carbon dioxide and Antarctic warmth. One sharp jump came at a known transition when Atlantic circulation weakened, around the Antarctic Cold Reversal into the Younger Dryas. Even that fastest past jump was slower than the long-term warming now projected. The authors take this as evidence that today's greenhouse push is without precedent in the record they measured.
pmc-13455064:
T. Baird and co-authors simulate the infrared spectra of protonated water clusters, tiny groups of water molecules carrying an extra proton, to learn about their structure and motion. Such spectra usually demand expensive quantum calculations. Their 2026 study combines machine-learned models of the clusters' energy and electric properties with a quantum thermal bath method that includes nuclear quantum effects cheaply.

Clusters from a single molecule up to four were simulated. The team compared their computed spectra with earlier theoretical and experimental work. They report that the combined approach reproduces spectral features suitably well while costing far less than standard alternatives such as ring polymer molecular dynamics. The authors present the method as a practical route to accurate spectra for these clusters, which serve as models for how water behaves around excess protons in many chemical environments.
pmc-13455164:
Qiaoli Yang and others tried pig gut-microbe transplants in 2026, to shield piglets from Clostridium perfringens type C gut harm. Piglet diarrhoea from this germ is a big swine trade woe. Duroc-Landrace-Yorkshire suckling piglets were split into a germ-hit control group and a transplant group that got Hezuo pig gut slurry before germ hit.

Transplants eased jejunum harm a lot, with taller villi and shallower crypts, plus more goblet cells. Tight-join genes Occludin, ZO-1, and Claudin-1 plus calm cytokine IL-10 rose, while flare cytokines TNF-alpha and IL-6 fell. Good germ kinds such as Akkermansia, Rothia, Peptococcus, and Proteocatella grew. Swine farms gain a gut-microbe shield for a costly germ.
pmc-13456964:
Mauricio Parada and nine colleagues assess, in a 2026 study, how well magnetic resonance scans of the pelvis joints flag axial spondyloarthritis in everyday practice. The disease inflames the spine and the joints linking spine to pelvis, yet back pain has many causes. The team reviewed 95 adults with chronic back pain who had joint and whole-spine scans for suspected disease.

Expert rheumatologists sorted the patients into two disease forms and one non-inflammatory group after follow-up. Scan-defined joint inflammation proved highly specific, at 91 percent, but caught only about four fifths of true cases. Spinal inflammatory lesions appeared in 40 percent of all patients, and in three quarters of the psoriatic form, often without joint inflammation. Age, regular exercise, expert-judged inflammatory pain, and the count of disease features each predicted joint inflammation. The authors say scans must join clinical judgment, not replace it.
pmc-13457464:
Peng Liu and colleagues develop a calculator that estimates a woman's chance of taking home a baby within a year of her first infertility consultation. The patients have polycystic ovary syndrome, renamed in 2026 as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome. Their retrospective study at one center enrolled 610 women: 389 treated from late 2021 through 2023 formed the development group, and 221 from 2024 formed a later validation group.

Live birth within 365 days occurred in 44.7 percent of the first group and 44.3 percent of the second. Seven routine variables made the final model: age, body mass index, years of infertility, prior pregnancies, the LH-to-FSH hormone ratio, tubal or pelvic problems, and uterine problems. Older age, higher weight, longer infertility, a higher hormone ratio, and uterine factors all trimmed the odds. Accuracy was moderate, with area-under-curve values of 0.735 and 0.738 and acceptable calibration. The authors want multicenter testing and impact studies before the tool guides care elsewhere.
pmc-13458164:
Lukas Ley and colleagues report a heart valve repair done with the patient awake, guided only by an ultrasound probe inside the heart. The patient, a multimorbid 74-year-old man, had severe leakage of the tricuspid valve, breathlessness at NYHA class III, swollen legs, and two heart-failure admissions in 14 months. Surgery was too risky, and the imaging route through the esophagus best avoided, so the heart team chose catheter-based edge-to-edge repair under local anesthesia.

Using three-dimensional intracardiac echocardiography as sole guide, the operators placed two clips, one anteroseptal and one posteroseptal in the clover arrangement, and cut the leak to a trace. The man left hospital without complications. Intracardiac probes usually play a supporting role beside esophageal imaging in these procedures. This 2026 case shows the probe can carry the guidance load, an option whenever esophageal imaging or general anesthesia is off the table.
pmc-13458764:
Federica Sordelli and colleagues report a salvage operation after penile surgery went badly wrong. A 36-year-old man arrived with spreading penile skin necrosis and infection after repair surgery elsewhere. That surgery had excised a plaque, placed Gore-Tex grafts on both sides, cut the suspensory ligament, and included circumcision and vasectomy. The synthetic grafts lay exposed under dead skin.

The team moved fast: radical debridement and removal of the grafts, leaving the erectile bodies exposed but alive, uncovered as stage one of the rebuild. Targeted antibiotics and hyperbaric oxygen therapy checked the infection and steadied the wound. Final coverage came later, pairing a split-thickness skin graft with Matriderm, a dermal template, and the graft took well with a good cosmetic result and a smooth recovery. The authors distill the lesson: with man-made material in play, speed, foreign-body removal, and staged repair protect tissue and erectile function.
pmc-13459164:
Shaghayegh Moradi Alamdarloo and colleagues examined life after a risky pregnancy complication in which the placenta grows too deeply into the womb. Women with this condition, placenta accreta spectrum, usually need a cesarean delivery plus removal of the uterus to control bleeding. Their 2026 study in Shiraz, Iran, interviewed 62 such women and 75 women who had repeated cesareans without the complication. They used standard quality of life and postnatal depression surveys.

The accreta group scored worse on physical function and bodily pain than the comparison group. Heavier blood loss, intensive care admission for mother or baby, and surgical complications each tracked with specific quality of life gaps. Yet probable depression appeared at similar rates, in 37 cases and 39 controls. Mental health after delivery, that suggests, depends on more than this diagnosis alone. The authors recommend targeted counseling and team follow up.
pmc-13459264:
Jinglun Wu and Zhaomo Zhang followed young adults over eight months to learn how social media feedback, the likes and comments posts attract, shapes mental health over time. Their 2026 three-wave study tracked 398 Chinese young adults, average age 21.34 years, measuring depressive and anxiety symptoms, self-esteem, and the tendency to compare oneself with others at each wave, then modeling the pathways between them.

Receiving fewer likes at the start predicted more depression and anxiety four months later, while the reverse direction showed no significant effect. Two mechanisms carried the influence: feedback worked through self-esteem, which explained 37.1 percent of the total effect, and through social comparison tendency, which explained 27.9 percent between them in the models. Together the mediators accounted for 65.0 percent of the link. The authors suggest building self-esteem resilience as protection.
pmc-13459364:
Nor Asiah Muhamad and co-authors measured smartphone addiction and its mental health links among Malaysian public university students. Their 2026 survey ran online between July 2022 and January 2024 and collected 7,278 students from twenty public universities. Validated questionnaires scored smartphone addiction, depression, anxiety, and loneliness. Regression models identified which student characteristics and mental health states were linked with problematic phone use in this large sample on their own.

Smartphone addiction affected 30.1 percent of the students surveyed. Depression was present in 42.6 percent, anxiety in 41.9 percent, and loneliness in a striking 83.8 percent of respondents on the instruments used. Using a phone more than ten hours daily carried the largest association, with an adjusted odds ratio of 5.277 for addiction in the model. Female gender, higher academic year, certain ethnic backgrounds, and depression, which roughly doubled the odds, also predicted addiction.
pmc-13459464:
Nur Aliah and co-authors folded an underused edible fern into date energy bars and measured what the plant adds nutritionally. The fern, Stenochlaena palustris, is eaten across Southeast Asia but rarely studied inside manufactured foods. In their 2026 laboratory study, bars were made with fern powder at 2.5 percent and 5 percent inclusion alongside a plain control, and an accredited laboratory measured basic composition, sugars, minerals, antioxidant activity, and water activity, which affects shelf life.

Adding the fern raised dietary fiber, ash, and protein in the bars, with generally higher levels of calcium, magnesium, iron, and zinc than the control formulation. Total energy stayed comparable across all three recipes, so the nutritional gains did not come from extra calories. Water activity remained in ranges compatible with a stable packaged product. The data serve as a validated baseline for product developers, the authors say.
pmc-13460864:
Nicholas Aderinto and colleagues conducted in 2026 an umbrella review, a synthesis of existing syntheses, on mechanical thrombectomy for acute ischemic stroke caused by a blocked large vessel. pmc-13461064:

pmc-13461164:

pmc-13461364:

pmc-13461464:

pmc-13461564:

pmc-13461664:
Boriana S Gagaouzova and co-authors revisit, in a 2026 study, how well a fall in blood pressure on standing explains the symptoms people notice. pmc-13462164:

pmc-13462264:

pmc-13462364:

pmc-13462464:

pmc-13462764:

pmc-13462864:

pmc-13464264:

pmc-13464564:

Tissue stored up to fifteen years still yielded clean reads. pmc-13464964:

pmc-13465064:

pmc-13465664:

pmc-13465964:

pmc-13466264:

pmc-13466964:

pmc-13467864:

pmc-13467964:

pmc-13468164:

pmc-13468364:

pmc-13468764:

pmc-13469664:

pmc-13470664:

pmc-13471364:

pmc-13471464:

pmc-13472064:

pmc-13472264:

pmc-13472964:

pmc-13473564:

pmc-13473664:

pmc-13473964:

pmc-13474364:

pmc-13474664:

pmc-13474764:

pmc-13474864:

pmc-13474964:
Yuanlei Gao and co-authors compare two airway devices in 2026 for orthopedic trauma surgery under general anesthesia. A trial of 198 adults split between a new noninflatable device and a standard gel device. A camera scope graded how well each lined up with the voice box right after placement. Seal pressure, placement time, and sore throat were also tracked.

The new device lined up well far more often at first check, about eighty-five percent versus sixty-five percent. Its edge held at one hour and again before removal. Success and placement speed matched between devices, as did seal pressure. Stomach tube passage was faster with the new device.
pmc-13478064:
Sihan Wang and coauthors published a 2026 randomized crossover trial testing whether endurance exercise changes eating in ways that blunt its blood sugar benefits. Fifty-four healthy college students completed five-day periods of moderate exercise, vigorous exercise, and no-exercise control in turn. Food was freely available and weighed daily, while blood sugar was checked fasting and after a glucose drink.

Neither exercise level raised total calorie intake. Vigorous exercise did cut vegetable intake by about 16 percent and raised added cooking oil intake. Both exercise levels lowered glucose after the test drink. The team also checked the exercise-diet pattern against diabetes risk in the UK Biobank cohort. The findings suggest compensation shows up in food choices rather than total amount, a nuance for exercise advice.
pmc-13478464:
Xin Lan and seven colleagues rebuilt in 2026 the human protein arginylation pathway inside bacteria. ATE1 is an enzyme that adds arginine to proteins, a tag that can mark them for disposal and shape stress responses.

By pairing ATE1 with human helper enzymes ADO, NTAN1, and NTAQ1 in E. coli, they turned starting forms of cysteine, asparagine, and glutamine into forms open to tagging. They found end-of-chain tagging efficient and favored over mid-chain tagging, with the brain protein alpha-synuclein tagged only rarely and no clear split between ATE1 forms. The bacterial setup gives a scalable way to measure which proteins ATE1 tags and how sharply it chooses.
pmc-13479564:
Gayathry R. Menon and coauthors published a 2026 comparison of how weather and air quality shaped COVID-19 spread in two Korean cities, Daegu and Seoul, during the first half of 2020. Nine meteorological and pollution factors were modeled with flexible curve methods that allow non-linear effects. Risk zones were identified by percentiles, and days were grouped by clustering.

Daegu's transmission was driven mainly by climate, with the model explaining about 63 percent of variation and risk rising at both temperature extremes. Its worst days averaged about 279 cases under cool, moderately dry conditions. Seoul showed a stronger pollution signature, with risk climbing steadily alongside temperature and two traffic-related pollutants. The authors argue pandemic preparedness plans must be tuned city by city rather than copied nationally.
pmc-13479864:
Abdmagidu Menya and coauthors published a 2026 interview study of how Ugandan health workers live the work of caring for people with disabilities. Workers hold the keys to fair care, yet many lack training for it. Thirteen staff in Luuka district were questioned in late 2022: nurses, midwives, lab workers, and clinical officers, plus four key voices from district and national health offices.

The title quotes a view heard again and again: patients with disabilities are seen as hard work. The talks dug into the knowledge gaps, time pressures, talk struggles, and views behind that stance. Workers told of making do without training or gear, and officials told of policy plans that rarely reach rural clinics. The authors use these accounts to spell out what training and service design must actually change.
pmc-13480264:
Meiqi Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study of low mood and unhealthy habits among Chinese teens, tracked over three years. The team surveyed 5,988 adolescents from 2022 to 2024 with yearly questionnaires. Eight habits counted as unhealthy, from smoking and drinking to poor sleep and heavy screen time, and a standard scale scored low mood at each wave.

Low mood in one year predicted more unhealthy habits the next year, while habits did not predict later mood. Mood paths split into three shapes: a large low group, a middle group that rose and fell, and a small group that peaked high. Teens in the two troubled groups carried more unhealthy habits by the final year than the low group. Early help for low mood may therefore cut later habit build-up, the authors argue.
pmc-13480864:
Adovich Rivera and co-authors compare biological aging across adult groups in this 2026 study. Sexual and gender minority adults face stigma that might wear the body down faster. Chemical clocks in DNA can estimate biological age. The team used a long-running United States heart cohort with blood samples from two time points.

The sample held 817 adults, about eighteen percent of them minority group members. Most aging clocks showed no clear gap between groups. One internal clock ran slightly faster for minority adults at the later point. Computer simulations checked whether biased dropout could fake that gap and suggested not. The authors call the overall evidence weak and ask for stronger studies.
pmc-13481964:
Ruijun Xu and co-authors offer a 2026 review of brain-computer interfaces as a tool against brain injury caused by radiation therapy. Such injury creeps in months after tumour treatment, harming memory, movement, and mood, while current care mostly eases symptoms. The review gathers database proof on how the injury forms and how interface systems might step in.

Promising roles include early detection through brain signal changes, calming inflammation, easing daily symptoms, and flagging complications before they bloom. Interfaces that read and nudge brain activity could one day tailor rehab to each patient's damaged circuits. The authors stay measured: most uses remain at the proof stage, and trials in this exact injury group are scarce. Still, the map of where the technology fits gives trial designers a starting grid.
pmc-13482364:
Adabara and colleagues build an intrusion response system in 2026 for hospital device networks that must answer not only whether it catches attacks, but whether its automatic reactions are safe for patients. Their framework layers three parts. A random forest detector flags suspicious traffic, a reinforcement learning agent picks one of four responses, and an ethics rule engine can veto unsafe actions. Every decision lands in an audit log for later review.

On its home dataset the triage agent scored a weighted F1 of 0.978, and the governance layer cut mistaken blocking of harmless traffic from 25.3 percent down to 17.3 percent of cases. Under shifted, unfamiliar traffic the scores fell hard. In replayed real-time streams the governed system still caused less decision harm than the ungoverned one, 0.434 against 0.502 on their harm cost scale. The authors stress these are simulations, not proof for live hospital use.
pmc-13483064:
Wu Wang and co-authors report a 2026 study linking resting brain rhythms to how finely people feel angles by touch. Eighty-one healthy right-handed adults rested with scalp electrodes on, then judged angle differences by fingertip. The team split the resting signal into five brief repeating patterns called microstates and timed how often each appeared.

One pattern, labelled A, predicted touch sharpness best: people whose brains visited it more often felt finer angle gaps. Its total time share and average stay pointed the same way. A model using pattern switch rates also held up, though no single switch stood out. Group splits echoed the pattern, with sharp feelers favouring A-linked switches. Resting brain tempo may quietly set the stage for touch skill.
pmc-13486664:
Diaz and team spent a week measuring waves washing up a terraced beach while running a detailed water model beside the instruments. Swash, the rush of water up the sand after a wave breaks, drives erosion and flooding, yet models rarely face week-long field tests. Their 2026 experiment combined laser scanners, cameras, and current meters on a low-tide terrace beach, then simulated the same days with the CROCO model in a wave-resolving mode.

The model reproduced the main swash rhythms and the extreme run-up events that matter for flooding. Small shifts in wave period, around one second, changed swash response surprisingly strongly in the sensitivity tests. Run-up grew with tide under calm conditions but shrank with tide when waves were energetic. Diaz flags weak spots, including simplified friction, while backing the model's overall robustness.
pmc-13487164:
Yi Li names a sugar-coated protein as an upstream driver of the growth signal that keeps colorectal cancer stem cells renewing. Published in 2026, data mining first flags SPOCK1, which makes the protein Testican-1, as a Wnt-linked marker whose high levels predict poor outlook and shorter benefit from first-line chemotherapy. Cell, graft, and patient-organoid experiments then test cause.

Lowering Testican-1 kept the signal carrier beta-catenin out of the nucleus, quieted its target genes, and curbed both growth and sphere formation. Raising Testican-1 did the opposite, and a targeted inhibitor erased the advantage, proving dependence on that pathway. Tumors engineered to overproduce the protein grew faster with more nuclear signal carrier inside. A druggable driver sitting above a famous pathway could matter for resistant disease.
pmc-13487964:
Xuexue Zhang and co-authors link a metabolic score for insulin resistance with new stroke in a 2026 national cohort study from China. The score combines routine measures such as blood sugar, fats, and body size. Data came from more than four thousand middle-aged and older adults followed to 2020, with the score tracked from 2011 to 2015 to capture both total exposure and change patterns.

People in the highest quarter of accumulated score had notably higher stroke risk than those in the lowest quarter. One change pattern, starting high then falling, also carried raised risk, which warns against assuming a drop erases past exposure. Blood pressure explained a small part of the link. The authors propose repeated scoring to sharpen risk assessment.
pmc-13488264:
Yang Zhu and co-authors review percussive therapy for recovery from exercise muscle damage in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Handheld devices deliver rapid tapping to sore muscle, and gyms promote them widely, yet dose guidance is thin. Twelve randomized trials through late 2025 were graded for bias and evidence certainty, with outcomes covering jump performance, maximal strength, soreness, and a blood marker of muscle damage called creatine kinase.

Jump recovery improved and the damage marker fell with treatment in pooled results, both with low or very low certainty. Maximal strength recovery and soreness relief showed no clear benefit in the reported analyses. Longer sessions hinted at better jump effects, while some dose patterns tied to worse soreness scores. The authors warn against treating dose hints as prescriptions.
pmc-13488564:
Yismaw Muluye Abate and colleagues identify risk factors for uterine rupture at the University of Gondar hospital in northwest Ethiopia in a 2026 case-control study. The tear in the womb wall is a leading cause of severe harm and death in childbirth in lower-income settings. Records from 2018 to 2022 covered 150 women who suffered a rupture and 300 comparison women who gave birth at the same hospital without one.

Living in a rural area raised the odds of rupture in adjusted models. So did long distance from the hospital and missing antenatal visits. Labor care without a partograph, a chart tracking labor progress, also raised the odds. Referral patterns mattered in the reported figures as well. The authors urge birth preparedness counseling and wider use of antenatal care and labor monitoring.
pmc-13489564:
Akbarzadeh and colleagues published a 2026 trial on psyllium fiber for fatty liver disease. Fatty liver tied to metabolism is now the world's commonest liver condition. Weight loss is the standard advice, but sticking to it is hard. The team gave 80 overweight patients psyllium or a look-alike powder for ten weeks.

Both groups followed a weight-loss diet and activity advice during the trial. Seventy-eight patients finished, with the fiber group faring better overall. Their waist size, weight index, and one key liver enzyme fell further. Liver scarring scores also dropped more in the fiber group. The authors present psyllium as a helpful add-on, not a cure. Liver function panels were checked before and after the program.
pmc-13490364:
Samuel O. Antwi and others evaluate genetic risk scores for pancreas ductal gland cancer, a cancer usually found too late for cure. In 2026, the study builds genome-wide scores with several statistical methods and tests them with thirteen published scores in an independent sample of over four thousand cases and forty-six thousand controls. Risk scores sum many small genetic effects into one number.

A score built with the LDpred2 method performed best, raising odds by about fifty-seven percent per standard deviation and improving discrimination beyond known risk factors. Crucially, it worked consistently across African, Admixed American, and EU ancestry groups, while the best published score worked only in Europeans. The work supports multi-ancestry risk stratification to target early finding.
pmc-13491764:
Siqi Wu and six colleagues review in 2026 how plant-derived vesicles, tiny particles shed by plant cells and loaded with active molecules, might be combined with engineered materials to repair skin. The particles are gentle on the immune system and carry useful cargo, but they degrade quickly, target poorly, and clear from the body fast. Pairing them with biomaterials is the field's current answer.

Combined systems are being tested for wound healing, sun-related skin aging, and inflammatory skin diseases. The review explains how the pairings calm immune overreaction, encourage new blood vessel growth, and restore chemical balance in damaged tissue. Clinical use still faces manufacturing and regulatory obstacles, which the authors map out alongside the scientific progress.
pmc-13493364:
Cheng Chen and six co-authors show in 2026 that tiny vesicles shed by stored red blood cells can stoke dangerous inflammation, and that an existing drug can mute them. Transfusing older blood worsens outcomes in critically ill patients, and these vesicles are prime suspects. The team characterized vesicles from human and mouse blood units and tested their effects on immune and vessel-lining cells, then in mice with sepsis.

The vesicles dialed up inflammatory signals through a known alarm pathway and left vessel cells dysfunctional, with effects growing by dose. In septic mice they deepened lung injury and cut survival. Calpeptin, a compound that blocks vesicle release, softened every one of those harms. The authors suggest filtering or blocking these vesicles could make transfusion safer for the sickest patients.
pmc-13493464:
Mustafa Akyurek and three colleagues evaluate in 2026 a muscle-flap trick for filling the hollow that can gape above the eye after upper eyelid surgery. Fat grafting, the usual fix for a sunken upper sulcus, can shrink unpredictably or, rarely, threaten vision. From 481 eyelid operations performed between 2017 and 2024, forty-five women also received a flap of the eyelid's own closing muscle, swung on a medial stalk into the hollow.

Early swelling and incomplete eye closure settled on their own in the flap group. Temporary numbness above the eye affected most flap patients yet faded within months, and no flap tissue died. Scarring at the inner eye corner troubled the conventional group more, with four patients needing revision. Satisfaction questionnaire scores matched between groups, and the authors call the flap safe and reproducible for selected cases.
pmc-13493664:
Ibba and a large Italian team report a 2026 real-world study of secukinumab, a biologic drug for psoriasis, tracked for up to seven years. Records came from 15 dermatology units covering 769 adults with moderate-to-severe disease who stayed on treatment at least four years. Effectiveness was judged with the PASI score, which grades how much skin is affected and how badly, and the team also logged every reported side effect.

Response deepened steadily over time, with about nine in ten remaining patients reaching at least 90 percent skin improvement by year six. Complete skin clearance also became more common as the years passed, and results held up in patients with other health problems or hard-to-treat body areas. People who also had psoriatic arthritis cleared fully at especially high rates in years five and six. No new safety concerns appeared over the long follow-up.
pmc-13494164:
Jiaxing Yang and Nan Gao write a 2026 editorial on how new gene-reading tools are reshaping study of the gut, its food, and its immune defenses. The gut lining meets food, helpful microbes, and germs at once, so its cells talk constantly with immune cells nearby. Single-cell methods read gene activity one cell at a time, while spatial methods keep track of where each cell sits.

The authors point to recent studies that used these tools to map gut cell types, spot rare cells, and trace signals between the lining and immune cells during infection and bowel inflammation. They argue that adding spatial maps and live labeling in animals can show true cell-to-cell contact, not just likely signals. That detail could reveal how nutrients steer gut immunity and where diet-based treatments might act.
pmc-13494564:
Eman Tadros, Thita Lamsam, and Chandni Anandha Krishnan offer a scoping review of relational therapy for people coming home after incarceration in the United States. About 600,000 people leave prison each year and face stigma, money strain, and tense family reunions, all of which can strain mental health and partnerships. Relational therapy treats ties with partners and family as the core of well-being, rather than focusing on the person alone.

Following standard review steps, the authors screened 304 articles and kept 19 for full review. Hard proof for relational methods in this group proved scarce. They found no tested therapy models that marriage and family therapists can pick up and use with people after release. The review ends with a call for research built for this population, arguing that family ties are often the ground on which a fresh start stands or falls.
pmc-13494664:
Ma, Wang, and Chen studied two predictors of cardiovascular events in people with high blood pressure, in a 2026 retrospective study. The predictors were how much blood pressure swings during a day and whether it fails to dip at night. Five hundred adults underwent twenty-four-hour blood-pressure monitoring and were followed for a median of four years. Variability was measured from the spread of systolic readings, and night patterns were classed as dippers, non-dippers, or reverse dippers whose pressure rises at night.

Ma found one in four patients suffered an event: heart attack, stroke, heart-failure hospitalization, or cardiovascular death. Patients with variable pressure had double the event rate of steadier patients, and high variability raised risk by about ninety percent after adjustment. Reverse dipping added risk, and patients carrying both problems faced the highest danger. The authors argue that monitoring reveals a pattern and should guide treatment.
pmc-13495164:
Weiqiang Wang and colleagues test, in a 2026 feeding trial, swapping corn silage for triticale silage in Pingliang Red Cattle on China's Loess Plateau. Corn silage there is squeezed by scarce water and rising costs, and triticale, a wheat-rye cross, offers a hardier forage. How the swap affects growth, digestion, and the rumen's microbes in this breed was unknown.

Thirty young bulls were split into five groups, from no swap to a full swap, over a ninety-day trial after a settling period. As the triticale share rose, gut enzyme activity, rumen fermentation, and helpful microbe groups improved, and waste nitrogen fell. Yet feed intake and daily weight gain slipped at high shares. A combined scoring method that weighs all measures at once picked a thirty percent swap as best: growth held near the corn-only level while digestion, metabolism, and rumen health all gained.
pmc-13495364:
Hui Zhang and co-authors hunt, in a 2026 study, for warning signs that the lens capsule will prove lax during cataract and glaucoma surgery in eyes with angle closure. A loose capsule raises the risk of complications mid-operation, and surgeons would rather know in advance. The team studied 241 eyes, sorting them after surgery by whether the front capsule, the back capsule, both, or neither had been lax.

Two in three eyes showed some laxity. Shallow front chambers and an acute angle-closure diagnosis predicted looseness of the front capsule. For the back capsule, the predictors were the same diagnosis, a missing support band behind the lens, and a thicker ciliary body. Prediction models built on these signs scored respectably. The authors offer the markers as a preoperative checklist, so teams can brace for trouble before the first cut.
pmc-13498564:
Malik Yussupov and a large veterinary team trace in 2026 where and when anthrax outbreaks struck livestock in Kazakhstan over a decade. Anthrax is a serious animal disease that can also infect people, and its spores survive for years in soil despite vaccine programmes. The authors mapped outbreaks from 2015 to 2024 against climate, soil moisture, and vaccination practice to find patterns that surveillance could use.

Thirty-three outbreaks were recorded, almost all in cattle, clustered in long-known endemic regions and peaking in summer and early autumn. Outbreaks persisted even where reported vaccine coverage topped high levels, suggesting gaps in practice or spore persistence at play. Human cases followed animal outbreaks and were mainly tied to unapproved slaughter and handling of infected animals, supporting risk-based watch that links weather, place, and targeted vaccination.
pmc-13501564:
Mateusz Okrutniak leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 study of why worker ants of the same species come in different sizes. The team examined endoreduplication, a process where cells copy their DNA again and again without dividing, which enlarges cells and the body. Earlier work linked this mechanism to size differences in ant species with distinct castes. Here the researchers tested three monomorphic species, whose workers look alike apart from size variation, and which differ in ecology, colony structure, and life history.

Individual worker size correlated positively with nuclear DNA content, in a mixed-effects model and within each species. DNA content also varied by body part, reaching its highest levels in the abdomen. The authors conclude that endoreduplication helps set body size even without castes. They propose it as a developmental mechanism that may have laid the groundwork for the worker polymorphism seen in other ant lineages.
pmc-13501764:
Liv Engel and others argue that rodent models should account for gender-like norms, not only biological sex. In 2026, the commentary distinguishes sex, grounded in chromosomal and hormonal traits, from gender, grounded in social norms, roles, and self, then challenges the assumption that rodents cannot express gender-like actions. Rodents are the most common preclinical model.

Sex-specific rodent actions shift with natural versus vivarium environments, cage type and enrichment, and cage social composition including rank and familiarity. The authors call these consistent, context-dependent patterns gender-like norms and offer design recommendations to measure them explicitly. Better models could improve reproducibility and protein building, where most drugs strong in animals fail in human trials.
pmc-13501864:
Rongqiang Yuan leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 genome-wide census of plant defensin genes in soybean. Defensins are small cysteine-rich peptides that form a first line of plant immunity. Searching the Williams82 version 4 genome with sequence matching and profile models, the team found 27 genes producing 31 protein versions. Family history sorted them into four subfamilies, the largest holding eleven genes, over 40 percent of the family. The genes scatter across thirteen of soybean's twenty chromosomes, with chromosome eight alone carrying six.

Three tandem clusters and nineteen collinear pairs show both local copying and a whole-genome duplication expanded the family, with all pairs evolving under purifying selection. Promoter scans found hormone response elements for jasmonate, abscisic acid, and salicylate in most genes. When plants met the fungus Fusarium oxysporum, eighteen of the twenty-seven genes changed activity, four sharply. The catalogue is offered for breeding disease-resistant soybeans.
pmc-13503064:
Abraham Kaggwa and others examine how morbidity changes the link between lifestyle and mortality in Korean adults. In 2026, the Health Examinee cohort analysis follows 111,537 adults aged forty to sixty-nine from 2004 to 2020. It joins smoking, alcohol, action, sleep, and diet quality into a weighted lifestyle score, stratified by no disease, one condition, or many ills. Over ten years median follow-up, 3,366 deaths occurred.

The least healthy third faced higher mortality than the healthiest third in every stratum, with hazard ratios of 1.40, 1.68, and 1.62 respectively, and stronger effects in women with many ills. At age forty, the least healthy group with many ills lost about five years of life in men and four years in women. Healthy habits matter even, and mainly, with chronic disease.
pmc-13503764:
Ömer Hatipoğlu and four colleagues compare two families of deep learning models that spot faulty dental fillings on X-rays, in a 2026 study. A filling that sticks out past the tooth edge can trap food and harm the gum, yet the flaw is faint on standard bitewing images.

The team marked 1,236 X-rays by hand and tagged each filling as sound or sticking out. One-stage models that scan an image once faced two-stage models that scan, then refine. All models found fillings well at loose overlap. Two-stage models held up better when tight overlap was required, which means cleaner edges. A refined two-stage model led on the faulty class.
