Bigger one-stage models did not help.
pmc-13503864:
Dongyu Liu leads a team comparing the carbon cost of budget chain hotels built two ways in Hangzhou, China, in a 2026 study. Hotels built from factory-made parts may cut emissions, yet shape also matters. The team read both forces together across the full life of each building.

They assessed 200 hotels, counting emissions from making materials through transport, building, upkeep, and demolition. Factory-built hotels cut carbon more, most clearly for neat shapes like rectangles. In both build types, a higher shape factor, which marks a less compact form, went with higher emissions per area. The authors say compact shapes and factory building together give the strongest savings for hotel chains.
pmc-13504564:
Xiaowei Xue leads a team reviewing what air purifiers do for health, in a 2026 systematic review. People spend most of their time indoors, where dirty air can build up from outdoor drift and indoor sources. The team gathered studies from 1990 to 2025 on purifier use at home.

Across the studies, purifiers cut indoor pollution levels by a clear margin. Health gains showed most strongly for breathing and heart outcomes, above all in high-risk groups like children and people with asthma. Proof for brain and thinking outcomes stayed thin. Study designs varied a great deal, which tempers firm claims. The authors judge purifiers a likely cost-effective step and call for device standards plus policies that widen access.
pmc-13505064:
Lulu Zhu leads a team pooling trials of virtual reality rehab after knee replacement for osteoarthritis, in a 2026 meta-analysis. VR promises engaging therapy after joint surgery, but single trials gave scattered results. The team asked whether VR beats standard rehab on pain, function, and quality of life.

Ten randomized trials with 588 patients met the rules. VR groups scored better on a joint function index at one and three months, yet the edge was gone by six months. A timed walking test also favored VR early. Knee bend range improved and held. Pain results split by scale, and quality-of-life data were too thin to judge. Wide differences between trial designs urge caution, and the authors ask for standard protocols and longer follow-up.
pmc-13505464:
Mi Hyeon Cho and her thirteen co-authors, publishing in 2026, profile single extracellular vesicles, the tiny parcels cells shed into blood, to catch lung cancer early. Vesicles carry cargo from their parent cells, but tumor signals are rare and vanish in bulk averages. Their workflow, Cygnus, images individual vesicles in cycles, reading many proteins per parcel and rolling the results up into a sample fingerprint.

In mice engineered to develop lung tumors, the system spotted a distinctive vesicle subgroup before scans could see any tumor. In a pilot group of 35 people, blood vesicle patterns separated cancer patients from controls. A three-marker combination was nominated for validation. The authors present single-vesicle profiling as a route to blood tests that report cancer while it is still curable.
pmc-13505964:
Sourish Mukhopadhyay and others overturn the view that urine scent marking is a male-only mouse actions. In 2026, the study shows that simple modifications to standard lab assays reveal exuberant urine marking by females, earlier excluded because no protocol stimulated female marking. Mice communicate largely through chemical signals in urine, conveying self, sex, rank, and reproductive status.

Both sexes marked toward a broad set of targets, including breeding-incapable partners, regardless of sexual motivation or partner self. Chemogenetic blocking of estrogen receptor-1 neurons in Barrington's nucleus showed both sexes use a similar mechanistic plan for marking. Sex parity reframes urine marking as broad social communication rather than a male-specific reproductive display.
pmc-13506964:
Divakar Budda, Coen van Hasselt, and Elizabeth de Lange ask if drug levels in brain fluid outside cells forecast receptor occupancy read by PET scans, for dopamine D2 ligands. Their past model frame joined body based drug spread, binding speeds, and receptor shifts. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

For one very fat loving drug, fluid based forecasts strayed far from scan reads. That gap points to drug build up in cell membranes as the true driver. The team gathered human studies with blood drug data and scan occupancy, across a range of fat loving traits. They then tested how fat loving nature, receptor shifts, and illness linked body changes sway forecast skill.
pmc-13507264:
Wei Yan leads a 2026 team that trains interpretable machine learning to spot skip metastasis in papillary thyroid cancer. Skip spread reaches side neck nodes while skipping the central nodes, defying the usual stepwise route. It appeared in about one in seven patients with side-node disease among 739 studied, and missing it distorts surgical planning.

Ten algorithms competed on routine clinical variables, with the XGBoost model winning across development plus two external cohorts. Calibration and benefit analyses held up well. Explanation tools ranked dissected central node count, side node burden, tumor site, age, and size as top drivers. Tailored neck surgery, sparing needless central dissection, is the practical payoff.
pmc-13508264:
D Erdody and four co-authors lay out a plan to standardize how scientists label the jobs of sugar-cutting enzymes, in 2026 work. These enzymes, called glycoside hydrolases, break down complex carbohydrates and matter for fuels, food, and medicine. Labs once found their roles by direct testing, but genome reading now names far more enzymes than testing can keep up with. Families overlap in what they cut, and test conditions and reporting vary widely. The review traces that shift from test-first to sequence-first discovery.

The authors catalog 169 measured enzyme activities, with the materials each one acts on and the methods used. They also build a substrate list for each enzyme family as a starting guide for testing new finds. Their roadmap calls for shared standard materials, uniform reporting, and open data pooling. The goal is annotation that can predict an enzyme's job before lab testing.
pmc-13508564:
Dana Aldughim surveys Saudi public views on gene editing as an answer to inherited disorders tied to marriage between relatives, in 2026 work. Such marriages remain common in Saudi Arabia and raise rates of diseases like sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia. The survey ran in late 2025 through messaging groups and an online form, reaching 139 people across the country. Seventeen questions covered awareness of CRISPR editing, views on related marriage and disease risk, and openness to editing as treatment.

About six in ten people had heard of CRISPR, yet over half showed little or no real grasp of how it works. Even so, more than ninety-six percent said they would accept editing-based treatment for inherited disease. Safety proof, religious considerations, and cost weighed most in their answers. Pairing public teaching with careful cell-based editing programs could cut the inherited disease burden over time.
pmc-13510064:
Basil Almutairi and colleagues test in 2026 whether placing a calming layer under whitening gel can speed up in-office tooth bleaching without losing whitening power. Sensitivity is the most common complaint after bleaching, and a potassium nitrate layer is meant to reach the nerve before the peroxide does.

Sixty extracted molars were split into three groups: peroxide alone, a two-layer method, and a mixed gel. Color was measured with a precision instrument after thirty and forty-five minutes. No group whitened significantly more than another at either time. Notably, the two-layer teeth at thirty minutes matched the others at forty-five. The authors say the layered approach may shorten chair time while keeping results, pending tests in real patients.
pmc-13510164:
Grace Clouse and nine co-authors test whether breathing in THC, the main active compound in cannabis, during early adulthood worsens bone loss after the ovaries are removed, in 2026 work. Young adult female rats breathed THC or plain air daily for eight weeks, then had ovary removal or a sham operation. Tissue was collected four weeks after surgery and scanned in fine detail.

Ovary removal alone cut spongy bone volume in the thigh bone, matching the expected menopause-like loss. Rats that had breathed THC before ovary removal lost far more, with spongy bone volume down sharply compared with the air and sham group. The authors read the pattern as a lasting THC effect that leaves bone more open to later hormone loss. They note the finding comes from rats and needs care before any reading for people.
pmc-13510664:
Amaury Bignaud and eight colleagues watch a virus genome fold and unfold as it infects a bacterium, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The phage attacks Pseudomonas, a germ known from hospitals. How phage DNA arranges itself inside a host was nearly unknown. The team mapped contacts in the DNA through infection.

The phage genome spread out fast and took a set shape. That shape matched which of its genes were switched on. The host genome, in turn, loosened as its own genes went quiet. Its transcription-based domains faded away. The phage also touched the host chromosome at set points. It seems to use the host's layout to run its own program. The work shows folding as a tool of infection.
pmc-13510864:
Lea Wagner and six colleagues published this 2026 study on uncoupling protein 2, a mitochondrial protein most abundant in the spleen, whose job was unclear. Using rats lacking the protein, with and without drug-induced high blood pressure from blocking nitric oxide production, the team examined spleen size and gene activity. Nitric oxide is a blood vessel signal, and its synthase gene turned out to be one of the silenced genes in the knockout animals.

Without the protein, spleens grew enlarged. Genes for mitochondrial energy machinery, including pyruvate dehydrogenase and reactive oxygen detoxifiers, were reduced. That profile favours sugar glycolysis and cell proliferation over mitochondrial burning. Blocking nitric oxide in normal rats mimicked much of the knockout pattern, tying the protein's effect to nitric oxide availability. Neither the knockout nor the hypertension changed inflammation. The authors conclude UCP2 steers fuel choice in spleen cells in a nitric-oxide-dependent manner.
pmc-13511464:
Fengxia Lin and co-authors build a DNA carrier for a heart drug in this 2026 study. Ginsenoside Rg1 comes from ginseng and can protect heart tissue. The compound reaches the heart poorly on its own. The team loaded it onto a tiny pyramid-shaped DNA frame tagged with a heart-seeking peptide.

The loaded frames held a uniform size and stayed stable in fluid. In mice with heart attack damage, they gathered in heart tissue after injection. Treated mice survived better and kept stronger heart function. Stress markers in cells fell, and fewer heart cells died. The platform may boost other natural compounds the same way.
pmc-13511764:
Dario Colacurci and nine co-authors review gene sequencing for newborns with brain dysfunction whose cause may not be oxygen shortage alone, in 2026 work. Several genetic disorders can mimic or accompany hypoxic injury in the first days of life. Three databases were searched through June 2026 for studies of infants in their first month who received sequencing, and study quality was graded with a standard scale.

Seven studies qualified, with wide differences in patient picking, sequencing style, and reporting. Diagnostic yield across sequencing studies ran from about a quarter to just over half of cases. Found changes fell in genes tied to developmental and epileptic brain disorders, metabolic and mitochondrial diseases, and broader developmental syndromes. The authors say sequencing can crack cases that look like birth injury, though shared standards are still missing.
pmc-13514464:
Mortadah Alsalman leads a nine-author team investigating blood transfusion patterns among people with sickle cell disease in a 2026 cross-sectional study from Saudi Arabia. Transfusion is a mainstay of care for this inherited blood disorder, and safe matching depends on ABO and Rh blood groups. The researchers interviewed 309 clinic patients and pulled laboratory values from their records, looking for traits tied to having ever received blood.

Nearly nine in ten patients had a transfusion history. Older age, other chronic illness, and higher platelet and red-cell size measures went with more transfusion, while higher haemoglobin and fetal haemoglobin went with less. Patients with group O blood had notably lower odds of transfusion than those with other groups. Blood groups showed no link to acute chest syndrome. The authors caution that their snapshot design cannot prove cause and effect.
pmc-13515064:
Yueting Cai and colleagues review in 2026 the double-edged role of zinc in fights between the human body and Gram-negative bacteria, a group behind many drug-resistant infections. Zinc is essential for both sides: immune cells need it, and bacteria need it to grow and cause disease.

The review explains nutritional immunity, where the host starves invaders of zinc or floods them with toxic amounts. Bacteria answer with import pumps and export systems that also shape their virulence, surface films, and survival. Because both attack and defense hinge on zinc balance, the authors argue that metal handling is a promising target. They suggest drugs that jam bacterial zinc systems could help against resistant infections.
pmc-13515364:
Xianli Tang, Yonghao Jia, and Yuandong Gu propose an improved electrical model for surface acoustic wave resonators in a 2026 engineering article. These tiny devices sit inside the radio filters of wireless gear, and designers need circuit models that predict their behaviour, including stray extra resonances and swings in temperature. The authors extend the standard Butterworth-Van Dyke model by adding isolation capacitances that let each stray resonance sit at its own frequency.

They then let two key parts of the model, the motional resistance and inductance, drift with temperature. The model was tested across a wide span from minus fifty-five to eighty-five degrees Celsius. Simulated curves matched measured device data closely. Stray-mode frequencies proved fairly steady near room temperature and moved mainly at the extremes. Tang's team presents the model as a practical tool for filter design under harsh conditions.
pmc-13515564:
Zenon Pogorelić and four colleagues report surgical results for osteochondroma, the most common benign bone tumour of childhood, in a 2026 retrospective study. Most of these bony outgrowths cause no trouble, yet pain, snagging, or looks can push families toward removal. The team reviewed seventy-five children and teens treated at one centre between 2015 and 2026, with seventy-six single lesions in total.

The median age was thirteen, and nearly two-thirds were boys. The thigh bone hosted almost half the lesions, and pain was the leading complaint, ahead of cosmetic worry. X-rays correlated well with the true size found in surgery but understated it, missing the cartilage cap. Outcomes were kind: about ninety-five percent had no complications, infections and blood collections were rare, and no tumour returned over a median follow-up of sixty-three months. Size and site did not predict symptoms, the authors note.
pmc-13516664:
José Bel-Lacoma, Ángela Aguilera-Rubio, and Roberto Cano-de-la-Cuerda review virtual reality tests of arm function after neurological disease in a 2026 systematic review. Stroke, Parkinson's disease, and similar conditions often rob adults of arm use, and playful VR systems promise engaging ways to measure it. Following a registered protocol for measurement studies, the team gathered every VR-based upper-limb assessment and graded its measurement quality with standard tools.

Twenty assessments surfaced. A virtual box-and-blocks test carried the deepest evidence and worked across all immersion levels, in both stroke and Parkinson's groups. An immersive action arm test showed the strongest measurement profile in stroke. Two systems stood out for lifelike daily tasks. Repeatability and validity were the properties most often checked. Most systems earned a middle recommendation grade, yet the certainty behind them stayed low.
pmc-13518364:
Dragos Daniel Țarălungă and co-authors review AI methods for reading fetal heart signals without surgery in a 2026 article. A fetal electrocardiogram tracks the unborn baby's heart, but the standard method is invasive. Electrodes on the mother's belly offer a safer route, yet the baby's signal is faint and buried under the mother's heartbeat and other noise.

The review gathered twenty-two studies from 2014 to 2025 and sorted the AI methods into four families. AI beat classic signal methods at extracting and cleaning the fetal signal. Some designs best preserved the signal's shape, while mixed designs added robustness. Six studies used AI for diagnosis, such as estimating heart rate or spotting rhythm problems. The authors flag scarce labeled data and missing shared benchmarks as key gaps.
pmc-13518864:
Tianhua Jiang and nine colleagues identify in 2026 a gene switch that keeps chrysanthemums in their squat winter rosette form during long cold spells. Perennials survive winter by halting stem growth and flowering, yet the coordinator of both pauses was unknown. Prolonged chilling acted mainly at the shoot tip in their experiments.

Cold switched on a gene called CmDREBa in the apex rib zone. The gene's protein turned on MAF genes, known flowering brakes, which together enforced the rosette habit and blocked blooming. When warmth returned, CmDREBa levels fell and growth resumed. Jiang and co-authors present the gene as a key seasonal regulator that breeders might tune for climate resilience.
pmc-13518964:
Yuzhao Huang, Hao Sheng, and Seyed Mohsen Sadeghzadeh blend three modifiers into asphalt binder in 2026 and test the mix against heat, cold, and fatigue. Roads rut in summer, crack in winter, and age in service. Their recipe combines dendritic fibrous nanosilica for reinforcement, waste rubber powder from old tires for elasticity, and waste cooking oil for flexibility.

Seven formulations went through standard tests, shear and bending rheometry, fatigue sweeps, and thermal checks. The triple-modified binder raised the rutting factor at 52 degrees Celsius and lowered cold stiffness at minus 24 degrees. It also kept more of its stiffness after 10,000 seconds of fatigue loading than plain binder. Each ingredient, the authors argue, covers another's weakness.
pmc-13520164:
Sercan Küçükkurt runs a controlled computer simulation in 2026 on tilted rear implants in the All-on-4 full-arch dental method. Tilting back implants is usually bundled with a shorter prosthesis overhang, so the tilt's own effect was confounded. Four 3D jaw models paired axial versus 30-degree tilted rear implants with two commercial implant designs, keeping the prosthesis identical.

Under one-sided chewing loads of 300 newtons, tilted models showed higher peak bone and implant stresses than straight models in every comparison. One tilted pairing produced the highest cortical bone stress and rear implant stress under molar loading. NobelActive designs consistently stressed implants and connections more than Straumann BL designs. Küçükkurt cautions the linear model shows trends, not clinical failure predictions.
pmc-13520264:
Negash Wakgari leads a seven-author review in 2026 of how people experience abortion care across sub-Saharan Africa, where tight laws push many toward unsafe procedures. Eight databases were searched for studies from 2010 to 2025, and 35 of more than 20,000 records qualified for summary.

Patients described delays, stigma, privacy worries, and false claims during care, plus guilt, sadness, and anxiety about future pregnancies. Relief, happiness, and contentment also surfaced often, hinting services still spare many the consequences of unwanted birth. Wakgari's team found no proven tools exist for measuring patient-reported abortion experiences in the region, and they call for building them as a research priority.
pmc-13520364:
Xuebiao Yang and colleagues report in 2026 on using CT angiography scans before surgery to choose blood-vessel flaps for rebuilding soft tissue around the knee. Vessel paths vary between people, so advance mapping could cut guesswork during the operation.

Sixteen patients with 17 flap procedures between 2014 and 2024 were reviewed. Every vessel chosen from scans was found as expected in surgery. Skin paddles survived fully in 15 of 16 scan-guided flaps, with one partial tip loss that healed without further surgery. One patient needed a different local flap after scans showed no suitable vessel. The series supports routine mapping for these reconstructions.
pmc-13520464:
Jennifer Pett and colleagues study in 2026 daily exposures that may drive a kidney disease of unknown cause in rural Sri Lanka. The illness clusters in farm villages. Men are hit most often. Field teams visited twelve villages with varied disease levels in two districts.

Teams noted housing, water sources and farm work on site. Villagers shared habits that are hard to see on a short visit. Men did almost all farm chemical handling. Many worked with no gloves or masks. Cost and travel time blocked steady use of filtered water. Well water stayed in daily use. High-rate villages leaned more on farm work and chemical use.
pmc-13522164:
Tingting Zhan and Hang Cao study early blood changes in advanced lung cancer in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Patients get immune drugs that block PD-1 or PD-L1 as first treatment, but lasting benefit varies. Static markers before treatment capture only part of that variation.

The team built a recovery signature from blood markers at the second treatment cycle, sorting patients into favorable, middle, and failure groups. Among more than four hundred patients, the failure group had less lasting benefit and more early progression than the favorable group. Survival without progression was also shorter. The combined signature did not beat single dynamic markers, the authors note, which tempers its added value.
pmc-13522464:
Yifei Guo and colleagues mapped how losing male hormones reshapes the adult human testis, using hormone-deprived testes as a natural test case. They combined three mapping methods: single-cell gene reads, chromatin access reads, and gene maps that keep tissue position.

The atlas flagged hormone-controlled gene switches that keep Sertoli cells, the nurse cells of sperm production, working properly. One factor, Neuregulin 2, made by Sertoli cells under hormone control, pushed sperm precursor cells to multiply in tests. Hormone loss also switched on a Sertoli marker in support tissue cells, nudging some toward a Sertoli-like state. Guo offers the atlas as a resource for treating hormone-linked male infertility.
pmc-13522664:
Xiangrong Cao, Linzong Xu, and Weiwei Ta tested a pain strategy that spares opioids in patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a throat cancer whose spread causes severe head and face pain. The pain mixes nerve damage and inflammation, so the team combined two non-opioid drugs aimed at each side: celecoxib and gabapentin. They compared thirty patients on the pair with thirty on extended-release oxycodone, reviewing the first two days of records.

The combined group reported a greater drop in pain scores at forty-eight hours. Their sleep improved far more, by the study's insomnia scale. Nausea and vomiting were absent in the combined group against twenty percent on opioids, while other side effects matched. The authors call the pair an effective opioid-sparing option, while stressing the study is small and backward-looking. Prospective trials, they say, should test whether the early advantage holds.
pmc-13523364:
Anusri Kadam and colleagues build a multi-task learning system that names tomato leaf diseases and grades their severity from one image in a 2026 study. Severity matters for treatment decisions, yet most earlier systems only classified disease type. A shared image backbone with attention-based refinement feeds two task branches, and a cross-task attention step lets disease and severity features inform each other. Partially labeled data were handled with a masking strategy.

On a public tomato leaf dataset, the system classified diseases with accuracy near ninety-eight percent and predicted severity at just over three quarters accuracy. Both scores beat leading single-task models and earlier multi-task designs. Checks confirmed the model looks at biologically meaningful diseased regions. The authors offer the framework as a complete tool for integrated plant disease analysis in the field.
pmc-13523464:
Yun Lin and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective cohort study on doula care during vaginal birth. Doulas are trained supporters who give emotional, physical, and informational help around birth. The question was whether adding doula support during labor shortens labor and improves maternal outcomes compared with standard perinatal care alone.

The study covered 2,095 women with vaginal deliveries. Doula support included music, a labor ball, birth dance, positioning cushions, massage, and breathing exercises. Labor was shorter at every stage in the doula group. Episiotomy and second-degree tears were less common, forceps delivery was less frequent, and bleeding in the first day after birth was lower. Amniotic fluid features and fever before delivery did not differ. The authors support wider promotion of doula care for safer natural delivery.
pmc-13524464:
Zechariah J. Malel and others assess, in a 2026 facility-based cross-sectional study, how involved male partners are in antenatal care in Juba County, South Sudan. Partner involvement is promoted as a way to improve maternal and newborn outcomes, support pregnant women, and encourage timely use of services. Involvement still stays low in many settings.

Women attending public antenatal services between November and December 2025 answered structured questionnaires. Just over half, 50.4 percent, reported a partner accompanying them to at least one visit. Women's education, partner age and education, health worker encouragement, and a welcoming clinic environment were each linked with involvement. Work commitments were the main barrier, named by about six in ten. The authors urge education and clinic changes to draw partners in.
pmc-13524764:
AlMuhanna and co-authors wrote a review from 2026 on advanced therapy medicines in Saudi Arabia. These are gene, cell, and tissue-based treatments that can address diseases once thought out of reach. Rich regions built rule systems for them years ago. Far less was known about how an emerging market such as Saudi Arabia handles them. The team reviewed the national drug authority's guidelines, past papers, and trial records from 2010 to 2025.

By 2025 the authority had approved eight such products, among them engineered immune cell therapies for cancer and gene therapies. Trial work keeps growing, clustered in cancer, blood disease, and rare genetic disease. Two national research centers lead local production of the immune cell therapies, and biobanks feed the wider effort. Gaps remain in trained staff, factory standards, and payment routes. Still, the team sees the kingdom on a path to regional leadership in the field.
pmc-13524864:
Yiting Li and others quantify, in a 2026 Medicare cohort study, dementia risk in older adults with advanced kidney disease and how that risk varies by race, ethnicity, and neighborhood. Vascular injury and chronic inflammation may raise dementia risk in kidney disease, possibly more in minoritized groups and deprived or rural areas.

The sample held 211,321 older adults with kidney disease stages 3 to 5 drawn from a five percent Medicare sample spanning 2010 to 2022. Adjusted models showed stage 4 raised dementia hazard modestly and stage 5 raised it substantially than stage 3. Associations were stronger among Black and Hispanic adults, and stage 5 risk was higher in high-deprivation neighborhoods. The authors suggest targeted early detection of cognitive decline in advanced kidney disease.
pmc-13525164:
Ang and colleagues studied in 2026 how long the front surface of the eye takes to settle after surgery for pterygium. A pterygium is a fleshy growth that creeps from the white of the eye onto the cornea, the clear front window. Their records came from a large hospital in the Philippines. Knowing when the surface is stable matters, because later eye surgery needs steady measurements.

The team reviewed 58 eyes operated on during 2022 and 2023, and tracked when shape readings stopped shifting. Half the eyes settled by about four weeks, about nine in ten by three months, and all by six months. Growths that reached farther onto the cornea took longer to settle. The authors advise waiting at least three months before cataract measurements, and about six months for the largest growths.
pmc-13525564:
Cecilia Catania leads a large team in a 2026 retrospective study of why seizures return in new-onset epilepsy, arguing that drug resistance is only part of the story. Recurrence can also stem from missed doses, inadequate treatment, nonepileptic events, or seizures provoked by acute illness. Mislabeling these as drug failure can drive needless treatment escalation.

Geneva University Hospital records covered adults diagnosed between 2005 and 2019, with 330 patients followed over five years. About 61 percent relapsed at least once, and 181 relapses followed the start of antiseizure medication. Only about a third reflected true drug ineffectiveness, while inadequate treatment led early relapses and poor adherence stayed common across years. Drug-resistant epilepsy was ultimately diagnosed in seven percent of the cohort. Seizure type at relapse also hinted at cause.
pmc-13526364:
Landrit Mehaj and co-authors report a rare late failure of a chest implant. A seventy-two-year-old man had his sternum removed for a low-grade cartilage cancer ten years earlier, rebuilt with titanium. After four quiet years he noticed redness at the scar's lower edge. The spot slowly opened into a channel leaking fecal matter to the skin, yet he waited four more years before seeking care.

Scans showed the titanium implant had migrated into the bowel. Surgeons removed the implant, took out the right half of the colon, rejoined the bowel, and braced the chest wall with a corset. The authors warn that survivors of such surgery need long-term imaging checks, and that even mild skin changes over an implant deserve a prompt scan.
pmc-13526864:
Aida Šermukšnytė and colleagues synthesized hybrid pyridine-triazole compounds and tested them against cancer and microbes. Published in 2026, the study built triazole-thiol derivatives and screened them in cell monolayers and 3D tumor spheroids against lung, triple-negative breast, and melanoma cell lines. New cancer drugs and new antimicrobials are both urgently needed as resistance grows.

Compounds with a dibromopyridyl fragment proved most toxic to cancer cells, and compound 34 led the set, killing all three lines at low micromolar doses. In spheroids, compound 34 slowed growth of breast and melanoma models, while two others cut viability without shrinking size. Compound 26 also beat a standard antifungal and matched a standard antibacterial in lab tests. Computer docking hinted at MEK and BRAF targets, awaiting lab confirmation.
pmc-13527164:
Erlich and colleagues built a glowing reporter test to measure, inside living cells, whether stray ribonucleotides embedded in DNA help the mismatch repair system fix copying errors. Ribonucleotides are RNA building blocks that differ slightly from DNA ones, and test-tube work suggested they can flag which DNA strand is newly made. Their 2026 assay places a deliberate mismatch near a single placed ribonucleotide in a reporter that lights up when corrected.

Erlich found that a nearby ribonucleotide clearly boosted mismatch correction in repair-competent cells, in either orientation along the strand. Cells lacking the repair system fixed the reporters weakly overall, yet still showed ribonucleotide-driven improvement in one orientation. Removing RNaseH2, an enzyme that normally strips ribonucleotides from DNA, only modestly blunted the effect. Its loss did not protect cells from a chemotherapy drug, implying other enzymes share this work and the pathway is a minor backup in mammals.
pmc-13527664:
Armina Fani and colleagues introduce, in a 2026 methods paper, MindGrab, a lightweight deep-learning model for skull stripping, the step that removes non-brain tissue from neuroimaging scans. Deployment complexity and high-end hardware demands keep many strong models out of routine hands. MindGrab was designed from spectral principles governing its dilated convolutions.

Across the tested datasets and imaging types, the fully convolutional model averaged a Dice overlap score near 95.9 percent, matching state-of-the-art accuracy while running up to forty times faster with far lower memory. Its small footprint allows full-volume processing on modest machines and even directly inside a web browser. Distribution runs through the BrainChop platform as an installable command-line tool and a zero-installation web application, aiming to widen access for clinicians and researchers.
pmc-13527964:
Zhuoling Bi and fifteen colleagues describe a 2026 gel-based cancer vaccine tested in mice. The idea is to turn a patient's own tumor into the vaccine source. A hydrogel placed at the surgery site holds two agents. One is doxorubicin, a chemotherapy drug that kills tumor cells in a way that alerts the immune system. The other is a charged polymer that grabs the released tumor proteins.

The polymer also helps those proteins escape inside immune cells, where they can be presented to T cells. Lab tests showed stronger dendritic cell maturation and antigen display. In mouse models of breast tumor recurrence, treated animals resisted both regrowth and tumors on the opposite side. Memory T cell responses rose as well. The authors see a flexible route to personalized immunotherapy.
pmc-13528064:
Zaid Bin Sahaq and twelve colleagues weigh early versus delayed dialysis start in sepsis with kidney failure in a 2026 meta-analysis. Starting renal replacement early may prevent fluid overload. Starting late may spare patients unneeded procedures. The team searched four databases through February 2026. Fifteen studies with 6,289 patients qualified. Four were randomized trials and eleven were look-back cohorts.

Early treatment linked with lower death at twenty-eight days. The risk ratio was about 0.81. A bias check weakened that result, making it non-significant after adjustment. Death at ninety days did not differ clearly. Organ failure scores and time in intensive care or hospital also matched. The authors say timing alone may not change long-term fate. They call for care matched to each patient rather than one rule.
pmc-13528864:
Rawa Bapir and nine colleagues published a 2026 case report of shrapnel that stayed in a patient's kidney for eighteen years. Retained foreign bodies in the kidney after blast or firearm injuries are rare, and they usually cause symptoms soon after the injury. A presentation delayed by years is a diagnostic challenge.

Imaging showed a 24 millimeter stone grown around the retained metal fragment at the left kidney's hilum, blocking urine flow. The kidney was severely swollen and contributed only 27.4 percent of total function. After a stent was placed by ureteroscopy, surgeons broke up the stone through a percutaneous procedure. The report, paired with a literature review, shows how blast fragments can surface as disease decades later.
pmc-13529764:
Kun Zeng, Yixiao Cao, and Hui Sun borrow a trick from bacteria to coordinate power grid agents in a 2026 paper. Bacteria sense crowd density by chemical signals, called quorum sensing. Each grid agent here sends one tiny number rating local urgency. A central trainer pools those signals during learning. The pooled view steers exploration noise for the whole team.

At run time the noise drops away. Each agent acts alone from its local network view, with no heavy message traffic. Tests used three standard grid cases, up to the 118-bus system. Rewards beat the best rival by up to twenty-five percent. Voltage breaches fell by thirty-one percent. Training finished up to forty percent sooner. Answers came in milliseconds and held up under noisy readings. The authors target grids rich in solar, wind, and batteries.
pmc-13530164:
Shenghua Qin, Yingjie Wang, and Shuyuan Chu build 2026 screening models for silent ischemic stroke that need no brain scan. Diagnosis normally rests on CT or MRI imaging, which primary clinics may lack. Health-check records supplied age, body measures, blood pressure, blood fats, blood sugar, and illness history instead.

Four learning methods trained on people with two stroke subtypes plus healthy controls. A random forest model performed best, with a neural network close behind. Blood pressure, blood fats, and fasting sugar carried the greatest weight. The authors suggest such tools could help front-line doctors flag hidden stroke for confirmatory imaging.
pmc-13530264:
Jialu Wei and colleagues explore in 2026 how losing a nerve-cell protein called NRSN2 affects memory in mice. Human work had tied the gene to a deletion syndrome with learning disability, yet its brain role stayed unclear. Knockout mice faced behavior tests, tissue measurement, and electrical recording at two young ages.

Mutant mice moved slightly awkwardly and performed worse on spatial and fear memory tasks by eight weeks. Brain wiring looked normal in shape, yet key receptor parts for a learning-related signal fell in the hippocampus. Signal flow and long-term strengthening weakened there, while a second brain region showed its own distinct changes.
pmc-13530864: Fatemeh Bonyadimanesh and Mohammadreza Abrishami tell of a tooth with neck root wear cured by root work and cuts. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The tooth also bore tip root wear. Care joined root canal work with a set plug at the tip, cut clean of worn cloth at the neck spot, and a seal of the flaw. The join of cures was need to clear the germ ill at the tooth.
pmc-13531164:
Chang-Lung Wu and co-authors published this case report in 2026. A healthy man of thirty fell ill with severe meningoencephalitis, a fierce swelling of the brain and its linings. He sank into coma, his lungs failed, and his body burned with inflammation. Blood tests over time showed an immune system in disarray: worn-out fighter cells, odd shifts in the cells that calm attacks, and a surge of antibody-making cells.

Care mixed standard intensive support with IVIG, pooled antibodies given by drip, and a hydrogen-based add-on the team calls HydroBox. The swelling eased fast, immune profiles moved back toward normal, and the man's brain function came back in full. The authors say tracking immune patterns over time can guide care in such crises, and that the pairing deserves wider trials.
pmc-13531964:
Chang Xiong and co-authors harness in 2026 tiny vesicles shed by dying eosinophil immune cells to repair fatty livers after blood-flow injury. Fatty donor livers tolerate transplant stress poorly. The vesicles carry working mitochondria, the cell power units, which merge with damaged ones in liver and vessel lining cells.

Treated cells recovered energy balance, grew better, and steered immune cells toward a calming state. A hydrogel patch built on amniotic membrane released vesicles steadily onto mouse livers, boosting vessel growth and liver cell division while damping inflammation. The patch offers a transplant-ready strategy for marginal organs.
pmc-13532264:
Elisa Piperni and co-authors recheck in 2026 stool samples from a feeding trial of two resistant starch types to see how each reshapes gut microbes. Resistant starch escapes digestion and feeds gut bacteria, with possible metabolic benefits. Shotgun gene sequencing compared two starch types against an ordinary digestible control.

Each type left a distinct yet temporary fingerprint. One boosted a keystone starch degrader and a partner species, while the other favored a common gut resident and an unnamed relative. Even strains within one friendly species split in response. Carbohydrate-handling genes rose broadly, supporting tailored fiber advice.
pmc-13533464:
Grzonka and colleagues survey how intensive care staff in Switzerland actually understand brain death, the legal and medical line their daily work depends on. The DISCOVER survey gathered 338 physicians and nurses from three hospitals, asking about diagnostic criteria, personal beliefs, and emotional attitudes. Their 2026 results show a workforce that knows the official rules well and rates its own understanding highly, with median self-scores near the top of the scale.

Beneath the confidence sit telling fractures: wrong ideas about which tests are essential persisted. Respondents firmly rejected the claim that a brain-dead patient is simply a corpse, scoring it near the bottom of the scale even while approving the diagnosis itself. Physicians approved of the concept more than nurses and treated brain death as the same as ordinary death more readily, while understanding grew with intensive care experience and case exposure.
pmc-13533564:
Despoina Kesidou and co-authors review the dark genome and its role in heart and vessel medicine, in this 2026 paper. Only about one to two percent of human DNA codes for proteins. The rest, long dismissed, holds switches, repeated stretches, and genes for non-coding RNA. These parts steer gene activity, cell identity, and disease risk.

The review covers the dark genome parts tied to cardiovascular disease. Non-coding RNAs get special focus, since their control roles are coming into focus. New genome tools have sharpened the links between these regions and heart traits. The authors argue that growing insight opens paths to targeted drugs for prevention and care. They stress that much of the map is still being drawn.
pmc-13533864:
Wafaa Alharbi and colleagues report in 2026 three new cases of Cousin syndrome, a rare disorder caused by changes in both copies of the TBX15 gene. The condition brings short stature, unusual face traits, and poorly formed shoulder and pelvic bones. Only six gene-confirmed cases had been reported before this work.

The new cases came from two unrelated families, each with a new gene change carried in both copies. Review of all cases shows common hip dislocation, fused arm bones, hearing loss from the ear canal, and eye misalignment. Learning ability varied a lot, so more case reports are still needed.
pmc-13534164:
Xiaojun Wu and colleagues build in 2026 a machine learning model to predict heart failure within one year after a heart attack. Current models rest on resting tests and miss how the body performs under effort. Their data held 3,172 patients from three hospitals who had exercise tests from 2018 to 2023.

After screening, 2,221 patients remained and one in ten developed heart failure. The best combined model scored very high in training and strong in outside testing. Adding exercise test data clearly improved sorting of risk, and a web calculator lets clinics flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13534864:
Sebueng Ramatsokotla and colleagues gather in 2026 forensic stakeholder views on adding point-of-care diagnostics to unnatural death investigations in South Africa. Fast bedside-style tests could speed scene and autopsy choices, yet legal and quality hurdles remain. Eight key stakeholders ranked benefits, enablers, and barriers in a structured group session.

Guidance for investigation, faster turnaround, and resource savings ranked as top benefits. Scientific validity, quality checks, and fit with legal rules were named as key enablers, while technical limits and legal uncertainty were the main barriers. Standard protocols and training were stressed.
pmc-13536564:
Sümer Münevveroğlu, Duygu Basegmez, and Hasan Burak Karaca run in 2026 a randomised trial comparing dry needling with two local anaesthetics for jaw muscle pain tied to jaw joint disorders. Trigger point care is common, yet direct comparisons in the face region are few. Seventy-five patients with active trigger points on both sides joined three weekly sessions.

All three methods cut pain, depressive symptoms, and disorder scores within one week. Mepivacaine gave the largest pain drop and beat dry needling clearly, while lidocaine matched dry needling. Longer follow-up is needed to judge lasting benefit and true ranking.
pmc-13536664:
In a 2026 survey, Bağdagül Al Kocaoğlu and Yasemin Özer Güçlüel measured how much health sciences students know about cancer. A total of 233 students completed a questionnaire and a standard awareness scale covering warning signs, risk factors, and screening. The study compares scores across student groups to find where knowledge is weakest and what teaching should address first.

Average awareness fell in the middle range, with the weakest scores for early warning signs of cancer. What students knew about risk factors and screening options also ran thin. Women scored higher than men, and students who exercised often or learned about cancer from health staff or coursework also scored higher. The authors recommend stronger practical teaching on warning signs and screening within health sciences courses.
pmc-13536764:
Dandan Kou and colleagues develop DNA markers for telling bamboo types apart in a 2026 genome study centered on moso bamboo. Looks alone often fail to separate close forms and species. The team scanned whole genome data for short repeating DNA stretches, then tested hundreds of marker pairs for variation across moso forms and related species in the same genus. Fingerprints and identity cards were built from core markers.

Millions of repeat sites were found, mostly between genes, with the most common type holding two repeating units. Tested markers showed moderate variation. Most genetic differences lay between species rather than within them, while moso forms stayed close with weak separation. Related species grouped into three clusters. The authors offer the markers for identification, conservation, and breeding work.
pmc-13536964:
Moustapha Faye and colleagues validate a Wolof kidney disease quality of life questionnaire in Senegal in a 2026 study. The thirty-six item tool must fit local language and culture before scores can be trusted. A total of 575 adults with mid-stage kidney disease or on dialysis, followed for at least three months, completed the version between June and November 2024. Structure, consistency, repeat stability, group differences, and sensitivity to change were tested.

Structure checks supported a layered general module plus three kidney-specific parts covering burden, symptoms, and effects. Consistency was sufficient and repeat stability ran moderate to good. Scores differed as expected between dialysis and non-dialysis patients and between men and women. Several parts also shifted clearly with change over time. The authors judge the Wolof version valid and reliable for Senegalese care.
pmc-13537464:
Anjana Subramoniam and co-authors examine heart rhythm activity during a daytime nap and its links to mood in younger and older adults in a 2026 study. Aging tends to lift positive mood and soften negative mood, and sleep plus body control systems may help explain the shift. Brain and heart signals were recorded during a midday nap, while mood ratings along pleasantness and arousal lines were taken before and after sleep.

Younger adults felt more positive about calm feelings than intense feelings after the nap, while older adults showed no such gap. Body control activity ran lower in older adults during wake and sleep stages. Higher activity in one rhythm band tracked with stronger positive mood after the nap, while the other band tracked the reverse. Mood before sleep did not predict rhythm activity.
pmc-13537764:
Jackson Scheib and a large team published a neuroscience study in twenty twenty-six on how mouse frontal cortex neurons encode movement differently in their dendrites and cell bodies. Layer five neurons receive input on tuft dendrites that can fire powerful local events. Whether those tufts carry information distinct from the cell's output was unknown.

Using two-photon calcium imaging during learning of a cued paw action, the team watched tufts and bodies in the same neurons. Bodies tracked both cues and action, while tufts mainly tracked cues. After movement errors, extra tuft activity appeared only when the mouse corrected itself. Learning changed tuft and body responses in opposite directions, suggesting separate channels for instruction and execution.
pmc-13538164:
Chen and five co-authors studied hormone testing in early breast disease in this paper from twenty twenty-six. Ductal carcinoma in situ is a non-invasive breast lesion. Hormone therapy after surgery may cut later cancer events, but use varies widely. The team linked a national breast register with drug records for over five thousand New Zealand women.

Only about fifteen percent ever had the estrogen receptor test that guides therapy. Testing peaked mid-period, then fell back. One region, Waikato, did most of the testing, tied to trial activity there. Of women with hormone-positive lesions, just a quarter started therapy. Their later event risk looked lowest, though not firmly so. The authors back standardized testing across regions.
pmc-13538264:
Yinhua Zhao, Jiaxing Ma, Bo Li, and Huang Lin published a review in twenty twenty-six on using energy devices, lasers and kin, to push drugs through scar tissue instead of injecting them. Thirty studies covered raised hypertrophic scars and keloids treated with fractional lasers, plasma radiofrequency, ultrasound, or thermomechanical injury paired with medicines.

For corticosteroids, device-assisted delivery matched injections on results while hurting less and risking less skin thinning, a particular mercy for children. Adding a chemotherapy drug improved scar thickness, and one photosensitizer combination showed strikingly low recurrence in acne scars. Keloids, stubbornly, still answered better to injected botulinum toxin than to laser-assisted delivery. The review maps where the needle can retire and where it cannot.
pmc-13539764:
Sudjit Liblub and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-six on a joint aid for mental health in pregnancy: peer support plus a mindfulness app. Pregnancy is a peak time for anxiety and low mood. Each aid has shown gains alone. Their mix was near untested. The team ran a four week pilot at a public hospital clinic in Australia.

A small group of pregnant women took part, and all stayed to the end. Stress fell in the general group next to the high risk group. Other gauges, from mood to felt support, did not shift in a clear way. Women praised the sense of kinship and calm the plan gave. They said they would commend it to others.
pmc-13539864:
Krakowsky and seven co-authors test adding a polygenic score to breast cancer risk checks for families with inherited risk, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Standard risk models blend gene faults with life and family factors. A score from three hundred thirteen common variants may sharpen those estimates. The team applies it to patients and their healthy relatives.

In healthy carriers of strong gene faults, median risk barely moves. Yet single estimates shift by up to twenty-five points either way. In affected carriers, risk to the other breast shifts widely as well. Among healthy relatives of test-negative families, a few cross into intensive screening. A similar few drop out of it. The score tailors prevention at the person level.
pmc-13540164:
Hélène Guegan and four co-authors show how a mold found in cystic fibrosis lungs wakes guard cells fast and strong. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The mold, Scedosporium apiospermum, is the next most known lung guest in this ill past Aspergillus. Human guard cells were faced with each mold for four and twelve hours, and gene use, flare signs, and mold life were read.

The Scedosporium mold lit more flare paths and three times more genes at four hours than its kin mold. Its spores were also killed more by six hours past touch. Flare signs like IL-6 and TNF ran high. The team say the fast flare may clear the mold yet harm the lung.
pmc-13540864:
Frederike Basedow and co-authors studied who fails to answer patient outcome surveys in Swiss rehabilitation in two thousand twenty-six. Such surveys add the patient's view to quality checks, but missing answers can bias results. The study spans cardiac, psychosomatic, and pulmonary rehab.

They used routine data for tens of thousands of patients treated between two thousand sixteen and two thousand twenty-two. Non-response was highest for the heart and lung surveys, near a quarter or more. It linked strongly to a proxy for non-native language, care-home stays, and discharge to acute care. Older age, worse health, and lack of extra insurance also mattered. Clinic differences explained much of the gap.
pmc-13540964:
Kaitlyn Carver and colleagues tested one dose of weed killer on mouse memory and brain firing. Published in 2026, the study gave male and female mice a single oral dose of glyphosate at 0, 250, or 500 mg per kilo and ran a new-object memory test. Glyphosate, the main agent in Roundup, reaches the brain and may harm genes, yet single-dose effects on learning were murky.

No strong proof emerged that the weed killer impaired memory overall, though females on the top dose failed to favor the new object over the known one. DNA breaks in the memory hub fell at the top dose in both sexes, yet early-gene firing fell only in males. The authors read the split pattern as a complex sex-linked effect needing more work. Readers get a caution that one weed-killer dose may not act the same in both sexes.
pmc-13541564:
Mohammed Mhanna and colleagues present a 2026 case report. The patient was a 63-year-old man. He developed a pause-dependent heart block after repeat surgery. The surgery redid his aortic root. His history held valve replacement and a Bentall procedure. It also held infection of the prosthetic valve.

Monitoring showed early extra beats triggering the block. This was phase 4 block, a failure after long pauses. High-grade block and long gaps followed. A chaotic fast rhythm appeared over two days. A temporary pacemaker steadied the rhythm by shortening pauses. He later received a leadless pacemaker with success. The authors stress early recognition of this pattern.
pmc-13542164:
Abdu Salam and colleagues design a protected control system in 2026. The setting is water distribution networks. Industrial internet devices run those networks. Sensors and controllers automate the flow of water. That same wiring opens doors for attackers. Attackers can falsify readings or hijack commands.

Sensor data goes onto a permissioned blockchain. Records there cannot be quietly rewritten. Smart contracts verify the identity of each device. A hybrid detector watches the data stream for attacks. It fuses cyber signals with physical signals. Tests used three public benchmark datasets. Detection scores beat classical and modern rivals. Transfer between systems varied with sensor density.
pmc-13543064:
Hong Zhao and co-authors review a force-sensing channel that links physical load to bone and muscle health in this 2026 paper. The channel, called Piezo1, sits in cell membranes in bone, cartilage, muscle, and tendon. When tissue is pressed, stretched, or sheared, the channel opens and lets calcium in, starting signals that steer cell growth and repair.

Under normal loads the channel helps keep these tissues in balance. Under heavy or constant load it can fire too much, upsetting calcium levels, feeding inflammation, and pushing cells toward death. The review ties that overdrive to joint wear, bone thinning, muscle injury, and tendon breakdown. It also surveys early attempts to aim drugs, gene methods, and stem-cell approaches at the channel in lab models. The authors say the channel's roles differ by tissue and need more study before clinic use.
pmc-13543164:
Zainab and co-authors published this 2026 perspective on the modern management of thalassemia, an inherited blood disorder that cripples red cell production. Lifelong care rests on regular transfusions, drugs that strip out the iron those transfusions leave behind, and wide supportive care; stem cell transplant can cure a lucky few. Newer gene therapies remain fenced in by cost, access, and unproven long-term safety.

The review walks through standards for both alpha and beta forms, then spotlights a newcomer. Mitapivat, an oral pyruvate kinase activator recently approved by the FDA, coaxes red cells to work better. Drawing on guidelines, trials, and regulatory sources, the authors weigh where the pill fits beside luspatercept, hydroxyurea, and gene therapy. Their message is cautious optimism.
pmc-13543364:
In a 2026 study, Élise Arsenault Knudsen and colleagues tested whether nurses who sit centrally in a unit's communication network view teamwork more positively during practice-change efforts. Two intensive care units took part: 145 nurses completed a teamwork survey and a sociometric survey naming who they communicate with about changing practice. From those answers the team calculated each nurse's centrality and coreness in the network, then compared network position with teamwork scores.

Teamwork perceptions were high overall. Yet few links between centrality and teamwork scores reached significance, in the whole network or in smaller subnetworks. Nurses who talked closely with each other did not hold similar views of teamwork, either. The expectation that central nurses would rate teamwork highest was not supported. Communication structure and felt teamwork, the authors suggest, may influence improvement work through separate paths.
pmc-13543564:
Eric Kim, Sara Diaz Saravia, and Gagan Sahni published a 2026 case report of fulminant heart inflammation caused by talquetamab. The drug, a bispecific antibody for multiply relapsed myeloma, produced an illness that mimicked a heart attack. A 69-year-old man developed fainting and chest pain four weeks after starting the drug. Tests showed heart-damage markers, new tracing changes, and a weakened heart on ultrasound, yet vessel procedures and a heart biopsy found no blockage or clear culprit.

Heart MRI showed the swelling and scar pattern of acute myocarditis, and high-dose steroids began. He improved briefly, then deteriorated despite four further immune-suppressing treatments, and his heart function kept falling until he died. Immune myocarditis is known with checkpoint drugs; this case warns that newer T-cell-engaging antibodies can trigger the same catastrophe and may not yield to standard escalation.
pmc-13544364:
Zhang and coauthors tag gene carriers with a glow dye to track them in the body. Branched polymers can carry genes into cells without viruses. Their fate in the body has been hard to track live. A near-infrared dye can be watched through tissue.

The team bound the dye to the polymer at rising doses. Six dye levels gave six tagged polymer forms. Tests checked that tagging kept gene binding strong. Gene packs from each form were gauged for size and charge. Tagged packs were then tracked in live animals. Safety checks weighed organ harm from the packs.
pmc-13544864:
Adhya and colleagues write to the editor in 2026 about a 65-year-old man whose illness imitated dementia with Lewy bodies almost perfectly. It matched down to a signature brain scan pattern, yet turned out curable. Over a year he had slowed, stiffened, and lost balance, with apathy and failing attention, plus three episodes of clouded consciousness lasting days, formed visual hallucinations, and dream-enacting sleep behaviour. His PET scan showed the cingulate island sign, a metabolic pattern treated as a fingerprint of Lewy body dementia.

The true culprit was his liver: cirrhosis of unknown cause had opened a portosystemic shunt. That is a detour letting gut blood bypass the liver's filter and poison the brain, a condition called acquired hepatocerebral degeneration. Treating the shunt produced a striking recovery, the letter's central drama. Their case argues for liver imaging in atypical parkinsonism with fluctuating consciousness.
pmc-13545264:
Rukundo and colleagues release annotated image datasets meant to teach robots to spot batteries hiding inside electronic waste, a fire hazard that plagues recycling plants as lithium cells spread through gadgets. Their 2026 data paper describes the first release from the XBAT+ project. Workers pulled small battery-containing devices from cages of general e-waste at recycling facilities and collection events. They sorted them into categories and photographed them with ordinary cameras and X-ray imaging, which sees the battery inside a sealed casing.

From fifty initial categories, a frequency rule kept fifteen, covering 421 devices and just over three thousand images. They were organised into quality tiers and split into training and test portions, with a fifth held back for testing. Two modern detection models trained on the data reached promising accuracy and recall for device identification and for the simpler battery-versus-no-battery decision.
pmc-13546664:
Plamen Bokov and eight co-authors test two airway exams in children with sleep apnea in a 2026 study. A European statement had suggested both exams may help manage the condition. One uses sound echoes to size the throat, and the other uses head X-ray measures of jaw and airway angles.

The study enrolled 205 children sent for treatment of moderate to severe apnea. Each child had both exams in sitting and lying positions where relevant. The team compared exam indices with the standard count of breathing pauses per hour. Children with enlarged tonsils formed one large subgroup in the sample. Results show how far these quick exams track disease severity before treatment begins.
pmc-13547164:
Lou Thomas and co-authors present a 2026 study of how autistic and non-autistic children make quick perceptual choices. The team asked whether autistic children can bend their strategy when a task pushes speed over accuracy, or the reverse. Past results with decision models in autism had been inconsistent.

Fifty children in each group, aged six to fourteen, judged visual orientation and motion under different instructions. A decision model split their choices into parts such as evidence gathering and caution. Across tasks and modelling styles, no firm group differences appeared. Autistic children adjusted their strategy to the instructions, which the authors read as evidence that flexibility is not uniformly reduced in autism.
pmc-13547564:
Tae-Young Ha, Seung Min Lim, Hyunjun Park, and Keun-A Chang traced in 2026 a small RNA whose loss helps kill neurons in Alzheimer's disease. In the hippocampus of mice bred to develop the disease, the regulator miR-204 was sharply reduced. Its direct target turned out to be NPTX1, a protein that rises when miR-204 falls silent.

Blocking the remaining miR-204 worsened everything, while restoring it, or silencing NPTX1, preserved the energy factories and kept neurons alive. The authors propose restoring miR-204 as a therapeutic idea for Alzheimer's and related oxidative diseases.
pmc-13548264:
Nuran Aypar Akbağ and Buse Güler survey how Turkish women cope with monthly symptoms and how coping tracks with partner fit and felt support, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Three hundred ninety-five women filled online scales in late two thousand twenty-three into early two thousand twenty-four. Near a third screened as likely severe cases.

Partner fit ran lower in the likely severe group. Self-care and harm-dodging coping tied to better partner fit. Talking coping tied most to felt support gains. Energy-tuning coping cut the other way on fit. The authors urge routine screening and partner-inclusive teaching. Readers get coping styles with social prices and prizes attached.
pmc-13549164:
Artor Pogosean and three colleagues published this 2026 pilot study asking whether muscle ultrasound shows structural change in junction disorders. The junction is the nerve-muscle connection. These disorders are seen as functional rather than structural diseases. The team looked back at 18 patients with the condition. They had congenital myasthenic syndromes or autoimmune myasthenia. All had electrical testing and ultrasound scored against standard values.

Electrical testing flagged 13 of the patients. It was normal in 14. Only 4 patients showed abnormal or borderline muscle brightness, including two with myasthenia gravis. Every patient with an abnormal scan also had abnormal electrical findings, never the reverse pattern alone. The authors read this as a sign that muscle change does occur in some junction patients. But ultrasound is far weaker than electrical testing. At best it complements that testing for tracking disease.
pmc-13551764:
Víctor García-García and co-authors published this case series in 2026. It tries focused radiation as an alternative to brain surgery for stubborn temporal lobe epilepsy. Removing the seizure source works, but risks memory and language, and many patients refuse or cannot risk it. Seven patients with drug-resistant one-sided disease got a single high radiation dose aimed at the hippocampus, delivered by a linear accelerator. Seizure counts were tracked for twenty-four months.

Median monthly seizures fell from twelve to three and a half, a cut of about three quarters. No patient became fully seizure free. Still, about seventy-one percent kept at least a halving of seizures across the follow-up. The team frames radiation as a gentler fallback for patients shut out of surgery. pmc-13552364:
Benatar and coauthors argue ALS trial claims often outrun the proof. Early trial data have long been used to claim patient gains. Those claims then fail in large final trials again and again. The team blames flawed logic fed by skewed rewards.

Faults hold false base claims and misuse of lab marks. Design may clash with the stated trial goal as well. Cherry-picked results and post hoc cuts add to the skew. Open-label follow-up data get more weight than they merit. Rosy framing of weak data caps the list of faults. The team urges tighter rules for claims and reports.
pmc-13554064:
Manish Jangra and eleven colleagues test foliar salicylic acid and silicon sprays on sorghum under salt stress. Foliar salicylic acid and silicon improved water content, chlorophyll, and yield traits and reduced damage markers under salt stress. The pair thus eased salt damage and raised stress tolerance in greenhouse sorghum. Field trials and molecular work are still needed to confirm long-term gains.
pmc-13554264:
Nima Mohammadizadeh, Alireza Tabarsa, and Mohammadhadi Aryaie Monfared test paper sludge ash as a soil strengthener for building in a 2026 study. Paper mills produce ash waste that often ends up dumped. The team mixed ash into clay soil at four rates and cured samples for up to twenty-eight days. Tests covered packing, stiffness, crushing strength, acidity, and fine structure.

More ash lightened the packed soil while raising the water it wanted. Bending behaviour eased as ash and curing time grew. Crushing strength climbed with ash, curing, and packing density, peaking near twenty times the raw soil's strength. Acidity rose with ash, then drifted down as curing lengthened. Microscope views showed the ash reshaping the soil's inner structure.
pmc-13554364:

Shrinking tissue marks Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, and foreseeing its pace aids research. Models using past change beat single-scan models at every target. Adding age, sex, a risk gene, and diagnosis helped further. Top correlations ran strongest for shrinkage of the memory hub. A second cohort in Australia confirmed the pattern. Forecast shrinkage flagged people headed from normal thinking to impairment better than today's sizes did.
pmc-13554764:
Takahiro Tokuda leads a nine-author team weighing a calcium-drilling step before balloon treatment of hardened leg arteries in a 2026 study. Thick calcium blocks balloons from opening thigh and knee arteries fully. Records covered 582 fresh lesions with the heaviest calcium grades. After matching, 153 lesion pairs compared drug-coated balloons alone against drilling plus balloon.

Drilled lesions ended the procedure with less leftover narrowing. One year on, drilled arteries stayed open more often than balloon-only ones. By two years the edge had faded and no longer stood firm. Adjusted models still favoured drilling modestly for lasting openness. Complications ran higher with drilling, chiefly debris washing downstream, so the authors advise selective use.
pmc-13554864:
Ahmed Eisa and three colleagues report a hidden heart wiring fault unmasked by exercise in a forty-three-year-old man in a 2026 case report. The active man had felt dizzy spells and palpitations with no prior heart complaints. A treadmill test provoked bursts of extra beats that escalated into a dangerous rhythm as he recovered. Scans then revealed his right coronary artery branching from the wrong side, threading between the great vessels and through the artery wall.

Such routes can squeeze the vessel during effort and trigger sudden death. Surgery to unroof the trapped segment fixed the fault, and his symptoms cleared at follow-up. The authors urge artery scans for adults whose exercise tests stir dangerous rhythms.
pmc-13555064:
Ricardo Fernando Cosio Borda leads a large team comparing mango exports from Peru and Colombia across two decades in a 2026 study. Mango holds strategic weight in tropical fruit trade, yet growth lasts only with spread markets and steady demand. Trade, bank, and distance data from 2004 to 2024 fed several measures of advantage and buyer power. A gravity model tested what drives export flows.

Peru's mango exports grew about eightfold and kept a competitive edge throughout. Colombia's grew far faster in percentage terms, yet its edge turned positive only from 2020. France, Spain, the Netherlands, and the United States stood out as the strongest demand markets. Bigger economies, larger destination populations, and trade deals all lifted exports in the model. Peru looks consolidated, Colombia still expanding.
pmc-13555564:
Atsuta Ozaki leads a sixteen-author team transplanting lab-grown retinal tissue into monkeys with macular damage in a 2026 study. The grafts came from human stem cells edited to lack their own signal-relay cells. Host relay cells in the monkeys' eyes were the test: could they wire into the graft's light sensors? Laser injury first stripped the central retina of its sensors.

Host relay cells stretched new arms toward the graft and formed working connections. Electrical tests showed signal flow in some eyes. In two of four grafted eyes, one relay path improved by up to about a fifth and held steady for two years. A second path matured slowly in one eye after thirteen months. Durable wiring in the primate macula is shown for the first time.
pmc-13555964:
Michail Delis leads a seven-author team pooling evidence on how celiac disease affects menstrual and hormone health in a 2026 analysis. Celiac disease, an immune reaction to gluten, harms the gut and can ripple outward. Three databases were searched for studies up to August 2025. This is the first full pooling of the topic, the authors note.

Girls with celiac disease reached their first period about two thirds of a year later than peers. Abnormal womb bleeding was about twice as likely, and absent periods about four times as likely. Menopause timing did not differ clearly between groups. Gluten-free eating showed no clear link to first-period age. Blood hormone levels, surprisingly, matched controls across every marker tested.
pmc-13556964:

The virus HSV-1 already draws interest as a tumor-killing agent thanks to its copying power, big cargo room, and mild toxicity. A variant that fuses infected cells into giant syncytia hits tumors harder and longer.

The authors trace the path from molecule to clinic, weighing what must be solved before the therapy can spread. The survey aims to guide teams building fusion-based oncolytic drugs.
pmc-13558564:

Their 2026 study trains on 850 patients from Union and validates on 403 from Hefei and 217 from Shihezi. Seven time-to-event models were tested, with SHAP used to explain predictions.

SHAP flagged CEA, CA125, age, MPV, CA19-9, INR, and monocyte count as top predictors. The model helps oncologists spot high-risk patients early for tailored care. Routine blood indices thus offer a convenient path to accurate survival prediction.
pmc-13558764:
M. A. Madshal and three colleagues melted in 2026 a family of phosphate glasses laced with increasing selenium to make a better gamma radiation shield. Seven compositions replaced part of the sodium oxide with selenium, at levels from zero to thirty mole percent. The glasses were checked with diffraction, infrared and electron imaging, and light spectroscopy. Computed shielding figures covered a wide energy range.

Diffraction confirmed every sample stayed glassy rather than crystalline, while infrared spectra showed selenium rearranging the phosphate network. Added selenium darkened the optical response, narrowing the band gap, raising the refractive index, and packing the glass denser as molar volume shrank. Shielding improved in step: at the lowest test energy the mass attenuation multiplied several fold, and the thickness needed to halve a beam fell throughout. The authors propose the glass for protective windows and enclosures.
pmc-13559264:
Wu and colleagues ran a 2026 multicentre trial comparing two ultrasonic devices for sealing lung blood vessels during keyhole chest surgery. Sealing vessels five to seven millimetres wide is hard because staplers are bulky in tight spaces and clips can slip. The trial tested a new Y20 device against the widely used Harmonic HD 1000i.

Patients having a lung segment or lobe removed were assigned at random to one device, with branding hidden from outcome assessors. Sealing succeeded in all ninety Y20 cases and in eighty-eight of eighty-nine control cases within a ten minute watch for bleeding. The small gap sat well inside the preset limit, so Y20 counted as not worse. Blood loss, surgery time, drainage, and complications were also tracked.
pmc-13559464:
Carlos D Solano Iglesias and four colleagues map published findings on chemical pleurodesis for non-traumatic chylothorax, a rare condition where milky lymph fluid collects around the lung. Their 2026 scoping review followed PRISMA-ScR guidance and screened studies under blinded review. Most chylothorax cases trace back to cancer, and standard first care, drainage plus nutrition support, fails fairly often.

Across the literature, sealing the pleural space chemically, most often with talc, controlled the fluid in a high share of selected patients. Major complications stayed uncommon, giving the procedure a favorable safety profile in these reports. Success depended on picking suitable patients, on the underlying cause, and on the lung re-expanding fully. Even so, the authors found the option underused, partly because high-quality trials and shared selection criteria are scarce. They place pleurodesis inside a combined strategy and call for studies that pin down timing and benefit.
pmc-13559564:
Xiu Chen and colleagues compare two thyroid cancers at single-cell resolution: medullary carcinoma, an aggressive type from hormone-making C cells, and papillary carcinoma, the commonest thyroid cancer. Their 2026 exploratory study sequenced tissue from one patient of each type, profiling over nineteen thousand cells between the two samples. Follow-up lab tests checked two transcription factors in cell lines and tissue.

The medullary sample carried more epithelial and fibroblast compartments, while T cells and natural killer cells clustered mainly in the papillary sample. Two regulators, CEBPB and PAX8, showed their strongest activity in a poorly differentiated epithelial cluster yet faded along its developmental path. Laboratory assays confirmed both ran lower in medullary tissue and cells. The authors propose that losing these factors may weaken immune surveillance in medullary cancer. They stress the work is hypothesis-generating, built on just two tumor samples.
pmc-13560664:
Ryan and co-authors wrote a 2026 protocol for applying OPTIMA-ID, a prescribing checklist built for older adults with intellectual disability, to Irish longitudinal ageing data. The team translated the criteria into codable statements and built computer functions in the R language to apply them. Of sixty-seven criteria, fifty-two could be applied to the fifth wave of the Irish intellectual disability ageing dataset. Ryan explains each function returns true or false for whether a criterion is met for a given participant. Where a criterion fails, the responsible medicine is identified by its standard drug classification code for follow-up.
pmc-13562264:
Arruda and colleagues hunt in 2026 for warning signs of alcohol use disorder in patients who have had Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. After this weight-loss operation, alcohol problems often go undetected because screening relies on self-report.

The single-center Brazilian study analyzed 130 adults who completed two standard alcohol questionnaires during routine follow-up. About a quarter screened positive on the stricter questionnaire. Two factors independently predicted a positive screen: being male, and having a father who used alcohol, each raising the odds roughly fivefold. A simple model using only those two factors sorted patients from low predicted risk, under one in ten, to high risk, three in four, when both factors were present. A liver enzyme was higher in screen-positive patients but failed stricter statistical correction, and the authors require outside validation before clinical use.
pmc-13562664:
Oluwatofunmi Jemima Bankole and nine colleagues compare activity of two genes in Nigerians with type 2 diabetes and in healthy peers. Both genes, APOL1 and NOTCH2, have been tied to blood sugar handling, body fat, and diabetic complications. Patients showed the pattern of higher glucose, worse long-term control, and more insulin resistance. Their APOL1 activity ran lower than controls, while NOTCH2 activity did not differ. Lower APOL1 tracked with lower glucose and control markers, an inverse pattern worth follow-up. NOTCH2 dipped with age and glucose. The team argues that molecular readings add value beside clinic measures, especially in African populations that diabetes genetics has skipped.
pmc-13563064:
Qing Du and six co-authors map how depression, thinking problems, and disability intertwine after stroke, in a multicenter cohort study from twenty twenty-six. Depressed mood and psychiatric anxiety sat at the network's center. Suicidal thinking, loss of interest, anxiety, and the disability score bridged the clusters.
