Disability tied positively to suicidal thinking and lost interest, and negatively to language. Brain lesion mapping in an imaging subgroup pinned language trouble to one left-side fiber region. The mood symptoms showed no single lesion site, pointing to spread-out network failure instead.
pmc-13563964:
Chen Wang and colleagues pool, in a 2026 meta-analysis, twenty-nine randomized trials of exercise for sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle and strength, covering 1,524 patients. Trials were sorted by how closely their exercise programs matched American College of Sports Medicine guidance, then outcomes for muscle mass, strength, and movement tests were compared.

Programs with high guideline compliance improved the muscle mass index and showed gains on some strength and sit-to-stand measures. Grip strength results shifted with the cutoff used, and walking tests showed no clear advantage, so several findings remain unstable. Clinicians get a careful case for following established exercise dosing rather than assuming any activity works equally.
pmc-13564964:
Silla George Raju, Ramin Hosseinnezhad, and Andrzej Galeski study how mixing speed shapes the foam structure of a plant-based plastic in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The plastic, PLA, was foamed with two fillers: a clay in tiny tubes and a Teflon-like plastic. A twin-screw machine made the foams at speeds from slow to fast.

With the clay, faster mixing spread the filler better and shrank cell size by about half. With the second filler, fast mixing stretched it into a web of fine threads inside the foam. That web sped crystal growth far more than the clay did and gave much stronger foam. The work shows how process settings, not just recipe, set foam quality.
pmc-13565664:
Jiangyue Pi and six co-authors build food emulsions that carry a spice compound in a 2026 study. Thick emulsions can deliver fat-loving nutrients, but classic recipes need lots of protein and fail under heat or salt. A natural gum called sanxan may fix those limits.

Mixed with whey protein at modest levels, the gum formed a stable gel network. The emulsion held nearly all its oil even after salt exposure and half an hour of strong heating. It trapped most of the curcumin load and boosted its antioxidant power over protein-only versions. In simulated digestion, almost none escaped in stomach fluid. The design suits clean-label foods that deliver nutrients to the gut.
pmc-13566864:
Roman Zonov leads an eight-author team reporting a synthetic route to lopsided phenanthroline ligands, in a chemistry paper from two thousand twenty-six. The target molecules are 1,10-phenanthroline-2,9-dicarboxamides. They are claw-like binders for metals, and of use in a range of work. To make unsymmetrical versions of them efficiently has been a hard task till now.

Their start stock holds both a halogen and an oxo group. The two of them react on their own, each in its own way. Nucleophiles swap out the halogen at one position under mild conditions. The oxo group, for its part, undergoes selective O-functionalization. A broad range of carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen nucleophiles gave products in high yields. Azido and hydroxy derivatives were taken on more to show how wide the method can reach. The strategy opens a broad path to unsymmetrical ligands of diverse forms.
pmc-13568564:
Shuhan Yang and nine colleagues published a case report with a literature review in two thousand twenty-six on a rare drug side effect. A forty-four-year-old woman with an aggressive womb tumour received the immunotherapy drug sintilimab with chemotherapy. After three cycles she developed painful, urgent, frequent urination.

Antibiotics failed, and scans showed swollen bladder and ureter walls, pointing to immune-driven inflammation. Steroid treatment eased her symptoms sharply, and a later-found bacterial infection cleared with added antibiotics. She later restarted sintilimab with only mild urinary trouble, and a switch to a sister drug caused none. The authors review similar cases to guide diagnosis and safe reuse of these drugs.
pmc-13569264:
Yuzhi Gong and colleagues observe, in a 2026 study, cannibalism and cross-predation involving Buchananiella whitei, a minute pirate bug newly sold in New Zealand for biological pest control. Seven predatory mite species were tested alongside it. Enclosed tests varied whether other prey, dried fruit mites, were available to distract the predators.

Bugs ate each other only in adult-versus-young pairings, and extra prey sharply reduced that behavior. Young bugs preyed on most mite species, while only two mite species preyed back, partly reflecting body size. No eggs were eaten in any pairing. With alternative prey around, these conflicts look unlikely to undermine the bug's pest control value.
pmc-13569464:
Marie A. Doyle and colleagues traced how abstinence reshapes brain activity and drinking in mice prone to compulsive alcohol use, publishing the study in 2026. Alcohol use disorder varies widely in relapse risk, and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, a hub for stress and alcohol behaviour, was a candidate source of that variation. Using an operant task, the team sorted mice into high, low, and aversion-resistant drinkers and tracked a dorsal BNST signal.

Aversion-resistant drinkers showed stronger BNST activity during drinking despite similar intake, and only they kept seeking alcohol through protracted abstinence, with BNST signals rising in parallel. Abstinence itself strengthened later aversion-resistant intake. Because causality was not established, the authors present BNST dynamics as a marker of vulnerability and a target for mechanistic follow-up.
pmc-13571464:
Takuma Hayami, Masayo Kimura, Harumitsu Suzuki, Miho Nozaki, and Tsutomu Yasukawa clear a blocked eye drain with a needle in this two thousand twenty-six case report. A seventy-five-year-old man had an Ahmed valve fitted for glaucoma in both eyes, a small tube that lets fluid out to hold eye pressure down. Pressure in his left eye rose again after surgery. A laser freed tissue stuck at the tube tip, yet pressure stayed high.

Scans then showed tissue-like matter inside the tube itself. The team passed a fine needle, size thirty gauge, through the front chamber of the eye and into the tube, and drew the block out with suction. Pressure fell to normal at once. A year on, the tube was still clear. The authors say the method works with no cut to the eye's outer skin, sparing the drainage blister the valve needs.
pmc-13571664:
Nine authors present a study dated two thousand twenty-six cataloging gut parasites of wild mammals in Gabon. Parasite communities reflect host biology, behavior, and environment, but baseline data for Central Africa are thin. The team sampled two forest sites, a national park and a second locality.

Droppings from five mammal kinds, two hundred seventy-nine samples in all, were floated and settled to reveal parasite eggs and forms. Half the samples tested positive, yielding twenty-five parasite kinds after cleaning the list. Strongylid worms were most common, followed by whipworms. Richness differed sharply between host species.
pmc-13571764:
Hou, Li, Liu, Zhang, and Zheng study a gene that shapes birch branch angle, in work from twenty twenty-six. Tree shape matters for forestry, since canopy form affects growth and wood yield. Genes that set branch angle in trees were largely unknown.

White birch is a pioneer tree of cool forests. The team made mutants with gene editing in a gene for a histone modifying enzyme. Mutant trees showed altered branch angles. The enzyme changed chemical marks on a key histone and altered a cellulase gene that loosens cell walls. The work links an epigenetic control to visible tree architecture for the first time in birch.
pmc-13572164:
Wenfeng Jia and colleagues build, in a 2026 research note, a two-in-one vaccine virus for ducks by editing duck enteritis virus with a CRISPR-based method. The enteritis virus is a stable herpesvirus already used as a vaccine strain. First the team compared insertion sites using a glowing marker gene, then combined protective genes from two other duck viruses into one construct.

Genes from duck hepatitis A virus and duck Tembusu virus rode together in the engineered virus, which grew like its parent and kept the inserted genes stable and active. The best expression site was identified for future inserts. Duck producers could one day protect flocks against several major viral diseases with a single vaccine strain.
pmc-13572364:
Xiaoxuan Liu, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 computer method for guessing how strongly a drug binds to its target protein. Good guesses help drug makers pick which pairs to test in the lab. Many older tools study the drug and the protein apart and join them only at the end, which can miss how the two shape each other.

The new method, called BiT-Fusion, lets drug and protein data flow both ways and mix step by step. It draws on graphs of drug structure and on protein letter sequences. On two known test sets, Davis and KIBA, the method gave steady gains over past tools. Tests that removed one part at a time showed the two-way flow and the mixing step drove most of the gain.
pmc-13572464:
Akio Nakashima, with nine colleagues, ran a 2026 study of a blood test for vessel hardening risk in people on dialysis. The hormone Klotho, tied to slower ageing, may guard vessels against calcium build-up. A lab score called T50 gauges how fast blood starts that build-up, yet its link to Klotho had not been tested.

The cross-sectional study enrolled 199 dialysis patients with a mean age of 65.2 years. Blood Klotho sat at a median of 408 picograms per millilitre, and the T50 score had a median of 78 minutes. Regression models then weighed how Klotho levels lined up with T50 once other factors were counted. The setup gives clinics a first read on whether a low hormone level flags blood that hardens vessels fast. Such a flag could help target checks and care.
pmc-13572564:
Carolina Muñoz Olivar, with 21 colleagues, reports a 2026 mixed-methods study of supportive care for breast cancer patients in Chile. A national program guarantees diagnosis and treatment, yet access to physical therapy, nutrition advice, and mental health support lags. The team asked what blocks and what helps those services reach patients.

Records from 2019 to 2023 for one health service joined interviews and group talks with staff and patients at a public and a private centre. Referrals to supportive care fell from 30.2 percent in 2019 to 11.9 percent in 2023. Barriers named were missing referral rules, staff shortages, thin facilities, and split coordination. Teamwork across fields and electronic referrals helped. Patients and staff prized physical therapy most. The authors urge stronger referral paths inside cancer care.
pmc-13572964:
Yao Fu, Martin Stroet, and Megan O'Mara present a graph based learning frame that assigns force field values to new molecules for motion simulations. Such simulations drive drug search, but exact values for new molecules are hard to get. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Quantum chem-ical math can give values one molecule at a time, yet it costs far too much at scale. The graph frame scales far better with molecule size, with vast speed gains for larger molecules. Shown on bond stretch constants, it beat a popular method when checked against lab data. The authors credit a smoothing effect that calms noise in training data, and note better transfer to fresh molecules.
pmc-13573464:
Yakup Şen and Sümeyye Coşgun Baybars report a 2026 study of pulp stones, small hard lumps inside teeth, and their links to body diseases. The lumps show on dental X-rays and had been tied anecdotally to heart and metabolic disease. The team tested those ties on a large film archive in Türkiye.

One thousand panoramic films from 2019 to 2025 split into a healthy control group and groups with heart disease, diabetes, or kidney stones. Pulp stones showed in just over a quarter of all films. Raw rates ran higher in each disease group than in controls, with diabetes on top. Yet once age and sex were counted, the links flipped below the null, which marks age as the true driver. Women showed more stones than men, and first molars hosted them most.
pmc-13573564:
Mukesh Gautam, with nine colleagues, details a 2026 study of early damage in motor neurons in a mouse model of hereditary spastic paraplegia. This inherited disease slowly wastes the upper motor neurons that drive voluntary movement. Faults in the spastin gene cause about 40 percent of cases, yet how mutant spastin first harms those cells was unknown.

The team pulled pure sets of the neurons from reporter mice at two ages before symptoms and read their protein mix. The mix shifted over time, and faults centred on cell structure and on the health of key organelles, the cell's inner parts. A compound called NU-9, given for 100 days, stopped tract decay in the model. It also restored organelle shape and cut dense build-ups in the cells. The work names early targets for a disease with no modifying therapy.
pmc-13574664:
Maartje Rietdijk and five co-authors present a method for profiling immune cells in human blood using two complementary measurement panels. Their paper came out in 2026. The technique, spectral flow cytometry, reads many fluorescent markers on each cell to identify cell types and states.

Together the panels cover sixty distinct markers, more than a single panel on current instruments allows. They resolve more than fifty immune populations, including rare ones that need many markers to identify. The panel reads each population's maturation, activation, and exhaustion states. The team demonstrated the method on blood from healthy donors and from patients with a brain tumor, bowel inflammation, and COVID-19. The protocol supports both manual and automated analysis. It is designed for large monitoring studies that need standard, repeatable workflows across many batches.
pmc-13576164:
Francesca Piazza leads a 2026 study of how bacteria break down a natural phosphorus compound, 2-hydroxyethylphosphonate, often shortened to HEP. Phosphonates carry a direct carbon-phosphorus bond and serve microbes as a phosphorus source. The breakdown route for HEP was poorly mapped until now.

Gene analysis and lab work showed a dedicated pathway: HEP is first oxidised into an activated form that known enzymes can finish processing. Two unrelated enzyme families can run that key step, one kin to a known biosynthetic enzyme and one newly described, named PbfG. Both use zinc, yet they differ sharply in shape and efficiency, a case of convergent evolution. The new family worked faster and seemed specialised for the job. Related pathways for a sister compound often stay separate, the authors note.
pmc-13576364:
Jinwen Chen leads a 2026 genome study of Parrotia subaequalis, an endangered relict tree from China prized for leaves that start red and turn green. The team assembled its first chromosome-level genome and combined gene activity and chemical profiling across leaf development. Young leaf colour comes from anthocyanin pigments, the same family that colours many autumn leaves.

One pigment, a malvidin sugar form, built up early then faded as its production genes wound down. Networks of co-active genes tied a set of WD40 regulator genes to pigment building, alongside hormone and enzyme activity signals. The genome also showed bursts of jumping elements and growth in gene families for making and moving secondary compounds. Families tied to flower shaping had shrunk. The authors offer the genome as a base for breeding colour and resilience together.
pmc-13576564:
Heierli and colleagues review trials of microbreaks, brief pauses for stretching taken mid operation, to ease surgeons' work related pain and fatigue. Long cases in fixed postures load the neck, back, and shoulders, and worn surgeons may operate worse. Their 2026 systematic review searches three databases to October 2024. It keeps clinical trials that test breaks during real or simulated surgery, grading effects on pain, discomfort, focus, accuracy, and case length.

Ten trials with 284 participants qualified, most of them crossover designs, but break length, spacing, and exercises varied widely. Six trials found at least one improved outcome. Pain and discomfort improved in five of the eight trials that measured them, mental focus improved in all three that measured it, and accuracy improved in one of three. No trial found that breaks lengthened operations. The authors back microbreaks as promising, while demanding standard protocols and long term data.
pmc-13578864:
Maeva Terrapon and colleagues test how lab prep steps bend isotope readings in killer whale teeth, in a methods study. Isotopes, atom variants that act as tracers, let tooth layers replay a whale's diet and travels across its life. Teeth were sliced, yearly layers were drilled, and powders were split across prep routes: acid bath, peroxide soak, plasma burn, heat drying, or no prep at all.

Acid prep stripped nearly all mass yet gave clean collagen for carbon and nitrogen reads, with a small carbon shift to correct. Both organic removal routes skewed the carbonate reads badly, the plasma burn worst of all. Gentle oven drying at the lower heat kept readings steadiest. The authors advise acid prep for collagen work and plain dried powder for carbonate work, with a prep test before any new study.
pmc-13579164:
Chen Yu, Jiarui Yang, Deyan Luan, and Xiong Wen Lou design a host frame for lithium metal battery anodes, in a 2026 study. Lithium metal promises far more stored energy than today's cells, yet it plates unevenly and swells, which ruins cycle life. Leaning on excess lithium hides the flaw but wastes the gain. Their host is a hollow iron phosphate rod wrapped in a nitrogen laced carbon shell.

Electrodes cast with the rods guided smooth, even lithium plating and curbed swelling. Deep chemical probes showed the iron compound seeds a helpful surface film rich in two lithium salts. Cells ran steady for fourteen hundred hours of plating and stripping with small voltage drift. A full cell with a lean lithium share kept about four fifths of its capacity past one hundred cycles.
pmc-13582164:
Qi Yu and colleagues pitted two immune therapies against each other in new membranous nephropathy with early kidney impairment. Cyclophosphamide plus steroids, and rituximab, are both widely used for this kidney disease, but data in untreated patients with reduced kidney function were scarce. Their look-back study tracked 113 patients from one Chinese hospital, 55 on cyclophosphamide and 58 on rituximab, for at least six months.

Remission rates were similar at 6, 12, and 18 months, reaching about 74 percent in both groups by 18 months. In patients with kidney scores below 60, rituximab got kidney function back up at six months while cyclophosphamide did not, and rituximab caused fewer mild side effects. The authors suggest rituximab as the first choice here, pending bigger forward-looking checks.
pmc-13582264:
Jana Teuscher and co-authors argue it is time to rethink how newborn group B streptococcal disease is prevented. Their review appeared in 2026. Antibiotics during labor have cut early infections sharply. Late infections, up to half of all cases, have not fallen. The same antibiotics also thin helpful gut bacteria in infants, with possible links to asthma and obesity later. The review weighs the germ's tools for sticking, invading, and dodging newborn immunity, from hair-like pili to its sugar capsule.

Those tools, the authors say, are targets a smarter prevention could hit directly. Newborn immune cells also respond differently by strain, which argues for tailored strategies. The authors call for prevention that protects babies without carpet-bombing their early microbiome.
pmc-13582364:
Graham, Dvorsky, Yeguez, Holbrook, and Sibley compare ADHD coaches who started before and after the pandemic in twenty twenty-six. Demand for ADHD support rose during COVID-19 beyond what clinics could supply. Online coaching grew as an alternative source of help. The team asked whether newer coaches differ from established ones.

They analysed a national survey of four hundred sixty-five self identified coaches in the United States. Post pandemic coaches were younger and more likely to report having ADHD themselves. They were more professionally isolated, with lower referral rates to therapy and prescribing services. They also had lower rates of licensure and liability insurance. Clinical topics such as medication adherence and suicide risk were discussed less by newer coaches. The authors flag needs for training standards and clearer boundaries.
pmc-13584064:
Sergej Ostojic, writing alone in 2026, reviews how creatine supplements might interact with prescription drugs. His piece is a narrative review, with a map of the proof. It deals with a pair that is in wide use, but that has been studied in few cases.

Creatine is in wide use among athletes, and its use grows among older adults and people with chronic states who take medicines too. Searches of the main databases found hundreds of records. After screening, none had tested, in a direct way, how creatine and drugs interact in humans. Databases on drug interactions were also checked, to set any hints in their right place. Paths in biology that deal with how the kidney handles drugs, and with how biomarkers are read, hint at interactions that may take place. If they count in clinics is still not clear, Ostojic ends, from the proof in hand now.
pmc-13584564:
Montag and Elhai warn that muddy naming is slowing research on digital well-being. The jingle jangle fallacy covers two naming errors. One error gives two different things the same label. The other gives one thing many labels. Both errors leave a field unable to stack up its own findings.

Terms like excessive technology use and life satisfaction can mean very different things across studies. One team may mean hours online, another a felt loss of control. With no shared meaning, results cannot be compared or built on. The authors call for agreement on what digital well-being is. Clear terms, they argue, are the base for steady, cumulative science in this fast-growing field.
pmc-13585464:
Iwanek and colleagues built a machine learning tool in 2026 to forecast how much urine a patient with acute heart failure will make after a water pill. That output is a key sign of whether treatment is working. The prospective study enrolled 296 patients at one center to build the model, then tested it in a separate group of 50. Just three inputs feed the model: kidney function and two urine measures taken two hours after the intravenous drug.

In the test group, forecast and actual six-hour urine output tracked each other closely. The model sorted 88 percent of patients into the right output band, against 58 percent for a standard formula. Error shrank steadily as more training patients were added, by roughly 200 milliliters per hundred patients. The calculator is freely available online. The authors present it as a practical aid for early, personal adjustment of diuretic therapy.
pmc-13585564:
Pedro Jiménez-Sandoval and co-authors show how a sulfur bond shapes a plant signal peptide for its receptor. Plant receptor kinases must tell near-identical signals apart to run growth and defense. Their target pair is the HSL3 receptor and the CTNIP4 peptide in Arabidopsis. Binding tests pinned the smallest peptide stretch that grips the receptor tightly.

A crystal picture at fine detail shows the peptide's ring locked by the bond. The receptor's end pocket cradles that ring with mixed water-shy and polar grips. Kin receptors lack that pocket, which explains the sharp choice. The peptide also bridges the receptor to its SERK partner. Shape tweaks thus buy exact signaling in a crowded family.
pmc-13585964:
Giovanni Anobile, Sofia Ditano, and five colleagues test whether children with ADHD have a fuzzier basic number sense, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-six. These children often struggle with mathematics, and one candidate cause is the approximate number sense itself: the gut ability to judge how many things there are without counting.

Twenty children with ADHD and forty-three typically developing controls estimated briefly shown dot arrays. They also judged sequences of flashes in time and counted their own button presses. Precision and bias were measured for each child. Before adjustment, the ADHD group estimated less precisely overall. After accounting for age, reasoning ability, and math performance, the group difference vanished. Nothing separated the groups on accuracy. The result cuts against a pure number-sense deficit story. It suggests ADHD's math troubles ride on broader cognitive factors instead.
pmc-13586064:
Björn Nashan, Miao Pu, Jie Zhao, and Haibo Wang compare how three places run organ transplant quality systems, in a 2026 paper. Transplant care mixes surgery, tailored immune drugs, training, and quality checks. Programs are growing worldwide. The authors compare Chinese Mainland with the United States and Germany. Western systems lean on decentralized, profession-led training and oversight.

Chinese Mainland instead uses a central framework. It joins regulation, standard schooling, and data-based monitoring. The paper traces how immune therapy, surgeon training, and quality checks interact in each system. Both sides are moving toward data-driven quality work and skill-based training. Still, their governing ideas differ. The central model favors uniformity and scale. Western models favor flexibility and new ideas. The authors suggest each side can inform a future shared approach.
pmc-13586464:
Young-Il Kim and four co-authors followed healthy adults to see how often a stomach bacterium newly infects them, in a 2026 paper. Helicobacter pylori is a common cause of stomach disease, and Korean studies using blood tests put new infections at two to three percent a year. The team used the more direct urea breath test instead.

They enrolled 192 adults who had tested negative by two stomach checks in a national screening program. After an average of about four years, only six people, about three percent, had become infected. Older age and a worn stomach lining looked linked at first pass, but no factor held up as independent. New infection in adults, they conclude, is rare.
pmc-13586664:
Ali Bagheri and four co-authors study self-care in people with multiple sclerosis in a survey from 2026. The disease brings lasting physical and mental strain, and daily self-care shapes quality of life. The team asked 360 patients at Sina Hospital in Tehran about kindness toward themselves, how they view their illness, and how well they care for themselves.

Being kind to oneself linked directly to better self-care. It also helped through three views of illness: a sense of personal control, a clear grasp of the disease, and steadier feelings about it. Other views, such as trust in treatment, showed no such link. Training in self-kindness is suggested.
pmc-13586864:
A research team led by Jeanne Neuffer presents a two thousand twenty-six study seeking a blood signature of the MIND diet in older adults. The diet is designed to protect the ageing brain. Knowing who actually follows it is hard from questionnaires alone.

Participants came from a long French cohort of dementia-free older adults. Over one hundred fifty food-related blood compounds were measured. Samples nested inside the cohort compared people by later cognitive decline. The team built and checked a multi-compound panel marking diet adherence. Such a panel could flag people at risk and target help earlier.
pmc-13587464:
Purvi Kaur Khanuja and colleagues published a 2026 review of diet strategies for fatty liver disease. The disease is common and varies widely between patients. Liver scarring stage best predicts long-term danger. Ketogenic diets and intermittent fasting are popular proposed remedies. Both aim to flip the body's fuel use.

The review separates several diet variants carefully. Human evidence remains short-term and mixed. Some benefits seen in animals are unproven in patients. Gut microbes and liver signaling may mediate effects. The authors warn against one-size-fits-all claims. Careful trials must define which patients benefit safely.
pmc-13588364:
Jingjin Gong and seven colleagues published a 2026 study on a nutrient that may ease a pregnancy disorder. Preeclampsia is a serious risk in pregnancy, marked by harm to the lining of blood vessels. The test substance is L-(+)-ergothioneine, a compound found in foods like mushrooms.

The team used a cell model of placenta tissue harmed by a bacterial toxin. They ran a battery of tests on cell health, movement, and repair. The compound acted through a chain of three signals, named Nrf2, PPARγ, and sFlt-1 in the title. Adjusting that chain eased the vessel-lining harm in the model. Cell results are an early step, but they mark a path for later animal and human tests.
pmc-13588864:
Mehdi Borjkhani and two colleagues model how the visual cortex keeps its activity lively without tipping into chaos. Brain circuits fire irregularly yet answer the same stimulus reliably, a paradox that suggests they hover near instability. Their 2026 model shrinks the primary visual cortex to three interacting populations, excitatory, inhibitory, and modulatory cells, built on a classic chaotic system.

Three feedbacks drawn from real biology did the taming: excitatory cells recruiting inhibition, a homeostatic brake on modulatory drive, and sensory input tuned to line orientation. Together they converted chaotic wandering into steady cycles and cut the activity's variance by over ninety percent. The model matched real orientation tuning, the calming of variability when a stimulus arrives, and true-to-life spiking patterns in coupled neuron runs. The authors argue the cortex owns the machinery for chaos but keeps it leashed.
pmc-13589164:
Andrea Nemethova and co-authors report, in a 2026 paper, two cases of a nerve disease that mimics a well-known paralysis syndrome but needs different treatment. Both patients arrived with severe, fast-climbing weakness like that syndrome. Standard immune therapy gave no gain or only a brief mild one, then both sank toward near-total paralysis with breathing failure.

Further immune treatments also failed, which pushed the team to test for antibodies against a nerve junction protein. Both patients carried them, which confirmed the mimic diagnosis. A targeted antibody drug then brought full and lasting recovery in both cases. The report urges early antibody testing when standard treatment fails in such presentations.
pmc-13589664:
Heather Davila and twelve colleagues compare home-based care use between rural and urban veterans. Home and community services let aging or disabled people stay in their own homes, but rural areas often offer fewer of them. Their 2026 study drew on fiscal 2022 records for over six million veterans in the VA health system, adjusting step by step for health, poverty, and the facility each veteran used.

Raw use ran close: about five percent in both groups. After full adjustment, rural veterans came out about eight percent less likely to use the services than urban peers. Facility differences swamped that average, with rural odds at some centers running from sixty percent below urban levels to well above them. The authors argue the standout centers prove the rural gap is fixable rather than fated.
pmc-13589864:
Biniam Paulos and co-authors looked at a plant oil as a likely antimicrobial in 2026, at a moment when drug resistance keeps pushing research staff toward natural products. They steam-distilled the needed oil from the leaves of Vepris salicifolia and profiled it chemically, identifying twenty-six compounds that made up most of the oil. One of them, delta-cadinene, dominated the mixture, with intermedeol and germacrene D next in amount.

Both the whole oil and isolated delta-cadinene were tested against germs and fungi using disc diffusion and agar dilution methods. And both inhibited a wide range of Gram-positive and other microbes in the lab. To go beyond the petri dish, the authors modeled delta-cadinene computationally, docking it against microbial targets to suggest how it might act. And profiling its absorption, toxicity, and drug-likeness to judge whether the compound could plausibly become a medicine.
pmc-13590764:
Jinwan Shi, Jieting Xia, Huanqiong Li, Shuyan Zhang, and Bowen Shi build a fair benchmark for detecting children's drug side-effect signals across national reporting systems, in a two thousand twenty-six pharmacovigilance paper. Pediatric reactions are hard to judge because trial evidence is thin and databases name products inconsistently.

The benchmark harmonizes the American FAERS system with Canada Vigilance and Japan's JADER across six hundred twenty-eight drug-endpoint rows. Simple co-reporting statistics performed nearly as well as machine learning models once duplicates were screened and endpoints conditioned on; chemical structure helped only until truly novel scaffolds appeared. Future support concentrated in anaphylaxis. The resource targets reproducible pediatric signal triage.
pmc-13590864:
Bolormaa Sainbayar and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, braces-only treatment of an adult whose bite showed a class III pattern with crossbites front and back. Surgery plus braces is the usual path for such jaw mismatch in grown patients. In mild cases, moving teeth alone can mask the jaw gap, a method called camouflage.

The patient, a thirty-three-year-old Mongolian woman, also had crowding and worn jaw bone support. Treatment took seventeen months with a fixed brace system and removal of two upper premolars. Both crossbites were fixed, crowding cleared, and the midlines lined up. Changes were mostly in tooth position, not jaw shape, which suits carefully picked mild cases.
pmc-13591164:
MohammadHossein Sahami Gilan and colleagues mapped work on metaverse and deep-immersion tech for brain rehab. They combed seven data banks through April 2025, from 5,681 hits down to nineteen works on deep-immersion tech in people with brain and nerve ills. Two readers each logged design, group, tech, dose, and gains.

Virtual reality led, in 63 percent of works, and more than half the works showed clear gains in move, thought, or mood skills. Just a fourth were gold-standard trials with random groups, and methods swung wide. The field holds hope for stroke, brain harm, and nerve ills that wear down, but big strict trials with long follow-up are still due.
pmc-13591364:
Aiyu Ma and co-authors report a 2026 study of a circular RNA circuit that speeds nasopharyngeal cancer spread. The reading protein YTHDF2 breaks down one circular RNA. That loss frees a small RNA to silence a guard gene, easing cancer cell movement.

Cell tests tracked migration, invasion, and shape-change markers after tweaking each link. Sequencing screened the circular RNA options, and chemical tests pinpointed the change site involved. Tests of how fast the RNA breaks down completed the chain of proof. The work maps a fresh route in a cancer common in parts of Asia, giving targets for future blocking drugs.
pmc-13591664:
Yunheum Lee leads a 2026 team weaving a single fiber that can feel both a faint pulse and a wide joint swing. Most stretch sensors trade range for sharpness: tuned for tiny signals, they fail at big strain, and wide range types miss faint ones. Their fiber stacks two rubber layers filled with carbon, drawn together in one strand. One layer reacts strongly to small stretch, the other keeps working at large stretch.

At low strain the sharp layer proved over four times as responsive as its partner, and the layers kept working to very different stretch limits. Sewn into a glove, the fiber raised gesture reading accuracy by more than a tenth over single mode controls. Lee and the team see uses from health checks to human machine links.
pmc-13592364:
Seyed Reza Mousavi and six co-authors report a rare spinal tumor case in a 2026 paper. A woman in her thirties arrived with growing weakness in all four limbs, a weak gag reflex, and a stiff gait. Scans pointed to a slow-growing tumor inside the cord where the spine meets the brain, a spot where full removal is hard.

Surgeons removed the whole tumor through the back of the neck, with nerve monitoring throughout. Tissue tests confirmed the tumor type. A year later her strength had returned to full and her function grade was normal. Follow-up scans showed no regrowth, supporting complete removal as a curative aim in such cases.
pmc-13593064:
Chunxiang Niu and co-authors published this 2026 mapping study of research on stroke centers. Stroke centers, hospitals organized for fast, expert stroke care, have drawn a fast-growing literature. The team used CiteSpace software to chart the shape of that literature across five databases, Chinese and international.

They gathered 3,730 papers, most in English, and traced yearly output, leading authors and institutions, and hot keywords. Output keeps climbing. Current hotspots include clot-busting drugs given by vein, catheter-based clot removal, fast-track emergency channels, and patient outcomes. The frontiers point to machine learning and information systems for stroke care. The map is meant to steer both nursing practice and future studies.
pmc-13593164:
Xia Zhang and Juhua Duan study a blood ratio as a marker of heart disease in patients with chronic lung disease, in work from 2026. The ratio joins a white cell count with the good cholesterol level, so it reflects both swelling and fat handling. Lung patients often carry heart disease as well, which worsens outlook.

Data came from a United States health survey spanning 2007 to 2018, with 1,033 lung patients aged forty and up. About a fifth also had heart disease. Higher ratios tracked higher odds of heart disease, even after many traits were held steady. The link bent at a middle value rather than rising in a straight line. Subgroup checks held the pattern.
pmc-13594064:
Syahmi Nuqman Sarifulnazwan and a team of co-authors review recent progress in hormone-based medicines for cancers that feed on hormones, chiefly estrogen-driven breast cancer and androgen-driven prostate cancer. Standard hormone therapy works well for many patients, yet tumors often learn to resist it, switch on backup growth routes, and return.

Newer options surveyed include oral drugs that destroy the estrogen receptor rather than merely block it. The review also covers oral blockers of the hormone signal that releases sex hormones. A third strand is combinations chosen by tumor genetics, adding cell-cycle or growth-pathway inhibitors. A further class uses targeting chimera technology to drag the androgen receptor to the cell's disposal machinery. The authors see the field shifting from simple blockade toward guided combinations and deliberate protein destruction, while simple receptor blocking remains the backbone of care.
pmc-13594964:
Zhongyang Wu, Jinfu Liang, and Chang Gao present a study dated two thousand twenty-six on a single bubble wobbling in a sound field. A bubble held in a standing sound wave can pulse as a perfect sphere or break into wobbling shapes. That change stirs tiny flows around the bubble, called microstreaming.

The team levitated one bubble with ultrasound and filmed its shape change at high speed. Particles around it traced the flow, and stacking their paths rebuilt the streaming pattern. Computer simulations of the same setup reproduced the shift and the swirling flow. Tests then varied the sound frequency and bubble size to see what drives the change.
pmc-13595664:
Peng Gao and co-authors present a 2026 case report on freeing a trapped vein filter. Such filters are placed in the large vein that returns blood from the legs, to catch clots, and they should later be removed. In this rare case, a surgical stitch had fixed the filter in place, which blocked the usual removal route.

Working through a leg vein, the team first used a balloon inside the filter frame to gently force it open and tear it loose from the stitch site. Once the struts broke free and the grip was released, a snare pulled the whole filter out under the cover of a large sheath. The authors describe the approach, which they call balloon-assisted radial release, as a low-invasive option for this rare problem. They note the trick had not been reported before.
pmc-13596764:
Kuan-Chen Huang and co-authors pooled the research on artificial intelligence tools that watch transplanted tissue flaps after reconstructive surgery and flag failing blood flow before the flap dies. Their systematic review and meta-analysis followed diagnostic accuracy reporting standards, searching five databases and gathering eighteen studies, seventeen of them pooled.

Across studies the AI systems caught roughly eighty-three percent of compromised flaps and correctly cleared about eighty-seven percent of healthy ones, with overall discrimination rated high. Image-based systems performed best of all. Certainty checks and bias assessments were built into the review, and the protocol had been registered in advance. The authors caution that the wide prediction ranges show performance varies a lot between settings, so AI should assist surgical teams' vigilance rather than replace the bedside checks that remain standard.
pmc-13598964:
Yumei Chen and co-authors published this study in 2026. It scans the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub, in Parkinson's patients with mild thinking trouble. The sample held thirty-four such patients, thirty-four Parkinson's patients with clear thinking, and eighteen healthy controls. Standard scans measured the sizes of hippocampus subfields. Diffusion scans measured how water moves inside the tissue, a sign of its fine structure.

No size measure separated the groups once strict corrections were applied. Diffusion measures told a different story: forty-two showed group effects. Most gaps sat between the impaired patients and both other groups. The two Parkinson's groups barely differed from each other, and healthy brains differed from impaired ones widely. Diffusion scores also tracked memory test results. The authors read the fine-structure damage as an early marker of decline.
pmc-13599764:
Manore and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation of a daily wildfire smoke report in Quebec. Eeyou Istchee, a Cree region, endured a record fire season in 2023. Health officials turned daily spoken updates into a written smoke report in 2024. The team interviewed six report recipients about its use in decisions.

Recipients called the report useful and said it calmed worry during fires. It pulled public data on smoke, fire, and heat into one place. Readers asked for more pictures and plainer wording in future editions. They also wanted pointers to deeper local detail beyond regional summaries. A shorter version for calm days joined the 2025 update list. Other Indigenous groups could adapt the report model, they suggest.
pmc-13600064:
Diana García Dilba and Alejandro Castro Solano tested whether the High Five Model of positive traits predicts optimal functioning in university students. The model groups five traits, erudition, peace, joviality, honesty, and tenacity, drawn from everyday language about positive character. One hundred thirty-six students, averaging 30.8 years of age and 83 percent female, completed trait, well-being, symptom, and grade measures.

Honesty and tenacity carried the strongest predictive power for high complete mental well-being after twenty months, with standardized coefficients of 0.64 and 0.49. The model explained 35 percent of variance cross-sectionally but only 17 percent longitudinally. Positive traits can therefore flag flourishing students, though their long-term predictive reach is more modest.
pmc-13600864:
Group B streptococcus often sits harmlessly in pregnant women's guts and birth canals, yet it can threaten newborns. Yao Zhu and co-authors shift attention to the gut in this 2026 study of eighty-seven pregnant women, comparing the microbes and fatty acids in stool between carriers and non-carriers.

Carriers held different mixes of several gut genera and less butyrate, a fatty acid that feeds the gut lining. More butyrate and more of one key genus tracked with healthier birth weights and lower inflammation in cord blood. After adjustments, butyrate still looked protective, hinting that gut health may soften this infection's risks.
pmc-13601964:
Rinrada Naka and co-authors follow, in a 2026 cohort study, whether fine dust in city air worsens chronic rhinitis in children over time. The Bangkok study tracked 146 children for about a year, with weekly symptom scores and estimated dust exposure for the week before each score. Medication use and infections were logged as rival explanations.

Each ten-unit rise in the fine dust measure came with a clear rise in symptom scores. Wet season weeks, infections, and medication use also tracked with worse scores, which the models weighed in. The dust link held for both allergic and non-allergic rhinitis. The authors call for exposure cuts as part of care.
pmc-13603164:
Guang Yi and co-authors field-test a wireless sensor node that watches barn air around the clock in commercial beef cattle housing. Their study appeared in 2026. The node measures temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide, ammonia, air speed, and light, sending data by long-range radio. At one farm it ran beside reference instruments, minute by minute, for direct comparison. Nine nodes then ran for fourteen days across three sites.

Temperature and humidity matched the references almost perfectly; light, air speed, and carbon dioxide tracked well. Ammonia was weaker, improving when readings were averaged over ten minutes, and low levels were partly estimated rather than proven. The system delivered 99.66 percent of expected data. The authors say such nodes can give farmers continuous, trustworthy barn records at production scale.
pmc-13604064:
Aslı Geçgel and co-authors compare two chemotherapy plans given after surgery for a rare ovarian tumor. Their 2026 study covers adult granulosa cell tumors, slow-growing cancers with a lingering risk of late return. Doctors disagree on the best drug plan for higher-risk patients because comparative evidence is thin.

The team reviewed patients treated at five centers in Türkiye over more than a decade. Some received a cisplatin and etoposide based plan, sometimes with a third drug, and others received carboplatin with paclitaxel, chosen by local practice. The main measure was time without disease return. Treatment delivery and side effects were compared as well. With under sixty patients, the study cannot settle the question alone, but it adds rare real-world numbers for a tumor few trials can recruit.
pmc-13604264:
Martyna Szachniewicz, Michał Baran, Maciej Gagat, and Marta Hałas-Wiśniewska test diabetes drugs in bladder cancer cells. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The drugs block a sugar carrier and have drawn note for possible anti-cancer acts. Their effect in bladder cancer was poorly known.

In a human bladder cancer line, all three drugs cut cell metabolic work in step with dose. Cells pile up in the first phase of the cycle, with no rise in cell death in a day. Wound closing and cell motion change as well. The carrier protein is found in the cells and falls with treatment. The doses top those seen in patients, so care is urged in reading the finds.
pmc-13604864:
Francesca Pescosolido and co-authors report research from two thousand twenty-six on germ-killing coatings made from ordinary paint. Busy, high-risk places such as hospitals, schools, and public transport need surfaces that curb bacteria. Mixing active agents into a commercial water-based paint is a practical route, since it suits large-scale use.

The team added curcumin, a natural compound from turmeric, to the paint, and for comparison a silver-based additive. Sprayed films on two plastics passed standard tests for adhesion and hardness. After five days in water, the films showed no cracking or color change. In contact tests, both coatings cut the recovery of live bacteria sharply, including a common hospital germ. The work supports paint as a hygiene tool.
pmc-13604964:
Nina Nouraeyan and co-authors review how bedside ultrasound helps doctors handle shock in newborn babies, in this 2026 paper. A newborn's circulation shifts fast and reacts to many factors, so shock is hard to spot early. Staff long relied on pulse, blood pressure, and blood tests. Ultrasound at the bedside adds a direct view of the heart and other organs in real time.

The review sets out two tools. One, called POCUS, gives quick focused checks of lungs, heart, belly, and head to find urgent causes. The other, targeted heart ultrasound, gives a fuller, repeated picture of heart function over hours. The authors stress the two tools complete each other. Used together with clinical judgment, they can guide fluids, drugs, and breathing support for each baby.
pmc-13606164:
Gelatin gels carry cells in many medical products, and the animal the gelatin comes from quietly shapes how the gel behaves. Antonio David Abreu-Rejón and five co-authors compared cow, pig, and cold-water fish gelatins head to head in a 2026 study. They checked chemistry, heat stability, structure, and stickiness. They also watched how two cell types fare on each gel.

Fish gelatin had fewer linking groups, weaker heat stability, and a looser structure. Skin-like cells did equally well on all three, but bone cells fared worse on fish gel and sat more contracted. Fish gel also peeled away more gently in pull tests. The authors call fish gelatin promising but in need of strengthening.
pmc-13606264:
Warantron Potarin and co-authors present a 2026 case-control study of pressure injuries gained during hospital stays. Such injuries are a major safety problem for high-risk patients. Knowing what drives them is key to stopping them. The study was run at a hospital in Thailand over close to three years. It compared forty patients who developed such injuries with forty who did not. Records and structured forms supplied the data.

The team first compared the groups trait by trait. Traits with even a weak link to injury moved on to deeper checks. Many personal and care factors were in the pool of candidates. The aim was a risk picture built from many factors, not just one score. Wards can use such a picture to target bedding, turning, and skin checks. The study adds data from a setting often missing in this field.
pmc-13608364:
Filiz Mizrak, Turhan Karakaya, and Burcak Vatansever Durmaz build a test of how well staff think when an AI tool gives advice. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Staff must not just use AI tips, but judge when those tips are wrong and when to trust them. Past work looked at trust acts, not at skill as a trait that can be scored.

Their test uses set work scenes and scores error spotting, use of proof, and control of reliance. It also logs confidence and time. In a large sample of working adults, scores track known tests of reasoning and memory. Scores also track the quality of choices made at work, past what other traits explain.
pmc-13609464:
Magdalena Król, Witold Jastrzębski, and Włodzimierz Mozgawa study, in a 2026 materials paper, how two toxic oxyanions enter the structure of ettringite, a mineral that forms in cement. The mineral can trap such pollutants, which makes it useful in waste settings. How arsenate and chromate change its inner structure was poorly known.

The team made the mineral with each pollutant present and probed it with X-ray and infrared methods. The mineral stayed the main phase in all samples, with no new crystals formed. Chromate caused only small shifts in the lattice. Arsenate shrank the cell, mostly along one axis, and left clearer local changes. Such trapping comes with real structural cost.
pmc-13611064:
Rodríguez and Martín-Rodríguez review whether physical activity improves mental flexibility in children with ADHD. The condition often weakens executive skills, which hurts school work and daily life. Exercise is a drug-free candidate to support those skills. Yet studies vary in exercise type and in how strong their findings are. The review followed PRISMA rules and searched six databases. It kept studies of primary school children with ADHD who took part in activity programs.

The protocol was logged in a public registry before write-up. Outcomes centered on cognitive flexibility, the skill of shifting rules and focus. The authors set out to sort which activity forms show the clearest gains. The review guides schools weighing exercise as support.
pmc-13611964:
Hakkı Öztürk and Berrak Itır Aylı published this infodemiology study in 2026. It examines what the public searches for during Ebola outbreaks, using the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak in Congo and Uganda as its focus. That outbreak, the first of its kind without a licensed vaccine, was shadowed by conspiracy claims, violence against response teams, and attacks on treatment centers. The authors combined search suggestions with trend data across six outbreaks from 2014 to 2026.

From 83 seed terms they gathered 7,347 unique suggested queries in English and French. Risk and transmission questions dominated. Search interest in false claims rose and fell together with overall Ebola interest. The French suggestions carried six times more misinformation and conspiracy content than the English ones, and nearly nine times more fear-related content. The authors argue that response messaging designed for English speakers misses the audiences most at risk.
pmc-13612264:
Eman O Alsheikh leads a nine-author team surveying self-medication among pharmacy students in Makkah, Saudi Arabia. Future pharmacists should model safe medicine use, yet students everywhere dose themselves freely. Between November and December 2025, the team questioned 244 Doctor of Pharmacy students at Umm Al-Qura University with a validated electronic survey covering habits, medication knowledge, and stress-related attitudes. They then modeled what predicts frequent self-medication.

Self-medication was nearly universal: 94.3 percent reported it, led by painkillers at 82.2 percent of users, topical products, and cough syrups. Men cited saving money and time more often and used more cough syrup; women used more sleeping aids. Two factors independently predicted doing it often: higher medication knowledge, with an odds ratio of 1.21 per unit, and stronger stress-related attitudes, at 1.11. Knowledge alone plainly does not protect. The authors recommend weaving stress management into pharmacy curricula beside medication safety.
pmc-13612364:
Xinyang Sun leads a six-author team dissecting how a bacterial pigment sabotages chlamydia. Pyocyanin, made by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, was known to cripple chlamydia's infectious particles at low doses. The team pinned down where in the pathogen's two-stage life cycle the damage lands. Delayed-treatment experiments and infection assays probed newly formed elementary bodies, the spore-like particles that spread infection between cells.

Complete suppression of progeny took 16 micromolar pyocyanin, while direct attack on incoming particles achieved only about 60 percent. The real action was intracellular: treated bacteria still produced normal numbers of new elementary bodies, but those bodies could barely infect fresh cells. The drug also slowed the growth cycle rather than freezing it, and its grip was reversible. The authors offer pyocyanin as a lab probe for chlamydia biology and a lead compound for a new drug class.
pmc-13612464:
Parul Sirohi leads a ten-author team fusing two metabolic hormones into a single drug for fatty liver disease in 2026. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis scars the liver, and approved treatments remain scarce. GLP-1 and FGF21 each help through different routes, one governing appetite and glucose, the other liver chemistry. The team linked both hormones with a heat-responsive elastin-like polypeptide, creating one molecule that forms a slow-release depot under the skin.

Cell assays confirmed the chimera still activates both hormone receptors. In mice with diet-driven steatohepatitis and fibrosis, treatment improved body weight, liver mass, blood glucose, and cholesterol. Liver swelling and scarring eased, fat accumulation fell, and liver cells proliferated more. Inflammation and fibrotic gene markers dropped alongside. The authors present the dual agonist as proof that one long-acting molecule can press two metabolic levers at once, a strategy they argue deserves development.
pmc-13612864:
Rebecca L. W. Hansford and colleagues compare cancer care in a 2026 Ontario study of stage IV non-small-cell lung cancer. It covers diagnoses from 2010 to 2022. Patients were split by whether they have intellectual or developmental disabilities. Only 106 patients in the group had such disabilities, yet the gaps were wide. These patients were far less likely to see a cancer specialist or to receive cancer-directed treatment, radiation, or drug therapy.

Receipt of palliative care, which focuses on comfort and quality of life, showed no clear gap between the groups. The authors say the pattern points to barriers in how care is offered and decided, not simply to health differences. They call for research centred on the patients themselves, so that end-of-life lung cancer care can be made fairer and easier to reach.
pmc-13613464:
Samir Mallick wrote a solo computational study dated two thousand twenty-six on plant compounds that might fight fungi. Phenolics from plants are a renewable source of candidate antifungal drugs. Wood vinegars hold many such compounds, but which features of their structure drive the activity was unclear.

Mallick modeled nine phenolics from corncob and areca wood vinegars on a computer. He computed how easily each gives up a hydrogen atom and how the resulting radical spreads its spin, both signs of scavenging power. A fat-solubility estimate gauged membrane crossing. Twelve more phenols widened the set, and a propagator-versus-terminator scheme frames the results.
pmc-13614464:
Jyoti Choudhary and four co-authors report a rare heart case in a grown man. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The man had Tetralogy of Fallot, a set of heart faults present from birth, plus a lung artery that grew from the aorta in the wrong way. Life to adult age with no repair is itself rare.

He came in with cough and blood in his spit. A gated scan of the heart showed the classic Fallot traits, a blocked main lung artery, and the odd right-sided source. Small side vessels fed the left lung artery. The case shows how heart scans can map such a hard build and guide care plans.
pmc-13616264:
Shufeng Ma and colleagues show how influenza A virus hijacks a host protein, PARP1, to pause the cell's own gene-reading machinery and steal parts for making viral RNA. A gene-screening sweep flagged PARP1 as a helper the virus needs. The viral protein NS1 grabs a coiled section of PARP1 and locks it into a stiff, gel-like droplet state, changing how the protein gathers inside the cell.

That frozen gathering traps the gene-copying enzyme, polymerase II, in a long pause near gene starts, stocking the spot with pausing factors and keeping release factors out. The virus raids the paused site for the caps it needs to start its own messages. The trick does not even use PARP1's known enzyme action. Blocking the NS1 grip could free the host machinery and slow flu at a step few current drugs touch.
pmc-13616464:
Shimoga Nagaraj Sriharsha and a large team shared a study in twenty twenty-six. They designed nucleoside analogues to hit HIV's reverse transcriptase. That is the enzyme the virus uses to copy itself. Six compounds were made and tested. Each one swaps an oxazolidine ring into the classic nucleoside frame. The question was plain. Does the ring change keep the antiviral punch?

The fluorine and bromine versions blocked the enzyme most strongly. They did so at low micromolar concentrations. Docking simulations showed both grip the active site well. They form hydrogen bonds and stacking interactions there. All six passed standard drug-likeness rules. All six had favorable absorption profiles. The authors argue that halogen decoration plus the oxazolidine scaffold is a promising direction. They concede that potency still trails real HIV drugs.
pmc-13617064:
Abbie-Louise Smith, Charlotte Doidge, and Jasmeet Kaler study how the framing of welfare messages shapes what United Kingdom citizens decide about separating dairy calves from their mothers at birth. The practice is standard on dairy farms yet widely criticized by the public. Their factorial survey presented five hundred three participants with varied welfare scenarios and recorded how each version shifted agreement.

Positive outcomes in four of the five welfare domains, covering environment, health, behavior, and mental state, made respondents more willing to accept separation and kinder in judging its effect on the calf. Age, dairy knowledge, diet, personal links to farming, and prior views also moved the ratings. The authors say knowing which welfare facts actually sway citizens can help farmers and the public talk past each other less and rebuild trust in the industry.
pmc-13617664:
Kundur and colleagues review in 2026 radiomics in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the commonest inherited heart muscle disease. Its thickened heart walls can mimic other conditions and can end in sudden death. Radiomics mines medical images for quantitative texture and shape patterns invisible to the eye.

The review covers studies applying radiomics, texture analysis, and machine learning to heart imaging, mostly magnetic resonance scans with a smaller, newer set using ultrasound and computed tomography. Reported uses include telling true hypertrophic cardiomyopathy apart from look-alike causes of thickening, and detecting scar tissue without contrast dye. They also include improving prediction of sudden death and heart failure beyond standard markers such as wall thickness. The authors caution that studies remain small, retrospective, and methodologically varied, with too little testing on outside data, so standardization must come before clinical use.
pmc-13618064:
Mohammed O. H. Jaber and two colleagues brew silver nanoparticles with white tea and benchmark them head-to-head against a citrate-made preparation. Silver nanoparticles kill a broad range of bacteria, but green tea versions dominate the literature. Potency is rarely tied to particle quality or to actual damage of the bacterial envelope. Both products were made and tested in parallel against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus.

Diffraction showed pure face-centered silver in the tea product, while the chemical benchmark carried a silver chloride impurity. Tea particles were smaller, more uniform, and more strongly charged. Normalized to total silver, they stopped bacterial growth at roughly eightfold lower concentrations than the benchmark. Even below killing doses, flow cytometry and microscopy showed envelope damage with cell contents leaking within an hour, in both Gram types. The team caught a processing artifact that distorts a leakage assay.
pmc-13618564:
Stephen Mwangi Njoroge and eight colleagues evolve malaria drug resistance in the laboratory, exposing a mouse malaria parasite to repeated rounds of the combination artemether-lumefantrine. Resistance to this therapy is a rising worry in human malaria, yet how it builds stepwise is poorly understood. Using the standard four-day suppressive test in mice, they measured the parental line's drug sensitivity, then applied twenty rounds of rising drug pressure over twenty-six weeks.

The doses needed to suppress the parasite climbed to nearly triple starting values, evidence of progressively selected resistance. After five drug-free generations and a freeze-thaw cycle in deep cold, the line kept slight resistance, indicating a stable inherited trait rather than a temporary tolerance. Resistant lines showed clearly weaker suppression than sensitive controls. The authors offer the system for studying how combination resistance emerges and persists, and for hunting genetic markers to monitor it.
pmc-13619664:
Jakub Żurowski and seven colleagues examined how cannabidiol, the non-intoxicating cannabis compound, reshapes inflammation signals and gene activity in male mice. Animals received one of three doses for either two days or twenty-eight days. The team measured three inflammatory proteins in blood and sequenced gene activity in liver and spleen tissue.

Short treatment lowered two of those blood proteins across doses, while the third fell mainly with longer exposure. The liver showed sweeping, dose- and time-dependent changes in gene activity, touching energy, fat handling, and daily rhythm pathways. The spleen changed far less, responding clearly only after short high-dose treatment. The authors read CBD as a body-wide immune and metabolism modulator rather than a simple immune suppressor, with the liver carrying most of the response.
pmc-13621364:
Mohammad Shahbakhti and six colleagues asked whether false alarms from a children's seizure monitor cluster at certain hours of the night. NightWatch is a wearable armband that watches movement and heart rate to catch major nighttime seizures in children with epilepsy. False alarms wear families down and can breed dangerous alarm fatigue. The team analyzed 2,876 alarms from sixty-five children aged three to sixteen, recorded between evening and morning.

True and false alarms followed clearly different clocks. Nearly a third of false alarms landed in the final stretch, between six and nine in the morning, when children stir and wake. Real seizures spread differently across the night. The authors suggest the device could change its trigger threshold by time or sleep state, tightening up when morning movement fools it most. Such tuning, they argue, could cut false alerts without dulling real protection.
pmc-13621464:
Bryan Chin Hou Ang and twelve colleagues followed two tiny drainage stents for glaucoma in eyes with high myopia, where the eyeball's stretched shape complicates surgery. Both devices, iStent inject and Hydrus, prop open the eye's natural drainage channel and were almost always paired with cataract surgery. The multicenter review covered 252 eyes from 207 patients treated between 2019 and 2023, tracked for up to two years.

About a third of eyes held a pressure cut of at least a fifth while still on drops, and fewer managed it drop-free. Roughly half to two thirds reached the low target pressure range with medicine help. The commonest problem was a sharp pressure spike after surgery, seen in about one eye in twenty. Neither device beat the other on any measure, and neither cleared the bar set for a meaningful added benefit from such surgery. The authors call both options modest but safe.
pmc-13621664:
Danfeng Zhang and colleagues report that heart failure may drive breast cancer progression through a collagen-linked signalling pathway. Their 2026 study investigates the clinical observation that failing hearts worsen breast cancer outcomes.

Data mining with network and machine learning methods screened shared hub genes, singling out one collagen gene. Its expression ran higher in breast cancer patients who also had cardiovascular disease. Raised levels accompanied activation of a growth signalling pathway and a cell-state transition promoting spread. In mice, the heart failure environment markedly accelerated tumour growth with the same pathway switched on. Heart-muscle-derived collagen protein boosted cancer cell growth, migration, and invasion in dishes, while silencing it blunted those behaviours.
pmc-13621764:
Remo Fortunato and co-authors report a 2026 survey of heat strain among home health care workers in Switzerland. These workers visit patients at home, do physical tasks, and travel between visits, so hot weather can hit them hard. Little was known about how much heat stress they feel or which parts of the job make it worse.

An anonymous online survey drew 359 workers from the north-east and the warmer south of the country. Most, eighty-six percent, reported heavy heat strain, and strain rose with heavier workload, heat symptoms, and trouble drinking enough water. Workers in the south reported more strain than those in the north-east. The authors argue that heat protection plans should fit this mobile workforce, with attention to workload, water access, and region.
pmc-13622964:
Christian Cochrane and co-authors present a report of a woman whose swollen right eye area turned out to signal a blood vessel problem in the skull. A carotid-cavernous fistula is an abnormal link between a major neck artery and a vein-filled space beside the brain. Such links usually follow head injury or occur in people with connective tissue disorders.

This patient had neither risk factor, yet she reported two months of swelling, redness, and mildly painful eye movement. A CT angiogram, a scan that outlines blood vessels, showed a high-flow fistula on the right side. Doctors used catheter imaging to confirm the problem and sealed the link with an embolization procedure, which blocks the abnormal channel. Her symptoms cleared. The authors stress that doctors should keep this rare diagnosis in mind even when the usual warning signs are missing, since delays can cost vision.
pmc-13623264:
Four authors present a case series dated two thousand twenty-six on an unusual symptom: sexual arousal linked to food in people with psychiatric disorders. The phenomenon, sometimes called sitophilia, is rarely reported and has no established standing as a diagnosis. The authors describe it as a side phenomenon in three contrasting cases.

One case was a teenage girl with anorexia whose arousal at food images fed her restriction. Another was a man with depression who found arousal while cooking, as a substitute pleasure. The third was a woman with obsessive-compulsive disorder aroused by culinary perfection. In each case the symptom stayed hidden and tied to the main illness.
pmc-13623364:
Sefa Gümrük Aslan and colleagues review inpatient rehabilitation results for people with acquired brain injury, damage to the brain from trauma or illness after birth. The team described who these patients were, which complications they carried, and how much function they regained during a structured hospital programme between 2019 and 2024.

Fifty patients met the study rules after screening. Three quarters had traumatic injuries, and most had severe damage on the coma scale. Long confusion after trauma clustered in the severe group. Stiff muscles affected nearly two thirds of patients, and tight joints, speech problems, and swallowing trouble were each common. Walking scores improved clearly by discharge: the share unable to walk at all fell, while the share walking with little or no help nearly doubled. The authors credit the team-based programme but note that without a comparison group, the gains cannot be pinned on rehabilitation alone.
pmc-13624364:
Anna Nicolaou leads a review of how machine learning is moving stem cell research from the bench toward the clinic. Stem cells promise disease models and replacement tissues, yet their behaviour varies, their maturation stalls, and quality checks strain under mountains of molecular, imaging, and clinical data. Algorithms that learn patterns in that data now touch every stage of the pipeline.

The review organises the field three ways: by data source, by model family, and by job. The jobs run from reprogramming adult cells back to stemness, through guided differentiation and maturation, to quality control, disease modelling, drug development, and bedside decisions. Transformer-based foundation models and methods that fuse several data types get special attention. The authors set criteria for choosing benchmark datasets, stressing biological diversity, methods, complete records, and public access. Their closing call is for models that clinicians can interpret and trust, not accurate black boxes.
pmc-13625664:
Johan Jacobus Maasz and colleagues survey South African speech-language therapists about young people in the justice system. Therapists could plausibly help rehabilitate youth offenders, since many struggle with communication, yet hidden bias among health workers can warp care. An online mixed-method survey drew thirty-five registered therapists working in the country, and the team linked numbers with written answers.

Nine in ten had never trained for justice-system work, and seven in ten had never served a young offender. Still, three in five agreed offenders can be rehabilitated and rejoin society, and almost all blamed public attitudes for part of the hardship returnees face. Therapists noted that communication disorders can feed emotional and behavior troubles, a gap training could close.
pmc-13625964:
Jinxiu Zhang and colleagues climb a dry-hot valley in Yuanjiang, China, to learn what orders the worms of the soil. These nematodes, tiny roundworms that graze bacteria, plants, and each other, run much of the underground food web. Arid mountains, though, have been little studied. The team sampled plots at four heights, measuring worms and soil together, and asked which soil traits steer abundance, diversity, and community makeup.

Wetter soil at higher plots carried more worms, making moisture the main driver of numbers. Diversity answered instead to nutrients, with ammonium nitrogen lifting plant-parasite diversity while trimming bacteria-eaters, and microbe carbon shaping the overall mix. Moisture filtered nothing directly, which suggests these worms are already hardened to dry ground, a useful baseline as arid valleys warm.
pmc-13626164:
George Bcharah and co-authors ask whether a surgeon's fellowship training changes results when stiff knees are freed by keyhole surgery. After knee replacement, scar tissue can lock the joint, and arthroscopic lysis cuts those adhesions. The team reviewed ninety-four such operations at one academic system, reaching back to 1989. Cases split by whether the surgeon had completed an arthroscopy fellowship. The comparison covered motion gained in surgery and motion kept afterward.

Both groups won similar motion on the table. Months later, fellowship-trained surgeons' patients had kept far more of it, losing only a few degrees of bend, while the other group lost much more and even fell below their pre-replacement bend. Revision rates leaned the same way. For this niche operation, the authors argue, subspecialty hands protect the gain.
pmc-13626364:
Marek Lenarczyk leads a team exposing rats to the twin hazards of deep space: cosmic radiation and weightlessness. Male rats were suspended by their hind limbs to mimic floating, for five days before, during, and twenty-five days after a whole-body dose of simulated galactic cosmic rays. Hearts, blood, spleen, and genes were checked across many months, with the last look at 270 days, to see whether the two stressors multiply each other.

Both irradiated groups, floated or not, grew extra collagen around heart vessels, the main endpoint, and the pairing added nothing beyond radiation alone. Floating by itself trimmed several immune signals and a spleen cell type, while radiation blocked a floating-linked rise in blood lymphocytes, the one clear interaction. Calcium balance, reassuringly, held steady under every combination.
pmc-13626864:
Sophie Mounouchos and colleagues present a 40-year-old man in London with malignant pleural mesothelioma, a cancer of the lung lining that usually follows workplace asbestos by decades. He arrived breathless, losing weight, with fluid around his right lung that would not clear after pneumonia, and imaging showed nodular thickening wrapping the pleura with lymph node spread. Biopsy confirmed the epithelioid type of the disease, strikingly early for a cancer of men in their seventies.

No job had exposed him to asbestos. His childhood homes, though, stood in Kabul, Afghanistan, and Peshawar, Pakistan, cities where environmental asbestos in soil and building dust is documented. Migration, the authors warn, will bring more such patients to rich-country clinics, and exposure histories must reach back to childhood streets, not just workplaces.
pmc-13627264:
Anna Giczewska and colleagues read the RNA inside blood platelets for signs of glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain cancer. Platelets soak up signals from tumors, and their RNA patterns may betray a tumor's presence in a simple blood draw. The team analyzed platelet RNA from eighty-four patients and 319 healthy people. Two lenses were used. One scans whole gene sets for enriched themes. The other builds a compact predictive signature under a strict penalty method.

The broad scan lit up clotting, wound healing, immune control, and cell skeleton themes, while the signature method added immune activation, signaling, and protein folding. Together they sketch how a brain tumor echoes through the blood's repair crews. The work is a resource for building a non-invasive test, and for understanding the tumor's whole-body footprint.
pmc-13627664:
Srinivas Akula and co-authors publish the first single-cell map of healthy horse skin. Horse skin suffers immune conditions such as insect bite hypersensitivity, yet nobody had charted its normal cell mix one cell at a time. Two horses each gave one biopsy, split for manual and machine tissue breakup, and sequencing captured over eighty-five thousand high-quality cell transcriptomes between them.

The data resolved twenty-two distinct cell populations: layered skin cells at every stage of their climb to the surface, follicle and gland lineages, support and vessel cells, and resident immune sentries. Marker genes and pathway scores back each identity. As an open reference, the atlas lets veterinarians and biologists ask what changes in allergy, wounds, and healing, and it enriches comparisons of skin across species.
pmc-13627764:
Katherine Lenz and Coral Zhou review frog egg extracts as a lab for genome remodeling in a paper from 2026. The eggs of the African clawed frog yield a cytoplasm packed with everything needed to build nuclei. Adding outside DNA triggers fast, repeatable chromatin assembly and replication. Researchers watch the process by microscopy, gels, or genomics. The system historically revealed how chromosomes are built and copied.

The review gathers the main assays the extract enables. Recent work stretches from division to differentiation transitions. New directions include using the system to study speciation and polyploidy. Biochemical control is the draw: reactions can be tweaked molecule by molecule. The authors map where the field can go next.
pmc-13628164:
Larisa Bayova, Nikita Grigorev, Victor Kazantsev, and Susanna Gordleeva review the body signals that mark top skill in precision shooting, in a paper from 2026. Great shooting rests on many body systems working as one. The review gathers studies on brain, heart, eye, muscle, balance, and breath signals. It asks which signals split experts from beginners.
