Expert shooters show calm brain waves tied to focus and less word-based thought. Their hearts beat slower, with shots timed well inside the heart cycle. Their gaze stays steady, their muscles stay loose, and their stance holds firm. Breath is timed with the shot as well. Most past studies track one signal at a time, the authors note. They call for combined tracking and smart feedback tools that coach each shooter in real time.
pmc-13628964:
Céline Mestres and two colleagues watched how same-day surgery paths truly run in France. They studied nine health sites, public and private. Their 2026 study aimed to build a fairer way of judging running quality. They watched the full hospital stay from three angles. Those were the site itself, the patients moving through it, and staff practice.

Coding the notes produced five quality strands. They cover patient flow, working conditions, and staff-patient talk. They also cover health outcomes and patient experience. No measured item fed only one strand. Three levers cut across all of them. Those were the staff-patient bond, path organisation, and the facts given to patients. The authors offer the scheme as a base for judging tools. Hospitals and regulators could both use them.
pmc-13629064:
Tang, Dang, and Wang tune DeepSeek-OCR-2 to read chem forms from print shots. Form reads turn drawn forms in books to code text for machines. Sight-word tools show hope for end-to-end reads in such tasks. Yet chem reads strain them, and full tune oft fails cold. Their fix casts the task as shot-led SMILES text birth. A two-stage tune plan steadies the train runs in the work.

Stage one uses low-rank adds, a lean tune form, to start. Stage two swaps to picked full tune with split pace marks. Train sets join fake PubChem draws with real sheet shots. The tuned tool takes the name MolSeek-OCR in the text. Its true-match scores tie the best chain-form peer in runs. Graph-form tools still top it on those same runs.
pmc-13629164:
Itkin and five co-authors present a single tube workflow for multi omics profiling, in work from twenty twenty-six. Mass spectrometry can read many molecule types in fine detail. Detecting several biomolecule classes robustly from one sample remains hard.

Their platform measures metabolites, lipids, proteins, and native peptides together from a single tube, at high throughput. A proof of concept profiled deep, dynamic molecular changes in a test system. One tube per sample cuts cost, sample use, and mismatch between separate assays. Such unified profiling suits studies where material is precious and time points are many.
pmc-13629264:
Erin Rachel Davis and two colleagues followed nurses' views of a combined practice bundle designed to improve hospital care for adults with cognitive impairment, such as dementia or delirium. Their 2026 longitudinal study ran focus groups and interviews with seventeen nurses at two points in time.

Nurses said the bundle strengthened drug-free supportive practices and improved communication, collaboration, and relationships with patients. Two forces seemed to carry the change: visible leadership pushing the new practices, and a close fit between the bundle and nurses' own professional and personal values. The authors suggest that multi-part bundles travel well between services when leaders stay engaged and the content matches what nurses already believe good care means.
pmc-13629564:
Sunarno Sunarno and twenty colleagues sequenced the genomes of diphtheria bacteria stored from Indonesian outbreaks. The outbreaks ran from 2010 to 2017. The aim was to map how the disease spread. The team also checked whether control measures were working. Eighty-nine stored samples from ten provinces went into the study. Seventy passed quality checks.

Fifteen types appeared, led by two main ones. The typing resolved dozens of genetic clusters. Several clusters spanned many provinces and islands. Some Indonesian strains closely matched samples from Malaysia, India, and Europe. That hints at spread links across borders. Resistance genes pointed mainly to older drug families. Resistance to penicillin and erythromycin stayed rare. The authors recommend routine genome sequencing for diphtheria watching in Indonesia.
pmc-13629964:
Anup Radhakrishna Warrier and Jyothi Antony published a 2026 study on how hospitals can plan for fuel shortages in wartime. Their test case is a 455-bed top-level hospital in South India. Fuel and cooking gas cuts can stall care, from ambulances to sterilizers and kitchens.

They used a method called failure mode and effects analysis, which scores risks before they strike. Each failure gets marks for severity, chance, and how hard it is to spot, all from 1 to 10. The marks combine into a priority number. A team from many hospital roles did the scoring. The result is a tiered plan that ranks which failures to prepare for first.
pmc-13631664:
Yaqing Gao and colleagues examine two-way links between severe infection and thinking decline in older adults. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses an English ageing cohort. Severe infections are tied to dementia risk in past work. Whether weak cognition also invites later infection was less clear.

Hospital records covered infections before and after cognitive testing. Twenty-one tests fed general and four domain scores. Memory, language, executive, and visual-spatial skills separated. Earlier infections tracked poorer performance in specific domains. Lower cognition also predicted later hospital infections. The relationship runs in both directions over time. Infection prevention may protect brains, and vice versa.
pmc-13632564:
Hilah Gal and Valery Krizhanovsky published this 2026 review of what pushes cells into senescence, a lasting state where they stop dividing yet stay alive and active. Senescent cells help suppress tumors and heal wounds early in life. When they build up with age, their secretions fuel inflammation, tissue decline, and age-related disease. The review gathers the many triggers that can start this program.

Triggers range from damaged DNA and worn chromosome ends to oxidative stress, overactive growth genes, and cells fusing together. Senescence can even spread from one cell to its neighbors. The authors trace the molecular routes each trigger uses and show how many routes merge into the same core arrest machinery. Knowing which trigger acted in a given tissue may explain why senescent cells differ so much. That knowledge guides efforts to control senescence in aging and disease.
pmc-13633364:
Coerts and colleagues examine in 2026 which scan measures predict survival in anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, a rare and fast-moving cancer whose typical survival is measured in weeks. They test metabolic imaging taken before treatment.

The retrospective study covered 34 patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2024 who had FDG PET/CT staging scans, which light up tissue burning sugar quickly. Median survival in the group was 48 days. Of the scan measures, metabolic tumor volume was the one tied to shorter survival in single-factor analysis: larger volumes meant worse outcomes. Metabolic tumor volume means the total volume of tumor taking up the tracer. Patients who received surgery or radiotherapy each showed a lower risk of death than those who did not in this small cohort. The authors present the volume measure as a practical prognostic marker for this disease.
pmc-13633864:
Chaocheng Liu, Jean Carruthers, and Alain Michon review a new cosmetic toxin in work from two thousand twenty-six. Standard type A toxins relax facial muscles for months, which some patients fear if they dislike the result. The new product, a type E toxin, starts working fast and wears off much sooner.

The review sums up lab studies and trials for frown lines between the brows. Improvement often appeared within a day, peaked near one week, and faded toward baseline by about three weeks. In large trials, many treated patients reached a clear gain by day seven, and most reported high satisfaction with a natural look. Side effects tied to treatment were uncommon, and no cases of blocking antibodies were reported in the cited work.
pmc-13634164:
Abdelwahed Abougazia and a large team of co-authors score two ultrasound rating systems for thyroid lumps, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. They studied 284 surgically removed nodules from 233 patients. Lab tissue results served as the truth standard for cancer.

Both the American and European systems were applied to each lump. Scores covered hit rate, false alarms, and overall accuracy at set cut points. Single ultrasound traits were weighed for their own sorting power. Errors at each threshold were charted, and results split by cancer subtype. The aim is sharper calls on which lumps need surgery.
pmc-13634264:
Mengsun Li and seven co-authors test virtual reality as an add-on to recovery care after severe lung failure in a 2026 trial. Survivors of acute respiratory distress syndrome often leave intensive care with weak thinking, anxiety, and low quality of life. Immersive virtual reality offers engaging practice, but proof in this group has been thin.

Eighty-eight patients were split evenly between usual care and a four-week package that added immersive sessions to usual care. After four weeks the added group gained more on a thinking test, reported better quality of life, and felt less anxiety. The authors note the package also added staff time and attention, so the gain cannot be credited to the headset alone.
pmc-13635764:
Vinesh Jarajapu and five co-authors compare two versions of a cancer-driving gene mutation in eye melanoma. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Most of these tumors carry a change in the gene GNAQ at one hot spot, but the exact swapped letter varies.

The team built mouse models that differed only in that swap, alongside the same other cancer changes. Tumors from both versions looked alike under the microscope. One version, though, grew faster in the body and cut survival. Cells from the other version grew hardier in dishes and leaned on a signaling path called FAK-YAP. The contrast suggests treatment should be matched to the exact version a patient carries.
pmc-13638864:
Héctor Vázquez-Lorente and eight colleagues report a 2026 cohort study linking telomere length to muscle mass in older adults. Telomeres are caps on chromosome ends that shorten with age, and the study asked whether their length predicts how much lean tissue people keep in their arms and legs.

The sample held 185 adults aged fifty-five to seventy-five with overweight or obesity and metabolic syndrome, followed for six years. Those with longer telomeres at the start kept more lean mass, especially in the legs. The authors caution that an observational link cannot prove telomeres themselves drive muscle aging.
pmc-13640164:
Fatma Dilara Baysan and four colleagues published a 2026 study of how obesity affects children's mouths, including bad breath. Earlier work on weight and oral health in children was limited, and no study had focused on halitosis in this age group.

The sample held 295 children aged ten to thirteen, of whom 111 were overweight or obese. Tooth decay and gum scores did not differ between weight groups. Bad breath, however, appeared in about a quarter of the heavier children versus a smaller share of the others. The authors urge that parents hear weight can affect breath and confidence.
pmc-13642064:
Chien-Feng Chien led a 2026 study of an all-dielectric chiral metasurface that twists light strongly in the visible range through high-order multipolar resonances. Natural chiral materials show only weak circular dichroism, the different response to left- and right-handed circularly polarized light, because light-matter coupling at tiny scales is inefficient. The team broke the mirror symmetry of a gammadion-shaped unit cell, building a low-loss array whose resonances concentrate fields sharply.

Simulations and experiments found two strong response peaks near 652 and 735 nanometers, exceeding 50 percent and 40 percent respectively. Multipole analysis traced the stronger peak to selective excitation of high-order electric and magnetic modes under right-handed light, creating a large scattering imbalance and local chiral fields. The quadrupole-dominated peak also held up well at oblique angles. The work gives rules linking asymmetry, multi-mode excitation, and robust chiral response in low-loss devices.
pmc-13642164:
Xiaoqin Bai led a 2026 theoretical study proposing a new anti-twig edge for the honeycomb lattice that hosts two symmetric high-energy edge states. Edge states matter because they can carry signals along boundaries while the bulk stays insulating, and the recently proposed twig edge instead hosts a zero-energy flat band. The authors ask what a complementary anti-twig edge offers, and how strain reshapes both kinds of edge states.

Stretching the lattice along the edge merged the high-energy band into the bulk and suppressed that state, while the zero-energy state spread out. Compressing along the edge localized both states strongly. Rebuilding the anti-twig edge produced degenerate flat bands and strain-driven multiple flat bands, with topologically protected vacated edge states demonstrated. Photonics researchers get a richer edge toolkit: strain and edge geometry together can switch, suppress, or multiply edge channels.
pmc-13643764:
Eli Isael Maciel and ten colleagues present a 2026 methods paper on a droplet digital PCR test that counts chromosome copies in the pathogenic yeast Candida albicans. Gaining or losing chromosomes helps this fungus adapt to hosts and antifungal drugs, so measuring copy number precisely matters.

Their single reaction uses six colors and sixteen probe combinations to read every chromosome arm at once. After tuning probe amounts, cycling, and DNA preparation, the assay matched whole-genome sequencing results across normal and abnormal isolates. The authors pitch it as faster, cheaper, and easier to scale than sequencing for tracking genome instability in large isolate collections.
pmc-13644164:
He Lu and seven colleagues present a 2026 UK Biobank cohort study linking circadian syndrome with new cases of gastroesophageal reflux disease. The syndrome bundles metabolic problems with short sleep and depression, and its forward link with reflux was untested.

The sample held 330,925 adults free of reflux at the start, followed for a median of about thirteen years, during which 28,554 developed the disease. Meeting the syndrome raised reflux risk by about a fifth, and every one of its seven components raised risk alone, with depression and short sleep strongest. More components meant more risk in a clear dose pattern.
pmc-13644764:
Ke Gao and co-authors explain how butterflies gained richer color vision and how the brain coped with the new input, in a study from 2026. Most insects have two types of a key light-sensing cell per eye unit. Butterflies have three, thanks to a second copy of one cell type. Each cell picks its type by chance, which widens the eye's mosaic.

The team found the gene switch that drove the change. Nearby cells were converted to a new fate, which then called in the extra sensor. They rebuilt the same trick in a fruit fly by tweaking gene switches. The fly brain held spare partner cells that linked up with the new sensors at once. Extra partners are culled when they find no match. The work shows how new senses can plug into old brains.
pmc-13646764:
Varissara Kaewchaivijit and five colleagues study infections in children whose livers are scarred by biliary atresia, a blocked bile duct disease of infancy, in a 2026 paper. Records from 2014 to 2023 covered 150 children at their center. Infections were classed as proven or suspected bacterial, presumed viral, or none. The team weighed risk factors, a blood marker's sorting power, and how long children kept their own liver before transplant or death.

Nearly two thirds of the children had infections, often repeatedly, and bile duct infection was the most common bacterial type. A CRP blood level cut-off separated bacterial from viral episodes with fair accuracy. Children with bacterial infections had worse disease scores and, after adjustment, lower survival with their own liver. The authors argue that preventing and promptly treating bacterial infection should help more of these children keep their native liver longer.
pmc-13647264:
Mona Mohammed Fouad Mohammed El-Sawaf and Nayera Mohamed Shousha survey 360 Egyptian adults aged eighteen to twenty-one about ongoing abuse by parents they still live with. Most studies ask about childhood abuse in hindsight; this one measures ongoing abuse and ties it to well-being. Gender was tested as a factor that changes the link. Age, field of study, and living arrangement were held steady in the models.

Nearly two thirds reported moderate to high parental abuse, with women far above men. The well-being cost differed by gender in shape: for women, abuse tied to lower life satisfaction and less positive feeling, while for men satisfaction oddly tilted the other way. Bad feelings rose with abuse in both genders, more steeply in men. The authors call for culturally grounded work on family dynamics and economic dependence, with help shaped to each gender's distinct vulnerability.
pmc-13647964:
Helinara L V Capucho and nine colleagues build an isotope fingerprint library to tell where massaranduba timber was cut, a tool against illegal logging in the Amazon. The tree, Manilkara huberi, is heavily traded, and paperwork about origin is easily faked. The team sampled 130 living trees across four Brazilian states, taking 350 wood samples in all. Carbon and nitrogen isotope ratios were measured by mass spectrometry and tested as geographic signatures.

Both isotope ratios differed significantly between places, tracking soil, vegetation, and local conditions. Nitrogen carried the sharper geographic signal, while carbon reflected broader environmental patterns. A classification model assigned origin with accuracy ranging widely by site, reaching the high nineties for particular municipalities. Because the library rests on living, located trees, agencies can check suspect timber against it directly. The authors offer the database as technical backing for Brazil's forest origin documents.
pmc-13648064:
Guoqiang Ma and ten colleagues examine how green space and mixed air pollution relate to biological aging patterns among adults in a high-pollution Chinese city. Using repeated measures from 11,760 adults aged twenty to sixty-five, they grouped people into slow, moderate, and accelerated aging trajectories based on how far biological age ran ahead of calendar age.

More green space near home was linked with lower odds of belonging to the accelerated group, while higher fine particles, sulfur dioxide, and ozone raised those odds. About a quarter of the green space benefit ran through reduced pollution exposure, in their mediation analysis. The authors argue that urban greening and pollution control should advance together to support healthy aging.
pmc-13649164:
Alexander Muacevic and six colleagues report a seventy-eight-year-old former heavy smoker whose fast-growing chest wall nodule turned out to be skin spread from a hidden lung cancer. Skin metastases are uncommon and usually signal advanced disease, and here they were the very first sign.

Biopsy showed a poorly differentiated glandular cancer, but two stains normally pointing to lung origin came back negative, complicating the search. Chest imaging then found a tumour in the right lower lobe, confirmed by airway biopsy, with spread already in brain, adrenal glands, and bone. A tumour board chose brain radiotherapy with palliative chemotherapy, and disease stayed stable at six months. The authors stress integrated diagnosis over single stains.
pmc-13649464:
Wengao Zhang and six colleagues built a machine learning tool to forecast how older adults will function two years after a burst brain aneurysm bleeds. Outcomes vary a lot in this group, and care paths differ by hospital. Their study drew on four hospitals in North China plus a separate check cohort, for 1,413 patients in total.

A gradient boosting model kept fair sorting power on the outside cohort, though it did not top every score. A method that shows each factor's push ranked bleed severity, age, a clinical grade, and treatment choice as the top drivers. Raw survival also split by treatment type and hospital capacity. The authors call for fresh recalibration and fairness checks before any real use.
pmc-13649764:
Sophia Sachs and two colleagues draft a plan to test open-plan multi-space offices at a big German teaching hospital. Such offices split space into zones by task, in place of fixed closed rooms. Hospital work is dense and team-based, and staff health rides on the room round them. Proof on open plans in clinics is thin and split.

Two office types will be matched head to head. At least 40 staff from mixed roles will fill a survey, keep a daily diary on their phones, and sit for talks. Scores span tiredness, body gripes, job joy, loyalty, air at work, and social strain. The plan is a protocol, so end finds are yet to come.
pmc-13650064:
Ganz and a large team describe OpenNeuroPET, building open infrastructure for molecular brain imaging, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. PET and SPECT reveal molecular targets in the living brain. High costs, small samples, and lab-specific pipelines long limited sharing. The initiative develops standards and open tools across continents.

A PET extension of the brain imaging data structure standardizes data sets. Conversion tools help labs curate data into that format. Open repositories host shared data, with controlled access for privacy law. Automated workflows support reproducible analysis across centers. Collaborative reuse of costly scans becomes practical.
pmc-13650464:
Ying Liu and eight colleagues study a thyroid-related index in women who have polycystic ovary syndrome together with a traditional Chinese medicine pattern called phlegm-dampness. Insulin resistance drives much of the metabolic trouble in this group, and the index, which gauges how strongly the pituitary responds to thyroid hormone, has emerged as a possible metabolic marker.

Among 486 patients, the 264 with the phlegm-dampness pattern were split by whether they had insulin resistance, and most of them did. That subgroup showed higher blood pressure, weight measures, blood fats, and thyroid values, including the index itself. Higher index values lined up with worse insulin resistance across several markers, yet after full adjustment the link shrank to borderline. The index separated the groups only weakly compared with rival measures. The authors present the association as real but limited in diagnostic power.
pmc-13651064:
Wenji Wang and four colleagues, publishing in 2026, survey caregivers of children with dry eye disease at a hospital clinic in Yuxi, China. They measure what the caregivers know, how they feel, and what they actually do. Children's dry eye is rising with screen use and pollution, and home care depends entirely on the adults around the child.

Five hundred fifteen valid questionnaires came back, mostly from mothers, and most children had been affected for under three months. Knowledge scores landed low against their scale, attitudes were generally positive, and practices were moderately good but inconsistent. The three scores rose together, and modeling traced paths from knowledge through attitude to practice, with income, marital status, and urban or rural residence also playing roles. The authors conclude that targeted teaching could close the knowledge gap and steady daily management, rather than relying on goodwill alone.
pmc-13651464:
Rakshita Kaskar and four colleagues coax more yellow pigment from a cold-loving bacterium pulled from an Arctic fjord in Svalbard, Norway. Pigment-making microbes from polar waters are nearly unexplored, and their natural, biodegradable colors could serve textile and food industries that now rely on synthetic dyes.

The isolate proved a close relative of the genus Citricoccus, and chemical profiling identified its pigment as a zeaxanthin-like carotenoid, the family that colors egg yolks and marigolds. A stepwise optimization, first varying one factor at a time and then applying a statistical surface method, tripled the pigment yield per batch. Adding titanium dioxide nanoparticles to the tuned recipe pushed production about thirty percent higher again, for a near fourfold gain overall. Early cell tests in a kidney cell line showed no harm from the pigment. The authors highlight textile dyeing as a promising use.
pmc-13651664:
Ziqi Gao and three colleagues review osteoarthritis through the lens of mechanobiology, the science of how cells feel force. Wear-and-tear framing misses the point, they argue: distorted mechanical loading is both the disease's main driver and its calling card, in a condition affecting roughly a quarter billion people.

At the joint level, bad loading comes from trauma, obesity, and deformity, compounded by changes in the cartilage matrix itself. Cartilage cells sense the distortion through force-gated channels, adhesion complexes, and hair-like primary cilia, converting it into calcium signals and cytoskeletal change that converge on inflammatory and growth pathways. The endpoint is cell death, senescence, matrix chewing, and chronic inflammation. Therapeutic ideas follow the same chain: correct the gross mechanics, tune the signaling, or implant biomaterials that support, lubricate, deliver drugs, and calm immunity. The goal throughout is restoring mechanical balance so tissue can regenerate.
pmc-13651764:
Yauba Saidu and twenty colleagues report the findings of Cameroon's national commission on non-communicable diseases and injuries, created to weigh a burden that global health funding largely passes by. The commission combined global burden data, two decades of literature, and spending records, then ranked conditions and interventions through scoring and expert agreement.

The numbers are stark. These diseases and injuries caused over two fifths of all deaths in 2019, and nearly three in ten of those deaths struck people under forty. Most of the disability burden sits outside the big four disease families, and over half cannot be blamed on the usual measured lifestyle or metabolic risks. Yet only a small single-digit share of prevention funding reached this whole category. The commission named forty-nine priority conditions and over a hundred interventions for rollout across community, primary, and hospital care, arguing for rebalanced financing inside universal health coverage.
pmc-13652064:
Susmita Das and five colleagues review how plant cells protect their proteins when soil turns salty. Salt stress disrupts protein making, folding, and disposal, so survival depends on the nucleus, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi apparatus working in coordination. Earlier work described each compartment on its own, and the review asks how the parts signal to one another as a single system.

Four questions organize the discussion, covering changes to gene activity, selective protein production under stress, expanded folding capacity, and the sorting of transporters that manage salt and water balance. Two signaling layers tie the compartments together: chemical tags placed on proteins, and plant hormones and gas signals. By naming the connection points between organelles, the authors point breeders and engineers toward targets for building crops that tolerate salty ground.
pmc-13656964:
Hang Zhou and colleagues built a rat model of bone infection with two germs at once. Such mixed infections resist treatment, and how the germs interact is poorly known. The pair studied, MRSA and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, often appear together in patients. Titanium screws carried the germs into the rats' thigh bones.

The screws were tagged with glowing markers so each germ could be tracked. Groups got one germ, both in either order, or none. Blood tests, scans, and tissue slices tracked spread, clumping, and bone damage over time. The team also checked how well drugs still killed each germ. Gene readouts probed what each germ switched on in company. The model lets researchers watch which germ takes charge, and why mixed infections prove so stubborn.
pmc-13671464:
Dongdong Li and co-authors wrote this 2026 review on mRNA vaccines against shingles. Shingles erupts when the chickenpox virus, dormant for decades, wakes up, mostly in older adults, and can leave lasting nerve pain. A current vaccine works well but often causes strong short-term reactions and is hard to make at scale.

The review surveys how mRNA designs could do better. It covers how to build the antigen, how fat-based particles deliver the message, and what animal studies show about immune response. Leading candidates now moving into human trials get a status check. The authors see mRNA as a path to safer, easier-to-scale shingles shots, pending proof in the clinic.
pmc-13673164:
Zak Buhmann, Amanda Robinson, Jason Mattingley, and Reuben Rideaux time the moment when sound bends sight in the brain, in a 2026 study. In the ventriloquist effect, a voice seems to come from a seen source rather than its true spot. Volunteers located paired sights and sounds while scalp electrodes recorded activity. Decoders trained on single-sense trials were then read against the paired trials.

Behavior showed the usual pull, with vision weighted slightly more. Brain decoding found each sense's spatial map intact early on. Only after about 200 milliseconds did the maps bend toward each other, hearing first, then sight. The authors say integration arrives late, through feedback, while early senses stay honest. That timing explains the illusion's mechanics.
pmc-13675964:
Lizhi Lin, Monika Bauden, Roland Andersson, and Daniel Ansari present a 2026 study of pancreatic cancer cells that survive after breaking free from a tumor. To spread, cancer cells must live without their normal anchor, a state that kills most cells. The survivors' tricks are still not fully known.

The team grew two pancreatic cancer cell lines in floating culture again and again until resistant lines formed. They then read the full gene activity of these cells. A self eating process, in which cells digest their own parts, stood out as turned up. Programs for cell division were turned down. The study also flags gene marks that may predict patient outcomes.
pmc-13682064:
Yi Ren and four co-authors compare two ways to fill large inner knee bone defects in a computer model study from 2026. In knee replacement, a big defect on the inner shin bone is hard to bridge, above all in older patients. One design bridges it with an asymmetric cone; the other rebuilds the shape with a symmetric cone plus a metal block.

In healthy bone both designs held steady under walking loads. In osteoporotic bone the bridging cone lifted and sheared, rocking the stem. The rebuilt design stayed stable at any bone quality. The authors favor the block-and-cone build where bone is weak.
pmc-13689964:
Vallentine Miranda and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how gum disease is less an infection than a hijacking. Periodontitis grows from a bacterial community fallen out of balance, but the damage is done by the host's own immune system, chronically fired up and aimed at the tissue it should protect. Keystone bacteria such as Porphyromonas gingivalis play both sides: they stir inflammation to feed on its debris while dodging the clearances that should remove them.

The review follows the osteoimmune pathway, where a T cell signal chain links the microbial imbalance to the bone loss that loosens teeth. Treatment, the authors argue, must go beyond scraping away biofilm. They survey add-ons that resolve rather than suppress inflammation: pro-resolving mediators, a complement blocker, and probiotics. The goal is a truce in the gum, with the immune system back to guarding instead of destroying.
pmc-1413964:
Schroeder, Mueller, Stocker, and co-authors introduce the RIN, an RNA integrity number for grading RNA samples. RNA is fragile, and its quality decides whether a gene activity snapshot is trustworthy. Before their work, labs had no reliable standard score, relying on rough ratios from gel images.

The RIN gives each sample a single clear grade of how intact its RNA is. Labs can then drop poor samples before costly tests, or note quality limits when reporting results. A shared score made studies easier to compare and helped raise standards across gene expression research.
pmc-2557064:
Baird, Etter, Atwood, and co-authors show how sequenced RAD markers speed SNP discovery and genetic mapping. SNPs are single-letter DNA differences, and finding them is essential for mapping traits to genes. A simple, cheap platform for finding many SNPs in large groups was still needed.

The team sequenced DNA cut at restriction sites, a method that samples the same spots across many individuals. That sampling uncovers dense sets of markers at low cost. Breeders and ecologists adopted the approach to track inheritance in species that lack a finished reference genome.
pmc-3637064:
Chen, Tan, Kou, and co-authors present Enrichr, an interactive web tool for gene list enrichment analysis. Profiling genes and proteins across whole mammalian cells produces lists of changed items. Those lists must be analysed for collective functions before they yield new knowledge.

Enrichr lets users test a gene list against many curated libraries through a collaborative, browser-based interface. Fast, shared analysis helps teams spot pathways and regulators behind their data. The tool's growing libraries and simple design made it a routine stop in functional genomics workflows.  Users can contribute gene lists and annotations, so the resource grows collaboratively over time.
pmc-4406164:
Nilsen wrote in 2015 about making sense of implementation theories, models, and frameworks. Implementation science had moved toward using theory to explain how and why efforts to change practice succeed or fail. The terms in use, though, were often mixed up.

The article proposes a taxonomy, a sorting scheme that separates the different categories of theory used in the field. Clear categories help researchers pick the right lens for their question. They also make studies easier to compare and build on. For health systems trying to adopt proven care, that clarity can mean the difference between a plan that lands and one that fades.
pmc-4623764:
Bossuyt, Reitsma, Bruns, and their colleagues issued STARD 2015 for diagnostic accuracy studies. Reports that leave out key facts waste research effort and money, the authors note. Study reports often omit essential information, which blocks appraisal and replication.

STARD gives an updated list of essential items that a diagnostic study report should include. It covers how patients were recruited, how tests were done, and how accuracy was calculated. Better reporting lets readers judge whether a test truly works before clinics adopt it. The checklist is used by journals worldwide to lift the quality of diagnostic research.
pmc-4879264:
Kobayashi, Suzuki, Funayama, and their team wrote in 2016 on Nrf2, a gene switch in cells. Nrf2 turns on the cell's guard against stress from harsh chemicals and oxidants. It also calms inflammation, but how it did that was not clear.

The team showed that Nrf2 blocks the genes that make pro-inflammatory signals in macrophages, the immune cells that drive swelling and pain. It acts right at those genes to stop them being read. That direct block helps explain how Nrf2 cools an immune attack. The find matters for drugs that aim to raise Nrf2 in diseases driven by too much inflammation.
pmc-6514564:
Anchal Singh, Ritushree Kukreti, Luciano Saso, and coauthors reviewed oxidative stress in brain diseases in 2019. Oxidative stress means oxidants overwhelm the body's antioxidant defenses. That imbalance is proposed as a driver of aging and nerve disorders.

Excess reactive molecules damage proteins, fats, and DNA inside brain cells. The review links this damage to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and related conditions. It surveys natural and drug-based antioxidants tested so far, with mixed results. Readers get a map of a popular theory and the reasons proof in patients has been hard to win.
podcast-joerogan-vJCzvb-6R64:
Bigfoot gets a supernatural twist in this Joe Rogan Experience segment asking whether the creature is inter-dimensional. Some believers now say Sasquatch slips between worlds, which would explain why no body is ever found. Rogan, a longtime Bigfoot watcher, airs the wild idea out.

The talk runs through sightings where the creature seemed to vanish and tracks that simply stop. Portals and other realms get floated as answers where a hidden ape will not do. Rogan keeps one foot in doubt, asking what proof could separate either claim. It is the mystery podcast habit at its most playful and strange.
puylaurens-chronique-1864:
William of Puylaurens lived through the Albigensian war's long tail and wrote its chronicle in Latin. The version here is Du Mège's French rendering of 1864, complete in one volume. His account runs from 1202 to 1272, well past the last battles.

Puylaurens was a southerner who served under the new northern rule, and his tone is cooler than the crusaders' own. He tells of the war on the Cathars, the fall of the southern lords, and the slow peace that followed. The chronicle shows conquest settling into rule, year by year. It balances Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay's hotter, camp-side tale.
quatrefages-moulin-quignon-1864:
Armand de Quatrefages, a lead voice of the French Academy, wrote this memoir in French on the Moulin-Quignon jaw in 1864. The jaw had been dug near Abbeville in 1863, in the same beds as Boucher de Perthes's flints. At once a row broke out on fraud and proof.

Quatrefages stands by the jaw as a true find of great age, and by its finder. He sets out the dig, the men who saw it, and the beds it came from. The memoir is the French learned world's shield for the jaw at the peak of the row.
sclater-mammals-madagascar-1864:
Philip Lutley Sclater published his paper on the mammals of Madagascar in 1864. Sclater was a leading British zoologist and an expert on animal distribution. Lemurs in Madagascar and India, but nowhere between, posed his puzzle.

His answer was a drowned continent spanning the Indian Ocean. He named that hypothetical land Lemuria in this short paper. The idea thrilled Victorian science and explained other distribution puzzles too. Plate tectonics later replaced sunken continents with drifting ones. Occult writers seized on Lemuria and built legends around the name. Sclater's paper remains a turning point in biogeography and a myth's birth certificate.
solinus-de-mirabilibus-mundi-mommsen-186:
Gaius Julius Solinus wrote De mirabilibus mundi, a catalogue of the world's wonders, in the third century. Theodor Mommsen, the great German scholar, made this critical Latin edition in 1864. Solinus drew most of his matter from Pliny, and the Middle Ages drew theirs from Solinus.

His pages list dog-headed men, griffins, and marvels of far-off lands. He reports strange births, giant gems, and rivers that change the nature of beasts. Medieval mapmakers and monster writers fed on this book for a thousand years. Mommsen's edition gives scholars the Latin text in careful form. It is the classic world's own cabinet of curiosities.
speke-what-led-discovery-nile-1864:
John Hanning Speke published What Led to the Discovery of the Source of the Nile in 1864 to defend his great claim. Speke had traveled with Burton in 1857 and 1859 and found Lake Victoria. He argued the lake was the Nile's source, and Burton disputed him.

Speke tells how the expedition split, how he reached the lake, and why he trusted his reading of the land. The feud with Burton, once his close partner, runs bitterly under the narrative. Speke died in a shooting accident the day before a planned public debate. His lake was later confirmed as the source he claimed.
statesmans-yearbook-1864:
Frederick Martin edited the first Statesman's Year-Book in 1864, a compact survey of the world's states. Victorian readers faced a fast-changing map of new nations, wars, and empires, and Martin offered the facts in one yearly volume. The book was meant for officials, merchants, and anyone who needed to know how countries were run.

Each country gets a short account of its rulers, government, people, trade, money, and armed forces. The facts came from official returns and were revised for each new edition. The formula worked so well that the year-book is still published today, more than 160 years later. The first volume shows the world of 1864 as its own clerks and statesmen measured it.
swedenborg-divine-providence-1764:
Divine Providence, from 1764, rounds out Swedenborg's core set of faith books. Emanuel Swedenborg wrote it in Latin late in his long life. It stands with Heaven and Hell and Divine Love and Wisdom. The theme is how God guides the world and each soul in it.

Swedenborg holds that God lets men go free, yet steers all ends to good. Ill deeds are let be, he says, lest free will die. He tells how prayer, chance, and pain fit the great plan. The book gives the calm core of his thought on God's care.
taylor-battle-of-standards-1864:
John Taylor pressed his claim for a god given unit in The Battle of the Standards, a tract of 1864. Taylor had writ in 1859 that the Great Pyramid holds a true unit, the pyramid inch. Now the halls of law weighed a shift in weights and measures for the realm. He begged them to keep the old inch.

His case rests on stone, scripture, and pride of realm. The tract is brief, hot, and full of zeal. It shows how a stone claim could stir law and faith. Taylor is held the sire of this whole school.
the-arabian-nights-entertainments-volume: Volume one of the Aldine Edition of The Arabian Nights Entertainments is present in front matter only. Pickering and Chatto of London printed it in 1890, with pictures by S. L. Wood and text taken from Dr. Jonathan Scott, across four volumes. The American small paper printing ran to 500 copies, and this copy is numbered 217. A publishers' preface says the edition opens a planned series of reprints of standard English fiction, chosen for readers who want handsome, well-printed books for their shelves.
the-brochure-series-of-architectural-ill:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, Volume I, Number 5, for May 1895, treats Two Florentine Pavements. The pavements are those of San Miniato al Monte, just outside the walls southeast of Florence, and of the Baptistery, the church of San Giovanni Battista, in the city. Both churches rank among the finest of the Tuscan Romanesque style. Both most likely date from the early twelfth century.

The two churches share much, though their plans differ wholly. San Miniato's inner space is held one of the most beautiful in Italy, for its basilican plan, its crypt, and its rich detail and mosaics. The Baptistery is famed for its bronze doors by Ghiberti, eight-sided in plan and 108 feet across outside. The piece weighs whether the pair owes aught to Byzantine art, and sides with Tuscan refinement of classic forms.
the-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-1-janua: Volume V of The Continental Monthly, covering January to June 1864, is shown here by its title page and index rather than by the January number itself. John F. Trow of New York printed the volume and entered it for copyright in 1864. The index lists Robert J. Walker's American Finances and Resources, a serial tale of slave life in Rome called AEnone, Lieut.-Col. C. W. Tolles on army organization, and aphorisms by the Rev. Asa Colton. Only the volume front matter and index are present here.
the-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-4-april:
April 1864 brings the fourth number of volume V of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its lead piece treats Sir Charles Lyell on the antiquity of man, a question then pressing hard on church teaching.

The writer recalls Thomas Chalmers lecturing at St. Andrews sixty years earlier, daring to say that the writings of Moses do not fix the age of the globe. Most clergy of that day held the opposite view, and Chalmers risked cries of heresy. As geology's proof of an old earth grew too strong to resist, he lived to see his claim broadly accepted. A divine who now said Moses does not fix the age of man, the piece warns, might face church censure, since that proof is still young and open to dispute.
the-lances-of-lynwood-pg4364:
Charlotte M. Yonge's tale appears in this second record with identical opening matter. Its sibling record in this set shows the same preface and first chapter. The duplication is stated plainly. The preface sends young readers to Froissart's chronicle. The Orthon tale is copied nearly word for word from him, it notes. The old French life of Bertrand du Guesclin supplied more material. Tiphaine la fée's gift of lucky and unlucky days is explained. An apology ages Henry of Lancaster by a year or two.

Chapter I opens on Edward III's England at peace. Turbulent spirits are busy in foreign wars. Wise government gives plenty and security at home. The island had never known such calm before. Both records show the same wording throughout. A reader choosing between them loses nothing in the opening. Yonge's romance of knighthood follows from that tranquil start. The Black Prince's wars frame it.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Switzerland, part of The Eternal Quest in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows the 1894 London edition translated by Arthur Machen, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Chapter Thirteen carries the surprising summary that Casanova resolves to become a monk. Arriving from Zurich on foot, he visits a church first and takes dinner with its abbot. The abbot, delighted by his pilgrim's air of compunction, joins his hands and lifts them to heaven.

The monks are fasting, yet host and guest will eat meat under a dispensation from Benedict XIV. The abbot shows the framed brief hanging opposite his table for curious visitors. Casanova replies that the Holy Father granted him a similar dispensation, which excites the abbot's curiosity about his guest. The chapter promises confession, a fortnight's delay, and pranks at an inn before the resolve dissolves. Readers enjoy a hardened traveler taken, briefly, for a great sinner come to repent.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, August 16, 1828, No. 327, illustrates Rosamond's Well and Labyrinth at Woodstock. Two correspondents' sketchbooks supplied the engravings. The editors add few words, since fair Rosamond Clifford's fortunes are familiar to readers. Drayton's lines from Elizabeth's reign attest the ruins: the well paved with square stones, the tower, and vaults wound almost inextricably within one another.

Those vaults let Rosamond escape if Queen Eleanor ever beset her lodging, with secret issues opening many furlongs around Woodstock. Sir Walter Scott's novel Woodstock has revived interest in the spot, the article notes. Tradition sets Rosamond's surrender to Eleanor's menaces on the bank above the well. One correspondent sends the labyrinth plan without the silken cord that guided Eleanor, trusting readers' ingenuity instead. Romance geography is offered as a puzzle the reader must thread alone.

Volume 20, No. 570, dated October 13, 1832, prints notes from a walking tour of the Isle of Wight by a correspondent. Roads on the island had improved enough for stage coaches in twenty years, the writer says, yet walking remained the best way to see it. The route begins at Ryde.

A footpath crosses the park of St. John's toward Brading. Nunwell, seat of Sir W. Oglander, stands about a mile short of the town, opposite views over Bembridge and Brading Harbour. Brading itself kept a mayor and corporation, an ancient church said to be the island's first, and a churchyard noted for epitaphs above the ordinary run. One, to Miss Barry, had been set to music by Dr. Calcott.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-08:
Motley's eighth volume covers 1563 and 1564. Chapter four follows a joint protest from three nobles. Orange, Egmont, and Horn write to Philip together. Egmont quarrels with Aerschot and with Aremberg meanwhile. Philip answers the three with instructions to the Duchess. Egmont declines a royal invitation to visit Spain. A second letter from the seigniors follows that refusal.

Secret letters from Granvelle carry insinuations against colleagues. He chronicles anecdotes discrediting Berghen and Montigny in private. Their lukewarmness toward the inquisition draws his complaints. Schwendi's correspondence marks an approaching crisis in the provinces. A banquet and a foolscap livery lighten the summary's tail. Backstairs letter-writing becomes a quiet weapon of state here.
the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-ancien:
George Rawlinson's Seven Great Monarchies continues in this record, labeled volume two. Its section here concerns the fourth monarchy, Babylonia. A map precedes chapter one, which treats the extent of the empire. Rawlinson heads it with a verse from Daniel. The verse pictures a great tree whose height reached unto heaven.

Babylonia Proper was the tract where the dominant power of the fourth monarchy dwelt, Rawlinson writes. Its limits are almost identical with those already described under Chaldaea. For that reason he will not describe them again at length. The chapter opening shown here is brief. It sets up a geography of the Babylonian empire within Rawlinson's larger history of seven ancient eastern monarchies.
the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-egypt-:
Book four of Gilbert Parker's Weavers occupies this volume record, chapters twenty-eight to thirty-four. Chapter twenty-eight, Nahoum Turns the Screw, finds fat Higli Pasha laughing in a courtyard of Nahoum Pasha's Cairo palace, a narghileh stem in his mouth. He waits with hilarious patience on a pretext of finance.

Higli alone survives of the old conspirators against David Claridge: Achmet sits at the Place of Lepers, and Diaz died of a tarantula bite. Higli doubts Nahoum's alliance with David is genuine and hopes to judge the true position himself. Nahoum, meanwhile, trusts no one save Mizraim, his chief eunuch, who is secret and terrible. Parker's Egypt is a nest of smiling, watchful plotters.
thoreau-maine-woods-1864:
Henry David Thoreau's The Maine Woods saw print in 1864, after his death, a wilderness narrative set. The book gathers his three Maine trips of 1846, 1853, and 1857 into one posthumous volume for readers. Many call it the founding text of American wilderness writing in the modern sense of the craft.

Thoreau climbs Katahdin and feels nature raw, savage, and not made for man at all there. With Penobscot guides, above all Joe Polis, he canoes lakes and reads moose, pine, and rapid. Polis's skill and lore correct the Concord man's bookish pride in some of the finest pages here. Logging camps and dams raise his fear that Maine's wilds will fall to the axe for profit. The book's awe at untamed land helped seed the American conservation movement after him.
tob-10264:
Helena Petrovna Blavatsky published Isis Unveiled in New York in 1877, a huge two-volume work subtitled a master-key to the mysteries of ancient and modern science and theology. She had co-founded the Theosophical Society two years earlier. The book made her name on two continents.

The first volume attacks the science of her day, the second its theology, arguing that an ancient wisdom stands behind both. Blavatsky ranges over Egypt, India, Kabbalah, magic, and early Christianity in a flood of learning and claim. Critics charged her with borrowing without credit, yet the book launched Theosophy and still opens the history of modern occultism.
tob-10464:
George Fox, founder of the Religious Society of Friends, dictated the journal published here as his autobiography late in life. Fox tells how an inner light led him to reject paid clergy, oaths, hat-making deference, and war. His preaching across England filled jails with Friends who refused to bend.

The narrative is blunt, vivid, and utterly convinced, moving from spiritual despair in his youth to public confrontation with magistrates and priests. Fox records travels, imprisonments, and the gathering of a movement. As the founding document of Quakerism, the Journal shows one of history's most stubborn faiths explaining itself in its founder's own words.
tob-14364:
The Sophia of Jesus Christ, preserved at Nag Hammadi, stages a talk between the risen Christ and his disciples on a mountain. They ask him about the world above and their own origin. The text belongs to the Sethian branch of Gnosticism.

Christ explains how Sophia, divine wisdom, fell through her own act, and how blind rulers, the archons, made and misruled this world. He tells the disciples they carry a spark of the true light and can wake from forgetfulness. Dense with myth, the dialogue sets out Sethian teaching at a high and solemn pitch.
tob-4264:
An anonymous French work of 1689, ascribed to Limojon de Saint-Didier, defends alchemy against its scoffers under the title The Hermetical Triumph. The English translation of 1723 carried the argument across the Channel. Two speakers debate whether the philosopher's stone is a fraud or a sober fact of nature.

Reasoned and elegant, the dialogue answers chemists who dismissed the old art as greed and delusion. The defender marshals authorities and experiments with a lawyer's calm. Verified from the 1919 edition, the Triumph shows alchemy arguing for its life in the age of Newton, and arguing well. It is the thinker's stone, defended as fact.
un-doc-consensus-on-gibraltar-by-the-un-:
The Special Committee on decolonization, known as the Committee of 24, adopted its consensus on Gibraltar in 1964. The committee had studied the Rock's status as a non-self-governing land. It heard the British, who ran the place, and Spain, which claimed it. Locals from both sides also spoke.

The text says the 1960 freedom declaration covers Gibraltar in full. It notes a plain row, even a dispute, between London and Madrid over the Rock. Both are asked to start talks at once. The goal is a settled deal that fits the Charter and the declaration. The wishes of the Rock's people must count in the talks.
un-ga-res-52-164:
With Resolution 52/164, adopted on December 15, 1997, the General Assembly approved the International Convention for the Suppression of Terrorist Bombings. The text came out of the fifty-second session; catalog copies dated 1998 reflect the year it opened for signature. States had spent years building law piece by piece against attacks on the public.

The treaty makes it a crime to set off bombs in public places, state buildings, and transport systems with intent to kill or cause great damage. Signers must try offenders found on their soil or hand them over for trial elsewhere. It carved out no excuse for such attacks. The convention took effect in 2001 and joined a growing web of anti-terror law.
un-ga-res-a-69-64:
Trust between states, built in the open, is the theme of Resolution A/69/64, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Its subject is trust-building steps in the field of standard arms: tanks, guns, and the like, short of mass-kill arms. Such steps, taken by free choice of the states involved, can lift the whole state of peace and safety in a region.

The text holds that swapping facts on these steps builds grasp and trust between states. It notes the two-way gain: calmer regions make arms cuts easier, and arms cuts calm regions in turn. Past votes from 2004 on are recalled as the base for the call.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Hosted under the Resolution 52/164 label, the text here is the International Convention for the Suppression of Terrorist Bombings. The General Assembly adopted the treaty through that resolution. Its opening pages note the spread of attacks with bombs and other lethal devices. They also note the gaps in older treaties. Those gaps left such attacks hard to punish across borders.

The convention makes it a crime to set off an explosive or other lethal device in certain places. The places are a public place, a government site, public transport, or a key public system. The act must mean to kill, injure, or cause major loss. States must punish these acts at home. They must claim the right to try offenders. They must extradite or prosecute those found on their soil.

Resolution 69/64, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns information on confidence-building measures in the field of conventional arms. It welcomes the measures states have taken and the information they have supplied voluntarily. It asks the Secretary-General to keep the database of such measures up to date. He is to help states, on request, organize seminars and workshops. Those events share practical experience.
un-sc-res-1364:
Abkhazia, the breakaway region of Georgia, is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1364. The Council adopted it on 31 July 2001. Killings and hostage takings in the Gali district that spring and summer had frozen peace talks. The Abkhaz side had walked out of a planned meeting in protest.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 31 January 2002. It presses both sides, above all the Abkhaz side, to return to talks on core issues. It demands the release of hostages and justice for those behind the attacks. Refugees, the Council repeats, keep the right to go home in safety and dignity.
un-sc-res-1464:
Côte d'Ivoire's political forces had signed a peace deal in France in January 2003. On 4 February 2003 the Security Council endorsed the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement. West African states had already decided to send a peacekeeping force. The Council backed that effort and the African Union's work for a settlement. It restated Côte d'Ivoire's sovereignty and unity. Good relations between neighbors framed the text.

The deal provided for a government of national reconciliation. The Council called on all Ivorian forces to build it without delay. A balanced and stable government was the goal. The agreement also set up a monitoring committee. Its members had to watch compliance closely. All parties were urged to cooperate with that watch.
un-sc-res-1564:
Darfur's crisis brought a warning and an inquiry on 18 September 2004. The Secretary-General's report of 30 August found Sudan had not met all its duties under resolution 1556 (2004). Aid access had improved, but security had not. The African Union's president had appealed for support to grow the Union's mission in Darfur. Four Council members abstained.

The Council declared its grave concern at Khartoum's failure to meet its obligations. It backed the African Union's plan to enlarge its Darfur mission and urged states to give gear, money, and transport. Sudan and the rebels were called to work fully with the Union's force and to stop all violence. The Council asked the Secretary-General to set up an international commission of inquiry at once. It would study reports of grave breaches in Darfur, decide whether genocide had occurred, and name those responsible.
un-sc-res-1664:
Lebanon asked for a court to try the killers of its former prime minister. Rafiq Hariri died in a bombing in February 2005. An international team was investigating the attack. On 29 March 2006 the Security Council welcomed the Secretary-General's report on the probe. It asked him to negotiate a deal with Lebanon's government. The deal would create a tribunal of an international character. It would rest on the highest standards of criminal justice.

Setting the court's legal base would not fix its start date. Its parts could be phased in over time. Timing would follow the investigation's progress. The Secretary-General had to update the Council as talks advanced. The tribunal that resulted sat in the Netherlands. It tried suspects in the Hariri case in their absence.
un-sc-res-1764: Under the number 1764, a formal decision of the fifteen-member Security Council survives through a Wikisource transcription of the record. The body's texts are built to be quoted: each operative paragraph stands alone and numbered. The entry preserves the quotable whole, from the opening grounds the members stated to the final instruction they issued.
un-sc-res-1864:
Nepal's mission was kept on with a drawn-down shape on 23 January 2009. The constituent assembly elections of 10 April 2008 had been held with success. The assembly's first session had declared Nepal a federal democratic republic. A democratically elected government now sat in Kathmandu. A special committee had formed to oversee the Maoist army's integration and rehabilitation. The government asked for the mission to stay.

The Council extended UNMIN's mandate in line with the government's request and the Secretary-General's advice. A phased, gradual drawdown of the mission's staff was endorsed as the way ahead. The current arms monitoring arrangements would stay while the parties finished the integration question. All parties were called to use the mission's expertise as the peace process closed out. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed. Kathmandu was pressed to complete the steps needed for the mission's orderly end.
un-sc-res-264:
South Africa's hold on Namibia faced a direct legal challenge in 1969. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate over the territory in 1966. It had taken direct responsibility for Namibia until independence. On 20 March 1969 the Security Council recognized that act as valid. France and Britain abstained in the vote. The rest of the Council backed the Assembly's move.

South Africa's continued presence, the Council said, is illegal. It runs against the Charter and past United Nations decisions. It also harms the people of the territory. South Africa had to withdraw its administration at once. Pretoria refused, and the occupation lasted two more decades.
un-sc-res-364: Resolution 364 of the Security Council reaches readers here as an official record text, catalogued under the year 1966. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades.
un-sc-res-464: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines was recommended for United Nations membership by the Security Council on 19 February 1980. The Council had weighed the young Caribbean state's bid to join. It told the General Assembly that Saint Vincent and the Grenadines should be admitted. The one-paragraph text is the standard admission step, sending the application on to the Assembly for the final vote.
un-sc-res-564:
Street fighting in Lebanon in 1985 fell heavily on civilians. Palestinian refugee camps suffered some of the worst attacks. On 31 May 1985 the Security Council voiced its deepest concern. It counted a heavy cost in lives and in destroyed property. The Council's president had already spoken on the rising violence a week earlier. Members now put their alarm into a resolution.

All concerned had to end violence against civilians at once. That duty applied above all in and around the refugee camps. The Council restated Lebanon's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It called for steps to ease suffering and to let aid groups work. The United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees needed room to operate.
un-sc-res-64: Four days after it ordered the release of Indonesia's leaders, the Council found them still held. On 28 December 1948 it told the Dutch government to free the president of the Republic of Indonesia at once. All other political prisoners had to go free as well. The Dutch also had to report back within a day. The whole text is one sentence. It backed up the demand made in resolution 63 of 24 December.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Violence in Georgia's Abkhazia conflict zone mars Resolution 1364, adopted on 31 July 2001. Killings and hostage-taking in the Gali district and elsewhere in April, May, and July had halted talks, and the Abkhaz side had pulled out of the planned Coordinating Council session. Two UNOMIG observers had been seized in the Kodori Valley. Both sides had held military drills that broke the 1994 Moscow ceasefire deal.

The Council extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, until 31 January 2002. It regrets that the draft paper on sharing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi has not yet gone to the sides and stresses its early delivery as a spur to talks. It calls on the parties, above all the Abkhaz side, to get past the deadlock and settle the status of returnees to Gali as a first step. It demands the hostages be freed and those to blame face justice.

Côte d'Ivoire split in two after a rebellion in September 2002. Peace talks in France produced the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement on 24 January 2003. Resolution 1464, adopted unanimously on 4 February 2003, threw the Council's weight behind that deal. Ivorian leaders were told to build a balanced reconciliation government.

Members condemned rights abuses committed since the uprising began. Perpetrators had to face justice. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backed regional troops already on the ground. ECOWAS soldiers and supporting French forces could protect their own people. They could also shield civilians facing immediate violence. The authority lasted six months. A special UN representative for the country was requested as well.

Darfur's crisis deepens in Resolution 1564, adopted on 18 September 2004. Sudan's government had promised in Resolution 1556 and a July joint statement to protect civilians and disarm the Janjaweed militias. The Secretary-General reported that those promises were not fully kept. The Council deplored fresh ceasefire breaches, including helicopter attacks and militia raids on villages in late August.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backs a much larger African Union monitoring mission in Darfur and urges states to supply it with gear, money, and support. It asks the Secretary-General to set up an international commission of inquiry at once to probe abuses in Darfur, judge whether acts of genocide had occurred, and name those to blame. It warns that if Sudan fails to comply, the Council will weigh measures under Article 41, including steps aimed at the oil sector.

Fighting between France and Tunisia produced Resolution 164, adopted on 22 July 1961 by ten votes to none. French forces still held the naval base at Bizerte after Tunisian independence, and a Tunisian move to blockade it had triggered open clashes. The Council said it was acting while debate on the question continued, given the gravity of the situation.

Its orders were interim but firm: a cease-fire at once, with all armed forces back at the spots they held before the clash. The Council then decided to keep debating the item rather than close the file. The brief text shows the Council working as an emergency brake, stopping the shooting first and leaving the harder argument over the base's future for later sessions.

Resolution 1664, adopted on 29 March 2006, moves Lebanon closer to a court for the bombing that killed former Prime Minister Rafiq Hariri. Lebanon's government had asked for a court with an international character to try those blamed for the February 2005 attack. UN and Lebanese officials had reached a shared understanding on the court's main features.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to negotiate an agreement with Lebanon to create that tribunal, built to top world standards of criminal justice. It noted that setting the legal basis would not fix the timing, which depended on the investigation's progress. Progress reports were requested as talks moved forward, and the process led to the Special Tribunal for Lebanon.

A new High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina is welcomed on 29 June 2007. The Peace Implementation Council's Steering Board had designated Miroslav Lajčák on 19 June 2007, in succession to Christian Schwarz-Schilling. The designation is agreed to, and tribute is paid to the outgoing holder's work in the post.

The importance of the High Representative's role in driving the peace agreement's implementation is restated. That role includes guiding and coordinating the civilian organizations and agencies helping the parties carry out the agreement. Support for Bosnia and Herzegovina's path toward closer ties with European institutions is also reaffirmed, and the situation stays under review.

Nepal's peace process after a long civil war is the subject of Resolution 1864, adopted on 23 January 2009. The government and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) had signed a Comprehensive Peace Agreement in November 2006. Votes for a Constituent Assembly followed in April 2008, and that body chose to make Nepal a federal democratic republic. The UN Mission in Nepal, UNMIN, watched over arms and fighters.

Nepal asked for a smaller UNMIN for six more months, and the Council renews the mandate until 23 July 2009. It backs a slow, phased drawdown of UNMIN staff, including arms monitors. It calls on all parties to finish the work on managing arms and armed personnel. It also calls on them to free minors held in cantonment sites. It calls for terms that let the mission close and leave by the end of the period.

AMISOM is kept in Somalia and ordered to grow in Resolution 1964, adopted on 22 December 2010. Al Shabaab's attacks on the Transitional Federal Government, AMISOM, and civilians continued. Humanitarian funding was falling. The African Union's July summit and October Peace and Security Council meeting pressed for a stronger mission. Uganda and Burundi supplied the troops.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes African Union member states to maintain AMISOM until 30 September 2011 with its mandate. It asks the AU to raise its strength from 8,000 to 12,000. The Secretary-General must keep providing the UN logistical support package for up to 12,000 troops, excluding fund transfers. Future decisions will track benchmarks: progress on transitional tasks and constitution-making, a national security plan and Somali forces, reconciliation outreach, and AMISOM-backed consolidation of security. The Council also recalls its intent to consider a UN peacekeeping operation once conditions allow.

South Africa's grip on Namibia faced a blunt legal verdict in 1969. The land had been run by Pretoria since the First World War. The Assembly had cut that mandate in 1966 and claimed the land for the UN. Pretoria refused to leave. Resolution 264 passed on 20 March 1969 by thirteen votes to none. France and Britain held back.

The Council backed the Assembly's move in full. South Africa's stay was ruled against the law. Its rule had to be pulled out at once. Plans to split the land into tribal zones were banned. A new South African law for the land was ruled out of bounds. If Pretoria kept defying the UN, the Council warned, it would meet fast to weigh firm steps.

Five months after the Cyprus crisis of the summer, the island's peacekeeping force came up for a new term. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 6 December 1974, said the force was still needed. Its work maintained the cease-fire and helped the search for a peaceful settlement. Cyprus agreed it should remain beyond 15 December. Resolution 364 was adopted on 13 December 1974.

The Council reaffirmed its older Cyprus resolutions. It also reaffirmed the run of crisis texts passed in July and August 1974. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint and to speed up their joint efforts. The force's stay was extended to 15 June 1975. Progress toward a final solution might then allow a withdrawal or a reduction. All parties were again asked to cooperate fully with the force.

Resolution 464, adopted unanimously on 19 February 1980, recommends Saint Vincent and the Grenadines for United Nations membership. The Council had examined the Caribbean island chain's application. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines had become independent from Britain the previous October, one of the last British Caribbean territories to take that step.

The single operative sentence asks the General Assembly to admit the new state. Small island countries placed real value on that seat: a General Assembly vote counts the same for them as for a superpower. The resolution's brevity is typical of admissions, where agreement is reached in advance and the Council's recommendation simply unlocks the Assembly's vote.

Lebanon was deep in civil war when the Council adopted Resolution 564 unanimously on 31 May 1985. Fighting had spread into civilian neighborhoods and Palestinian refugee camps, causing heavy deaths and destruction. The members said they were alarmed at how the violence kept growing and spreading.

The text calls on everyone involved to stop attacks on civilians, above all in and around the camps, and it repeats the Council's support for Lebanon's sovereignty and unity. It also asks all parties to ease suffering by letting UN aid agencies and the Red Cross reach victims safely, and it asks the Secretary-General to follow up and report.

The Dutch had four days to free Indonesia's leaders, and this text is the chase-up. On 28 December 1948, the Council adopted Resolution 64. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. Belgium, France, and Britain held back. Resolution 63, passed on Christmas Eve, had ordered the release. The Council now records that no release has come.

The Netherlands must set the prisoners free at once, the text says. It must report to the Council within twenty-four hours of the vote. Deadline pressure this sharp was rare for the young Council. The order showed how far Dutch standing had fallen after the December offensive. Within a year, The Hague handed sovereignty to Indonesia.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1964:
Section 1964 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with systems of safety for the Capitol buildings and grounds. It sits in Chapter 29, on the Capitol Police, in a part on their powers and duties. A first clause deals with the design and the set-up of such systems. From 1 October 1995, the left sums of grants named in a second clause are moved. Those sums go to the fund for the general costs of the Capitol Police.

The sums so moved are to be used for the design and the set-up of the safety systems. The second clause names the grants in view. They are the left sums of grants for safety works, named under the heads for Capitol buildings in the act of the year past. The text shown is cut off at the head of that list.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2164:
Section 2164 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers rides for House Pages by the Capitol Grounds shuttle service. It sits in Chapter 30 of that title, on the operation of the Capitol complex. The passenger vehicles cleared by section 2163 give a shuttle service for Members and staff of Congress. This section lets those vehicles be used for House Pages as well.

The Pages may be carried to and from special events tied to their schooling. Such use must be approved by the House of Representatives Page Board. A proviso in the text adds a further term on that use. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s364:
Section 364 of Title 2 of the United States Code is a provision on some other pay adjustments. It sits in Chapter 11 of that title, on the Citizens' Commission on Public Service and Compensation. The first rule in the text sets a delay on a class of pay rises. A law that raises the rate of pay for an office or post in named classes of section 356 is covered.

Such a law is not to take effect before the start of the Congress that follows the Congress in which it is passed. The second rule in the text fixes how a span of time is to be counted for that end. It names a span that starts on the Tuesday after a stated day, as the passage goes on. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
van-helmonts-workes-1664: Van Helmont's Workes of 1664 gathered the Flemish physician's writings. The Helmont corpus. Early modern medicine. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe for everyone. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
verne-journey-centre-of-the-earth-1864:
Jules Verne wrote A Journey to the Centre of the Earth in 1864. F. A. Malleson gave the tale its English dress used here. A German sage finds an old note that tells of a path down. The note points to a peak in Iceland with a shaft at its heart.

The sage, his kin, and a stout guide climb down through old lava tubes. They find a vast cave sea, lit by strange light, with live beasts of the old world. Storms, thirst, and a blocked path tax their strength to the end. The tale is the great subterranean trip of the age.
vogt-lectures-on-man-1864:
Carl Vogt, a Swiss-German man of science, gave these bold talks on man in Geneva, and James Hunt put them in English in 1864. Vogt was a famed voice for the view that all life is stuff and force alone. The talks deal with man's place in the world of beasts.

He makes the full case for man's ape kin, from skulls, brains, and the races of men. His scheme came before Darwin's own book on man's descent, and it reached a wide public. The book is the most strong famed plea of its kind from those years.
wallace-origin-human-races-1864:
Alfred Russel Wallace read this paper on the races of man to a London learned group in 1864. It was the first use of the new law of natural selection on the theme of man. Wallace had found that law on his own, far from Darwin's home and desk.

He holds that man's body was shaped by selection in a far past age. Once the mind grew strong, he says, selection bore on the mind more than on the frame. The step set him on the path that led, in time, to his split with Darwin on man.
walpole-castle-of-otranto-1764:
Horace Walpole wrote The Castle of Otranto in 1764. He first said it was a tale turned from old Italian print. The tale is set in a grim pile in the south of Italy. Prince Manfred holds the pile by a claim of thin right.

A vast helm falls from the sky and crushes Manfred's son on his wed day. Portraits sigh, statues bleed, and a hid curse drives all the fates. Walpole's brief tale set off the whole Gothic line in prose. Its stock of ghosts, tyrants, and hid sins still feeds tales now.
warren-commission-report-1964:
President Lyndon Johnson set up the Warren Commission days after President John Kennedy was shot in Dallas in November 1963. Chief Justice Earl Warren led the inquiry, which worked for ten months with a large staff. Its report, issued in September 1964, runs to 888 pages with volumes of evidence behind it.

The commission concluded that Lee Harvey Oswald fired the shots that killed Kennedy, and that he acted alone. It also found that Jack Ruby acted alone when he killed Oswald on live television. Doubts about those findings began at once and have never faded. The report remains the official account of the assassination, and the most argued-over government inquiry in American history.
whittier-in-war-time-1864:
John Greenleaf Whittier published In War Time, and Other Poems in 1864, while the Civil War still raged. Whittier, a Massachusetts Quaker, had spent thirty years as abolitionism's bard, editing antislavery papers and risking mobs. This volume is his wartime voice at full power.

The poems cheer Union soldiers, mourn the dead, and demand emancipation as the war's true purpose. Barbara Frietchie, his most famous ballad, tells of an old Maryland woman waving the Union flag at Stonewall Jackson's troops. Other pieces honor nurses, chaplains, and the enslaved people walking to freedom. Whittier's plain Quaker verse spoke to farmhouses and camps alike. The collection stands as the home front's own record of the war years.
